segments.text: This is the opening chapter of the book. The author himself says: ‘Having once lived through a dream, I have concealed the true events, a phrase that in Chinese echoes the name Zhen Shi-yin, and written this Story of the Stone. Hence the words “Zhen Shi-yin encounters the Spiritual Jade in a dream”.’ But what does the book record, and why was it written? In his own words: ‘Now, worn down by the dusty business of the world, with nothing accomplished, I suddenly think of all the women I knew in those days. When I consider them one by one, I find that in conduct and understanding every one of them was my superior. How could I, a full-grown man, truly be less worthy than those women?

segments.text: ‘These are days when shame is plentiful, regret useless, and nothing can be done. At such a time I wish to set down a record of my offences for all the world to see: how, favoured by Heaven above and sheltered by my ancestors’ virtue below, I lived in fine silks and feasted on delicacies; how I betrayed my parents’ loving instruction and my teachers’ and elder brothers’ guidance, until I came to this, half my life spent in failure and want, with nothing achieved. My guilt cannot be excused. But the women of those inner rooms were distinct and living people. My own unworthiness must never be allowed to efface them all.

segments.text: ‘Even now, with rough rafters, a brushwood window, an earthen stove and a cord-strung bed, the breezy mornings and moonlit evenings, the willow by the steps and the flowers in the courtyard have done no harm to my spirits or my pen. Why should I not use fictitious words and homely speech, a phrase that in Chinese echoes the name Jia Yu-cun, to unfold a story that will give people pleasure? Hence “in straitened circumstances, cherishes a woman of the inner rooms”.’ This is the true meaning of the heading to the first chapter. Since the book opens with those words about cherishing the women of the inner rooms, we know that the author’s intention was to record the friends and affections of those days, not to rail at the world or abuse his times. Where he touches on the ways of the world, these things have had to be told; they are not his main purpose. Reader, bear this well in mind.

segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, where do you suppose this book came from? Its origins may sound absurd, but examine them closely and there is much to interest you. Let me explain them, so that you may read without bewilderment. When Nüwa smelted stones to mend the sky, she made thirty-six thousand five hundred and one rough blocks at Fable Cliff on the Mountain of Great Desolation, each twelve zhang high and twenty-four zhang square. The goddess used only thirty-six thousand five hundred. The one block left unused she abandoned at the foot of Green Ridge Peak on that mountain.

segments.text: Now, after passing through the furnace, this stone had acquired consciousness. Seeing all the other stones chosen to repair the sky, while it alone lacked the qualities required, it reproached itself and sighed, crying out in shame and sorrow day and night. One day, in the midst of its lamentations, it saw a Buddhist monk and a Taoist approaching in the distance. Their bearing was extraordinary, their appearance quite unlike that of ordinary men. Talking and laughing, they came to the foot of the peak, sat beside the stone, and launched into a spirited conversation. At first they spoke of cloud-wrapped mountains and misty seas, of immortals and mysteries. Then they turned to the splendour, wealth and honours of the dusty world. As the stone listened, worldly desire stirred within it. It too longed to enjoy that wealth and splendour among men. Distressed by its own coarse, clumsy nature, it could do nothing but speak in a human voice to the monk and the Taoist. ‘Masters, your disciple is a clumsy thing, unable even to salute you. I have just heard you speaking of the glory and prosperity of the human world, and I long for them with all my heart. Though my substance is coarse and clumsy, I have a little understanding. From your immortal appearance and bearing, I know you can be no ordinary beings. Surely you possess the ability to mend the heavens and save the world, and the goodness to aid all creatures and help mankind.

segments.text: ‘If you would show me a little mercy and take your disciple into the dusty world, to enjoy a few years among the rich and noble, in the tender company of women, I should treasure your great kindness for ever and never forget it through ten thousand ages.’ Both immortals gave a hearty laugh. ‘Excellent, excellent! There are pleasures in that dusty world, certainly, but you cannot count on them lasting. And the two four-character sayings “Perfection has its flaw” and “Good things meet many obstacles” are never far behind. In an instant, joy carried to its height gives birth to sorrow; people and things are changed. In the end it is all a dream, and every scene returns to emptiness. You would do better not to go.’ But the stone was burning with worldly desire. It would not listen, and begged them over and over again. Knowing it could not be restrained, the two immortals sighed. ‘This too is ordained: stillness carried to its utmost seeks movement, and something arises out of nothing. Very well, we shall take you to enjoy yourself. Only do not regret it when things cease to please you.’ ‘Of course not, of course not,’ said the stone. The monk went on: ‘You may have understanding, but your substance is still so coarse, and there is nothing rare or precious about you. As you are, you would be good for nothing but a stepping-stone.

segments.text: ‘Very well. I shall use the power of the Buddha to help you. When your appointed trials are over, you will return to your original substance, and the matter will be closed. What do you say?’ The stone could not thank him enough. The monk recited a spell, drew a charm, and exercised his magic. In an instant the great stone became a beautiful piece of jade, bright and translucent, reduced to the size of a fan-pendant, small enough to wear or hold. Resting it on his palm, the monk smiled. ‘In appearance you are a treasure now. But you still have no real virtue. I must engrave a few words on you, so that anyone who sees you will know at once that you are something extraordinary.

segments.text: ‘Then I shall take you to a flourishing and enlightened country, to a family of learning, ceremony and high office, to a place bright with flowers and willows, where tenderness and wealth abound, and there you may settle and enjoy your life.’ The stone was beside itself with delight. ‘What special qualities have you bestowed on your disciple, and where are you taking me? Please explain, so that I may understand.’ The monk smiled. ‘Do not ask yet. In time you will understand for yourself.’ He slipped the stone into his sleeve and floated away with the Taoist. No one knew where they went or whose house they sought.

segments.text: Who knows how many lifetimes and ages passed? Then a Taoist called the Taoist of Emptiness, travelling in search of the Way and immortality, happened to pass beneath Green Ridge Peak, by Fable Cliff on the Mountain of Great Desolation. On a great stone he saw writing, clear and distinct, setting out a story in detail. He read it from the beginning. It was the story of a stone unfit to mend the sky, transformed and brought into the world by the Boundless Master and the Ethereal Adept, there to experience parting and reunion, sorrow and joy, and the warmth and coldness of human dealings. At the end was a verse:

segments.text: After the poem came the place where the stone had fallen, the household into which it had been born, and an account of all that it had experienced. The small affairs of family and inner rooms, with poems written in idle moments, were recorded quite fully and might offer amusement or relieve boredom. But dynasty and dates, countries and geography had all been omitted and could not be traced. The Taoist of Emptiness said to the stone: ‘Brother Stone, you say your story has some interest, and that is why you have written it here, hoping it will be made known as a tale. But as I see it, first, there is no dynasty or date to be verified; and second, there are no wise and loyal ministers whose good government puts the court in order and reforms the people’s manners. All you have are a few unusual women, some loving, some foolishly devoted, some with a little talent or goodness, but none with the virtue and accomplishments of Lady Ban or Lady Cai. Even if I copy it out, I fear people will not care to read it.’

segments.text: The stone laughed. ‘My master, why be so foolish? If it is a matter of supplying a dynasty, how hard would it be for you to borrow some dates from the Han or Tang and insert them? But the unofficial histories have always followed the same old track. By avoiding that convention, I can offer something fresh and different. All that matters is that the events and feelings ring true. Why be so particular about dynasties and dates? Besides, very few ordinary people enjoy books about government. Far more like something entertaining to read at leisure. The unofficial histories are full of slanders against rulers and ministers, or insults to other men’s wives and daughters, and accounts of villainy and debauchery without end. Then there are those writings on love and lust, so filthy that they poison the very pen and paper and corrupt the young. They too are beyond counting. As for stories of beautiful women and gifted scholars, a thousand books are cast in the same mould. Inevitably they stray into licence, filling their pages with Pan Ans and Zi-jians, Xi Shis and Wen-juns. The author only wants a chance to display his own couple of amorous poems and rhapsodies, so he invents a man and woman, gives them names, and introduces some villain to make trouble between them, like the clown in a play.

segments.text: ‘And the maids cannot open their mouths without spouting classical particles, literary learning or moral principles. Examine the stories one by one and they are full of contradictions and wildly improbable talk. Better these women I have seen and heard myself during half a lifetime. I dare not claim they surpass everyone in the books of former ages, but the events of their lives may at least dispel some sorrow and boredom. There are also a few poor verses and familiar sayings, enough to make you choke with laughter over your rice or enliven a cup of wine. As for their partings and reunions, joys and griefs, their rise and fall and changes of fortune, I have followed each step and trace. I have not dared invent the slightest detail merely to entertain readers and so falsify the account. Nowadays the poor spend their days struggling for food and clothing; the rich never feel they have enough. Even when they have a little leisure, there are lusts to pursue, beauties to dote on, wealth to covet and troubles to seek. Where would they find time for books about government? I do not ask people to hail my story as a marvel, nor insist that they take pleasure in reading it. I only hope that, when they might otherwise lie about after gorging themselves or indulge in drunken lust, or when they wish to withdraw from the world and escape their cares, they will turn to it for amusement. Would that not save them some of their life and strength?

segments.text: ‘Compared with chasing illusions and pursuing what is false, it would spare them the harm of quarrelsome tongues and the weary running about of their legs. It might also give them something new to look at, unlike those old manuscripts stuffed with absurd coincidences, sudden partings and meetings, gifted men and virtuous women, Zi-jians and Wen-juns, Hong-niangs and Xiao-yus, all the same familiar routine. What do you think, master?’ The Taoist of Emptiness considered this for a while, then went through The Story of the Stone again. He saw that, though it contained words exposing treachery, reproving flatterers and condemning wickedness, its purpose was not to attack the times or rail at the world. Indeed, wherever the proper human relationships were concerned, it praised the achievements and virtues of benevolent rulers and good ministers, loving fathers and dutiful sons, with unending devotion. In this it was quite unlike other books. Though its main subject was love, it only recorded what had happened, and could not be compared with inventions full of lascivious invitations, secret assignations and clandestine pledges. Since it had nothing to do with the affairs of the day, he copied it from beginning to end and brought it back to circulate as a tale. Thereafter, through emptiness he perceived form; from form he came to love; by transmitting love he entered form; and from form he awakened to emptiness. So the Taoist of Emptiness changed his name to the Monk of Love, and renamed The Story of the Stone The Monk of Love’s Record.

segments.text: Wu Yu-feng called it Dream of the Red Chamber. Kong Mei-xi of Eastern Lu called it The Mirror of Love and Desire. Later, Cao Xueqin spent ten years reading it in the Studio of Mourning the Red, adding and deleting five times, making a table of contents and dividing it into chapters. He entitled it The Twelve Beauties of Jinling.

segments.text: According to the writing on the stone, after the earth sank in the south-east there was, in that corner of the world, a place called Gusu, with a city known as Changmen, one of the foremost places in the dusty world for wealth, elegance and pleasure. Outside Changmen lay Ten-li Street, and in that street, Renqing Lane. In the lane stood an old temple, so cramped that everyone called it Gourd Temple. Beside it lived a retired local official, surnamed Zhen, whose personal name was Fei and courtesy name Shi-yin. His lawful wife, née Feng, was gentle and virtuous, with a thorough understanding of propriety. Though not particularly rich or exalted, the family was counted among the distinguished households of the neighbourhood. Zhen Shi-yin had a tranquil disposition and cared nothing for rank or fame. He spent his days enjoying flowers, tending bamboo, drinking wine and reciting poems, leading a life worthy of an immortal. There was only one thing lacking: now fifty he had no son, only a daughter whose infant name was Ying-lian. She was just three years old.

segments.text: The monk laughed. ‘It is an amusing business, quite unheard of in all the ages. On the bank of the Spirit River in the west, beside the Stone of Three Lives, there grew a Crimson Pearl plant. The Divine Luminescent Attendant from the Palace of Vermilion Flaw used to water it daily with sweet dew, and so the plant lived on for many years. Nourished by the essence of heaven and earth, as well as rain and dew, it finally shed its plant’s substance and took human shape, attaining the form of a girl. All day she wandered beyond the Heaven of Parting Sorrow, eating Honey-green Fruit when hungry and drinking water from the Sea of Grief when thirsty. But she had not repaid the kindness of that watering, and a lingering feeling knotted itself within her and would not end. Now, recently, the Divine Luminescent Attendant happened to be seized by worldly longing. Wishing to take advantage of this enlightened and peaceful reign to descend to earth and experience the bonds of illusion, he has registered his name before the Fairy Disenchantment. Disenchantment also raised the matter of the unpaid debt for the watering: this would be a chance to settle it. The fairy Crimson Pearl said, “His gift was sweet dew. I have no such water to give him in return.

segments.text: ‘That certainly is unusual,’ said the Taoist. ‘I have never heard of a debt repaid in tears. This story should be still more intricate and delicate than the love affairs of the past.’ ‘Of the lovers of the past,’ said the monk, ‘only the outlines of their lives, and their poems and other writings, have been handed down. Not so much as a meal or a drink in their homes and inner rooms has ever been recorded. Besides, most love stories are only about seductions, secret trysts and elopements. They have never revealed even a little of the true feelings of young men and women. Among this company entering the world, the fools for love and slaves to lust, the wise, the foolish and the worthless will all be different from those described before.’

segments.text: ‘Why should we not go down as well and deliver a few of them?’ said the Taoist. ‘Would that not be a meritorious undertaking?’ ‘Exactly what I had in mind,’ the monk replied. ‘Come with me to the Fairy Disenchantment’s palace first, and we shall hand over this stupid thing properly. Once this whole company of love’s doomed spirits has descended, we shall go too. Half of them have already entered the dusty world, but they are not all there yet.’ ‘In that case,’ said the Taoist, ‘I shall come with you.’

segments.text: Zhen Shi-yin had heard all this clearly, but had no idea what the ‘stupid thing’ might be. Unable to restrain himself, he went forward, bowed and greeted them with a smile. ‘My respects, immortal masters.’ The monk and the Taoist hastily returned his salutation. Shi-yin went on: ‘What I have just heard you say about causes and consequences is something rarely heard in the human world. But your disciple is dull and ignorant, and cannot fully comprehend it. If you would enlighten my foolishness and let me hear the particulars, I would listen with the utmost attention. Even a little understanding might spare me the suffering of being lost in the world.’

segments.text: The two immortals smiled. ‘This is a mystery that cannot be revealed beforehand. When the time comes, do not forget the two of us, and you will be able to leap out of the fiery pit.’ Shi-yin could not press them further. Instead he smiled and said, ‘The mystery cannot be revealed beforehand, but you spoke just now of a “stupid thing”. What is it? Might I perhaps see it?’ ‘As for that,’ said the monk, ‘you are indeed destined to meet it once.’ He took it out and handed it to Shi-yin. Shi-yin saw a beautiful piece of shining jade, clearly engraved with four characters: ‘Spiritual Jade’. On the back were several lines of smaller writing. He was about to examine them when the monk announced that they had reached the realm of illusion, snatched the jade from his hand, and went with the Taoist through a great stone archway. Four large characters above it read ‘Land of Illusion’. On either side was a line of a couplet:

segments.text: Shi-yin cried out. Opening his eyes, he saw the fierce sun blazing and the plantain leaves swaying gently. Half the dream had already slipped his mind. Then he saw the nurse coming towards him with Ying-lian in her arms. His daughter was growing prettier every day, as pretty as a painted jade carving, clever and endearing. He held out his hands for her, took her in his arms and played with her for a while, then carried her to the street to watch the bustle of a passing festival procession. He was about to go back in when a monk and a Taoist came along. The monk had a scabby head and bare feet; the Taoist was lame and shaggy-haired. They gestured, talked and laughed like a pair of madmen. When they reached the gate and saw Shi-yin holding Ying-lian, the monk burst into loud weeping. ‘Good sir,’ he said, ‘why are you holding that thing in your arms, born to live but not to prosper, and to bring trouble on her parents?’

segments.text: Shi-yin heard the words distinctly. Uneasy, he wanted to ask who they were. But the Taoist was already saying, ‘We need not travel together. Let us part here, each to his own business. After three ages I shall wait for you at Mount Beimang. Once we meet, we can go together to the Land of Illusion and strike our names from the register.’ ‘Excellent, excellent!’ said the monk.

segments.text: With that they went off, leaving not a trace. Shi-yin thought to himself: ‘Those two must have some history. I ought to have asked them. It is too late to regret it now.’ While he stood lost in thought, a poor scholar who lodged next door in Gourd Temple came out. His surname was Jia, his personal name Hua, his courtesy name Shi-fei, and his literary name Yu-cun. Jia Yu-cun came from Huzhou, from a family of scholars and officials. But he had been born into an age of decline: the resources left by his parents and forebears were exhausted, and the family had dwindled until he alone remained. There was nothing for him in his native place, so he had set out for the capital to win a degree and office and restore the family fortunes. He had reached this place the year before last and become stranded here. Lodging temporarily in the temple, he earned his daily living by selling his calligraphy and writing essays. Shi-yin therefore often spent time with him. Seeing Shi-yin now, Yu-cun hastened to bow and asked with a smile, ‘Are you standing at your gate, sir, because there is some news in the streets?’

segments.text: Yu-cun passed the time leafing through books. Suddenly he heard a woman cough outside the window. He rose and looked out. A maid was gathering flowers. She had a pleasing bearing and clear, well-shaped features. Though no great beauty, she was decidedly attractive. Without knowing it, Yu-cun stood staring. The Zhen family’s maid had finished picking flowers and was about to leave when she looked up and saw someone at the window. His cap was shabby and his clothes worn; he was plainly poor. But he had a solid waist and broad back, a wide face and a square mouth, with sword-like eyebrows, bright eyes, a straight nose and high cheekbones. The maid quickly turned away, thinking: ‘What a fine, sturdy figure, and yet so ragged! He must be that Jia Yu-cun my master is always mentioning. He has often wanted to help him, but has never found a good opportunity. We have no friends or relations as poor as this. It must be him. No wonder my master says he will not be down on his luck for long.’ Thinking this, she could not help looking back twice.

segments.text: Yu-cun saw her turn her head and assumed that she had taken a fancy to him. He was overjoyed. Here, he thought, was a remarkable woman with a discerning eye, someone who understood him in his obscurity. Presently the boy came in. Learning that the visitor in the front hall was staying for a meal, Yu-cun felt he ought not to linger, and let himself out by the side passage. When Shi-yin’s guest had gone, he found that Yu-cun had left, and did not send for him again.

segments.text: Before long it was the Mid-Autumn Festival. After the family feast, Shi-yin had another table laid in the study and walked over to the temple in the moonlight to invite Yu-cun. Ever since the Zhen family’s maid had looked back at him twice, Yu-cun had believed she understood him, and had kept her constantly in his thoughts. Now that it was Mid-Autumn, the moon inevitably stirred his feelings. He improvised a regulated poem in five-character lines:

Yu-cun hastily smiled in return. ‘I was merely reciting a couple of lines by an earlier poet. How could I presume to make such extravagant claims?’ Then he asked, ‘What brings you here, sir?’

segments.text: Shi-yin smiled. ‘It is Mid-Autumn tonight, what people call the festival of reunion. I thought that, lodging far from home in a monk’s cell, you must feel a little lonely. So I have prepared some wine and come to invite you to drink with me in my poor study. Would you accept this modest offering?’ Yu-cun made no attempt to decline. ‘Since you are so kind,’ he replied with a smile, ‘how could I refuse your generous invitation?’ He went back with Shi-yin to the study.

segments.text: Tea was soon finished, and the cups and dishes were already laid out. The fine wine and excellent food need no description. They took their seats, at first pouring with care and drinking slowly. Then, as their talk grew livelier, the cups began to pass rapidly. Throughout the neighbourhood pipes were playing in every house, strings and singing sounded at every door. Overhead the full moon shed its brilliant, gathered light. The two men’s spirits rose still higher, and every cup was drained as soon as it was filled. Yu-cun was now decidedly drunk. Unable to contain his exuberance, he addressed the moon, putting his feelings into an improvised quatrain:

segments.text: ‘Wonderful!’ Shi-yin cried. ‘I have always said you would not remain beneath others for long. In these lines you have just recited I can already see the sign of your ascent. Before long you will be stepping among the clouds. Congratulations, congratulations!’ He filled a cup with wine himself to celebrate. Yu-cun drained it and sighed. ‘This is not drunken boasting, sir, but in the learning required these days I might perhaps make up the numbers and earn a name. Only I cannot raise anything for luggage or travelling expenses. The capital is a long way off. Selling calligraphy and writing essays will never get me there.’ Before he had finished, Shi-yin said, ‘Why did you not tell me sooner?

segments.text: ‘I have often had it in mind, but whenever we met you never mentioned it, so I did not like to presume. Now that the matter has come up, little ability as I have, I do know the difference between right conduct and self-interest. Fortunately next year is the year of the great examinations. You should hurry to the capital and try your strength in the spring examinations, so that your learning will not have been wasted. As for the travelling expenses, leave those to me. Then your good opinion of me will not have been entirely misplaced.’ He immediately told the boy to go inside and have fifty taels of silver wrapped up, together with two suits of winter clothes. ‘The nineteenth is an auspicious day,’ he added. ‘You can hire a boat and set off westwards then. When you have soared to the heights, we can meet again next winter. Would that not be a splendid thing?’ Yu-cun accepted the silver and clothes with only a brief word of thanks, making little of the matter, and went on drinking, talking and laughing. It was not until the third watch that they parted.

segments.text: After seeing Yu-cun off, Shi-yin returned to his room and slept until the sun was high. Thinking over the previous night’s conversation, he decided to write two letters of introduction for Yu-cun to take to the capital, so that he could call on an official household and find somewhere to stay. He sent a servant to invite him over. The man returned and said, ‘The monk says Mr Jia left for the capital at the fifth watch this morning. He left a message for you with the monk: “A scholar should not concern himself with lucky or unlucky days. What matters is the sense of the thing. I could not wait to take my leave in person.”’ Shi-yin could only let it rest. Time passes quickly in leisure. Almost before one knew it, the Lantern Festival had come round. Shi-yin told the servant Huo Qi to take Ying-lian out to see the festive performances and lanterns. In the middle of the night Huo Qi needed to relieve himself, and left Ying-lian sitting on a doorstep. When he returned to pick her up, there was no sign of her. Frantic, he searched for the rest of the night. At dawn she was still missing. Afraid to face his master, Huo Qi fled to another district.

segments.text: When their daughter failed to return all night, Shi-yin and his wife knew something was wrong. They sent several people out to look, but all came back without a word of news. She was the only child they had had in half a lifetime. How could they not pine for her, lost in a moment like this? They wept day and night, almost driven to take their own lives. As a month went by, Shi-yin fell ill; his wife too became sick with longing for their daughter. Doctors were called every day to treat them. Then, on the fifteenth day of the third month, the monks at Gourd Temple were frying offerings. Through carelessness, fire leapt from the oil pan and caught the paper windows. Most houses in that district had bamboo fences and wooden walls. Perhaps it was their appointed calamity: the flames spread from one to another until the whole street was like the Mountain of Flames. Soldiers and townspeople came to help, but the blaze had already taken hold. How could they put it out? It burned all night before gradually subsiding. No one knew how many houses had gone. Poor Zhen’s house, next door to the temple, had long since become a field of broken tiles and rubble.

segments.text: Only their lives were spared: Shi-yin, his wife and a few servants were unhurt. In his distress Shi-yin could do nothing but stamp his feet and sigh. After consulting his wife, he decided they must go and live on their farm. But in recent years floods and droughts had ruined the harvests, and bands of thieves were springing up everywhere, seizing land and fields, robbing and stealing, leaving the people no peace. Government troops were sent to hunt them down, and it was impossible to settle there. Shi-yin had to sell the farm and take his wife and two maids to his father-in-law’s home.

segments.text: His father-in-law, Feng Su, was a native of Daruzhou. Though a farmer, he was fairly well-to-do, and he was not pleased to see his son-in-law arrive in such a plight. Fortunately Shi-yin still had some of the money from the sale of his land. He handed it over to Feng Su, asking him to buy a modest house and some land at a suitable price, within his means, to provide for their future. By a mixture of deception and cheating, Feng Su gave him only a little poor land and a dilapidated house. Shi-yin was a scholar, unused to business or farming. He struggled on for a year or two, growing poorer all the time. Whenever they met, Feng Su had some easy advice to offer. In front of them and behind their backs he complained that they did not know how to manage, that they were lazy and thought only of eating, and so on. Shi-yin realised he had sought help from the wrong person and could not help regretting it. The shocks, anguish, anger and grief of the preceding year had already done him lasting harm. At his age, assailed by poverty and illness, he gradually began to look like a man whose life was drawing to its end.

segments.text: The mad, lame Taoist clapped his hands and laughed. ‘Exactly! Exactly!’ Shi-yin laughed too. ‘Let us go!’ He snatched the pouch from the Taoist’s shoulder and slung it over his own. Without going home, he went lightly away with the mad Taoist.

segments.text: The whole neighbourhood was stirred, and everyone passed the story on as a piece of news. When his wife heard, she wept until she was almost senseless. She could only consult her father and send people out to search in every direction. But where were they to find any word of him? There was nothing for it: she had to depend on her parents. Fortunately she still had two of her old maids with her. Mistress and servants, all three, did needlework day and night to sell, helping with her father’s household expenses. Feng Su complained every day, but could do nothing about it.

segments.text: One day the Zhen family’s senior maid was buying thread at the gate when she heard the cries of men clearing the street. Everyone said the new prefect had arrived to take up office. She stood concealed inside the doorway to watch. Guards and runners passed in pairs. Presently a great sedan chair came by, bearing an official in a black hat and scarlet robe.

segments.text: The maid stared, thinking that his face was very familiar, as if she had seen him somewhere before. Then she went back into the room and put it out of her mind. That evening, just as they were about to go to bed, there was a loud hammering at the gate. Many voices shouted, ‘His Honour has sent for someone from this house to answer questions!’ Feng Su was struck dumb with fright, not knowing what disaster had come upon them.

segments.text: Now Feng Su, hearing the officers calling for him, hurried out and asked their business with an obliging smile. They only shouted, ‘Fetch Mr Zhen out at once!’
‘My name is Feng, gentlemen, not Zhen,’ he said, still smiling. ‘My son-in-law’s name was Zhen, but he left to enter religion a year or two ago. Could he be the man you want?’

segments.text: ‘We know nothing about your Zhens and your Fakes,’ the officers said. ‘Our prefect sent us to ask. If he’s your son-in-law, we’ll take you along to explain it to His Honour yourself. Save us running about.’ Without allowing Feng Su another word, they crowded round and hustled him away. Everyone in the Feng household was frightened, not knowing what this might mean.

segments.text: It was about the second watch that night before Feng Su came home, delighted with himself. Everyone pressed him to explain.

‘Our newly appointed prefect is a man named Jia Hua, originally from Huzhou. He used to be a friend of my son-in-law. He passed our door just now and saw that maid Jiao-xing buying thread, so he supposed my son-in-law had moved in here. I explained everything. His Honour was quite distressed and sighed over it. Then he asked after my granddaughter. I told him she had been lost while looking at the lanterns. “Never fear,” he said. “I shall send my men out and have every effort made to find her.” We talked for a while, and when I left he actually gave me two taels of silver.’
Mrs Zhen could not hear this without sorrow. Nothing more happened that night.

segments.text: Early next morning Yu-cun sent two packets of silver and four lengths of brocade to thank Mrs Zhen. He also sent Feng Su a private letter, asking him to approach Mrs Zhen on his behalf: he wanted Jiao-xing as a secondary wife. Feng Su was so beside himself with joy he all but shat and pissed himself. Eager to curry favour, he urged his daughter so insistently that she agreed, and under cover of night Jiao-xing was carried in to the prefect in a single small chair. Yu-cun’s delight need hardly be described. He sent Feng Su a packet of a hundred taels of silver and gave Mrs Zhen many other gifts, telling her to take good care of herself while they sought news of her daughter. Feng Su went home, and there we may leave him.

segments.text: This maid Jiao-xing was the very one who had looked back at Yu-cun that year. A casual glance had brought all this about: an extraordinary turn of fate she could never have foreseen. Who would have thought her destiny and her luck would serve her so well? Within a year of going to Yu-cun she unexpectedly bore him a son. Another six months passed; his lawful wife suddenly fell ill and died, and Yu-cun formally raised Jiao-xing to the position of principal wife. As the saying goes:

segments.text: Able as he was, he was not free from greed and harshness. Confident of his talents, he treated his superiors with contempt, and his fellow officials all looked askance at him. Before a year was out, his superior found an opening and drew up a memorial impeaching him for ‘a deceitful and crafty disposition, the unauthorised prescription of ceremonial rules, and the pursuit of a reputation for purity and uprightness while secretly associating with men who are wolves and tigers, bringing troubles upon the district and making the people’s lives unbearable’, among other charges. The emperor was furious and ordered his dismissal. When the notice arrived from the ministry, every official in the prefecture rejoiced. Yu-cun was deeply ashamed and bitter at heart, but showed not a trace of resentment. He went on smiling and joking as though nothing had happened. After handing over his duties, he sent the money he had accumulated in office, together with his family and dependants, back to his native place. Once all was properly arranged, he set off alone, with the wind on his shoulders and moonlight in his sleeves, to visit the famous sights of the empire. His travels happened to bring him to the Huaiyang region. There he heard that Lin Ru-hai had been appointed to oversee the salt revenue that year. This gentleman’s surname was Lin, his personal name Hai and his courtesy name Ru-hai. He had placed third in the previous palace examination and had now risen to be an officer of the Imperial Library. A native of Gusu, he had been specially appointed by the emperor as Salt Inspector and had been in his new post a little over a month.

segments.text: An ancestor of Lin Ru-hai had held a hereditary marquisate; Ru-hai was now the fifth generation. Originally the title had been granted for three generations only. But the munificence and virtue of the present sovereign so far surpassed those of earlier reigns that an additional favour had allowed Ru-hai’s father to inherit it for a fourth generation. Ru-hai himself had entered official life through the examinations. His family belonged to the hereditary nobility, with its bells and bronze vessels, but it also had a tradition of learning. Unfortunately, the Lin clan had few branches and few descendants. There were several households, but these were only collateral relations of Ru-hai’s, with no close kin in his direct line. He was now forty. His only son, a boy of three, had died the previous year. He had several concubines, but no son was allotted to him by fate, and nothing could be done about it. His lawful wife, a lady of the Jia family, had borne him a daughter, known from infancy as Dai-yu, who was just five. Having no son, husband and wife treasured her. She was bright and delicate-looking, too, and they wished her to study and learn a few characters, merely to stand in, as it were, for the son they were not raising, and ease their sorrow at the emptiness about their knees.

segments.text: Yu-cun had caught a chill and lain ill at an inn for nearly a month before beginning to recover. Worn out in body and running short of travelling money, he was looking for a suitable place where he could settle for a while. Fortunately, two old friends lived in the district. Hearing that the Salt Inspector wanted a tutor, he asked for their help and secured the post, as a means of providing himself with a home for the time being.

segments.text: The beauty of it was that he had only one girl to teach, with two maids studying beside her. She was very young and extremely frail, and no fixed amount of work was required of her, so his duties were light. Almost another year had passed when his pupil’s mother fell ill and died. The girl had attended her with broth and medicine and now observed her mourning with the utmost grief. Yu-cun was about to leave the post and look elsewhere, but Lin Ru-hai wished his daughter to continue her studies during mourning, and kept him on. Lately, however, grief had overwhelmed the girl. Always frail and sickly, she had suffered a return of an old illness and had missed lessons for several days. Yu-cun had nothing to do. Whenever the weather was sunny and mild, he would go out for a walk after his meal.

Its gateway and approach were falling in, its walls crumbling. Over the entrance a board bore the words ‘Temple of Understanding’; beside the door hung an old, damaged couplet:

segments.text: Yu-cun read it and thought: ‘The words are plain enough, but the meaning goes deep. I have visited famous mountains and great temples without ever seeing a saying like this. Perhaps someone here has taken a tumble and come through it. Why not go in and find out?’

He went in. There was only a decrepit old monk cooking gruel, and Yu-cun took little interest in him. When he did ask him a question or two, the old monk proved deaf and muddle-headed, toothless and slow of speech; his answers had nothing to do with the questions.

segments.text: Yu-cun grew impatient and went out again. He thought he would have a few cups at the village tavern to round off his enjoyment of the countryside, and strolled towards it. Just as he was entering, one of the drinkers rose with a loud laugh and came to meet him.
‘What a meeting! What a meeting!’

Yu-cun looked and recognised a man known as Leng Zi-xing, an antiques dealer in the capital whom he had met there in former days. Yu-cun had always praised him as a capable man who could accomplish things; Zi-xing, for his part, profited by Yu-cun’s reputation as a scholar. They therefore found plenty to talk about and got on very well.
‘When did you come here, my dear fellow?’ Yu-cun asked with a smile. ‘I had no idea. What a lucky chance to meet you today!’

‘I came home at the end of last year,’ said Zi-xing. ‘Now I am on my way back to the capital, and stopped here to have a word with a friend. He was kind enough to keep me for a couple of days. I have no pressing business, so I’m staying a little. I shall set off about the middle of the month. My friend is busy today. I happened to stroll out here and thought I would rest my feet.’

segments.text: ‘Who could have expected such a lucky meeting?’
As he spoke he invited Yu-cun to sit with him, and ordered fresh wine and dishes. They drank at leisure and talked of what had happened since their last meeting.
‘Any news in the capital lately?’ Yu-cun asked.
‘Nothing much. Though there has been one little oddity in the family of your distinguished kinsmen.’
Yu-cun laughed. ‘None of my clan live in the capital. Whom can you mean?’
‘You share a surname,’ said Zi-xing, smiling. ‘Doesn’t that make you one clan?’
Yu-cun asked which family he meant.

segments.text: ‘The Jias of the Rong mansion. Surely that would bring no discredit on your family?’

‘Oh, that family!’ Yu-cun said with a smile. ‘As it happens, our humble clan has quite a number of members. Since Jia Fu of the Eastern Han, its branches have multiplied and spread through every province. Who could trace them all? The Rong branch does belong to the same genealogy as ours, but with all their splendour we could hardly presume on the connection. So by now we have grown still further apart and scarcely know each other.’
Zi-xing sighed. ‘Don’t say that, sir. Both houses, Ning and Rong, are in decline now. They are not what they were.’
‘There used to be a great many people in those two mansions. How have they declined so soon?’
‘Ah,’ said Leng Zi-xing, ‘that is a long story.’

‘Last year,’ said Yu-cun, ‘I went to Jinling to see the remains of the Six Dynasties. One day I entered the Stone City and passed their ancestral mansions. The Ning mansion lay to the east, the Rong mansion to the west; together they took up more than half the street.’

segments.text: ‘The great gates were quiet and deserted, but over the enclosing walls I could see halls and towers, all still lofty and imposing. Even the trees and rocks in the gardens behind had a rich, flourishing look. How could that be a family in decline?’

segments.text: Leng Zi-xing laughed. ‘And you a jinshi! You understand nothing of it. As the old saying has it, “A hundred-footed creature does not fall stiff even when dead.” They may not flourish as they did, but they still look very different from an ordinary official’s household. There are more mouths every day, and more affairs to attend to. From the masters down to the servants, plenty enjoy the wealth and honour, but not one does any planning. Yet they cannot bring themselves to cut down the expense of their daily show. The outer structure has hardly begun to totter, but inside the purse is nearly empty. Even that is a small matter. There is something worse. Who would have thought that in a house of bronze vessels and dinner bells, a family of books and poetry, the sons and grandsons would grow worse with every generation?’

Yu-cun was astonished. ‘How could a family so steeped in learning and propriety neglect its children’s education? I cannot speak for other houses, but Ning and Rong are particularly good at bringing up their sons.’
Zi-xing sighed. ‘Those are the very two I mean. Let me tell you.’

segments.text: ‘The first Duke of Ning and the first Duke of Rong were brothers born of the same mother. Ning was the elder and had four sons. After his death Jia Dai-hua inherited his rank. Dai-hua himself had two sons. The elder, Jia Fu, died at eight or nine, leaving only the younger, Jia Jing, to inherit. Nowadays Jing thinks of nothing but the Tao. He loves firing his elixirs and refining mercury; nothing else concerns him. Luckily he had a son in his early years, called Jia Zhen. So intent was the father on becoming an immortal that he handed his rank over to the son. He will not return to his native place, but stays outside the capital, muddling about with Taoist priests. This Master Zhen has a son in his turn, Jia Rong, who is just sixteen this year. Old Mr Jing leaves everything alone. As for Master Zhen, he has no mind for books: pleasure is all he cares about. He has turned the Ning mansion upside down, and nobody dares control him.

‘Now listen to the Rong side. That is where the strange thing I mentioned happened. After the Duke of Rong died, his eldest son Jia Dai-shan inherited. His wife was a daughter of the Marquis Shi’s family, another house of hereditary distinction in Jinling. They had two sons: the elder Jia She, the younger Jia Zheng.’

segments.text: ‘Dai-shan has long been dead, but his widow is still alive. The elder son, Jia She, inherited the rank. The younger, Jia Zheng, was devoted to books from childhood and was his grandfather’s favourite. He had meant to make his way through the examinations. But when Dai-shan’s dying memorial reached the emperor, His Majesty, out of regard for his late servant, not only ordered the eldest son to succeed him but asked how many other sons there were, and summoned them at once. As an additional favour he gave Mr Zheng the title of secretary and sent him to a ministry to learn its business. He has now been promoted to assistant director.

‘Mr Zheng’s wife, a lady of the Wang family, first bore a son called Jia Zhu. He qualified as a licentiate at fourteen; before he was twenty he had married, fathered a son, and died of an illness. Her second child was a girl, born on New Year’s Day. That was remarkable enough, but later she had another boy, and this was stranger still: he came out of the womb with a piece of lustrous, many-coloured jade in his mouth, with a good many characters written on it. So they named him Bao-yu, “Precious Jade”.’

segments.text: ‘Wouldn’t you call that something new and strange?’
‘Strange indeed,’ said Yu-cun, smiling. ‘He may have no ordinary origin.’

Zi-xing gave a cold laugh. ‘That is what everyone says. His grandmother treasured him from the start. On his first birthday Mr Zheng wanted to test what his future inclinations would be, and set out a great collection of all sorts of things for him to choose from. He would touch none of them, but reached straight for the rouge and powder, hairpins and bracelets. His father was furious. “He’ll be nothing but a wine-bibber and a lecher!” After that he took a great dislike to him. Old Lady Shi alone still cherished him as her very life.

‘And here is another odd thing. He has grown to seven or eight now, and though he is extraordinarily naughty, a hundred other children together could not match his intelligence and quickness. Even his childish talk is strange. “Girls’ flesh and bones are made of water,” he says. “Men’s are made of mud. When I see girls, I feel fresh and clear; when I see men, their muddy stink comes pressing in on me.” Isn’t that laughable? He is certain to grow into a sex-mad devil!’

segments.text: Yu-cun’s expression abruptly hardened. He hurried to stop him.

‘No! What a pity you do not understand where such a person comes from. I suspect that Mr Zheng too has mistaken him for a lecherous monster. Unless one has read widely and learnt about the world, laboured at investigating things and extending knowledge, and striven to apprehend the Way and explore its mysteries, one cannot understand.’
Seeing how seriously he took it, Zi-xing at once asked him to explain.

‘Of all the people Heaven and Earth produce,’ said Yu-cun, ‘there are two exceptional kinds: the supremely benevolent and the supremely wicked. The rest do not differ greatly. The supremely benevolent are born in answer to an auspicious turn of fortune; the supremely wicked in answer to a time of calamity. Those born of fortune bring order to the world; those born of calamity bring danger. Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Kings Wen and Wu, the Dukes of Zhou and Shao, Confucius and Mencius, Dong Zhong-shu and Han Yu, Zhou Dun-yi, the Cheng masters, Zhang Zai and Zhu Xi: all were born in answer to fortune. Chi-you, Gong-gong, Jie, Zhou, the First Emperor, Wang Mang, Cao Cao, Huan Wen, An Lu-shan and Qin Hui: all were born in answer to calamity. The supremely benevolent set the world in order; the supremely wicked throw it into turmoil.’

segments.text: ‘Clarity, illumination, spirit and refinement are the upright force of Heaven and Earth, with which the benevolent are endowed. Cruelty and perversity are its evil force, with which the wicked are endowed. In our present dynasty, with its flourishing fortune and enduring blessings, in this peaceful age of effortless rule, those endowed with the clear, luminous, spiritually refined force are everywhere, from the court above to the countryside below. What remains of that refined force wanders with nowhere to go, and becomes sweet dew and gentle breezes, spreading moisture and harmony throughout the four seas. The evil force of cruelty and perversity cannot range abroad in the bright light of day. It congeals and fills deep ravines and great chasms instead. A gust of wind may stir it, or a cloud drive it on; a slight movement or response is awakened, and a thread or half a wisp escapes by accident. If the spiritually refined force happens to pass at that moment, the upright cannot tolerate the evil, and the evil in turn resents the upright. Neither will yield. Like wind, water, thunder and lightning meeting underground, they can neither die away nor make room for each other. They must clash and burst forth before their strength is spent. Such a force, too, must therefore be bestowed on human beings; only when it has discharged itself completely can it disperse. Men or women born by chance with this mixed endowment can neither rise to be benevolent men and gentlemen nor sink to be the greatly vicious and wicked.’

segments.text: ‘Set them among a hundred million people, and their intelligence, quickness, spirit and refinement will put them above them all; but in their perversity, waywardness and disregard for common human feeling, they will rank below them all. Born into a rich and noble house, they become fools for love, creatures of passion. Born into a poor but learned family, they become lofty recluses. Even if born into a humble household with scant blessings, they can never become common runners or sturdy serving-men, content to be driven and ruled by mediocrities. They must become extraordinary actors or celebrated courtesans. Think of Xu You, Tao Qian, Ruan Ji, Ji Kang, Liu Ling, the Wang and Xie families, Gu Hu-tou, the Last Emperor of Chen, Emperor Ming-huang of the Tang, Emperor Hui-zong of the Song, Liu Ting-zhi, Wen Fei-qing, Mi Nan-gong, Shi Man-qing, Liu Qi-qing and Qin Shao-you in earlier times; or, more recently, Ni Yun-lin, Tang Bo-hu and Zhu Zhi-shan. Then there are Li Gui-nian, Huang Fan-chuo, Jing Xin-mo, Zhuo Wen-jun, Hong-fu, Xue Tao, Cui Ying and Chao-yun. Change their circumstances, and they would all be the same kind of people.’

segments.text: ‘Then by your account,’ said Zi-xing, ‘“Success makes a prince; failure makes a bandit.”’

‘Precisely,’ said Yu-cun. ‘And there is something else you do not know. In the two years since my dismissal I have travelled through the provinces and met two unusual children. So as soon as you mentioned this Bao-yu, I could guess that he was very probably of this kind. There is no need to look far. Do you know the Zhen family in Jinling, whose head is imperial commissioner and president of the Institute of Benevolence in Jinling province?’
‘Who doesn’t? The Zhens and the Jias have long been related by marriage and are old family friends besides. They are extremely close. I myself have had dealings with the Zhens for a good while.’

‘Last year, when I was in Jinling,’ Yu-cun said with a smile, ‘someone recommended me as a tutor to that family. Once inside, I found that, exalted as their position was, they were rich yet mindful of propriety. It was a rare household to teach in. But this one pupil, though only beginning his letters, cost me more trouble than a student preparing for the examinations.’

segments.text: ‘His talk was more ridiculous still. “I must have two girls beside me while I study,” he said. “Then I can recognise the characters and understand them. Otherwise my mind is all muddled.” He would often say to the pages who attended him, “The word ‘girl’ is supremely noble and supremely pure. Even the sacred names of Amitabha Buddha and the Primordial Lord of Heaven cannot equal it in honour. You must never profane it with your filthy mouths and stinking tongues. Remember that! Whenever you wish to say it, you must first rinse your mouths with clean water and fragrant tea. If you slip up, I’ll have your teeth knocked out and your cheeks pierced!” His cruelty, impatience, wilfulness and foolish infatuation were extraordinary in every way. Yet the moment lessons ended and he went indoors to see the girls, he became gentle and peaceable, intelligent and polished: quite another person. His father had beaten him almost to death several times for it, but nothing would change him. Whenever the pain of a beating grew unbearable, he would start crying out, “Sister! Little sister!”’

segments.text: ‘Later I heard the girls indoors teasing him. “Why do you keep calling for your sisters when the beating gets bad? Do you want us to plead for you and get you off? Aren’t you ashamed?” His answer was marvellous. “When the pain is terrible,” he said, “I thought that just saying ‘sister’ or ‘little sister’ might perhaps ease it. And when I tried it, I really did feel no pain. That was how I discovered the secret. Whenever the pain is at its worst, I call out for my sisters over and over.” Isn’t it ridiculous? His grandmother’s blind indulgence made matters worse. Time and again, for her grandson’s sake, she insulted his tutor and reproached her son. So I resigned and left. I am now teaching in the household of Lin, the Salt Inspector. You see, children of that sort will never preserve what their forefathers established or follow the guidance of their teachers and elders. The pity is that the girls in his family are so remarkable.’

‘The three girls now at the Jia house are good, too,’ said Zi-xing. ‘Mr Zheng’s eldest daughter, Yuan-chun, has been chosen for her goodness, filial devotion, talent and virtue to serve as a lady clerk in the palace.’

segments.text: ‘The second young lady, Ying-chun, is Mr She’s daughter by a concubine. The third, Tan-chun, is Mr Zheng’s daughter by a concubine. The fourth, Xi-chun, is Master Zhen’s full sister, from the Ning house. Old Lady Shi is so fond of the granddaughters that they all live with her and study together. I hear they are all excellent.’

segments.text: ‘That is not quite it,’ said Zi-xing. ‘The eldest girl was born on the first day of the first month, so she was called Yuan-chun, “First Spring”, and the others merely followed her in using “spring”. The women of the previous generation were named on the same pattern as their brothers. There is a case in point: your present employer Mr Lin’s wife was the full sister of Messrs She and Zheng of the Rong house. Before she married she was called Jia Min.’

segments.text: ‘If you doubt it, make some inquiries when you go back.’

Yu-cun slapped the table and laughed. ‘So that is why! Whenever my pupil comes to the character min in her reading, she pronounces it mi instead. She does it every time. When she writes it, she leaves out a stroke or two. I had wondered about that. Now you tell me this, there can be no doubt of the reason. And no wonder the girl speaks and behaves so differently from other girls nowadays. I had thought her mother must have been an unusual woman to have such a daughter. Now that I know she is a granddaughter of the Rong house, there is nothing surprising in it. Sadly, her mother died only last month.’

Zi-xing sighed. ‘There were four sisters in that generation, and she was the youngest. Now she too is gone. Not one of the older generation’s sisters remains. We can only wait and see what husbands these younger girls will find.’

segments.text: ‘Quite so,’ said Yu-cun. ‘Now, you said Mr Zheng has the son born with jade in his mouth, and a young grandson left by his eldest son. Has Mr She no son at all?’

‘After Mr Zheng’s jade boy was born, a concubine bore him another son. I don’t know what sort he is. At any rate, he has two sons and a grandson living now; what will become of them remains to be seen. Mr She has two sons as well. The elder, Jia Lian, is about twenty. He strengthened an existing family tie by marrying the niece of Mr Zheng’s wife, Lady Wang: her brother’s daughter. They have been married two years. Master Lian has purchased the title of sub-prefect. He has no taste for books either, but he is quick and adaptable in worldly affairs and can talk well enough. So he lives at his uncle Mr Zheng’s house and helps manage the household business. But since he married, everyone from top to bottom has praised his wife, and Master Lian has fallen a bowshot behind. She is extremely good-looking, brisk and fluent in speech, and remarkably shrewd and calculating. You would not find her equal in ten thousand men.’
Yu-cun smiled. ‘Which shows I was not wrong.’

segments.text: ‘For all we know, these people we have been discussing may belong to that same class, endowed with both the upright and the evil forces.’
‘Evil or upright,’ said Zi-xing, ‘you’ve been so busy reckoning up someone else’s affairs, you ought to have a cup of wine.’
‘True,’ said Yu-cun. ‘Though in all this talking I have actually drunk a few cups too many.’
Zi-xing laughed. ‘Other people’s gossip is the perfect relish for wine. What harm in a few extra cups?’
Yu-cun looked out of the window. ‘It’s getting late. Mind they don’t shut the city gates on us. We might walk slowly back and go on talking.’
They rose and settled their bill. Just as they were about to leave, someone called from behind them: ‘Brother Yu-cun, congratulations! I have come especially to bring you good news.’

segments.text:
When Yu-cun hurriedly turned to look, the man proved to be an old colleague, Zhang Ru-gui, who had been impeached and dismissed in the same case as himself. Zhang was a native of this district and had been living at home since his dismissal. He had now heard that a memorial requesting the reinstatement of former officials had been approved in the capital, and was looking everywhere for connections and a way forward. Happening upon Yu-cun, he had hastened to congratulate him. They exchanged greetings, and Zhang Ru-gui told him the news. Yu-cun was naturally delighted. After a few hurried words they parted, each to return home. On hearing of this, Leng Zi-xing at once suggested that Yu-cun ask Lin Ru-hai to intercede with Jia Zheng in the capital. Yu-cun took his meaning, said goodbye and returned to his lodgings, where he immediately sought out the Court Gazette to make sure. The next day he discussed the matter with Ru-hai in person.
‘Heaven has arranged this very conveniently,’ said Ru-hai. ‘Since my wife’s death, my mother-in-law in the capital has been concerned that my little girl has no one to care for her and bring her up. She has already sent men and women servants, with boats, to fetch her. The child has not yet fully recovered, so they have not been able to leave.

‘I was just reflecting that I had done nothing to repay your kindness in teaching her. How could I fail to do my utmost for you when such an opportunity presents itself? Set your mind at rest. I have already made provision for this and written a letter of recommendation, asking my brother-in-law to give you every assistance. Only then shall I have done something, however little, to show my gratitude. As for any customary expenses, I have made that quite clear in my letter too. You need not trouble yourself about them.’
Yu-cun bowed repeatedly, thanking him without cease. He also asked, ‘May I inquire what office your distinguished relative now holds? I am afraid of being too hasty. I should not like to rush up to the capital and impose upon him.’
‘My relations are of your own clan, if one goes by the genealogies,’ Ru-hai said with a smile. ‘They are grandsons of the Duke of Rong. The elder of my wife’s brothers has inherited the title of General of the First Rank. His name is She, his courtesy name En-hou. Her second brother, Zheng, whose courtesy name is Cun-zhou, is an assistant director in the Board of Works. He is modest, courteous and generous, with much of his grandfather’s character. He is not one of those frivolous men born to wealth who happen to hold office. That is why I have written to ask his help. Otherwise it would not only compromise your integrity: I should scorn to do it myself.’
Only now did Yu-cun feel sure of what Zi-xing had told him the day before. He thanked Lin Ru-hai once more.

Ru-hai went on, ‘We have chosen the second day of next month for my daughter’s journey to the capital. Would it not suit you both to travel together?’
Yu-cun readily agreed to everything, inwardly delighted. Ru-hai then arranged gifts and a farewell entertainment, all of which Yu-cun accepted.

Dai-yu, the young pupil, was only just recovering. At first she could not bear to leave her father, but her grandmother had sent word insisting that she come, and Ru-hai himself said, ‘Your father is nearly fifty. I have no intention of marrying again. You are often ill and still so young, with no mother to bring you up and no brothers or sisters to support you. If you go to your grandmother and your uncles’ family, with your girl cousins for company, I shall have less cause to worry about your care. Why do you still say you will not go?’
Only then did Dai-yu take leave of him, bowing through her tears,

segments.text: and board the boat with her nurse and several elderly women from the Rong household. Yu-cun had a boat of his own and two young servants, and travelled in Dai-yu’s company. In due course they reached the capital and entered the imperial city. Yu-cun first put his clothes and cap in order, then took his boys to the gate of the Rong mansion and sent in a visiting card describing himself as a nephew of the same clan. Jia Zheng had already read his brother-in-law’s letter and promptly invited him in. Yu-cun was an imposing figure and spoke well. Jia Zheng had a particular regard for men of learning: he honoured talent without standing on his own rank, helped the weak and relieved those in distress, much as his forebears had done. With his brother-in-law’s request added to these considerations, he treated Yu-cun with exceptional favour and worked strenuously for him behind the scenes. When the memorial was submitted, it was a simple matter to secure his reinstatement, pending a vacancy. In less than two months the prefecture of Yingtian, at Jinling, fell vacant, and this post was obtained for him. Yu-cun took leave of Jia Zheng, chose a day and went off to assume office. We need say no more of that.

segments.text: When Dai-yu left her boat and came ashore, a sedan chair and carts for her luggage had long been waiting, sent by the Rong household. She had often heard her mother say that her grandmother’s family was unlike other families. Even the third-ranking women servants whom she had seen in the last few days ate, dressed and spent in a manner far from ordinary. What must the house itself be like? She therefore watched every step and took care at every moment, unwilling to say one word too many or take a single unnecessary step, for fear of making herself ridiculous. Once seated in the chair and carried into the city, she looked out through its gauze window. The busy streets and crowded population were indeed unlike anything elsewhere. After they had gone on for some time, she suddenly saw two great stone lions crouching on the north side of the street, before a three-bay gateway ornamented with animal heads. Ten or more men in splendid caps and clothes sat in rows outside. The central gates were shut; people came and went only through the smaller gates to east and west. Above the main entrance a tablet bore five great characters: ‘Ning Mansion, Built by Imperial Command’.

segments.text: ‘This must be my grandfather’s elder branch of the family,’ Dai-yu thought. As she was thinking this, they went a little farther west and came to another three-bay gateway just like it. This was the Rong mansion. They did not use the main entrance, but went in through the small western gate. The bearers carried her about a bowshot inside, then set down the chair as they were about to turn a corner, and withdrew. The women following behind had already got out of their chairs and now came hurrying up. Three or four neatly dressed young servants of seventeen or eighteen took the bearers’ places and lifted the chair again. The women walked round it as it was carried to an inner gate with pendant-flower carving and set down.

segments.text: The young servants withdrew. The women came forward to lift the curtain and help Dai-yu out. With her hand resting on one of the women’s, Lin Dai-yu passed through the flower-carved gate. Covered walks ran round both sides; in the centre stood a passage-hall, with a great marble screen on a rosewood stand. Beyond the screen was a small three-bay hall, and behind that the main courtyard of the inner apartments.

The principal range facing them had five bays, all carved beams and painted woodwork, with covered walks passing through the gables to side rooms on either hand. Parrots, hwamei and other birds hung in cages along them. Several maids in red and green were sitting on the terrace. The moment they saw the party they came forward, smiling.
‘Her Old Ladyship was only just asking about you. And here you are!’
Three or four competed to raise the door-curtain. Someone could be heard announcing, ‘Miss Lin has arrived.’

As Dai-yu entered, she saw an old lady with silver hair coming towards her, supported by two attendants, and knew at once that this was her grandmother. Before she could make her obeisance, the old lady had caught her in her arms and burst into loud weeping, calling her her heart and her darling flesh. Everyone standing in attendance covered their faces and cried. Dai-yu too wept without stopping. After a time the others gradually persuaded them to be calm, and only then could Dai-yu greet her grandmother formally. This was the old Lady Shi of whom Leng Zi-xing had spoken, the mother of Jia She and Jia Zheng. Grandmother Jia now introduced the others one by one.
‘This is your elder uncle’s wife. This is your second uncle’s wife. And this is your late Cousin Zhu’s wife, your sister-in-law.’
Dai-yu paid her respects to each in turn.
‘Ask the girls to come,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Our visitor has only just arrived from far away. They need not go to their lessons today.’
The servants answered, and two went off.

Before long three girls arrived, surrounded by three nurses and five or six maids. The first was moderately tall, her figure a little full, her cheeks as smooth as freshly peeled lychees, her nose as creamy as goose fat. Gentle and quiet, she looked easy to approach. The second was tall and slender, with sloping shoulders, a narrow waist, an oval face, lovely eyes and finely shaped brows. Her eyes moved with spirit; there was a brilliance about her that made one forget the commonplace. The third had not yet grown to her full height and still looked quite a child. All three wore the same ornaments, skirts and jackets. Dai-yu rose quickly to greet them. They exchanged courtesies and learned who each other was, then all sat down again. The maids poured tea. They spoke only of how Dai-yu’s mother had fallen ill, the doctors and medicines, her death and the funeral arrangements. Grandmother Jia could not help grieving again.
‘Of all my children, your mother was the one I loved most. And now she has gone before me, and I could not even see her face. How can I look at you without feeling heartbroken?’
She held Dai-yu to her again and began to sob.

Everyone hurried to console her, until she was a little calmer. They could see that young as Dai-yu was, her speech and manner were far from common. Though her face and body seemed frail almost beyond endurance, there was a natural grace about her. They recognised that she suffered from a constitutional weakness and asked what medicines she regularly took, and why no prompt treatment had been undertaken.
‘I have always been like this,’ Dai-yu said. ‘I began taking medicine as soon as I could eat, and I have never stopped. Any number of famous doctors have written prescriptions and prepared medicines, but none has done any good. I am told that when I was three a scabby-headed monk came and asked my parents to give me up to the religious life. Of course they refused. He said, “If you cannot bear to part with her, I fear her illness will never be cured.

‘Just as well,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘I am having pills made up here. They need only prepare an extra batch.’
Before she had finished, laughter sounded in the courtyard behind, and a voice called, ‘I’m late! I wasn’t here to welcome our visitor!’
Dai-yu wondered, ‘Everyone here has been holding their breath and speaking so quietly, so solemn and respectful. Who can this be, behaving with such abandon and so little ceremony?’

While she was thinking this, a woman came in through the rear doorway, surrounded by married women servants and maids. She was dressed quite differently from the girls. Brilliant in coloured embroidery, she might have been a goddess or an immortal. Gold filigree adorned her coiled hair, set with pearls and the Eight Treasures; her hairpin showed five phoenixes facing the rising sun, with hanging pearls. Round her neck she wore a pure-gold circlet of coiling hornless dragons. From her skirt hung a pea-green palace sash and rose-coloured stone pendants carved as paired fish beneath two crosspieces. Her close-fitting scarlet foreign-satin jacket was worked in gold with a hundred butterflies among flowers. Over it she wore a dark-blue coat lined with ermine and patterned in five-coloured silk tapestry, and below it an emerald-green skirt of foreign crêpe scattered with flowers. Her phoenix eyes tapered to sharp corners; her brows curved like willow leaves, lifting at the ends. She was slender and alluring. Her powdered face held a springtime warmth, its authority concealed; her laughter reached one before her red lips parted.
Dai-yu rose at once to meet her.
‘You don’t know her,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘She’s our famous little rogue, our good-for-nothing. Down south they call such a person a “peppercorn”. Just call her “Peppercorn Feng”.’
Dai-yu was still unsure how to address her when the girls hurried to explain, ‘This is Cousin Lian’s wife.’
Though she had never met her, Dai-yu had heard her mother say that Jia Lian, the son of her elder uncle Jia She, had married a niece of her second aunt, Lady Wang. The girl had been brought up as a boy from childhood; her formal name was Wang Xi-feng.

Dai-yu smiled in response and paid her respects, calling her ‘Sister-in-law’. Xi-feng took her hand and looked her carefully up and down, then led her back to sit beside Grandmother Jia.
‘So there really are such beauties in the world!’ she said, smiling. ‘I had never seen one till today. And with that bearing, you would never take her for your daughter’s child, Grandmother. She looks like your own son’s daughter. No wonder you think and talk of her all day long.

‘Only it’s so pitiful that this dear little cousin should have such a hard lot. Why did Aunt have to die?’ She wiped her eyes with her handkerchief.
‘I had only just stopped, and here you are setting me off again,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘Your cousin has had a long journey, and she’s frail too. We had only just consoled her. Now, no more about that!’
Xi-feng immediately changed from sorrow to cheerfulness.
‘Of course! The moment I saw her, I could think of nothing else. I was so glad and so sad that I quite forgot you, Grandmother. I deserve a good beating!’
She took Dai-yu’s hand again. ‘How old are you, my dear? Have you been to lessons? What medicine are you taking? You mustn’t pine for home here. If there’s anything you’d like to eat or play with, just tell me. And if the maids or old women don’t behave, tell me that too.’
She turned to the women servants. ‘Has Miss Lin’s luggage been brought in? How many people came with her? Get two rooms in the servants’ quarters cleaned up at once, and let them have a rest.’

While they were talking, tea and fruit had been laid out. Xi-feng herself presented Dai-yu with both. Dai-yu then heard her second aunt ask Xi-feng, ‘Have the monthly allowances been paid?’
‘They’ve all been paid. I was just taking some people up to the back storey to look for satin. We hunted for ages and couldn’t find the kind you mentioned yesterday. Perhaps you remembered it wrongly, ma’am?’
‘It hardly matters whether there is any,’ Lady Wang said. Then she added, ‘You should have taken out a couple of lengths while you were there, to make clothes for your cousin. Remind me this evening to have someone fetch them. Don’t forget.’
‘I had thought of that already,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Knowing she was due any day now, I’ve set some aside. Once you’ve been back and seen them, I can send them over.’
Lady Wang smiled and nodded without speaking.

When the tea and fruit had been cleared away, Grandmother Jia told two old nurses to take Dai-yu to pay her respects to her two maternal uncles. Jia She’s wife, Lady Xing, rose too.
‘It would be convenient for me to take my niece over,’ she said with a smile.
‘Yes, do go,’ Grandmother Jia replied, smiling. ‘You needn’t come back here.’
Lady Xing answered, ‘Yes,’ and took Dai-yu to say goodbye to Lady Wang. Everyone accompanied them as far as the passage-hall. Outside the flower-carved gate the young servants had already brought up a carriage with green curtains and a blue silk cover. Lady Xing took Dai-yu inside. The women lowered the curtains before ordering the young servants to lift and draw it to a wider space, where a docile mule was harnessed to it. They too went out through the small western gate, turned east past the main entrance of the Rong mansion and entered a great black-lacquered gateway, stopping before the ceremonial inner gate. Only after the young servants had withdrawn were the carriage curtains raised. Holding Dai-yu by the hand, Lady Xing led her into the courtyard. From the arrangement of the buildings and courtyards, Dai-yu judged that this must have been partitioned off from the Rong mansion’s garden.

After they had passed through three ceremonial gates, she found that the main rooms, side rooms and covered walks were all small and finely arranged, quite unlike the lofty splendour of the apartments she had just left. Trees and ornamental rocks stood everywhere in the courtyard. They entered the principal room, where a number of concubines and maids in splendid dress came to meet them. Lady Xing asked Dai-yu to sit down and sent someone to fetch Jia She from the outer study. Presently the messenger returned.
‘His Lordship says, “I have been unwell for several days. Seeing the young lady would only grieve us both, and for the moment I cannot bear it. Tell her not to be sad or homesick. With her grandmother and her aunts, it will be just as though she were at home. Her cousins may be dull girls, but their company will help to relieve her loneliness. If anything troubles her, she must say so, and not treat us as strangers.”’
Dai-yu stood up quickly and listened to the whole message. After sitting a little longer, she asked leave to go.

Lady Xing pressed her to stay for supper, but Dai-yu replied with a smile, ‘It is very kind of you to offer me supper, Aunt, and I ought not to refuse. But I have still to pay my respects to my second uncle. I am afraid it would be discourteous to go only after I had eaten. May I accept your kindness another day? I hope you will forgive me.’
‘Of course,’ Lady Xing said, smiling.

segments.text: Soon Dai-yu was back at the Rong mansion and alighted from the carriage. The nurses led her round to the east, through an east–west passage-hall, to a large courtyard inside the ceremonial gate behind the great south-facing hall. The principal building had five bays. Side rooms and low-roofed annexes joined it through the gables, with passages leading in every direction. Its imposing magnificence was quite different from Grandmother Jia’s apartments. Dai-yu recognised this as the principal inner residence. A broad paved walk led straight out to the main gate. On entering the hall, the first thing she saw when she looked up was a great blue tablet bearing nine dragons in gold. Three enormous characters read ‘Rong-xi Hall’. A small inscription behind them said, ‘Written and bestowed upon Jia Yuan, Duke of Rong, on such-and-such a day, month and year’, followed by the imperial seal, ‘Treasure of the Imperial Brush Amid Myriad Affairs’. On a great rosewood table carved with hornless dragons stood an ancient bronze tripod, some three chi high, with a blue-green patina. Above hung a large ink painting of a dragon, entitled ‘Awaiting the Water-clock to Attend Court’. On one side was a golden ape-shaped ritual vessel; on the other, a large glass drinking vessel. Below, sixteen nanmu folding chairs stood in two rows. A couplet, its engraved silver characters inlaid in ebony boards, read:

segments.text: Below, in smaller characters, was written: ‘Respectfully inscribed by Mu Shi, hereditary Prince of Dong’an, a junior fellow countryman bound to you by generations of family friendship.’ Lady Wang did not ordinarily sit or rest in this main hall, but in the three-bay suite to its east. The old nurses now led Dai-yu through the eastern doorway. The great kang beneath the window was covered with a scarlet foreign woollen rug. A scarlet backrest with a pattern of coin-roundels and mang dragons stood against the wall, with dark-blue bolsters and a long olive-yellow mattress in the same design. On either side was a little plum-blossom-shaped table in foreign lacquer. On the left stood a King Wen-style tripod incense burner, with its spoon, tongs and incense box; on the right a slender ‘beauty’ vase of Ru ware, filled with flowers in season, as well as tea bowls, a spittoon and other things. Four chairs faced west below the kang, each draped in a pink floral cover, with four footstools beneath. A pair of tall stands flanked the chairs, also furnished with tea bowls and vases of flowers.

segments.text: There is no need to describe the remaining furnishings in detail. The old nurses invited Dai-yu to sit on the kang. But there were two brocade cushions set opposite one another along its edge, and, judging the precedence of the places, she declined to mount it and sat instead on a chair to the east. The maids of these apartments hurried to bring tea. As Dai-yu drank, she observed their clothes and ornaments, their bearing and movements. They too were indeed unlike the servants of other households.
