Before she had finished her tea, a maid in a red silk-twill jacket and a blue satin waistcoat with piped edges came in, smiling.
‘Her Ladyship asks Miss Lin to come and sit in the other room.’
The nurses led Dai-yu out and into a small three-bay range off the eastern covered walk. A low table stood across the kang in the main room, piled with books and tea things. Against the eastern wall, facing west, were a somewhat worn blue satin backrest and bolsters. Lady Wang sat at the lower place to the west, on a cushion with a backrest of the same worn blue satin. ‘Your uncle has gone to observe a fast today,’ Lady Wang said. ‘You can see him another time. There is just one thing I must tell you. Your three girl cousins are all very good. Dai-yu had often heard her mother speak of a boy cousin, the son of her second aunt, who had been born with a piece of jade in his mouth. He was extraordinarily unruly, hated studying, and liked nothing better than to spend his time among the women and girls. His grandmother doted on him, and no one dared discipline him. From Lady Wang’s words Dai-yu knew that this must be the cousin she meant.
She smiled politely. ‘Do you mean the cousin who was born with the jade, Aunt? At home I often heard Mother speak of him. She said he was a year older than me and his childhood name was Bao-yu; although he was very wilful and mischievous, he was wonderfully affectionate towards his sisters and girl cousins. Now that I am here, I shall naturally be with the girls. The boys have their own rooms in another courtyard. How could I have occasion to provoke him?’
‘You don’t understand,’ Lady Wang said, smiling. ‘He is not like other boys. From his earliest years your grandmother has spoilt him, bringing him up with the girls, and he is used to being indulged among them. On a day when they pay him no attention, he is rather quieter. Even if he feels neglected, he only goes outside the inner gate and takes it out on his two little pages where no one can see. A little muttering, and it is over.

Dai-yu agreed to each of these instructions. A maid then came to announce, ‘Supper is being served at Her Old Ladyship’s.’
Lady Wang at once took Dai-yu through the rear doorway, west along the covered walk and out through a side gate into a broad north–south passage between walls. To the south stood a small three-bay hall, its back towards the outer approach, with a projecting covered porch; to the north was a great screen wall painted white. Behind it were a smallish gateway and a small set of rooms.
Lady Wang pointed them out with a smile. ‘Those are your Cousin Feng’s rooms. You can come and find her here later. Whatever you need, just tell her.’
Four or five young servants, still with their hair tied in little children’s tufts, stood by the courtyard gate with their hands at their sides. Lady Wang led Dai-yu through another east–west passage-hall into Grandmother Jia’s rear courtyard. They entered by the back door, where many attendants were already waiting. Only when Lady Wang arrived were the table and chairs set in place. Jia Zhu’s wife, née Li, brought the rice; Xi-feng laid out the chopsticks; Lady Wang presented the soup.

Grandmother Jia sat alone on the couch facing the room, with four empty chairs, two on either side. Xi-feng hurried to draw Dai-yu to the first chair on the left, but Dai-yu was most reluctant to accept it.
‘Your aunts and your cousins’ wives don’t eat here,’ Grandmother Jia said, smiling. ‘You are our guest. That is where you ought to sit.’
Only then did Dai-yu ask leave to be seated and sit down. Grandmother Jia told Lady Wang to sit. Ying-chun and the other two girls likewise asked leave before coming forward. Ying-chun took the first chair on the right, Tan-chun the second on the left, and Xi-chun the second on the right. Maids stood beside them holding fly-whisks, rinsing bowls and towels. Li and Xi-feng stood by the table, serving and inviting them to eat. Though many women servants and maids waited in the outer room, not so much as a cough was heard. The meal ended in silence. Maids brought each of them tea on small trays. Lin Ru-hai had taught his daughter to cherish her good fortune and preserve her health: after a meal she must be sure that every grain of rice had been swallowed and wait a while before drinking tea, so as not to harm the digestion. But Dai-yu had already seen many things here that differed from the customs at home and that she would have to follow. She must change her ways one by one. Accordingly she accepted the tea.

Someone promptly brought a rinsing bowl, and Dai-yu followed the others in rinsing her mouth. After they had washed their hands, more tea was brought. This was the tea for drinking.
‘You may go now,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Let us talk at our ease.’
Lady Wang rose at once. After a few more casual remarks she took Xi-feng and Li away. Grandmother Jia asked Dai-yu what she was studying.

‘I have only just been studying the Four Books,’ Dai-yu said. She then asked what her cousins were reading.
‘Reading?’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘They only learn a few characters, so that they won’t be blind with their eyes open!’

She had scarcely finished when footsteps sounded outside. A maid came in, smiling.
‘Bao-yu is here!’
Dai-yu was wondering, ‘What sort of idle scamp is this Bao-yu? What sort of muddle-headed, naughty child?’

She would have been quite content not to meet the stupid creature at all. Before the maid had finished announcing him, however, a young gentleman had entered. His hair was held by a coronet of reddish gold set with gems; level with his brows lay a golden band worked with two dragons contending for a pearl. He wore a scarlet, tight-sleeved robe patterned in two shades of gold with a hundred butterflies among flowers, a palace sash of five-coloured silk tied in flower-knots with long tassels, and over it a dark-blue Japanese-satin coat with eight roundels in raised weave and a fringe of tassels. On his feet were little court boots of blue satin with white soles. His face was like the mid-autumn moon, his colour like a flower at spring dawn. The hair at his temples was trimmed as if with a knife, his brows drawn in ink; his cheeks were peach petals, his eyes autumn waters. Even in anger he would seem to smile; even a reproachful glance would hold affection. About his neck was a gold circlet of hornless dragons, and on a cord of five-coloured silk hung a beautiful piece of jade.
Dai-yu was astonished at the sight of him. ‘How strange! It is as though I have seen him somewhere before. How can he look so familiar?’
Bao-yu greeted Grandmother Jia. ‘Go and see your mother,’ she told him, and he turned and went out.

segments.text: When he returned a little later, he had changed his clothes and headgear. The short hair round his head was plaited into little braids tied with red silk, all gathered into the lock left to grow from infancy at the crown, and woven into a single long plait, black and shining as lacquer. A row of four large pearls ran from crown to tip, with a golden Eight Treasures ornament hanging at the end. He wore a somewhat worn pink long jacket scattered with flowers, and still had on his neck circlet, jade, the lock marking his dedication to a religious guardian, his protective charms and the rest. Below showed part of his pine-pollen-green flowered silk-twill trousers, ink-splashed stockings edged with brocade, and thick-soled scarlet shoes. His face looked more than ever as if it had been powdered, his lips as though touched with rouge. Affection moved in his glances; laughter was never far from his speech. All his natural charm was gathered in the tips of his brows, a lifetime’s countless feelings crowded into the corners of his eyes. His appearance was certainly superb, but what lay beneath it was harder to know. A later writer composed two lyrics to the tune ‘Moon over the West River’ which judged Bao-yu very aptly:

Wayward in conduct, perverse in disposition,
What does he care for the world’s slander?

segments.text:
‘Nonsense again!’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘When could you ever have met her?’
Bao-yu smiled. ‘Even if I have never met her, her face is familiar. In my heart she counts as an old acquaintance. Why shouldn’t we treat today as a meeting after a long separation?’
‘Better still! Better still!’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘Then you will get on all the better.’
Bao-yu moved over to sit beside Dai-yu and studied her again.
‘Have you done any reading, Cousin?’
‘No,’ Dai-yu said. ‘I only went to lessons for a year. I know a few characters, that’s all.’
‘What are the two characters of your name?’
Dai-yu told him. He asked her courtesy name.
‘I haven’t one.’

‘Let me give you a wonderful one,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Nothing could be better than Pin-pin, “Frown-frown”.’
Tan-chun asked where he had found it.
‘The Comprehensive Survey of Persons Past and Present says, “In the west is a stone called dai, which can be used instead of ink for painting eyebrows.” And Cousin Lin’s brows look as though they are drawn together in a frown. Don’t those two characters make it doubly apt?’
‘I’m afraid you’ve made that up again,’ Tan-chun said, laughing.
Bao-yu laughed too. ‘Apart from the Four Books, there’s plenty that’s made up. Why am I the only one accused of inventing things?’
He asked Dai-yu another question. ‘Have you a jade too?’

No one understood what he meant. Dai-yu considered: ‘He has a jade himself, so he wants to know if I have one.’
‘I haven’t anything like that,’ she answered. ‘It must be something very rare. How could everyone have one?’
At this Bao-yu instantly flew into one of his fits of madness. He tore off the jade and flung it down with all his strength.
‘What’s rare about it?’ he cried angrily. ‘It can’t even tell the better people from the worse, and they call it “spiritual”! Spiritual indeed! I don’t want the wretched thing!’
Everyone rushed in alarm to pick it up. Grandmother Jia clasped him to her in great distress.
‘You wicked boy!

‘If you’re angry, you can easily hit someone or scold them. Why must you throw away your very life?’
Bao-yu sobbed, his face streaked with tears. ‘None of the girls at home has one. I’m the only one, and I said it was no fun. Now this cousin has come, lovely as an immortal, and she hasn’t one either. That proves it’s no good.’
Grandmother Jia hurried to soothe him. ‘Your cousin did have one. But when your aunt died, she couldn’t bear to leave her little girl, and there was nothing else to be done, so she took your cousin’s jade with her. It served as a burial offering, to express your cousin’s devotion, and it let your aunt’s spirit feel that she could still see her daughter. That’s why your cousin says she hasn’t one. She doesn’t like to boast about herself. How can you compare yourself with her now? Put it on again and take good care of it. Mind your mother doesn’t hear of this!’
She took the jade from a maid and put it back on him herself. Bao-yu thought this explanation made excellent sense and raised no further objections. Just then Dai-yu’s nurse came to ask where she was to sleep.

‘For now, move Bao-yu out to the warm side-room with me,’ Grandmother Jia said, ‘and put Miss Lin inside the gauze-screened alcove. Once the rest of the winter is over, we can get rooms ready for them in the spring and make fresh arrangements.’
‘Dearest Grandmother,’ Bao-yu said, ‘I shall be perfectly comfortable on the bed outside the gauze screen. Why move me out to disturb your peace?’
Grandmother Jia considered. ‘Very well.’
Each child was to have a nurse and a maid in attendance, with the others keeping watch in the outer room, ready to answer a call. Xi-feng had already sent over a flowered mauve bed-curtain, together with brocade quilts, satin mattresses and other bedding.

segments.text: Dai-yu had brought only two attendants: Nurse Wang, who had nursed her from infancy, and a little maid of ten named Snowgoose, who had also been with her since she was very small. Grandmother Jia saw that Snowgoose was still thoroughly childish and Nurse Wang extremely old, and thought neither would be able to spare Dai-yu trouble or serve her as she wished. She therefore gave her one of her own second-ranking maids, called Ying-ge. In other respects Dai-yu was provided for on the same terms as Ying-chun and the others. Besides the nurse who had suckled each girl, there were four matrons to guide her conduct; besides the two personal maids who looked after her hair ornaments, washing and bathing, there were five or six little maids to sweep the rooms and run errands. Nurse Wang and Ying-ge now attended Dai-yu inside the green gauze screen. Outside, by the large bed, were Bao-yu’s wet-nurse, Nurse Li, and his senior maid, Aroma.

Aroma too had originally been Grandmother Jia’s maid, and her name had been Pearl. Doting on Bao-yu, Grandmother Jia had feared that none of his maids would give herself wholly to his service. She had always liked Aroma for her simple, good heart and the thoroughness with which she performed her duties, and had therefore given her to him. Bao-yu knew that her surname was Hua, ‘flower’, and had seen the phrase ‘the flowers’ aroma steals upon one’ in an old poem. He reported his wish to Grandmother Jia and changed her name to Aroma. Aroma had a certain single-mindedness of her own: when she served Grandmother Jia, the old lady alone filled her heart and eyes; now that she served Bao-yu, there was no one in her heart or eyes but Bao-yu. His perverse disposition, however, led her to remonstrate with him often and made her deeply anxious. That night, after Bao-yu and Nurse Li had gone to sleep, she saw that Dai-yu and Ying-ge were still awake inside. Having taken off her make-up, she slipped quietly in.
‘Why aren’t you resting yet, miss?’ she asked with a smile.
‘Please sit down, Sister,’ Dai-yu said at once.
Aroma sat on the edge of the bed.
‘Miss Lin has been upset,’ Ying-ge said, smiling. ‘She was crying and wiping her eyes, saying, “I had only just arrived, and already I brought on your young master’s madness. If he had broken the jade, wouldn’t it have been my fault?” That’s what was troubling her. I’ve only just managed to comfort her.’
‘Please don’t feel that way, miss,’ said Aroma. ‘You’ll probably see much stranger goings-on than that in future!

‘If you take his behaviour to heart and let it grieve you, I’m afraid there will be no end to your grieving. Please don’t fret over it!’
‘I shall remember what you both tell me,’ Dai-yu said. ‘But where did that jade come from, after all? Does it have writing on it?’
‘No one in the family knows where it came from,’ Aroma said. ‘There was already a hole in it. They say it was taken out of his mouth when he was born. Let me fetch it and you’ll see.’
Dai-yu stopped her at once. ‘No, never mind. It’s late now. Tomorrow will be soon enough.’
They talked a little longer, then at last went to bed.

segments.text: Next morning, after getting up and paying her respects to Grandmother Jia, Dai-yu went to Lady Wang’s apartments. Lady Wang and Xi-feng were together, opening letters from Jinling. Two married women servants had also been sent with a message from Lady Wang’s brother and his wife. Dai-yu knew nothing of the circumstances, but Tan-chun and the others knew that they were discussing Xue Pan, their maternal cousin, the son of Aunt Xue in Jinling. Relying on his wealth and influence, he had beaten a man to death, and the case was now before the Yingtian prefecture. Their uncle Wang Zi-teng had heard the news and sent members of his household to tell Lady Wang’s family, with the intention of having the Xues called to the capital.

segments.text: Now Dai-yu and the other girls went to Lady Wang’s rooms, where they found her discussing household business with a messenger from her brother and his wife. There was also talk of a homicide case involving the girls’ aunt’s family. Seeing how much Lady Wang had to attend to, they withdrew and went instead to the rooms of their widowed sister-in-law, Mrs Li.

segments.text: This Mrs Li was Jia Zhu’s wife. Though Zhu had died young, he had fortunately left a son, Jia Lan, now just five years old and already attending school. Mrs Li too came from a distinguished official family of Jinling. Her father, Li Shou-zhong, had been Chancellor of the Imperial Academy, and there was not a man or woman in the clan who did not study books and recite poetry. Once Li Shou-zhong became head of the family, however, he maintained that ‘A woman’s virtue lies in having no accomplishments.’ When his daughter was born, therefore, he did not have her taught very much. Three or four works, such as the Four Books for Women, the Lives of Exemplary Women and the Collected Lives of Worthy Ladies, would suffice: she need only learn to recognise a few characters and remember a few virtuous women of earlier dynasties. Spinning and weaving, drawing water and pounding grain were what mattered. Accordingly, he named her Li Wan and gave her the courtesy name Gong-cai.

Thus Li Wan, though widowed in the bloom of youth and living amid fine food and silks, was like dead wood and cold ashes. She took notice of nothing, heard nothing, and knew only the service of her elders and the upbringing of her son. Beyond these duties, she kept her young sisters-in-law company at their needlework and reading. Though Dai-yu was a guest beneath another’s roof, she now had these girls with her every day. Apart from her elderly father, there was nothing more she need trouble about.

segments.text: Let us turn for the moment to Yu-cun. He had been appointed to fill the vacant prefecture of Yingtian, and scarcely had he taken up his post when a report of a homicide came before him. Two families had tried to buy the same maid; neither would give way, and the quarrel had ended in a fatal beating. Yu-cun summoned the complainant for examination.

‘The man they beat to death was my master,’ the man said. ‘He bought a girl one day, never knowing she had been kidnapped and was being sold by her kidnapper. The fellow had already taken our money. Our young master said that the third day from then was an auspicious day, and he would wait till then to bring her home. But the kidnapper secretly sold her a second time, to the Xues. We found out and went to seize the seller and recover the girl. The Xues are one of the tyrants of Jinling. They used their power to intimidate us, and a gang of their brutal servants beat my young master to death. Both the murderer and his servants have fled without a trace. Only a few people who were not involved are left. I have been lodging complaints for a year, and no one will see justice done. I beg Your Honour to arrest the killers, root out these evil men and protect the widowed and the orphaned. The dead man’s gratitude for your boundless kindness would know no end!’

segments.text: Yu-cun flew into a rage.
‘What damned nonsense is this? Beat a man to death and simply walk away, never to be caught?’

He was about to issue a warrant ordering his runners to arrest members of the murderer’s clan at once and question them under torture until they revealed where he was hiding. A general warrant for his arrest would also be circulated. Just as he was going to issue the order, however, an usher standing beside the tribunal desk caught his eye and signalled to him not to do so. Greatly puzzled, Yu-cun stayed his hand. He dismissed the court and retired to a private room, where he sent all his attendants away except the usher.
The man hurried forward to pay his respects.
‘Your Honour has been rising in rank and growing richer all this time,’ he said with a smile. ‘Have eight or nine years been enough to make you forget me?’
‘Your face is certainly very familiar. I simply cannot place you for the moment.’
The usher smiled. ‘Great men do have short memories, sir! Have you forgotten the very place you started from? Can you not remember the Gourd Temple?’

Yu-cun started as though struck by thunder. Only then did it come back to him. This usher had been a little novice in the Gourd Temple. After the fire he had had nowhere to live. He had thought of entering another temple to continue his religious life, but could not bear its bleak austerity. An usher’s work, he thought, would be lighter and offer more company and bustle. So, while still young enough, he had grown his hair again and taken up the occupation.

segments.text: Yu-cun had never dreamed it could be he. He hastily took him by the hand and smiled.
‘An old friend, then!’
He invited him to sit down so that they could talk. The usher dared not accept.

‘One must never forget the friends of one’s poor days,’ Yu-cun said, smiling. ‘You and I are old friends. Besides, these are my private rooms. If we are to have a long talk, you cannot possibly remain standing.’
Only then did the usher thank him for the seat and perch sideways on its edge.

segments.text: Yu-cun asked why he had signalled to stop the warrant.
‘Now that Your Honour has received this distinguished appointment in our province,’ the usher said, ‘surely you have had a copy made of the provincial “Charm for Protecting Officials”?’
‘What is this “Charm for Protecting Officials”?’ Yu-cun asked at once. ‘I know nothing of it.’
‘That will never do!’ said the usher.

segments.text: ‘How can you expect to last in office if you do not even know that? Every local official nowadays keeps a private list of the great gentry families in his province, the richest, noblest and most powerful of them all. It is the same in every province. If you do not know who they are and happen to offend one of them, you may lose more than your rank. You may not even keep your life. That is why we call it the “Charm for Protecting Officials”. How could Your Honour touch the Xues we have just been speaking of? There is nothing difficult about the case itself. It has dragged on like this only because no one wants to offend their connections.’
As he spoke, he took a handwritten copy of the charm from his pouch and handed it to Yu-cun. It consisted of popular sayings about the great local clans and families of high officials.

segments.text: The sayings were neatly set out, each with notes below giving the rank and title of the family’s founding ancestor and the branches descended from him. The Stone once copied this list too. Here is what was written on it:

The Jias are no sham:
Their halls are white jade, their horses gold.

Three hundred li of Epang Palace
Cannot house the Shi clan of Jinling.

When the Eastern Sea lacks a white-jade bed,
The Dragon King comes to ask the Wangs of Jinling.

A splendid fall of snow for a year of plenty:
Pearls are dirt to them, and gold is iron.

Before Yu-cun had finished reading, the sound announcing a visitor was heard, and someone reported, ‘Mr Wang has come to call.’ Yu-cun hurriedly put on his formal robes and cap and went out to receive him. Not until the time it took to eat a meal had passed did he return to ask further questions.

‘These four families are all linked by marriage,’ the usher explained. ‘Harm one and you harm them all; when one prospers, they all prosper. They support one another, cover up for one another, and see that everything is looked after. The Xue accused of this killing is the “snow” in that line about the year of plenty. Nor does his family depend only on the other three. They have plenty of old family friends and relatives of their own, both in the capital and elsewhere. Whom is Your Honour going to arrest now?’
Hearing this, Yu-cun smiled and asked, ‘If that is so, how are we to settle the case?

segments.text: ‘I suppose you also know very well where the murderer is hiding?’

The usher smiled. ‘To tell Your Honour the truth, I know more than where the murderer is. I know the kidnapper too, and I knew the dead buyer very well indeed. Let me tell you the whole story. The fellow who was killed was a local minor landowner’s son called Feng Yuan. Both his parents died when he was a child, and he had no brothers. He lived alone on the little property they had left him. By the time he was eighteen or nineteen he was passionately fond of men and detested women. It must have been some unhappy debt from a former life: he happened to see this kidnapper offering the girl for sale and took a fancy to her at first sight. He made up his mind to buy her as a concubine and swore he would have no more dealings with men,

segments.text: ‘nor take another woman after her. That was why she was to enter his household three days later. Who could have known the kidnapper would secretly sell her again to the Xues? He meant to pocket both families’ money and escape to another province. But he failed to get away. Both families caught him and beat him within an inch of his life. Neither would take its money back; each insisted on having the girl. Young Master Xue was hardly one to yield. He shouted to his men to lay into them, and they beat young Feng to a pulp. Feng was carried home and died three days later. Now, this young Master Xue had already fixed the day for going up to the capital. He happened to come upon the girl two days before he was due to leave, and meant to buy her and take her with him. Then all this trouble broke out.

segments.text: ‘But leave that aside. Who do you suppose the girl being sold was, sir?’
‘How should I know?’ Yu-cun said with a smile.
The usher gave a cold laugh. ‘In a manner of speaking, sir, she is one of your great benefactors. She is the daughter of Mr Zhen, who lived beside the Gourd Temple. Her name is Ying-lian.’
Yu-cun was astonished. ‘So it was she! I heard that she was kidnapped when she was five. Has she only now been put up for sale?’

segments.text: ‘That sort of kidnapper specialises in stealing children of five or six,’ said the usher. ‘He keeps them somewhere out of the way until they are eleven or twelve, then takes them to another district and sells them according to their looks. We used to play with Ying-lian and amuse her every day. Seven or eight years have passed, and she must be twelve or thirteen now. She has grown much prettier, but her features are still much the same. Anyone who knew her would recognise her easily. Besides, she had a red birthmark the size of a grain of rice between her eyebrows. She was born with it. That was how I recognised her.

‘As it happened, the kidnapper had rented some rooms of mine. One day when he was out, I questioned her. But he had beaten her till she was terrified of him, and she dared not tell me a thing. She would only say that he was her own father, and was selling her because he had no money to pay his debts. I tried coaxing her again and again. Then she cried and said only, “I cannot remember when I was little!” That left me in no doubt.

‘The day young Feng came to look at her and paid over the silver, the kidnapper got drunk. She sighed to herself, “At last I must have paid for all my sins!” But when she heard that Feng had ordered her to be brought home three days later, she grew troubled again.

segments.text: ‘I could not bear to see her like that. When the kidnapper went out, I sent my wife to comfort her. “Young Master Feng insists on waiting for a lucky day to fetch you,” she told her. “That shows he does not mean to treat you as a maid. Besides, he is a very handsome, charming young man, and comfortably off. He has always hated women; yet now he is paying such a price for you. You can imagine what that means for your future. You have only two or three days to wait. Why be so unhappy?” That eased her mind a little, and she thought she had found a home at last.

‘Who could have dreamed things would turn out so badly? The very next day the man sold her again, to the Xues. It might have been all right if he had sold her to anyone else. But this young Master Xue, the one they call the “Stupid Tyrant”, is the most wilful, overbearing creature in the world, and spends money like dirt. So he had them thrashed to pieces and Ying-lian was dragged away by force. I do not even know whether she is alive or dead. Poor Feng had all that happiness for nothing. Before he could realise a single hope, he had lost both his money and his life. Is it not pitiful?’
Yu-cun sighed too. ‘Their burden of past sins had brought them to this unhappy pass. There was nothing accidental about it.

segments.text: ‘Otherwise, why should Feng Yuan have set his heart on Ying-lian of all people? After all those years of torment at the kidnapper’s hands, she had at last found a way out, with someone who loved her too. It would have been a happy thing if they could have come together. Instead, this had to happen.

segments.text: ‘The Xues may be richer and grander than the Fengs, but, from the sort of man he is, I imagine he has any number of concubines and indulges himself without restraint. He may be very far from Feng Yuan, who gave his heart to one woman only. A bond of love as fleeting as a dream, and two ill-fated young people brought together! But let us leave them. What I need to know is how best to decide this case.’

The usher smiled. ‘Your Honour used to be so clear-headed and decisive. How is it that you cannot make up your mind today? I hear it was through the Jia and Wang families that you obtained this new appointment. Xue Pan is a relative of the Jias. Why not go with the current, do them a thorough good turn and settle the case? Then you will have something to say when you next call on the Jias and the Wangs.’

‘There is much in what you say,’ Yu-cun replied. ‘But a man’s life is involved. His Majesty’s great kindness in reinstating me and entrusting me with office has given me a second life. This is the very time when I ought to devote every effort to repaying him. How can I set the law aside for private interests? I truly could not bring myself to do it.’
The usher gave a cold laugh. ‘Your Honour’s principles are excellent. Only they will not work in the world as it is today.

segments.text: Yu-cun kept his head lowered for a long time. At last he spoke.
‘What would you do?’

‘I have already thought of an excellent plan,’ the usher said. ‘When Your Honour takes your seat in court tomorrow, make a great show of authority. Issue documents and warrants for arrests. Naturally, the actual killer will not be found. The complainant is bound to insist that some of the Xue clansmen and servants be arrested and questioned under torture. I shall arrange things behind the scenes and have them report that Xue Pan has died of a sudden illness. His clansmen and the local people can jointly submit a written guarantee of the fact. Your Honour need only claim to be skilled at spirit-writing and summoning immortals. Have an altar set up in court, and invite soldiers and civilians alike to watch. Then announce: “The immortal has given his verdict through the writing-planchette. Feng Yuan and Xue Pan were brought together by a debt from a former life. Having met on a narrow path with no room to pass, they were bound to settle it. Xue Pan has now succumbed to a nameless illness. Pursued by Feng’s ghost, he has died. All the trouble was caused by a certain kidnapper, a man of such-and-such a name from such-and-such a place. He is to be dealt with according to law; no one else need be implicated.” Something of that sort. I shall privately instruct the kidnapper to make a confession agreeing with it.

segments.text: ‘Once people see that the immortal’s pronouncement agrees with the kidnapper’s confession, they will naturally believe the rest of it too. The Xues have money enough. Your Honour may order them to pay a thousand taels, or five hundred, towards the Feng family’s funeral expenses. There is no one of any consequence among the Fengs. All they want is money, and once they get it, I imagine they will have nothing more to say. What does Your Honour think of the plan?’
‘No, that will not do,’ Yu-cun said with a smile. ‘Let me think it over again. Perhaps there is a way to silence the talk.’

segments.text: It was already late by the time they had finished their discussion, and there is nothing more to tell of that evening. The next day Yu-cun took his seat in court and summoned all those named in the case. He examined them closely and found that, as he had been told, there were few people left in the Feng household, and they were merely using the case to obtain a larger sum for funeral expenses.

segments.text: The Xues, relying on their power and connections, had refused to yield, which was why the affair had been turned this way and that without a settlement. Yu-cun now bent the law to favour his patrons and disposed of the case in a muddle. The Fengs received a substantial sum for funeral expenses and had little more to say. As soon as he had decided the case, Yu-cun hurriedly wrote two letters, one to Jia Zheng and the other to Wang Zi-teng, Commander of the Metropolitan Garrison. They said little more than, ‘Your nephew’s affair has been settled. There is no need for further concern.’

The whole arrangement had originated with the former novice of the Gourd Temple, now an usher. Yu-cun, however, feared that he might tell people about his earlier days of poverty and low estate, and was deeply uneasy. In the end he found some fault with the man and had him sent far away into penal exile. Only then was he satisfied.

But we need say no more of Yu-cun for the present. Let us return to the young Master Xue who had bought Ying-lian and had Feng Yuan beaten to death. He too was a native of Jinling, born into a family with a tradition of scholarship. He had lost his father as a child, however, and his widowed mother, cherishing him as her only son, had spoilt and indulged him until he grew up good for nothing. The family possessed a fortune reckoned in millions, and currently received funds from the imperial privy treasury to purchase miscellaneous supplies.

segments.text: The young man’s formal name was Xue Pan, and his courtesy name Wen-long. Even at five he had been extravagant in his tastes and arrogant in his speech. He had attended school, but knew little more than a few characters, and spent his days at cockfights and horse races, or roaming the hills and enjoying the scenery. Though an imperial purveyor, he knew nothing at all of business or practical affairs. Old ties with his grandfather and father kept his name nominally on the Board of Revenue’s books and allowed him to draw the allotted funds. Everything else was attended to by the clerks and the old family servants.

segments.text: His widowed mother, née Wang, was a younger sister of Wang Zi-teng, the present Commander of the Metropolitan Garrison, and a sister by the same mother of Lady Wang, Jia Zheng’s wife at the Rong mansion. She was only about forty, and Xue Pan was her only son. She also had a daughter, two years younger than Xue Pan, whose childhood name was Bao-chai. The girl’s skin had a smooth, lustrous bloom, and her manner was composed and graceful. Her father had adored her and had her taught to read, and she was ten times the scholar her brother was. After her father’s death, seeing that her brother could do little to comfort their mother, she gave up making books her chief concern and turned instead to needlework and household affairs, hoping to ease her mother’s worries and spare her some labour.

Now the present sovereign, who honoured poetry and ritual and sought out talent, had recently bestowed an extraordinary favour. In addition to the selection of imperial consorts, the names of daughters from distinguished official families were all to be submitted to the appropriate board, so that some might be chosen as study companions for princesses of the imperial and princely houses, with appointments as Ladies of Talent and Ladies of Instruction. There was another consideration too. Since Xue Pan’s father had died, the managers and clerks of the family’s businesses and supply agencies in the provinces, seeing how young and inexperienced Xue Pan was, had seized the opportunity to cheat him. Several of the businesses in the capital were dwindling away as well.

segments.text: Xue Pan had long heard that the capital was the most splendid and prosperous place in the world, and had been thinking of going there. He took this opportunity to do so: first, to escort his sister there for the selection; second, to visit relatives; and third, to settle the old accounts in person at the Board and arrange for new advances. His real purpose was to see the sights of the imperial city.

He had accordingly packed his baggage and valuables well beforehand, together with local specialities and other gifts for relatives and friends. Just as an auspicious day had been chosen and his departure fixed, he happened to encounter the kidnapper selling Ying-lian a second time. Struck by her unusual beauty, he was determined to buy her. When the Fengs came to claim her, he relied on his superior strength and ordered his brutal servants to beat Feng Yuan to death. Then, having entrusted every detail of the household’s affairs to his clansmen and a few old servants, he set off on his long journey with his mother and sister. To him a homicide case was child’s play. He thought there was nothing that a little filthy money would not settle.

We need not count the days they spent on the road. As they were nearing the capital, they heard that his maternal uncle Wang Zi-teng had been promoted to Commander-in-Chief of Nine Provinces and ordered to leave the capital on an inspection of the frontiers.

segments.text: Xue Pan was secretly delighted.

‘I was just worrying that my own mother’s brother would be there to keep me in order,’ he thought, ‘and I would not be free to spend and enjoy myself as I pleased. Now he has been promoted and sent away! Heaven does give a man what he wants.’
He broached the matter with his mother.

‘We have several houses in the capital, but none of us has lived there for ten years or more. The caretakers are sure to have been letting them out on the quiet. We ought to send a few men ahead to clean up and put things in order.’

‘Why make such a fuss?’ his mother said. ‘The first thing we ought to do on reaching the capital is visit our relatives and friends. We can stay either with your uncle or with your aunt’s husband. Both houses have very convenient accommodation. Why not settle in at one of them first, and then have our own house put in order at leisure? It would be much less trouble.’

‘But my uncle has just been promoted to a post outside the capital. His household will be busy getting ready to leave. Surely it would be rather tactless for the whole lot of us to descend on them just now.’

segments.text: ‘Even if your uncle is moving away, there is still your aunt’s husband,’ his mother replied. ‘And for years now both your uncle’s and your aunt’s households have been sending letters and messages inviting us to come. Now that we are here, your uncle may be busy leaving, but your aunt at the Jias’ is sure to press us to stay. If we rush about getting our own house ready, will people not take offence? I know what you are thinking. Living with your uncle or your aunt’s husband would put a check on you. You would rather live on your own and do just as you please. Very well, then. Go and choose a house for yourself. Your aunt and I have not seen each other for years, and I want to spend a few days with her. I shall take your sister and stay at her house. How does that suit you?’
Xue Pan knew from this that he could not get his way. He had to tell the men to take them straight to the Rong mansion.

segments.text: Lady Wang had already heard how Jia Yu-cun had intervened to settle Xue Pan’s case, and her mind was now at ease. Then came the news of her brother’s promotion to a frontier post. She was feeling rather lonely at the thought that there would be one fewer member of her own family to see. A few days later a servant suddenly announced, ‘Your sister has brought the young master and young lady to the capital. The whole family is outside, getting out of the carriages.’

Delighted, Lady Wang hurried out to the main hall with the girls and daughters-in-law to welcome Aunt Xue and bring them in. The sisters were meeting again in their later years: there is no need to describe their mingled grief and joy, their tears and laughter as they spoke of their long separation. Lady Wang hastened to take them to pay their respects to Grandmother Jia, and the various presents and local specialities were offered. When everyone in the household had greeted them, a welcoming feast was quickly prepared.

segments.text: Xue Pan had already paid his respects to Jia Zheng, and Jia Lian took him to see Jia She, Jia Zhen and the others. Jia Zheng sent a message in to Lady Wang:

‘Your sister is getting on in years, and our nephew is young and knows nothing of the world. If they live outside, I fear someone may make trouble for them. There are a dozen rooms standing empty in Pear-tree Court, in the north-east corner of our grounds. It would be an excellent arrangement to have them cleaned and invite your sister and the two young people to stay there.’
Before Lady Wang could urge them to stay, Grandmother Jia too sent to say, ‘Ask your sister to make her home here, so that we can all be closer.’

Aunt Xue had wanted just such an arrangement, which would allow her to keep a tighter hold on her son. If they lived separately, she feared he would give his temper free rein and get into trouble again. She therefore thanked them warmly and accepted. In private, however, she made one point clear to Lady Wang:
‘You must leave all our daily expenses and provisions to us. That is the only way we can go on comfortably together.’
Lady Wang knew that her sister’s family could well afford them, and agreed. From then on Aunt Xue and her children lived in Pear-tree Court.

segments.text: Pear-tree Court had been the old Duke of Rong’s retreat in his later years. It was a neat little place of a dozen rooms or so, complete with a hall at the front and living quarters behind. A separate gate opened on to the street, and the Xue servants used it to come and go. In the south-west corner a side gate led into a narrow passage, which emerged on the east side of Lady Wang’s principal rooms. Every day, either after a meal or in the evening, Aunt Xue would come over to chat with Grandmother Jia or spend time with Lady Wang. Bao-chai passed her days with Dai-yu, Ying-chun and the other girls, reading, playing chess or doing needlework, and was very happy.

Xue Pan had originally been unwilling to live in the Jia household, fearing that his uncle would keep him in order and give him no freedom. But his mother was determined to stay, and the family pressed them so warmly that he had to remain for the time being. Meanwhile, he sent men to prepare one of his own houses, intending to move there later. Yet before he had been there a month he had become well acquainted with half the sons and nephews of the Jia clan. Every one of its idle young rakes was delighted to make his acquaintance. There was a drinking party today, an outing to see the flowers tomorrow; then came gambling parties and visits to prostitutes, until by degrees there was nothing they would not do. Under their influence Xue Pan grew ten times worse than before.

segments.text: Jia Zheng had sound methods of bringing up his sons and firm rules for his household. But in the first place, the clan was too large, with too many members, for him to supervise all this. In the second, its present head was Jia Zhen, the eldest grandson of the Ning branch, who had also inherited its rank. Clan affairs were his responsibility. Thirdly, Jia Zheng had more than enough public and private business to attend to, and was by nature a man of easy detachment who set little store by mundane affairs. In his hours away from official work he merely read or played chess, paying little attention to anything else. Moreover, Pear-tree Court was two ranges of buildings away and had its own street gate, through which anyone could come and go at will. The young men were therefore quite free to enjoy themselves as they pleased, and Xue Pan gradually abandoned all thought of moving out.

segments.text: Ever since her arrival at the Rong mansion, Grandmother Jia had lavished affection on her. In everything, from meals and sleeping arrangements to the ordering of her day, she was treated just like Bao-yu; the old lady’s own three granddaughters, Ying-chun, Tan-chun and Xi-chun, had to take second place. The closeness and affection between Bao-yu and Dai-yu were quite unlike their relations with anyone else. By day they went about together and sat together; at night they rested in the same quarters. In word and thought they were in perfect accord, with scarcely a moment’s estrangement. But now Xue Bao-chai had suddenly appeared. Although only a little older, she had a composed, upright manner and a full, lovely face, and many thought Dai-yu no match for her. Bao-chai was easygoing, accommodating herself to people and circumstances, unlike Dai-yu, who held herself proudly apart and disdained anything she thought beneath her. Consequently she was far more popular with the servants. Even the little maids generally preferred to go and play with Bao-chai. This left Dai-yu feeling somewhat depressed and resentful, though Bao-chai was entirely unaware of it. Bao-yu was still a child. Moreover, with the simple-minded, contrary nature he had been born with, he felt the same towards all his brothers, sisters and cousins, making no distinction between close relations and distant ones.

segments.text: regretting his own rash words, went to make peace with her. Only then did she gradually relent. The plum blossom was now at its height in the garden of the Ning mansion to the east, and Jia Zhen’s wife, You-shi, arranged a party for Grandmother Jia, Lady Xing, Lady Wang and the others to enjoy it. That day she brought Jia Rong’s wife with her to deliver the invitation in person. Grandmother Jia and her party went over after breakfast and amused themselves in the Garden of Gathered Fragrance, taking tea first and wine afterwards. It was merely a small family gathering of the women from the Ning and Rong households; there were no other novelties or amusing incidents to record. Presently Bao-yu grew tired and wanted his midday nap. Grandmother Jia told his attendants to coax him gently to sleep and bring him back when he had rested. Jia Rong’s wife, Qin-shi, promptly answered with a smile, ‘We have a room all ready for Uncle Bao. Don’t worry, Great-grandmother. Just leave him to me.’ Then she turned to his nurse and maids. ‘Mamma, sisters, please bring Uncle Bao this way with me.’ Grandmother Jia had always known Qin-shi to be thoroughly capable. Delicate and graceful in appearance, gentle and even-tempered in her dealings, she was the old lady’s favourite among her great-grandsons’ wives. With Qin-shi seeing to Bao-yu, she naturally felt quite at ease.

segments.text: Qin-shi led the whole party to an inner room in the main apartments. Bao-yu looked up and saw a picture mounted on the wall. The figures were beautifully painted, but its subject was The Burning Goosefoot Staff, and without even looking to see who the painter was, he began to feel displeased. Beside it hung a pair of scrolls: ‘A thorough knowledge of worldly affairs is learning; / A practised understanding of human dealings is literature.’ Once he had read those two lines, he would not stay, however exquisite the room and sumptuous its furnishings. ‘Let’s go out! Quickly!’ he cried. ‘If this won’t do, where can we go?’ Qin-shi said, laughing. ‘Unless you come to my room.’ Bao-yu nodded and smiled. ‘Who ever heard of an uncle sleeping in his nephew’s room?’ one of the old women objected. ‘Oh, dear me!’ Qin-shi laughed. ‘I hope he won’t be offended, but how old is he, that we should already worry about such things? Didn’t you see my brother when he came last month? He’s the same age as Uncle Bao, but put them side by side, and I rather think my brother would be the taller.’ ‘How is it I’ve never seen him?’ Bao-yu asked.

Bao-yu’s eyes grew heavy, his limbs relaxed, and he kept saying, ‘What a lovely scent!’

segments.text: On the table stood the precious mirror that had once furnished Wu Ze-tian’s mirror chamber. To one side was the golden platter on which Flying Swallow had danced; in it lay the quince An Lu-shan had thrown, bruising Tai-zhen’s breast. Further in stood the couch on which Princess Shou-chang had slept below the Hanzhang Hall, hung with the strung-pearl curtains Princess Tong-chang had had made. ‘This is lovely!’ Bao-yu said again and again, smiling. ‘I dare say even an immortal could live in this room of mine,’ Qin-shi said with a laugh. With her own hands she spread a gauze coverlet washed by Xi Shi and moved into place a lovers’ pillow once held by Hong-niang. The nurses settled Bao-yu in bed and gradually withdrew, leaving only the four maids Aroma, Winsome, Skybright and Musk to keep him company. Qin-shi told the little maids to keep a good watch under the eaves in case the cats and dogs started fighting.

segments.text: Bao-yu had scarcely closed his eyes before he drifted off to sleep. It still seemed that Qin-shi was before him, and he floated along behind her until they reached a place of red balustrades, white stone, green trees and clear streams, where human footsteps seldom came and no dust could reach. Delighted in his dream, he thought, ‘What an interesting place! I’d willingly spend my whole life here, even if it meant losing my home. segments.text:
She leaves the willow hollow, steps from her flowery bower.
Where she walks, birds start in the courtyard trees;
as she approaches, her shadow crosses the winding gallery.
Her immortal sleeves stir: musk and orchid breathe around her;
her lotus robe begins to move: her girdle pendants chime.
Her dimples smile like peach blossom in spring beneath cloud-dark coils of hair;
her lips part, red as cherries, her pomegranate-seed teeth hold fragrance.
Her slender waist turns like snow dancing in a circling wind;
pearls and kingfisher jewels gleam above a brow adorned with yellow.
Among the flowers, now hidden, now seen, she is lovely in anger or joy;
beside the pool she lingers, seeming to rise and fly.
Her moth-fine brows smile and frown; she is about to speak, but has not spoken.
Her lotus steps begin: she would pause, yet means to go.
Admire the beauty of her being: clear as ice, lustrous as jade;
admire her splendid robes, their patterns flashing bright.
Love her face, as though nurtured on fragrance and carved of jade;
praise her bearing, a phoenix soaring, a dragon in flight.
Her unadorned fairness? Spring plum blossom opening in snow.
Her purity? An autumn chrysanthemum mantled in frost.
Her stillness? A pine growing in an empty valley.
Her splendour? Rosy clouds reflected in a clear pool.
Her elegance? A dragon moving through a winding lake.
Her spirit? Moonlight striking a cold river.
Xi Shi must feel ashamed beside her, Wang Qiang abashed.
How wondrous! Where was she born, from what country does she come?
Indeed, the Jasper Pool has no second such beauty, the Purple Palace no equal.
Who can she be, so lovely as this?

segments.text: The immortal smiled. ‘I dwell above the Heaven of Parting Sorrow, amid the Sea of Grief. I am Fairy Disenchantment, of the Land of Illusion, in the Cave of Dispersed Fragrance on Mount of Released Spring. I oversee the debts of love and desire among mortals, and govern women’s resentments and men’s infatuations in the dusty world. Lately certain tangled debts of passion have become bound up with this place, so I have come to examine the opportunities and spread the longing of lovers. Our meeting today is no accident either. My domain is not far away. I have little to offer: just a cup of immortal tea I picked myself, a jar of fine wine of my own brewing, a few singing girls practised in enchanted dances, and twelve newly written immortal songs called Dream of the Red Chamber. Will you come and visit it with me?’ Hearing this, Bao-yu forgot all about where Qin-shi might be and followed the fairy. They reached a stone archway bearing the great inscription ‘LAND OF ILLUSION’. On either side was a couplet:

segments.text: ‘So that’s how it is,’ Bao-yu thought after reading it. ‘But what is this love through all the ages? What are these debts of love? From now on I must find out about them.’ He merely thought it to himself, little knowing that he had already invited evil influences into the deepest recesses of his being. Following the fairy through a second gateway, he came to the side halls. All had plaques and couplets, too many to read at once. He noticed only a few: ‘Office of Infatuation’, ‘Office of Accumulated Resentment’, ‘Office of Morning Tears’, ‘Office of Night-time Grievances’, ‘Office of Spring Longings’ and ‘Office of Autumn Sorrow’. Having read them, he asked the fairy, ‘Could I trouble you to show me round these different offices? Would that be allowed?’ ‘These offices hold the records of the past and future of every woman under heaven,’ she said. ‘With your mortal eyes and earthly body, you cannot be permitted to know them beforehand.’ Bao-yu would not take no for an answer, and begged her again and again.

segments.text: On a cupboard over to one side he saw a seal marked in large characters ‘MAIN REGISTER OF THE TWELVE BEAUTIES OF JINLING’. ‘What does “Main Register of the Twelve Beauties of Jinling” mean?’ he asked. ‘It records the twelve foremost women of your province,’ Disenchantment replied. ‘That is why it is called the Main Register.’ ‘People always say Jinling is enormous,’ said Bao-yu. ‘How can it have only twelve women? In our household alone, counting high and low, there are several hundred girls.’ Disenchantment gave a cold laugh. ‘There are indeed many women in your province. We have selected only those of consequence to enter here. Those in the two cupboards below rank next. As for the ordinary run of women, there are no registers for them.’ Looking at the two lower cupboards, Bao-yu saw that one was indeed labelled ‘SUPPLEMENTARY REGISTER OF THE TWELVE BEAUTIES OF JINLING’, and the other ‘SECOND SUPPLEMENTARY REGISTER OF THE TWELVE BEAUTIES OF JINLING’.

segments.text: Bao-yu wanted to read on, but the fairy knew how bright his natural gifts were, how quick his understanding, and feared that heaven’s secrets might be disclosed. She closed the volume and said with a smile, ‘Come and see the marvels with me. Why stay here puzzling over these riddles?’ In a haze, Bao-yu let the register go without quite knowing it and followed Disenchantment to the rear. There were pearl curtains, embroidered hangings, painted beams and carved eaves: words could not exhaust the light that played on crimson doors and floors of gold, or the snowy brilliance of jasper windows and palaces of jade. Immortal flowers and rare grasses filled the air with fragrance. It was a wonderful place indeed. Disenchantment called out, laughing, ‘Come quickly and welcome our honoured guest!’ Before she had finished, several immortals came out of the rooms, their lotus sleeves fluttering, their feather robes swaying, lovely as spring flowers and alluring as the autumn moon. The moment they saw Bao-yu, they reproached Disenchantment. ‘We wondered what “honoured guest” this could be, and hurried out to meet him! You said that at this very hour today our little sister Crimson Pearl’s living soul would come to visit, and we have been waiting for so long.

segments.text: ‘Why have you brought this filthy creature instead, to pollute our pure realm of girls?’ Hearing them, Bao-yu was so frightened that he wanted to retreat but could not, and truly felt himself unutterably unclean. Disenchantment quickly took his hand and said to her sisters, ‘You do not know the circumstances. Today I meant to go to the Rong mansion to fetch Crimson Pearl, but as I passed the Ning mansion I happened to meet the spirits of the Dukes of Ning and Rong. They charged me with this request: “Since our dynasty was established, our family has enjoyed distinction in generation after generation, passing wealth and honour down for a hundred years. But now our allotted fortune is spent, and nothing can turn it back. Though we have left many descendants, not one can carry on our work. Only Bao-yu, a grandson in the legitimate line, offers some hope. His disposition is perverse, his nature strange and unpredictable, but he is intelligent and quick-witted, and something might be made of him. Unfortunately our family’s term of fortune is due to end, and we fear there will be no one to guide him to the proper path. Since you have chanced to come, fairy, we beg you first to warn his stubborn, infatuated nature through matters of passion and desire, music and beauty. Perhaps he may break out of their beguiling circle and then enter the right way. That would be a blessing to us brothers.” Because they asked this of me, I took pity and brought him here.

segments.text: ‘First I let him study the lifelong records of the women of his household in all three ranks, upper, middle and lower, but still he did not awaken. So I have brought him here to experience further illusions of feasting, music and beauty. Who knows? Perhaps he will one day understand.’ With that, she led Bao-yu indoors. A thread of delicate scent reached him, but he had no idea what was burning, and could not help asking. Disenchantment gave a cold laugh. ‘How could you know it, when no such incense exists in the mortal world? It is made of the essence of rare flowers at their first budding in famous mountains and places of beauty, blended with oils from precious forests and jewelled trees. Its name is Marrow of All Flowers.’

segments.text: Bao-yu could only admire it. They all sat down, and little maids brought tea. He found its fresh fragrance and unfamiliar flavour extraordinarily pure and delicious, and asked its name as well. ‘This tea comes from the Cave of Dispersed Fragrance on Mount of Released Spring,’ said Disenchantment. ‘It is brewed with dew that has lain overnight on immortal flowers and numinous leaves. Its name is A Thousand Reds in One Cavern.’ Bao-yu nodded appreciatively. Looking round the room, he saw that nothing was lacking: a precious qin, fine incense tripods, old paintings and new poems. He was still more pleased to find bits of embroidery floss spat out beneath the window and occasional powder stains among the dressing boxes. A couplet hung on the wall:

segments.text: Bao-yu admired everything he read. He then asked the names of the immortals. One was the Fairy of Infatuated Dreams, another the Great Being of Devoted Love, another the Golden Maiden Who Draws Sorrow, and another the Bodhi of Passage beyond Grief. Each had a different religious name. Presently little maids came to arrange tables and chairs and lay out food and wine. Truly, precious nectar brimmed in glass goblets; rich jade liquor filled the amber cups.

segments.text: There is no need to dwell on the abundance of the dishes. Finding the wine unusually fragrant, sweet and clear, Bao-yu could not resist asking about it too. ‘This wine is brewed from the stamens of a hundred flowers and the sap of ten thousand trees,’ Disenchantment told him, ‘with a ferment of qilin marrow and a starter of phoenix milk. That is why it is called Ten Thousand Beauties in One Cup.’ Bao-yu could not praise it enough.

segments.text:
Since primal chaos first broke open,
who was born a creature of love?
It all springs from love’s passion for the moon and wind.
In this helpless heaven,
on this sorrowing day,
in this lonely hour,
let me try to give voice to my foolish heart.
And so we perform this Dream of the Red Chamber,
cherishing gold, mourning jade.

segments.text:
They all proclaim the happy match of gold and jade;
I think only of the former pledge of wood and stone.
In vain I face the mountain recluse’s glittering snow;
I cannot forget the lonely forest of that fairy beyond the world.
Alas, only now do I believe
that human happiness is never whole.
Even were the tray raised level with the brows,
still my heart would find no peace.

segments.text:
One is a flower of the immortal garden,
one a flawless piece of precious jade.
If no strange destiny unites them,
why have they met in this life?
If a strange destiny unites them,
why must their heart’s desire dissolve at last?
One sighs to no purpose;
one wastes all care in vain.
One is the moon in water,
one a flower in a mirror.
How many tears can there be in those eyes,
to endure the flow from autumn to winter’s end,
from spring into summer?

segments.text:
Joy in splendour just at its height;
resentment that impermanence has come again.
With open eyes, all things must be abandoned;
drifting, drifting, the fragrant soul is spent.
I look towards home: the road is long, the mountains high.
So I seek my parents in their dreams to tell them:
‘Your child’s life has entered the Yellow Springs.
My dear ones, step back and get free while there is time!’

segments.text:
In swaddling clothes, alas, both parents lost.
Even dwelling amid fine silks,
who knows the care that cherishes a child?
Fortunately, she was born open-hearted, bold and generous;
never did the private feelings of lovers entangle her heart.
She was like a moon after rain and a clear fresh wind,
shining through a hall of jade.
Matched with a handsome, gifted husband, fair as an immortal,
she won a union that would last as long as heaven and earth,
surely enough to make amends for childhood’s hardships.
Yet in the end the clouds disperse from Gaotang,
the Xiang River’s waters run dry.
Such are the destined ebb and flow of this dusty world.
Why grieve to no purpose?

segments.text:
Her nature lovely as an orchid,
her abundant gifts an immortal’s equal;
born solitary, unlike anyone else.
You call the eating of meat and fish rank,
and find silk finery vulgar and repellent.
Yet you do not know: the loftier you stand, the more they envy;
the purer you are, the more the world dislikes you.
Alas, she will grow old by a dim lamp in an ancient hall,
wasting the fading spring of a painted face in crimson chambers.
In the end there is still the grime of the dusty world,
against her heart’s desire.
As though flawless white jade were sunk in mud.
Why then should princes and young gentlemen
lament that no destined bond was theirs?

segments.text:
Wolf of Zhongshan, heartless beast,
forgetting entirely how it all began!
Nothing but arrogance, extravagance, lust and greed, and further scheming.
He regards that noble beauty as a common willow,
degrades a duke’s daughter as though she were the lowest of the low.
Alas for her lovely, fragrant soul,
drifting away within a year.

segments.text:
See through the three springs:
what then can red peach blossom and green willow do?
Extinguish the splendour of youth;
seek a heart free of passion, at peace with heaven.
What talk of peach trees blooming high in heaven,
of countless apricot stamens among the clouds!
In the end, who endures beyond autumn?
Look: among the white poplars, people sob;
beneath the green maples, ghosts chant.
And withered grass, stretching to the sky,
hides the graves.
Truly, poor yesterday, rich today, people toil;
flowers flourish in spring and fade in autumn, worn away.
Who can escape life’s barriers and death’s ordeals?
They say a precious tree in the West is called the Sala,
and on it grows the fruit of everlasting life.

segments.text:
Every device calculated, clever beyond measure,
she calculates away her own dear life.
Before death her heart is broken;
after death her spirit is empty and free.
A wealthy house, its people at peace:
still there comes the family’s ruin,
its members scattering, each to flee alone.
All for nothing, half a lifetime’s anxious heart,
like a dream adrift at the third watch.
A crash, as a great mansion falls;
a gathering darkness, as a lamp burns low.
Ah! All that joy, suddenly grief and bitterness.
Alas for this world: nothing can be settled!

segments.text:
Blessings left behind, blessings left behind:
a benefactor met by chance.
Fortunate in her mother, fortunate in her mother,
who stored up hidden merit!
Let all people take this counsel:
help the distressed, support the poor.
Do not be like my cruel uncle and treacherous elder cousin,
who love silver and forget their own flesh and blood!
Multiplication, division, addition, subtraction:
heaven above keeps the account.

segments.text:
Affection in a mirror,
and worse, distinction in a dream!
How swiftly lovely youth is gone.
Speak no more of embroidered curtains and lovers’ quilts.
Even wearing a pearl coronet
and a phoenix-patterned robe
cannot offset the impermanence of life.
Though they say none should suffer poverty in old age,
there is still a need to store hidden merit for one’s descendants.
Head held high beneath an official’s hat and tassels;
a golden seal hanging bright at the waist;
rank and stipend mounting in imposing splendour:
then darkness, and the road to the Yellow Springs draws near.
Where are the generals and ministers of old?
Only empty names remain for later people to admire.

segments.text:
Spring ends at the painted beam; fragrant dust falls.
Skilled in love, possessed of a moonlike face:
these become the roots of the family’s ruin.
The ancestral calling falls to pieces, all from Jing;
for the household’s destruction, Ning bears the first blame.
Old karmic wrongs always spring from passion.

segments.text: When they had finished, they were about to sing the supplementary songs. Seeing how little interest Bao-yu showed, Disenchantment sighed. ‘The foolish child still has not awakened!’ Bao-yu hastily stopped the singers from going on. Feeling dazed and confused, he pleaded drunkenness and asked to lie down. Disenchantment had the remains of the feast removed and took him to a fragrant, embroidered bedchamber, furnished with splendours such as he had never seen.

segments.text: Still more astonishing, a young woman was already inside. In the rich freshness of her beauty she resembled Bao-chai; in her graceful charm and slender bearing she was like Dai-yu. He had no idea what this meant. Suddenly Disenchantment spoke. ‘In so many wealthy, distinguished households in the mortal world, the moonlit pleasures behind green windows and the misty splendour of embroidered chambers have all been defiled by debauched young wastrels and loose women. More hateful still, how many frivolous libertines through the ages have excused themselves by saying, “I love beauty but am not lustful,” or pleaded, “I have passion, but not lust.” These are all words to dress up wrongdoing and conceal ugliness.

segments.text: ‘To love beauty is already lust; to know passion is greater lust still. The meetings on Mount Wu, the pleasures of cloud and rain, all come from delighting in someone’s beauty and then becoming attached to their affection. What I value in you is that you are the foremost creature of lust in all the world, ancient or modern.’

segments.text: Bao-yu was so alarmed that he answered hastily, ‘You are mistaken, fairy. My parents are always scolding me for being lazy about my books. How could I dare to incur the name of “lustful” as well? Besides, I’m still young. I don’t know what “lust” is.’ ‘No,’ said Disenchantment. ‘Though lust has one underlying principle, its meanings differ. Those who delight in lust in the ordinary world merely enjoy good looks, singing and dancing, endless flirting, lovemaking at every hour. They wish all the beauties in the world could serve their momentary pleasure. Such creatures are fools whose excess goes no deeper than the skin. You, however, were born with a strain of devoted feeling that we call “lust of the imagination”. This can be understood in the heart, but not passed on by mouth; grasped in spirit, but not conveyed in words. You alone now possess this quality. It can make you a good companion in the women’s quarters, but out in the world you will inevitably seem impractical and strange, mocked by every tongue, glared at by every eye. Having met your ancestors, the two Dukes of Ning and Rong, and heard their heartfelt entreaty, I cannot bear that you should bring distinction only to our world of women and be rejected by society. That is why I have brought you here: to intoxicate you with numinous wine, steep you in immortal tea, warn you through marvellous songs, and then give you my younger sister in marriage. Her childhood name is Jian-mei, “Beauty Combined”, and her courtesy name Ke-qing.

segments.text: ‘Tonight is auspicious; you may marry at once. You need only learn that even this immortal bedchamber in an illusory realm offers no more than this. How much less, then, can the mortal world offer? Henceforth you must free yourself from these entanglements, awaken from your former passions, attend to Confucius and Mencius, and devote yourself to the work of governing the world.’ She then privately instructed him in the business of cloud and rain, pushed him into the room, closed the door and went away.

segments.text: Still dazed, Bao-yu followed Disenchantment’s instructions, and the intimacies of lovers took their course, which cannot be fully recounted. By the next day he and Ke-qing were bound to each other in tender feeling and gentle words, unable to bear parting. As they went out hand in hand to amuse themselves, they suddenly came to a place overgrown with thorns and brambles, where wolves and tigers ran together. A black stream blocked their path, with no bridge across it. While they hesitated, Disenchantment came running up behind them. ‘Do not go any further! Turn back at once!’

segments.text: Bao-yu stopped hurriedly. ‘What is this place?’ ‘This is the Ford of Delusion,’ Disenchantment said. ‘It is ten thousand zhang deep and stretches a thousand li. No boat can cross it. There is only a wooden raft: Layman Wood steers it and Attendant Ash poles it. They accept no gold or silver in thanks, but ferry across only those with whom they have a destined bond.

segments.text: ‘You have happened to wander here today. If you were to fall in, you would gravely betray all the earnest warnings I gave you.’ Before she had finished, the waters of the Ford of Delusion thundered, and a host of yakshas and sea-demons came to drag Bao-yu down. Sweat poured off him like rain; in terror he cried out, ‘Ke-qing, save me!’ Alarmed, Aroma and the other maids hurried to hold him. ‘Don’t be afraid, Bao-yu! We’re here!’

segments.text: Now Qin-shi, hearing Bao-yu call her childhood name in his dream, was naturally puzzled, but could hardly question him closely. Bao-yu himself was dazed, as though something had slipped away from him. The others hurried to bring him some longan soup. After sipping two mouthfuls, he got up to straighten his clothes. As Aroma reached to tie his trouser-sash, her hand happened to brush his thigh and felt a patch of cold dampness. Startled, she snatched it away and asked what had happened. Bao-yu flushed scarlet and gave her hand a squeeze.

segments.text: She finished putting his clothes in order, and they went to Grandmother Jia’s. After a hasty supper he came back to his own rooms. When the wet nurses and other maids were out of the way, Aroma hastily fetched him a fresh undergarment and helped him change.
‘Dear sister,’ Bao-yu pleaded, blushing, ‘whatever you do, don’t tell anyone.’

segments.text: ‘Where did all that dirty stuff come from?’
‘It’s a long story,’ Bao-yu said.

He told Aroma his dream in detail. When he came to the love of cloud and rain that Disenchantment had taught him, she hid her face and bent double, laughing with embarrassment. Bao-yu had always been fond of Aroma’s gentle, winning ways and her pretty looks, and now pressed her to join him in what Disenchantment had taught. Aroma had long known that Grandmother Jia had given her to Bao-yu, and felt that even now this would not be a breach of propriety. So they secretly tried it together; fortunately no one came upon them. From then on Bao-yu treated Aroma differently from all the others, and she served him with still greater devotion. For the moment there is nothing more to tell of them.

Taking the Rong household as a whole, there were not so very many people: three or four hundred, from highest to lowest. Nor were there so very many affairs: ten or twenty a day. Yet they were as tangled as a skein of hemp, with no end to catch hold of and draw into order.

segments.text: Just as we were wondering which affair and which person would make the best beginning, there happened to come, from a thousand li away, a tiny household, insignificant as a mustard seed or a bean. Through a slight connection with the Rong family, members of it were on their way to the mansion that very day. This little household will therefore give us a thread to follow.

What was their surname? Who were they, and what connection did they have with the Rong mansion? If you gentlemen find such things petty and vulgar, put this book down at once and seek a better one to refresh your eyes. But if you think they may pass an idle hour, let this blockhead tell you all about them.

segments.text: The little household just mentioned belonged to the Wang family, natives of the district. An ancestor had held a very minor post in the capital and had known Lady Wang’s father, Xi-feng’s grandfather. Coveting the influence and advantages of that family, he had claimed kinship through their shared surname and acknowledged himself a nephew. At the time, only Lady Wang and her eldest brother, Xi-feng’s father, had been living in the capital, so they alone knew of this branch of nominal relations; the others knew nothing of it. That ancestor was now dead. His only son, Wang Cheng, had seen the family fortunes decline and moved out of the city to their old village. Wang Cheng too had recently died of illness, leaving only his son, known by the childhood name Gou-er. Gou-er in turn had a son, called Ban-er, and his lawful wife, née Liu, had also borne him a daughter, Qing-er. This family of four still lived by farming. As Gou-er did other work during the day to earn a living, and his wife was busy drawing water, grinding grain and doing the housework, no one was left to look after the two siblings, Qing-er and Ban-er. Gou-er therefore brought his mother-in-law, Grannie Liu, to live with them. She was an old woman who had been widowed for many years, with no children at her side, subsisting on two mu of poor land.

segments.text: Naturally she was glad to have her son-in-law take her in and support her, and she devoted herself to helping him and her daughter get by. It was the end of autumn, the beginning of winter. The weather was turning cold, and nothing had yet been got ready for the season. Gou-er could not help worrying. After a few cups of wine drunk to drown his troubles, he began finding things to rage about at home. His wife dared not answer back. Grannie Liu could bear it no longer.

‘Son-in-law,’ she said, ‘don’t be cross with me for speaking out. We country people live honestly, don’t we? We eat as much rice as our bowl will hold. When you were little, you had your old father to thank for easy eating and drinking, and now you can’t keep yourself in hand. When you have money, you think of today and never tomorrow; when it’s gone, you fly into a temper. Is that how a grown man behaves? We may live outside the city, but we’re still at the Son of Heaven’s feet. There’s money everywhere in Chang’an, only nobody knows how to pick it up. Jumping up and down at home won’t do any good.’
‘All you can do is talk nonsense from the kang!’ Gou-er burst out. ‘Do you want me to rob people or steal?’
‘Who’s telling you to steal?

segments.text: ‘That’s not necessarily so,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘We make the plans; Heaven decides whether they work. Once we’ve done our part, who knows? With the Bodhisattva’s blessing, a chance may come. In fact, I’ve thought of one for you. Your family used to claim kinship with the Wangs of Jinling. Twenty years ago they treated you well enough. It’s only because you’ve been so stiff-necked, refusing to go near them, that you’ve drifted apart. Your wife and I went there once, back then. The second daughter was a lively, open-handed girl, knew how to treat people and never put on airs. She’s now the wife of the Second Master Jia at the Rong mansion. I hear that as she’s grown older she’s become still kinder to the poor and the old. She loves feeding Buddhist monks, honouring Taoist priests, giving out rice and money. The Wang family may have gone off to a frontier appointment on promotion, but I dare say that married daughter would still remember us. Why don’t you pay her a visit? She may remember old times and do something for us. If she takes it into her head to be kind, a single hair plucked from her body would be thicker than our waists.’
His wife put in, ‘What you say is true, Mother, but how could people like you and me show our faces at her door?

segments.text: ‘To begin with, the gatekeepers might not even take in a message. We’d only go there to be snubbed and make fools of ourselves.’
Gou-er, however, cared more for advancement and gain than anything else, and the suggestion had begun to stir him. Hearing his wife’s objection, he smiled.
‘Since you say so, Grannie, and you’ve met the lady once before, why don’t you go yourself tomorrow and see which way the wind blows?’
‘Good heavens!’ said Grannie Liu. ‘There’s a saying: “A great lord’s gate is as deep as the sea.” What sort of creature am I? The people there don’t know me. I’d be going for nothing.’

‘Never mind,’ Gou-er said, smiling. ‘I’ll tell you how to manage it. Take your grandson Ban-er, and ask first for Zhou Rui, the servant she brought with her from her own family when she married. If you see him, you may get somewhere. Zhou Rui and my father once had a piece of business together. We’re on very good terms.’
‘I know him too,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘But it’s been so long since we saw anything of him. Who knows how he is now?

segments.text: ‘Well, there’s no help for it. You’re a man, and with that face of yours you plainly can’t go. My daughter’s a young married woman, and she can hardly go showing herself about. I’d better risk this old face of mine and try. If anything good comes of it, we’ll all benefit. And even if I bring back no money, I’ll have seen something of the world inside a duke’s or a marquis’s gates. My life won’t have been wasted.’
They all laughed at this, and that evening settled what was to be done.

segments.text: Next day Grannie Liu rose before dawn to wash and comb her hair, and gave Ban-er a few instructions. The child was only five or six and understood nothing of it. Delighted to hear that his grandmother was taking him into town for an outing, he agreed to everything. She led him into the city and found her way to Ning-Rong Street. Before the stone lions at the Rong mansion’s main gate she saw such a crowd of sedan-chairs and horses that she dared go no further. She brushed down her clothes, gave Ban-er a few more instructions, then edged towards a side gate. Several men sat on a long bench, chests thrust out and bellies prominent, gesticulating as they talked of this and that. Grannie Liu had to sidle up to them.
‘Blessings upon you, masters.’
They looked her over for a while, then asked, ‘Where are you from?’
‘I’m looking for Master Zhou, Zhou Rui, Her Ladyship’s family servant,’ she said with an ingratiating smile. ‘Would one of you masters be so kind as to ask him to come out?’
