segments.text: They paid no attention. At length one said, ‘Go and wait over there by the corner of the wall. Someone from his household will be coming out presently.’

An older man among them said, ‘Don’t hold her up. Why make sport of her?’ He turned to Grannie Liu. ‘Master Zhou has gone south. His home’s in the row at the back, and his wife’s in. If you want her, go round this way to the street behind and ask at the back gate.’

segments.text: Grannie Liu thanked him and led Ban-er round to the back gate. Hawkers had set down their carrying-poles outside, some selling food, others toys. Twenty or thirty children were romping about in a noisy crowd. Grannie Liu caught hold of one.
‘Let me ask you, young fellow: is Mrs Zhou at home?’
‘Which Mrs Zhou?’ the children asked.

segments.text: Hearing this, Zhou Rui’s wife hurried out.
‘Who is it?’
Grannie Liu stepped forward. ‘How are you, Sister Zhou?’
Zhou Rui’s wife stared for a while before recognising her, then smiled.
‘Grannie Liu! How are you? Tell me, how many years has it been? I’ve quite forgotten. Come in and sit down.’
‘An important person like you has so much to remember,’ Grannie Liu said, smiling as she went in. ‘How could you remember us?’
Inside, Zhou Rui’s wife told a young maid she employed to pour tea.
‘How you’ve grown!’ she said to Ban-er.
After asking about various things that had happened since they last met, she turned to Grannie Liu.
‘Were you passing today, or have you come specially?’
‘I came specially to see you, Sister, and to pay my respects to Her Ladyship as well. If you could take me to see her, so much the better. If not, I’ll rely on you to pass on my respects.’
Zhou Rui’s wife had already guessed something of her purpose.

segments.text: ‘Strictly speaking, receiving visitors and announcing them is nothing to do with me. Everyone here has a particular job. My husband only looks after the rents in spring and autumn. At other times all he has to do is go out with the young masters. My job is to attend the ladies when they go out. But since you’re a relation of Her Ladyship’s, and you’ve thought enough of me to come to me for help, I’ll make an exception and take in a message for you. There’s just one thing you don’t know, Grannie. This place isn’t what it was five years ago. Her Ladyship hardly attends to business now. Mrs Lian manages the household. Do you know who Mrs Lian is? Her Ladyship’s own niece, the daughter of her eldest brother, the one they used to call Feng.’

segments.text: ‘So it’s her!’ Grannie Liu exclaimed in surprise. ‘Well, no wonder. I said in those days she was a fine girl. Then I’ll get to see her today as well?’

‘Of course,’ said Zhou Rui’s wife. ‘Her Ladyship has so much to trouble her now that she passes on any visitor she can, and Miss Feng sees to them all. Even if you don’t see Her Ladyship today, you must see her, or your journey will have been wasted.’
‘Blessed Buddha! I’m entirely in your hands, Sister.’
‘Don’t say that. As the saying goes, “Make things easy for others and you make them easy for yourself.” It only costs me a word. What harm can it do me?’
She sent the young maid to the front hall to find out quietly whether the meal had been laid in Grandmother Jia’s rooms. The girl went off, and the two women talked of other things.

segments.text: ‘Miss Feng can’t be more than twenty this year,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘To be so capable, and manage a household like this! That’s something you don’t often see.’

‘Oh, Grannie, I couldn’t begin to tell you!’ said Zhou Rui’s wife. ‘Young as she is, she can outdo anyone in the way she handles things. She’s grown into a real beauty, and has ten thousand little ways about her, at the very least. As for arguing, ten clever-tongued men couldn’t get the better of her. You’ll believe me when you see her. There’s only one thing: she’s rather too hard on the servants.’

segments.text: As they talked, the young maid returned.
‘The meal has been served in Her Old Ladyship’s rooms. Mrs Lian is with Her Ladyship.’
Zhou Rui’s wife got up at once and urged Grannie Liu to hurry.

‘Quick, quick! When she comes back to have her own meal, there’ll be a moment free. Let’s get there first. If we’re late, people will be coming to report on business and it’ll be hard to get a word in. Then she’ll have her nap, and there’ll be no time at all.’
They climbed down from the kang, brushed their clothes, gave Ban-er a few more instructions and followed Zhou Rui’s wife by a winding route towards Jia Lian’s quarters.

segments.text: At the front hall Zhou Rui’s wife settled Grannie Liu to wait a little, then went past the screen wall and through the courtyard gate herself. Finding that Xi-feng had not yet returned, she first sought out Patience, one of Xi-feng’s trusted senior chamber-maids, who also shared her master’s bed. Zhou Rui’s wife explained who Grannie Liu was and how she came to be there.

‘She’s come all this way today specially to pay her respects. Her Ladyship used to see her often, so we really couldn’t refuse to see her today. That’s why I’ve brought her in. When the mistress comes back, I’ll explain it all. I don’t think she’ll blame me for taking too much on myself.’
Patience made the decision.
‘Bring them in. They can sit here for the time being.’

segments.text: Only then did Zhou Rui’s wife go out and bring the two of them into the courtyard. They mounted the steps of the main rooms, and a young maid lifted a scarlet felt curtain. As soon as they entered the central room, a wave of fragrance struck Grannie Liu’s face. She could not tell what scent it was and felt as though she were floating among clouds. Everything in the room glittered and shone, dazzling her eyes and making her head swim. All she could do was nod, click her tongue and invoke the Buddha.

They went into the room on the east, where Jia Lian’s little daughter, Da-jie, slept. Patience stood by the edge of the kang, looked Grannie Liu over once or twice, then greeted her and offered her a seat. Seeing Patience dressed from head to foot in fine silks, wearing gold and silver, with a face as lovely as flowers and jade, Grannie Liu took her for Xi-feng. She was just about to address her as ‘Madam’ when she heard Zhou Rui’s wife call her ‘Miss Patience’, and Patience in turn address the other woman as ‘Mrs Zhou’. Only then did she realise that this was merely a maid of some standing. Grannie Liu and Ban-er were invited up on to the kang; Patience and Zhou Rui’s wife sat facing each other on its edge. A young maid poured tea for them.

segments.text: Grannie Liu heard a steady clack-clack, very like the sound of someone working a flour-sifting chest, and could not help looking this way and that. Suddenly she noticed a box hanging on a pillar in the central room. Beneath it hung something like a weight from a pair of scales, swinging ceaselessly to and fro.
‘What a curious thing!’ she thought. ‘Whatever is it for?’
As she stared, there came a clang like a metal bell or a bronze chime. Taken unawares, she blinked in fright. Eight or nine more strokes followed in quick succession.

Zhou Rui’s wife and Patience rose hurriedly.
‘Just wait here,’ they told Grannie Liu. ‘We’ll come and fetch you when it’s time.’
With that they went out to meet her.

segments.text: Grannie Liu waited without a sound, her head tilted to listen. Laughter came from a distance, and some ten or twenty women, their clothes and skirts rustling, gradually entered the central room and went into the room on the other side. Two or three more women came into the room where she sat, carrying large lacquered food-boxes, and waited. From the other side came the command, ‘Serve the meal.’ Little by little the crowd withdrew, leaving only the few who were serving the dishes.

After a long spell of utter silence, two people appeared carrying a low kang-table and set it on the kang beside her. It was thickly covered with bowls and dishes still full of fish and meat; only a few had been touched. Ban-er clamoured for meat as soon as he saw it, and Grannie Liu slapped him away. Just then Zhou Rui’s wife came over, all smiles, and beckoned to her. Understanding the signal, Grannie Liu brought Ban-er down from the kang and into the central room. Zhou Rui’s wife whispered to her for a little while before taking her into the other room.

segments.text: A soft scarlet curtain scattered with flowers hung at the doorway from chased copper hooks. Beneath the south window stood a kang spread with a strip of scarlet felt. Against the wooden partition on the east were a backrest of chain-patterned brocade and a bolster. A large seat-cushion was covered in satin shimmering gold and green; beside it stood a carved-lacquer spittoon.

Xi-feng was dressed informally in a Zhaojun hood of autumn sable, encircled by a band of clustered pearls. She wore a peach-red jacket scattered with flowers, a dark-blue silk-tapestry cloak lined with grey squirrel, and a scarlet foreign-crêpe skirt lined with ermine. Bright with powder and rouge, she sat perfectly upright, stirring the ashes in her hand-warmer with a little pair of copper tongs. Patience stood at the edge of the kang holding a small tea tray decorated with filled-in lacquer, with a little covered teacup on it. Xi-feng neither took the tea nor raised her head, but went on stirring the ashes.
‘Why haven’t they been asked in yet?’ she said slowly.
As she spoke, she lifted herself to take the tea and saw that Zhou Rui’s wife had already brought two people in. They were standing on the floor before her.

segments.text: She at once made as if to rise but, before actually doing so, greeted them with a face all smiles and reproached Zhou Rui’s wife for not telling her sooner. Grannie Liu had already bowed several times from where she stood.
‘My respects to you, Madam.’

‘Sister Zhou, quick, help her up. No more bowing,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Please sit down. I’m young and don’t know all our relations. I’m not sure which generation you belong to, so I daren’t venture on a form of address.’
‘This is the grannie I was telling you about,’ Zhou Rui’s wife hastened to explain.
Xi-feng nodded. Grannie Liu was now sitting on the edge of the kang, with Ban-er hiding behind her. No amount of coaxing could persuade him to come out and bow.

segments.text: ‘When relations seldom visit, they drift apart,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘Those who know the circumstances say you’ve taken a dislike to us and won’t come. But spiteful people who don’t know may think we look down on everyone.’
Grannie Liu hurried to invoke the Buddha.
‘We’re badly off. We can’t afford to make visits. If we came here, we’d only bring shame on you, Madam. Even your stewards would think we looked out of place.’

‘That’s a dreadful thing to say,’ Xi-feng replied, smiling. ‘We only live on our grandfather’s empty reputation and a poorly paid official post. What has any of us got? Just an empty shell left over from the old days. As the saying goes, “Even the imperial court has three branches of poor relations.” How much more must you and I?’
She asked Zhou Rui’s wife whether she had informed Lady Wang.
‘I was waiting for your instructions, ma’am.’

segments.text: ‘Go and see. If she has someone with her on business, leave it. If she’s free, tell her and see what she says.’

Zhou Rui’s wife assented and went. Xi-feng had someone bring a handful of fruit for Ban-er, and had just begun to ask a few casual questions when a number of married women servants with household duties arrived to report on business. Patience announced them.
‘I have a visitor,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Let them come back this evening. If anything is very urgent, bring them in and I’ll deal with it now.’
Patience went out and presently returned.
‘I’ve asked them all. There was nothing urgent, so I sent them away.’
Xi-feng nodded. Zhou Rui’s wife came back and addressed her.

‘Her Ladyship says she has no time today. If you keep them company, ma’am, it will be just the same. She thanks them for thinking of her. If they’ve simply come for a visit, very well. If there’s anything they want to say, they should tell you. It will be just the same.’
‘There’s nothing particular to say,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘We only came to see Her Ladyship and you, Madam, as relations ought.’
‘If there’s nothing, very well,’ said Zhou Rui’s wife. ‘But if there is, you need only tell Mrs Lian. It’s the same as telling Her Ladyship.’

segments.text: As she spoke, Zhou Rui’s wife gave Grannie Liu a meaningful look. Grannie Liu understood. Her face flushed before she could speak. She wanted to say nothing, but then what had she come for today? She could only swallow her shame.
‘By rights, Madam, I shouldn’t speak of it on our very first meeting. But I’ve come such a long way to see you that I can hardly leave it unsaid.’
She had got no further when the pages at the inner gate announced, ‘The young master from the Ning mansion is coming in.’
‘No need to say any more,’ Xi-feng broke in hastily. Then she asked, ‘Where is Master Rong?’

Booted footsteps sounded all the way in, and a young man of seventeen or eighteen entered. He had delicate, handsome features and a fine figure, and wore light furs, a jewelled belt, splendid clothes and an ornate cap. Grannie Liu did not know whether to sit or stand, and there was nowhere to hide.
‘Stay where you are,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘This is my nephew.’
Only then did Grannie Liu settle awkwardly on the edge of the kang.

segments.text: Jia Rong said with a smile, ‘Father sent me to ask a favour, Aunt. You know that glass screen for the kang your uncle’s wife gave you last time? We’re entertaining an important visitor tomorrow. Could we borrow it to set out for the occasion? We’ll send it straight back.’
‘You’re a day too late,’ Xi-feng said. ‘I gave it away yesterday.’
Jia Rong grinned and, kneeling on one knee on the edge of the kang, pleaded with her.
‘If you won’t lend it, Aunt, he’ll say again that I don’t know how to ask properly, and I’ll get another good beating. Have pity on your nephew!’
‘As though everything from our Wang family had to be better than anyone else’s!’ Xi-feng said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘You have just the same things at home. You’re never content once you’ve seen mine.’
‘Nothing there is as good as this,’ Jia Rong said with a smile. ‘Do be merciful!’
‘If you so much as chip it, look out for your skin!’
She told Patience to get the key to the upstairs rooms and send a few reliable people to carry it over. Jia Rong’s whole face lit up.
‘I’ll take the men myself. I won’t let them knock it about.’
He got up and went out.

Jia Rong hurried back and stood with his hands at his sides, waiting for her instructions.

segments.text: Xi-feng merely went on sipping her tea, lost in thought for a long while. Then she smiled.
‘Never mind. Off you go. Come after supper, and we’ll talk then. I have someone here now, and I haven’t the energy.’
Jia Rong assented and slowly withdrew.
Only now did Grannie Liu recover her composure and begin again.

‘I’ve brought your nephew today for nothing else but this: his father and mother at home haven’t even anything to eat. And now it’s turned cold. However much we think, we can see no way out. So I had to bring your nephew and come to you.’
She nudged Ban-er.
‘What did your dad tell you at home? What did he send us here for? All you think about is eating fruit.’
Xi-feng had long since understood. Hearing how poorly she put it, she stopped her with a smile.
‘There’s no need to say more. I understand.’

segments.text: Presently Zhou Rui’s wife had a meal for the visitors laid in the room on the east and came to take Grannie Liu and Ban-er in to eat.
‘Sister Zhou, see that they have plenty,’ Xi-feng said. ‘I can’t join them.’
They went into the east room. Xi-feng called Zhou Rui’s wife back and asked what Lady Wang had said when she reported to her.

‘Her Ladyship said they weren’t really of the same family. They only happened to share a surname, and their old gentleman had held office alongside her father in those days, so they’d casually claimed kinship. They haven’t visited much these last few years. When they came that time, though, they were not sent away empty-handed. It’s kind of them to come and see us today, and we mustn’t slight them. If there’s anything they want to say, you’re to decide what’s best, ma’am.’
‘That explains it,’ said Xi-feng. ‘I wondered how they could be relations without my having the faintest idea who they were.’

segments.text: ‘As relations, we really ought to have looked after you without waiting for you to come to our door. But there are so many things to attend to in this household, and Her Ladyship is getting on. It’s quite possible for something to slip her mind. As for me, I’ve only lately taken over some of the business, and I didn’t even know we had these relations. Besides, for all the grand show we make outside, a large household has difficulties of its own. People might not believe it if we told them. Still, you’ve come such a long way today, and it’s the first time you’ve asked me for anything. How could I let you go back empty-handed? It so happens that yesterday Her Ladyship gave me twenty taels of silver for clothes for my maids. I haven’t touched it yet. If you don’t think it too little, take that for the time being.’

When Grannie Liu first heard her speak of difficulties, she thought nothing was coming and her heart began to thump. Then she heard that she was to have twenty taels, and joy set her itching all over.
‘Ah, I know what difficulties are. But as they say, “Even a camel starved to death is bigger than a horse.” Whatever happens, a single hair plucked from your body is thicker than our waists!’
Finding her language coarse, Zhou Rui’s wife kept signalling with her eyes for her to stop.

segments.text: ‘Don’t be offended by what I say, but even if he were her own nephew, you ought to have put it more gently. Master Rong is her proper nephew. Where did this other nephew spring from?’
‘Oh, Sister,’ Grannie Liu said, laughing, ‘I liked her so much the moment I saw her, I couldn’t find the words.’

Talking together, they went back to Zhou Rui’s home and sat for a little while. Grannie Liu wanted to leave a piece of silver for the children to buy fruit. segments.text: After seeing Grannie Liu off, Zhou Rui’s wife went to report to Lady Wang. But Lady Wang was not in her principal rooms. On asking the maids, she learnt that Her Ladyship had gone to chat with Aunt Xue. She accordingly went out through the eastern side gate, crossed into the eastern courtyard and made her way to Pear-tree Court. Just outside its gate she saw Lady Wang’s maid Golden playing on the sloping approach to the steps with a little girl whose hair had only lately been allowed to grow. Seeing Zhou Rui’s wife, they knew she had something to report, and gestured towards the room with their lips. She lifted the curtain softly and went in. Lady Wang and Aunt Xue were deep in a long conversation about household affairs and their dealings with relatives and friends.

segments.text: Not daring to interrupt, Zhou Rui’s wife went into the inner room. There sat Xue Bao-chai in her everyday clothes, her hair loosely coiled in a simple bun. She was sitting towards the inner end of the kang, leaning over its little table to trace embroidery patterns with her maid Oriole. At the sight of her visitor Bao-chai put down her brush and turned, her face all smiles. ‘Do sit down, Sister Zhou.’
Zhou Rui’s wife hastened to smile back. ‘Are you well, miss?’

segments.text: She sat down on the edge of the kang. ‘We haven’t seen you over our way for two or three days. Surely your cousin Bao hasn’t offended you?’
‘Of course not,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘It’s only that my old complaint has come back. I haven’t been out of my room these last two days.’

‘Ah, yes. But what is it that keeps troubling you, miss? You ought to have a doctor as soon as possible, get a proper prescription and take a few doses faithfully, to clear it up once and for all. It’s no laughing matter to have a chronic illness at your age.’

Bao-chai smiled. ‘Please don’t speak of medicine! I don’t know how much money we’ve thrown away on doctors and remedies for this complaint. The most famous doctors and the most miraculous medicines never did the slightest good. In the end it was a bald monk who helped. He said he specialised in nameless complaints, so we asked him to examine me. He said I had a heat-toxin that I’d brought with me from the womb. Luckily, my constitution was strong to begin with, so it wasn’t doing any harm.

segments.text: ‘Ordinary medicines would be no use. He told us a rare prescription and gave us a packet of medicinal powder to activate it, with the most extraordinary fragrance. I don’t know where he got it. He said one pill when the trouble came on would put it right. Strange to say, his medicine really has done me some good.’
‘What sort of rare prescription is it?’ asked Zhou Rui’s wife. ‘Tell us, miss, so that we can remember it and pass it on. If we ever meet anyone with the same illness, it would be a good deed.’

Bao-chai smiled at the question. ‘You’d be better off without it. If you tried to use it, the fuss and bother would be the death of you. The ingredients themselves are nothing very special. The difficulty is getting everything to happen just right. You need twelve taels of stamens from white peonies that flower in spring, twelve taels from white lotuses that flower in summer, twelve taels from white hibiscus in autumn and twelve taels from white plum blossom in winter. On the day of the Spring Equinox the following year you dry these four kinds of stamens in the sun, mix them with the medicinal powder and grind the whole lot together.

segments.text: ‘Then you need twelve qian of rainwater that falls on the day of Rain Water…’
‘Good gracious!’ Zhou Rui’s wife broke in. ‘By that reckoning it would take three years! And suppose it didn’t rain at all on Rain Water day? What would you do then?’

‘That’s just what I mean,’ Bao-chai said, smiling. ‘Where are you to find rain that comes so conveniently? If it doesn’t rain, you can only go on waiting. Then twelve qian of dew from the day of White Dew, twelve qian of frost from the day of Frost’s Descent and twelve qian of snow from the day of Lesser Snow. Blend those four waters thoroughly and mix in the medicine. Add twelve qian of honey and twelve qian of white sugar, make it into pills the size of longans and put them in an old porcelain jar, which you bury under the roots of a flowering plant. When the illness comes on, take out one pill and swallow it with a decoction of twelve fen of phellodendron bark.’
Zhou Rui’s wife laughed. ‘Merciful Buddha! What a torment! You might wait ten years and still not have everything happen just so.’
‘Luckily for us, everything did come just right within a year or two of his telling us. We managed at last to make up one batch.

segments.text: ‘We’ve brought it north from the south, and it’s buried under the pear tree at this very moment.’
‘Does the medicine have a name?’ Zhou Rui’s wife asked.
‘Yes. The scabby-headed monk gave us that too. They’re called “Cold Fragrance Pills”.’
Zhou Rui’s wife nodded. ‘And just how do you feel when the illness comes on?’
‘Nothing very much. I only get a little wheezy and cough. Once I’ve taken a pill, I feel rather better.’
Zhou Rui’s wife was about to speak again when she suddenly heard Lady Wang ask, ‘Who’s in there?’

She hurried out to answer, and took the opportunity to report about Grannie Liu. After waiting a little while and finding that Lady Wang had nothing more to say, she was just going to withdraw when Aunt Xue stopped her with a smile. ‘Wait a moment. I’ve something for you to take with you.’ She called for Caltrop.

segments.text: The doorway curtain rattled, and the little maid who had been playing with Golden came in. ‘What did you want me for, ma’am?’
‘Bring the flowers in the box,’ said Aunt Xue.
Caltrop assented and brought over a little brocade-covered box.

‘These are twelve gauze flowers in the newest palace fashion,’ Aunt Xue said. ‘It occurred to me yesterday that it was a shame to leave them lying idle. Why not let the girls wear them? I meant to send them over yesterday, but then I forgot. You’ve come at just the right moment to take them. A pair for each of your three young ladies. Of the six left over, give two to Miss Lin, and the other four to our Feng.’

segments.text: ‘Keep them for Bao-chai to wear,’ Lady Wang said. ‘You’re always thinking of the others.’
‘You don’t know what a peculiar girl she is, Sister,’ said Aunt Xue. ‘She’s never cared for flowers and powder and such things.’
Zhou Rui’s wife took the box and went out. Golden was still there, basking in the sun.

segments.text: ‘That little Caltrop,’ she asked Golden, ‘is she that girl people keep talking about, the one they bought just before coming to the capital and got into a murder case over?’
‘The very one.’

As they were speaking, Caltrop came up smiling. Zhou Rui’s wife took her hand and studied her for a while, then turned to Golden with a smile. ‘She really is a pretty creature. There’s quite a look of Mrs Rong at the Ning mansion about her.’
‘That’s just what I say,’ Golden answered, smiling.

Zhou Rui’s wife asked Caltrop how old she had been when she entered service here, and then where her parents were now, how far into her teens she was and where she came from. To every question Caltrop shook her head and answered, ‘I can’t remember.’ Hearing this, Zhou Rui’s wife and Golden fell to sighing and grieving for her instead.

segments.text: Presently Zhou Rui’s wife carried the flowers round to the back of Lady Wang’s principal rooms. Grandmother Jia had recently declared that there were too many granddaughters crowding together for comfort. She had kept only Bao-yu and Dai-yu with her to amuse her, and moved Ying-chun, Tan-chun and Xi-chun into three small rooms in the annex behind Lady Wang’s apartments, with Li Wan to keep them company and look after them.

segments.text: As this lay on her way, Zhou Rui’s wife went there first. Several little maids were waiting in the annex to be called. Ying-chun’s maid Chess and Tan-chun’s maid Scribe were just coming out through the curtain, each carrying a teacup. From this she knew the sisters were sitting together. She went into the inner room and found Ying-chun and Tan-chun playing Go by the window. She presented the flowers and explained where they had come from. Both girls stopped their game at once, half rose to offer their thanks and told the maids to put the flowers away.

‘Isn’t she just in here?’ said the maids.

‘When did you get here?’ Zhou Rui’s wife asked Sapientia. ‘And where’s that bald old rascal, your teacher, gone?’
‘We came early this morning. My teacher went on to Mr Yu’s house after seeing Her Ladyship. She told me to wait for her here.’
‘Have you had your monthly silver for incense offerings, due on the fifteenth?’
Sapientia shook her head. ‘I don’t know.’
‘Who looks after the monthly allowances for the temples now?’ Xi-chun asked.
‘Yu Xin does.’
‘So that was it!’ Xi-chun said, laughing. ‘As soon as her teacher arrived, Yu Xin’s wife came hurrying over, and they whispered together for ages. I suppose that was what they were talking about.’

Zhou Rui’s wife rose at once, handed her the box and explained about the flowers. Patience opened it, took out four and went back. A little later she reappeared with two in her hand. segments.text: Zhou Rui’s wife now set off for Grandmother Jia’s quarters. As she passed through a passage hall, she looked up and saw her daughter, smartly dressed, just arrived from her husband’s home.
‘What have you come running over here for at this hour?’ she asked.

‘Have you been keeping well, Mother?’ her daughter said with a smile. ‘I’ve been waiting at home for ages, but you never came out. What’s keeping you so busy that you can’t get home? I got tired of waiting and came in myself to pay my respects to the Old Lady. Now I’m on my way to Her Ladyship. What errands have you still got to finish? What’s that you’re carrying?’

‘Oh!’ her mother said, smiling. ‘Of all days, this Grannie Liu had to turn up today. I took it upon myself to help her and spent half the day running about. Then Her Ladyship’s sister caught sight of me and sent me off with these flowers for the young ladies and young mistresses. I haven’t even finished delivering them yet.

segments.text: ‘There must be something the matter, for you to come hurrying here like this.’

‘How good you are at guessing!’ her daughter said with a smile. ‘To tell you the truth, your son-in-law had a glass or two too many the other day and quarrelled with someone. So I’ve come to ask your advice. Who could we ask to do us a favour and settle it?’

‘I knew it! What’s so dreadful about that? Go home and wait for me. As soon as I’ve taken Miss Lin her flowers, I’ll come back. Her Ladyship and Mrs Lian are both busy just now. Go home and wait. It’s nothing to make such a fuss about.’

‘What flowers?’ Bao-yu asked before anyone else could speak. ‘Give them to me.’ His hand was already out to take the box. When he opened it, they proved to be exquisitely fashioned artificial flowers of gathered gauze, made in the palace. Dai-yu merely glanced at them in Bao-yu’s hands.
‘Are these just for me, or have the other girls some too?’
‘All the young ladies have had theirs. These two are yours, miss.’
Dai-yu gave a cold laugh. ‘I knew it. Nothing comes to me till the others have had their pick.’
Zhou Rui’s wife said not a word.
‘What took you over there, Sister Zhou?’ Bao-yu asked.
‘Her Ladyship was there, and I went to report to her. Her sister took the opportunity to ask me to bring these over.’

‘She hasn’t been very well.’

Snowpink answered that she would go, and set off.

segments.text: Zhou Rui’s wife went away, and we need say no more of that. Her son-in-law was in fact Yu-cun’s friend Leng Zi-xing. He had lately become involved in a lawsuit over the sale of antiques, and had sent his wife to ask for help from her connections. With her masters’ power and influence behind her, Zhou Rui’s wife thought little of such matters. That evening she had only to ask Xi-feng, and it was settled.

segments.text: At lamp-lighting time, Xi-feng, having taken off her make-up, came to report to Lady Wang.
‘I’ve received the things the Zhen family sent today. Their boat that brought the fresh provisions for the New Year will be going back. Shall we give them our return gifts to take with them?’
Lady Wang nodded.
‘And the birthday presents for the old lady of the Earl of Lin’an’s household are ready. Who shall we send with them?’
‘See who’s free and send four of the women. Why come asking me again as though it were some great matter?’
Xi-feng smiled. ‘Cousin Zhen’s wife came today and asked me to go over tomorrow for a little visit. There doesn’t seem to be anything to do tomorrow.’

segments.text: ‘Whether there is or not makes no difference,’ said Lady Wang. ‘Usually, when she asks us all, you can’t feel quite at ease with us there. Since this time she’s asked only you, it’s clear she really wants you to relax and enjoy yourself. Don’t disappoint her. You ought to go even if you do have things to attend to.’
Xi-feng assented. Li Wan, Ying-chun, Tan-chun and the other girls then came to pay their evening respects and returned to their own rooms. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: Next morning, after washing and dressing, Xi-feng first told Lady Wang she was going, then went to take leave of Grandmother Jia. When Bao-yu heard about the visit, he wanted to go too. Xi-feng had to agree, and stood waiting while he changed his clothes. The two cousins got into the carriage and soon arrived at the Ning mansion. Jia Zhen’s wife You-shi and her daughter-in-law Qin-shi, Jia Rong’s wife, had already come out through the ceremonial gate to welcome them, with a great many concubines, maids and married women servants. As always when she saw Xi-feng, You-shi began with a laughing bout of teasing. Then, taking Bao-yu by the hand, she led them into the main room and they sat down. Once Qin-shi had served the tea, Xi-feng spoke.
‘What have you invited me here for? If you have anything nice to offer me, bring it out quickly. I’ve things to do.’

Before You-shi or Qin-shi could reply, several of the concubines standing below them began to laugh. ‘If you hadn’t come today, ma’am, that would have been another matter. But now you’re here, you can’t have everything your own way.’

segments.text: ‘What a coincidence,’ Qin-shi said with a smile. ‘My brother’s here today, Uncle Bao, the one you wanted to see that very instant last time. I think he’s in the study. Why don’t you go and see him?’
At this Bao-yu climbed straight down from the kang and was off.

‘Careful! What’s the hurry?’ You-shi and Xi-feng both cried. Then they told his attendants, ‘Stay close and take good care of him. Don’t let him feel neglected here, as though it were not the same as coming with the Old Lady.’
‘If that’s so, why not ask young Master Qin in?’ Xi-feng said. ‘I should like to see him too. Is there some reason why I can’t?’

segments.text: ‘No, no, you needn’t see him!’ You-shi said, laughing. ‘He’s not like our children, used to all their rough-and-tumble ways. Other people’s children have been brought up to be quiet and well-mannered. If he suddenly came face to face with a rowdy like you, he’d laugh himself to death at us.’
‘Anyone in the whole wide world should be glad enough if I don’t laugh at them,’ Xi-feng retorted with a laugh. ‘And you think I’m going to let a mere child laugh at me?’
‘That’s not what we mean, Aunt,’ Jia Rong said, smiling. ‘He’s shy by nature and unused to grand occasions. If you saw him, you might only be annoyed.’
‘Pah!’ said Xi-feng. ‘I’d want to see him even if he were Nezha himself! Stop your damned nonsense. If you don’t bring him here, I’ll give you a good slap.’
‘I wouldn’t dare go against you,’ Jia Rong said with a grin. ‘I’ll bring him at once.’

He went out and returned with a youth a little slimmer than Bao-yu, with finely drawn brows, lovely eyes, a fair face and red lips. His figure was handsome, and there was a grace in his movements that seemed to surpass even Bao-yu’s. But he was bashful and timid, with something of a young girl’s air. Shy and faltering, he slowly made his bow to Xi-feng and greeted her.

segments.text: Delighted, Xi-feng first gave Bao-yu a push. ‘You’ve been outdone!’ she said, laughing. Then she leant forward, took the boy’s hand and told him to sit beside her. She gently questioned him about his age and his studies, learning in the course of it that his school name was Qin Zhong. Meanwhile, her maids and married women servants, seeing that this was her first meeting with him and that she had brought no introductory gift, hurried back to tell Patience. Patience knew how close Xi-feng was to Qin-shi. Though the visitor was only a young boy, the gift must not be too meagre. On her own authority she therefore took a bolt of cloth and two small gold ingots bearing the auspicious words ‘First Place in the Palace Examination’, and gave them to the messenger to take over. Even so, Xi-feng laughingly protested that they were far too little, and Qin-shi and the others thanked her.

segments.text: After they had eaten, You-shi, Xi-feng, Qin-shi and the others played dominoes, but we need not dwell on that. Bao-yu and Qin Zhong sat or stood as they pleased, talking together. The moment Bao-yu had seen Qin Zhong’s outstanding looks and bearing, he had felt a sense of loss, and had been spellbound for some time. Now his foolish fancies stirred again. ‘Can there really be someone like this in the world?’ he thought. ‘Beside him I’m nothing but a muddy pig, a mangy dog.

segments.text: ‘Why, oh why, was I born into this household of marquises and dukes? If only I’d been born into a poor family of minor officials, I could have made friends with him long ago, and my life would not have been wasted. For all my higher station, all this brocade, silk and gauze is only wrapping for a dead log. Fine wine and tender lamb merely fill a dung-pit, a muddy ditch. To think that “wealth and honour” should have suffered such abuse at my hands!’

Qin Zhong, for his part, had seen Bao-yu’s extraordinary beauty and his unaffected manner, together with his golden headpiece, embroidered clothes, haughty maids and extravagant pages. He too was thinking to himself. ‘This Bao-yu! No wonder everyone dotes on him. Why must I have been born into a family that is genteel but poor, so that I can’t be close beside him, day in, day out? That “rich” and “poor” should set bounds to people is one of the great vexations of this world.’

Both were lost in equally fanciful thoughts when Bao-yu suddenly asked what books Qin Zhong was reading. Qin Zhong answered him plainly. They exchanged a dozen or so remarks and found themselves growing closer all the time.

segments.text: Presently tea and fruit were brought in.
‘Neither of us drinks wine,’ Bao-yu said. ‘Put the fruit on the little kang in the inner room. We’ll sit there, out of your way.’
The two boys went in to take their tea. While seeing that wine and fruit were set before Xi-feng, Qin-shi hurried in to speak to Bao-yu.
‘Uncle Bao, if your nephew should say anything thoughtless, please overlook it for my sake. Shy as he is, he can be stubborn and contrary, and is not always easy to get on with.’
‘Off you go,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘I understand.’
Qin-shi gave her brother a few admonitions as well, then returned to keep Xi-feng company.

segments.text: A little later Xi-feng and You-shi sent someone to ask Bao-yu if he wanted anything to eat. ‘There’s plenty out here. Just ask for it.’
Bao-yu assented, but had no interest in food or drink. He only wanted to ask Qin Zhong about his present circumstances at home.

‘My tutor died of an illness last year,’ Qin Zhong told him. ‘My father is elderly and infirm, and has so much official business to attend to that there has been no discussion yet of engaging another. For the moment I’m simply revising my old lessons at home. Besides, if one is to make any progress in one’s studies, one really needs one or two congenial companions to discuss things with regularly.’

Before he had finished, Bao-yu answered. ‘Exactly! We have a family school. Anyone in the clan who can’t afford to engage a tutor can go there, and relations of the boys are allowed to attend too. My own tutor went home last year, so I’ve been neglecting my lessons as well. Father wants to send me there for the time being to revise what I’ve already learnt. When my tutor comes back next year, we can each study at home again. But Grandmother says there are so many boys at the school that she’s afraid they’ll get up to mischief and do me no good. Then, too, I was ill for a few days, so it’s been put off for the present.

segments.text: ‘From what you say, your father must be worrying about the same thing. Why not speak to him when you get home today and come to our humble school? I’d be there with you, and we could help one another. Wouldn’t that be splendid?’

Qin Zhong smiled. ‘When Father spoke the other day of engaging a tutor, he did mention that the charitable clan school here was a good one. He meant to ask my sister’s father-in-law to recommend me. But everyone here is so busy that he didn’t like to bother them with such a small matter. Uncle Bao, if you really think your nephew might be fit to grind your ink and wash your inkstone, why not arrange it as soon as possible? Then neither of us would neglect his lessons. We could meet and talk often, put our parents’ minds at rest and enjoy each other’s friendship. What could be better?’

‘Don’t worry, don’t worry,’ said Bao-yu. ‘We’ll tell your brother-in-law, your sister and Cousin Lian’s wife presently. When you get home today, you speak to your father, and I’ll speak to Grandmother when I get back. There’s no reason why it shouldn’t be settled at once.’
Having agreed on their plan, the two boys came out and watched the others play for a while longer. By now it was time to light the lamps.

segments.text: Some time after the married women servants had passed this order outside, Qin Zhong rose to take his leave.
‘Who’s been appointed to go with him?’ You-shi asked.
‘They’ve sent Jiao Da. But he’s drunk, and he’s swearing again.’
‘Why pick on him?’ You-shi and Qin-shi both exclaimed. ‘With all those lads standing about, couldn’t they send any one of them? They have to go and stir him up!’
‘I’m always telling you that you’re too soft,’ Xi-feng said. ‘How can you let the servants carry on like this?’

‘You know what Jiao Da is like,’ You-shi said with a sigh. ‘Even Father leaves him alone, and so does your cousin Zhen. As a boy he went on three or four campaigns with the old masters. He carried the old master out of a heap of dead bodies and saved his life. He went hungry himself, but stole food for his master to eat. Once, when they’d had no water for two days, he got hold of half a bowl and gave it to his master, while he drank horse piss. He’s traded on those services and old ties ever since. Our forebears used to make special allowances for him. Who’s going to make things difficult for him now?

segments.text: ‘Besides, he’s old, and cares nothing for his dignity. All he does is drink, and when he’s drunk there’s no one he won’t abuse. I keep telling the stewards not to give him any duties. They should simply treat him as though he were dead and leave it at that. But today they’ve sent him out again.’

‘Of course I know about Jiao Da,’ Xi-feng said. ‘It’s you who can’t make up your minds. With a man like that, why not send him off to some distant estate and have done with it?’ Then she asked, ‘Are our carriages ready?’
‘All ready and waiting,’ the attendants answered.

segments.text: Xi-feng rose to take her leave and walked out hand in hand with Bao-yu. You-shi and the others accompanied them as far as the great hall, where lamps and candles blazed and the young male servants stood waiting in the red-paved forecourt. Jiao Da was emboldened by Jia Zhen’s absence. Even if his master had been at home, there was not much he could have done to him, so now he could let himself go all the more freely. With drink to spur him on, he began by abusing the chief steward Lai Er for being unfair, bullying the meek and fearing the strong.

‘Whenever there’s a nice job, you give it to somebody else. But taking someone home in the dead of night, that’s for me! You heartless son of a whore! Playing at being steward! You’d better remember that if old Master Jiao Da lifts his foot, it’s higher than your head.

segments.text: ‘Twenty years ago, who did old Master Jiao Da give a damn about? Never mind a pack of bastard sons of whores like you!’

He was still swearing with great relish when Jia Rong came out to see Xi-feng’s carriage off. The others shouted at him to stop, but he would not listen. Unable to bear it any longer, Jia Rong cursed him a couple of times and ordered the men to tie him up. ‘Tomorrow, when he’s sober, we’ll ask if he still wants to get himself killed!’

segments.text: But Jiao Da thought nothing of Jia Rong. Instead he raised his voice and came after him, shouting, ‘Rong, my boy, don’t put on your master’s airs with Jiao Da. Never mind you: even your father and grandfather wouldn’t dare stand up to me! If it hadn’t been for Jiao Da alone, would you be holding office and enjoying all this glory and wealth?

segments.text: ‘Your ancestors came within a hair of death to win this family fortune. And now, instead of repaying what you owe me, you start playing the master! Keep your mouth shut and I’ll say no more. One more word, and it’ll be red blade in, white blade out!’

From the carriage Xi-feng said to Jia Rong, ‘See that you get rid of this lawless creature as soon as possible. Keeping him here is asking for trouble. If our relatives and friends heard of this, wouldn’t they laugh at a family like ours, with no order or discipline at all?’
‘Yes,’ Jia Rong answered.

segments.text: Seeing that he was quite out of hand, several of the lads had no choice but to seize him, throw him down, tie him up and drag him towards the stables. Jiao Da grew more outrageous still, bringing Jia Zhen into his ravings.

‘I’m going to the ancestral hall to weep for the old master! Who could have thought his descendants would turn out to be such beasts? Fooling around on the sly every day, “stealing dogs and teasing hens”! Some raking the ashes, some keeping their husbands’ younger brothers as lovers! What don’t I know? We all “hide the broken arm inside the sleeve”!’
At these appalling words the lads were frightened out of their wits. They could think of nothing else: they bound him fast and stuffed his mouth full of earth and horse manure.

segments.text: Xi-feng, Jia Rong and the others could hear him from a distance too, but pretended they had heard nothing. Bao-yu, watching the drunken uproar from the carriage, found it rather entertaining.
‘Sister,’ he asked Xi-feng, ‘did you hear him say “raking the ashes”? What does “raking the ashes” mean?’

Her eyebrows shot up and her eyes flashed. ‘Stop that nonsense!’ she snapped. ‘It’s a drunkard’s filthy babble. A boy in your position ought to pretend he hasn’t heard it, not start asking questions! I’ll tell Her Ladyship when I get home, and we’ll see if you don’t get a beating!’
Frightened, Bao-yu hurried to plead with her. ‘Dear sister, I won’t do it again!’
At once Xi-feng softened her expression and coaxed him. ‘That’s better.

segments.text: Now Xi-feng and Bao-yu returned home and paid their respects to everyone. Bao-yu at once told Grandmother Jia that Qin Zhong wanted to attend the family school. He would have a friend to study with now, just the thing to spur him on. He warmly praised Qin Zhong’s character and behaviour, which made him such an endearing boy. Xi-feng helped him along, remarking that the boy would come another day to pay his respects to the venerable old lady. Between them they quite delighted the old lady. Xi-feng took the opportunity to invite her to the plays the day after next. Old as Grandmother Jia was, she still had a great zest for pleasure. When the day came, You-shi called to invite her again, and she took Lady Wang, Lin Dai-yu, Bao-yu and the others over to watch. At noon Grandmother Jia returned to rest. Lady Wang, who preferred peace and quiet, came back when she saw the old lady leaving.

segments.text: Xi-feng then took the seat of honour, and they enjoyed themselves until evening, with nothing further to relate. Bao-yu, meanwhile, had escorted Grandmother Jia home. Once she had taken her midday nap, he wanted to go back and enjoy the plays, but feared he might trouble Qin-shi and the others. Then he remembered that Xue Bao-chai had been ill at home lately, and that he had not yet visited her himself. He would go and see her. If he went through the side gate behind the main apartments, however, he might get caught up in some other business, or, worse still, happen to meet his father. Better to take the long way round.

segments.text: His nurses and maids came to help him change, but he went straight out through the inner gate in the clothes he was wearing. They could only follow, still assuming that he was going to the other mansion for the plays. Once he reached the passage hall, however, he turned east and then north, round the back of the hall. There he came face to face with two of the household’s literary dependants, Zhan Guang and Shan Pin-ren. At sight of Bao-yu both hurried up with beaming faces. One put an arm round his waist, the other took his hand.
‘Our dear little bodhisattva! I knew that dream meant something good. At last we’ve had the luck to meet you!’
They paid their respects, enquired after his health and talked on and on before finally moving away. An elderly nurse called them back.
‘Have you two gentlemen just come from the Master?’
They nodded. ‘The Master is having his midday nap in the little study at Mengpo Studio. There’s nothing to worry about.’

They walked off as they spoke, making Bao-yu smile too. He turned north towards Pear-tree Court. Just then Wu Xin-deng, the head of the silver treasury, and Dai Liang, who was in charge of the stores,

segments.text: together with several other stewards, seven men in all, came out of the accounts office. Seeing Bao-yu, they hurried over and stood with their hands at their sides. Only the purchasing agent Qian Hua, who had not seen him for some days, stepped forward and made a formal kneeling salute. Bao-yu promptly took his hand and raised him, smiling.
‘We saw a square sheet of your calligraphy somewhere the other day, Master Bao,’ the men said with smiles. ‘Your brushwork is finer than ever. When will you favour us with a few sheets to put up?’
‘Where did you see it?’ Bao-yu asked, smiling.
‘In several places. Everyone praises it to the skies. They’ve even been asking us for some.’
‘It’s nothing much,’ said Bao-yu with a smile. ‘Just tell my pages.’
He walked on as he spoke. The men waited until he had passed before going their separate ways.

segments.text: But enough of these incidental matters. Bao-yu reached Pear-tree Court and went first to Aunt Xue’s room, where she was arranging sewing work with the maids. He hastened to pay his respects. She caught hold of him at once and drew him into her arms.
‘My dear boy, how good of you to think of coming on such a cold day! Come up and sit on the kang.’
She ordered piping-hot tea.
‘Is Cousin not at home?’ Bao-yu asked.
‘He’s a horse without a bridle,’ Aunt Xue sighed. ‘Off roaming every day. As if he would stay home for a single day!’
‘Is Cousin Bao-chai quite well again?’

‘Yes, indeed. And you were kind enough to send someone to ask after her the other day. She’s in the inner room. Go and see her. It’s warmer in there than here. Sit there, and I’ll come and talk to you when I’ve put these things in order.’

Bao-yu climbed down from the kang and went to the inner doorway, where a soft curtain of somewhat worn red silk hung. Lifting it and stepping inside, he saw Xue Bao-chai sitting on the kang at her needlework. Her glossy black hair was coiled in a bun. She wore a honey-coloured padded jacket, a rose-purple sleeveless coat worked in two shades of gold and lined with ermine, and a padded skirt of spring-onion-yellow figured silk. None of her clothes was quite new or old, and there was nothing ostentatious about her appearance.

segments.text: Her lips were red without rouge, her brows dark without being painted. Her face was round as a silver basin, her eyes like glistening apricots. She spoke little, which people called hiding her simplicity; she kept her place and accommodated herself to circumstances, which she herself called keeping to her unassuming ways. As Bao-yu looked at her, he asked, ‘Are you quite well again, Cousin?’
Bao-chai looked up and saw him coming in. She rose at once and answered with a smile, ‘Much better now. Thank you for thinking of me.’

She invited him to sit on the edge of the kang and told Oriole to pour tea. While asking after Grandmother, her aunt and the other girls, she looked at Bao-yu. On his head was a purple-gold filigree coronet set with jewels, and across his forehead a gold band with two dragons contending for a pearl. He wore an olive-yellow robe with upright python patterns, close-fitting archer’s sleeves and a lining of white fox underarm fur. At his waist was a five-coloured sash with a butterfly design. Round his neck hung a longevity locket and an amulet of religious dedication, as well as the precious jade that had been in his mouth when he was born.
‘I hear about this jade of yours every day,’ Bao-chai said with a smile, ‘but I’ve never really had a good look at it. Today I mean to.’
She moved closer.

segments.text: The stone had also recorded this transformed appearance and the seal-script inscriptions engraved by the scabby monk. These are reproduced below according to its drawing. Its actual body was tiny, small enough to be held in the mouth of a child emerging from the womb. Were we to draw it at its true size, the writing would be so minute that readers would have to strain their eyes, which would hardly be agreeable. We have therefore kept only the shape and enlarged the proportions a little, so that it may be read by lamplight or when tipsy. By explaining this now, we forestall such objections as: ‘How large can an unborn child’s mouth be, to hold such a huge, clumsy lump?’

segments.text: After reading it twice, she turned to Oriole with a smile.
‘Why are you standing here in a daze instead of pouring the tea?’
Oriole giggled. ‘Those two lines sound as though they make a pair with the two on your necklace, miss.’
‘So you have eight characters on your necklace too, Cousin!’ Bao-yu exclaimed, smiling. ‘Let me admire them as well.’
‘Don’t listen to her,’ said Bao-chai. ‘There’s no writing on it.’
‘Dear Cousin,’ Bao-yu pleaded with a smile, ‘why did you look at mine, then?’

Unable to resist his pestering, Bao-chai said, ‘Someone gave us a couple of auspicious sayings, so they were engraved on it, and I was told to wear it every day. Otherwise, what pleasure is there in carrying such a weight?’

As she spoke, she undid the row of buttons and drew out from over her scarlet inner jacket a jewelled necklace, its gems glittering and its gold ablaze. Bao-yu promptly took the locket in his hand. Sure enough, there were four seal-script characters on each side, eight altogether, forming two auspicious pronouncements.

segments.text: Its appearance, too, had been drawn to show the design. The front of the necklace bore, in ordinary transcription: ‘Never part, never forsake.’ The reverse bore: ‘Youth and beauty, ever renewed.’ Bao-yu read these twice, then read his own twice.
‘These eight characters of yours really do make a pair with mine, Cousin,’ he said with a smile.
‘They were given by a scabby-headed monk,’ said Oriole, smiling. ‘He said they had to be engraved on something made of gold—’

Before she could finish, Bao-chai reproved her for not pouring the tea and asked Bao-yu where he had come from. Sitting so close to her, Bao-yu kept catching a delicate scent, sweet and cool, whose nature he could not make out.
‘What incense have you been using on your clothes, Cousin?

segments.text: Bao-yu and the others rose at once, smiling and inviting her to sit down.
‘What makes you say that?’ Bao-chai asked with a smile.
‘If I’d known he was coming, I wouldn’t have come,’ Dai-yu said, smiling.
‘Now I understand you even less.’

‘Either everyone comes in a crowd, or nobody comes at all. If he comes today and I come tomorrow, and we take turns like that, won’t you have someone here every day? Then you won’t be too lonely, or have too much company either. How is it you don’t understand, Cousin?’
Seeing that Dai-yu wore a scarlet camlet coat fastening down the front, Bao-yu asked, ‘Is it snowing?’
‘Snow pellets have been falling for quite a while,’ the women standing below the kang replied.
‘Has anyone brought my cloak?’ Bao-yu asked.
‘There, you see,’ said Dai-yu. ‘As soon as I come, it’s time for you to go.’
‘When did I say I was going?’ Bao-yu laughed. ‘I only want it here in case I need it.’
His wet-nurse, Nurse Li, said, ‘It’s snowing, and getting rather late. You might as well stay here and amuse yourself with your cousins.

segments.text: ‘Your aunt is laying out tea and refreshments. I’ll send a maid for your cloak and tell the pages they can go.’

Bao-yu agreed. Nurse Li went out and dismissed the pages, of whom no more need be said. Aunt Xue had set out several dainty things to eat and was keeping her visitors to tea. Bao-yu praised the delicious goose feet and duck tongues he had eaten at Cousin Zhen’s wife’s in the other mansion the other day. Aunt Xue promptly brought him some of her own, preserved in wine lees, to taste.
‘These really need wine with them,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
Aunt Xue sent for some of the very best wine.

segments.text: Nurse Li came forward. ‘Madam, perhaps no wine.’
‘Mamma, just one cup,’ Bao-yu pleaded.

‘No, that won’t do! In front of Her Old Ladyship or Her Ladyship, I wouldn’t mind if you drank a whole jar. But the other day I took my eyes off you for a moment, and some ill-bred creature, thinking only of pleasing you and not caring what happened to anyone else, gave you a sip of wine. I was scolded for two days because of it. You don’t know, madam, what an aggravating temper he has. Wine only makes him more wilful. One day Her Old Ladyship is in a good mood and lets him drink as much as he likes; another day she won’t let him touch it. Why should I suffer for nothing in between?’
‘You old thing,’ Aunt Xue said, laughing, ‘go and have a drink yourself, and stop worrying.

segments.text: ‘I shan’t let him have too much either. If Her Old Ladyship asks, I’ll answer for it.’
She told a young maid, ‘Come, see that your mammas have a cup too, to keep out the snowy chill.’
Hearing this, Nurse Li could only go with the others to have some wine. Bao-yu now said, ‘There’s no need to warm it. I only like it cold.’
‘That will never do,’ Aunt Xue said at once. ‘Cold wine makes your hand shake when you write.’

Bao-chai smiled. ‘Cousin Bao, with all the odds and ends you pick up every day, surely you know that wine is intensely heating by nature? Drink it warm and it disperses quickly. Drink it cold and it congeals inside you, and your five internal organs have to warm it. How can that fail to do harm? Do give up drinking it cold.’
Bao-yu thought this reasonable. He put down the cold wine and had it warmed before drinking.

segments.text: Dai-yu sat cracking melon seeds, with only a close-lipped smile. Just then her little maid Snowgoose brought her a small hand-warmer.
‘Who told you to bring that?’ Dai-yu asked, smiling. ‘How very thoughtful! As though I were about to freeze to death!’
‘Nightingale was afraid you’d be cold, miss, and sent me with it,’ Snowgoose replied.

segments.text: Dai-yu took it and clasped it to her bosom.
‘How good of you to listen to her!’ she said, smiling. ‘Everything I say to you goes in one ear and out the other. Why is it that when she speaks, you obey faster than if it were an imperial decree?’
Bao-yu knew she was using this to make fun of him, but could think of nothing to say in reply. He merely gave a couple of little laughs. Bao-chai knew Dai-yu’s ways of old and took no notice.

segments.text: ‘You’ve always been delicate,’ Aunt Xue said. ‘You can’t stand the cold. Is it wrong of them to think of you?’

‘You don’t understand, Aunt,’ Dai-yu said with a smile. ‘It’s fortunate I’m here with you. If it were someone else’s house, mightn’t they be offended? It looks as though I thought they couldn’t even provide a hand-warmer, so I had to have one specially sent from home. Instead of saying my maids are over-anxious, they would think I was always so ill-mannered and presumptuous.’
‘You do imagine things!’ Aunt Xue said. ‘You may think of that, but I never would.’

segments.text: During this conversation Bao-yu had already drunk three cups. Nurse Li came forward to stop him again. He was feeling thoroughly content, talking and laughing with Bao-chai and Dai-yu. How could he be willing to stop? He had to swallow his pride and plead.
‘Dear Mamma, just two more cups, and then no more.’
‘Mind yourself,’ said Nurse Li. ‘The Master is at home today. He may ask you about your books!’

segments.text: This made Bao-yu thoroughly uneasy. He slowly put down his wine and lowered his head. Dai-yu spoke at once.
‘Don’t spoil everyone’s fun! If Uncle sends for you, just say Aunt is keeping you here. This mamma has had a drink herself, and now she wants to amuse herself at our expense!’
She gave Bao-yu a secret nudge to stir him to defiance, and murmured, ‘Don’t mind the old thing. Let’s enjoy ourselves.’
Nurse Li knew Dai-yu’s ways too.
‘Miss Lin, don’t encourage him. Do try to persuade him. He might listen to you.’

‘Why should I encourage him?’ Dai-yu said with a cold laugh. ‘And I’ve no call to persuade him either. You’re far too anxious, Mamma. Grandmother often gives him wine. Surely an extra mouthful here at Aunt’s can’t hurt him. Unless, of course, Aunt is an outsider, and perhaps he oughtn’t to be here at all.’

segments.text: ‘I’ve nothing very good to offer you when you come here. If you’re frightened into letting even this little bit lie heavy on your stomach, you’ll make me feel bad. Go on and enjoy it. I’ll answer for everything. Stay for supper too. If you get drunk, you can sleep here with me.’
She gave orders: ‘Warm some more wine! I’ll have a couple of cups with you, and then we’ll eat.’
Only then did Bao-yu’s spirits rise again.

segments.text: Nurse Li gave the young maids their instructions.
‘Watch him carefully while you’re here. I’m going home to change my clothes, and then I’ll be back. Have a quiet word with Her Ladyship: she mustn’t give him his way and let him drink too much.’

With that she went home. There were still two or three older women present, but none felt particularly concerned. When they saw Nurse Li leave, they too quietly slipped away to see to their own needs. Only two young maids remained, delighted at the chance to please Bao-yu. Fortunately, after coaxing him again and again, Aunt Xue allowed him only a few cups before hastily having the wine taken away. Soup was made with sour bamboo shoots and chicken skin. Bao-yu drank two bowls with relish and ate half a bowl of green-grained rice gruel. Presently Bao-chai and Dai-yu finished their meal too, and strong tea was brewed for everyone. Only then did Aunt Xue feel at ease. Snowgoose and the other maids, three or four in all, had eaten and came in to attend them.
‘Are you going?’ Dai-yu asked Bao-yu.
Bao-yu looked sideways at her through heavy eyelids. ‘If you’re going, I’ll go with you.’
Dai-yu rose when she heard this. ‘We’ve been here all day. It’s time we went back.

segments.text: ‘Who knows how they may be looking for us over there?’

With that, the two took their leave. A young maid brought his rain-hat. Bao-yu inclined his head a little and told her to put it on. She shook out the scarlet felt hat and had only just set it on his head when he protested.
‘Stop, stop! Clumsy thing, be a little gentler! Haven’t you ever seen anyone put one on? Let me do it myself.’
Dai-yu stood on the edge of the kang.
‘What a fuss! Come here and let me see.’

Bao-yu went over at once. Dai-yu adjusted the hat with her hands, settling it gently over the coronet that held his hair and tucking its brim above his forehead band. She raised the walnut-sized crimson floss tassel on his hairpin so that it quivered outside the hat. When she had finished she looked him over.
‘There. Now put your cloak on.’
Only then did Bao-yu take the cloak and put it on.
‘Your nurses haven’t come back yet,’ Aunt Xue said hastily. ‘There’s no hurry. Wait a little.’
‘Why should we wait for them?’ said Bao-yu. ‘The maids are quite enough to go with us.’
Aunt Xue was uneasy and would not be satisfied until she had ordered two women to accompany the cousins.

segments.text: The two thanked her for her hospitality and went straight back to Grandmother Jia’s rooms. She had not yet had supper, and was all the more pleased when she heard they had come from Aunt Xue’s. Seeing that Bao-yu had been drinking, she sent him to rest in his room and forbade him to come out again. She ordered that he be carefully looked after. Then, remembering his attendants, she asked, ‘Where is Li, his wet-nurse?’
No one dared say she had gone home. ‘She was here just now,’ they answered. ‘She must have gone off on some errand.’
Bao-yu staggered and turned his head. ‘She has an easier life than you do, Grandmother. What do you want with her? I might live a couple of days longer without her.’
Talking as he went, he reached his bedroom. Brush and ink were on the table. Skybright came forward to meet him, smiling.

‘Well, well! You made me grind all that ink, and in your fine mood this morning you wrote just three characters, threw down the brush and went off. You’ve kept us waiting all day. Come and use up the ink before you do anything else!’
Bao-yu suddenly remembered what had happened that morning.
‘Where are the three characters I wrote?’ he asked with a smile.
‘He really is drunk!’ Skybright said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘Before you went to the other mansion, you told us to put them up over this doorway. Now you ask that! I was afraid someone else would spoil them, so I climbed the ladder and put them up myself. My hands are still stiff with cold.’
‘I forgot,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘If your hands are cold, let me warm them.’
He reached out and took her hand, and they looked up together at the three freshly written characters above the doorway. Presently Dai-yu came in.
‘Dear Cousin, tell me honestly,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Which of those three characters is best?’
Dai-yu looked up at the three characters newly pasted above the inner doorway. They read ‘Crimson Rue Studio’.

segments.text: ‘They’re all good,’ Dai-yu said with a smile. ‘How have you come to write so beautifully? You must write a name-board for me tomorrow.’
‘You’re coaxing me again,’ Bao-yu chuckled. Then he asked, ‘Where’s Aroma?’
Skybright pointed with her lips towards the kang in the inner room. Bao-yu looked and saw Aroma lying there asleep, still dressed.

‘Well, that’s rather early to be tucked up so snugly,’ he said with a smile. Then he asked Skybright, ‘At breakfast in the other mansion today there was a plate of bean-curd-skin parcels. I remembered you liked them, so I spoke to Mrs Zhen. I just said I wanted to keep them for tonight, and had someone send them over. Did you eat them?’

‘Don’t speak of it. As soon as they came I knew they were for me. But I’d only just eaten, so I put them aside. Then Mamma Li came and saw them. “Bao-yu probably won’t eat these,” she said. “I’ll take them for my grandson.” And she had someone carry them home.’
Just then Snowpink brought in the tea.

segments.text: ‘Have some tea, Cousin Lin,’ Bao-yu said.
The others laughed. ‘Miss Lin left some time ago, and you’re still offering her tea!’

Bao-yu drank half a bowl. Suddenly he remembered the morning’s tea and asked Snowpink, ‘There was a bowl of Maple Dew tea brewed this morning. I said it only comes into its own after three or four infusions. Why have you brewed this instead?’
‘I did keep it,’ said Snowpink. ‘But when Mamma Li came, she wanted to taste it, so I gave it to her.’
At this Bao-yu flung the cup he was holding straight to the floor.

segments.text: It shattered with a crash, splashing tea all over Snowpink’s skirt. He sprang up and demanded of her:

‘What sort of mamma is she to you, for you all to be so dutiful? All she has to go on is that I drank her milk for a few days when I was little. Now you’ve let her set herself up above my ancestors. I don’t need her milk any more. Why keep an ancestor here doing nothing? Turn her out, and we’ll all have some peace!’
He was about to go that very instant and ask Grandmother Jia to dismiss his wet-nurse.

segments.text: Aroma, in fact, had not been asleep at all. She had only pretended, to tempt Bao-yu into coming to tease her. When she first heard the talk about the writing and the parcels, there had been no need to get up. But when he smashed the teacup and lost his temper, she quickly rose to explain matters and soothe him. Grandmother Jia had already sent someone to ask what had happened.
‘I was bringing in the tea just now,’ Aroma said quickly, ‘and slipped on the snow. The cup fell out of my hand and broke.’

Then she tried to calm Bao-yu. ‘Very well, if you’ve set your heart on turning her out. We’d all like to go too. You might as well turn us all out together. It would suit us, and you needn’t worry about finding better people to wait on you.’

This silenced Bao-yu at last. Aroma and the others helped him to the kang and changed his clothes. They could not make out what he was still saying: his tongue was growing thick, his eyelids heavier and heavier. They hurried to settle him to sleep. Aroma took the Spiritual Jade from his neck, wrapped it in her own handkerchief and tucked it under the mattress, so that it would not chill his neck when he put it on next morning.

segments.text: Bao-yu fell asleep as soon as his head touched the pillow. Nurse Li and the others had come back by then. Hearing that he was drunk, they dared not come forward and provoke him further. They quietly made sure he was asleep before dispersing, relieved. When he woke next day, someone reported that Master Rong from the other mansion had brought Master Qin to call. Bao-yu hurried out to welcome them and took Qin Zhong to pay his respects to Grandmother Jia. Delighted by the boy’s good looks and gentle manners, she thought him a worthy companion for Bao-yu’s studies. She kept him to tea and a meal, and had him taken to see Lady Wang and the others. They had always been fond of Qin-shi, and seeing what a fine boy Qin Zhong was, they too were pleased. Each gave him a gift when he left. Grandmother Jia gave him a purse and a gold figure of Kui Xing, to signify ‘harmony under the star of learning’. She also told him:

‘You live a long way off. If ever the heat or cold, or getting your meals, makes things awkward, stay here. There’s no need for a fixed rule. Just keep company with your Uncle Bao, and don’t learn the ways of those good-for-nothing creatures.’
Qin Zhong assented to each instruction, then went home and told his father.

segments.text: His father, Qin Ye, currently held office as a secretary for building works. He was nearly seventy, and his wife had long been dead. Having had no children in his earlier years, he had adopted a boy and a girl from a foundling home. The boy had died, leaving only the girl, whose childhood name was Ke-er. She grew into a slender, graceful young woman with a charming disposition. Qin Ye had some longstanding connections with the Jias, and a marriage was arranged: she was betrothed to Jia Rong. Qin Ye was over fifty before Qin Zhong was born. The boy’s tutor had died the previous year, and there had been no opportunity to engage another accomplished teacher, so for the time being he had been reviewing his old lessons at home. Qin Ye had been thinking of approaching his daughter’s family by marriage about sending him to their school, so that his studies would not be neglected in the meantime, when this chance encounter with Bao-yu occurred. He knew too that the Jia school was now in the charge of Jia Dai-ru, a venerable scholar of the day. Qin Zhong was bound to improve there, and might hope to make a name for himself. Qin Ye was therefore delighted. His official purse, however, was poorly filled, and everyone in the Jia household, high and low, had eyes only for wealth and rank. A modest sum would hardly do, yet he feared harming his son’s prospects for life. There was nothing for it but to scrape together twenty-four taels, respectfully wrap them as an introductory gift to the teacher and take Qin Zhong himself to pay a call at Dai-ru’s house.

segments.text: Now Qin Ye and his son were waiting for someone from the Jia household to bring word of the day chosen for starting school. Bao-yu, impatient to be with Qin Zhong, could think of nothing else, and fixed on the day after next. ‘Ask Master Qin to come here early that morning, so that we can set off together.’ He sent a messenger with these instructions.

segments.text: Early on the appointed morning, when Bao-yu woke, Aroma had already packed his books, brushes and other writing things, putting everything neatly in order, and was sitting disconsolately on the edge of his bed. Seeing him awake, she had to help him wash and do his hair. Bao-yu noticed her gloomy look and asked with a smile, ‘Dear sister, what’s troubling you again? Surely you don’t blame me for going to school and leaving you all lonely?’

‘What a thing to say!’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘Studying is an excellent thing. You can’t drift along all your life. Where would that end? There’s only one thing: when you’re studying, keep your mind on your books, and when you’re not, spare a thought for home. Don’t go fooling about with the others. If your father catches you, it will be no laughing matter. Of course you want to work hard and do well, but it would be better to take on a little less. For one thing, if you bite off too much you can’t chew it, and for another, you must look after your health. That’s all I mean. Do try to understand.’
Bao-yu agreed to everything she said, point by point.
‘I’ve packed your thick furs too,’ Aroma went on, ‘and sent them out to the boys.

segments.text: ‘It’s cold at school. Do remember to put on extra things or change what you’re wearing. It isn’t like home, with someone to look after you. I’ve sent out charcoal for your foot-warmer and hand-warmer as well. You must make them keep those filled. Those lazy rascals are only too pleased to do nothing unless you tell them, and you’ll be frozen for no reason.’
‘Don’t worry,’ Bao-yu said. ‘I can manage all that for myself when I’m out. And don’t sit here in this room, bored to death. Go and laugh and play with Cousin Lin as often as you can.’

By now he was fully dressed, and Aroma urged him to go and pay his respects to Grandmother Jia, Jia Zheng, Lady Wang and the others. Bao-yu still had a few instructions for Skybright and Musk before he went out to see Grandmother Jia. She too, naturally, had some parting advice for him. Then he went to Lady Wang, and from her rooms out to the study to see Jia Zheng.

segments.text: As luck would have it, Jia Zheng had come home rather early that day and was in the study chatting with his literary dependants. Bao-yu suddenly appeared, paid his respects and said he was going to school.

‘If you mention the word “school” again, you’ll make even me die of shame,’ Jia Zheng said with a cold laugh. ‘If you take my advice, you’ll simply go and play. That’s what you’re fit for. Mind you don’t soil my floor by standing on it, or my door by leaning against it!’
The literary gentlemen had all risen and were smiling.

‘Come, sir, why speak like that? Once our young friend starts today, in two or three years he’ll have made a name for himself. He certainly won’t go on behaving like a child as he did before. It’s nearly time for the morning meal. Do be on your way, young sir.’
Two of the older men took Bao-yu out by the hand.

A couple of answering calls came from outside, and three or four strapping men promptly entered and made formal kneeling salutes. Looking at them, Jia Zheng recognised Bao-yu’s wet-nurse’s son, Li Gui.

segments.text: ‘You go to school with him every day,’ he said to Li Gui. ‘What books has he actually read? All he’s filled his head with is gossip and nonsense, and all he’s learnt is ever more elaborate mischief. When I have a moment to spare, I’ll flay you first and settle with that good-for-nothing afterwards!’

Terrified, Li Gui dropped on both knees, took off his cap and knocked his head audibly on the floor, saying ‘Yes, sir’ over and over. Then he ventured, ‘The young master’s got as far as the third volume of the Book of Poetry. Something about “The deer go yoo-yoo, lotus leaves and duckweed.” I wouldn’t dare lie, sir.’
The whole room burst out laughing. Even Jia Zheng could not help joining in.

‘He might read thirty volumes of the Book of Poetry, and it would still be like stopping his ears to steal a bell: nothing but an attempt to fool people. Go and give my respects to the old gentleman at the school. Tell him I said there is no need to go through the motions with the Book of Poetry or classical prose or any of that. What matters most is to explain the Four Books straight through first and have him learn them thoroughly by heart.’
Li Gui hastily assented. Seeing that Jia Zheng had nothing more to say, he withdrew.

segments.text: and hurried to her room. She was sitting by the window in front of her mirror, doing her hair. When he said he was going to school, she smiled.
‘Splendid! You’re sure to pluck the cassia in the Moon Palace this time. I can’t come to see you off.’
‘Dear cousin, wait till I come back from school before you have supper,’ Bao-yu said. ‘And wait for me before you mix the rouge paste.’
He went on and on before he could bring himself to leave. Dai-yu hastily called him back.
‘Why don’t you go and say goodbye to your Cousin Bao-chai?’
Bao-yu smiled without answering and went straight off to school with Qin Zhong.

The Jia family’s charitable clan school was not far away, only a li or so. It had been founded by their first ancestor so that boys of the clan whose families were too poor to engage a tutor could study there. All members of the clan who held office or rank contributed silver towards its expenses in proportion to their salaries. They chose a man of years and virtue to be schoolmaster, with the sole duty of teaching and supervising the boys. Bao-yu and Qin Zhong now arrived, exchanged formal greetings with everyone in turn, and began their lessons.

Grandmother Jia was fond of Qin Zhong too, and often kept him to stay for three or five days, cherishing him as if he were her own great-grandson. Seeing that he was not well off, she also helped him with clothes, shoes and other things.

segments.text: In less than a month Qin Zhong was quite at home in the Rong mansion. Bao-yu, however, was never one to keep within bounds: he simply followed his own inclinations. Another of his odd notions took hold of him, and he made a point of whispering to Qin Zhong, ‘We’re the same age, and we’re schoolfellows too. From now on, let’s forget about being uncle and nephew and treat each other as brothers and friends.’

segments.text: At first Qin Zhong refused, but Bao-yu would not have it and insisted on calling him ‘brother’, or using his courtesy name, Jing-qing. Qin Zhong had no choice but to follow suit and abandon the proper forms of address.

Now although the pupils at this school were all boys of the clan or sons of its relatives, the proverb puts it well: ‘One dragon has nine kinds of offspring, and no two kinds are alike.’ With so many of them, dragons and snakes were bound to be mixed together; there were some low characters among them.

segments.text: Both the newcomers were as lovely as flowers. Qin Zhong was shy and gentle, blushing before he spoke, his hesitant, modest manner like a girl’s. Bao-yu, for his part, had an inborn readiness to make himself small, to yield and defer, with considerate ways and endlessly affectionate talk. The two therefore grew still closer, and one could hardly blame those schoolfellows for becoming suspicious. Behind their backs one boy passed a word to another, until abuse and scandal filled the classroom and spread beyond it.

Since coming to live with Lady Wang, Xue Pan had discovered that there was a family school with plenty of young lads in it. This occasionally stirred in him the inclinations of Longyang, and he too made a pretence of coming to study. His attendance was fitful, fishing for three days and drying his nets for two. He gave Jia Dai-ru tuition gifts for nothing and made no progress whatever. All he wanted was to acquire male favourites.
