segments.text: Indeed, several of the younger pupils, tempted by Xue Pan’s money and the food and clothes he provided, had already been enticed into his keeping. We need not record the details. There were also two amorous young pupils whose family connections were unknown, and whose real names had not been ascertained. So charming and graceful were they that the whole school called them by a pair of nicknames: one was Xiang-lian, the other Yu-ai.

segments.text: Everyone admired them in secret, with intentions that boded no good for the lads, but fear of Xue Pan’s power kept anyone from approaching them. When Bao-yu and Qin Zhong arrived and saw the two, they too could not help feeling drawn to them. Knowing that they were intimate with Xue Pan, however, they dared make no rash advance. Xiang-lian and Yu-ai in turn felt just as fond of Bao-yu and Qin Zhong. All four thus cherished feelings which had yet to declare themselves. Each day at school they sat apart, but their eight eyes sought one another out. A casual remark might carry a hidden meaning, a verse about mulberry trees allude to willows: from a distance they understood each other, while outwardly avoiding notice. Yet a few sly rogues had seen what was happening and would wink and make faces behind their backs, or cough loudly and raise their voices. This had been going on for some time.

segments.text: It so happened that Dai-ru had business that day and had gone home early, leaving a seven-character line for the boys to match with the second half of a couplet before their next lesson the following day. He put Jia Rui in temporary charge of the school. Happily, Xue Pan no longer came very often even to put in an appearance, so Qin Zhong took the opportunity to exchange winks and signals with Xiang-lian. Pretending that they needed to relieve themselves, they went into the back courtyard for a private talk.
‘Do the grown-ups at home mind who you make friends with?’ Qin Zhong began.

Before he had finished, someone coughed behind them. Startled, both hastily turned. It was a schoolfellow called Jin Rong. Xiang-lian was rather quick-tempered, and embarrassment and anger together provoked him.
‘What are you coughing for? Aren’t we allowed to talk?’

‘If you’re allowed to talk, why shouldn’t I cough?’ Jin Rong said with a laugh. ‘Just tell me this: why can’t you say what you have to say out in the open? What are you up to, sneaking about like this? I’ve caught you now. No use denying it!

segments.text: ‘Give me my cut first, and I won’t say a word. Otherwise we’ll all join in.’
Qin Zhong and Xiang-lian flushed scarlet with agitation.
‘What have you caught us doing?’ they demanded.
‘I’ve caught you at it, all right,’ Jin Rong said, laughing. He clapped his hands and shouted in amusement, ‘Fine griddle cakes you’ve slapped together! Won’t any of you buy one to eat?’
Furious and distressed, Qin Zhong and Xiang-lian hurried back inside to complain to Jia Rui that Jin Rong had been bullying them for no reason.

segments.text: Jia Rui was a thoroughly unscrupulous creature, always on the lookout for an advantage. At school he used his authority to serve his private ends, forcing the boys to treat him. Later he had attached himself to Xue Pan for the sake of a little money, wine and meat, allowing him to bully and tyrannise as he pleased. Far from restraining him, Jia Rui helped him in his villainy to win his favour. But Xue Pan’s affections drifted like duckweed: one day he loved this one, the next day that. Lately he had made new friends and cast Xiang-lian and Yu-ai aside. Jin Rong himself had once been an intimate, only to be dropped when Xiang-lian and Yu-ai appeared; now they too had been abandoned. Jia Rui was consequently left without anyone to speak for him or lend him a hand. Instead of blaming Xue Pan for throwing over old friends for new, he blamed Xiang-lian and Yu-ai for failing to help him with Xue Pan. Jia Rui, Jin Rong and their set were therefore already jealous of the pair. When Qin Zhong and Xiang-lian came to complain about Jin Rong that day, Jia Rui felt immediately resentful. He could hardly scold Qin Zhong, so he vented his displeasure on Xiang-lian instead, accusing him of making trouble and giving him a sharp dressing-down.

segments.text: Xiang-lian had only brought a rebuff on himself. Even Qin Zhong felt abashed, and they went back to their respective seats. Jin Rong was more triumphant than ever, shaking his head, smacking his lips and continuing to make remarks. Yu-ai happened to hear and could not swallow his indignation. The two began a muttered quarrel across the intervening seats.

‘I plainly saw them in the back courtyard just now, kissing and feeling each other’s bottoms,’ Jin Rong insisted. ‘Just the two of them, breaking off grass stalks and drawing for long and short. Whoever got the longer one went first.’
He was too pleased with himself to care what nonsense he talked, and forgot that others were listening. Already he had angered someone else. And who do you suppose that was?

segments.text: His name was Jia Qiang, and he was a great-great-grandson in the legitimate line of the Ning branch. His parents had died when he was very young, and he had grown up in Jia Zhen’s household. Now sixteen, he was even more handsome and graceful than Jia Rong. The two cousins were particularly close and were often together. There were many people and many tongues in the Ning mansion, and servants who felt slighted were especially adept at inventing slanders against their masters. Who could say what malicious tales had been set going this time? Jia Zhen, it seemed, had heard something of the unsavoury gossip and wished to avoid suspicion himself. He had now allotted Jia Qiang quarters of his own and told him to move out of the Ning mansion and set up a separate household. Jia Qiang was as clever as he was good-looking. Though nominally a pupil, he attended only to keep up appearances, and went on cockfighting, coursing, enjoying flowers and dallying with willows. With Jia Zhen’s indulgence above and Jia Rong’s support below, who in the clan would dare cross him?

segments.text: Being so close to Jia Rong, how could he stand by and see Qin Zhong bullied? He wanted to step forward and take his part, but first he thought it over.

‘Jin Rong, Jia Rui and that lot are all friends of Uncle Xue’s, and I’ve always been on good terms with Uncle Xue myself. If I interfere and they tell old Xue, won’t it spoil our friendship? Yet if I do nothing, this sort of gossip makes things unpleasant for everyone. Why not find a way to bring them to heel, stop their mouths and save everyone’s face?’

Having decided this, he too pretended to need to relieve himself and went outside. He quietly beckoned over Bao-yu’s schoolboy attendant, Tealeaf, and put a few such suggestions into his head. Tealeaf was Bao-yu’s most useful boy, but young and ignorant of the world. Jia Qiang now told him that Jin Rong was bullying Qin Zhong and dragging his own master Bao-yu into it too: unless he was taught a lesson, next time he would be still more insolent and impossible to check. Tealeaf needed no excuse to throw his weight about. With this news, and Jia Qiang behind him, he rushed in to find Jin Rong. There was no ‘Master Jin’ now.
‘You there, Jin! What do you think you are?’
Jia Qiang stamped his boots, deliberately straightened his clothes and looked at the sun.
‘Time to go,’ he said, and told Jia Rui that he had business and must leave early.

segments.text: Jia Rui dared not make him stay and had to let him go. Meanwhile Tealeaf grabbed Jin Rong.

‘Whether we bugger anyone or not, what the fuck has it got to do with you? We haven’t buggered your dad, have we? If you’re such a fine fellow, come out and have a go at your lord and master Tealeaf!’

segments.text: All the boys in the room stared, dumbfounded. Jia Rui hastily shouted, ‘Tealeaf, none of your insolence!’
Jin Rong’s face had turned yellow with rage.
‘This is rebellion! Even a servant boy dares behave like this! I’ll have a word with your master.’

He wrenched his hand free and was about to seize Bao-yu and Qin Zhong and hit them. Before he could reach them, an inkstone came whizzing from behind his head. Who had thrown it was not yet clear. Luckily it missed, but landed on someone else’s desk: the desk shared by Jia Lan and Jia Jun.

segments.text: Jia Jun too was a great-grandson of a close branch of the Rong family. His mother had also been widowed young and had remained a widow, bringing him up alone. He and Jia Lan were particularly good friends, which was why they shared a desk. Young as Jia Jun was, however, he had tremendous spirit and was a very mischievous, fearless boy.

segments.text: Watching coolly from his seat, he had seen one of Jin Rong’s friends secretly come to his aid by throwing the inkstone at Tealeaf. It missed Tealeaf and landed on Jia Jun’s desk instead, right in front of him, smashing a porcelain water-pot for the inkstone to pieces and splashing black water all over a book. Jia Jun was not going to put up with that.
‘You filthy bastards! So we’re all fighting now, are we?’
As he cursed, he snatched up his own inkstone to throw back. Jia Lan, who preferred to stay out of trouble, hastily held it down and pleaded with him.
‘Dear brother, it’s nothing to do with us.’

segments.text: But Jia Jun could not contain himself. Taking his book-box in both hands, he hurled it towards the other side. He was too small and weak to throw so far, and it fell short on Bao-yu and Qin Zhong’s desk. It struck with a clatter, scattering books, loose sheets, brushes and inkstones all over the desk, and smashed Bao-yu’s tea-bowl as well, spilling the tea. Jia Jun jumped out to grapple with the boy who had thrown the inkstone. Jin Rong had meanwhile seized a long, broad bamboo board. In such a cramped, crowded space, how could anyone escape when he began swinging it? Tealeaf had already taken a blow.
‘Why aren’t you coming to help?’ he yelled.
Bao-yu had three other boys with him: Chu-yao, Sao-hong and Mo-yu. Not one of them was any less mischievous. They all shouted at once, ‘Sons of whores! They’re using weapons!’

Mo-yu picked up a door-bar, while Sao-hong and Chu-yao each had a riding-whip. They charged in together. Jia Rui rushed from one to another, trying to stop this boy and reason with that, but no one would listen. The brawl went on unchecked.

segments.text: Some of the unruly boys joined in for the fun of landing a few blows without risk to themselves. Others, more timid, hid to one side, while others stood on the desks, clapping, roaring with laughter and shouting encouragement to the fighters. In an instant the room was in uproar. Outside, Li Gui and several of the grown servants heard the commotion and hurried in, shouting together for everyone to stop. They asked what had caused it. Each voice told a different story: one said this, another that. Li Gui first gave Tealeaf and the other three a furious scolding and drove them out. Qin Zhong’s head had already met Jin Rong’s board, grazing the skin, and Bao-yu was rubbing it with the front of his jacket. When he saw that everyone had been silenced, he gave his orders.

‘Li Gui, pack up the books! Bring the horses. I’m going back to tell the old schoolmaster! We’ve been bullied. We didn’t say anything out of turn, but went politely to tell Master Rui. Master Rui blamed us instead. He let them abuse us and even put them up to beating our Tealeaf, and now Qin Zhong’s head is cut open too. What’s the use of studying here any more?

segments.text: ‘Tealeaf only did it because someone was bullying me. We’d be better off breaking up the school.’

‘Don’t be hasty, young master,’ Li Gui urged him. ‘The old gentleman’s gone home on business. If we trouble him with this little matter now, it’ll look as if we’re in the wrong. I say we should settle it here where it happened. Why disturb him?’ He turned to Jia Rui. ‘It’s all your fault, Master Rui. When the old gentleman’s away, you’re the head of the school, sir. Everyone takes their lead from you. If someone misbehaves, beat him if he needs beating, punish him if he needs punishing. How could you let things come to this without doing anything?’
‘I shouted at them, but none of them would listen,’ Jia Rui said.
‘I hope you won’t be angry with me, sir,’ Li Gui said, smiling, ‘but you aren’t always quite as proper as you might be. That’s why the lads won’t listen to you.

segments.text: ‘If this goes before the old schoolmaster, you won’t get off either, sir. You’d better find a way to sort it out, and quickly.’
‘What is there to sort out?’ Bao-yu said. ‘I’m going home, whatever happens!’
‘If Jin Rong stays, I won’t study here,’ Qin Zhong said, crying.

‘Why should that be?’ Bao-yu said. ‘Are other people allowed to come here and we aren’t? I’ll explain everything to everyone and have Jin Rong turned out.’ He asked Li Gui, ‘Which branch of the family is Jin Rong related to?’
Li Gui thought for a moment.
‘Better not ask. If we start going into whose relation he is, we’ll only make more bad feeling among the family.’

segments.text: From outside the window Tealeaf called, ‘He’s the nephew of Mrs Huang in the east lane. As if that were some mighty pillar to lean on! And he thinks he can frighten us! Mrs Huang’s his father’s sister. All that aunt of yours does is hang about pestering our Mrs Lian, going down on her knees to borrow things to pawn. I’ve no respect for a lady or a mistress like that!’
Li Gui kept shouting at him to stop.
‘You little dog-fucked bastard! You’re the only one who knows anything, are you, spewing out all that filth?’
‘So that’s whose relation he is!’ Bao-yu said with a cold laugh. ‘Sister-in-law Huang’s nephew. I’ll go and ask her about it myself.’
He made to leave, calling Tealeaf in to pack his books.

segments.text: As Tealeaf packed, he spoke up again, pleased with himself.

‘No need for you to go and see her yourself, Master Bao. Let me go to her house and say Her Old Ladyship has something to ask her. I’ll hire a carriage and bring her in, and you can question her in front of Her Old Ladyship. Wouldn’t that save trouble?’

segments.text: ‘Are you tired of living?’ Li Gui shouted. ‘Mind I don’t give you a good thrashing when we get home, and then report to the master and mistress that you’re behind all Bao-yu’s mischief! I’d only just managed to coax him halfway round, and here you are with another bright idea. You’ve made a riot of the school. Instead of finding some way to quiet things down, you want to make it worse!’
After that Tealeaf dared not say another word.

segments.text: By this time Jia Rui too was afraid of the affair growing bigger. His own hands were far from clean, so he had to swallow his pride and plead first with Qin Zhong and then with Bao-yu. At first neither would give way. Eventually Bao-yu said, ‘Very well, I needn’t go home. Just make Jin Rong apologise, and that will do.’
Jin Rong refused at first, but could not hold out when Jia Rui began pressing him to apologise as well. Li Gui and the others had to coax him.
‘You started it, after all. How else can it be settled?’

Unable to resist any longer, Jin Rong bowed to Qin Zhong with clasped hands. Bao-yu was still not satisfied: he insisted on a kowtow. Jia Rui wanted only to quiet the affair for the moment. He took Jin Rong aside and urged him in a whisper, ‘As the saying goes, “Even an execution ends with a head touching the ground.” You’ve made the trouble, so you’ll have to swallow a little pride. One kowtow, and it’s over.’
Jin Rong had no choice. He went forward and kowtowed to Qin Zhong. For what followed, listen to the next chapter.

Outnumbered, and ordered to do so by Jia Rui, Jin Rong had apologised and kowtowed to Qin Zhong. Only then would Bao-yu let the matter rest. When school was over and everyone had gone home, Jin Rong grew angrier the more he thought about it.
‘Qin Zhong is only Jia Rong’s wife’s younger brother,’ he said. ‘He isn’t a member of the Jia family. He’s allowed to study there, just as I am. He thinks he can look down his nose at everyone because Bao-yu is his friend. If that’s how he means to carry on, he ought at least to behave decently, so no one can say anything. He’s always up to something with Bao-yu, sneaking about as if the rest of us were blind and couldn’t see. And today he went after someone else, right under my eyes. What if there was a row? What have I got to be afraid of?’

His mother, née Hu, heard him grumbling on and on.
‘What are you working yourself up about now?’ she asked. ‘Do you know how hard it was for me to ask your aunt, and all the trouble she took before she could put in a word for you with Mrs Lian over at the Rong mansion? That’s how you got a place to study. Without their help, could we afford a teacher? Besides, they give you your tea and your meals at school. These two years you’ve been studying there have saved us a great deal in food alone. And you like to spend the savings on a nice bright new outfit. Then there’s Master Xue. Would you ever have got to know him if you hadn’t been at that school? Even when he hasn’t given much, one year with another, he’s helped us out with seventy or eighty taels over these two years.

‘If you make such a fuss now that you have to leave, let me tell you, finding another place like it will be harder than climbing to heaven! Be a good boy, amuse yourself for a bit and then go to bed. You’ll be far better off.’
Jin Rong swallowed his anger, and before long went off to sleep. Next day he went to school as usual.

segments.text: We need say no more of that. His aunt had married Jia Huang, a member of the direct line in the Jia clan’s generation whose names bore the jade radical. There is no need to explain that not every member of the clan enjoyed the wealth and standing of the Ning and Rong households. Jia Huang and his wife had a small property to live on. They paid frequent calls at the two mansions to enquire after the family’s health, and knew how to make themselves agreeable to Xi-feng and You-shi. The help these two ladies gave them from time to time enabled them to get by. On this particular day the weather was fine and there was nothing to do at home, so Mrs Huang took an elderly woman servant with her and drove over to see her widowed sister-in-law and her nephew.

segments.text:
Jin Rong’s mother was beside herself with alarm.
‘It’s all my fault for letting my tongue run away with me and telling you,’ she said hurriedly. ‘Please, sister, don’t go. Never mind who was right and who was wrong. If there’s a row, how is he to keep his place? And if he loses it, not only can’t we afford a teacher, but there’ll be all his food to find as well.’
‘Who can stop to think of all that?’ said Mrs Huang. ‘Wait till I’ve spoken and see what comes of it!’
She would not listen to her sister-in-law’s pleas, but told the old servant to see to the carriage, got in and set off for the Ning mansion. They drove through the carriage gateway, and she alighted at the little corner gate on the east. Going inside, she found Jia Zhen’s wife, You-shi. Here she did not venture to put on airs. She made warm and attentive enquiries after her health, exchanged a little small talk, and only then asked, ‘How is it we haven’t seen Mrs Rong today?’
‘I don’t know what’s come over her lately,’ You-shi replied. ‘It’s more than two months since she had her period.

segments.text: ‘“If anything should happen to her, where would you find another wife with her looks and her disposition? You could search with a lantern and never find one.” With the way she conducts herself, which of our relations, which of the elders in the family doesn’t like her? So these last two days I’ve been dreadfully worried, quite beside myself. And then this morning her brother came to see her. The child has no sense. He could see his sister wasn’t well. Even if something had happened, he shouldn’t have told her. Never mind such a trifle as this, even if he’d suffered the most terrible injustice, he ought not to have told her.

segments.text: ‘It turns out there was a fight at school yesterday. Some boy who’s been allowed to study there, I don’t know who, had been bullying him. There was some dirty talk mixed up in it too, and he told his sister everything. You know what she’s like, Aunt. She may be all smiles and conversation when she sees people, and she knows how to behave, but she notices everything and takes it all to heart. Whatever she hears, she’ll turn it over for three days and five nights before she lets it go. It’s that worrying disposition of hers that has made her ill. Today, hearing that someone had bullied her brother, she was angry and upset. Angry with that pack of scoundrels he calls his friends, stirring up mischief and setting people against one another, and upset because her brother won’t behave or attend to his books, so that he gets into these rows at school. After hearing all this, she wouldn’t even eat her breakfast. When they told me, I went over and comforted her for a while, and talked to her brother too, to calm him down. I sent him off to the other mansion to find Bao-yu, and stayed till I’d seen her take half a small bowl of bird’s-nest soup. Only then did I come back.

segments.text:
By the time she had heard all this, Mrs Huang, née Jin, had been so thoroughly frightened that the fiery determination to have things out with Qin-shi, which had filled her at her sister-in-law’s, had fled to the far side of the world. When You-shi asked whether she knew a good doctor, she hastened to reply.
‘We hear this and that, but I really haven’t heard anyone mention a good doctor. From what you say about Mrs Rong, though, it might still be a pregnancy. Don’t let them treat her at random, sister. It would be a dreadful thing if they mistook her condition.’
‘Exactly,’ said You-shi.
While they were speaking, Jia Zhen came in. Seeing the visitor, he asked You-shi, ‘Isn’t this Mrs Huang?’
Mrs Huang stepped forward to pay her respects.
‘Make our cousin stay for a meal,’ Jia Zhen told You-shi, and went on into the next room.
Mrs Huang had come to speak to Qin-shi about Qin Zhong’s bullying her nephew. Now that she had heard Qin-shi was ill, she not only could not speak of it, but dared not even mention it.

Besides, Jia Zhen and You-shi had received her so kindly that her anger turned to pleasure. She stayed to chat a little longer before going home.
After she had gone, Jia Zhen came back and sat down.
‘Did she have anything in particular to say today?’ he asked You-shi.
‘Not really. When she first came in, she looked as if something had put her out. But after we’d talked for a while and I’d told her about our daughter-in-law’s illness, she gradually looked calmer. Then you asked her to stay for a meal. Hearing how ill the girl is, she felt she oughtn’t to sit on and on, so she said a few more words and left. She didn’t ask for anything. But to come back to our daughter-in-law, the urgent thing is for you to find a good doctor to see her. Don’t let it drag on. What use are these doctors who come here now? Every one of them listens for what people want to hear, then repeats what they’ve said with a few learned phrases thrown in.

It’s really of no benefit to the patient.’

segments.text: ‘Quite,’ said Jia Zhen. ‘But the child is being foolish too. Why keep taking her clothes off and changing them? If she catches cold and adds another illness to this one, what then? However fine her clothes may be, what are they worth beside her health? Even a new outfit every day would cost nothing worth speaking of. I was just coming in to tell you: Feng Zi-ying called a little while ago. He noticed I looked downcast and asked what was wrong. I told him our daughter-in-law had suddenly become very unwell, and without a good physician we couldn’t find out whether she was pregnant or ill, or whether there was any danger. That was why I’d been so anxious these last two days. Feng Zi-ying told me about a teacher he studied under as a boy, a man called Zhang You-shi. He says he’s a most learned scholar and has a profound knowledge of medicine as well, and can even tell whether a person will live or die. He’s come to the capital this year to purchase an official appointment for his son, and is staying with Feng Zi-ying. Perhaps it’s our daughter-in-law’s good fortune, after all, to have him here to bring her safely through this illness.

‘Let’s wait till Mr Zhang has examined her.’
You-shi was delighted to hear this.
‘The old master’s birthday is the day after tomorrow,’ she said. ‘What are we going to do about it?’
‘I’ve just been to pay my respects to him,’ said Jia Zhen, ‘and to ask him to come home so the whole family could offer their congratulations. He said, “I’m used to peace and quiet. I don’t want to get caught up in that whirl of squabbles at your place. If you insist that, because it’s my birthday, I must come and have everyone kowtow to me, you’d do a hundred times better to have a fair copy made of the Tract on Hidden Virtue I annotated some time ago and get it cut on printing blocks. Far better than having people knock their heads to me for no reason. If the family are coming over for a day or two around my birthday, you stay at home and entertain them properly. There’s no need to send me anything, and you needn’t come yourself on the day. If that troubles your conscience, you can kowtow to me now before you go. If you do come on my birthday and bring a whole crowd after you to disturb me, I shan’t let you off!” He said it over and over, so I certainly shan’t dare go.

‘Send for Lai Sheng and tell him to prepare two days of feasting.’
You-shi had Jia Rong called in.
‘Tell Lai Sheng to arrange two days’ feasting as usual, and make it generous. Then go over to the Rong mansion yourself and invite Grandmother Jia, Lady Xing, Lady Wang and your Aunt Lian to come and spend some time with us. Your father has heard of a good doctor today and has already sent to ask him here. He’ll certainly come tomorrow, I should think. You must give him a full account of your wife’s symptoms over these last few days.’

Jia Rong agreed to each instruction and went out. He met the servant who had been sent to Feng Zi-ying’s house to fetch the doctor, just back from his errand.
‘I went to Master Feng’s with the master’s visiting card to ask the gentleman to come,’ the servant reported. ‘He said, “Mr Feng has just spoken to me about it too. But I’ve been out paying calls all day and have only just got back. I’m quite exhausted. Even if I went over now, I couldn’t examine the patient’s pulse.” He said he’d rest for the night and be sure to come tomorrow. He also said, “My knowledge of medicine is slight. I really don’t deserve so warm a recommendation. But since Mr Feng and your master have both asked me, I can hardly refuse. Please explain this to your master for me. I’m not worthy of the honour of his visiting card.” So he made me bring it back. Would you pass on the message for me, Master Rong?’
Jia Rong went back inside, reported to Jia Zhen and You-shi, then came out again and sent for Lai Sheng to give him the instructions for the two days’ feasting.

Lai Sheng heard his orders and went to make the customary arrangements. We need say no more of that. At noon the next day, a servant announced that the invited Mr Zhang had arrived. Jia Zhen showed him into the main hall and asked him to sit down. When they had taken tea, he began:
‘Mr Feng told me yesterday of your character and learning, sir, and of your profound knowledge of medicine. I cannot tell you how much I admire you.’
‘I am only a coarse, insignificant scholar, with very little knowledge or understanding,’ said Mr Zhang. ‘Mr Feng told me yesterday how graciously you and your family receive men of learning, however humble. When you were kind enough to send for me, how could I refuse? But I have no real attainments, and am all the more ashamed.’
‘You are too modest, sir,’ said Jia Zhen. ‘Please go in and see my daughter-in-law. We are relying on your skill to set my mind at rest.’
Jia Rong accompanied him inside. When they reached Jia Rong’s rooms and he saw Qin-shi, he asked, ‘This is your wife?’
‘Yes,’ Jia Rong answered. ‘Please sit down, sir. May I tell you about my wife’s illness before you feel her pulse?’
‘I think it would be better if I took her pulse first.

‘Please feel her pulse and see whether she can be cured, so that my father and mother may be reassured.’
The married women servants brought a large cushion and drew back Qin-shi’s sleeve to expose her wrist. When he had finished, he said, ‘Let us sit outside.’

segments.text: Jia Rong accompanied Mr Zhang to the outer room, where they sat on the bed. An older woman brought tea.
‘Please have some tea, sir,’ said Jia Rong.
He drank with Mr Zhang, then asked, ‘From the pulse, sir, do you think she can be cured or not?’

‘Your wife’s pulse is deep and rapid at the left cun position, deep and hidden at the left guan, fine and weak at the right cun, and deficient and lacking vitality at the right guan. A deep, rapid pulse at the left cun means that deficient heart-qi has generated fire. A deep, hidden pulse at the left guan means that qi in the liver is stagnant and its blood deficient. A fine, weak pulse at the right cun means that qi in the lung channel is greatly deficient. A pulse deficient and lacking vitality at the right guan means that spleen-earth is constrained by liver-wood. When deficient heart-qi generates fire, one should expect irregular periods and sleeplessness at night.

‘When the liver has deficient blood and stagnant qi, there must be pain and swelling beneath the ribs, delayed periods and a sensation of heat within the chest. segments.text:
Mr Zhang smiled.
‘Those gentlemen have certainly delayed the treatment of your mistress’s condition. If she had been given medicine when she first began menstruating, she would never have come to this. Indeed, by now she would have been quite well. As it is, the delay has brought her illness to this pass. It must be a misfortune she was destined to suffer. As I see it, there are still three parts in ten of hope for a cure. Let us see how she takes my medicine. If she can sleep at night, that will give me another two parts of confidence. Her pulse tells me that your mistress is strong-willed and exceptionally intelligent. When people are too intelligent, things often fail to satisfy them, and when that happens often, they think and worry too much. In this illness, anxiety has injured the spleen and liver-wood has grown too strong, so that the menstrual blood cannot come at the proper time. Ask about her periods in the past. The intervals will never have been regularly shortened; they must have been regularly prolonged. Am I right?’
‘Indeed you are,’ the woman replied. ‘They’ve never been shorter. She’s been two or three days late, and even as much as ten.’
‘Excellent!’ said Mr Zhang.

segments.text:
‘There is the source of the illness. If she had taken medicines to nourish the heart and regulate her periods earlier, how could it have come to this? Now she is clearly showing signs of deficient water and excessive wood. Let us try medicine and see.’
He wrote a prescription and handed it to Jia Rong. It read:

Decoction to Replenish Qi, Nourish the Blood, Fortify the Spleen and Harmonise the Liver

Ginseng, two qian; baizhu, two qian, stir-fried with earth; yunling, three qian; shudi, four qian.
Guishen, two qian, rinsed with wine; baishao, two qian; chuanxiong, one and a half qian; huangqi, three qian.
Processed xiangfu, two qian; vinegar-prepared chaihu, eight fen; huaishanyao, two qian, stir-fried; genuine ejiao, two qian, stir-fried with clam-shell powder.
Yanhusuo, one and a half qian, stir-fried with wine; prepared liquorice, eight fen.
To guide the decoction: seven Jian lotus seeds with the bitter centres removed, and two red dates.

‘Most skilful,’ said Jia Rong when he had read it. ‘There is one more thing I must ask, sir. Will this illness ultimately put her life in danger?’
Mr Zhang smiled.
‘You are a very discerning gentleman. An illness does not reach this stage overnight. Even with this medicine, much will depend on her good fortune in finding the right treatment. As I see it, she should come to no harm throughout this winter.

‘Once she is past the Spring Equinox, there will be hope of a full recovery.’
Jia Rong was an intelligent young man himself, and did not press him further. He saw Mr Zhang out, then took the prescription and the record of his findings to Jia Zhen. He repeated everything that had been said to both Jia Zhen and You-shi.
‘No doctor has ever spoken so plainly,’ You-shi said to Jia Zhen. ‘I imagine his medicine will be good too.’
‘He’s not one of those men who has spent his life practising medicine to earn his keep,’ said Jia Zhen.

‘It was only because Feng Zi-ying is a friend of ours that he managed, with some difficulty, to persuade him to come. Now that we’ve found him, perhaps our daughter-in-law will get well. There’s ginseng in his prescription. Use the one catty of good ginseng we bought the other day.’
When Jia Rong had heard these instructions, he went out and sent someone to get the medicine, have it decocted and give it to Qin-shi. To learn how her illness fared after she had taken it, you must read the next chapter.

segments.text: Now it was Jia Jing’s birthday. Jia Zhen first had sixteen large presentation boxes packed with the finest delicacies and some unusual fruits, and sent Jia Rong with a party of household servants to take them to Jia Jing.

‘Watch carefully and see whether your grandfather likes them,’ he told Jia Rong. ‘Pay your respects, then come back. Tell him, “My father has obeyed your instructions and has not ventured to come. He has led the whole household in paying their respects to you from home.”’
Jia Rong took his instructions and set off with the servants.

segments.text: Meanwhile the guests began to arrive. Jia Lian and Jia Qiang came first. They inspected the seating arrangements in the various rooms and asked whether there was to be any entertainment.

‘Our master had meant to invite the old master home today,’ the servants replied, ‘so we hadn’t dared arrange any. The day before yesterday we heard he wasn’t coming after all, and we’ve now been told to find a troupe of child actors and a shifan instrumental ensemble. They’re all waiting on the stage in the garden.’

segments.text: Next came Lady Xing, Lady Wang, Xi-feng and Bao-yu. Jia Zhen and You-shi welcomed them inside. You-shi’s mother was already there. After they had exchanged greetings and politely urged one another to take the seats of honour, Jia Zhen and You-shi served the tea themselves.

‘The old lady is the senior member of our family, and my father is her nephew,’ Jia Zhen said. ‘We should never have presumed to invite her on such an occasion. But the weather is so pleasantly cool just now, and the garden is full of chrysanthemums. We thought she might come over for a little diversion and enjoy seeing all the children and grandchildren making merry. That was all we meant. Who would have thought she would refuse to honour us?’
Before Lady Wang could answer, Xi-feng spoke up.

‘Only yesterday Grandmother was still saying she would come. But in the evening she saw Cousin Bao and the others eating peaches, and got a fancy for some herself. She ate more than half a peach, and during the fifth watch she had to get up twice in quick succession. This morning she felt a little tired. She sent me to tell you she really couldn’t come today. But she wants a few of the good things to eat, and they must be cooked very soft.’
Jia Zhen laughed. ‘I said there must be some reason. She does love a lively gathering. If that’s all it is, there’s nothing to worry about.’

segments.text: ‘The other day Xi-feng told me Rong’s wife was not quite well,’ said Lady Wang. ‘What exactly is the matter with her?’

‘It’s a strange illness,’ You-shi replied. ‘At the Mid-Autumn Festival last month she stayed up half the night enjoying herself with the old lady and all of you. She was perfectly well when she came home. But after the twentieth she grew more listless every day, and didn’t feel like eating either. That’s been going on for over half a month now. And she hasn’t had her period for two months.’
‘Could she be expecting?’ Lady Xing put in.
Just then a servant announced from outside, ‘The Elder Master and the Second Master have arrived with the other gentlemen of the family. They’re in the hall.’
Jia Zhen hurried out. Only then did You-shi continue.

‘Some of the doctors did say that at first. Yesterday Feng Zi-ying recommended a gentleman he used to study under, who knows a great deal about medicine. He examined her and said she wasn’t expecting at all: it was quite a serious illness. He wrote a prescription yesterday, and she’s taken one dose. Her dizziness is a little better today, but there hasn’t been much improvement in anything else.’
‘I know she’d have struggled up on a day like this,’ said Xi-feng, ‘if she could possibly have kept going.’
‘You saw her here on the third,’ said You-shi. ‘She forced herself to stay for half the day. It was only because you two are so fond of each other that she couldn’t bear to go.’
Xi-feng’s eyes reddened. For a long while she could say nothing. At last she said, ‘It’s true enough: “The sky may change without warning; fortune or disaster may overtake us in a day.”’

segments.text: ‘At her age, if this illness should carry her off, what pleasure would there be in being left alive ourselves?’
As they were talking, Jia Rong came in. He paid his respects to Lady Xing, Lady Wang and Xi-feng before making his report to You-shi.

‘I took the food to Grandfather just now. I told him Father was at home attending to the elder gentlemen and entertaining the rest of the family, and had obeyed his instructions by not venturing to come himself. Grandfather was very pleased. “That’s as it should be,” he said. He told me to tell Father and Mother to look after the elder gentlemen and ladies properly, and said I must attend to my uncles and aunts and the older cousins. He also said the Tract on Hidden Virtue was to be cut on printing blocks at once, and ten thousand copies printed to give away. I’ve told Father all this already. I must go out now and see that the elder gentlemen and the rest of the family have their dinner.’
‘Wait a moment, Rong,’ said Xi-feng. ‘How is your wife today, really?’
Jia Rong frowned. ‘Not well at all!’

segments.text: ‘Come and see her later, Aunt, and you’ll know.’
With that he went out. You-shi turned to Lady Xing and Lady Wang.
‘Would you rather have dinner here, or go and eat in the garden? The child actors are ready there now.’
‘Why don’t we eat first and go over afterwards?’ Lady Wang suggested to Lady Xing. ‘It will save a good deal of trouble.’
‘Very well,’ Lady Xing agreed.

You-shi ordered the married women servants and old women to bring in dinner at once. A chorus of assent came from outside the door, and each went to fetch her share of the dishes. Before long the meal was set out. You-shi persuaded Lady Xing, Lady Wang and her own mother to take the seats of honour; she herself sat at the side with Xi-feng and Bao-yu.
‘We came to wish the Elder Master a happy birthday,’ Lady Xing and Lady Wang said. ‘Anyone would think we had come to celebrate our own!’
‘The Elder Master has always liked peace and quiet,’ said Xi-feng. ‘He’s perfected his spiritual training by now. You might almost call him an immortal.’

segments.text: ‘So when you put it like that, ladies, it’s a case of “A thought in the heart is known to the gods.”’

Everyone in the room laughed. When You-shi’s mother, Lady Xing, Lady Wang and Xi-feng had finished dinner, rinsed their mouths and washed their hands, they began talking of going to the garden. Jia Rong came in and spoke to You-shi.

‘The elder gentlemen and all the uncles and cousins, older and younger, have finished too. The Elder Master said he had business at home, and the Second Master doesn’t care for plays and finds the noise too much for him, so they’ve both just left. Second Uncle Lian and Cousin Qiang have persuaded all the other gentlemen to go over and watch the plays. The four princely households, the Princes of Nan’an, Dongping, Xining and Beijing, have all sent servants with visiting cards and birthday gifts. So have the six households that include the Niu family of the Duke of Zhen, and the eight that include the Shi family of the Marquis of Zhongjing. I’ve reported everything to Father. The gifts are in the counting-house for the moment, and the gift lists have all been entered in the register. Father’s cards acknowledging the gifts and conveying his thanks have been handed to the messengers. They’ve all had the customary tips, and we saw that every one of them had a meal before leaving.’

segments.text: ‘You should invite the two ladies, Grandmother and Aunt over to sit in the garden now, Mother.’
‘We’ve only just finished,’ said You-shi. ‘We were about to go.’
‘If you’ll excuse me, Aunt,’ Xi-feng said to Lady Wang, ‘I’ll go and see Rong’s wife first, and join you afterwards.’
‘Quite right,’ Lady Wang said. ‘We would all like to see her, but we’re afraid she might find a crowd too much. Give her our love.’
‘There’s a dear sister,’ You-shi said. ‘She listens to you. If you can talk her out of her low spirits, I shall feel easier too. But do come along to the garden soon.’
Bao-yu wanted to go with Xi-feng to see Qin-shi.
‘Just look in on her, then come straight over,’ Lady Wang told him. ‘Remember, she is your nephew’s wife.’
You-shi led Lady Xing, Lady Wang and her mother into the Garden of Gathered Fragrance.

segments.text: Xi-feng and Bao-yu now went with Jia Rong to Qin-shi’s rooms. They entered quietly and approached the door of the inner room. At the sight of them Qin-shi tried to rise.
‘No, don’t get up,’ Xi-feng said. ‘You’ll make yourself dizzy if you get up too quickly.’
She hurried forward a couple of steps and took Qin-shi’s hand.
‘My dear girl! How can you have grown so thin in these few days?’
She sat down on the mattress beside her. Bao-yu asked how she was and took a chair opposite. Jia Rong called for tea.
‘Be quick! Aunt and Second Uncle haven’t had any tea in the main rooms yet.’

segments.text: Holding Xi-feng’s hand, Qin-shi forced a smile.

‘It’s my own lack of good fortune. To have married into a family like this! My father-in-law and mother-in-law treat me as their own daughter. Your nephew may be young, Aunt, but he has always treated me with respect, and I him. We’ve never had a cross word. As for the other members of the family, older or of my own generation, there isn’t one who hasn’t been kind to me, or with whom I haven’t got on well. I needn’t speak of you, Aunt. Now this illness has taken away every bit of the spirit I had to do things well. I haven’t had a single day to show my devotion to my parents-in-law. And you’ve been so loving to me, Aunt. Even if I longed with all my heart to show you the same devotion, I couldn’t do it now. I don’t think I shall last out the year.’

segments.text: Bao-yu had been gazing at Spring Sleep among the Crab-apple Blossoms and the couplet written by Qin Tai-xu:

A gentle chill confines the dream: spring is still cold;
Fragrance enfolds the sleeper: wine perfumes the air.

He could not help remembering the afternoon nap he had taken here and his dream of the Land of Illusion. As he sat lost in thought, Qin-shi’s words struck him like ten thousand arrows in the heart. Before he knew it, tears were running down his face. Xi-feng was deeply distressed herself, but feared that the sight of them all looking so would only make the sick woman more miserable. That would defeat their purpose in coming to comfort and encourage her. Seeing Bao-yu’s tears, she spoke to him.

‘Cousin Bao, you’re being an old woman! She only talks like that because she’s ill. It hasn’t come to that yet. And how old is she, after all? A little illness, and she starts thinking this and imagining that. Isn’t that enough to make her worse?’
‘There’s nothing else needed for this illness,’ said Jia Rong. ‘If she could only eat a little, there’d be nothing to fear.’
‘Cousin Bao,’ Xi-feng said, ‘your mother wants you to go over at once.’

segments.text: Left with Qin-shi, Xi-feng tried again to comfort her. They spoke for a long time in low voices, opening their hearts to one another. You-shi had sent two or three times to fetch her before Xi-feng finally took leave.
‘Look after yourself properly. I’ll come again. You must be meant to get well, or someone wouldn’t have recommended such a good doctor the other day. There’s nothing to be afraid of now.’
Qin-shi smiled. ‘An immortal himself might cure an illness, but he couldn’t cure one’s fate. Aunt, I know I’m only dragging out my days.’

‘How can you get well if you keep thinking like that?’ Xi-feng said. ‘You must try to put it out of your mind. Besides, I hear the doctor said if you weren’t treated, things might go badly in the spring.’

segments.text: ‘It’s only the middle of the ninth month now. There are still four or five months to go. What illness couldn’t be cured in all that time? If we were a family that couldn’t afford ginseng, that might be another matter. But if your father-in-law and mother-in-law heard it would cure you, never mind two qian of ginseng a day: they could afford two catties. Now take good care of yourself. I’m going over to the garden.’
‘You must forgive me for not going with you, Aunt,’ Qin-shi said. ‘When you have a little time, do please come and see me often. We can sit together, you and I, and have a few more talks.’
Xi-feng’s eyes reddened again in spite of herself.
‘Whenever I can get away, I’ll come.’

Taking the old women and maids who had accompanied her, together with the married women servants and old women of the Ning household, Xi-feng went round from the inner quarters and into the garden by a side gate. Here was a sight indeed: yellow flowers covered the ground, pale willows stretched across the slope. A little bridge might have led to the stream of Ruoye; a winding track might have joined the path to Tiantai. Clear water raced among the rocks; fragrance drifted from the hedges. Red leaves fluttered in the treetops, and the open woodland was a painting.

segments.text: The west wind freshened; the orioles’ song had only just ceased. In the warm sunshine, the crickets added their voices. Far off to the south-east, several open pavilions nestled against the hillside; to the north-west stood a three-bayed pavilion beside the water. The sound of reed pipes filled the air, bringing a charm all its own; silk-clad figures threaded the trees, lending the scene still greater grace.

‘My respects to you, Sister-in-law.’
Taken by surprise, Xi-feng drew back a step.
‘Why, isn’t this Master Rui?’
‘Don’t you recognise me any more, Sister-in-law?’ Jia Rui asked.

segments.text: ‘Who else could it be?’
‘It’s not that I don’t recognise you,’ Xi-feng said. ‘You startled me. I never expected to see you here.’

‘It must be that you and I were meant to meet, Sister-in-law,’ Jia Rui said. ‘I slipped out of the feast just now for a little stroll somewhere quiet. And here you are, coming this way too! If that isn’t fate, what is?’
As he spoke, his eyes kept straying to Xi-feng.

segments.text: Xi-feng was a clever woman. Seeing the way he behaved, how could she fail to guess most of what was in his mind? With a show of smiling friendliness she answered him.

‘No wonder your cousin Lian is always speaking of you and saying what a good fellow you are. Now I’ve met you and heard you talk, I can see at once how sensible and pleasant you are. I must go to the ladies just now, so I can’t stay and talk. We’ll have a chat another time, when we’re free.’
‘I’ve wanted to come to your house and pay my respects,’ Jia Rui said, ‘but I was afraid that, being so young, you might not care to receive visitors.’
Xi-feng put on another smile. ‘We’re all one family. What has being young to do with it?’
Jia Rui had never dreamed he would have such a stroke of luck that day. At these words, the look on his face and his whole manner became more unseemly than ever.
‘Do go back to your seat,’ Xi-feng said. ‘Take care they don’t catch you and make you drink a forfeit.’
By now Jia Rui felt half his body go numb. He walked slowly away, turning to look back as he went.

‘Your mistress is always in such a devil of a hurry,’ Xi-feng said.

segments.text: Still walking slowly, she asked how many scenes had been performed.
‘Eight or nine,’ one of the women replied.
As they spoke, they reached the back entrance of the Tower of Heavenly Fragrance. Bao-yu was playing there with a group of maids.
‘Cousin Bao, don’t get up to too much mischief,’ Xi-feng told him.
‘The ladies are all sitting upstairs,’ one of the maids said. ‘Please come up this way, ma’am.’

segments.text: Xi-feng gathered up her skirts and went leisurely upstairs. You-shi was waiting at the top.

‘You two are far too fond of each other,’ she said, laughing. ‘Once you’ve met, there’s no getting you to come away. You’d better move in with her tomorrow. Sit down. I must give you a cup of wine before anything else.’

Xi-feng asked Lady Xing and Lady Wang’s permission to be seated, then exchanged a few courtesies with You-shi’s mother before joining You-shi at her table to drink and watch the plays. You-shi called for the list and asked her to choose a scene.
‘With your mother and both our ladies here, how could I presume to choose?’ Xi-feng said.
‘We and our good kinswoman have chosen several already,’ Lady Xing and Lady Wang told her. ‘Choose a couple of good ones for us to hear.’
Xi-feng rose to acknowledge the invitation before taking the list. She read it from the beginning and chose Return to Life and The Ballad, then handed it back.
‘When they’ve finished The Double Investiture, which they’re performing now, let them do these two. By then it will be time.’
‘Indeed it will,’ Lady Wang said. ‘We ought to let your cousin and his wife have an early rest. They have enough to worry about.’
‘You don’t come over often,’ You-shi protested. ‘It’s much nicer when we can all sit together a little longer. There’s plenty of daylight yet.’
Xi-feng stood up and looked down from the tower.
‘Where have all the men gone?’
‘They’ve just taken the shifan ensemble over to the Pavilion of Gathered Morning Light to drink,’ an old woman beside her answered.
‘They couldn’t do as they pleased here, could they?’ Xi-feng said. ‘Who knows what they’ll get up to out of sight!’
‘Not everyone is as proper as you,’ You-shi said, laughing.

segments.text: So they talked and laughed until the scenes they had chosen were over. Only then were the wine tables cleared and the meal brought in. When they had eaten, they left the garden and sat down in the main rooms for tea. At last they ordered the carriages and took leave of You-shi’s mother. You-shi, accompanied by the concubines and the household’s old women and married women servants, saw them out. Jia Zhen and the younger men of the family were already standing respectfully beside the carriages, waiting for them.
‘Aunts, do both come over again tomorrow,’ Jia Zhen said to Lady Xing and Lady Wang.
‘No, we’ve sat here the whole day and we’re tired,’ Lady Wang replied. ‘We shall rest tomorrow.’

They got into their carriages. Jia Rui was still stealing glances at Xi-feng from time to time. After Jia Zhen and the others had gone in, Li Gui brought up Bao-yu’s horse. Bao-yu mounted and followed Lady Wang home. Back at the Ning mansion, Jia Zhen and the other men, older and younger, had supper together before they finally dispersed.

segments.text: The next day the members of the clan made merry for another whole day, of which we need give no detailed account. After this Xi-feng often went herself to see Qin-shi. Some days Qin-shi was a little better; on others she was just as before. Jia Zhen, You-shi and Jia Rong were desperately anxious. Jia Rui, meanwhile, called at the Rong mansion several times, but each time Xi-feng happened to be away at the Ning mansion.

That year the Winter Solstice fell on the thirtieth day of the eleventh month. During the days around the turn of the season, Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang and Xi-feng sent someone every day to ask after Qin-shi. The messengers all returned with the same report: ‘She hasn’t grown any worse these last few days, but she isn’t much better either.’

segments.text: ‘With an illness like this, if she can get through such an important turn of the season without growing worse, there’s a great deal to hope for,’ Lady Wang told Grandmother Jia.
‘Indeed there is,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Such a dear child! If anything were to happen to her, it would break our hearts.’

segments.text: The thought brought a pang to her heart. She called Xi-feng to her.

‘You two have been so close. Tomorrow is the first of the month; let tomorrow go by, then go and see her the day after. Look at her very carefully. If she’s a little better, come back and tell me, so that I can be glad too. And have them make the things she’s always liked to eat and send them over often.’
Xi-feng agreed to each of her requests.

segments.text: On the second, after breakfast, she went to the Ning mansion. Qin-shi’s illness had not grown much worse, but the flesh had wasted away from her face and body. Xi-feng sat with her for half the day, making conversation and once again assuring her that there was no cause for alarm.
‘We shall know in the spring whether I’m going to get well,’ Qin-shi said.

segments.text: ‘Now the Winter Solstice is past and nothing has happened, perhaps I may recover after all. Do tell the old lady and Her Ladyship not to worry, Aunt. I ate two of the yam cakes filled with jujube paste that the old lady sent me yesterday. I really seemed able to digest them.’
‘I’ll send you some more tomorrow,’ Xi-feng said. ‘I’m going to look in on your mother-in-law now, then I must hurry back and report to Grandmother.’
‘Please give the old lady and Her Ladyship my respects, Aunt,’ Qin-shi said.

segments.text: Xi-feng promised and went out. She took a seat in You-shi’s main room.
‘Now you’ve had a chance to judge for yourself, how do you think she is?’ You-shi asked.
Xi-feng kept her head lowered for a long time.
‘There really is nothing to be done. You ought to get the things ready that will be needed afterwards. It might even turn her luck.’
‘I’ve had people preparing them quietly,’ You-shi said. ‘Only we can’t find good wood for that one thing. We shall have to take our time over it.’
Xi-feng drank her tea and stayed talking for a while. Then she said, ‘I must hurry back now and tell Grandmother.’
‘Break it to her gently,’ You-shi said. ‘Don’t frighten her.’
‘I know.’

Xi-feng returned home. When she saw Grandmother Jia, she said, ‘Rong’s wife sends her respects and kowtows to you. She says she’s a little better, and begs you not to worry. As soon as she’s a little stronger, she wants to come and kowtow to you herself.’

segments.text: ‘What did you think of her?’ Grandmother Jia asked.
‘There’s no danger for the moment. She’s still quite bright.’
Grandmother Jia pondered this for a long while.
‘Go and change your clothes and rest,’ she told Xi-feng.

segments.text: Xi-feng assented and went out. After seeing Lady Wang, she returned to her own rooms, where Patience helped her change into the everyday clothes she had been warming for her. As soon as she sat down, Xi-feng asked, ‘Has anything happened at home?’
Patience brought her tea and handed it to her.

‘Nothing much. Wang-er’s wife brought in the interest on those three hundred taels of silver. I took it from her. And Master Rui sent someone to ask whether you were at home. He wants to call and pay his respects, and have a word with you.’

segments.text: Xi-feng gave a snort.
‘The brute is bent on getting himself killed. Let’s see what happens when he comes!’
‘Why does this Master Rui keep coming?’ Patience asked.
Xi-feng told her all about meeting him in the Ning garden in the ninth month, and what he had said.
‘A toad hankering after swan’s flesh!’ Patience said. ‘The shameless, good-for-nothing creature, with no respect for family decency! May he die a wretched death for thinking of such a thing!’
‘Let him come,’ said Xi-feng. ‘I know how to deal with him.’
What happened when Jia Rui came? To find out, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: Now Xi-feng was talking to Patience when someone came to announce, ‘Master Rui is here.’
‘Show him in at once,’ Xi-feng said promptly.
Jia Rui was overjoyed to find himself invited inside. He hurried in and greeted Xi-feng again and again, his face all smiles. She too made a show of eagerness, offering him a seat and tea.

segments.text: The sight of Xi-feng dressed as she was made Jia Rui melt still further. With languishing eyes he asked, ‘Why hasn’t Second Brother come back yet?’
‘I don’t know what’s keeping him.’
‘Perhaps someone has detained him on the road,’ Jia Rui said with a smile, ‘and he can’t bear to come away?’
‘Perhaps. There are men who fall in love with every woman they see.’
‘You’re wrong there, Sister-in-law,’ Jia Rui said with a smile. ‘I’m not like that.’
‘How many men are there like you?’ Xi-feng asked, smiling. ‘You couldn’t pick one out of ten.’
Jia Rui scratched his ears and rubbed his cheeks in delight. ‘You must find it very dull, day after day?’
‘Indeed I do. I keep hoping someone will come and talk to me, to relieve the boredom.’
‘I’m free every day,’ he said with a smile. ‘How would it be if I came every day to keep you company?’
Xi-feng smiled. ‘You’re teasing me. As if you’d want to come here!’
‘May Heaven strike me with a thunderbolt if I tell you a single lie, Sister-in-law!

segments.text: ‘It was only because I had heard people say you were so formidable, and one couldn’t put a foot wrong in front of you, that I was frightened off. Now I find you so ready to laugh and talk, and so kind, how could I stay away? I’d come even if it killed me!’

‘You really are a man of understanding,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘Far better than Jia Rong and the other one. With such a pretty face, I thought he must have some sense, and the other too. But they’re a pair of fools. They haven’t the least idea what anyone feels.’

segments.text: This went straight to Jia Rui’s heart. He could not help edging a little closer, peering at the purse Xi-feng wore, then asking what rings she had on.
‘Behave yourself,’ she said softly. ‘Don’t let the maids see you and laugh.’
To Jia Rui it was like hearing an imperial decree or the words of the Buddha. He hastily moved back.
‘You ought to go now,’ Xi-feng said, smiling.
‘Let me sit a little longer. How cruel you are, Sister-in-law!’

She lowered her voice again. ‘In broad daylight, with people coming and going, it’s hardly convenient for you to stay here. Go now, and come back tonight when the watches have begun. Wait quietly for me in the passage on the west side.’
Jia Rui received this like a precious treasure. ‘You won’t play me false? But so many people go through there. How can I keep out of sight?’
‘Don’t worry. I’ll give all the boys on night duty leave. Once the doors at both ends are shut, there won’t be anyone else.’
Delighted beyond measure, Jia Rui hurriedly took his leave, convinced that success was his.

segments.text: At last evening came. Sure enough, he felt his way into the Rong mansion in the dark and slipped into the passage as the doors were being shut. It was indeed pitch-black and deserted. The door towards Grandmother Jia’s quarters was already bolted; only the one to the east remained open. Jia Rui strained his ears, but a long time passed and no one came. Suddenly there was a clunk: the eastern door had been bolted too. In his alarm he dared not make a sound. He could only creep out and shake the door. It was shut as tight as an iron barrel. There was no getting out now.

segments.text: To north and south were the walls of great buildings, with no handhold by which he might climb over. The passage itself was bare and draughty. It was the twelfth month, the night was long, and the bitter north wind cut into his flesh and split his very bones. He all but froze to death that night.

segments.text: Jia Rui’s parents had died when he was young, and he had been brought up by his grandfather Dai-ru alone. Dai-ru was always very strict with him. He would not let him stray a step, for fear he might go drinking or gambling and neglect his studies. Now that he had stayed out all night, Dai-ru was certain he had been drinking or gambling, visiting brothels and sleeping with prostitutes. This particular adventure never entered his head, and he had been furious all night.
Jia Rui was in a cold sweat too. Once home, he had no choice but to lie. ‘I went to my mother’s brother’s house. It got dark, and they kept me for the night.’
‘You have never dared go out without telling me first,’ Dai-ru said. ‘Why did you go off on your own yesterday? That alone deserves a beating, let alone the lie!’

In his fury he gave him a full thirty or forty strokes with the board, forbade him any food, and made him kneel in the courtyard reciting his lessons. He was to make up ten days’ work before he could stop. After a whole night in the freezing cold, Jia Rui now had a savage beating, and knelt hungry in the wind reciting essays. His sufferings were beyond description. Yet his desire had not changed at all. It still never occurred to him that Xi-feng was making a fool of him.

segments.text: Two days later he found a chance to call on Xi-feng again. She deliberately reproached him for breaking his word, and in his agitation he swore oath after oath. Seeing him walk straight into the net, she had to devise another scheme to make him mend his ways.
‘Don’t wait in that place tonight,’ she told him. ‘Wait in the empty room in the little passage behind my rooms. And don’t blunder about.’
‘Do you mean it?’
‘Who’s deceiving you? If you don’t believe me, don’t come.’
‘I’ll come, I’ll come, I’ll come! I’ll come if it kills me!’
‘Go along now, then.’
Certain that everything would go well that night, Jia Rui left for the time being. Xi-feng began mustering her forces and laying her trap.

segments.text: Jia Rui could scarcely wait for nightfall, but some relatives happened to call at home and stayed until after supper. By the time they left, the lamps had already been lit. He had to wait again until his grandfather was in bed before he could slip into the Rong mansion and make straight for the room in the narrow passage. There he waited, turning helplessly round and round like an ant on a hot pan. He looked and looked, but saw no one; he listened and listened, but heard nothing. ‘Can she be staying away again?’ he wondered. ‘Am I to be left to freeze for another night?’

‘My darling sister-in-law! You’ve kept me waiting till I’m half dead!’

segments.text: He carried the figure inside to the kang, kissing and tugging at trousers, babbling ‘My darling mother!’ and ‘My darling father!’ The other remained silent. Jia Rui pulled down his own trousers and, stiff with excitement, was about to thrust himself in when a light suddenly flared.
‘Who’s in there?’ called Jia Qiang, holding up a lighted taper.
The figure on the kang laughed. ‘Uncle Rui is trying to shame me.’
Jia Rui looked: it was Jia Rong. He was so mortified he wished he could sink through the floor. At a loss what to do, he turned to run, but Jia Qiang caught hold of him.
‘Stay where you are! Aunt Lian has already complained to Her Ladyship that you’ve been making advances to her without the least encouragement.

‘That’s easy enough. Only there’s no paper or brush here.’

segments.text: ‘That’s easy enough too,’ said Jia Qiang. He went out at once. Paper and brush were ready to hand, and he brought them in and made Jia Rui write. After much bargaining between the two of them, the sum was brought down to fifty taels of silver. Jia Rui put his mark to the document, and Jia Qiang took it away.

Then there was Jia Rong to deal with. At first he was adamant. ‘Tomorrow I’ll tell the clan and let them judge,’ was all he would say. Jia Rui was so desperate that he went down on his knees and kowtowed. Jia Qiang coaxed and argued until another bond for fifty taels had been written; only then was it settled.

‘If I let you go now, I’m taking the blame on myself,’ Jia Qiang said. ‘The door on Her Old Ladyship’s side has long been shut, and His Lordship is in the hall looking at the things from Nanjing. You certainly can’t go that way. There’s only the back gate. But if you run into anyone going out, I’m done for too. Wait while we go and see whether the coast is clear, and then we’ll come and take you out. You can’t hide in this room, either. They’ll be bringing things in to store here in a moment. Let me find somewhere.’

He took Jia Rui by the arm, put out the light again, and led him into the courtyard. Feeling his way to the foot of a high flight of steps, he said, ‘This hollow will do. Crouch here and don’t make a sound. Don’t move until we come.’ Then the two of them went away.

segments.text: Jia Rui had no choice now but to crouch there. He was turning things over in his mind when he heard a noise above his head. Down came a whole slop-pail of urine and faeces, splashing over his head and body. He could not suppress a cry, but quickly covered his mouth, afraid to make a noise. His head, face and body were plastered with filth; he shivered with cold. Then Jia Qiang came running up.
‘Quick! Go, go!’

segments.text: As though granted his life again, Jia Rui ran home by the back gate in a few bounds. It was already the third watch, and he had to call for the gate to be opened. The person who opened the door saw the state he was in and asked what had happened. He had to lie again. ‘It was dark. I missed my footing and fell into the privy.’

He went to his room to change and wash. Only now did it dawn on him that Xi-feng had been playing with him, and for a while he hated her. Then he thought of her looks and longed to have her in his arms that very instant. He did not close his eyes all night.

segments.text: From then on his thoughts were full of Xi-feng, though he dared not go to the Rong mansion again. Jia Rong and his companion kept coming to demand their money, and he was afraid his grandfather would find out. His longing was hard enough to bear, and now there were debts as well; by day his studies left him little respite. He was a man in his twenties, still unmarried, and with Xi-feng so much in his thoughts, his fingers had inevitably been called upon to work themselves weary. Add to this the cold, vexation and exertion of those two nights: assailed from several sides at once, he fell ill before he knew it.

His chest felt distended, there was no taste in his mouth, his legs were like cotton, his eyes as though full of vinegar. He burned at night and was weary by day; semen passed with his urine, and he coughed blood in his phlegm. In less than a year he had acquired all these symptoms. At last he could hold out no longer and took to his bed. Even with his eyes shut he was still lost in disordered dreams, babbling wildly and frightened out of his wits. Doctors were summoned and every sort of treatment tried. He swallowed dozens of catties of such medicines as cinnamon bark, fuzi, soft-shelled turtle shell, maidong and yuzhu, without the slightest improvement.

segments.text: Before long the twelfth month had ended and spring returned, and his illness grew still worse. Dai-ru was alarmed now. He called in doctors from everywhere, but nothing they did had any effect. Later Jia Rui began taking a ginseng-only decoction. How could Dai-ru afford that? He had to go to the Rong mansion to ask for some ginseng.

segments.text: Lady Wang told Xi-feng to weigh out two taels for him.

‘The new supply was all used for Her Old Ladyship’s medicine the other day,’ Xi-feng replied. ‘And you said the whole roots were to be kept for Commander Yang’s wife to make up her medicine. As it happens, I sent them over yesterday.’

‘Even if we have none here, send someone to ask your mother-in-law, or try your Cousin Zhen’s household. Get some together for them. If it does him good and saves a life, that will be to your credit too.’

Xi-feng listened, but sent no one to look. Instead she scraped together a few qian of crumbs, dregs and little root fibres and had them sent over, with the message, ‘Her Ladyship sends you this. There isn’t any more.’

segments.text: She then reported to Lady Wang, ‘I’ve tried everywhere. We managed to get together over two taels and sent it all.’

By now Jia Rui wanted so desperately to live that there was no medicine he would refuse. It only wasted money; nothing helped. One day a lame Taoist came begging for food, proclaiming that his special skill was to cure afflictions born of karmic wrongs. Jia Rui happened to hear him from inside and cried at the top of his voice, ‘Quick, ask that Bodhisattva in to save me!’

segments.text: As he called, he knocked his forehead against his pillow. The others had to bring the Taoist in. Jia Rui seized him, crying again and again, ‘Bodhisattva, save me!’
‘Your illness is beyond medicine,’ the Taoist said with a sigh. ‘But I have a treasure for you. Look into it every day, and your life can be saved.’
From his shoulder-bag he took a mirror which reflected on both sides. Its handle bore the inscription ‘The Mirror of Love and Desire’, engraved in four Chinese characters. He handed it to Jia Rui.

‘This object comes from the Hall of Numinous Emptiness in the Land of Illusion. It was made by Fairy Disenchantment to cure the afflictions of wayward thoughts and unruly desires, and has the power to help the world and preserve life. That is why I have brought it into the world, solely for clever, gifted men and cultivated young nobles to look into.

segments.text: ‘Never, on any account, look into the front. Look only into the back. This is vital, vital! I shall return in three days to fetch it, and I guarantee you will be well.’
With that he went away. For all their entreaties, they could not keep him. Jia Rui took the mirror. ‘There’s something in what this Taoist says,’ he thought. ‘Why shouldn’t I try looking?’

segments.text: He picked up the Mirror of Love and Desire and looked into the back. There stood a skeleton. So frightened was he that he hastily covered the mirror.
‘Damn that Taoist! Why does he want to frighten me?’
‘I’ll have a look at the front and see what’s there,’ he thought.

He turned it over and looked. Xi-feng was standing inside, beckoning to him. His heart leapt with joy. He felt himself drifting into the mirror, where he lay with Xi-feng; afterwards she saw him out again. Back on his bed he gave a cry and opened his eyes. The mirror slipped from his hand and turned over, showing the skeleton in its reverse once more. He felt himself wet with sweat; beneath him he had spilled a pool of semen. Still unsatisfied, he turned the front towards him again. Xi-feng was still beckoning, and in he went.
This happened three or four times. On this occasion, just as he was about to come out of the mirror, two men approached, looped an iron chain about him and dragged him away.
‘Let me take the mirror before I go!’ Jia Rui cried. Those were the last words he could speak.

segments.text: The people attending Jia Rui at his bedside saw only that at first he kept looking into the mirror, dropping it, then opening his eyes and picking it up again. The last time the mirror fell, he did not move. They came to look: he had stopped breathing. Beneath his body lay a great cold, wet patch of semen. They hurried to dress him and move him to the bier.
Dai-ru and his wife wept until they were nearly dead themselves, cursing the Taoist. ‘What a devilish mirror! If we don’t destroy it at once, there’s no telling what harm it will do in the world.’
They ordered a fire made to burn it. But a voice inside the mirror began to weep.
‘Who told you to look into the front? You yourselves took the false for the true. Why must you burn me?’
While it was still crying, the lame Taoist came running in from outside.
‘Who would destroy the Mirror of Love and Desire? I have come to save it!’
He went straight into the central hall, snatched it up and floated away.

segments.text: Dai-ru set about arranging the funeral and sent word of the death to everyone. On the third day the chanting of scriptures began; on the seventh the funeral procession set out. The coffin was left temporarily at the Temple of the Iron Threshold, to be taken back to their native place at a later date. All the Jia clan came to offer condolences. Jia She of the Rong mansion gave twenty taels of silver, Jia Zheng another twenty, and Jia Zhen of the Ning mansion twenty too. The other members of the clan gave according to their means, three taels here, five there, too many to enumerate. Contributions from the families of his fellow students came to another twenty or thirty taels. Though Dai-ru’s household was poorly off, he was able to see the business through in considerable style.

segments.text: Now, at the end of that winter, a letter arrived from Lin Ru-hai. He was seriously ill and had written especially to ask for Lin Dai-yu to come home. The news added to Grandmother Jia’s worries and distress, but there was nothing for it: she hurried to prepare Dai-yu for the journey. Bao-yu was deeply unhappy; yet, with the bond between father and daughter to consider, he could hardly try to stop her going. Grandmother Jia insisted that Jia Lian should escort her and bring her back again. There is no need to dwell on the local gifts and travelling expenses: naturally everything was properly provided. A date was chosen without delay, and Jia Lian and Lin Dai-yu took leave of Grandmother Jia and the others. With their servants, they boarded a boat for Yangzhou.
To learn what followed, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: One night the two of them sat by the brazier, tired of their embroidery beneath the lamp. Xi-feng had already ordered the embroidered quilts to be well warmed and scented. They lay down and counted off the days of the journey on their fingers, reckoning how far the travellers ought to have gone. Before she knew it, the third watch had begun. Patience was fast asleep. Xi-feng’s bright eyes were only just growing heavy when, dimly, she saw Qin-shi come in from outside. Smiling, she said, ‘How soundly you sleep, Aunt! I am going back today, and you have not even come to see me on my way. We have always been so close that I could not bear to leave you. That is why I have come to say goodbye. There is also one wish I have not fulfilled. I must tell you about it, Aunt. Someone else might be of no use.’
Still in a haze, Xi-feng asked, ‘What is troubling you? Whatever it is, leave it to me.’

‘Aunt,’ said Qin-shi, ‘you are a hero among women. Even the men in their caps and girdles cannot outdo you. How can you not know a couple of common sayings? “When the moon is full it begins to wane; when water is full it spills over.” And again, “The higher the climb, the harder the fall.” Our family has now enjoyed almost a hundred years of splendour. Suppose one day joy turned to sorrow, and the saying came true: “When the tree falls, the monkeys scatter.” Would all our claims to be an old family of learning not have been empty words?’
These words greatly heartened Xi-feng and filled her with awed respect. ‘You have thought this out very well,’ she said quickly. ‘But what can we do to keep ourselves safe for ever?’
Qin-shi gave a cold laugh. ‘How foolish you are, Aunt.

segments.text: ‘At the furthest point of adversity, prosperity returns. Honour and disgrace have followed one another in a circle since ancient times. How could human effort keep things always as they are? Still, if we use our prosperity to provide an estate for the lean times ahead, that might indeed be called lasting security. Everything is in order now except for two things. If we dealt with them in this way, we could ensure our future.’

segments.text: Xi-feng asked what they were.

‘At present,’ Qin-shi replied, ‘sacrifices are offered at the ancestral graves in all four seasons, but there is no fixed fund of money and grain for them. Secondly, the clan school has been established, but it has no assured provision either. While we are prosperous, of course, there is no shortage of money for sacrifices or for the school. But where will these two expenses come from when we have fallen on hard times? My settled view is that, while we are rich and honoured, we should buy more farms, houses and land near the ancestral graves, so that their income will meet both expenses. Move the clan school there too. Bring the elders and younger members of the clan together to draw up rules. Each branch should take its turn for a year, managing the land, the money and grain, the sacrifices and the school’s provision. With this rotation there would be no rivalry, nor such abuses as mortgaging or selling the property. Even if we were convicted of a crime and everything else confiscated, the government would not seize an estate devoted to ancestral sacrifices. Should the family decline, our descendants could go home to study and farm. They would have somewhere to fall back on, and the sacrifices could continue for ever. To suppose our present glory will never end, and give no thought to the future, is no lasting plan.

segments.text: ‘Very soon, you will see, there is to be another extraordinary piece of good fortune. Our splendour will be like oil seething over a fierce fire, like flowers heaped on brocade. But remember: it is only a moment’s glory, a brief time of happiness. Never forget the saying, “Every great feast must break up.” Unless you make provision now, when the time comes regret may be of no use.’
‘What good fortune?’ Xi-feng asked eagerly.
‘Heaven’s secrets must not be revealed. But for the sake of the affection we have shared, Aunt, I will leave you two lines before I go. Be sure to remember them.’ And she recited:

segments.text: By then the whole household knew. Everyone was astonished, and all felt some misgiving. Those of the older generation remembered her filial devotion; those of her own, her warmth and affection; the younger generation, her kindness. Old and young among the servants remembered how she had pitied the poor, cared for the lowly, cherished the old and loved the young. There was not one who did not weep and wail.
