segments.text: But let us leave these matters. Since Lin Dai-yu had gone away, Bao-yu too had felt lonely and desolate. He no longer played with anyone, but went listlessly to bed each night. Now, hearing in his sleep that Qin-shi was dead, he rolled over and scrambled up. It was as though a knife had pierced his heart. Unable to bear it, he gave a cry and brought up a mouthful of blood. Aroma and the others hurried to support him, asking what was wrong. They were going to tell Grandmother Jia and send for a doctor.
‘Do not fuss,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘It is nothing. A sudden rush of fire has attacked the heart, and the blood has strayed from its channels.’

As he spoke he got up, called for clothes to change into and went to see Grandmother Jia, determined to go over at once. Aroma was still uneasy, but dared not stop him and could only let him have his way.
‘Someone has only just breathed her last there. The place is unclean,’ Grandmother Jia said when he asked to go. ‘Besides, the wind is strong at night. Tomorrow morning will be soon enough.’
Bao-yu would not listen. Grandmother Jia ordered a carriage and sent extra servants to escort and protect him.

segments.text: They went straight to the Ning mansion. Its gates stood wide open, with lanterns on either side making the entrance as bright as day. People hurried noisily in and out, and the wailing within seemed enough to shake the mountains. Bao-yu got out of the carriage and rushed to the room where the body lay. After weeping bitterly there, he went to see You-shi, only to find her in bed with a recurrence of her old stomach pains.

segments.text: He then came out to see Jia Zhen. Jia Dai-ru had arrived, bringing Jia Chi, Jia Xiao, Jia Dun, Jia She, Jia Zheng, Jia Cong, Jia Bin, Jia Heng, Jia Guang, Jia Chen, Jia Qiong, Jia Lin, Jia Qiang, Jia Chang, Jia Ling, Jia Yun, Jia Qin, Jia Zhen, Jia Ping, Jia Zao, Jia Heng, Jia Fen, Jia Fang, Jia Lan, Jia Jun and Jia Zhi. Jia Zhen was dissolved in tears. He was saying to Jia Dai-ru and the others, ‘Who among our household, old or young, our distant relations or our closest friends, did not know that this daughter-in-law of mine was ten times better than my son? Now she has stretched out her legs and gone. This senior branch of the family is finished. There is no one left.’ He began to weep again.
They hastened to comfort him. ‘She has passed away. Tears will do no good now. What matters is to decide how the arrangements are to be made.’

segments.text: Jia Zhen struck his hands together. ‘How are they to be made? I shall simply give everything I have!’

As he spoke, Qin Ye and Qin Zhong arrived, together with several of You-shi’s relations, including her sisters. Jia Zhen told Jia Qiong, Jia Chen, Jia Lin and Jia Qiang to attend to the guests, and sent for an official from the Yin-yang Office of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau to select the dates. It was duly determined that the coffin should remain for seven times seven, forty-nine days, with formal mourning and the dispatch of notices to begin three days later. For those forty-nine days, a hundred and eight Chan monks alone were engaged to perform the Great Compassion repentance rite in the main hall, delivering the souls of those who had died before and those who would die hereafter, and absolving the dead of their sins. A separate altar was set up in the Tower of Heavenly Fragrance, where ninety-nine Quanzhen Taoist priests were to conduct, for forty-nine days, a Taoist offering rite to reconcile grievances and cleanse karmic burdens. The coffin was then placed in the Garden of Gathered Fragrance. Before it, another fifty eminent monks and fifty eminent Taoist priests performed rites at facing altars at each seven-day observance.

When Jia Jing heard that his eldest grandson’s wife had died, he was so certain that he himself would soon ascend to immortality that he could not possibly return home to be tainted by worldly dust and throw away all his previous efforts. He therefore paid little attention, leaving everything to Jia Zhen.

segments.text: With his father taking no part, Jia Zhen indulged all the more freely in extravagant display. Several sets of fir boards were inspected for the coffin, but none was good enough. Xue Pan happened to come to pay his condolences and, seeing Jia Zhen in search of fine timber, said, ‘There is a set of boards in our timber shop. The wood is called qiang, or something of the sort. It comes from Iron-net Mountain in the Huang Sea region. Make a coffin of it and it will last ten thousand years without rotting. My late father brought it back years ago. His Highness Prince Yi-zhong originally wanted it, but when things went wrong for him, he never took delivery. It is still sealed up in the shop. Nobody has dared offer a price for it. If you want it, have it brought over.’

Jia Zhen was overjoyed and immediately ordered it to be fetched. When it arrived, they saw that the boards for the sides and bottom were all eight cun thick. Their grain resembled areca nut, their scent sandalwood and musk. Tapped with the hand, they rang like metal or jade. Everyone marvelled and praised them.
‘What is the price?’ Jia Zhen asked, smiling.
Xue Pan smiled too. ‘Even with a thousand taels of silver, you might not find anything like it. Why talk of a price? Just give the men a few taels for their trouble.’
Jia Zhen thanked him repeatedly and at once ordered the sawing, pasting and lacquering to begin.

segments.text: Jia Zheng tried to dissuade him. ‘I fear this is not something an ordinary person is entitled to use. Then news came that a maid of Qin-shi’s named Gem, on seeing that her mistress was dead, had dashed herself against a pillar and died too.

segments.text: The occurrence was extraordinary, and the whole clan praised her. Jia Zhen had her laid out and coffined with the rites due to a granddaughter, and her coffin too was placed in the Garden of Gathered Fragrance, in the Ascension Pavilion. A young maid named Jewel, seeing that Qin-shi had left no child, freely offered to become her adopted daughter and pledged herself to break the funeral earthenware basin and go before the coffin as chief mourner. Jia Zhen was delighted. He ordered at once that everyone was henceforth to address Jewel as Miss.

segments.text: By chance, on the fourth day of the first seven-day mourning period, Dai Quan, chief palace eunuch of Daming Palace, first sent someone ahead with funeral offerings, then came in person to present them. He arrived in a grand sedan-chair, with a ceremonial umbrella and gongs sounded before him. Jia Zhen hurried out to receive him and invited him into the Bee-enticing Pavilion for tea. Having made up his mind, he took the opportunity to mention buying an official appointment for Jia Rong.
Dai Quan understood. ‘To make a finer show at the funeral, I suppose?’ he said with a smile.
‘You see it exactly, sir,’ Jia Zhen replied, smiling eagerly.

‘Well, you are in luck. There is a very good vacancy. Two places are unfilled among the three hundred Dragon Guards. Yesterday the Marquis of Xiangyang’s younger brother, the third of the brothers, came to see me. He has already sent fifteen hundred taels of silver to my house. You know what old friends we are. For his grandfather’s sake, I had to promise him something, one way or another. That left one vacancy. Then who should come asking but Fat Feng, the military commissioner of Yongxing, wanting to buy it for his boy. I had no time to give him an answer.

segments.text: ‘But since our own boy wants the appointment, have his particulars written out at once.’
Jia Zhen immediately gave orders: ‘Tell the men in the study to prepare the young master’s particulars with all due care. Quickly!’
The pages dared not delay. A little later one returned with a sheet of red paper. Jia Zhen read it and hastened to hand it to Dai Quan. It ran:

Jia Rong, Imperial Academy student, aged twenty, of Jiangning county, Jiangning prefecture, Jiangnan. Great-grandfather: Jia Dai-hua, formerly Commander of the Metropolitan Garrison, hereditary General of Divine Might of the First Rank. Grandfather: Jia Jing, jinshi of the yimao examination. Father: Jia Zhen, hereditary holder of the third-rank title General of Martial Valour.

segments.text: After reading it, Dai Quan passed it back to a personal attendant to put away. ‘Take this later to old Zhao, the senior official at the Board of Revenue. Give him my respects and tell him to issue a warrant for a fifth-rank Dragon Guard, together with a certificate. He can enter these particulars on them. Tomorrow I will have the silver weighed out and sent over.’

The attendant assented. Dai Quan then took his leave. Jia Zhen urged him to stay, but could not prevail, and had to see him to the gate. Just before he entered his chair, Jia Zhen asked, ‘Should I take the silver to the Board to be weighed, or send the whole sum to your residence, sir?’
‘If you go to the Board, you will only be out of pocket.

segments.text: ‘Better send a full twelve hundred in silver to my house, and that will settle it.’
Jia Zhen could not thank him enough. ‘When the mourning is over, I shall bring my unworthy son to your residence to offer our thanks in person,’ was all he could say.

They parted. Soon there were more cries clearing the way: the wife of Shi Ding, Marquis of Zhongjing, had arrived. Lady Wang, Lady Xing and Xi-feng had scarcely welcomed her into the principal room when offerings from the households of the Marquis of Jinxiang, the Marquis of Chuanning and the Earl of Shoushan were set before the coffin. A little later the three men stepped out of their chairs, and Jia Zheng and the others hurried to receive them in the main hall. Friends and relations came and went in numbers beyond counting. Throughout those forty-nine days, the street before the Ning mansion was a flowing stretch of white-clad mourners, brightened by the many-coloured ranks of officials coming and going.

Jia Zhen told Jia Rong to put on his ceremonial robes the next day and collect his credentials. All the equipment and insignia displayed before the coffin were arranged according to the rules for a fifth-rank official. The spirit tablet and ritual petitions bore the words: ‘Spirit tablet of Qin-shi of the Jia family, invested by the Celestial Dynasty with the honorific title gongren.’ The street gate of the Garden of Gathered Fragrance stood wide open. Music pavilions were hastily erected on either side, where two bands of musicians in blue robes played at the appointed times. The paired ceremonial insignia stood in ranks as straight and even as if cut into line by axe and blade.

segments.text: ‘Here in the central land of the Four Great Continents, in this realm of peace which reverently receives Heaven’s mandate, Wan-xu, Chief of the Buddhist Registry, presiding over the teaching of emptiness and stillness, and Ye Sheng, Chief of the Taoist Registry, presiding over the teaching of the Primordial Origin and the Three-in-One, and their fellows, reverently perform the fasting rites, bowing to Heaven and prostrating themselves before the Buddha.’ There were also such passages as ‘Respectfully inviting the monastery guardians, the jiedi and the divine officers of merit’, and ‘May sacred grace be spread over all, and divine might hold distant evils in check: a Water-and-Land rite of forty-nine days to dispel calamity, cleanse karmic burdens and bring peace.’ We need not record it all.

segments.text: Although Jia Zhen was now satisfied on these counts, You-shi’s old illness had returned and she could not manage affairs inside. He feared that titled ladies coming and going would not receive the proper courtesies, and people would laugh at him. This made him uneasy. As he was fretting, Bao-yu, who stood beside him, asked, ‘Everything seems to be settled, Cousin. What is still worrying you?’
Jia Zhen told him there was no one to take charge inside.
‘That is easily put right,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘I can recommend someone to manage things for you this month. I guarantee she will do it properly.’
‘Who?’ Jia Zhen asked at once.

There were still many friends and relations sitting about, so Bao-yu could not say openly. He went to Jia Zhen and whispered a few words in his ear. Delighted, Jia Zhen rose at once. ‘Just the person! Let us go now.’ Taking Bao-yu with him, he excused himself to the company and made for the principal room.

segments.text: It happened not to be one of the principal days of observance, and there were few visitors. Only a handful of close female relations were inside, with Lady Xing, Lady Wang, Xi-feng and the women of the clan to keep them company. At the announcement, ‘The master is coming in,’ the married women of the household scattered in alarm, scarcely able to conceal themselves fast enough. Xi-feng alone rose unhurriedly.
Jia Zhen was somewhat ill himself, besides being worn down by excessive grief, and came slowly in on a stick.
‘You are unwell, and you have had so much to do these past few days,’ Lady Xing and the others said. ‘You ought to be resting. What have you come in for?’

Supporting himself on his stick, he struggled to bend his knees, meaning to kneel in greeting and acknowledge their trouble. Lady Xing and the others quickly told Bao-yu to support him, and ordered a chair to be brought. Jia Zhen firmly refused to sit. With a forced smile he said, ‘Your nephew has come to ask a favour of you two aunts, and of my sister here.’
‘What is it?’ they asked.
‘As you know, Aunt, your grandson’s wife is dead, and your nephew’s wife has fallen ill as well. Affairs inside here are in a very poor state.

segments.text: Xi-feng had always loved taking work upon herself and displaying her abilities. Though she managed the household well, she had never been responsible for a wedding or a funeral, and feared that people were not yet convinced of her powers. She had longed for just such an opportunity. When Jia Zhen made his appeal, she was already delighted. At first Lady Wang had refused, but now, seeing how earnestly he spoke and how Lady Wang was beginning to give way, Xi-feng said, ‘My cousin asks so sincerely, Your Ladyship. Do let me do it.’
‘Can you manage it?’ Lady Wang asked her quietly.
‘Why should I not? My cousin has already settled all the important business outside. It is only a matter of looking after things inside. If there is anything I do not know, I can ask Your Ladyship.’

Lady Wang found this reasonable and said no more. Seeing that Xi-feng had agreed, Jia Zhen smiled again. ‘There is no help for it: I must ask you to take the trouble, Sister. Let me pay my respects to you here first. When it is all over, I shall come to your house to thank you.’ He bowed with clasped hands, and Xi-feng hastened to return the courtesy.

Xi-feng did not venture to take the tally at once, but looked at Lady Wang.

segments.text: ‘Since your cousin puts it that way, you may look after things for him,’ Lady Wang said. ‘Only do not act on your own judgement. If anything comes up, be sure to send someone to ask your cousin or his wife.’
Bao-yu had already taken the tally from Jia Zhen and pressed it into Xi-feng’s hand.

Jia Zhen went on, ‘Will you stay here, Sister, or come over every day? Coming daily would be still more tiring. Why not let me have a courtyard made ready at once? You could stay here for these few days in comfort.’
‘No need,’ Xi-feng said, smiling. ‘They cannot do without me over there either. I had better come every day.’
Jia Zhen could only accept this. After a little more conversation, they went out.

segments.text: When the women visitors had dispersed, Lady Wang asked Xi-feng, ‘What are you going to do today?’
‘Please go back, Your Ladyship,’ Xi-feng replied. ‘I must first get some order into things before I can leave.’
Lady Wang accordingly went home with Lady Xing and the others. Of them we need say no more.

segments.text: Xi-feng went to sit in a three-bay side hall and considered the position. First, there were so many people coming and going without order that things went missing. Second, no one had a definite responsibility, so when something had to be done they passed it off on one another. Third, expenditure was excessive, with reckless disbursements and fraudulent claims. Fourth, duties were assigned without regard to their importance, leaving some people overworked and others at ease. Fifth, the servants were insolent and unrestrained: those with influence would not submit to control, while those without it could never advance. These five abuses were indeed the established ways of the Ning mansion. How Xi-feng dealt with them you must hear in the next chapter. As the couplet has it:

segments.text: Now Lai Sheng, the chief steward of the Ning mansion, heard that Xi-feng had been invited to take charge of affairs within. He assembled his fellow servants and told them, ‘They have asked Mrs Lian from the western mansion to manage things inside. If she comes to draw supplies or gives us any instructions, we must be more careful than usual. Everyone must come early and leave late. Better work hard for this one month and rest afterwards than lose face. She’s a famous spitfire, sour-faced and hard-hearted. Once her temper’s up, she’ll make no allowances for anyone.’ They all agreed that he was right.

segments.text: ‘To be fair,’ another said with a laugh, ‘we could do with her putting the inside of this house in order. Things have really gone too far.’ As they were talking, Lai Wang-er’s wife arrived with an authorisation tally to collect paper for formal announcements, large public notices and paper offerings. The quantities were marked on the requisition. They hurried to offer her a seat and tea, while someone was sent to fetch the specified amount of paper. He carried it alongside her as far as the ceremonial gate, where he handed it over for her to take inside herself.

segments.text: Xi-feng at once ordered Sunshine to stitch together the account-books. She then summoned Lai Sheng’s wife and asked for the register of the household’s servants and their families. She also ordered that all the married women servants be assembled early next morning to receive their duties. After glancing over the lists and figures and asking Lai Sheng’s wife a few questions, she went home in her carriage. Nothing happened that night to call for an account.

segments.text: Next morning she arrived at half past six. The married women servants of the Ning mansion had all gathered on hearing of her arrival. Seeing that she was still assigning duties with Lai Sheng’s wife, none dared enter unbidden. They listened and peered through the windows. They heard Xi-feng say, ‘Since you have entrusted this to me, I’m afraid you’ll have to put up with being annoyed. I’m not as good-tempered as your mistress, letting you do as you please. I want no more of “That’s how we’ve always done it in this house.” From now on you’ll do as I say. Cross me by so much as a hair and I shan’t care who has influence and who has none. Everyone will be dealt with openly and alike.’

She told Sunshine to read the register and called the women in one by one to look them over. When she had seen them all, she gave her orders. ‘These twenty are to be divided into two shifts of ten. Their only work each day will be serving tea to visitors in the inner rooms. They need attend to nothing else. These next twenty will also work in two shifts. They are to look after the tea and meals for members of the family and our relations, and nothing else.

segments.text: ‘These forty, again in two shifts, are to tend the incense and replenish the oil before the coffin, hang the mourning curtains, keep vigil, set out the offerings of tea and food, and join in the lamentations whenever they begin. Nothing else concerns them. These four will look after the cups, saucers and tea things in the inner tea-room. If one piece is missing, the four of them must make good the loss. These four will be responsible for the wine vessels and dishes. If a piece goes missing, they too must make good the loss. These eight will supervise the receipt of funeral offerings. These eight will look after the lamp oil, candles and paper offerings for every part of the house. I shall draw the whole supply and hand it over to you eight, who will distribute it according to the quantities I prescribe. These thirty will take turns on night duty, guarding the doors, watching for fire, and keeping the place clean. The rest will be assigned to the different rooms, each person responsible for a particular place. Everything there, from tables, chairs and antiques down to spittoons and dusters, every blade of grass and every plant, is their responsibility. If anything is lost or broken, I shall call the person in charge to account and make them pay for it. Lai Sheng’s wife will make a general inspection every day. If anyone is idling, gambling, drinking, fighting or quarrelling, report to me at once.

segments.text: ‘If you show favour and I find out, all the standing your family has built up in three or four generations won’t save you. Now that everyone has a fixed duty, if anything goes wrong in one branch of the work, it is the people in that branch I shall speak to. My own people always have a watch with them. For every task, large or small, I have a set time. You have a clock in the principal rooms here too. I shall come to call the roll at half past six in the morning. Breakfast will be in the middle of the si hour. Anyone needing a tally or wishing to report on business must come only at the first quarter of the wu hour. At the beginning of the xu hour, after the evening paper-offerings have been burnt, I shall inspect every part of the house myself. When I come back, the handover of keys for the night watch must be properly accounted for. Next morning I shall be here again at half past six. We shall all have to work hard for these few days. Once the business is over, your master will of course reward you.’

She then ordered tea, oil, candles, feather dusters, brooms and other supplies to be issued in the appointed quantities. Furnishings were also brought out: table-fronts, chair covers, cushions, felt mats, spittoons, footstools and the like. As each item was handed over she recorded it, setting down quite plainly who was responsible for each place and who had received each object.

segments.text: The women took their supplies away, each now with a definite task. It was no longer a matter of choosing the easiest jobs and leaving the hard ones for nobody to undertake. Nor could things disappear from the rooms under cover of confusion. Even the coming and going of visitors became orderly. No longer did someone setting out tea have to rush off to serve a meal, or someone joining the lamentations turn aside to receive a guest. All that disorder, confusion, shifting of responsibility, idling and pilfering had been swept away by the next day.

segments.text: Xi-feng was thoroughly pleased to find that her authority carried weight and her orders were obeyed. Seeing that You-shi was ill and that Jia Zhen, overcome with grief, was eating very little, she had delicate rice gruels and carefully prepared side dishes made at her own mansion every day and sent over to tempt them to eat. Jia Zhen, for his part, ordered the finest dishes to be sent daily to the annex for Xi-feng alone. She never shrank from hard work.

segments.text: Every day she arrived at half past six in the morning to call the roll and attend to business. She kept to the annex on her own instead of joining the other married women of the family, and did not go out to receive the visiting ladies either. This was the principal day of the fifth seventh-day observance. The Buddhist ritual monks were opening the ways and breaking open the prisons of hell, passing the lamps to light the dead on their way, paying homage to the Lord of the Underworld, summoning the ghost commanders, inviting Kshitigarbha, opening the golden bridge and leading the sacred banners. The Taoists were submitting their memorials and petitions, worshipping the Three Pure Ones and bowing before the Jade Emperor. The Chan monks were offering incense, performing the rite for feeding hungry ghosts and making their devotions in the Water Repentance rite. There were also thirteen Buddhist nuns, wearing embroidered robes and red shoes, silently reciting before the coffin the spells that would guide the departed. It was a scene of great activity.

Xi-feng knew there would be many visitors that day. Having spent the night at home, she was called by Patience in the middle of the yin hour to rise and make her toilette. By the time she was ready, had changed her clothes and washed her hands, eaten a few mouthfuls of rice gruel with milk and sugar, and rinsed her mouth, it was already half past six. Lai Wang-er’s wife and the other attendants had long been waiting. Xi-feng came out before the hall and got into her carriage. A pair of translucent horn lanterns went ahead, bearing three large Chinese characters meaning ‘Rong Mansion’, and the carriage moved at a measured pace to the Ning mansion.

segments.text: The lanterns over the main gate shone brightly. On either side stood matching rows of lanterns on poles, making the entrance as light as day. Servants in mourning white waited in lines to right and left. When the carriage had been ushered up to the main entrance, the pages withdrew and the married women servants stepped forward to raise the curtain. Xi-feng alighted, resting one hand on Felicity. Two women carried hand-lanterns as the attendants escorted her inside. The women of the Ning mansion came forward to greet her and pay their respects. She walked slowly into the Garden of Gathered Fragrance and up to the coffin in the Ascension Pavilion. At the sight of it, tears rolled down her face like pearls from a broken string. Many pages stood in the courtyard, hands lowered, waiting to burn the paper offerings. ‘Offer tea and burn the paper,’ Xi-feng ordered. A gong sounded and all the instruments struck up. Someone had already brought a great round-backed chair and set it before the coffin. Xi-feng sat down and began to weep aloud.

segments.text: As soon as they heard her, men and women, high and low, inside and outside, hurried to join in the wailing. After a while Jia Zhen and You-shi sent someone to comfort her, and only then did she stop. Lai Wang-er’s wife brought tea for her to rinse her mouth. Xi-feng rose, took leave of the members of the clan and went to the annex. She checked the attendance against the register. Every group was complete except for one woman whose duty was receiving and seeing off visiting relations. She had the woman summoned. The woman was already distraught with shame and fear.
Xi-feng gave a cold laugh. ‘I wondered who had kept us waiting. So it’s you! Of course, you have more standing than the rest. That must be why you needn’t obey me.’
‘I come early every day, ma’am. It was only today. I woke and thought it was still early, then dropped off again and came a little late. Please forgive me this once.’
As she spoke, Wang Xing’s wife from the Rong mansion appeared, peering in at the front.

segments.text: Leaving the first woman’s case unsettled for the moment, Xi-feng asked, ‘What does Wang Xing’s wife want?’ That woman had been longing to be asked first so that she could finish her errand. She hurried inside. ‘A tally to draw thread, ma’am, for the netted trimmings on the carriages and sedan-chairs.’ She handed up a slip. Xi-feng told Sunshine to read it. ‘Two large sedan-chairs, four small sedan-chairs and four carriages, requiring so many lengths of large and small netting, and so many catties of pearl-thread.’ The quantities tallied. Xi-feng told Sunshine to enter them in the register, then took a Rong mansion authorisation tally and tossed it down. Wang Xing’s wife left.

segments.text: Seeing Zhang Cai’s wife standing nearby, Xi-feng asked what she wanted. The woman hurried to produce her slip. ‘It’s for the carriage and sedan-chair covers just finished, ma’am. So many taels for the tailors’ work.’ Xi-feng took the slip and told Sunshine to record it. Only after Wang Xing’s wife had returned the tally and the buyer’s countersigned receipt had been checked against it did she give it to Zhang Cai’s wife to collect the money. She then had the remaining slip read. Bao-yu’s outer study had been completed and paper was needed for lining and papering it. She ordered the slip to be kept and the entry made. When Zhang Cai’s wife had cleared her account and returned the tally, she issued it to this applicant in turn.

segments.text: Then Xi-feng resumed. ‘Tomorrow she’ll oversleep, and the day after I’ll oversleep, and in the end there’ll be nobody here at all. I meant to let you off. But if I’m lenient the first time, I shan’t be able to manage anyone afterwards. Better settle it now.’ Her face hardened. ‘Take her outside and give her twenty strokes!’ she cried. She tossed down the Ning mansion’s authorisation tally. ‘Tell Lai Sheng she is to lose a month’s silver and rice as well!’ Hearing this and seeing her eyebrows bristle, the servants knew she was angry and dared not delay. Those charged with taking the woman out dragged her away, while the bearer of the tally hurried off with the order.

segments.text: The woman could do nothing. Dragged outside, she received twenty heavy strokes of the paddle and then had to come back in and kowtow her thanks. ‘If anyone is late tomorrow, it will be forty,’ said Xi-feng. ‘The day after, sixty. If you want a beating, by all means be late!’ Then she told them to disperse. Those listening outside the windows went off to their duties. All this time managers from both the Ning and Rong mansions kept coming and going, collecting and returning tallies. The beaten woman withdrew in shame, knowing now what Xi-feng was capable of. Nobody dared shirk. From that day they all worked diligently and cautiously to keep themselves clear of trouble. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: Let us return to Bao-yu. Seeing how crowded it was that day, he feared Qin Zhong might be put upon, and quietly suggested that they should go and sit with Xi-feng. ‘She has so much to do,’ said Qin Zhong, ‘and she doesn’t like people going there. Won’t we annoy her?’

‘How could she be annoyed with us? It doesn’t matter. Come along.’ Taking Qin Zhong by the hand, Bao-yu went straight to the annex. Xi-feng was just having her meal. At the sight of them she laughed. ‘What long legs you have! Come on up.’

segments.text: ‘We’ve already eaten, I’m afraid,’ said Bao-yu.
‘Out here on this side, or over at home?’
‘Why should we eat with those louts here? We ate at home, both of us, with Grandmother.’ As he spoke he went over and sat down.

segments.text: When Xi-feng had finished, a woman from the Ning mansion came for a tally to draw incense and lamp supplies. ‘I reckoned you were due for another issue today,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘When you didn’t come I thought you’d forgotten. So you’ve come for it after all! If you’d forgotten, of course, you would have had to pay for it yourselves. All the better for me.’
‘We did forget,’ the woman said, laughing. ‘We only just remembered. A little later and we wouldn’t have been able to get the tally!’ She took it and went away.

segments.text: Before long the entry was made and the tally returned. Qin Zhong laughed. ‘You use these tallies in both houses. What if someone secretly made one for himself, drew the silver and ran away?’
‘By your account there’d be no law left in the land,’ said Xi-feng, smiling.
‘Why does nobody from our house come for tallies to get things made?’ Bao-yu asked.

segments.text: ‘When they come for them, you’re still dreaming. Tell me, when are you going to start these evening lessons of yours?’
‘I wish we could start this very minute. But they’re so slow getting the study ready. There’s nothing I can do.’
‘Ask me nicely and I’ll guarantee it will be ready soon,’ Xi-feng said with a laugh.
‘It’s no use your wanting it done quickly. They’ll finish it when they get to it.’
‘Even if they do the work, they need supplies. And what are they to do if I won’t give them the tally?’
At that Bao-yu clambered all over her, demanding it at once. ‘Dear sister, give them the tally! Let them go and get what they need.’

‘I’m so tired my whole body aches. Do you think I can stand being pulled about as well? Don’t worry. They only collected the paper for the walls today. Do you suppose they wait to be told when they need something? What a goose you are!’ Bao-yu did not believe her, so she told Sunshine to find the entry in the register and show him.

segments.text: They were still playing about when someone announced, ‘Zhao-er, who went to Suzhou, is back.’ Xi-feng at once had him called in. He made a formal kneeling salute and paid his respects. ‘What have you come back for?’ she asked.

‘The Second Master sent me. Mr Lin died on the third day of the ninth month, in the si hour. The Second Master has taken Miss Lin to escort her father’s coffin to Suzhou. They should be back by the end of the year. He sent me to bring the news and pay his respects, to ask whether the Old Lady has any instructions, and to see that all is well with you at home, ma’am. He also wants a few of his heavy fur garments sent out.’
‘Have you seen the others yet?’
‘Yes, ma’am, all of them.’ With that he quickly withdrew.

‘Oh, how dreadful! Think how she must have been crying these last few days!’ Bao-yu frowned and gave a long sigh.

segments.text: Ever since Zhao-er’s arrival, Xi-feng had been anxious for news of Jia Lian. With other people present she had been unable to question him closely. She wanted to go home, but there were so many things to do that she feared leaving even briefly might cause delays and mistakes and expose her to ridicule. She had to endure it until evening. Once home, she summoned Zhao-er again and asked in detail whether all had gone safely on the journey. That very night she got the heavy fur clothes ready. She and Patience checked the bundles themselves, thinking carefully over everything else he might need and packing it all for Zhao-er to take. She also gave him minute instructions. ‘Look after your Second Master properly while you’re away. Don’t provoke him. Keep urging him to drink less, and don’t lead him into getting acquainted with disreputable women. If you do, I’ll break your legs when you come back.’ By the time all this bustle was over, the fourth watch was almost ended. When at last she lay down, she had gone past sleepiness. Before she knew it, the cocks were crowing at dawn. She hurried to wash and dress and go over to the Ning mansion.

segments.text: With the day for the funeral procession approaching, Jia Zhen took a clerk from the Yin-yang Office in his carriage to the Temple of the Iron Threshold, to inspect the place where the coffin was to rest temporarily. He gave the abbot, Se-kong, detailed instructions to prepare fresh furnishings and invite more eminent monks for the reception of the coffin. Se-kong hurried to provide a vegetarian supper. Jia Zhen had no appetite for food or tea. It was too late to get back into the city, so he passed an uncomfortable night in a quiet room at the temple. Early next morning he returned to the city to arrange the funeral procession. He also sent people ahead to the temple to work through the night, putting the place for the coffin in order and arranging the kitchens, tea-making facilities and accommodation for those who would receive it.

segments.text: Inside the mansion Xi-feng, seeing how little time remained, was arranging every detail in advance. She also had to assign the Rong household’s carriages, sedan-chairs and servants to accompany Lady Wang in the procession, and secure a place to stay for herself when she went. Just then the titled wife of the Duke of Shan had died, and Lady Wang and Lady Xing had to go to make offerings and attend her funeral. There was the Princess of Xi’an’s birthday, requiring a gift; the titled wife of the Duke of Zhen had given birth to her eldest son, requiring another. Xi-feng’s own elder brother, Wang Ren, was returning south with his family, so she had to write a family letter conveying her respectful greetings to her parents and prepare things for him to take. Ying-chun was ill, too. Physicians were called and medicines taken every day, and their written reports, accounts of her symptoms and prescriptions all needed attention. There was more than can be told. With the funeral procession so near, Xi-feng scarcely had time for food or tea, and could neither sit nor lie down in peace. No sooner had she reached the Ning mansion than people from Rong followed her there. Once back at Rong, she was pursued by those from Ning. Yet all this delighted her. She neither sought ease nor put things off on others. Anxious to give nobody grounds for criticism, she worked night and day, keeping everything in the strictest order.

segments.text: Everyone in the clan, high and low, praised her. On the evening of the final vigil, two troupes of young actors and performers of assorted entertainments kept the friends, relations and visiting ladies company within. You-shi was still confined to her room. All the arrangements and the reception of the guests fell to Xi-feng alone. There were plenty of other married women in the clan, but some were shy of speaking, some hesitant to move about, some unused to meeting strangers, and others awed by rank or frightened of officials. None could match her unhurried bearing, assured speech and dignified, expansive manner. Consequently she thought little of the rest, giving her orders freely and doing as she pleased, as though no one else were there. All night the lamps blazed as one guest was seen off and another official welcomed. There is no need to describe the bustle. At dawn, when the auspicious hour arrived, a company of sixty-four bearers in blue raised the coffin. On the funeral banner in front were written in large characters the words:

‘The coffin of Qin-shi of the Jia family, honoured with the title gongren by imperial patent under the dynasty grandly founded in obedience to Heaven and unchanging through countless ages; wife of the eldest grandson in the legitimate line of the Duke of Ning of the First Rank, and wife of a Dragon Guard, an Imperial Bodyguard defending the Inner Court and the ways of the Forbidden Palace; having enjoyed a full span of life.’

segments.text: All the ceremonial equipment and furnishings had been hurriedly made afresh, and everything shone with dazzling splendour. Jewel performed the rites of an unmarried daughter, broke the funeral earthenware basin and went before the coffin as chief mourner, in the deepest distress. Among the officials attending the procession were Niu Ji-zong, now holding the inherited title of Earl of the First Rank, grandson of Niu Qing, Duke of Zhen; Liu Fang, now holding the inherited title of Viscount of the First Rank, grandson of Liu Biao, Duke of Li; Chen Rui-wen, hereditary General of Subduing Might of the Third Rank, grandson of Chen Yi, Duke of Qi; Ma Shang, hereditary General of Far-reaching Might of the Third Rank, grandson of Ma Kui, Duke of Zhi; and Hou Xiao-kang, hereditary Viscount of the First Rank, grandson of Hou Ming, Duke of Xiu. The titled wife of the Duke of Shan had died, and her grandson Shi Guang-zhu was in mourning and could not attend. These six families, together with the houses of Rong and Ning, were those known in former days as the Eight Dukes. There were also grandsons of the Prince of Nan’an and the Prince of Xining; Shi Ding, Marquis of Zhongjing; Jiang Zi-ning, grandson of the Marquis of Pingyuan and hereditary Baron of the Second Rank; Xie Jing, grandson of the Marquis of Dingcheng, hereditary Baron of the Second Rank and a youji officer of the Metropolitan Garrison; Qi Jian-hui, grandson of the Marquis of Xiangyang and hereditary Baron of the Second Rank; and Qiu Liang of the Office of Military and Police Affairs for the Five Districts, grandson of the Marquis of Jingtian.

segments.text: Besides these there were Han Qi, son of the Marquis of Jinxiang; Feng Zi-ying, son of the General of Divine Might; Wei Ruo-lan, and more young gentlemen of princely and noble families than could be counted. The visiting ladies alone occupied some ten large sedan-chairs and thirty or forty small ones. With all the household’s own chairs and carriages, there were well over a hundred conveyances. Add the ceremonial attendants, equipment and entertainers in front, and the vast procession stretched for three or four li.

segments.text: They had not gone far before they came upon tall, brightly decorated pavilions beside the road, with feasting tables laid and harmonious music playing. These were the different families’ roadside funeral offerings. The first was the mourning pavilion of the Prince of Dongping’s household, the second that of the Prince of Nan’an, the third that of the Prince of Xining and the fourth that of the Prince of Beijing. Of these four princes, the Prince of Beijing alone had rendered such great services in former days that his descendants still inherited the princely title. Its present holder, Shui Rong, was not yet twenty, handsome in appearance and gentle in disposition. Hearing lately of the death of the wife of the Duke of Ning’s eldest grandson, he had thought of the friendship between their grandfathers, who had shared hardship and glory and never treated one another as men of different surnames. He therefore set aside his princely dignity. He had already visited the house of mourning and made offerings, and now had roadside offerings prepared as well, ordering the officials under him to wait here. He himself had attended court during the fifth watch. As soon as his official business was over he changed into plain clothes and came in his great sedan-chair, with gongs sounding and a ceremonial parasol borne before him. He alighted in front of the pavilion. His officers crowded about him on either side, and neither soldiers nor civilians were allowed to pass.

segments.text: Presently the great funeral procession from the Ning mansion appeared from the north, like a vast mountain of silver pressing over the earth. The Ning servants clearing the road and carrying messages saw the Prince and hurried back to inform Jia Zhen. Jia Zhen at once ordered the head of the procession to halt. With Jia She and Jia Zheng he hastened forward, and the three greeted the Prince with the formal courtesies required by his rank. Shui Rong inclined his body within the sedan-chair and returned their salute with a smile. He addressed and received them as old family friends, without assuming airs of superiority.

segments.text: ‘Your Highness has repeatedly condescended to honour the mourning for my unworthy daughter-in-law,’ said Jia Zhen. ‘How can we, who owe our standing to favours granted our ancestors, presume to deserve it?’

‘Between old family friends, why speak of such things?’ Shui Rong said with a smile. He turned and ordered his chief household officer to conduct the rite and make the libation on his behalf. Jia She and the others returned the ritual salutations from one side, then came forward again to thank him for his favour.

segments.text: Shui Rong was most courteous. He asked Jia Zheng, ‘Which is the boy who was born with jade in his mouth? I have wanted to see him several times, but other business has always intervened. I suppose he has come today. Why not ask him to join us?’ Jia Zheng hurried back and ordered Bao-yu to take off his mourning clothes, then brought him forward. Bao-yu had often heard his father, brothers, relations and friends praise Shui Rong in conversation as a worthy prince, gifted and handsome, elegant and free in his manner, who would not always be bound by official convention and the formalities of state. He had often wished to meet him, but his father kept him under such strict control that there had been no opportunity. Now that his father himself had sent for him, he was naturally delighted. As he walked along he had already caught a glimpse of Shui Rong sitting in his sedan-chair. What a striking figure he was! What would he look like at close quarters? For that, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: Bao-yu looked up at Shui Rong, the Prince of Beijing. He wore a prince’s hat with pure white tassels and silver wings, a white mang robe patterned with five-clawed dragons shown full-face above waves and jutting rocks, and a red leather belt set with green jade. His face was like fine jade, his eyes like bright stars: a remarkably handsome figure. Bao-yu hurried forward to pay his respects, but Shui Rong at once reached out of his sedan-chair and caught him by the hand. He saw a boy wearing a silver coronet over his bound hair and a brow-band patterned with two dragons rising from the sea, a white mang robe with close-fitting sleeves and a silver belt studded with pearls. His face was like spring blossom, his eyes like drops of lacquer.
‘You quite live up to your name,’ Shui Rong said with a smile. ‘A treasure indeed, and precious as jade. Where is the precious thing you were born with in your mouth?’
At the question Bao-yu hastily took it from inside his clothes and handed it over. Shui Rong examined it closely, read out its inscription, then asked, ‘Does it really have miraculous powers?’
‘So it is said,’ Jia Zheng answered quickly, ‘but we have never put them to the test.’
Shui Rong went on praising its wonders as he straightened the coloured cord and put it back on Bao-yu himself. Then, holding the boy’s hand, he asked his age and what books he was reading.

segments.text: Bao-yu answered each question. Finding his speech clear and his manner of speaking engaging, Shui Rong turned to Jia Zheng with a smile.

‘Your son is a dragon colt, a phoenix chick. Forgive me if I speak too freely before an elder of a family so long allied with mine, but one day “the young phoenix will sing more clearly than the old”. There is no measuring his prospects.’

Jia Zheng hastened to return the smile. ‘My poor boy could hardly deserve such lavish praise. Should Your Highness’s gracious blessing make it true, it would be a piece of good fortune for those of us who owe our standing to our forebears.’

‘There is only one thing,’ Shui Rong went on. ‘With such gifts, your son must naturally be the darling of his grandmother, his mother and the other ladies. Yet we young men are ill served by too much indulgence: it is all too easy to neglect our studies. I fell into that error myself once, and I imagine your son may not be altogether free of it. If he finds it hard to work at home, let him come often to my house. Though I have little ability myself, the distinguished men of our land are very kind to me: scarcely one comes to the capital without favouring me with a visit. Consequently quite a number of accomplished men gather under my roof. If your son comes to talk with them from time to time, his learning may improve day by day.’
Jia Zheng bowed his assent.

segments.text: Shui Rong slipped a string of prayer beads from his wrist and handed it to Bao-yu.

‘This is our first meeting, and in my haste I have brought no suitable gift. Here is a string of fragrant jiling prayer beads which His Majesty himself bestowed on me the other day. Pray accept it as a small token of my good wishes.’

segments.text: Bao-yu quickly accepted them, then turned and respectfully handed them to Jia Zheng. Father and son thanked the Prince together. Jia She, Jia Zhen and the others now came forward to ask him to turn his chair homewards.

‘The departed has ascended to the realm of immortals,’ Shui Rong said. ‘She is no longer one of the common mortals who toil here below, as you and I do. By the Emperor’s favour I have inherited a princely title which I do little to deserve, but how could I presume to go ahead of an immortal’s hearse?’

As he was determined not to yield, Jia She and the rest could only take their leave with further thanks. Returning to the procession, they ordered their men to silence the music. The whole great train streamed past before Shui Rong would allow his chair to turn for home. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: The Ning household’s funeral procession made a great stir along its route. Just before the city gate, more funeral canopies had been set up by colleagues and subordinates of Jia She, Jia Zheng, Jia Zhen and the others, whose households offered sacrifices as the coffin passed. When thanks had been given at each in turn, the procession left the city and took the road straight towards the Temple of the Iron Threshold. Jia Zhen brought Jia Rong to the elders to invite them to take their chairs or mount their horses. Those of Jia She’s generation got into their carriages and chairs, and those of Jia Zhen’s were about to mount.

Xi-feng was worrying about Bao-yu. Out in the country he might indulge himself, try to show off and refuse to listen to the servants; Jia Zheng did not concern himself with such small matters. If anything happened to the boy, how could she face Grandmother Jia? She therefore sent a page to fetch him. Bao-yu had no choice but to come to her carriage.

‘Dear brother,’ she said, smiling, ‘you are a precious creature, as fine and delicate as any girl. Don’t go playing the monkey on horseback like the rest of them. Come down and ride with me. We two sisters will be much better off together, won’t we?’
Bao-yu at once dismounted and climbed into her carriage. The two went on their way laughing and talking.

segments.text: Before long two riders came galloping along as though flying over the ground. Both leapt down near Xi-feng’s carriage, put their hands to it and reported, ‘There is a place to stop here, ma’am, if you would like to rest and change.’
Xi-feng at once sent to ask Lady Xing and Lady Wang what they wished. The messenger came back with the answer: ‘Their Ladyships say they need not stop. You are to please yourself, ma’am.’

On hearing this, Xi-feng decided to rest before going on. The pages turned the carriage horses out of the crowd and hurried north. From inside the carriage Bao-yu urgently told them to invite Master Qin.

Qin Zhong was riding beside his father’s sedan-chair when Bao-yu’s page ran up to ask him to come for refreshments. Looking ahead, he saw Xi-feng’s carriage heading north, with Bao-yu’s horse led behind it, the saddle-cover laid over the saddle. Realising that Bao-yu was riding with Xi-feng, he turned his own horse and caught them up. They went in together through the gate of a farmstead.

segments.text: The household servants had already driven all the farm men out. There were few rooms in the farmhouse, and the women had nowhere to withdraw to, so they had to be left where they were. How could the village girls and country women help wanting to look at Xi-feng, Bao-yu and Qin Zhong, with their fine looks and clothes, their manners and bearing?

segments.text: Xi-feng went into the thatched hall and told Bao-yu and the others to go out and amuse themselves for a while. Understanding her, Bao-yu came out with Qin Zhong, and they wandered about with the pages. Everything used on the farm was new to them. Bao-yu marvelled at the spades, mattocks, hoes and ploughs, with no idea what they were for or what they were called. The pages told him each name and explained its use. Bao-yu nodded and sighed.
‘No wonder the old poet wrote:

“Who knows that in the meal upon the plate
Each single grain has cost such bitter toil?”

segments.text: ‘This is just what he meant.’
As he spoke he came to another room, where he saw a spinning-wheel on the kang.
‘And what is this?’ he asked the pages.

They explained that too. Bao-yu went up and began turning it for amusement, quite delighted with himself. Just then a country girl of seventeen or eighteen ran in, crying out, ‘Don’t touch that! You’ll break it!’
The pages at once shouted her down and barred her way. Bao-yu quickly let go of the wheel and gave her an apologetic smile.
‘I’d never seen one before. I only wanted to try it.’
‘You wouldn’t know how to work it,’ the girl said. ‘Stand aside and I’ll spin for you to watch.’
Qin Zhong gave Bao-yu a secret tug and said with a smile, ‘Now here’s a young lady with quite a charm of her own.’
Bao-yu pushed him away, laughing. ‘You wretch! Say any more nonsense and I’ll hit you!’

Having washed her hands, changed her clothes and shaken out the dust, she asked whether they wanted to change too. Bao-yu did not, so she let the matter drop. The women servants brought in the teapot and cups, the tiered box of assorted refreshments and the various snacks they had brought for the journey. Xi-feng and the others took tea, waited while everything was packed away, then got up to return to the carriage.

segments.text: Outside, Wang-er had prepared packets of gratuities and handed them to the owner of the farmstead. The farm women came to kowtow in thanks. Xi-feng paid no particular attention, but Bao-yu looked carefully: Second Girl was not among them. They got into the carriage and had not gone far when they saw her coming towards them, carrying her little brother and laughing and talking with several young girls. Bao-yu longed to get down and follow her, but he knew the others would never allow it. He could only follow her with his eyes. The carriage was light, the horses swift: in a moment she had vanished from sight.

segments.text: They soon caught up with the funeral procession. Ahead of them, amid ritual drums and brass cymbals, banners, streamers and jewelled canopies, the monks from the Temple of the Iron Threshold had come out to receive the coffin. Before long they entered the temple, where further Buddhist rites were performed and the incense altar was set up afresh. The coffin was placed in a side chamber of the inner hall, and Jewel was lodged in an inner bedroom to keep it company.

Outside, Jia Zhen entertained all the friends and relations. Some stayed for a meal; others took their leave without eating. He thanked each for the trouble they had taken. The guests departed in groups, beginning with the dukes, then the marquises, earls, viscounts and barons. Not until the end of the wei hour had they all gone. Inside, Xi-feng attended to the women guests and saw to their reception. The ladies with imperial titles belonging to the highest officials’ households left first, and it was well past noon before the last of them had departed. Only a few of the closest relations remained: they would wait until the three days of rites for the resting coffin were over.

Lady Xing and Lady Wang knew that Xi-feng would be unable to return home, and were preparing to go back to the city. Lady Wang wanted to take Bao-yu with her, but he had only just reached the countryside and would not hear of leaving. He insisted on staying with Xi-feng. Lady Wang could do nothing with him; she left him in Xi-feng’s charge and went home.

segments.text: The Temple of the Iron Threshold had originally been built by the Dukes of Ning and Rong. It still had an endowment of farmland to support its religious services, and provided a convenient place where the coffins of members of the family who died in the capital could rest temporarily. Accommodation for both the dead and the living had been arranged, so that those attending the coffins could stay there too.

By now, however, their descendants had grown numerous. Some were rich, some poor, and their dispositions differed as widely as stars that never meet. Those whose means were straitened and who were content with their lot stayed at the temple. Others, with money, influence and a taste for display, declared it inconvenient and insisted on finding rooms at a farmstead or nunnery elsewhere, where they could retire once the ceremonies and feasting were over. For Qin-shi’s funeral the other members of the clan were all lodging for the time being at the Temple of the Iron Threshold. Xi-feng alone found it inconvenient. She had sent ahead to Jing-xu, the nun at Steamed-bun Hermitage, to have two rooms cleared for her.

segments.text: Steamed-bun Hermitage was in fact Water-Moon Hermitage. Its steamed buns were so good that they had earned it this nickname. It stood not far from the Temple of the Iron Threshold.

When the monks had finished their offices and the evening tea had been offered to the departed, Jia Zhen sent Jia Rong to ask Xi-feng to go and rest. Seeing that several other wives of her generation in the clan were still there to keep the women relations company, she took leave of them all and set out for Water-Moon Hermitage with Bao-yu and Qin Zhong. Qin Ye was old and frequently ill, and could not stay himself. He had merely told Qin Zhong to remain until the rites for the resting coffin were finished. Qin Zhong accordingly kept with Xi-feng and Bao-yu.

When they reached Water-Moon Hermitage, Jing-xu came out to welcome them with her two disciples, Zhi-shan and Sapientia. Everyone exchanged greetings. Xi-feng and her party went into the quiet rooms, changed and washed their hands. Seeing how much taller and prettier Sapientia had grown, Xi-feng said, ‘Why haven’t you and your disciples been to see us all this time?’

‘We really have had no time these last few days,’ Jing-xu answered. ‘There has been a son born in Mr Hu’s household. His wife sent us ten taels of silver to engage several nuns to recite the Blood-bowl Sutra for three days. We have scarcely had a moment free, so I have not been able to come and pay my respects to you, ma’am.’
Let us leave the old nun keeping Xi-feng company.

segments.text: Bao-yu and Qin Zhong were amusing themselves in the hall when they saw Sapientia coming.
‘Here’s Sapientia,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
‘What do you want with that creature?’ said Qin Zhong.

‘Don’t try your tricks on me,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘The other day, when there was nobody else in Grandmother’s room, what were you doing with your arms round her? And now you’re still trying to fool me!’
Qin Zhong laughed. ‘There’s no truth in that.’
Bao-yu smiled. ‘True or not, I shan’t bother you about it. Just tell her to pour me a cup of tea, and I’ll let you off.’
Qin Zhong laughed. ‘That’s a queer thing to say. Tell her yourself. Do you think she’ll refuse? Why must I ask?’
‘If I ask her, there’s no affection in the tea. It won’t be like the tea you ask her for: that will have affection in it.’
Qin Zhong had no choice but to say, ‘Sapientia, bring me a cup of tea.’

Sapientia had visited the Rong mansion since she was a small child. Everyone knew her, and she often played and joked with Bao-yu and Qin Zhong. Now that she was growing up and beginning to understand affairs of love, Qin Zhong’s handsome, graceful bearing had caught her fancy. He, in turn, was very taken with her pretty, winning ways. Though they had not yet been intimate, they were already drawn to one another.

segments.text: The sight of Qin Zhong now filled Sapientia with delight, and she went to pour the tea. When she brought it back, Qin Zhong said with a smile, ‘Give it to me.’
‘Give it to me!’ cried Bao-yu.
Sapientia smiled with her lips pressed together. ‘Fighting over a cup of tea! Have I got honey on my hands?’

Bao-yu snatched it first. He was drinking and about to ask her something when Zhi-shan came to call Sapientia away to set out the tea dishes. Presently they invited the boys in for tea, fruit and cakes. Neither was interested in food of that sort. They sat for a little while, then went out to amuse themselves again.

segments.text: Xi-feng too sat only a little while before returning to rest in the quiet rooms, with the old nun escorting her. Finding that there was nothing more to do, the women servants drifted away one by one to take their ease. Only a few trusted young maids who regularly attended her remained. The old nun took her opportunity.
‘There is a matter I was going to bring to Her Ladyship at the mansion. Might I first ask your advice about it, ma’am?’
Xi-feng asked what it was.

‘Amitabha! It began back when I first took my vows at Shancai Hermitage in Chang’an county. We had a benefactor there named Zhang, a very rich man. He had a daughter whose childhood name was Jin-ge. One year they all came to the hermitage to offer incense, and she happened to meet young Master Li, the younger brother of the prefect of Chang’an’s wife. He set his heart on marrying Jin-ge and sent someone to ask for her hand. But she had already accepted the betrothal gifts of the son of the former garrison commandant. The Zhang family were afraid that the commandant would object if they broke off the match, so they said she was already promised. Young Master Li would not accept that. He insisted on marrying the daughter.

segments.text: ‘The Zhang family could think of no way out, caught between the two sides. Then the commandant’s family heard of it. Without troubling to find out the rights and wrongs, they came and abused and insulted the Zhangs, asking how many families they meant to promise one girl to. They flatly refused to take back the betrothal gifts, and brought a lawsuit. The Zhangs were so distressed that they sent someone to the capital to find a way of getting help. Out of sheer anger, they were now determined to return the gifts. It occurred to me that Mr Yun, the military commissioner of Chang’an, is a very close friend of your household. If we could ask Her Ladyship to speak to His Lordship, and have him send a letter asking Mr Yun to put in a word with the commandant, I am sure the commandant would give way.

segments.text: ‘I am not short of money,’ Xi-feng said with a smile, ‘and I don’t do that sort of thing either.’
Jing-xu abandoned her hopes. After a long silence she sighed.

‘Of course. Only, the Zhangs already know I have come to ask your household for help. If nothing is done, they won’t understand that you have no time for it and have no interest in their gifts of thanks. It will look as though your household has not even the influence to manage this little thing.’
This stirred Xi-feng’s interest.

‘You have known me long enough. I have never believed in all that talk of the underworld, hell and retribution. Whatever it is, if I say it can be done, it can. Tell him to bring three thousand taels of silver, and I’ll see that he has his satisfaction.’

segments.text: The old nun was beside herself with joy. ‘Yes, yes! That will be no difficulty.’

‘I am not like those go-betweens who pull strings for money,’ Xi-feng went on. ‘The three thousand is simply for the travelling expenses of the servants I send to speak for him, and to let them earn a little for their trouble. I don’t want a single coin of it myself. I could lay my hands on thirty thousand taels this very moment.’
The nun hastened to agree. ‘Then perhaps you would be so kind as to do it tomorrow, ma’am?’
‘Just look at how busy I am. Where can they do without me? Since I’ve promised you, naturally I’ll settle it as quickly as I can.’
‘Anyone else would be quite overwhelmed by a matter like this, but for you, ma’am, even a few more would hardly give your abilities room to show themselves.

segments.text: ‘But as the saying goes, “The able bear the heavier load.” Her Ladyship sees how well you manage everything, great and small, and leaves more and more to you. You must take care of your precious health, ma’am.’
These flattering remarks pleased Xi-feng more and more. Forgetting her fatigue, she went on talking.

Meanwhile Qin Zhong took advantage of the darkness and the absence of other people to look for Sapientia. He came to a room at the back and found her alone, washing the teacups. He ran up, put his arms round her and kissed her. Sapientia stamped her foot in distress.
‘What do you mean by this? Do that again and I’ll shout!’
‘My dear, I’m desperate,’ he pleaded. ‘If you refuse me again today, I’ll die here.’
‘What do you expect? Only when I’m out of this prison and away from these people will I agree.’
‘That’s easy enough. But distant water won’t quench thirst here and now.’

He blew out the lamp, leaving the room pitch-dark, carried Sapientia to the kang and lay with her. She struggled in every way to get free, but could not; unable to bring herself to call out, she had no choice but to yield.

segments.text: Just as Qin Zhong was enjoying himself, someone came in and held them both down without a word. Not knowing who it was, they were too frightened to move. Then the intruder gave a snort and could no longer keep from laughing. Only when they heard his voice did they realise it was Bao-yu. Qin Zhong scrambled up.
‘What do you mean by this?’ he complained.
Bao-yu laughed. ‘If you’re going to object, I’ll shout.’
Sapientia slipped away through the darkness in shame. Bao-yu pulled Qin Zhong outside.
‘Will you still try to get the better of me?’
‘My dear fellow,’ Qin Zhong said with a smile, ‘just don’t shout and let everyone know. I’ll do anything you want.’
Bao-yu laughed. ‘No need to discuss it now. We’ll settle accounts properly when we go to bed.’

When it was time to undress and retire, Xi-feng slept in the inner room and Qin Zhong and Bao-yu in the outer one. The floor was covered with bedding for the household women who sat up on watch. Afraid that the Spiritual Jade might be lost, Xi-feng waited until Bao-yu was in bed, then had it brought to her and tucked it beside her own pillow.

segments.text: What accounts Bao-yu settled with Qin Zhong is not known. It was not clearly witnessed or recorded; the matter remains in doubt, and I would not venture to invent it.

The night passed without further incident. Early the next morning, Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang sent people to see how Bao-yu was, with instructions that he should put on a couple more layers of clothing and, if there was nothing to keep him, come home. Bao-yu would not hear of going. Qin Zhong, moreover, was reluctant to leave Sapientia and urged him to ask Xi-feng to stay another day.

Xi-feng considered it. The important funeral arrangements were all in order, but there were still one or two small matters to settle. She could use these as a reason to stay another day: would that not be doing Jia Zhen a handsome favour as well? Secondly, she could finish Jing-xu’s business; thirdly, Bao-yu would have his wish, and Grandmother Jia would surely be pleased to hear of it. With these three advantages in mind, she said to Bao-yu, ‘All my work is done. But if you want to stay here and enjoy yourself, I suppose I must put myself out for one more day. Tomorrow, though, we really are leaving.’

segments.text: Bao-yu called her his dear sister a thousand times over and begged, ‘Just one more day. We’ll go back tomorrow.’

So they stayed another night. Xi-feng had Lai Wang-er quietly informed of the matter the old nun had brought up the day before. He understood at once, hurried into the city and found the gentleman who handled the household’s correspondence. Pretending that Jia Lian had given the instructions, he had a letter written, then set off that very night for Chang’an county. It was only a hundred li away, and within two days everything had been arranged. The military commissioner, whose name was Yun Guang, had long been indebted to the Jia family. How could he refuse so small a request? He gave a letter in reply, and Wang-er returned. Let us leave that for the moment.

Xi-feng and the others stayed another day, then took leave of the old nun the following morning. Xi-feng told her to come to the mansion three days later for news. Qin Zhong and Sapientia could scarcely bear to part. Their secret promises and arrangements to meet need not be recounted in detail. At last they had to separate, full of regret. Xi-feng went to the Temple of the Iron Threshold once more to see how things stood.

segments.text: Now Bao-yu, finding the outer study put in order, arranged to read there at night with Qin Zhong. But Qin Zhong had always been exceedingly frail. Exposure to wind and frost in the country, together with his secret meetings and intimacies with Sapientia, had left him little chance to care for his health. He came home with a cold and a cough, no appetite and scarcely the strength to keep going. He dared not venture out, but stayed at home to recuperate. Bao-yu’s pleasure was spoiled. There was nothing for it but to wait quietly until he was quite recovered before making another arrangement.

segments.text: Xi-feng had meanwhile received Yun Guang’s reply: everything had been settled. The old nun informed the Zhang family, and the garrison commandant, swallowing his anger, duly accepted the return of the betrothal gifts. Who would have thought that parents so greedy for money and influence could have a daughter with such constancy and feeling? When she learnt that they had rejected the husband first promised to her, she quietly took a hempen cord and hanged herself.

segments.text:
The commandant’s son, who was no less devoted, heard that Jin-ge had hanged herself and drowned himself in the river, true to the pledge of the girl who should have been his wife. Neither the Zhangs nor the Lis had anything to rejoice at: they had lost both the girl and their money. Xi-feng, on the other hand, pocketed three thousand taels without stirring. Lady Wang and the others knew nothing whatever about it. Emboldened by this success, Xi-feng thereafter did as she pleased whenever such a matter arose. We need not record them all.

One day, on Jia Zheng’s birthday, everyone from the Ning and Rong mansions had assembled to congratulate him, and the celebrations were in full swing, when a gatekeeper hurried up to the banquet.

‘Mr Xia, chief eunuch of the Six Palaces, has come with an imperial command!’

Jia She, Jia Zheng and the rest were alarmed, with no notion what it could mean. They hastily stopped the play, cleared away the feast, set out an incense table and opened the central gate, then knelt to receive the visitor. Xia Shou-zhong, chief eunuch of the Six Palaces, rode up with a host of palace eunuchs before, behind and on either side of him. He carried neither a written proclamation nor a sealed decree. Dismounting below the eaves, he walked into the hall, all smiles, and stood facing south.

‘By special command: Jia Zheng is summoned to court at once, for an audience in the Hall of Reverent Attendance.’

Without even stopping for tea, he mounted and rode away.

Jia Zheng and the others could not tell what this portended. He could only hurry to change his clothes and go to court. Grandmother Jia and the whole family remained in an agony of uncertainty, constantly sending riders back and forth for news. About two double-hours had passed when three or four stewards, including Lai Da, came panting through the ceremonial gate with congratulations. Their master had ordered them to ask Her Old Ladyship to bring the ladies to court at once to give thanks for the imperial favour.

Grandmother Jia was standing anxiously under the verandah of the main hall. Lady Xing, Lady Wang, You-shi, Li Wan, Xi-feng, Ying-chun and her sisters, and Aunt Xue were all together there. On hearing the news, she called Lai Da in and questioned him closely.

‘We were waiting outside the Gate of Reverent Attendance,’ he reported, ‘and could learn nothing of what was going on within. At last the eunuch Xia came out to congratulate us. He said our eldest young lady had been promoted to Secretary of the Phoenix Splendour Palace, with the further title of Consort of Worthy Virtue.

‘Later, when the master came out, he gave us the same news and these instructions. He has now gone on to the Eastern Palace. Your Old Ladyship and the ladies are asked to go at once to offer thanks.’

Only then were Grandmother Jia and the rest reassured, and their faces shone with joy.

segments.text: They put on the full ceremonial dress appropriate to their ranks. Grandmother Jia set off for court with Lady Xing, Lady Wang and You-shi in four great sedan-chairs. Jia She and Jia Zhen also changed into court dress and, with Jia Rong and Jia Qiang, attended Grandmother Jia’s chair on the journey. Throughout the Ning and Rong mansions, high and low, within and without, everyone was jubilant. Every face wore a look of triumph, and talk and laughter rose in a ceaseless clamour.

segments.text:
But in recent days Sapientia had secretly fled from Water-Moon Hermitage into the city and made her way to Qin Zhong’s house to see him. Qin Ye discovered her there, drove her out and gave his son a beating. His anger brought on his old illness, and within three to five days he died. Qin Zhong, frail to begin with and still not recovered, had endured the beating only to see his old father die of anger. His grief and remorse came too late, and many more symptoms now appeared.

Bao-yu was deeply dejected, as though something had been taken from him. Even the news of Yuan-chun’s promotion did nothing to dispel his gloom. How Grandmother Jia and the others gave thanks, how they returned home, how friends and relatives came with congratulations, how busy and festive the two mansions had been lately, how pleased everyone was: he alone treated all this as though it were not happening and paid it no attention. People laughed at him for being more of a simpleton than ever.

Happily, Jia Lian and Dai-yu were on their way back. A messenger sent ahead reported that they would reach home the next day, and at this Bao-yu brightened a little. On asking for particulars, he learnt that Jia Yu-cun too was coming to the capital for an imperial audience. Wang Zi-teng had repeatedly submitted memorials recommending him, and he was now to await a vacancy in the capital. Since he and Jia Lian acknowledged a common clan, and Dai-yu had been his pupil, he was travelling with them.

Lin Ru-hai had been buried in the ancestral graveyard, and Jia Lian had only set out for the capital after all the arrangements were complete. They had not expected to reach home until the following month, but news of Yuan-chun’s good fortune had made them press on day and night. All had gone safely on the journey. Bao-yu heard only that Dai-yu was safe: the rest did not concern him.

At last, after a long wait, noon of the next day arrived, and with it the announcement: ‘Master Lian and Miss Lin are home!’ At their reunion grief and joy mingled, and there was another bout of weeping before they exchanged congratulations. Bao-yu thought Dai-yu had grown more ethereally lovely than ever. She had brought back many books and busied herself having her bedroom cleaned and her belongings arranged, as well as distributing paper, brushes and other things among Bao-chai, Ying-chun, Bao-yu and the rest. Bao-yu carefully brought out the string of fragrant jiling beads the Prince of Beijing had given him, to pass it on to her.

‘Some stinking man has handled them! I don’t want them.’

She flung them aside and would not take them. Bao-yu could only put them away again. We shall leave them for the moment.

Jia Lian, meanwhile, had paid his respects to everyone and returned to his own rooms.

Xi-feng had been so busy lately that she scarcely had a moment to spare, but with Jia Lian home from his long journey she had to find time to receive him. No outsiders were in the room.

‘Congratulations, my lord, the imperial brother-in-law!’ she said, smiling. ‘What dust and hardship Your Lordship must have endured on the road! Yesterday your humble servant heard from the first rider sent ahead that your august person would return today. I have prepared a poor cup of wine to wash away the dust. I wonder whether you would condescend to honour it with your presence?’

‘You are too kind! Too kind!’ Jia Lian answered with a laugh. ‘I hardly deserve it.’

Patience and the other maids had made their salutations and were serving tea. Jia Lian asked about everything that had happened at home in his absence and thanked Xi-feng for all the trouble she had taken.

‘As if I could manage such things!’ she said. ‘I know so little, I’m so clumsy with words, and I always take people at their word. Give me a washing-beater and I’ll believe it’s a needle. I haven’t the face to refuse anyone. Two pleasant words and my heart melts. Besides, I’ve never dealt with anything important, and I’m such a coward that the slightest sign of displeasure from Her Ladyship keeps me awake all night.

segments.text: ‘I begged her several times to let me off, but she wouldn’t hear of it. Instead she said I wanted an easy life and wouldn’t learn. Little did she know I was in a cold sweat all the time, afraid to say one word or take one step too many. You know those stewards’ wives of ours. Which of them is easy to deal with? Make the slightest mistake and they laugh and jeer. Show the least favour and they curse the mulberry to abuse the locust, letting you hear their complaints without naming you. “Sit on the hill and watch the tigers fight”, “Kill with a borrowed sword”, “Raise a wind to fan the fire”, “Stand safe on the bank”, “Never lift a hand to right a toppled oil bottle”: they’ve mastered every trick in the book.

segments.text: ‘And I’m so young. Above all, I haven’t the weight to keep them in order. No wonder they think nothing of me. The most ridiculous thing was when Rong’s wife suddenly died over there. Cousin Zhen went down on his knees to Her Ladyship again and again, pleading for me to help him for a few days. I refused over and over, but Her Ladyship wouldn’t allow it, and I had to obey. Of course I turned everything upside down and made it more of a shambles than ever. Cousin Zhen is still complaining and regretting it. Now you’re back, when you see him tomorrow, do try to smooth it over. Tell him how young I am and how little I’ve seen of the world. What possessed him to put me in charge?’

While she was speaking, voices were heard in the outer room.

‘Who’s that?’ Xi-feng asked.

Patience came in. ‘Aunt Xue sent Caltrop to ask me something. I’ve answered her and sent her back.’

segments.text:
‘That reminds me,’ said Jia Lian, smiling. ‘When I went to see Aunt just now, I came face to face with a young married woman. A very pretty creature! I couldn’t think who she was: I’d never seen her in our household. So I asked Aunt as we were talking, and it turned out she was the little girl they bought when they came to the capital, Caltrop. She’s become that great fool Xue’s bedfellow. She’s had her bridal face-threading and grown prettier still. He really is a disgrace to her.’

‘Oh!’ said Xi-feng. ‘You’d think a journey to Suzhou and Hangzhou would have taught you something, but your eyes are still hungry when your belly’s full. If you fancy her, that’s easily settled. Shall I take Patience and exchange her for you? That eldest Xue boy is another who keeps an eye on the pot while he eats from his bowl. Over the past year, what quarrels he’s had with Aunt because he couldn’t get Caltrop! Aunt thought her looks the least of it. The way she behaves is quite unlike other girls: so gentle and quiet that many a young lady of good family couldn’t match her. That was why Aunt went to all the trouble of a feast and guests, and had her made his concubine openly and properly.

‘Before half a month was out, he paid her no more attention than the wind blowing through a stable. I do feel sorry for her.’

She had scarcely finished when a page at the inner gate sent in word: ‘The master is waiting for Master Lian in the main study.’ Jia Lian hastily straightened his clothes and went out.
