Xi-feng now asked Patience, ‘What did Aunt want, to send Caltrop all this way?’

‘There wasn’t any Caltrop,’ Patience said, smiling. ‘I borrowed her name for a little lie. Really, ma’am, Wang-er’s wife has less sense every day.’ She came close to Xi-feng and lowered her voice. ‘That interest money of yours: of all the times to bring it, she had to choose now, when the master was here!

‘Luckily I ran into her in the hall. Otherwise she’d have walked straight in and told you, and if the master had asked what interest it was, naturally you wouldn’t have wanted to keep anything from him. You’d have had to tell him the truth. And with his ways, he’d fish money out of a pot of boiling oil if he could spend it. Once he knew you had these private savings, he’d spend without a care. So I took it from her at once and gave her a talking-to. Who would have thought you’d hear and ask? That was why I made up the story about Caltrop.’

‘I thought as much!’ Xi-feng laughed. ‘Aunt knew your master was back. Why would she suddenly send a concubine over? So it was you playing your damned tricks, you little baggage!’

As they spoke Jia Lian came in. Xi-feng ordered the food and wine, and husband and wife sat facing each other. Though she could drink well, she did not dare indulge herself, but merely kept Jia Lian company. Presently his wet nurse, Nurse Zhao, came in. Both urged her to have some wine and sit up on the kang.

Nurse Zhao firmly refused. Patience and the others had already set a stool and a little footstool below the kang, and she sat on the footstool. Jia Lian chose two dishes from the table and put them on the stool for her to eat.

‘Nurse can hardly chew that,’ said Xi-feng. ‘You’ll only hurt her teeth.’ She turned to Patience. ‘I said this morning that the pork knuckle stewed with ham was beautifully tender, just the thing for Nurse. Why haven’t you taken it to be heated? Hurry and tell them to warm it up.’

Then she said, ‘Nurse, try the Huiquan wine your son has brought back.’

‘I’m drinking it. You have a cup too, ma’am. What is there to be afraid of, so long as you don’t have too much? It wasn’t the wine that brought me here just now. There’s something serious I want you to remember, ma’am, and give me a little of your care. This young master of ours talks so prettily, but when it comes to doing anything, he forgets all about us. A fine reward for nursing you from a baby to this size! I’m old now, and all I have is those two sons. Give them a bit of special consideration and no one else would dare bare his teeth. I’ve asked you again and again. You promise beautifully, and to this day it’s all dried-up shit. Now here’s this wonderful good fortune dropped straight from heaven: where won’t people be needed?

‘So it’s to you I’d better speak, ma’am. If I depended on our young master, I’d starve.’

‘Don’t you worry, Nurse,’ Xi-feng said with a laugh. ‘Leave both his foster-brothers to me. You nursed him from a baby: don’t you know his ways yet? He presses himself on outsiders who have nothing to do with him. Here are his own foster-brothers. Which of them isn’t better than anyone else? If you took care of them, who would dare say no? Why give outsiders all the benefit? No, I’ve got that wrong. We think of them as “outsiders”, but you treat them as your “inside people”.’

The whole room laughed. Nurse Zhao could not stop laughing either, and invoked the Buddha.

‘Well, we’ve a very upright judge sprung up in this room! As for all that nonsense about “inside people” and “outsiders”, our young master does nothing of the kind. He’s just too soft-hearted to refuse when someone asks him a favour.’

‘Exactly,’ said Xi-feng, smiling. ‘With his “inside people” he’s all softness. It’s only with us women at home that he’s hard!’

‘You’ve said everything there is to say, ma’am!’ Nurse Zhao laughed. ‘It does me good. I’ll have another cup of this fine wine. Now our mistress has taken charge, I’ve nothing left to worry about.’

‘Yes, we mustn’t hold up important business,’ Xi-feng said.

‘What did the master want you for just now?’

‘The home visit,’ Jia Lian replied.

‘Has permission really been given?’ she asked eagerly.

‘If it’s not absolutely certain,’ he said with a smile, ‘it’s eight parts out of ten.’

‘What generosity our Emperor shows!’ said Xi-feng. ‘All the old stories I’ve heard and plays I’ve seen, and never anything like it.’

Nurse Zhao broke in. ‘That’s just it. I must be growing old and muddle-headed. I’ve heard everyone, upstairs and down, making a commotion these last few days about a home visit, but I never troubled myself over it. Now here it is again. What does it all mean?’

‘His Majesty understands the hearts of all his people,’ Jia Lian said. ‘There is nothing greater in the world than filial duty. The love between parents and children must surely be the same for everyone; rank makes no difference to that. Though His Majesty attends the Retired Emperor and the Empress Dowager day and night, he still feels he has not done enough. Seeing that the consorts and ladies of the palace have all been there for years, parted from the sight and sound of their parents, he thought: how could they fail to miss them? It is only right for children to long for their parents.

segments.text: ‘And he thought of the parents at home, always missing children they could never see. “If they should fall ill, or even die, on that account, it would be because I have kept their children confined, denying them the natural wish of every family. That would grievously offend the harmony of Heaven.” So he laid the matter before the Retired Emperor and the Empress Dowager, proposing that the families of the palace ladies should be allowed to visit them on dates ending in two or six each month. Their Majesties were delighted. They praised his perfect filial devotion and pure benevolence, his understanding of Heaven and the nature of things. Then the two elder sovereigns issued a further decree. When families came into the palace, they said, there must inevitably be rules of state and ceremonial restraints, so that even mothers and daughters could not speak their hearts freely. They therefore extended their gracious indulgence still further and specially informed the imperial ladies’ families that, in addition to the privilege of visits on dates ending in two or six, any family with suitable ranges of buildings and separate grounds, where an imperial visitor could lodge and be properly guarded, might petition to receive the imperial carriage from the inner palace at its own house. This would allow the affections of kin and the deepest feelings of family life some small fulfilment. Who could fail to rejoice and give thanks when that decree came out? Honoured Lady Zhou’s father has already begun building a villa at home for her visit.

‘And the family of Wu Tian-you, Noble Consort Wu’s father, have been looking at sites outside the city. Doesn’t that make it eight or nine parts certain?’

‘Amitabha!’ said Nurse Zhao. ‘So that’s it! Then we too must prepare to receive our eldest young lady?’

‘Of course!’ said Jia Lian.

‘What else do you suppose all this bustle is for?’

‘If it really happens, I shall see something of the world at last,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘What a pity I wasn’t born a few years earlier! Another twenty or thirty years and these old people wouldn’t look down on me for having seen nothing. When they talk about the founding emperor’s tours in imitation of Shun’s royal progresses, it sounds more exciting than a whole book of stories. I never had the luck to see it.’

‘Oh, my!’ said Nurse Zhao. ‘That was something you might not see in a thousand years! I was just old enough to remember things then. Our Jia family were supervising the building of seagoing vessels and repairs to the sea walls around Suzhou and Yangzhou. Just to prepare for that one imperial visit, they poured out silver like seawater. Why, to tell you—’

‘Our Wang family prepared for one too,’ Xi-feng broke in. ‘My grandfather had sole charge then of the tribute and ceremonial greetings from foreign countries. Every foreigner who came was maintained by our family. All the goods brought by foreign ships to Guangdong, Fujian, Yunnan and Zhejiang were ours.’

‘Who doesn’t know that?’ said Nurse Zhao. ‘There’s still a saying: “When the Eastern Sea lacks a white-jade bed,
The Dragon King comes to ask the Wangs of Jiangnan.” That’s your family, ma’am. And the Zhens who are still down in Jiangnan: oh, what a display they made! That family alone received the Emperor four times. If we hadn’t seen it with our own eyes, no one we told would believe it. Never mind treating silver like dirt: everything in the world was piled up in mountains and seas. They hadn’t a thought to spare for such words as “waste” or “sin”.’

‘I’ve often heard our old gentlemen say so,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Of course I believe it. What puzzles me is how that family came to be so rich and grand.’

‘I’ll tell you one thing, ma’am. It was only the Emperor’s own money being spent on the Emperor! Who has that sort of money to buy a show of empty glory?’

They were talking animatedly when Lady Wang sent someone again to see whether Xi-feng had eaten.

Xi-feng knew this meant there was business waiting for her. She hurriedly ate half a bowl of rice, rinsed her mouth and was about to go when the pages at the inner gate reported that the two young gentlemen from the Ning mansion, Rong and Qiang, had arrived. Jia Lian had just rinsed his mouth too, and Patience was holding a basin for him to wash his hands.

‘What is it?’ he asked them. ‘Speak up.’

Xi-feng stopped to hear what they had to say. Jia Rong spoke first.

‘Father sent me to tell you, Uncle, that the masters have settled it. Beginning on the east, taking in our garden and turning round to the north, they’ve measured it all: three and a half li in extent. That will do for the villa for the imperial home visit. Someone has been sent for to draw the plans, and they’ll be ready tomorrow. You must be tired after your journey, so there’s no need for you to come over tonight. If there is anything to discuss, they’ll ask you over early tomorrow morning.’

Jia Lian smiled and answered at once. ‘Thank your father for his thoughtfulness. I won’t come over, then. This plan really does save trouble, and it will be easy to build there. Buying another site would be much more work, and the result wouldn’t be at all fitting.

‘Tell him I think this is excellent. If the masters want to change their minds, we must rely on him to dissuade them. On no account should we look elsewhere. I’ll come over early tomorrow to pay my respects and discuss the details.’

Jia Rong repeatedly assented. Jia Qiang now stepped forward.

‘Uncle, Master Zhen has put me in charge of going to Suzhou to engage instructors, buy girls and provide instruments, costumes and the rest. I’m to take the steward Lai’s two sons, and the two literary gentlemen Shan Pin-ren and Bu Gu-xiu. That’s why he told me to come and see you.’

Jia Lian looked him up and down and smiled.

‘Do you know anything about that line of business? It’s not a particularly large undertaking, but there are plenty of things hidden under the surface.’

‘I can only learn as I go,’ Jia Qiang said, smiling.

Beside them, in the lamplight, Jia Rong secretly tugged at Xi-feng’s clothing. She took the hint.

‘You worry too much,’ she said with a smile. ‘Surely your father knows as well as you whom to employ? Yet here you are, afraid the boy doesn’t know the business. Who knows everything to begin with? These children are quite grown up now. Even if they’ve never eaten pork, they’ve seen a pig run.

‘Your cousin is only sending him to sit under the commander’s banner. Does he seriously expect him to bargain over prices and do all the trading himself? I think it’s a very good arrangement.’

‘Of course,’ said Jia Lian. ‘I wasn’t objecting. But I ought to help him think it through.’ He asked Jia Qiang, ‘Where is the money for this to come from?’

‘We were just discussing that too. Grandfather Lai says there’s no need to carry it down from the capital. The Zhen family in Jiangnan still hold fifty thousand taels of our silver. Tomorrow we’re to take a letter and a bill of exchange, draw thirty thousand first, and leave the other twenty thousand there to pay for candles, coloured lanterns, and all the curtains, blinds and hangings.’

‘A good idea,’ Jia Lian said, nodding.

Xi-feng at once turned to Jia Qiang.

‘In that case, I have two reliable men who know the business. Take them with you to do the work. That will make things easy for you.’

Jia Qiang was all smiles. ‘I was just going to ask you for a couple of men, Aunt. How fortunate!’ He asked their names, and Xi-feng turned to Nurse Zhao. The old woman had been listening in a daze. Patience laughed and nudged her, and she came to herself.

‘One’s Zhao Tian-liang, and the other’s Zhao Tian-dong,’ she said quickly.

‘Mind you don’t forget,’ said Xi-feng. ‘I must get on with my own business.’

She went out. Jia Rong hurried to escort her and spoke quietly.

‘If you want anything, Aunt, tell me. I’ll make a list for Qiang to take, and have him buy it all for you.’

‘Don’t talk such bloody nonsense!’ Xi-feng said with a laugh. ‘I haven’t anywhere to put the things I have already. Do you think I want your sneaking little favours?’

And she went straight on.

Jia Qiang likewise asked Jia Lian quietly, ‘Is there anything you would like? I could have it woven while I’m there, as a little token of respect.’

‘Don’t get carried away,’ Jia Lian said, smiling. ‘You’re only just learning to do business, and you’ve already learnt that trick. If I need anything, I’ll write and tell you. We needn’t talk about that now.’

segments.text: He dismissed them both. People then came in to report on business three or four times and more, until Jia Lian, worn out, sent instructions to the inner gate that no further messages were to be admitted: everything must wait until tomorrow. It was the third watch before Xi-feng at last came back to bed. The night passed without further incident.

segments.text:
Next morning Jia Lian rose, paid his respects to Jia She and Jia Zheng, and went over to the Ning mansion. With the old stewards and several literary dependants and family friends, he inspected the grounds of both houses, planned and drew the buildings for the imperial visit, and considered how to arrange the labour.

From then on, craftsmen of every trade gathered there. Gold, silver, copper and tin, earth, timber, bricks and tiles were carried in without a pause. First the workmen were told to take down walls and pavilions in the Ning mansion’s Garden of Gathered Fragrance, opening it directly into the Rong mansion’s great eastern courtyard. The whole range of servants’ quarters on the eastern side of the Rong mansion was demolished. Until then the two estates had been divided by a narrow lane, with no passage between them, but the lane was private property, not a public thoroughfare, so the grounds could be joined. A stream of running water already entered the Garden of Gathered Fragrance beneath the wall at its north corner. There was no need to bring in another supply.

segments.text: There were not enough rocks and trees, but Jia She lived in what had once been the Rong mansion’s garden. Its bamboos, trees, rocks, pavilions, balustrades and other fittings could all be moved over. The two places were very close, and combining their resources would save a great deal of money and labour. Even if they did not provide enough, comparatively little would have to be added. All the planning and construction owed much to an elderly gentleman who went by the name of Shan Zi-ye.

segments.text: Jia Zheng was unused to practical business and left the arrangements entirely to Jia She, Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Lai Da, Lai Sheng, Lin Zhi-xiao, Wu Xin-deng, Zhan Guang, Cheng Ri-xing and the others. Shan Zi-ye designed the artificial hills and excavated pools, the towers and pavilions, the planting of bamboos and flowers, and every other feature of the landscape. When free after court, Jia Zheng merely looked round the various parts and discussed the most important points with Jia She and the rest. Jia She himself stayed comfortably at home. Jia Zhen and the others reported every trifling matter to him, either in person or in a brief written account. If he had anything to say, he sent for Jia Lian, Lai Da and the others to receive his instructions. Jia Rong’s sole charge was the making of gold and silver vessels. Jia Qiang had already left for Suzhou. Jia Zhen, Lai Da and the rest also had to assign the workers, draw up registers and supervise the work. No single pen could describe it all. Enough to say that for a time there was extraordinary bustle and commotion. Let us leave them there.

Now with such a great undertaking in the family, Jia Zheng had stopped examining Bao-yu on his books, which was a great relief to him. Yet Qin Zhong’s illness grew worse day by day, and Bao-yu was too anxious to enjoy his freedom. One morning he had just washed and combed his hair, and was intending to ask Grandmother Jia’s leave to visit Qin Zhong, when he saw Tealeaf peering round the spirit-screen at the inner gate, his head bobbing in and out. Bao-yu hurried out.

‘What is it?’

‘Master Qin’s dying!’

Bao-yu started in alarm. ‘I only saw him yesterday, and he was quite clear-headed. How can he be dying?’

‘I don’t know. The old man from his house came specially to tell me just now.’

Bao-yu turned at once to tell Grandmother Jia.

‘Choose reliable people to go with him,’ she ordered. ‘Go and show your affection for your schoolfellow, then come back. You mustn’t stay too long.’

Bao-yu hurried to change and came out again. The carriage was not ready, and in his impatience he paced wildly round the hall.

At last, under repeated urging, the carriage arrived. He scrambled in, with Li Gui, Tealeaf and the others attending him. No one was at Qin Zhong’s gate. They all crowded into the inner room, frightening Qin Zhong’s two distant aunts and several male cousins so much that they could scarcely get out of the way in time. Qin Zhong had already lost consciousness two or three times. His bed had long since been moved and its mat changed in preparation for death. At the sight Bao-yu could not help crying out.

‘No, no!’ Li Gui hastily urged him. ‘Master Qin is suffering from weakness. Lying stiffly up on the kang must have made his bones uncomfortable, so they’ve moved him down for a while to give him some ease. Carrying on like this will only make him worse, young master.’

Bao-yu restrained himself and went closer. Qin Zhong’s face was white as wax. He lay breathing on the pillow with his eyes shut.

Bao-yu called urgently, ‘Brother Jing!

‘Bao-yu is here.’

He called two or three times, but Qin Zhong made no response.

‘Bao-yu is here,’ he said again.

Qin Zhong’s soul had already left his body; only a faint last breath lingered in his chest. He was seeing a crowd of ghostly officers coming to seize him with warrants and ropes. His soul was unwilling to go. He thought of the household with no one left to manage it, of the three or four thousand taels his father had saved, and of Sapientia, whose whereabouts were still unknown. He pleaded with the officers in every possible way, but they would make no exception. Instead they rebuked him.

‘And you call yourself an educated man! Don’t you know the saying, “If King Yama orders you to die at the third watch, who dares keep you till the fifth?” Here in the world below we are all strictly impartial, from top to bottom. We’re not like you up among the living, always considering people’s feelings and connexions, with a thousand things to stand in your way.’

In the midst of this wrangle, Qin Zhong’s soul suddenly heard the words ‘Bao-yu is here’. He hastened to plead again.

‘Honoured messengers, have a little compassion. Let me go back and say one word to this dear friend, and then I’ll come.’

‘What dear friend is this now?’ the ghosts asked.

‘To tell you the truth, gentlemen,’ said Qin Zhong, ‘he is the Duke of Rong’s grandson. His childhood name is Bao-yu.’

The chief judge was the first to take fright. He hastily rounded on the ghostly messengers.

‘I told you to let him go back for a little while, but you wouldn’t listen! You had to wait till he brought out the name of someone whose star is rising and whose luck is in.’

Seeing their chief judge so alarmed, the ghosts too became flustered, but they grumbled as well.

‘You were all thunder and lightning just now, sir. So it turns out you can’t bear to hear the name “Bao-yu”! In our humble opinion, he belongs to the living and we to the dead. Being afraid of them does us no good.’

The chief judge snapped, ‘Rubbish!

‘There’s a good saying: “An official of the world has a hand in all the world’s affairs.” Since ancient times, men and ghosts have followed the same ways. The living and the dead don’t have two different sets of rules. Never mind which world he belongs to. Let him go back, and we shan’t go wrong.’

The ghosts had no choice but to release Qin Zhong’s soul. He gave a groan and opened his eyes a little. Seeing Bao-yu beside him, he forced out a sigh.

‘Why wouldn’t you come sooner? A moment later and we couldn’t have seen each other.’

Bao-yu took his hand, tears falling.

‘Is there anything you want to say? Leave me a few words.’

‘There’s nothing else,’ Qin Zhong said. ‘You and I used to think our understanding was above everyone else’s. Only today do I see how I led myself astray. From now on you ought to set your heart on success in the examinations and an official career. Honour and distinction are what you should aim for.’

With that he gave a long sigh and quietly passed away.

Splendour may well be envied,
But parting is hard to bear.
An empty name is won;
Who knows the bitter and the sweet?

segments.text: Now that Qin Zhong was dead, Bao-yu wept inconsolably. Only after a long struggle did Li Gui and the others persuade him to stop, and he was still stricken with grief on the way home. Grandmother Jia contributed several dozen taels of silver and provided funeral offerings besides. Bao-yu went to mourn and burn paper for the dead. Seven days later the coffin was taken out and buried. There is nothing further to relate, except that Bao-yu remembered his friend and mourned him every day, though there was nothing he could do.

segments.text:
An uncertain number of days had passed when Jia Zhen and the others came to report to Jia Zheng.
‘All the work in the garden is finished. The Elder Master has inspected it. We are only waiting for you to look it over, sir, so that anything unsuitable can be altered. Then the plaques and couplets can be inscribed.’
Jia Zheng considered this for a while.
‘The plaques and couplets will be a difficult matter. By rights we should ask Her Highness to bestow the inscriptions. But until she has seen the garden herself, she will hardly be willing to compose them at hazard. On the other hand, if we wait until after her visit to ask, all this scenery, all these pavilions and terraces, will look rather bare and dull without any words to distinguish them. Flowers and willows, hills and water alone cannot give them their full lustre.’
The literary dependants standing beside him answered with smiles.
‘You are quite right, sir. We have a humble suggestion. The plaques and couplets are indispensable, but they must not settle the names once and for all.

segments.text:
‘For the present, why not devise phrases of two, three or four characters, appropriate to the scenery, that merely suggest its meaning? They can be made into illuminated plaques and couplets and hung up temporarily. When Her Highness visits, she can be asked to decide the names. Would that not meet both difficulties?’
‘An excellent suggestion,’ said Jia Zheng and the others.
‘Let us go and look today,’ he continued, ‘and propose whatever occurs to us. Anything suitable can be used. If it will not do, we can ask Yu-cun to come and devise something else.’
‘Whatever you devise today is certain to be excellent, sir,’ the guests said with a laugh. ‘Why wait for Yu-cun?’
‘You do not understand,’ Jia Zheng answered, smiling. ‘Even as a boy I was never much good at verses about flowers and birds or hills and streams. Now I am getting on in years, and official papers keep me so busy that I have grown still more unfamiliar with writing for pleasure. Whatever I produced would be pedantic and stiff. Instead of lending charm to the garden, it might be quite out of keeping and spoil the effect.’
‘That need not matter,’ said the literary dependants. ‘We can all look round and compose together. Each of us can contribute whatever he does best. Keep the good and discard the bad. Surely that would serve.’
‘Very true,’ said Jia Zheng.

‘And luckily it is warm today. Let us all take a walk.’
He rose and led the party out. Jia Zhen went ahead to warn the people in the garden. As it happened, Bao-yu’s grief for Qin Zhong had lately been so unremitting that Grandmother Jia often had him taken there to amuse himself. He had only just gone in when he saw Jia Zhen coming towards him.
‘Hadn’t you better get out?’ Jia Zhen said with a smile. ‘Your father is coming.’
Bao-yu fled from the garden with his nurses and pages. No sooner had he rounded a bend, however, than he came face to face with Jia Zheng and his guests. It was too late to hide. He could only stand to one side. Jia Zheng had recently heard the schoolmaster praise Bao-yu’s particular aptitude for composing couplets. He disliked his books, but apparently possessed a kind of wayward talent. Finding this unexpected opportunity, Jia Zheng ordered him to come along. Bao-yu had no choice but to follow, without the least idea why he was wanted.

As Jia Zheng reached the garden entrance, Jia Zhen came up with a large number of attendants, who stood waiting to one side.
‘Shut all the gates for the moment,’ Jia Zheng told him. ‘We will look at the outside before we go in.’
Jia Zhen had them closed. Jia Zheng first stood squarely before the main entrance to examine it. It was five bays wide, with rounded roof-tiles and a smooth, loach-back ridge. The railings and window lattices were finely carved in fresh designs, without any red paint or other coloured finish. The surrounding walls were of evenly dressed brickwork, and the white stone platform below was carved with curling foreign foliage. To either side stretched snow-white plaster walls, built on mottled stone foundations and following the lie of the ground. Jia Zheng was pleased: here was none of the usual ostentatious splendour. He ordered the gates opened. Immediately inside, a screen of green hills blocked the view.
‘Splendid hills! Splendid!’ cried the literary dependants.

‘Without this hill,’ said Jia Zheng, ‘you would see everything the moment you came in. Where would be the pleasure in that?’
‘Precisely. Only someone with hills and valleys in his breast could have thought of it.’
Looking ahead as they spoke, they saw jagged white rocks, some like demons, others like fierce beasts, rearing and leaning across one another. Moss mottled their surfaces, and creepers half concealed them. Between them showed a narrow, twisting path.
‘We will explore along this little path,’ said Jia Zheng, ‘and leave by the other side on our way back. Then we shall have seen everything.’

He sent Jia Zhen ahead to lead the way and, resting a hand on Bao-yu, wound his way into the opening between the hills. Looking up, he suddenly saw a slab of white stone with a surface smooth as a mirror, placed to face them and clearly intended for an inscription.
‘Gentlemen,’ he said, turning with a smile, ‘what would be a fitting title here?’
One proposed ‘Fold upon Fold of Green’, another ‘Brocade Screen’, another ‘Rival to Incense-burner Peak’, another ‘Little Zhongnan’. There were dozens of suggestions. In fact, the guests already understood that Jia Zheng meant to test Bao-yu’s progress, and were merely offering conventional phrases to oblige him. Bao-yu had guessed the intention too. Having heard the proposals, Jia Zheng turned and ordered him to devise one.
‘I have heard an old saying,’ Bao-yu replied. ‘“Better to transmit the old than compose the new; an ancient carving outshines a modern embellishment.” Besides, this is neither the principal hill nor the main scene. There is nothing here that really calls for a title. It is simply a first step towards discovering the garden. Why not inscribe the old line, “A winding path leads into seclusion”? It would have a certain breadth and dignity.’
‘Exactly!’ they all exclaimed.

‘Young Master Bao has a remarkable natural gift and an uncommon imagination. Nothing like us, with all the life read out of us!’
‘You must not flatter him,’ Jia Zheng said with a smile. ‘He is only a child, making one scrap of knowledge do the work of ten. We may laugh at him, that is all. We shall choose the inscription later.’

They went on into a rocky passage. Beyond it, fine trees grew in luxuriant masses and strange flowers blazed with colour. A clear stream wound out of the depths of the flowers and trees and poured beneath the clefts in the rocks. A few steps further, tending northwards, brought them into a broad, level space. On either side, upper storeys seemed to fly into the sky, their carved roof-ridges and richly worked balustrades half hidden among folds of the hills and the tops of trees. Looking down, they saw the clear brook tumble white as snow, with stone steps climbing into the clouds. A white stone railing curved round the pool. A stone bridge spanned three channels, and water spouted from the mouths of carved beasts. There was a pavilion on the bridge. Jia Zheng and his companions went up into it and sat beside the railing.
‘What would you inscribe here, gentlemen?’ he asked.
‘In his Account of the Old Drunkard’s Pavilion, Ouyang Xiu wrote, “There is a pavilion with wings outspread.” Call it “Wings Outspread”.’
‘A fine phrase,’ said Jia Zheng with a smile, ‘but this pavilion stands over water. The inscription ought to give particular attention to that. My poor judgement would favour another phrase of Ouyang’s: “Cascading out between two peaks.” I should take the word “cascading”.’
‘Exactly, exactly!’ said one of the guests.

‘“Cascading Jade” would be perfect.’
Jia Zheng stroked his beard thoughtfully, then looked up and saw Bao-yu attending at his side. With a smile he ordered him to offer a suggestion too.
‘What you proposed just now was certainly right, Father,’ Bao-yu replied hastily. ‘But if one examines it further, “cascading” was appropriate when Ouyang used it of Brewer’s Spring. Applied to this spring, it seems less suitable. Although this is only a country retreat for Her Highness to stay in on her home visit, the inscriptions should still follow the rules for writing by imperial command. A word of that sort seems rather coarse and inelegant. Might something more restrained and suggestive be found?’
‘What do you make of this argument, gentlemen?’ Jia Zheng asked with a smile. ‘When they composed something new, you said we should use the old. Now we use the old, you say it is coarse and unsuitable. Let us hear your own proposal.’
‘Instead of “Cascading Jade”, would not “Drenched Blossoms” be fresher and more elegant?’
Jia Zheng stroked his beard and nodded without speaking.

The guests hurried to follow his lead, praising Bao-yu’s exceptional talent.
‘Two characters for a plaque are easy enough,’ said Jia Zheng. ‘Now compose a couplet of seven characters to a line.’
Standing in the pavilion, Bao-yu looked about him. An idea came at once, and he recited:
‘Willows round the bank lend green to three poles’ depth of water;
Flowers across the shore share fragrance with a single stream.’
Jia Zheng nodded and smiled slightly. The others were already pouring out their praise.

They left the pavilion and crossed the pool, studying every hill and rock, every flower and tree. Suddenly they looked up to see a stretch of whitewashed wall ahead. Within it stood several bays of elegant rooms, half screened by hundreds upon hundreds of green bamboo stems.
‘What a lovely spot!’ they all said.

segments.text: They went in. A winding covered walk began just inside the gate, and below the steps a path was laid with pebbles. Above were two or three small rooms, with one open central room and two enclosed side rooms. The beds, small tables, chairs and desks had all been made to fit their places. A little door in one of the inner rooms led into a back courtyard, where tall pear trees in blossom stood among plantains. There were also two small rooms at the rear. An opening in the back wall admitted a stream through a channel only a foot or so wide. It wound round the steps and along the house to the front courtyard, then curved away beneath the bamboo.

‘This place is not bad,’ Jia Zheng said with a smile. ‘A man who could sit reading at this window on a moonlit night would not have lived in vain.’
He looked at Bao-yu as he spoke. Bao-yu lowered his head in alarm. The guests hastened to ease the moment with conversation.
‘The plaque here ought to have four characters,’ they said.
‘Which four?’ Jia Zheng asked, smiling.
One proposed ‘The Qi River’s Enduring Grace’.
‘Commonplace,’ said Jia Zheng.
Another suggested ‘Traces of Sui Garden’.
‘Commonplace too.’
‘Let Cousin Bao devise one,’ said Jia Zhen with a smile.
‘Before he has composed a thing himself,’ said Jia Zheng, ‘he must first pronounce on everyone else’s efforts. A sure sign of a frivolous nature.’
‘But his criticisms are quite right. What can one do?’ said the guests.
‘You must not indulge him so.’ Then he addressed Bao-yu. ‘Today you may talk all the wild nonsense you please. Give us your criticisms first, and only then will you be allowed to compose anything.

‘Were any of those proposals usable?’
‘None seems quite suitable,’ Bao-yu answered.
‘And why not?’ Jia Zheng asked with a cold laugh.
‘This is the first place where Her Highness will make a stop. There must be some tribute to the throne. If the plaque is to have four characters, there is a ready-made phrase in the old books. Why compose a new one?’

segments.text:
‘Are “Qi River” and “Sui Garden” not from the old books?’ asked Jia Zheng.
‘But they are so stiff and stale. “The Phoenix Comes in State” would be better.’
A chorus of delighted approval broke out.
‘You little brute!’ said Jia Zheng, nodding. ‘Little brute! A fine instance of looking at the heavens through a tube and measuring the sea with a shell.’

‘Now give us a couplet,’ he ordered.
Bao-yu recited:
‘Tea rests in the precious tripod; its steam is green still;
The game ends by the quiet window; the fingers are cool yet.’
Jia Zheng shook his head.
‘I see no improvement.’
He led the others out.

Just as they were leaving, another matter occurred to him.
‘These courtyards and houses are all provided for,’ he said to Jia Zhen, ‘and so are the tables, desks and chairs. But have the curtains and hangings, the ornaments and curios, all been selected to suit each place?’

segments.text:
‘A great many ornaments have already been added,’ Jia Zhen replied. ‘They will naturally be arranged to suit the rooms when the time comes. As for the curtains and hangings, Cousin Lian told me yesterday that they were not all here yet. When work first began, drawings were made for each place and exact measurements taken. People were sent to have them made then. I believe half had arrived by yesterday.’
Realising from this that Jia Zhen was not responsible for the business, Jia Zheng sent for Jia Lian.

Jia Lian hurried up presently. Jia Zheng asked how many kinds there were altogether, how many had arrived and how many were still outstanding. Jia Lian hastily took a folded paper memorandum from the pocket inside the shaft of his boot. He glanced at it and replied:
‘There are a hundred and twenty sets of large and small hangings: figured python designs and raised embroidery, silk-tapestry and ink-sprinkled work, and silks and damasks of various colours. Eighty sets arrived yesterday, leaving forty outstanding. All two hundred curtains arrived yesterday too. In addition, there are two hundred felt curtains, two hundred golden-cane and red-lacquered bamboo blinds, two hundred black-lacquered bamboo blinds, and two hundred curtains knotted in five-coloured thread with coiled floral patterns. Half of each kind has arrived, and they will all be here by autumn at the latest. We also have the chair covers, table skirts, bed valances and table covers, twelve hundred of each.’

They walked on as they talked, until a green hill cut across their way. Rounding its flank, they caught sight of a yellow mud wall topped with rice straw. Several hundred apricot trees blossomed there, like bursts of flame or banks of rosy cloud. Within were a few thatched rooms. Outside, young mulberry, elm, hibiscus and cudrania trees had their fresh shoots woven into two green fences that followed the winding ground. Beyond the fence, below the hillside, stood an earthen well with a counterpoised sweep, a windlass and other tackle. Beneath it, beds and plots of fine vegetables and flowering greens seemed to stretch without end.
‘Now this has something to recommend it,’ Jia Zheng said with a smile. ‘Man-made and contrived as it is, the sight of it makes me long to retire to the land. Let us go in and rest.’
He was about to enter the wicket when he noticed a stone tablet beside the path, also awaiting an inscription.
‘Better still!’ cried the guests. ‘A plaque hung up here would destroy every trace of the farmhouse character. This stone gives it so much more charm. Nothing short of Fan Shihu’s poems of rural life could do it justice.’
‘Then suggest an inscription, gentlemen,’ said Jia Zheng.
‘As your son said just now, “Better to transmit the old than compose the new.” The old poets have said everything about such a place already. “Apricot-blossom Village” would be perfect.’
Jia Zheng smiled and turned to Jia Zhen.
‘A timely reminder!

segments.text:
‘Everything here is excellent, but it still lacks a tavern flag. Have one made tomorrow, nothing elaborate, just like those in the villages outside, and hang it from a bamboo pole above the trees.’
Jia Zhen assented.
‘We must not keep any other sorts of birds here either,’ he added. ‘Geese, ducks and chickens are what we should buy. They would all be in keeping.’
‘Better still!’ said Jia Zheng and the others.
‘“Apricot-blossom Village” is good,’ Jia Zheng told the guests, ‘but it amounts to giving the place its actual name. That must wait until Her Highness is asked to name it.’
‘Of course,’ they agreed. ‘What words would merely suggest it for the present?’
While they were thinking, Bao-yu could wait no longer. Without being told to speak, he said:
‘There is an old line: “A tavern flag hangs above the red apricot tips.” Why not use “The Apricot Tavern Flag in Sight”?’
‘Excellent, that “in sight”!’ they all said. ‘And it hints at “Apricot-blossom Village” too.’
Bao-yu gave a scornful laugh.
‘To call the village “Apricot-blossom” would be unbearably commonplace.

‘Another old poet wrote, “A brushwood gate beside the water, rice blossom sweet in the air.” Why not call it “Sweet-rice Village”?’
They applauded with an even louder chorus of ‘Excellent!’
Jia Zheng cut them short with a shout.

‘How many poets do you know? How many familiar verses can you remember? Yet you dare show off before these gentlemen! All that nonsense of yours was only to let us test the quality of your mind and have a little amusement. You have begun to take yourself seriously!’
He led them into the thatched hall. With its paper windows and wooden couch, it had cast off every trace of wealth and rank. Jia Zheng was secretly delighted, but he glanced at Bao-yu.
‘What do you think of this place?’
The guests quietly nudged Bao-yu, urging him to praise it. He ignored them.
‘It is nothing like as good as “The Phoenix Comes in State”,’ he answered at once.
‘Ignorant fool!’ said Jia Zheng. ‘You know nothing but red towers and painted beams. Vulgar splendour is all you care for. What can you understand of this peaceful seclusion?

‘It all comes of not reading your books!’
‘Your rebuke is quite right, Father,’ Bao-yu answered quickly. ‘But the old writers often speak of “the natural”. What does that mean?’
Everyone was exasperated by his stubbornness. They thought the boy would never learn. At his question they hastened to explain:
‘You understand everything else. How can you not understand “the natural”? It means something that exists of itself in nature, without being made by human effort.’
‘There you are again!’ said Bao-yu. ‘To put a farm here is plainly a forced and laboured contrivance. There is no neighbouring village in the distance, no town wall near at hand. The hill behind has no range to belong to; the water in front has no source. There is no temple tower hidden on the heights, no bridge below leading to a market. It stands all by itself, abruptly, and scarcely makes a fine prospect. How can it compare with the other place, which has the pattern and spirit of nature? Bamboo has been planted and a stream brought in, but without any sense of strain. When the old writers spoke of “a natural picture”, surely their concern was precisely that one should not force a place to be what it is not, or a hill to be what it is not. However skilfully it is done, it can never fit…’
Before he could finish, Jia Zheng shouted furiously, ‘Throw him out!’
He had barely gone when Jia Zheng shouted again, ‘Come back!’

He ordered Bao-yu to compose another couplet.
‘And if it makes no sense, you shall have your mouth slapped into the bargain!’
Bao-yu could only recite:
‘New-risen water adds its green where kudzu cloth is washed;
Fair clouds shelter the cress-gatherer in fragrance.’
Jia Zheng shook his head.
‘Worse than ever.’
He led the party out, round the hillside and through flowers and willows, past rocks they brushed with their hands and springs they walked beside. They passed a rose trellis, entered a bower of fragrant climbing roses, crossed a peony pavilion and a herbaceous peony garden, went into a rose courtyard and out through a plantain hollow, twisting and turning all the way. Suddenly they heard water murmuring out of a rocky cave. Creepers hung down above it, and fallen blossoms floated below.
‘A lovely scene!’ they all said.
‘What inscription would you propose here, gentlemen?’ asked Jia Zheng.

‘That is more explicit still,’ said Bao-yu. ‘“The Qin Refugees’ Old Home” suggests escaping from disorder. How could that be suitable? Why not “Knotweed Banks and Flowering Inlets”?’
Jia Zheng condemned this as further nonsense. They were about to enter the water-cave when he remembered to ask whether there were any boats.
‘Four lotus-gathering boats and one passenger boat,’ Jia Zhen replied. ‘But they are not finished yet.’
‘A pity we cannot go in,’ Jia Zheng said with a smile.
‘There is also a winding path over the hill,’ said Jia Zhen.
He led the way, and they followed, pulling themselves along by creepers and steadying themselves against trees. The fallen blossom on the water grew ever thicker, and the water itself ever clearer. It spread and rippled, winding this way and that. Two rows of weeping willows lined the banks, interspersed with peach and apricot trees. They screened out the sky and sun; not a speck of dust could enter. Presently, in the willow shade, another wooden bridge appeared, turning at angles like a folded belt and furnished with a red balustrade. Across it, paths led in every direction. Ahead stood a cool, tiled house, its walls all of dressed brick, with grey roof-tiles and patterned walling. Spurs from the principal hill ran straight through the enclosing walls.

‘This house is very uninteresting,’ Jia Zheng said.
But as he stepped through the entrance, an enormous, intricately pierced rock suddenly rose before him, seeming to thrust into the sky. Other rocks of every shape stood round it, completely hiding the buildings behind. There was not a single tree or flowering shrub. Instead, strange herbs grew everywhere. Some sent out tendrils, others trailed long runners. They hung from the summit or pierced the clefts, drooped from the eaves and coiled round pillars, twined along the masonry and curled about the steps. Some fluttered like green ribbons; others twisted like golden cords. Some had fruit like cinnabar, others flowers like golden cassia. Their fragrance was rich and pervasive, beyond anything that ordinary flowers could rival.
‘How interesting!’ Jia Zheng said with an involuntary smile. ‘But I hardly recognise any of them.’
‘Climbing figs and creepers,’ someone suggested.
‘Those could not give out such an extraordinary scent,’ Jia Zheng said.
‘No, indeed,’ said Bao-yu. ‘There are some creepers and climbing figs among them, but the scented ones are du-ruo and heng-wu. That kind is probably chai-lan, this one probably qing-ge. Those are golden-canopy grasses, these jade-lu vines. The red ones are surely purple rue, and the green ones must be green zhi.

‘They must be the strange plants in the Li Sao and the Literary Selections and books like those. Some are called huo-na and jiang-xun, some lun-zu and zi-jiang; then there are stone-sails, water-pines, fu-liu, and something called green-yi, as well as red pepper, mi-wu and feng-lian. As the years go by, people lose the knowledge of them. They give them new names from their appearance, and gradually the names go wrong. That must sometimes happen too.’
Before he had finished, Jia Zheng snapped, ‘Who asked you?’

Bao-yu stepped back in alarm and dared say no more. Jia Zheng noticed covered walks running along both sides, and followed one in. Ahead were five bays of airy rooms joined to a rounded-roofed porch, with verandahs on all four sides. Their green windows and polished walls had a quiet elegance quite different from the places they had already seen.
‘Anyone brewing tea and playing the qin in here would have no need to burn incense,’ Jia Zheng said with a sigh. ‘This design has exceeded all my expectations. You gentlemen must devise something fine and fresh for its plaque, or we shall not have done it justice.’
‘Nothing could fit it better than “Orchid Breezes and Fragrant Dew”,’ the guests said with smiles.
‘Those four characters will serve,’ said Jia Zheng. ‘And the couplet?’
‘I have thought of one,’ said a guest. ‘I leave it to you all to criticise and improve.’
He recited:
‘Musk and orchid fragrance mists a courtyard in the setting sun;
The scent of du-ruo drifts across a moonlit isle.’

‘Very fine,’ they said, ‘but “setting sun” will not do.’
‘There is an old line,’ he replied. ‘“Hands full of mi-wu, she weeps in the slanting light.”’
‘Too despondent, too despondent!’
‘I have a couplet too,’ said another. ‘Let me have your judgement, gentlemen.’
He recited:
‘On three paths, scented breezes stir the jade-hui grass;
In one courtyard, bright moonlight shines on golden orchids.’
Jia Zheng stroked his beard and pondered, intending to compose a couplet himself. Looking up, he saw Bao-yu standing beside him, afraid to speak.
‘Why are you silent now that you ought to say something?’ he demanded. ‘Must we wait upon you for your opinion?’
‘There are no orchids and musk, no moonlight, no islands and islets here,’ Bao-yu replied. ‘If one is going to make such explicit references, two hundred couplets would not be enough.’
‘Who is holding your head down and forcing you to use those expressions?’ asked Jia Zheng.
‘In that case, the best inscription would be “Clear Fragrance of Heng and Zhi”.

‘And for the couplet:
“Cardamom verses done, the poet’s gift still glows;
Sleep among roses over, dreams are fragrant still.”’
‘You have copied “Writing on plantain leaves is done; the words are green still”,’ Jia Zheng said with a smile. ‘Nothing remarkable in that.’
‘Li Bai’s Phoenix Terrace is modelled entirely on Yellow Crane Tower,’ the guests answered. ‘All that matters is how well it is done. If we examine this couplet closely, it is more delicate and more lively than “Writing on plantain leaves”. One might almost think that line had been modelled on this.’
‘What an absurd idea!’ Jia Zheng said, laughing.

They went out as they spoke. Before long they came upon lofty pavilions and towering storeyed buildings, surrounded on every side by palatial halls and linked by long, winding covered galleries. Green pines brushed the eaves; magnolias clustered round the stonework. Carved beasts’ faces gleamed with gold, and dragon heads shone with colour.
‘This is the principal hall,’ said Jia Zheng. ‘Rather too magnificent.’
‘It has to be,’ they all replied. ‘Her Highness may value thrift and have a natural preference for simplicity over elaboration, but the dignity of her present rank demands these ceremonial forms. There is nothing excessive in it.’
As they walked and talked, a jade-stone gateway appeared directly ahead, exquisitely carved with coiling dragons and guardian dragon forms.
‘What should be written here?’ asked Jia Zheng.
‘“The Immortal Realm of Penglai” would surely be best,’ they said.

Jia Zheng shook his head without answering. At the sight of this place, something stirred in Bao-yu. He thought he must have seen it somewhere before, but could not for the moment remember when. Jia Zheng again ordered him to devise an inscription. Bao-yu was so intent on recalling that earlier scene that he had no attention to spare for the present one. The guests did not understand. They assumed that the long ordeal had exhausted him, and that his talent and his words had run dry. If he were pressed with further questions, he might become so distressed that something happened to him. That would put them in an awkward position. They hurried to remonstrate with Jia Zheng.
‘Enough, enough. Let the inscription wait until tomorrow.’
Jia Zheng was also afraid that Grandmother Jia might be growing anxious. He gave a cold laugh.
‘So there are times when even you can do nothing, you little brute!

‘Very well, I will give you a day. If you still cannot do it tomorrow, I shall certainly not let you off. This is an important place. You must take particular care with it.’
He led them out and looked round again. Since entering the garden they had seen only five or six parts in ten. Just then a servant reported that someone from Yu-cun’s house had come with a message.
‘We shall have to leave the remaining places,’ Jia Zheng said with a smile. ‘But we must go out by the other side. Even if we cannot inspect them closely, we can at least glance at them.’
He led the guests on until they reached a large bridge, beneath which water rushed in like a curtain of crystal. This was the sluice connecting the garden to the river outside and admitting its water.

‘What is this sluice called?’ Jia Zheng asked.
‘It is the source of the Drenched Blossoms stream,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Call it the Drenched Blossoms Sluice.’
‘Nonsense! I expressly refuse to use “Drenched Blossoms”.’
They went on past airy halls and thatched cottages, walls of piled stone and windows framed with woven flowers. Here a secluded Buddhist convent nestled below a hill; there a women’s Taoist retreat lay hidden in the woods. There were long corridors, twisting caves, square houses and round pavilions, but Jia Zheng had no time to enter any of them. He remarked that his legs were aching after so long without a rest. Just then another courtyard appeared ahead.
‘We must go in here and sit down,’ he said with a smile.
He led them straight towards it, round flowering peach trees and through a moon-shaped opening woven into a bamboo fence and flower screen. White walls enclosed the place, with green willows drooping all round. They entered and found covered walks joined on either side of the gate.

A few rocks were set about the courtyard. On one side grew several plantains; on the other stood a Xifu crab-apple, spreading like an umbrella, green threads of foliage hanging from it and flowers opening cinnabar-red.
‘Beautiful blossoms!’ cried the guests. ‘We have seen plenty of crab-apples, but never anything as fine as this.’
‘It is called the “Daughter’s Crab-apple”,’ said Jia Zheng. ‘A foreign variety. The common story is that it comes from the Daughters’ Kingdom, where it is said to flourish more than any other kind. A preposterous and unfounded tale, of course.’

‘Unfounded it may be,’ the guests said with a laugh, ‘but how has the name survived so long?’
‘Probably some poet thought the flowers’ rosy colour looked like rouge,’ said Bao-yu, ‘and their frail grace like a girl weakened by illness. They suggested a young lady’s manner, so he called them “Daughter’s”. Then some vulgar fool must have heard it and put it into an unofficial history as evidence. One vulgar tale bred another, one error passed into the next, until everyone took it for fact.’

The guests swayed with admiration and applauded his explanation. Still talking, they sat down on the couches built beneath the projecting porch outside the covered walk.
‘What fresh phrase can you think of for the inscription here?’ Jia Zheng asked.
‘“Plantain and Crane” would be excellent,’ said one guest.
‘“Radiance Spilling Colour” would be better,’ said another.

‘Excellent, that “Radiance Spilling Colour”!’ said Jia Zheng and the others.
‘Wonderful,’ said Bao-yu too. Then he sighed. ‘Only it is a pity.’
‘A pity in what way?’ they asked.
‘There are two plantings here, plantain and crab-apple, and their arrangement holds the idea of both green and red. Mention only the plantain, and the crab-apple is left out; mention only the crab-apple, and the plantain has no place. Plantain without crab-apple will not do, and crab-apple without plantain is still less possible.’
‘What would you have, then?’ asked Jia Zheng.
‘“Red Fragrance and Green Jade” would do justice to both.’
Jia Zheng shook his head.
‘No, no. That will not do.’

segments.text:
all carved and fretted by master craftsmen, finished in many colours with gold and inlaid gems. Recess after recess held books, a tripod, brushes and inkstones, flower vases or miniature landscapes. The openings took every shape: round heaven and square earth, mallow flowers and plantain leaves, interlocking rings and half-round panels. Everything was richly clustered, delicately pierced and open to the eye. Here an opening covered in five-coloured gauze turned out to be a little window; there, a light veil of patterned silk concealed a doorway. Moreover, the walls were full of recesses cut to the exact shapes of the curios and ornaments they held. A qin, a sword, a hanging vase or a table screen might be mounted on the wall, but its surface lay flush with it.
‘What exquisite ingenuity!’ they said. ‘How did anyone think of it?’
Yet Jia Zheng and his companions had gone through fewer than two sets of partitions before they lost track of the way they had come. To the left there seemed to be a door; to the right, a window partly barred the way. They approached, only to find a bookcase in front of them. Turning back, they saw light through a gauze window and what looked like a clear passage through a door. But on reaching it they suddenly confronted a party of people exactly like themselves coming the other way. It was their own reflection in a great glass mirror.

They went round the mirror and found more doors than ever.
‘This way, sir,’ Jia Zhen said with a smile. ‘That door leads to the back courtyard. Going out through there is actually shorter than the way we came.’
They passed round two more sets of gauze screens and brocade partitions and did indeed find a door. Outside, roses and baoxiang flowers covered the courtyard trellises. Beyond a screen of flowers, a clear stream blocked their path.
‘Where does this water come from?’ they asked in surprise.
Jia Zhen pointed into the distance.
‘It starts at that sluice and runs to the cave-mouth. Then it is brought round the north-eastern fold of the hill to the village. Another channel branches off towards the south-west. The water all flows here, joins together again and goes out beneath that wall.’
‘Marvellous!’ they all said.
As they spoke, a large hill suddenly barred the way.
‘We have lost ourselves!’
‘Follow me,’ said Jia Zhen with a smile.
He went ahead once more. They followed him, and one abrupt turn at the foot of the hill brought them onto a broad, level road. There, quite suddenly, was the main gate.

segments.text: Bao-yu could think of nothing but getting back to the inner rooms. But Jia Zheng gave him no instructions, and he had to follow him to his study. Only then did his father remember him. ‘Why are you still here?’ he barked. ‘Have you not had enough of wandering about? After all this time, have you never thought how your grandmother must be worrying? Get inside. All her affection is wasted on you!’ Bao-yu was at last able to withdraw. Outside the courtyard, several of Jia Zheng’s pages came up and caught him round the waist. ‘You have us to thank for the master’s being so pleased today. Her Old Ladyship sent out several times to ask, and every time we told her he was pleased. If she had called you in, you would never have had your chance to shine. Everyone says those poems of yours were better than anything other people write. Now you have done so well, you ought to give us something.’ Bao-yu laughed. ‘A string of cash apiece.’ ‘As though we had never seen a string of cash! Give us that purse.’ One began untying his purse, another his fan-case, and before he could protest they had stripped off every ornament he wore.

segments.text: Presently Aroma brought tea. Seeing that not one of his ornaments remained, she laughed. ‘Those shameless creatures have taken everything off you again.’ Lin Dai-yu came over to look. Sure enough, there was nothing left. ‘Did you give them the purse I made you too?’ she asked. ‘You need never expect anything else from me!’ She went angrily back to her room, seized the scent-bag she had half finished at his request a few days earlier, and took her scissors to it. Bao-yu knew he was in trouble the moment he saw her anger and hurried after her, but she had already cut it open. He had seen the bag before. Unfinished though it was, it was exquisitely made and had cost a great deal of work; to see it cut to pieces for no reason made him angry too. He hastily undid his collar, untied her purse from the front of the red jacket he wore underneath, and held it out. ‘Look! What do you call this?

segments.text: He tossed it into her lap and turned to go. This made her angrier still. Her throat tightened, she could hardly breathe for sobbing, and tears rolled down her face. She took up the purse and began to cut that too. Bao-yu hurried back and snatched it away. ‘Dear cousin, do spare it!’ he said with a smile. Dai-yu flung down the scissors and wiped her eyes. ‘You need not be nice to me one moment and horrid the next. If you are angry, have done with me. What is the point of all this?’ She climbed angrily onto the bed and lay facing the wall, wiping her tears. Bao-yu came up, calling her his dear cousin over and over again, and would not stop apologising.

segments.text: In the rooms in front, Grandmother Jia was loudly calling for Bao-yu. His nurses and maids hastened to answer, ‘He is in Miss Lin’s room.’ ‘Good, good, good!’ she said. ‘Let the cousins play together. His father has kept him under his thumb all this time; let him enjoy himself a little. Only do not let them quarrel, and she must not pinch him.’ They promised to see to it. At last Dai-yu could endure Bao-yu’s pestering no longer. She got up. ‘You mean to give me no peace, so I shall go away from you.’ She made for the door. ‘Wherever you go, I shall follow,’ he said, laughing.

segments.text: As he spoke, he picked up the purse and put it on again. Dai-yu reached to snatch it. ‘You said you did not want it, and now you are wearing it again. segments.text: Lady Wang’s quarters were a scene of great bustle. Jia Qiang had returned from Gusu with the twelve girls he had bought, the teachers he had engaged, and the theatrical costumes and other equipment. Aunt Xue had moved to a quiet set of rooms to the north-east. Pear-tree Court had long since been cleared and repaired, and the teachers were now to train the actresses there. Women of the household who had once learnt singing and performed themselves, but were now white-haired old women, had been appointed to supervise and look after them. Jia Qiang was put in charge of their daily expenditure and receipts, and the accounts for everything they required, large or small. Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife also came to report. ‘All ten of the young Buddhist and Taoist nuns we were to find and engage or buy are here, and the twenty sets of religious robes we ordered are ready too. There is one other young woman, practising the religious life without taking the tonsure. She comes from Suzhou, from a family of scholars and officials. She was always ill as a little girl. Her family bought any number of substitutes to enter religion in her place, but none did any good. Only when she entered the Buddhist life herself did she recover. That is why she practises without taking the tonsure. She is just eighteen this year, and her religious name is Adamantina.

She heard that there were relics of Guanyin and ancient palm-leaf scriptures in Chang’an, so she came up with her teacher last year. She is now living at the Muni Convent outside the western gate.

segments.text: ‘Her teacher was exceptionally skilled in the divine calculations of the Prior Heaven, but passed away last winter. Adamantina meant to escort her teacher’s coffin home. Before dying, however, her teacher told her, “For the ordering of your daily life, you ought not to return home. Remain here quietly. In time your future will take its course.”

segments.text: ‘So she has not gone back.’ Before she could finish her report, Lady Wang said, ‘In that case, why not bring her here?’ ‘We did invite her,’ Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife replied. ‘She said, “In the houses of marquises and dukes they are sure to use their rank and power to bully people. I will never go.”’ ‘As the daughter of an official, she is naturally rather proud,’ said Lady Wang. ‘What harm would there be in sending her a proper invitation?’ Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife agreed and went out to have one of the secretaries write an invitation to Adamantina. The carriage and sedan sent to fetch her the following day, and what followed, must be left for later; we cannot relate it now. At this point someone reported that the builders were waiting for gauze and figured silk to cover things, and asked Xi-feng to unlock the upper storeroom and select some. Someone else wanted her to open the treasury to receive the gold and silver vessels. Neither Lady Wang nor any of the maids in the main apartments had a moment to spare. ‘Let us get out from under their feet and find Tan-chun,’ said Bao-chai. She took Bao-yu and Dai-yu off to amuse themselves in Ying-chun’s rooms with the other girls, and we need say no more of them for the present.

segments.text: Lady Wang and the others remained busy day after day until, towards the end of the tenth month, everything was at last ready. The supervisors had settled all their accounts; the antiques and scholars’ curios had been arranged everywhere. Those responsible for buying birds and animals had obtained everything, from cranes and peacocks to deer, rabbits, chickens and geese, and delivered them to suitable places in the garden to be kept and tended. Jia Qiang’s company had mastered twenty different plays, and the young Buddhist and Taoist nuns had learnt to recite several volumes of scriptures and spells. Only now could Jia Zheng feel somewhat at ease. He invited Grandmother Jia and the others to inspect the garden, consider each detail, and settle the finishing touches. When there was no omission or unsuitable arrangement left, he chose a day to submit his memorial.

segments.text: On the day it was submitted, the vermilion endorsement granted his petition: the Noble Consort was graciously permitted to visit her family on the fifteenth of the first month of the following year, the Festival of the First Full Moon. Once the Jia household received this gracious decree, they were busier than ever, night and day. They could not even celebrate the New Year properly. In no time the Lantern Festival was almost upon them. From the eighth day of the first month, eunuchs came out to inspect the arrangements: where she would change, where she would sit informally, where receive homage, where banquet, and where retire to rest. Other eunuchs, charged with inspecting the premises and overseeing security, came with numerous junior eunuchs to guard the various approaches, put up screening curtains, and instruct the household where to withdraw, where to kneel, where to serve food and where to make reports. The rules of ceremony were endless. Outside, officers of the Board of Works and the military intendant of the Five Districts had the streets swept and idlers driven away. Jia She and the others supervised the craftsmen making ornamental lanterns, fireworks and the like. By the fourteenth, all was ready. No one, high or low, slept that night.

segments.text: At the fifth watch on the fifteenth, Grandmother Jia and everyone else entitled to rank put on full ceremonial dress according to their grade. Throughout the garden, dragons writhed on the hangings and coloured phoenixes flew across the curtains. Gold and silver blazed; pearls and jewels vied in brilliance. A hundred-blend incense burned in the censers, and ever-blooming flowers filled the vases. Not a cough broke the stillness. Jia She and the men waited outside the west street gate; Grandmother Jia and the women outside the main gate of the Rong mansion. Curtains screened every street end and alley entrance. They were growing impatient when a eunuch rode up on a large horse. Grandmother Jia hurried to receive him and ask for news. ‘There is plenty of time yet! Her Highness has her evening meal at the first quarter of the early wei hour, then worships the Buddha at Baoling Palace at the second quarter after mid-wei. At the first quarter of early you she attends the feast and views the lanterns at Taiming Palace. Only then can she ask leave to depart. I doubt she will set out before early xu.’ ‘In that case, Grandmother, Aunt, please go back to your rooms,’ said Xi-feng. ‘There will be time enough to come out when she is due.’ Grandmother Jia and the others retired for the moment. Xi-feng was left in charge of all arrangements in the garden, and stewards were told to take the eunuchs away for food and wine.

segments.text: Soon men were bringing in candles by the shoulder-load, and the lamps were lit everywhere. They had just finished when the sound of galloping came from outside. Ten or so eunuchs ran in, panting and clapping their hands. Those already there understood the signal: ‘She is coming!’ Each took his assigned station. Jia She led the sons and nephews of the whole clan outside the west street gate, while Grandmother Jia led its women outside the main gate to receive her. For a long time all was silent. Then two red-robed eunuchs came slowly into view on horseback. At the west street gate they dismounted, sent their horses outside the screening curtains, and stood facing west with their hands at their sides. After another long interval, a second pair did the same. Presently ten or so pairs had arrived, and only then could the faint sound of delicate music be heard. In pairs came dragon banners and phoenix fans, pheasant plumes and kui-crested standards, followed by portable censers decorated with gold, burning imperial incense. Then came a golden-yellow canopy with a curved handle and seven phoenixes, followed by the ceremonial crown, robe, girdle and shoes. Attendant eunuchs bore fragrant beads, embroidered handkerchiefs, rinsing bowls, fly-whisks and other articles.

segments.text: When these successive parties had passed, eight eunuchs came slowly along carrying a golden-topped palanquin embroidered with phoenixes on golden yellow. Grandmother Jia and the others hurriedly knelt beside the way. Several eunuchs ran ahead to raise Grandmother Jia, Lady Xing and Lady Wang to their feet. The palanquin passed through the main gate and the ceremonial gate, then turned east. At the entrance to a courtyard a eunuch carrying a fly-whisk knelt and invited the Consort to alight and change.

segments.text: The palanquin was carried through the entrance, and the eunuchs withdrew. Only the zhaorong and caipin attendants remained to help Yuan-chun down. The courtyard blazed with lanterns of every kind, exquisitely fashioned from gauze and figured silk. Above was an illuminated tablet bearing the words ‘Embodying Benevolence, Bathed in Virtue’. Yuan-chun went inside, changed, and came out to re-enter her palanquin and proceed into the garden. There incense drifted in curling clouds, flowers and coloured decorations shone on every side, lantern answered lantern, and delicate music sounded continually. No words could exhaust that scene of peace and prosperity, of wealth and cultivated pleasure. At that moment I thought back to the desolation and loneliness beneath Green Ridge Peak in the Mountain of Great Desolation. Had the scabby-headed monk and the lame Taoist not brought me here, how could I ever have seen such a world? I wanted to compose a ‘Rhapsody on Lanterns and Moonlight’ or an ‘Ode to the Imperial Home Visit’ to record the occasion, but feared falling into the stale conventions of other books. A rhapsody and a panegyric together could not do full justice to the scene. Without either, you readers can surely imagine its splendour for yourselves.

segments.text: We may therefore save the time, paper and ink, and get on with the story. From her chair, Consort Jia surveyed the magnificence inside and outside the garden and sighed to herself at the extravagance and expense. A eunuch carrying a fly-whisk now knelt to invite her aboard a boat, and she alighted. A ribbon of clear water wound like a moving dragon. Along the stone balustrades on either bank hung lanterns of crystal and coloured glass, shining like silver light on snowy waves. The willows, apricots and other trees had neither blossom nor leaf, but these had been fashioned from pith, silk, figured silk, paper and gauze to suit each tree and stuck onto its branches. Several lamps hung from every tree. Even the lotus, water-plants, ducks and egrets in the pool had been made from shells, feathers and similar materials. Above and below, the lanterns competed in brilliance: a world of glass, a universe of jewels. Of the exquisite miniature landscapes and lanterns aboard the boat, its beaded curtains and embroidered hangings, its cassia oars and orchid paddles, we need hardly speak. Presently they entered a stone-lined inlet. Above it an illuminated tablet clearly displayed ‘Knotweed Banks and Flowering Inlets’. Now, those words, like ‘The Phoenix Comes in State’ and the other inscriptions, had only been devised in the previous chapter when Jia Zheng happened to test Bao-yu’s lessons and poetic talent. Why should these tablets and couplets now be used in earnest?

segments.text: Jia Zheng came from generations of scholars; the guests who attended him standing or sat in his company were all men of ability. Could none of them produce a fine inscription? Why make do with a child’s playful efforts? That would be like some newly rich family squandering money on paint and varnish, then writing up ‘Green willows at the front gate droop with golden locks; blue hills behind the house stand like a brocade screen’, and imagining the result a spectacle of the highest taste. Could that be the conduct of the Ning and Rong households portrayed throughout The Story of the Stone? On the face of it, there is a glaring contradiction.

segments.text: An explanation of the circumstances will make everything clear. Before she entered the palace, Consort Jia had been brought up from childhood by Grandmother Jia. When Bao-yu was born, she was already the elder sister and he the little brother. Knowing that her mother had borne this son only as she was growing older, she loved him with a tenderness quite different from her feelings for her other younger brothers. They were both with Grandmother Jia, and scarcely ever apart. Before Bao-yu went to school, when he was only three or four, she guided his hand and taught him by word of mouth until he had learnt several books and some thousands of characters. In name they were sister and brother; in their affection, almost mother and son. After entering the palace, she repeatedly sent messages to her parents: ‘Take the greatest care over his upbringing. Without firmness he will never amount to anything; with too much, I fear something unforeseen may happen and bring you sorrow.’ She never ceased to think of him with anxious love. A few days earlier, Jia Zheng had heard that the schoolmaster praised Bao-yu behind his back for considerable talent of an unconventional kind. He had not believed it. When the garden happened to be completed, he therefore asked Bao-yu to devise inscriptions, simply to test the quality of his imagination.

segments.text: The tablets and couplets he produced were no masterpieces, but for a young boy they had some merit. It would have been easy to engage an eminent writer to compose others, yet the flavour of something made within the family seemed more pleasing. Besides, when the Consort saw them and knew they were her beloved brother’s work, they might fulfil something of her long-held hopes for him. That was why Bao-yu’s inscriptions had actually been used. Those he had not finished that day had since been supplied. But enough of this digression. Consort Jia looked at the four Chinese characters and smiled. ‘“Flowering Inlets” is quite right. Why do we need “Knotweed Banks”?’ The eunuch seated beside her hurried into a little boat, landed, and sent the message flying to Jia Zheng, who immediately had the inscription altered. Presently the boat reached the inner landing. She left it and returned to her palanquin. Before her rose graceful palaces like those of jade, and lofty halls like those of cassia. A stone archway clearly bore the words ‘Precious Mirror of the Celestials’. She at once ordered these replaced with ‘Villa for the Family Visit’. Then she entered the temporary palace. Courtyard torches blazed into the sky; fragrant chips were strewn upon the ground. Trees of fire and jewelled flowers shone before golden windows and jade balustrades.

segments.text: ‘Why has this hall no tablet?’ the Consort asked. An attendant eunuch knelt to reply. ‘This is the principal hall. Your subjects outside the palace did not presume to devise one.’ She nodded without speaking. A master of ceremonies knelt to invite her to ascend the throne and receive homage. Music rose on both sides of the steps. Two eunuchs led Jia She, Jia Zheng and the other men into their appointed ranks below the terrace. From the hall a zhaorong announced the command: ‘The ceremony is dispensed with.’

segments.text: The eunuchs led Jia She and the others away. Another party conducted the Dowager Lady of Rong and the women up the eastern steps to their ranks on the terrace. Again the zhaorong announced, ‘The ceremony is dispensed with.’ They too were led away. When tea had been offered three times, the Consort left her throne and the music ceased. She retired to a side hall to change, and only then was her conveyance prepared to take her out of the garden for the family reunion.

segments.text: In Grandmother Jia’s main room, she wished to make the customary family obeisances, but Grandmother Jia and the others kept kneeling to prevent her. With tears filling the Consort’s eyes, they came forward at last to greet one another. She held Grandmother Jia with one hand and Lady Wang with the other. All three had so much in their hearts to say, and none could say a word. They could only sob and weep together. Lady Xing, Li Wan, Wang Xi-feng, and Ying-chun, Tan-chun and Xi-chun stood round them, silently shedding tears. At length the Consort mastered her grief, forced a smile, and tried to comfort her grandmother and mother. ‘You sent me away to that place where I can see no one. Now at last I have come home, and we can be together for a little. Why cry instead of talking and laughing? Soon I must go, and who knows when I shall come again?’ At these words she choked once more. Lady Xing hurried forward to comfort her. Grandmother Jia and the others persuaded her to sit, and came up to greet her one by one, with more unavoidable tears. Then the male stewards and household officers of both mansions paid their respects outside the hall, followed by the married women in charge of household affairs, leading the maids.

segments.text: ‘Why are Aunt Xue, Bao-chai and Dai-yu not here?’ the Consort asked. Lady Wang replied, ‘As relatives outside the household without official rank, they did not presume to enter unbidden.’ The Consort at once sent for them. Aunt Xue and the girls came in and were about to perform the state obeisances, but these too were dispensed with. Each came forward to exchange news and speak of their separation. Bao-qin and the other maids whom the Consort had taken into the palace then came to kowtow. Grandmother Jia and the others hastened to raise them and ordered that they be entertained in another room. The Ning mansion and Jia She’s household had people ready to entertain the attendant eunuchs, the caipin and zhaorong, and the rest of the retinue. Only three or four junior eunuchs remained to answer calls. Mother, daughter, sisters and cousins could now speak freely of their separation and of private family affairs.

segments.text: Jia Zheng came to the curtain to enquire after her well-being. The Consort lowered it and made her obeisance to him. Through the curtain she said tearfully, ‘A farming family may live on pickled vegetables and salt, wearing plain cloth, but they can still enjoy being together. We have wealth and honour beyond measure, yet our flesh and blood are scattered. What pleasure is there in it?’ With tears in his own eyes Jia Zheng replied, ‘Your subject comes of a humble, obscure family. Among a flock of doves and crows, who could have expected the auspicious appearance of a phoenix? Your Highness receives Heaven’s favour from above and makes manifest our ancestors’ virtue below. The rare essences of mountains and rivers, sun and moon, and the far-reaching virtue of our forebears have gathered in one person, and good fortune has reached my wife and me. Our present sovereign has revealed the great life-giving virtue of Heaven and Earth, bestowing a generosity without precedent in any age. Though we subjects dashed our brains and livers to the ground, how could we repay one ten-thousandth of it? We can only labour faithfully at our duties from morning to night and pray that our sovereign may live for ten thousand years, to the good fortune of all beneath Heaven. Your Highness must not trouble your precious heart over the declining years of my wife and myself. We beg you instead to cherish your own health. By serving His Majesty with constant diligence, care and reverence, you may prove worthy of the immense grace of his tender concern.’ The Consort in turn urged him to put affairs of state first, tend his health whenever he had leisure, and not worry about her.
