segments.text: Jia Zheng further reported, ‘The inscriptions for all the pavilions, terraces, studios and houses in the garden were composed by Bao-yu. If one or two are at all worthy of your notice, we should be honoured if you would bestow new names.’ Hearing that Bao-yu could compose such inscriptions, Consort Yuan smiled. ‘He really has made progress.’ Jia Zheng withdrew. The Consort saw that the Xue and Lin cousins stood out even among the other girls: they were indeed like lovely flowers and yielding jade. ‘Why has Bao-yu not come to see me?’ she asked. Grandmother Jia replied, ‘Without a command, no male from outside the palace would venture in.’ The Consort ordered him brought at once. A junior eunuch went out and led him in. After he had performed the state obeisances, she called him nearer, took his hand and drew him into her arms. Stroking his head and neck, she smiled. ‘How much taller you have grown since…’ Before she could finish, her tears were falling like rain.

segments.text: Entering the garden, they first visited ‘The Phoenix Comes in State’, ‘Red Fragrance and Green Jade’, ‘The Apricot Tavern Flag in Sight’ and ‘Clear Fragrance of Heng and Zhi’. They climbed towers, walked through galleries, crossed water and followed the hills, lingering to admire each view. Every place had a different arrangement, every ornament some novelty. The Consort praised it all most warmly, but added, ‘There must not be such extravagance in future. All this goes far beyond what is necessary.’

segments.text: They came at last to the principal hall. The Consort dispensed with ceremony and took her seat, and the great banquet began. Grandmother Jia and the others sat below her; You-shi, Li Wan and Xi-feng served the soup and wine themselves. Consort Yuan called for brush and inkstone, took a spotted-bamboo brush in her own hand, and bestowed names on the places she liked best. Her inscriptions ran as follows. For the tablet: ‘Remember Grace and Consider Duty’.

segments.text: ‘Pure Scent of Heng and Zhi’ was named ‘Allspice Court’; ‘The Apricot Tavern Flag in Sight’ became ‘Kudzu-washing Grange’. The main tower was ‘Prospect Tower’, the soaring building to the east ‘Brocade-adorned Pavilion’, and the obliquely set building to the west ‘Fragrance-bearing Pavilion’. There were also such names as ‘Knotweed Breeze Pavilion’, ‘Lotus Pavilion’, ‘Amaryllis Eyot’ and ‘Leafy Islet’. More than ten further tablets had four-character inscriptions, among them ‘Pear Blossom in Spring Rain’, ‘Autumn Wind Cuts the Paulownia’ and ‘Night Snow on Reeds’; it is difficult to record them all here. She ordered that none of the existing tablets and couplets need be taken down. Then she began by writing this quatrain:

segments.text: When she had finished, she smiled at her sisters and cousins. ‘You all know very well that I have never been quick-witted, nor much good at verse. Tonight I have merely done what was required, so as not to fail such a setting. Some other day, when I have a little leisure, I must write an “Account of Prospect Garden”, an “Ode to the Imperial Home Visit” and other pieces to record this occasion. Each of you must also compose an inscription and a poem. Do the best you can on the spur of the moment, and do not let my poor efforts constrain you. I am delighted that Bao-yu has learnt to compose inscriptions and verse. It is more than I expected. Of these places, I love Naiad’s House and Allspice Court most, and next to them the House of Green Delights and Kudzu-washing Grange. These four principal sites deserve poems of their own. The couplets you wrote before were good, but now you must compose an eight-line poem in five-character lines for each. Let me test you here in person, and feel that the trouble I took over teaching you as a child was not wasted.’ Bao-yu could only agree. He withdrew to think.

segments.text: When the Consort had read them, she praised them all, then smiled. ‘Our Xue and Lin cousins’ poems are different from the rest, after all. We foolish sisters cannot rank with them.’ Dai-yu had intended to display her extraordinary gifts that evening and outshine everyone. But the Consort had ordered only one inscription and one poem apiece. She could hardly disobey by writing more, and had merely tossed off an eight-line poem in five-character lines to suit the occasion. Bao-yu had not yet finished. He had completed only the poems on Naiad’s House and Allspice Court and was working on the House of Green Delights. His draft contained the line ‘Green jade stays furled in spring’. Bao-chai caught sight of it. While the others were paying no attention, she quickly turned, nudged him, and whispered, ‘She disliked “Red Fragrance and Green Jade” and changed it to “Delight in Red and Joy in Green”. If you insist on “green jade” now, will it not look as though you mean to challenge her? There are plenty of other expressions for plantain leaves. Think of one and change it.’ Bao-yu wiped his brow. ‘I cannot remember a single allusion or source just now.’ Bao-chai smiled. ‘Just change the word “jade” in “green jade” to “wax”.’ ‘Is there a source for “green wax”?’ At his question, Bao-chai quietly clicked her tongue and nodded,

segments.text: then said with a smile, ‘If you are like this tonight, I suppose that when you answer questions in the golden hall you will forget even “Zhao, Qian, Sun, Li”! Have you forgotten the first line of Qian Xu’s Tang poem on the plantain: “A cold candle, smokeless, its green wax dry”?’ Bao-yu felt his mind suddenly clear. ‘What an idiot I am!’ he said, laughing. ‘It was there before my eyes and I could not think of it. You really are a “one-word teacher”. From now on I shall call you Teacher, never Sister again.’

segments.text: Dai-yu was naturally disappointed at having had no chance to fulfil her ambition. segments.text: The Consort was delighted with what she read. ‘He really has improved!’ She singled out ‘The Apricot Tavern Flag’ as better than the preceding three and changed ‘Kudzu-washing Grange’ to ‘Sweet-rice Village’. She then ordered Tan-chun to copy on coloured paper all the dozen or more poems just composed, and had a eunuch carry them to the men outside. Jia Zheng and the others read them with endless praise. Jia Zheng also presented an ‘Ode to the Homecoming’. The Consort ordered delicacies, including fine milk pastries and golden sliced fish, to be given to Bao-yu and Jia Lan. Jia Lan was still very young and understood little of what was happening. He merely followed his mother and kept close to his uncle to perform the ceremonies, so there is no separate account of him. Jia Huan, who had fallen ill before the New Year and had not recovered, was being nursed in a quiet place; there is therefore no account of him either.

segments.text: Meanwhile, Jia Qiang and the twelve actresses were waiting impatiently below the tower. A eunuch came hurrying up. ‘The poems are finished. Bring the list of plays at once!’ Jia Qiang hastily presented the brocade-covered programme, together with the roster of all twelve girls. Soon the eunuch returned. Only four scenes had been selected: first, ‘The Lavish Feast’; second, ‘Praying for Skill’; third, ‘An Immortal Encounter’; and fourth, ‘The Soul’s Departure’. Jia Qiang hurried to get the performers ready. Their singing outdid voices that could split stone, and they danced with the allure of heavenly demons. Though all was costume and acting, they conveyed every shade of sorrow and joy. They had just finished when a eunuch came in carrying a golden tray of cakes and other dainties. ‘Which is Ling-guan?’ he asked. Jia Qiang knew at once that these were gifts for her. Delighted, he hastened to receive them and told her to kowtow. ‘Her Highness commands,’ the eunuch continued, ‘“Ling-guan is excellent. Let her perform two more scenes, any two she pleases.”’ Jia Qiang eagerly agreed and told Ling-guan to perform ‘A Walk in the Garden’ and ‘A Dream Interrupted’.

segments.text: Ling-guan considered neither scene proper to her own theatrical role and flatly refused. She insisted on ‘The Rendezvous’ and ‘The Quarrel’. Jia Qiang could not prevail against her and had to let her have her way. The Consort was delighted. ‘Do not make things difficult for this girl,’ she ordered. ‘See that she is well taught.’ She gave her an additional reward of two lengths of palace satin, two purses, small gold and silver ingots, food and other things. The banquet was then cleared away, and they toured the places they had not yet visited. Suddenly, seeing a Buddhist temple encircled by hills, the Consort had her hands washed afresh and went in to burn incense and worship. She wrote another tablet, ‘Mercy’s Vessel across the Sea of Suffering’, and bestowed additional favours on the secluded Buddhist and Taoist nuns.

segments.text: Presently a eunuch knelt to report, ‘The gifts are all ready. Please examine their distribution according to rank.’ He presented a summary. The Consort read it from beginning to end, found everything appropriate, and ordered it carried out. The eunuchs withdrew to distribute the gifts one by one. Grandmother Jia was to receive one gold ruyi and one jade ruyi, an aloeswood walking-stick, a string of kyanam-wood prayer beads, four lengths of palace satin patterned with ‘Wealth, Honour and Lasting Spring’, four lengths of palace silk patterned with ‘Long Life and Enduring Happiness’, ten ingots of purple gold with the ‘Brush, Ingot and Ruyi’ design, and ten silver ingots with the ‘Auspicious Celebration and Fish’ design. Lady Xing and Lady Wang each received the same, less the four articles comprising the two ruyi, the stick and the beads. Jia Jing, Jia She and Jia Zheng each received two sets of new books by the Emperor, two boxes of fine ink, two gold and two silver jue wine-cups, and ceremonial gifts of silk as above. Bao-chai, Dai-yu and the other girls each received one set of new books, a fine inkstone, and two pairs of gold and silver ingots in the newest designs. Bao-yu received the same. Jia Lan received two gold and silver neck-rings and two pairs of gold and silver ingots. You-shi, Li Wan and Xi-feng each received four gold and silver ingots and four lengths of silk.

segments.text: A further twenty-four lengths of silk and one hundred strings of good copper cash were for the nurses and maids in the rooms of Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang and the girls. Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Jia Huan and Jia Rong each received one allotment of ceremonial silk gifts and a pair of gold ingots. Another hundred lengths of coloured satin, a thousand taels of gold and silver, imperial wine and a splendid feast were granted to everyone in both mansions who had supervised the garden building, arranged its furnishings, attended to service, managed the plays or tended the lamps. A further five hundred strings of good copper cash were for the kitchen hands, actors, variety performers and miscellaneous workers.

segments.text: When everyone had thanked her for these favours, the attendant eunuch reported, ‘It is already the third quarter after the middle of the chou hour. We beg Your Highness to return to the palace.’ Tears welled up again in the Consort’s eyes. Forcing a smile, she held Grandmother Jia’s and Lady Wang’s hands tightly, unable to let them go. Again and again she urged them, ‘Do not worry about me. Take good care of yourselves. His Majesty’s grace is boundless: you may now come into the palace to see me once a month. We shall have plenty of chances to meet. Why be so miserable? If his favour allows me to come home again next year, you must on no account spend so extravagantly.’ Grandmother Jia and the others were sobbing too hard to speak. Unwilling as the Consort was to part, the rules of the imperial household could not be broken. She had to harden her heart, enter her palanquin and go. Those who remained at last managed to comfort Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang, and supported them out of the garden.

segments.text: After Consort Jia returned to the palace, she had an audience with the Emperor the following day to thank him for his favour and report on her visit home. His Majesty was greatly pleased, and made further gifts of coloured satins, gold, silver and other articles from the imperial privy treasury to Jia Zheng, the other imperial consorts’ families and those concerned. We need not give the particulars.

segments.text: For days the two mansions, Rong and Ning, had strained every nerve. Now everyone was exhausted in body and mind, and putting away all the furnishings and other things used in the garden took another two or three days. Xi-feng, above all, had a multitude of duties and a heavy burden to carry. Others might steal a little ease or find a quiet corner to hide in; she alone could not get away. Besides, she was too proud by nature to give anyone grounds for criticism, and struggled to look as though she had had nothing to do.

Bao-yu, by contrast, had less to do and more leisure than anyone. As it happened, Aroma’s mother came early that morning, obtained Grandmother Jia’s permission and took her home for New Year tea. She would not be back until evening. Bao-yu therefore stayed with the other maids, playing a dice game with Go counters. He was finding their games indoors rather dull when some maids came to announce, ‘Master Zhen from the East Mansion invites you over for the plays and the lanterns.’

Bao-yu told them to change his clothes. Just as he was leaving, a gift of sweet steamed milk curd arrived from Consort Jia. Remembering how much Aroma had enjoyed it the last time, he ordered it to be kept for her.

segments.text: He himself reported to Grandmother Jia and went over to see the plays. Jia Zhen’s programme, however, consisted of Ding Lang Acknowledges His Father, Huang Bo-yang Marshals the Ghostly Host, Pilgrim Sun Wreaks Havoc in Heaven, Jiang Zi-ya Beheads the Generals and Invests the Gods, and other pieces of that kind. Gods and ghosts suddenly swarmed out, only to give way to a full display of monsters and demons. There were even processions with banners, invocations of the Buddha and offerings of incense; gongs, drums and shouts could be heard beyond the lane. Everyone in the street declared, ‘What a lively show! You wouldn’t see anything like this at another house.’

segments.text: Bao-yu found all this magnificent commotion quite unbearable. He sat through very little of it before wandering off to amuse himself elsewhere. First he went into the inner quarters and spent a while laughing and talking with You-shi, the maids and the concubines, then came out through the second gate. You-shi and the others supposed he had gone back to the plays and thought no more about him. Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Xue Pan and their companions were too busy with guessing games, drinking forfeits and every sort of merriment to pay him any attention. If they noticed his empty seat, they merely assumed he had gone inside, and did not ask. As for Bao-yu’s pages, the older ones knew that once he had arrived here he would not leave until evening. Some slipped away to gamble, others to take New Year tea with friends or relations, and others again to visit brothels or go drinking. They dispersed in secret, intending to return that evening. The younger boys had all squeezed into the actors’ dressing room to watch the excitement.

segments.text: Finding himself quite alone, Bao-yu thought, ‘There’s that little study here, called [text missing], where they used to hang a scroll of a beautiful woman, painted so wonderfully true to life. With all this bustle today, I suppose the place must naturally [text missing], and the beauty is bound to be lonely too. I must go and see her, to cheer her up.’

With this in mind he made for the study. As he reached the window, he heard a sound of moaning within. It gave him quite a fright. Could the beauty have come to life? Summoning his courage, he licked a hole in the paper window and peeped inside. The painted beauty had not come to life at all. It was Tealeaf, holding a girl beneath him, engaged in what Disenchantment had taught.
‘Good heavens!’ Bao-yu cried involuntarily. He kicked the door open, startling the two apart; they trembled as they shook their clothes into place.

segments.text: Seeing that it was Bao-yu, Tealeaf dropped to his knees and pleaded over and over again.
‘In broad daylight! What do you mean by it?’ Bao-yu said. ‘If Master Zhen knew, would you get out of it alive?’

Meanwhile he looked at the girl. Though not a beauty, she had a clear, fair complexion and something rather pleasing about her. Her face and ears scarlet with shame, she stood with lowered head and said nothing.

segments.text: Bao-yu stamped his foot. ‘Why don’t you run?’
That brought her to her senses, and she fled as fast as she could. Bao-yu hurried out after her, calling, ‘Don’t be frightened! I shan’t tell anyone!’
‘My lord and master!’ Tealeaf cried behind him in dismay. ‘You’re telling everyone as it is!’
Bao-yu then asked, ‘How old is that girl? In her teens?’
‘Sixteen or seventeen at most,’ said Tealeaf.
‘You haven’t even asked her age or birth-year animal. Naturally you’ll know still less about anything else. A fine thing for her to have known you!

segments.text: ‘Poor girl, poor girl!’ He went on, ‘What’s her name?’

Tealeaf burst out laughing. ‘That’s a long story. Such an extraordinary tale, you couldn’t put it in a book! She says that when her mother had her, she dreamed she’d been given a length of brocade with a five-coloured pattern of wealth and honour and an unbroken wan motif. So they called her Wan-er, after the wan in the pattern.’
‘That really is unusual,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Perhaps she has some good fortune ahead of her.’ He fell silent for a while, thinking.

segments.text: Tealeaf asked, ‘Why aren’t you watching such fine plays, Master Bao?’
‘I watched for ages and got dreadfully bored. I came out for a stroll and found the two of you. What shall we do now?’
Tealeaf grinned. ‘No one knows where we are. I could quietly take you outside the city for a look round, and we’d come back here in a little while. They’d never know.’
‘No. We might get carried off by beggars. And if they found out, there would be an awful fuss. We’d better go somewhere familiar and close by, where we can get back at once.’
‘Somewhere familiar and close by? Whose house could we go to? That’s a difficult one.’
‘I know,’ said Bao-yu, smiling. ‘Let’s go and find your big sister Hua, and see what she’s doing at home.’
‘Yes, yes!’ Tealeaf laughed. ‘I’d forgotten about her house. But if they find out and say I took you roaming about, won’t they beat me?’
‘You’ve got me,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
At that Tealeaf brought the horses, and the two went out by the back gate.

Aroma’s mother had brought her home along with several nieces, some her sisters’ daughters and some her brothers’, and they were taking tea and fruit.

segments.text: Hearing someone outside call ‘Brother Hua!’, Hua Zi-fang hurried out. The sight of master and servant left him speechless with surprise and apprehension. He quickly lifted Bao-yu from his horse and called into the courtyard, ‘Master Bao is here!’
The news might mean little to the others, but Aroma had no idea what could have brought him. She ran out to meet him, caught him by the arm and asked, ‘What have you come for?’
‘I was so bored. I came to see what you were doing.’
Only then did she feel reassured. With a sigh and a smile she said, ‘What a way to behave! Whatever did you want to come here for?’ Then she asked Tealeaf, ‘Who else came with you?’

segments.text: ‘Nobody knows,’ Tealeaf said, grinning. ‘It’s just the two of us.’

Aroma became alarmed again. ‘This is too much! Suppose you’d met someone, or run into the master? The streets are crowded with people, carts bumping into one another, horses and chairs everywhere. What if there had been an accident? Is that something to play about with? You’ve got more nerve than sense, the pair of you. Tealeaf put you up to it. I shall certainly tell the mammas to beat you when I get back.’
Tealeaf stuck out his lips. ‘Master Bao ordered me to bring him, with threats and blows, and now it’s all my fault. I said we shouldn’t come. We’d better go away again.’
‘Never mind,’ Hua Zi-fang interposed. ‘You’re here now. There’s no need to say any more. Only this poor little place of ours is so cramped and dirty. Where can the young master possibly sit?’

segments.text: Aroma’s mother had already come out to welcome him. Aroma led Bao-yu inside, where three or five girls lowered their heads in shy embarrassment as he entered. Hua Zi-fang and his mother were terribly afraid that he would be cold. They urged him to sit on the kang, hurried to set out a fresh table of fruit and bustled about pouring good tea.
‘Don’t put yourselves to all that trouble,’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘I know what to do. There’s no need for the fruit either. We can’t just give him anything to eat.’

As she spoke, she took her own cushion and spread it on a kang for Bao-yu to sit on, setting her own foot-warmer beneath his feet. She took two plum-blossom incense cakes from her purse, lifted the lid of her hand-warmer and put them in to burn. Then she replaced the lid and put the warmer in his arms. Finally she filled her own teacup and handed it to him.

segments.text: Meanwhile her mother and brother had busily arranged a separate table of fruit, all very neat. Aroma could see nothing suitable for him to eat.
‘Now you’ve come,’ she said with a smile, ‘we can’t let you go without something. You must at least taste a little, to mark your visit to my home.’
She picked out a few pine kernels, blew away the thin skins and offered them to Bao-yu on her handkerchief.

‘Crying? I haven’t. I got something in my eye and rubbed it,’ she said with a smile, covering the matter up.

segments.text: Bao-yu was wearing a scarlet narrow-sleeved robe with golden python designs, lined with fox-underarm fur, and over it a dark blue sable-fur jacket with rows of tassels.
‘You even changed into new clothes to come here?’ Aroma asked. ‘Didn’t they ask where you were going?’
‘I changed to go and see the plays at Cousin Zhen’s.’
Aroma nodded. ‘Stay a moment, then go back. This isn’t a place for you to come to.’
‘It would be much better if you came home now,’ said Bao-yu, smiling. ‘I’ve saved you something nice.’
‘Hush!’ she said with a quiet smile. ‘What will they think if they hear you?’
She reached up and took the Spiritual Jade from his neck.

‘Here, have a look,’ she said to her cousins. ‘Whenever it’s mentioned, you all think it’s so wonderful and long to see it. Now you can look to your hearts’ content. However rare a thing may be, when you actually see it, it’s only a thing like this.’
She handed it round, then hung it on Bao-yu’s neck again. She told her brother to hire either a small sedan-chair or a little carriage to take him back.

‘It’s not a question of being all right. It’s meeting people.’
Hua Zi-fang hurried away and hired a small chair. No one dared press Bao-yu to stay; they could only see him out.

segments.text: Aroma gave Tealeaf a handful of fruit and some money to buy fireworks, warning him, ‘Don’t tell anyone. You’re to blame too, remember.’

She accompanied Bao-yu right to the door, watched him into the chair and lowered its curtain. Hua Zi-fang and Tealeaf followed, leading the horses. When they reached the street outside the Ning mansion, Tealeaf had the chair stopped.
‘Master Bao and I must go back into the East Mansion and mingle with the others a little before he goes home,’ he told Hua Zi-fang. ‘Otherwise people will suspect something.’
Hua Zi-fang agreed. He lifted Bao-yu out of the chair and helped him on to his horse.
‘I’ve put you to a lot of trouble,’ Bao-yu said, smiling.
They went in again by the back gate. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: Once Bao-yu was out, the maids in his room had given themselves over to still freer merriment. Some played the dice game with Go counters, others threw dice or played cards, and melon-seed shells littered the floor. His wet-nurse, Nurse Li, happened to come in leaning on her stick, to pay her respects and see Bao-yu. Finding him out and the maids absorbed in their games, she thoroughly disapproved.

‘Since I left and stopped coming in so often,’ she sighed, ‘you’ve grown more and more unruly. The other mammas scarcely dare say a word to you now. That Bao-yu is a lampstand a zhang and eight chi tall: lights up other people, but can’t see what’s beneath him. Always complaining how dirty other people are, yet here’s his own room and he lets you turn it into a pigsty. There’s less decency here every day.’

The maids knew very well that Bao-yu did not mind such things. Besides, Nurse Li had retired from her duties and no longer had any authority over them. They went on playing and took no notice. Nurse Li persisted with her questions: how much rice did Bao-yu eat at a meal now, what time did he go to bed, and so on.

segments.text: The maids gave whatever answers came into their heads. One said, ‘What a tiresome old thing!’
‘Is that milk curd in the covered bowl?’ Nurse Li asked. ‘Why wasn’t it sent to me? I’ll eat it now.’ She took a spoon and began.

‘Don’t touch that!’ one of the maids said. ‘He specifically told us to save it for Aroma. There’ll be another row when he comes back. You’ll have to own up yourself, mind, and not get us into trouble.’

Nurse Li was both angry and ashamed. ‘I don’t believe he’s become as bad as that. A bowl of milk! I’d have every right to it if it cost a great deal more. Does he think more of Aroma than of me? Doesn’t he remember how he grew up? My blood turned to milk, and he drank it to grow as big as he is. Now he’ll be angry because I eat one bowl of his milk? I’ll eat it, and we’ll see what happens! You think Aroma’s someone wonderful. She’s a slip of a girl I trained with my own hands. What is she, after all?’
Talking all the while, she defiantly finished the curd.

segments.text: Another maid laughed. ‘They don’t know how to speak to you. No wonder you’re angry. Master Bao is always sending you things to show his respect. Why should he be upset about this?’

‘You needn’t put on your wheedling ways to coax me,’ said Nurse Li. ‘Do you think I don’t know about Snowpink being driven out over that tea last time? When there’s trouble tomorrow, I’ll come and take the blame!’
She went off in a huff. A little later Bao-yu returned and sent to fetch Aroma. Seeing Skybright lying motionless on the bed, he asked, ‘Are you ill? Or did you lose?’
‘She’d been winning,’ Ripple said. ‘Then old Nurse Li came in and interfered, and she lost. She was so cross she went to bed.’
‘Don’t take her so seriously,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Just let her be.’

By now Aroma had arrived, and they greeted one another. She asked Bao-yu where he had eaten and what time he had come back, and passed on her mother’s and cousins’ greetings to her fellow maids. Then she changed her clothes and took off her finery.

segments.text: Bao-yu asked for the curd. ‘Nurse Li ate it,’ the maids told him.

Before he could speak, Aroma said quickly, smiling, ‘So that was what you saved me! How thoughtful of you. It tasted lovely when I had it the other day, but afterwards I got such a stomach-ache. I wasn’t better until I’d been sick. It’s just as well she ate it. Left here, it would only have been wasted. What I really want is dried chestnuts. Peel some for me while I make up the bed.’

Bao-yu believed her. He forgot the curd, fetched some chestnuts and sat picking them over and peeling them by the lamp. Seeing that the others were out of the room, he asked Aroma with a smile, ‘Who was that girl in red today? How is she related to you?’

segments.text: ‘She’s my mother’s sister’s daughter, my younger cousin.’
Bao-yu gave two murmurs of admiration.
‘What are you sighing about?’ Aroma asked. ‘I know what you’re thinking. You suppose she isn’t fit to wear red.’
‘No, no!’ he said, smiling. ‘If someone like her can’t wear red, who dares? I thought she was so lovely. If only we could have her here with us somehow!’
Aroma gave a cold laugh. ‘It’s enough for me to have a servant’s fate. Must all my relations have one too? Only the very prettiest girls are to be brought into your house, are they?’
‘Now you’re taking it the wrong way again,’ Bao-yu said hastily, with a smile. ‘Must coming to our house mean being a servant? Couldn’t she come as a relation?’

segments.text: ‘We’re not a fit match for that either,’ Aroma said.
Bao-yu would say no more, and went on peeling chestnuts.
‘Why so silent?’ she asked, smiling. ‘Have I been too forward and offended you? You can spend a few taels tomorrow and buy them in, just to spite me.’

‘What answer can I make when you talk like that?’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘I was only admiring her. She’s just the sort who ought to have been born in a great house like this. Instead, it’s filthy creatures like us who are born here.’

segments.text: ‘She hasn’t had that good fortune,’ Aroma said, ‘but she’s been brought up as carefully as any young lady. She’s the apple of my aunt and uncle’s eye. She’s seventeen now, and they’ve got every bit of her dowry ready. She’s to be married next year.’
The word ‘married’ drew another two sighs from Bao-yu. While he was still feeling unhappy, he heard Aroma sigh as well.
‘All these years since I came here, we cousins haven’t been able to be together.

segments.text: ‘Now I’m going home, they’ll all be gone.’
Hearing something behind these words, Bao-yu started. He dropped the chestnuts and asked urgently, ‘What do you mean, you’re going home?’
‘I heard my mother and brother discussing it today. They want me to put up with another year, and next year they’ll come and buy my release.’
Bao-yu was still more bewildered. ‘Why do they want to buy your release?’
‘What a question! I’m not a servant born into the household. My whole family is elsewhere, and I’m the only one here. How can that go on for ever?’
‘But you could hardly go if I wouldn’t let you.’

segments.text: ‘There’s no such rule,’ said Aroma. ‘Even in the imperial palace they have fixed regulations: a selection every so many years, an intake every so many years. Even there they have no right to keep people for ever, let alone you!’
Bao-yu thought this over. It did seem reasonable.
‘But if Grandmother wouldn’t let you go?’

‘Why wouldn’t she? If I were really someone quite out of the ordinary, I might have moved Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship so much that they’d insist on keeping me. Perhaps they’d give my family a few more taels and retain me. That could happen. But I’m only an ordinary person. There are plenty and plenty better than me. I came here as a little girl to attend Her Old Ladyship, served Miss Shi for several years, and now I’ve served you for several more. If my family comes to buy me back, it’s only right to let me go. They might even be kind enough to send me off without asking for my purchase money. As for keeping me because I’ve looked after you well, that’s out of the question.

segments.text: ‘Looking after you properly is my duty, not some extraordinary achievement. When I leave, someone else just as good will come. Things won’t fall apart without me.’
To Bao-yu it sounded as though there was every reason for her to go and none for her to stay. He grew more anxious.
‘Even so, if I’m determined to keep you, Grandmother will certainly speak to your mother. She could give her plenty of silver, and then your mother would hardly have the face to take you back.’

‘Of course my mother wouldn’t dare insist,’ Aroma said. ‘Never mind speaking nicely to her and giving her more silver. Even if they weren’t nice at all and gave her nothing, if they were set on keeping me by force, she wouldn’t dare refuse. But our family has never bullied people with its rank and power like that. I’m not some object they can get for you because you fancy it, at ten times its value. The seller loses nothing by that, so it can be done. But to keep me here for no reason does you no good, and separates us from our own flesh and blood. Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship would never do such a thing.’
Bao-yu pondered for a long while. ‘Then, by your account, you’re definitely going?’
‘Definitely.’

‘Who would have thought someone like her could be so cold and unfeeling?’ he thought. Then he sighed. ‘If I’d known you were all going away, I should never have had you brought here. In the end I’ll be left all by myself, a lonely ghost.’
He went off to bed in a sulk.

segments.text: In fact, when Aroma had heard her mother and brother propose buying her back, she had told them that she would never come home, not to her dying day.

‘You sold me because you had nothing to eat,’ she said. ‘I was the only thing left worth a few taels. If I hadn’t let you sell me, was I to stand by and watch my own parents starve? Luckily I was sold here, where I eat and dress like the masters and mistresses, and I’m not beaten in the morning and cursed at night. Father may be dead now, but you’ve put the household and your livelihood in order and got back on your feet. If you were still in difficulties and wanted to buy me back to squeeze a little more money out of me, that would be another matter. But you’re not in difficulties. What do you want to buy me back for now? Think of me as dead, and never entertain the idea again!’

There had been a bout of tears and protest. Her mother and brother saw how determined she was; plainly she would not come out. Besides, she had originally been sold under a deed of outright sale. They had been counting on the Jia family’s kindness and generosity: they need only make a plea, and quite possibly even the purchase money would be waived as a gift.

segments.text: Moreover, the Jia household had never ill-treated its servants, showing far more kindness than severity. The personal maids who attended its old and young members were treated quite differently even from the other servants. Young ladies in ordinary poor families would not have been accorded so much consideration. Mother and son accordingly gave up the idea of buying her back. Then Bao-yu unexpectedly arrived. Seeing how the two behaved together, mother and son understood still more. Their last fears fell away; here was something beyond their expectations. Each felt reassured, and neither thought any more of buying her release.

Now Aroma had known Bao-yu since childhood and had seen how unusual his disposition was. His mischief, his foolish playfulness, went far beyond that of other children. There were also several quite extraordinary habits she could scarcely bring herself to speak of.

segments.text: Recently, with his grandmother’s indulgence to rely on, he had become harder even for his parents to restrain. He was growing more unruly and unbridled, following every whim and impulse, and disliked nothing so much as attending to proper business. Aroma had often wanted to advise him, but reckoned he would not listen. Today’s talk of buying her release had given her the chance: first she would use a pretence to sound out his feelings and take down his pride, and then she could lay down some rules. Seeing him go silently to bed, she knew he could not bear to lose her, and that his spirit was subdued.

She had never wanted the chestnuts. Her only fear was that the curd would cause another incident like the trouble over Snowpink’s tea. Chestnuts had been an excuse to divert Bao-yu and let the matter drop. She now told the little maids to take them away and eat them, and went to nudge Bao-yu. His face was covered with tear-stains.
‘What is there to be so miserable about?’ she asked with a smile. ‘If you really want to keep me, of course I won’t go.’
Sensing a condition behind this, Bao-yu said, ‘Then tell me how else I’m to keep you. I can’t think of anything more.’
‘We needn’t talk about how fond we’ve always been of each other,’ Aroma said, smiling.

segments.text: Bao-yu smiled at once. ‘Tell me. What are they? I’ll agree to anything. Dear sister, my own dear sister, never mind two or three things: I’d agree to two or three hundred. All I ask is that you all stay and watch over me, and keep me company until the day I turn to flying ash. No, not ash: ash still has shape and leaves a trace; it still knows something.

segments.text: ‘Wait until I’ve turned to a wisp of smoke that scatters at a breath of wind. Then you’ll have no hold on me, and I shan’t be able to think of you. Let me go then, and I’ll let you go wherever you please.’

segments.text: Before he had finished, Aroma hastily clapped a hand over his mouth.
‘There now! That’s just what I wanted to stop you saying, and here you are saying worse.’
‘I won’t say it again,’ Bao-yu promised quickly.
‘That’s the first thing you must change.’
‘Changed! If I say it again, pinch my mouth.

segments.text: ‘What else?’

‘Second, whether you really like studying or only pretend to, don’t keep criticising and sneering at it in front of your father or other people. At least make a show of liking it. That will spare your father some anger and give him something to boast of when he’s with people. He thinks, “Every generation of our family has studied, and now there’s this boy. I never expected him to dislike books.” That’s enough to make him angry and upset already. Then you talk all that nonsense, to people’s faces and behind their backs, calling everyone who studies to get on a “salary-grub”. You say there are no books worth the name beyond “Making Bright Virtue Shine”; the rest were cobbled together by people in earlier times who couldn’t understand the sages’ books and invented notions of their own. When you say things like that, how can you blame your father for being angry and beating you so often? What are other people to think of you?’

‘I won’t say it again,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘That was when I was little and didn’t know how high the sky was or how deep the earth. I said whatever came into my head. I wouldn’t dare say it now.

segments.text: ‘What else?’

‘No more abusing Buddhist monks and slandering Taoist priests, or meddling with rouge and powder. And one thing matters still more: no more eating the rouge from people’s lips, or this mania of yours for red.’
‘I’ll change it all, all of it. What else? Tell me quickly.’

‘Nothing else,’ she said, smiling. ‘Only be a little more careful in everything, instead of following every whim and fancy. If you really do all that, even an eight-bearer sedan-chair won’t carry me out of here.’
‘Stay here long enough,’ Bao-yu said with a smile, ‘and you needn’t fear you’ll have no eight-bearer chair to ride in.’
Aroma gave a cold laugh. ‘That’s nothing I hanker after. Even if I had the good fortune, it wouldn’t be proper. And if I did ride in one, what pleasure would there be in it?’
While they were talking, Ripple came in.
‘It’s almost the third watch. Time for bed. Her Old Ladyship sent a mamma to ask just now, and I said you were asleep.’
Bao-yu asked for the clock. Sure enough, its hand already pointed to the middle of the hai hour. They washed again, undressed and settled for the night. There is no more to tell of that.

segments.text: Early next morning, Aroma rose feeling heavy all over, with a headache, aching eyes and burning limbs. At first she struggled on, but soon she could no longer bear it and wanted only to sleep. She lay down on the kang without undressing. Bao-yu hurried to tell Grandmother Jia, and a physician was summoned to examine her.
‘Only a slight attack of wind-cold,’ he said. ‘One or two doses to disperse it will put her right.’

After he had written a prescription and gone, the medicine was fetched and boiled. As soon as Aroma had taken it, she was told to cover herself with a quilt and sweat. Bao-yu went off to visit Dai-yu.

Dai-yu was resting on her bed after the midday meal. Her maids had all gone out to attend to their own affairs, and the room was perfectly still. Bao-yu lifted the soft embroidered curtain and went into the inner room. Seeing her asleep, he hurried over and nudged her.
‘Dear cousin, you’ve only just eaten, and now you’re asleep again!’
He woke her up.

segments.text: Seeing Bao-yu, Dai-yu said, ‘Go out for a stroll. I was up all night the other day, and I still haven’t recovered. I ache all over.’
‘Aches are a small matter. Making yourself ill by sleeping is much worse. I’ll amuse you until the drowsiness passes, and then you’ll be all right.’
With her eyes still shut, Dai-yu said, ‘I’m not drowsy. I only want a little rest. Go and make a nuisance of yourself somewhere else, then come back.’
Bao-yu nudged her. ‘Where am I to go? I get so tired of seeing anyone else.’

segments.text: ‘There’s no pillow. Let’s share yours.’
‘Balls! Aren’t there pillows outside? Go and get one.’
Bao-yu went into the outer room, looked round and came back smiling.
‘I don’t want that one. Who knows which dirty old woman it belongs to?’
Dai-yu opened her eyes and sat up, laughing. ‘You really are the demon star fated to plague me! Kindly use this one.’
She pushed her own pillow towards him, then got up and fetched another of hers for herself. They lay down facing one another.

segments.text: Dai-yu noticed a blood-red mark the size of a button on Bao-yu’s left cheek. She raised herself, leaned closer and touched it, examining it carefully.
‘Whose fingernail scratched you this time?’
Bao-yu turned aside to evade her, smiling. ‘It’s not a scratch. I was rinsing and straining rouge paste for them just now. I must have rubbed some on myself.’
He began looking for a handkerchief to wipe it off. Dai-yu used her own to clean his cheek.

‘You’ve been at it again! Doing it is one thing, but must you hang out a sign to advertise it? Even if my uncle doesn’t see you, someone else will. They’ll make a fine new story of it and carry tales to curry favour. It will reach my uncle’s ears, and then everyone will be in trouble and there’ll be another fuss.’
Bao-yu heard none of this. A delicate fragrance came from Dai-yu’s sleeve, intoxicating him, making his very bones melt. He caught hold of her sleeve to see what she had concealed inside.

segments.text: ‘Who wears perfume in the winter cold of the tenth month?’ Dai-yu asked, smiling.
‘Then where does this fragrance come from?’
‘I don’t know myself. Perhaps it’s the scent in the chest, and the clothes have picked it up.’
Bao-yu shook his head. ‘I don’t think so. This is an unusual fragrance, nothing like incense cakes or scent-balls or sachets.’
Dai-yu gave a cold laugh. ‘Do you suppose some “arhat” or “perfected immortal” has given me a special fragrance too?

segments.text: ‘Even if I had some marvellous perfume, I haven’t a dear elder or younger brother to gather flowers and blossoms, frost and snow, and prepare it for me. I’ve only ordinary, vulgar scents!’
‘Every time I say one thing,’ Bao-yu said, smiling, ‘you drag in all that. You won’t learn until I give you what you deserve. I’m not sparing you today.’

He rolled over and sat up, breathed on his hands twice, then darted them under Dai-yu’s arms and tickled her sides. She had always been helplessly ticklish. As his hands ran over her sides, she laughed until she could scarcely breathe.
‘Bao-yu! If you go on, I shall be angry.’
Only then did he stop. ‘Will you say that sort of thing again?’
‘I wouldn’t dare.’ Smoothing her hair, she smiled. ‘I have a special fragrance. Have you any “Warm Fragrance”?’
Bao-yu could make nothing of this. ‘What “Warm Fragrance”?’
Dai-yu nodded, sighing and laughing. ‘You fool, you fool!

segments.text: ‘You have jade, and someone else has gold to match you. Someone else has “Cold Fragrance”, so haven’t you any “Warm Fragrance” to make the pair?’
At last Bao-yu understood.
‘You were begging for mercy a moment ago, and now you’re worse than ever,’ he said, smiling, and reached for her again.
‘Dear cousin, I daren’t!’ Dai-yu cried, laughing.
‘I’ll let you off if you let me smell your sleeve.’
He pulled it over his face and kept breathing in the fragrance. Dai-yu snatched her hand away.
‘Now you really must go.’
‘Go? I can’t. Let’s lie here and talk nicely.’

He lay back down. Dai-yu did the same and covered her face with her handkerchief. Bao-yu talked nonsense on and off; she paid no attention. He asked how old she had been when she came to the capital, what scenery and ancient sites she had seen on the journey, what old remains and stories there were in Yangzhou, and what the people and their customs were like. Dai-yu would not answer.

segments.text: Afraid that sleeping would make her ill, Bao-yu tried to coax her out of it.
‘Oh! There’s a great story about your Yangzhou yamen. Have you heard it?’
He spoke so solemnly, with such a stern, serious face, that Dai-yu took him at his word.
‘What story?’
At this Bao-yu suppressed a smile and began inventing whatever came into his head.
‘There’s a mountain in Yangzhou called Dai Mountain, and on it there’s a cave called Lin’s Woodland Cave.’
‘You’re lying already,’ Dai-yu said, laughing. ‘I’ve never heard of any such mountain.’
‘There are plenty of mountains and rivers in the world. How could you know them all? Wait till I’ve finished before you criticise.’
‘Go on, then.’

Bao-yu continued his invention. ‘Now, a colony of mouse spirits lived in Lin’s Woodland Cave. One year, on the seventh day of the twelfth month, the old mouse took his seat to hold council. “Tomorrow is Laba, the eighth,” he said, “when people everywhere make laba porridge. We’re short of fruit and nuts in our cave. This would be an excellent chance to raid a few supplies.” So he drew a command-arrow and sent a capable young mouse to scout about.

segments.text: ‘Presently the young mouse returned to report. “I’ve searched and made enquiries everywhere. The temple at the foot of the mountain has by far the most fruit and grain.”
‘“How many sorts of grain? How many kinds of fruit?” asked the old mouse.

‘“There are whole granaries of rice and beans, too much to count. There are five kinds of fruit and nuts: first, red dates; second, chestnuts; third, peanuts; fourth, water-chestnuts; fifth, fragrant taro.”
‘The old mouse was delighted and began choosing mice to send at once. He drew a command-arrow. “Who will steal the rice?”

segments.text: ‘One mouse accepted the order and went to steal rice. The old mouse drew another arrow. “Who will steal the beans?” Another mouse accepted that order and went off for beans. One by one, they all took their orders and left. Only the fragrant taro remained. The old mouse drew another arrow and asked, “Who will steal the fragrant taro?”
‘A very tiny, very feeble little mouse piped up, “I’m willing to steal the fragrant taro.”
‘The old mouse and all the others looked at him. They were afraid he lacked experience, besides being timid and weak, and none of them would let him go.
‘“I may be young and small,” the little mouse said, “but my magic has no limits, my tongue is nimble and my schemes are deep. I guarantee I can steal more cleverly than any of them.”

segments.text: ‘“How can you be cleverer than they are?” the other mice asked eagerly.

‘“I shan’t steal outright like them. I’ll shake myself and turn into a piece of fragrant taro, then roll into the pile of taro. No one will see or hear a thing. Secretly I’ll use my magic of dividing into many selves to carry it off, little by little, until the lot is gone. Isn’t that cleverer than simply stealing and grabbing?”
‘“Very clever indeed,” they all said. “But we don’t know how you do this transformation. Change for us first, and let us see.”
‘The little mouse laughed. “Nothing easier. Watch me.”

segments.text: ‘He shook himself and said, “Change!” And there he was, transformed into a most exquisite, beautiful young lady.
‘“Wrong, wrong!” the other mice cried, laughing. “You said you’d turn into something to eat. How have you turned into a young lady?”

‘The little mouse resumed his own shape and laughed. “I told you you hadn’t seen the world. You only know fragrant taro, xiangyu, the food. You don’t know that the daughter of Mr Lin, the Salt Inspector, is the real fragrant jade, xiangyu!”’
Dai-yu rolled over, scrambled up and pinned Bao-yu down, laughing.
‘May your wicked mouth rot! I knew you were making it up about me.’
She pinched him until he begged her again and again, ‘Dear cousin, spare me! I’ll never dare do it again. Your fragrance suddenly reminded me of that old tale.’
‘You insult me, and then call it an old tale!’ Dai-yu said, laughing.

segments.text: Before she had finished, Bao-chai came in.
‘Who’s talking about old tales?’ she asked with a smile. ‘Let me hear one too.’
Dai-yu quickly invited her to sit down. ‘Who do you think? He insults me, then says it’s an old tale.’

‘Oh, Cousin Bao,’ Bao-chai said, smiling. ‘You can’t blame him. He has a bellyful of old tales and allusions. The pity is that whenever he needs one, he forgets it. If he’d remembered the other night as well as he does today, he should have remembered one for his plantain poem. He couldn’t think of what was right under his nose. Someone else was so cold, and he was in such a fluster that he did nothing but sweat. Now, suddenly, his memory works again.’
‘Amitabha!’ Dai-yu laughed. ‘You really are my dear good sister. So you’ve met your match too! It just shows that every deed gets its return, without the slightest mistake.’
At that very moment, a clamour broke out in Bao-yu’s room. Truly:

segments.text: Now Bao-yu had been telling Dai-yu about the mouse spirits in her room when Bao-chai came upon them and teased him for not knowing the allusion to ‘green wax’ at the Lantern Festival. The three were still there, laughing and making fun of one another. Bao-yu had been afraid that Dai-yu would indulge in a nap after her meal and either suffer from indigestion or be unable to sleep that night: neither was any way to look after her health. Fortunately Bao-chai’s arrival had set them all talking and laughing, so that Dai-yu no longer felt like sleeping, and he could stop worrying.
Suddenly they heard an uproar in his rooms. They all listened for a moment.

‘That’s your mamma shouting at Aroma,’ Dai-yu said with a laugh. ‘Whatever Aroma may have done, if your mamma is seriously making a scene with her, she must be getting very muddle-headed in her old age.’
Bao-yu hurried to go, but Bao-chai caught his arm.
‘You mustn’t quarrel with your mamma. She’s old and confused. You ought to give way to her a little.’
‘I know,’ said Bao-yu.
He went over and found Nurse Li standing in the middle of the room, leaning on her stick and abusing Aroma.
‘You little whore! Forgotten where you came from, have you?

segments.text: ‘I made something of you, and now when I come here you lie on the kang as grand as you please and don’t so much as take notice of me. All you think about is playing the little vixen and bewitching Bao-yu, till he won’t have anything to do with me and listens to you lot instead. You’re nothing but a chit bought for a few stinking taels of silver. Do you think you can make mischief in this room? I’ll have you dragged out and married to one of the boys, and then we’ll see whether you can still play the witch and charm Bao-yu!’

At first Aroma thought Nurse Li was merely angry at finding her lying down. She tried to explain that she was ill, had just begun to sweat and had had her head covered, so that she had not seen the old lady come in. But when the accusations of ‘bewitching Bao-yu’ and ‘playing the vixen’ went on and on, followed by the threat of marrying her to one of the boys, she felt so ashamed and wronged that she could not help crying.

segments.text: Bao-yu heard all this but could do little about it. He could only explain on Aroma’s behalf that she was ill and taking medicine.
‘If you don’t believe me, ask the other maids.’
This made Nurse Li angrier still.

‘You do nothing but protect those vixens. What am I to you now? Who am I to ask? Which of them wouldn’t take your side? Which of them hasn’t Aroma brought to heel? I know all about their doings. I’ll just have to take you before Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship and tell them. I nursed you till you grew this big, and now you have no use for my milk you push me aside and let the maids lord it over me.’
She too began to cry as she spoke. Dai-yu and Bao-chai had followed him over and tried to soothe her.
‘Mamma, you’re older and wiser. Just put up with them a little.’

At the sight of the two girls, Nurse Li seized on them to hear her grievances. On and on she rambled about the tea she had drunk that other day, Snowpink’s dismissal, yesterday’s milk curd and all the rest.

segments.text: As it happened, Xi-feng had just finished settling the gambling accounts in Grandmother Jia’s rooms. Hearing the uproar at the back, she knew Nurse Li was at her old tricks again, scolding Bao-yu’s attendants. Nurse Li had lost money that day and was taking it out on someone else. Xi-feng hurried over, took her by the arm and said with a smile:

‘Now, my dear mamma, don’t be angry. It’s the holiday, and Her Old Ladyship has only just had one happy day. You’re one of our old people. If anyone else raised their voice, you’d be the one to stop them. Surely you know better than to shout here yourself and upset Her Old Ladyship? Just tell me who’s been naughty, and I’ll beat her for you. There’s a pheasant cooking at my place, piping hot. Come and have some wine with me.’
Talking all the while, she pulled Nurse Li away.
‘Felicity! Carry your Grannie Li’s stick, and her handkerchief for wiping her eyes.’
Nurse Li was swept off her feet and away with Xi-feng, still protesting:
‘I don’t care if I die! I might as well forget my manners today, make a proper scene and disgrace myself. Anything’s better than being put upon by that little whore!’
Bao-chai and Dai-yu had followed them out. Seeing how Xi-feng managed it, they clapped their hands and laughed.
‘Thank goodness for that gust of wind! It whisked the old woman away.’
Bao-yu nodded and sighed.
‘Who knows whose score she’s settling this time? She always picks on someone who won’t answer back.

segments.text: Still crying, Aroma caught Bao-yu’s hand.
‘You’ve offended an old lady on my account, and now you’re offending all these people for me as well. Haven’t I enough to bear already, without your dragging in everyone else?’

Seeing her so ill, with all this trouble added to it, Bao-yu hurriedly swallowed his resentment and soothed her into lying down again to sweat. She was burning hot. He stayed beside her, reclining there and urging her to think only of getting well, not to vex herself over things that did not matter.
Aroma gave a bitter laugh.

‘If I let things like that upset me, I couldn’t stay in this room for a moment. But when it goes on and on, day after day, what is one to do? I’m always telling you not to offend people for our sake. You only think of standing up for us at the time, but they remember it. When they get a chance, out it all comes, and it’s very unpleasant to hear. What good does that do any of us?’
As she spoke she could not hold back her tears. Afraid of distressing Bao-yu, however, she forced herself to check them.

segments.text: Presently an old woman who did odd jobs brought in a second decoction of the medicine. Seeing that Aroma had only just begun to perspire, Bao-yu would not let her get up. He took the bowl himself and held it to her as she lay on her pillow, then told the little maids to make up the kang.

‘Whether you’re going to eat or not,’ Aroma said, ‘at least go and sit with Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship for a while, and spend a little time with the young ladies before you come back. Then I can lie here quietly too.’

segments.text: Bao-yu could only do as she asked. He took off her hairpins and earrings, saw her lie down, and went to Grandmother Jia’s rooms. After they had eaten, she wanted to amuse herself at cards with the old senior serving-women, but he was thinking of Aroma and returned to his room. She had drifted into a doze. He thought of going to bed himself, but it was still too early.
Skybright, Mackerel, Ripple and Emerald had all gone off in search of amusement with Faithful, Amber and the others. Only Musk remained, laying out dominoes by lamplight in the outer room.
‘Why haven’t you gone to play with them?’ he asked, smiling.
‘I haven’t any money.’
‘There’s all that money piled under the bed. Isn’t that enough for you to lose?’

‘If everyone goes off to play, who’s to look after the room? She’s ill, too. There are lamps up above and fires down below, all over the place. Those poor old mammas, at their age, have been waiting on us all day. They ought to have a rest. And the little maids have been working all day too. If they can’t go and play now, when can they?

segments.text: ‘So let them all go. I’ll stay here and keep an eye on things.’
Hearing this, Bao-yu thought she was positively another Aroma.
‘I’ll sit here,’ he said with a smile. ‘Off you go, and don’t worry.’
‘Now you’re here, there’s even less reason to go. Wouldn’t it be nice for the two of us to talk and have a laugh?’
‘What shall we do, though?’ said Bao-yu. ‘It’s rather dull. Oh, I know. You said this morning your head was itching. There’s nothing to do just now. Let me comb your hair.’
‘That’s just the thing,’ said Musk.

She brought over her fitted mirror case, took off her hairpins and bracelets, and let down her hair. Bao-yu took the fine-toothed comb and worked through it, strand by strand. He had made only three to five strokes when Skybright hurried in for some money. At the sight of them she gave a scornful laugh.
‘Oh! You haven’t drunk the wedding cups yet, and already you’re dressing her hair like a bride!’
‘Come here,’ said Bao-yu, laughing. ‘I’ll comb yours too.’
‘I’m not so blessed.’
She took her money and flung the curtain down behind her as she went out.

segments.text: Bao-yu was behind Musk, who sat facing the mirror, and their eyes met in the glass.
‘Of everyone in this room, she’s the only one who’s always sniping,’ he said with a smile at her reflection.
Musk hastily waved a warning hand in the mirror. Bao-yu understood. Suddenly the curtain swished, and Skybright ran in again.
‘How am I always sniping? Come on, let’s hear it.’
‘Off you go,’ said Musk, laughing. ‘Back again to question people!’
‘And you’re protecting him again!’ Skybright laughed. ‘I know all about your sneaking and your tricks. Wait till I’ve won my money back. Then we’ll talk.’
And straight out she went.

segments.text: Bao-yu finished combing Musk’s hair and had her help him quietly to bed, unwilling to disturb Aroma. Nothing more need be said of that night.

By the time they rose next morning, Aroma had sweated during the night and felt somewhat easier. She took only a little rice water and rested quietly. Bao-yu, relieved, went over after breakfast to Aunt Xue’s to while away some time. It was the first month: the school was closed for the New Year, and needlework was forbidden in the women’s apartments, so everyone was at leisure.

Jia Huan had also come to play. He found Bao-chai, Caltrop and Oriole, the three of them, amusing themselves with a dice game played with Go counters, and wanted to join in. Bao-chai had always treated him just as she treated Bao-yu, without any other thought. Hearing that he wanted to play, she invited him up to sit with them. The cash lay in piles of ten. He won the first time and was delighted. But after losing several games in succession, he began to grow anxious. In the current game it was his turn to throw the dice. A seven would win it for him; with a six, Oriole would only need to throw a three on her next turn to win. He picked up the dice and flung them down hard. One settled on five; the other spun round and round.

segments.text: Oriole clapped her hands and kept calling, ‘One!’ Jia Huan glared, shouting out ‘Six! Seven! Eight!’ indiscriminately. As ill luck would have it, the die came up one. In a panic he snatched it up, then reached for the money, claiming it had been a six.
‘It was a one, plain as anything!’ said Oriole.
Seeing Jia Huan’s agitation, Bao-chai gave Oriole a warning look.
‘The older you get, the worse your manners. Would a young master cheat you? Put that money down at once!’
Oriole felt deeply wronged, but after her mistress’s rebuke she dared not argue. She had to put down the money, though she muttered:

‘A young master, cheating us out of a few cash! He doesn’t even show me any respect. The other day, when I was playing with Master Bao, he lost all that money and never got cross. The little maids snatched up what he had left, and he only laughed.’

segments.text: Bao-chai sharply cut her off before she had finished.
‘How can I compare with Bao-yu?’ said Jia Huan. ‘You’re afraid of him. You all like him, and you all pick on me because I wasn’t born to Her Ladyship.’
He began to cry.
‘My dear boy, don’t say things like that,’ Bao-chai hastened to soothe him. ‘People will laugh at you.’
She scolded Oriole again.

segments.text: Just then Bao-yu came in. Seeing the state they were in, he asked what had happened. Jia Huan dared not make a sound. Bao-chai knew the rules of their household: younger brothers were all afraid of their elders. What she did not know was that Bao-yu wanted no one to be afraid of him. His reasoning was this: ‘My brothers all have parents to teach them. Why should I interfere and only make them shy of me? Besides, I was born to the lawful wife, and he to a concubine. People talk behind our backs as it is. What would they say if I started ordering him about?’ He also cherished another foolish notion.

segments.text: What foolish notion, you ask? From earliest childhood he had grown up among girls. There were his own sisters Yuan-chun and Tan-chun, his paternal cousins Ying-chun and Xi-chun, and other relations such as Shi Xiang-yun, Lin Dai-yu and Xue Bao-chai. He had therefore concluded that, though human beings were born the most spiritual of all creatures, the purest essence of mountains and rivers, sun and moon, was bestowed on girls alone. Bearded men were merely the dregs and dirty froth.

With this foolish notion in his head, he considered all males muddy, undifferentiated creatures whom one could quite well do without. There was an exception for his father, uncles and brothers: Confucius, the foremost man of all time, had said one must not defy or slight them, and Bao-yu could only obey his injunction. So, with his brothers, he did no more than observe the broad requirements of affection and propriety. He never thought that, as a man, he ought to set an example to the younger members of the family. Jia Huan and the rest were consequently not afraid of him, though fear of Grandmother Jia made them show him a little deference.
Now Bao-chai, afraid that a lecture from Bao-yu would only make matters awkward for Jia Huan, hastily made excuses for him.

segments.text: ‘What are you crying for in the New Year holidays?’ said Bao-yu. ‘If you don’t like it here, go and play somewhere else. You read every day, and all your reading seems to have muddled you. Suppose this thing isn’t any good: something else is bound to be better. You leave this one and take the other. Do you think sitting here crying over it will make it any better? You came to enjoy yourself. If you can’t enjoy yourself here, go somewhere else and find some fun.

segments.text: ‘Can you call it enjoying yourself, sitting here crying? You’re only making yourself miserable. You’d do better to go at once.’
Jia Huan could only go home. Aunt Zhao, seeing his face, asked:
‘Who’s been using you for a kicking-block this time?’
He did not answer her first question. When she asked again, he said:
‘I was playing with Cousin Bao-chai. Oriole bullied me and cheated me out of my money, and Brother Bao-yu sent me away.’

segments.text: Aunt Zhao spat in disgust.
‘Who told you to go mixing with your betters? You shameless little wretch! Couldn’t you find anywhere else to play? Who told you to go there and make a fool of yourself?’
Xi-feng happened to pass outside the window just then and heard every word. She spoke through the window:

‘What’s all this, in the middle of the New Year holidays? Huan’s only a child. If he does something a little wrong, you should teach him better. What’s the good of all this nonsense? Whatever he does, there are still Her Ladyship and His Lordship to look after him. How dare you spit abuse at him! He is one of the masters of this house. If he misbehaves, there are people to correct him. What business is it of yours? Huan, come out and play with me.’
Jia Huan had always been more afraid of Xi-feng than of Lady Wang. At her summons he hurried out, murmuring his obedience. Aunt Zhao did not dare utter a word either.

‘And you’re a spineless creature too,’ Xi-feng told Jia Huan. ‘How often have I told you? If you want something to eat or drink, or a game or a laugh, go to whichever sister, cousin, brother or sister-in-law you like.

segments.text: ‘Instead of listening to me, you let these people teach you their crooked, spiteful ways, all sly tricks and bullying. You have no self-respect, you’re determined to sink as low as you can, you harbour all these nasty little thoughts, and then you complain that other people are partial. How much did you lose, to get into such a state?’
Questioned, Jia Huan could only stammer an answer.
‘One or two hundred.’

segments.text: ‘And you call yourself a young master!’ said Xi-feng. ‘All this over one or two hundred cash!’
She turned to Felicity.
‘Go and fetch a string of cash. The girls are all playing at the back. Take him there to play.’
Then, to Jia Huan:

‘And if you behave like this again, you sly little wretch, I’ll beat you first and then send word to the school. They’ll flay you alive! Your brother’s so furious at your disgraceful ways he’s grinding his teeth. If I hadn’t stopped him, he’d have kicked your guts out.’
‘Off you go!’ she ordered.
Jia Huan meekly followed Felicity, received the money and went to play with Ying-chun and the others. Of him we need say no more.
Bao-yu was still talking and laughing with Bao-chai when someone announced, ‘Miss Shi has come.’ He sprang up to go.

segments.text: ‘Wait,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘Let’s go and see her together.’

She got down from the kang and went with him to Grandmother Jia’s rooms. They found Shi Xiang-yun talking and laughing at the top of her voice. When she saw the two of them, she hurried to exchange greetings. Dai-yu was there too.
‘Where have you been?’ she asked Bao-yu.
‘At Cousin Bao-chai’s.’
Dai-yu gave a cold laugh.
‘I thought as much. Lucky something kept you there, or you’d have flown here long ago.’
‘So I’m only allowed to play with you and keep you amused?’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘I go to see her once in a while, and this is what you say.’
‘What a tiresome thing to say! What do I care whether you go or not? I never asked you to keep me amused. You’re quite welcome never to speak to me again!’
With that, she went back to her room in a huff.

segments.text: Bao-yu hurried after her.

‘What’s made you angry again, all of a sudden? Even if I said something wrong, you could have stayed there and talked and laughed with the others for a while. Instead you’ve come back to sit here making yourself miserable.’
‘What business is it of yours?’
‘I wouldn’t dare interfere,’ he said with a smile. ‘But I can’t just watch you ruin your health.’
‘If I ruin my health and die, what’s that to you?’
‘Why talk about living and dying in the New Year holidays?’
‘I will talk about dying! I’ll die this very minute! If you’re afraid of death, you can live to be a hundred. How’s that?’
‘Do you think I’m afraid of dying, if this is to go on and on?’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Better to die and have done with it.’
‘Exactly!’ Dai-yu said at once. ‘If this is to go on, better to die and have done with it.’
‘I meant it would be better if I died. Don’t mishear me and then blame me for it.’

segments.text: While they were talking, Bao-chai came in.
‘Cousin Xiang-yun is waiting for you.’

She pushed Bao-yu out with her. Left behind, Dai-yu felt more wretched than ever and sat by the window weeping. Before two cups of tea could have been drunk, Bao-yu was back. At the sight of him her sobs grew louder and would not stop. He knew it would be hard to put matters right, and marshalled a thousand tender, soothing things to say. But before he could open his mouth, Dai-yu spoke.

‘What have you come back for? You’ve someone to play with now who reads better than I do, and writes better poetry, and has better handwriting, and is better at talking and laughing. And she’s so afraid you’ll get angry that she pulls you away. What have you come back for? Leave me to live or die as I please!’
Bao-yu hurried up to her and spoke softly.
‘You’re so sensible. Surely you know the saying, “Nearer kin should not be displaced by remoter kin, nor earlier ties by later ones”?

segments.text: ‘Muddle-headed as I am, I understand those two things. First, your mother and my father were sister and brother, whereas Cousin Bao-chai’s mother and mine are sisters. In terms of kinship, she isn’t as close to me as you are. Second, you came here first. We’ve eaten at the same table and slept in the same bed, and grown up together to this age. She’s only just come. How could I neglect you for her?’
Dai-yu gave a little snort.
‘Am I asking you to neglect her? What sort of person would that make me? It’s my heart I’m thinking of.’
‘And it’s my heart I’m thinking of. Do you know only your own heart, and not mine?’
Dai-yu lowered her head and said nothing. At last she spoke.
‘You’re always complaining that I take offence at everything you do. You never know how you torment me.

segments.text: ‘Just take the weather today. It’s so obviously cold, yet you’ve taken off your dark fox-flank cloak. Why?’
‘I had it on,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘But when I saw how angry you were, I got all hot and took it off.’
Dai-yu sighed.
‘You’ll catch cold, and then you’ll be kept on an empty stomach and make a fuss for something to eat again.’

segments.text: As they were talking, Xiang-yun came up to them with a smile.
‘Second Cousin! Cousin Lin! You two can play together every day. I hardly ever manage to come, and now I’m here you won’t take any notice of me.’
‘You do love to talk, for someone who lisps,’ Dai-yu said, laughing. ‘You can’t even say “Second Cousin”. It’s always “Dear Cousin, Dear Cousin”!

segments.text: ‘And when we play the counter game later, you’ll be at it again: “One, ai, three, four, five!”’
Bao-yu laughed.
‘Keep on copying her, and one of these days you’ll be lisping yourself.’

‘She never lets anyone off,’ said Shi Xiang-yun. ‘She does nothing but pick on people’s faults. Even if you’re better than everyone else, that’s no reason to make fun of everyone you meet. There’s one person I could name: if you dare find fault with her, I’ll admit you’re the clever one.’
Dai-yu promptly asked who it was.
‘Cousin Bao-chai. Dare to find fault with her, and I’ll give you credit. I may not be as good as you, but how is she any worse?’
Dai-yu gave a cold laugh.
‘Oh, so that’s who you meant! How would I dare find fault with her?’
Before she could finish, Bao-yu hastily turned the conversation.

segments.text: Now Shi Xiang-yun ran outside, afraid that Lin Dai-yu would catch her. Behind her Bao-yu called hurriedly, ‘Mind you don’t trip! She’s nowhere near you yet!’
When Dai-yu reached the door, he stretched his arms across the frame to bar her way.
‘Let her off this once,’ he urged with a smile.
Dai-yu tugged at his arms. ‘If I let Yun-er off, may I never live another day!’
Seeing Bao-yu block the doorway, Xiang-yun judged that Dai-yu could not get out, and stopped to laugh.
‘Dear sister, let me off this once!’
Just then Bao-chai came up behind her and said with a smile, ‘For Cousin Bao’s sake, I think you should both let go.’

segments.text: ‘I won’t!’ Dai-yu said. ‘You’re all in league against me. Do you mean to make fun of me together?’
‘Who would dare make fun of you?’ Bao-yu coaxed. ‘If you hadn’t teased her, would she have dared say anything about you?’

The four were still at an impasse when someone came to call them to dinner, and only then did they go to the front rooms. By lamplighting time that evening, Lady Wang, Li Wan, Xi-feng, Ying-chun, Tan-chun, Xi-chun and the others had all come to Grandmother Jia’s. They chatted for a while, then went their separate ways to bed. Xiang-yun again slept in Dai-yu’s room. Bao-yu saw the two of them back to their room. It was well into the second watch, and Aroma had come several times to hurry him, before he returned to his own room to sleep.

At daybreak he threw on his clothes, slipped his feet into his shoes and went over to Dai-yu’s room. Neither Nightingale nor Kingfisher was there. The two cousins were still in bed. Dai-yu lay peacefully asleep, her eyes closed, wrapped snugly in an apricot-red figured-silk quilt. Xiang-yun’s black hair trailed beside her pillow; her quilt came only to her chest, and a snow-white arm curved outside it, with two gold bracelets on it.

segments.text: Bao-yu sighed at the sight.
‘You can’t keep still even in your sleep! When a draught catches you, you’ll be complaining of a sore shoulder again.’
As he spoke, he gently covered her up. Dai-yu was already awake. Sensing someone there, she guessed it must be Bao-yu, and turned over to find that she was right.
‘What have you come running over for at this hour?’
‘You call this early?’ he said with a smile. ‘Get up and have a look.’
‘Go outside first and let us get up.’
Bao-yu turned and went out.

segments.text: Dai-yu rose and woke Xiang-yun, and both dressed. Bao-yu came back and sat beside the dressing-table as Nightingale and Snowgoose came in to help them wash and do their hair. When Xiang-yun had washed her face, Kingfisher was about to throw out the used water.
‘Wait,’ Bao-yu said. ‘I’ll wash in it while it’s here. It will save the trouble of going back.’
He came over, bent down and splashed his face twice. Nightingale offered him scented soap.
‘There’s plenty in the basin already. No need to rub any more.’
He splashed his face twice more, then asked for a towel.
‘Still the same old habit!’ said Kingfisher. ‘When will you ever give it up?’
He took no notice, but hurriedly asked for green salt, cleaned his teeth and rinsed his mouth. Xiang-yun’s hair was now finished. He went over to her with a smile.
‘Dear cousin, do my hair for me.’
‘No, I can’t do that.’
‘Dear cousin, why did you do it for me before, then?’
‘I’ve forgotten how. How can I do it now?’
‘I’m not going out. I shan’t wear a cap and headband. You only need to put it in a few loose plaits.’
He went on begging her, with a thousand ‘dear cousins’ and ten thousand more.

segments.text: Xiang-yun had to draw his head towards her and work through his hair, first with a comb and then with a fine-toothed one. At home, without a cap, he did not wear his hair in paired tufts. The short hairs round his head were simply made into little plaits, gathered in with the hair at the crown, and braided into one large plait tied with red cord. Four pearls were set along it from crown to tip, with a gold pendant at the bottom.
As she plaited, Xiang-yun said, ‘There are only three of these pearls now. This one is different. I remember they all matched. What happened to the other one?’
‘I lost it.’
‘It must have fallen off when you were out, and someone picked it up without your knowing. What a piece of luck for them!’
Dai-yu was washing her hands beside them. She gave a cold laugh.
‘Who knows whether it was really lost, or given to someone to have set in something to wear?’

Bao-yu did not answer. The dressing-table was flanked by cosmetic boxes and other toilet things, which he picked up idly to examine. Without thinking, he took up some rouge and was about to put it to his lips, but feared that Xiang-yun would scold him. While he hesitated, she caught sight of it from behind. Holding his plait in one hand, she reached round with the other and knocked the rouge out of his hand with a smack.
‘When will you ever grow out of that wretched habit?’
Before she had finished speaking, Aroma came in. Seeing what was going on, she knew that his washing and grooming were already attended to, and could only go back to do her own.

segments.text: Suddenly Bao-chai appeared and asked, ‘Where has Cousin Bao gone?’
‘As if Cousin Bao had any time to stay at home!’ Aroma replied with a smile.
Bao-chai understood. Then she heard Aroma sigh.

‘It’s all very well for cousins to be fond of one another, but there are limits, and there are proprieties. They can’t go romping about together night and day! Whatever anyone says to him goes in one ear and out the other.’
‘I mustn’t misjudge this maid,’ Bao-chai thought. ‘There’s some sense in what she says.’
She sat down on the kang.

segments.text: In casual conversation she gradually drew Aroma out, asking about her age, her home and so on. She watched her closely, and found much to respect and like in both her conversation and her outlook. Presently Bao-yu came in, and Bao-chai left.
‘What were you and Cousin Bao-chai talking about so merrily?’ he asked Aroma. ‘Why did she run away as soon as I came in?’
His first question went unanswered. When he asked again, Aroma said, ‘Are you asking me? How should I know what goes on between you?’
Hearing this, and seeing an expression quite unlike her usual one, Bao-yu smiled.
‘What, are you really angry?’

Aroma gave a cold laugh. ‘How should I dare be angry? Only don’t come into this room again from now on. You have people to look after you. Don’t come ordering me about. I’ll go back to waiting on Her Old Ladyship.’

segments.text: As she spoke she lay down on the kang and closed her eyes. Deeply dismayed, Bao-yu hurried over to comfort her, but she kept her eyes shut and paid him no attention. He was at a loss. Seeing Musk come in, he asked, ‘What’s the matter with your sister?’
‘How should I know? Ask yourself, and you’ll have your answer.’
Bao-yu sat dumbfounded for a while. Feeling thoroughly rebuffed, he rose with a sigh.
‘Don’t speak to me, then. I’ll go to sleep too.’

He got down from the kang and lay on his own bed. After a long silence Aroma heard him snoring softly. Supposing that he was asleep, she rose and brought a cloak. She had only just laid it over him when, with a sudden swish, he flung it off, still keeping his eyes closed and pretending to sleep.
Knowing perfectly well what he meant, Aroma nodded with a cold laugh.
‘There’s no need for you to be angry either. From now on I’ll pretend I’m dumb and never say another word against you. Will that do?’
Bao-yu could bear it no longer. He sat up.
‘What have I done now?
