segments.text: ‘There you go, advising me again! I wouldn’t mind your advice, but you didn’t give me any just now. As soon as I came in, you wouldn’t speak to me and lay down in a huff. I still don’t know why, and now you say I’m angry. When did I hear you give me any advice?’
‘Don’t you know in your own heart?’ said Aroma. ‘Must you wait for me to tell you?’

While they were quarrelling, Grandmother Jia sent for him to eat, and he went to the front rooms. He hastily swallowed half a bowlful, then returned to his own room. Aroma was lying on the outer kang, with Musk beside her playing dominoes. Knowing how close the two were, he would have nothing to say to Musk either. He lifted the soft curtain and went into the inner room. Musk had to follow him. He pushed her out.
‘I wouldn’t dream of troubling any of you.’
She could only come out smiling and send in two little maids. Bao-yu took a book and lay reading for some time. Wanting tea, he looked up to find the two young maids standing on the floor before him.

‘What’s your name?’ Bao-yu asked her.
‘Hui-xiang.’
‘Who gave you that name?’
‘I was called Yun-xiang before. Sister Aroma changed it to Hui-xiang.’

segments.text: ‘Four,’ Hui-xiang said.
‘Which are you?’
‘The fourth.’
‘Then from tomorrow you’re Si-er, Number Four. None of this Hui-xiang and orchid fragrance. Which of you deserves to be compared with such flowers? You only disgrace good names.’
As he spoke he told her to pour him some tea. Aroma and Musk heard him from the outer room and pressed their lips together to hide their smiles.

That day Bao-yu scarcely left his room. He neither romped with his cousins nor teased the maids, but sat gloomily by himself, turning to a book for distraction or playing with brush and ink. He gave the others no orders, calling only on Si-er. She proved a remarkably quick-witted, obliging girl and, finding herself in favour, tried every means of winning him over.

After supper, two cups of wine had left his eyes drowsy and his ears warm. On any other evening he would have had Aroma and the rest about him, laughing and enjoying themselves. Now he sat alone before the lamp in dismal silence, with no pleasure in anything. He wanted to go after them, but feared that this would only gratify them and encourage still more admonitions. To assert his authority as master and frighten them into obedience seemed altogether too unfeeling.

segments.text: There was nothing for it but to harden his heart and suppose them dead. He would have to go on living even then. So he imagined for the moment that they were dead, and found that, with nothing to tie him to them, he could actually be quite content. He told Si-er to trim the lamp and brew tea, and read for a while in The Classic of Nanhua. He came to this passage in ‘Breaking Open Chests’, one of the Outer Chapters:

‘Therefore, cut off sagehood and cast out knowledge, and great thieves will cease. Cast away jade and destroy pearls, and petty thieves will not arise. Burn tallies and break seals, and the people will be simple and unsophisticated. Smash measures and snap scales, and the people will not contend. Destroy utterly the sages’ laws throughout the world, and only then can one begin to reason with the people. Disrupt the six pitch-pipes, melt down and destroy the reed-organs and zithers, stop the ears of Kuang the blind musician, and only then will everyone in the world retain their own powers of hearing. Blot out ornament, disperse the five colours, glue shut the eyes of Li Zhu, and only then will everyone in the world retain their own powers of sight. Destroy hooks and marking-lines, throw away compasses and squares, break the fingers of the craftsman Chui, and only then will everyone in the world possess skill of their own.’
Delighted by what he read, and carried along by the wine, he could not help taking up his brush to add a continuation:

‘Burn the flowers and scatter the musk, and only then will everyone in the women’s chambers keep their counsel to themselves. Mutilate Bao-chai’s immortal beauty, reduce Dai-yu’s subtle understanding to ashes, destroy and diminish love and affection, and only then will fair and foul in the women’s chambers be alike.

segments.text: ‘If they keep their counsel to themselves, there will be no fear of estrangement, like the stars Shen and Shang that never meet. Mutilate their immortal beauty, and there will be no heart for love. Reduce their subtle understanding to ashes, and there will be no feeling for wit and invention. For hairpin and jade, flowers and musk, all spread their nets and dig their pitfalls, to bewilder, entangle and ensnare the world.’

His continuation finished, Bao-yu threw down the brush and went to bed. His head had scarcely touched the pillow before he was fast asleep. All night he knew nothing of where he had gone, and did not wake until daybreak. Turning over, he saw Aroma lying fully dressed on top of the quilt. Yesterday’s quarrel had already gone out of his mind. He nudged her.
‘Get up and go to bed properly. You’ll catch cold.’

segments.text: Now Aroma, seeing him romp with his cousins at all hours of the day and night, had judged that plain remonstrance would never change him. She therefore used his affection to bring him to his senses, supposing that in half a day, or even a little while, they would be on good terms again. Instead, Bao-yu had held out all day and all night. It was she who no longer knew what to do, and she had scarcely slept. Now that he behaved like this, she judged that his feelings had softened, and ignored him all the more.

When she did not answer, Bao-yu reached out to undo her clothes. He had just unfastened the buttons when she pushed his hand away and did them up again. Helpless, he could only take her hand and ask with a smile, ‘What is the matter with you?’
After he had asked several times, Aroma opened her eyes.
‘Nothing is the matter with me. You’re awake now. Go over to the other room to wash and have your hair done. If you wait much longer, you’ll be too late.’
‘Where am I to go?’

Aroma gave a cold laugh. ‘You ask me! How should I know? Go wherever you please. From now on, let’s have nothing to do with each other. It will save all this cock-and-goose squabbling for other people to laugh at.

segments.text: ‘When you’ve had your fill over there, you can come back here and have some Number Four or Number Five wait on you. Creatures like us do nothing but “disgrace good names”.’
‘You still remember that today!’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
‘I’ll remember it in a hundred years! I’m not like you, who let my words blow past your ears. What I say at night you’ve forgotten by morning.’
The sight of her face, so full of tender displeasure, stirred him beyond restraint. He picked up a jade hairpin beside the pillow and dashed it down, breaking it in two.
‘If I ever refuse to listen to you again, may I end up like this!’
Aroma hurriedly gathered up the pieces.
‘Why do a thing like that first thing in the morning? What does it matter whether you listen? Is it worth such a fuss?’
‘You don’t know how desperate I feel!’
‘So you know what it is to feel desperate?’ she said with a smile. ‘Then you can imagine how I feel. Come along, get up and wash your face.’
Only then did they both get up and attend to their washing and grooming.

segments.text: After Bao-yu had gone to the main rooms, Dai-yu happened to call. Finding him out, she turned over the books on his desk and chanced upon the volume of Zhuang-zi he had been reading the day before. When she reached his continuation, she was both angry and amused. She too could not resist taking up a brush and adding a quatrain:

Who idly takes his brush in hand
To mock Nanhua’s Zhuangzi yin?

segments.text:
He feels no shame for his own lack of sense,
But heaps foul words on others, laying blame.

When she had finished, she too went to the main rooms to see Grandmother Jia, and afterwards to Lady Wang’s. As it happened, Xi-feng’s daughter Da-jie had fallen ill, and there was a flurry of people fetching a doctor to feel her pulse.
‘My congratulations to Her Ladyship and the ladies,’ the doctor said. ‘The little girl’s fever is the auspicious eruption of smallpox, not some other illness.’
Lady Wang and Xi-feng hurriedly sent someone to ask whether she would be all right.
‘The illness is dangerous, but it is taking a favourable course,’ he replied. ‘There should be no great difficulty. The important thing is to have mulberry worms and pig tails ready.’

Xi-feng sprang into action. Rooms were cleaned for worship of the Smallpox Goddess, and orders went round the household that nothing was to be fried or stir-fried. She told Patience to put together bedding and clothes so that Jia Lian could sleep in a separate room, and brought out lengths of scarlet cloth to make clothes for the wet-nurse, the maids and all who attended the child closely. A clean room was also prepared in the outer quarters, where the two doctors were hospitably lodged. They took turns considering the case, feeling the pulse and prescribing medicines, and were not allowed home for twelve days. Jia Lian had to move into the outer study and observe fasting and abstinence. Every day Xi-feng and Patience joined Lady Wang in worshipping the goddess.

segments.text: As for Jia Lian, he had only to be away from Xi-feng to start looking for mischief. After two nights alone he found it unbearable, and for the time being picked out the better-looking male page-servants to relieve his desire.

Now in the Rong mansion there was a thoroughly worthless, disreputable drunkard of a cook called Duo-guan. He was so weak and ineffectual that everyone called him Duo the Dullard. While he was still young, his parents had found him a wife from outside the household. She was now in her early twenties, with looks that won the admiration of everyone who saw her. Flighty by nature, she delighted in sexual adventures. Duo the Dullard took no notice: so long as he had wine, meat and money, he let everything else go. Thus the men of both the Rong and Ning mansions had access to her. For her remarkable beauty and boundless wantonness, everyone knew her as ‘Mrs Duo’.

Jia Lian, now chafing in the outer quarters, had seen her before and lost his head over her. But fear of his lovely wife at home and his male favourites outside had kept him from making an approach. Mrs Duo had designs on him too; she had only lacked the opportunity.

segments.text: When she heard that Jia Lian had moved into the outer study, she began finding excuses to go that way and provoke him. He was soon like a starving rat. He had to consult his trusted pages, promising them liberal rewards of money and silk if they would arrange matters and cover for him. Why would the pages refuse? Besides, they were all on intimate terms with the woman themselves. One word settled it.

That night, at the second watch, when everyone had gone to rest and Duo the Dullard lay dead drunk on the kang, Jia Lian slipped over to meet her. One glimpse of her as he came in sent his senses flying. There was no need for affectionate talk or tender preliminaries; he undressed and set to work. The woman had a peculiar gift by nature: at a man’s touch her whole body became so soft and yielding that he seemed to be lying on cotton. Her lewd manner and licentious talk outdid a prostitute’s. What man at such a moment would spare his very life? Jia Lian wished he could melt his whole body into hers.

From beneath him, deliberately teasing him with wanton talk, she said, ‘Your daughter has the pox, and you’re worshipping the goddess at home. You ought to abstain for a couple of days, yet here you are, defiling yourself for my sake.

segments.text: ‘Go on, get away from me.’
Moving vigorously, Jia Lian answered between gasps, ‘You’re my goddess! What do I care about any other goddess?’
The more wanton the woman grew, the more completely Jia Lian abandoned all restraint. Afterwards they pledged their love by sea and mountain, unable to bear parting, and from that time became lovers.

In due course the poison left Da-jie’s body and the spots subsided. At the end of twelve days the goddess was ceremonially sent away. The whole family made offerings to Heaven and the ancestors, fulfilled their vows, burned incense, celebrated and distributed rewards. Jia Lian moved back into the bedroom. At his reunion with Xi-feng, it was just as the saying has it: ‘Newlyweds cannot match a couple long parted.’ Their tenderness was boundless, and need not detain us.

segments.text: Early next morning, after Xi-feng had gone to the main rooms, Patience was putting away the clothes and bedding Jia Lian had used outside when a lock of black hair unexpectedly fell from his pillowcase. She understood at once and hastily tucked it into her sleeve. Then she went into the other room, took it out and held it up to Jia Lian with a smile.
‘What’s this?’
He was alarmed and rushed to snatch it. Patience ran, but he caught her, pinned her to the kang and tried to prise her hand open.
‘You little baggage,’ he said, laughing, ‘give it here at once, or I’ll snap your arm!’
‘You heartless thing!’ she laughed. ‘I was kind enough to hide it from her and ask you privately, and now you threaten me!

segments.text: ‘Go on threatening. When she comes back I’ll tell her, and then we’ll see what you do.’
Jia Lian promptly put on a coaxing smile. ‘Be a darling and let me have it. I won’t threaten you again.’

Before he had finished, Xi-feng’s voice was heard approaching. He released his hold. Patience had only just got up when Xi-feng came in and told her to open the box at once and find a pattern for Lady Wang. Patience quickly assented and began to look. The sight of Jia Lian suddenly reminded Xi-feng of something.
‘Have you brought back everything that was taken out?’ she asked Patience.
‘Yes.’
‘Nothing missing?’
‘I was afraid a thing or two might have been left behind, so I checked very carefully. Nothing’s missing.’
‘That’s good. So long as nothing extra has turned up.’

segments.text: ‘It’s lucky enough not to have lost anything,’ Patience laughed. ‘Who would be adding to it?’

Xi-feng gave a cold laugh. ‘There’s no guarantee he’s kept himself clean this fortnight. Some intimate friend might have left something behind. A ring, a kerchief, a scent-bag, even hair or fingernails. They all count.’
Her words turned Jia Lian’s face yellow. Behind her back he stared at Patience, grimacing and jerking his head in frantic signals. Patience pretended not to see.

‘Why, ma’am, you and I think exactly alike!’ she said with a smile. ‘I was afraid of just such things. I searched very carefully, but there wasn’t the least sign of anything. If you don’t believe me, I haven’t put the things away yet. You can go through them yourself.’
‘Silly girl!’ Xi-feng laughed. ‘If he had anything like that, would he leave it where we could find it?’
With that, she found the pattern and went back to the main rooms.

segments.text: ‘Treat me well, and all’s well. If you don’t, I’ll let this out.’
‘Just keep it safe,’ Jia Lian said with a smile. ‘Whatever you do, don’t let her know.’
As he spoke, he watched for an unguarded moment and snatched it from her.
‘It will always be a danger in your hands,’ he said, laughing. ‘Better burn it and have done with it.’
But as he said this, he tucked it inside the top of his boot.

segments.text: Patience gritted her teeth. ‘You heartless creature! Pull down the bridge as soon as you’re across! And you expect me to lie for you again?’
Her pretty, spirited manner stirred Jia Lian. He clasped her and asked her to make love, but she wrenched herself free and ran. Bent double in his frustration, he cursed.
‘You damned teasing little slut! You have to set a man on fire, and then you run away.’
From outside the window Patience laughed. ‘I can tease if I please. Who told you to catch fire? Am I to give you one moment’s pleasure and have her turn against me again when she finds out?’

segments.text: ‘From now on I won’t let her see anyone either!’

‘She has a right to be jealous of you,’ Patience said. ‘You have no right to be jealous of her. Everything she does is above board. You can’t move without some wicked idea in your head. Even I don’t trust you, never mind her.’
‘You’re a pair of rogues, singing the same tune! Everything you do is right, and every move I make has some wicked idea behind it. One of these days I’ll kill the pair of you!’

segments.text: He had not finished speaking when Xi-feng came into the courtyard. Seeing Patience outside the window, she asked, ‘If you two want to talk, why don’t you talk indoors? What does it mean, one of you running outside and talking through the window?’
From inside, Jia Lian answered, ‘Ask her. You’d think there was a tiger in here waiting to eat her.’
‘There’s no one else in the room,’ Patience said. ‘What should I stay beside him for?’
‘No one else there? All the better,’ Xi-feng said, smiling.
‘Is that meant for me?’
‘Who else would I mean?’
‘Don’t make me say something nice in return.’
Without holding up the door-curtain for Xi-feng, Patience went in first, let it fall sharply behind her and went off into the other room. Xi-feng lifted it herself and came in.
‘Patience has gone mad! The little baggage really means to get the upper hand of me. You’d better look out for your skin!’

segments.text: Jia Lian had collapsed on the kang, clapping his hands and laughing.
‘I never knew Patience had such a temper! From now on I bow to her.’
‘You’ve spoiled her,’ Xi-feng said. ‘I shall have it out with you!’
‘You two fall out, and you make me the scapegoat again!’ Jia Lian said hastily. ‘I’m keeping out of your way.’
‘I’d like to see where you can hide.’

segments.text: When Jia Lian heard Xi-feng say that she had something to discuss with him, he stopped and asked what it was.
‘Cousin Xue’s birthday is on the twenty-first. What do you mean to do about it?’
‘How should I know? You’ve managed any number of grand birthday celebrations. Have you suddenly run out of ideas?’

segments.text: ‘For grand birthdays there are rules to go by. But hers is neither a great occasion nor quite an ordinary one. That’s why I’m asking you.’
Jia Lian lowered his head and thought for a while.
‘You’re being foolish today. There’s a precedent ready to hand: Cousin Lin. Whatever we did for Cousin Lin’s birthdays in past years, we can do for Cousin Xue now.’

segments.text: Xi-feng gave a cold laugh.

‘Do you suppose I don’t know even that? I had settled on the very same thing. But yesterday I heard Her Old Ladyship asking everyone’s age and birthday. She heard that Cousin Xue would be fifteen this year. Though it isn’t a round-number birthday, she is approaching the hairpin age, and Her Old Ladyship said she wanted to give her a birthday party. If she really does, it will naturally have to be different from Cousin Lin’s in past years.’
‘In that case, make it a little more than Cousin Lin’s.’
‘That’s what I thought. I only wanted to know how you felt. If I added things on my own, you’d blame me for not telling you properly.’
Jia Lian laughed. ‘Enough, enough. I’m not thanking you for that empty show of consideration.

segments.text: ‘It’s all I ask that you don’t pry into my affairs. As if I would blame you!’
With that he went straight off, and we need say no more of him for the present. Shi Xiang-yun, meanwhile, had stayed two days and was about to go home.
‘Wait until after your cousin Bao-chai’s birthday,’ Grandmother Jia told her. ‘See the plays, and then go.’
Xiang-yun could only stay. She sent someone home to fetch two kinds of needlework she had done earlier, as her birthday gifts for Bao-chai.

segments.text: Ever since Bao-chai’s arrival, Grandmother Jia had been pleased with her steadiness and even temper. Now that her first birthday since coming to the house had arrived, the old lady contributed twenty taels of her own money, summoned Xi-feng and entrusted her with arranging the feast and plays.

Xi-feng entered into the fun with a laugh. ‘When our revered ancestress gives one of the children a birthday party, who would dare find fault, whatever she chose to do? There’s no need for feasts and plays at all. Still, if you want some merrymaking, I’m afraid you’ll have to spend a few taels of your own. You go to all the trouble of digging out these twenty mouldy, rotten taels to play the hostess, and expect me to make up the rest! If you really couldn’t afford it, I’d say nothing. But gold and silver, round pieces and flat, are breaking through the bottoms of your chests, while you squeeze us dry. Look about you. Aren’t we all your children? Will Cousin Bao be the only one to carry you up Mount Wutai one day? You’re saving all your private treasure for him. Even if we aren’t fit to use it, don’t make life hard for us. Is this enough for the feast? For the players?’
The whole room burst out laughing.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia laughed too. ‘Just listen to that tongue! I thought I could talk, but I can’t get the better of this monkey. Your mother-in-law wouldn’t dare answer me back, yet here you are, chattering away at me.’
‘My mother-in-law dotes on Bao-yu just as much as you do,’ said Xi-feng, laughing. ‘There’s nowhere I can go for justice, and now you accuse me of answering back!’

segments.text: This set Grandmother Jia laughing again and left her in excellent spirits. That evening, after everyone had paid their respects, the mothers and daughters and cousins were chatting and laughing around her when she asked Bao-chai what plays she liked to hear and what she liked to eat. Bao-chai knew very well that the old lady enjoyed lively plays and sweet, soft food, and named all the things Grandmother Jia herself had always liked. Grandmother Jia was more delighted than ever. Next day she sent over her gifts of clothes and curios in advance. Lady Wang, Xi-feng, Dai-yu and the others all gave presents according to their means; there is no need to list them.

segments.text: By the twenty-first a neat little stage for a family performance had been put up in Grandmother Jia’s inner courtyard. A newly formed company of child players had been engaged, offering both the Kun and Yiyang styles. Several tables for the family feast were laid in Grandmother Jia’s principal room. There was not a single visitor from outside: only Aunt Xue, Shi Xiang-yun and Bao-chai counted as guests; everyone else belonged to the household.
Early that morning, finding Lin Dai-yu nowhere about, Bao-yu went to look for her in her room. She was reclining on the kang.
‘Get up and come to breakfast,’ he said with a smile. ‘The plays will be starting soon. Which would you like to see? I’ll ask for it.’
Dai-yu gave a cold laugh. ‘If that’s how you feel, engage a company specially and have them perform the plays I like. There’s no need to ask me now, taking advantage of somebody else’s occasion.’
‘Nothing could be easier,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘We’ll do just that tomorrow, and let the others take advantage of ours.’ He pulled her up as he spoke, and they went out hand in hand.

segments.text: After breakfast, when it was time to choose the plays, Grandmother Jia insisted that Bao-chai should choose first. Bao-chai tried to decline the honour, but in the end had to ask for an episode from Journey to the West. Grandmother Jia was naturally delighted. She next called on Xi-feng, who also knew the old lady’s liking for lively plays, and her still greater liking for comic business and jokes. She chose Liu Er Pawns His Clothes. Sure enough, Grandmother Jia was even more pleased. She then asked Dai-yu to choose. Dai-yu tried to defer to Aunt Xue, Lady Wang and the others.

‘I arranged today specially to have some fun with you young ones,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Let’s please ourselves and leave them out of it. Do you think I went to all the trouble of a feast and plays for their sake? They’re getting food and entertainment for nothing. That’s quite enough of a bargain without letting them choose the plays as well!’
Everyone laughed. Dai-yu then made a choice. Bao-yu, Shi Xiang-yun, Ying-chun, Tan-chun, Xi-chun and Li Wan each chose in turn, and the plays were performed one after another.

segments.text: When the wine was served, Grandmother Jia again asked Bao-chai to choose. She chose Lu Zhi-shen Runs Riot Drunk on Mount Wutai.
‘Must you always choose things like that?’ said Bao-yu.
‘You’ve listened to plays all these years for nothing. What do you know of the merits of this one? The staging is splendid, and the words are finer still.’
‘I’ve always dreaded all that noise and bustle.’
Bao-chai laughed. ‘If you think that’s all there is to this play, you really don’t understand the theatre.

segments.text: ‘Come here. Let me tell you whether it’s just noise and bustle. It’s a northern Rouged Lips suite, ringing and measured by turns. The beauty of its rhythms goes without saying. But there’s one song in it, Clinging Grass, whose words are wonderfully written. What would you know of that?’
At this glowing account Bao-yu moved nearer and begged, ‘Dear cousin, do recite it for me.’

Bao-chai recited:
‘Vainly I wipe a hero’s tears,
And take my leave of the recluse’s home.
I thank your mercy for my tonsure beneath the lotus throne.
No bond was destined: in an instant we must part.
Naked I come and go, with nothing to bind me.
Where can I find a straw cape for mist and a hat for rain, to roll my bedding and go alone?
Let me beg as chance may lead, in straw sandals, with a broken bowl!’
Bao-yu slapped his knee with delight and traced circles of approval in the air. He praised it over and over, then praised Bao-chai for knowing every book there was.
‘Be quiet and watch the play,’ said Lin Dai-yu. ‘They haven’t even started At the Monastery Gate, and you’re already performing Feigning Madness.’
This made Xiang-yun laugh too. They all settled down to watch.

segments.text: When the performance ended that evening, Grandmother Jia, who had taken a great fancy to the child playing the young heroine and to one playing a clown, sent for both to be brought in. Seen close to, they seemed more touching still. She asked their ages: the child playing the young heroine was only eleven, the clown-player only nine. Everyone sighed over them. Grandmother Jia ordered extra meat and fruit for the two children, with a further reward of two strings of cash.
‘This child in costume is the very image of someone,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘Surely you can see who it is?’
Bao-chai knew, but merely smiled, unwilling to say. Bao-yu had guessed too, but dared not speak.
‘Why, the very image of Cousin Lin,’ Shi Xiang-yun said, laughing.
Bao-yu glanced at Xiang-yun at once and gave her a warning look. But everyone had heard. They looked closely and began to laugh, agreeing that the likeness was unmistakable.

segments.text: Presently they dispersed. That evening, as Xiang-yun was changing, she told Kingfisher to open her clothes-bundle, put everything in order and pack it all up.
‘What’s the hurry?’ said Kingfisher. ‘There’ll be time enough to pack on the day you leave.’
‘I’m going first thing tomorrow. What am I staying here for? To watch other people’s faces and take my cue from their looks? Where’s the pleasure in that?’
Hearing this, Bao-yu hurried over and took her hand.

‘Dear cousin, you’ve misunderstood me. Cousin Lin takes things to heart. The others knew perfectly well, but wouldn’t say anything for fear of upsetting her. Then you spoke before you thought. How could she help being angry with you? I was afraid you would offend her; that was why I gave you that look. Being angry with me now is worse than wasting my good intentions. It’s treating me unfairly. If it had been someone else, what would I care if they offended ten people?’

Xiang-yun flung his hand off. ‘Don’t try your pretty speeches on me. Of course I’m not as good as your Cousin Lin. Anyone else can talk about her and make fun of her, but the moment I say anything, I’m in the wrong.

segments.text: ‘Of course I’m not fit to speak of her. She’s a young lady, a mistress, and I’m a servant, a slave-girl. I mustn’t offend her!’
‘I was trying to help you,’ Bao-yu cried in distress, ‘and now I’ve only made things worse. If I had any other thought, may I turn to ashes this instant and be trampled by ten thousand people!’

‘It’s the New Year. Don’t let your tongue run on with such nonsense. Keep those pointless curses, that foolish, crooked talk, for the touchy people who are always taking offence and know how to keep you in order. Don’t make me spit in your face.’
She went straight into Grandmother Jia’s inner room and lay down, still seething.

segments.text: Bao-yu hung his head unhappily and searched for his fault. Aroma already knew what had happened, and that this was no moment to try to reason with him. Bao-yu simply stood there in a daze. Dai-yu, supposing that he had gone back to his room, rose and opened the door, only to find him still standing outside. Now she felt awkward. She could hardly shut it again, so she withdrew and lay down on the bed. Bao-yu followed her in.
‘There must be a reason for everything,’ he said. ‘If you tell me, at least I needn’t feel unjustly treated. What can have made you suddenly so angry when everything was perfectly all right?’

segments.text: Lin Dai-yu gave a cold laugh. ‘A fine thing to ask me! How should I know the reason? I’m only here for you all to laugh at, to be compared to a player for your amusement.’
‘I didn’t compare you to anyone. I didn’t laugh. Why be angry with me?’
‘So you want to compare me too? You want to laugh? You’re worse without comparing or laughing than the people who did both!’
Bao-yu had no answer to this and said nothing.

segments.text: ‘That much I could forgive,’ Dai-yu went on. ‘But why did you make signs to Yun? What did you mean by that? Was joking with me beneath her dignity? Of course she’s a nobleman’s daughter, and I’m a poor nobody’s girl. If she joked with me and I answered back, wouldn’t she have invited contempt for herself? Wasn’t that what you meant? Very kind of you, too. Only she wouldn’t accept your kindness either, and got angry just the same. So then you used me to win her over, saying I was touchy and always taking offence. And you were afraid she would offend me and I would be angry with her. If I was angry with her, what business was that of yours? If she offended me, what business was that of yours?’

Bao-yu realised that she had overheard his private talk with Xiang-yun. Thinking it over, he had only tried to mediate for their sake, afraid that the two would quarrel and grow estranged. Yet he had not reconciled them at all; instead he had earned reproaches from both. It was just as he had read the other day in The Classic of Nanhua: ‘The skilful labour and the clever worry; those without ability seek nothing. They eat their fill and wander at ease, drifting like an unmoored boat.’ And again: ‘The mountain tree invites its own plundering; the spring invites its own draining.’

segments.text: The more he thought about it, the less pleasure he found in anything. For the moment there were only these two people, and he could not even keep on good terms with them. What did he hope to manage in the future? At this point he felt there was no need to defend himself or make an answer. He turned and went back to his own room. Seeing him leave without a word, Dai-yu knew that his reflections had disheartened him and that he had gone off in a huff. This only made her angrier.
‘Now that you’ve gone, don’t ever come back,’ she said. ‘And don’t ever speak to me again.’

segments.text: Bao-yu took no notice. Back in his room he lay on the bed, staring blankly. Aroma knew the whole story, but dared not speak of it yet. She tried to distract him with something else.
‘Today’s plays will lead to several more days of them. Miss Bao is sure to give a party in return.’
Bao-yu gave a cold laugh. ‘And what business is it of anyone’s whether she does or not?’
This was not his usual tone. Aroma tried again, smiling. ‘What a thing to say! Here we are at the New Year, with all the ladies and girls enjoying themselves. What has made you like this?’
‘Whether the ladies and girls enjoy themselves has nothing to do with me either,’ he said with another cold laugh.
Aroma smiled. ‘If they’re friendly and you’re friendly, won’t everyone have a pleasant time together?’
‘What do you mean by “everyone together”? They can have their “everyone together”. As for me, “Naked I come and go, with nothing to bind me.”’
At these words the tears began to fall.

segments.text: Having written it, he understood his meaning himself, but feared others might not. He therefore composed a song to the tune Clinging Grass and wrote it after the verse. He read the whole thing through once more, felt free of every encumbrance and, thoroughly pleased with himself, went to bed.
Dai-yu, meanwhile, had seen how resolutely Bao-yu had left her this time. On the pretext of looking for Aroma, she came to see what was happening.
‘He’s asleep already,’ Aroma told her with a smile.

Dai-yu was about to go back when Aroma said, ‘Do stay a moment, miss. Here’s something he’s written. Will you see what it means?’ She quietly brought over the song and verse he had just composed and gave them to Dai-yu.
Dai-yu read them and knew that Bao-yu had written them in a fit of vexation. She hardly knew whether to laugh or sigh.
‘It’s only something he’s written for amusement,’ she told Aroma. ‘It’s nothing to worry about.’

segments.text: After reading the song, she read the verse too and laughed.

‘He’s found enlightenment! It’s all my fault. It all started with the song I recited yesterday. Taoist books and Chan conundrums can change a person’s whole nature. If he really takes to talking this nonsense and fixes on these ideas, it will all have come from that one song. I shall be the chief culprit.’

segments.text: All three went to Bao-yu’s room. The moment they entered, Dai-yu said with a smile, ‘Bao-yu, answer me this. What is most precious is called “bao”, a treasure; what is hardest is “yu”, jade. What is precious in you? What is hard in you?’
Bao-yu could not answer at all. The three clapped their hands and laughed. ‘So dull and stupid, yet you want to investigate Chan!’

‘Your verse ends,’ Dai-yu continued, ‘“Nothing can be called realisation:
That is a ground to stand on.” That’s all very well, but to my mind it isn’t quite perfect. I’ll add two lines.’ She recited:
‘With no ground to stand on,
Only then is all swept clean.’

‘At the time, Hui-neng was pounding rice in the kitchen. When he heard the verse, he said, “Fine it may be, but understanding is still to come.” Then he recited a verse of his own:
“Bodhi was never a tree;
Nor is the bright mirror a stand.
From the first there was not a single thing:
Where could dust settle?”
The Fifth Patriarch handed down his robe and bowl to him.

segments.text: ‘Today’s verse has the same meaning. But that question you put to him just now has still not been settled. Are you going to let it drop?’

‘You couldn’t answer then,’ said Dai-yu with a smile, ‘so you’ve lost. It would be nothing remarkable if you found an answer now. Only you mustn’t talk about Chan again. You don’t even know what we two know, or do what we two can do, yet you want to investigate Chan!’

Bao-yu had thought himself enlightened. Then a single unexpected question from Dai-yu had left him speechless, and Bao-chai had produced sayings of the masters to illustrate the point. He had never seen either of them display these abilities before. He considered it for a moment. ‘So their understanding was ahead of mine, and even they haven’t reached enlightenment. Why should I go looking for trouble?’

segments.text: Then he laughed. ‘Who was investigating Chan? It was only a passing joke.’ And the four were as they had been before.

Suddenly someone announced that Her Highness had sent out a lantern riddle for them all to guess. Those who guessed it were each to make one of their own and send it in. The four hurried to Grandmother Jia’s principal room. There they found a young eunuch carrying a flat-topped, four-sided lantern of white gauze, made specially for riddles, with one already written on it. Everyone crowded round to read it and call out guesses.

The young eunuch conveyed a further command. ‘When the young ladies have guessed it, they mustn’t say the answer aloud. Each should write it secretly on a piece of paper. The papers will all be sealed together and sent into the palace for Her Highness to judge.’

Bao-chai and the others went closer and saw a quatrain of seven-character lines, with nothing particularly novel about it. They were obliged to praise it, of course, and said how hard it was, deliberately appearing to ponder, though in fact they had guessed it at first sight. Bao-yu, Dai-yu, Xiang-yun and Tan-chun had all solved it too. Each spent some time secretly writing down an answer.

segments.text: Jia Huan, Jia Lan and the others were summoned as well. All applied their wits, made their guesses and wrote them down. Each then chose an object, composed a riddle about it, copied it out in careful regular script and hung it on the lantern. The eunuch left. That evening he returned with a message.

‘All the answers to Her Highness’s riddle were correct except those of the Second Young Lady and the Third Young Master. Her Highness has also guessed the young ladies’ riddles, but does not know whether she is right.’

He produced her written answers. Some were right and some wrong, but everyone indiscriminately declared them correct. The eunuch then presented the gifts to those who had guessed rightly: a palace-made poetry tube and a tea whisk for each. Only Ying-chun and Jia Huan received nothing.

segments.text: Seeing Yuan-chun enter into the spirit of the game, Grandmother Jia became merrier still. She ordered a small, exquisitely made lantern screen to be prepared at once and set up in the middle of the room. The girls were each to compose their riddles in secret, write them out and paste them on the screen. Fragrant tea, choice fruits and all sorts of curios were laid ready as prizes for correct answers.

Returning from court, Jia Zheng saw how pleased his mother was. As it was the festive season, he too came that evening to entertain her and join in the fun. Wine and fruit were set out, prizes prepared, and coloured lanterns hung in the principal room. Grandmother Jia was invited to enjoy the lanterns. At the table of honour sat Grandmother Jia, Jia Zheng and Bao-yu. Below them, Lady Wang, Bao-chai, Dai-yu and Xiang-yun shared another table, while Ying-chun, Tan-chun and Xi-chun had one to themselves. The floor was crowded with women servants and maids. Li Gong-cai and Wang Xi-feng sat at a separate table in the inner room.
Noticing Jia Lan’s absence, Jia Zheng asked, ‘Where is Lan?’

A woman servant hurried into the inner room to ask his mother. Mrs Li rose and answered with a smile, ‘He said that the Master hadn’t sent for him, so he wouldn’t come.’ The woman took this answer back to Jia Zheng.

Jia Zheng at once sent Jia Huan and two women to fetch Jia Lan. Grandmother Jia had him sit beside her and gave him handfuls of fruit to eat. They all talked and laughed together.

Xiang-yun, though a young lady of the sheltered inner rooms, had always been fond of conversation, but with Jia Zheng at the table she too kept her mouth shut.

segments.text: Dai-yu was by nature reluctant to mix with others and had little wish to talk. Bao-chai, never given to careless speech or hasty action, remained as composed as ever. Thus, although it was a family party intended for pleasure, everyone seemed constrained and ill at ease. Grandmother Jia knew that Jia Zheng’s presence alone was the cause. After three rounds of wine she began sending him off to rest. Jia Zheng understood her intention too: with him gone, the young people could enjoy themselves. He hastened to put on a smile.

‘I heard that you were holding a grand gathering for elegant spring lantern riddles, Mother, so I brought prizes and a feast specially to join you. Must all your affection go to your grandsons and granddaughters? Can’t your son have a little of it?’

segments.text: ‘While you’re here they don’t dare talk or laugh,’ Grandmother Jia said, smiling. ‘It only makes it dull for me. If you want to guess riddles, I’ll give you one. But you’ll have to pay a forfeit if you can’t guess it.’
‘Of course I shall,’ Jia Zheng said quickly, laughing. ‘And if I do guess it, I shall expect a prize.’

segments.text: Having recited it, he whispered the answer to Bao-yu. Bao-yu understood and whispered it in turn to Grandmother Jia. She thought it over, found that it fitted perfectly and said, ‘An inkstone.’
‘Just as one would expect of you, Mother,’ said Jia Zheng, laughing. ‘Right at the first guess!’ He turned round. ‘Bring up the prizes at once.’

segments.text: The women standing below answered and carried up large and small trays together. Grandmother Jia examined the contents one by one. They were all new and ingenious things to use or play with during the Lantern Festival, and she was very pleased.
‘Pour your father some wine,’ she ordered. Bao-yu held the pot, and Ying-chun carried over the cup.
‘Look at the screen,’ Grandmother Jia told Jia Zheng. ‘The girls made all those. Try some more, and let me hear your answers.’

segments.text: ‘That must be a great votive lamp before the Buddha,’ said Jia Zheng.
‘Yes, a great votive lamp,’ Xi-chun replied, smiling.

Jia Zheng pondered inwardly. ‘Her Highness’s firecracker goes off with a bang and scatters. Ying-chun’s abacus falls into a tangle of confusion at a touch. Tan-chun’s kite is a thing that drifts and floats about. Xi-chun’s votive lamp is lonelier and more secluded still. This is the joyous Lantern Festival. Why should they all make games out of such ill-omened things?’

The more he thought about it, the gloomier he became. In his mother’s presence he dared not let it show, and forced himself to go on looking. Next came a regulated poem of eight seven-character lines, written by Bao-chai. He read it aloud:

segments.text: When he had finished, Jia Zheng thought, ‘The object itself is not so very bad. But for children so young to write such lines is still more ominous. None of them is destined for lasting happiness and long life.’ This thought made him more distressed than ever, and he looked deeply grieved. Eight or nine tenths of his earlier animation had drained away. He merely bowed his head and brooded.

segments.text: Seeing him like this, Grandmother Jia wondered whether he might be physically tired. She was also afraid that his presence would prevent the girls from enjoying themselves freely.
‘You needn’t guess any more,’ she told him. ‘Go and rest.

segments.text: ‘We’ll sit a little longer and then break up ourselves.’

At these words Jia Zheng hurriedly assented several times. He made another effort to persuade Grandmother Jia to drink, then withdrew. Back in his own room he could not stop thinking. He tossed and turned, unable to sleep, overcome with sorrow and foreboding. Of him we need say no more for now.

segments.text: Once Jia Zheng had gone, Grandmother Jia said, ‘Now you can enjoy yourselves freely.’

She had barely finished when Bao-yu was already at the lantern screen, gesticulating and criticising everything. This line in one riddle was poor; the answer to another did not quite fit. He was like a monkey let out of its cage.
‘Wouldn’t it be more civilised to sit as we were before,’ said Bao-chai, ‘and all talk and laugh together?’

Xi-feng hurried out of the inner room and joined in. ‘Your father ought to make you stay within a step of him every day. I forgot just now. Why didn’t I suggest, while he was here, that you should compose a verse riddle too? If I had, you’d be sweating over it this very moment.’

This made Bao-yu frantic. He caught hold of Xi-feng and clung to her like twisted toffee, pestering her and refusing to let go. Grandmother Jia chatted and laughed a little longer with Li Gong-cai and the girls, until she too began to feel tired. Listening, she heard that the water-clock had already marked the fourth watch. She ordered the food cleared away and distributed among the servants, then rose.
‘Let’s go to bed.

segments.text: After Jia Yuan-chun returned to the palace from her visit to Prospect Garden, she ordered Tan-chun to make a careful copy, in sequence, of all the poems and inscriptions composed that day. She herself arranged them and assessed their merits, and ordered them to be engraved on stone in the garden, to commemorate this elegant occasion for ages to come. Jia Zheng therefore had skilled and celebrated craftsmen sought out everywhere to dress the stones and cut the inscriptions. Jia Zhen supervised the work with Rong, Ping and the others. Jia Qiang was also responsible for the twelve actresses, including Wen-guan, and their costumes and other theatrical equipment, and could not readily spare the time, so Jia Zhen summoned Jia Chang and Jia Ling to help supervise. One day the hot wax was applied and the lettering transferred in vermilion: work was under way. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: Now the twelve young Taoists of the Temple of the Jade Emperor and the twelve Buddhist novices of the Bodhidharma Hermitage had been moved out of Prospect Garden. Jia Zheng was intending to send them to live in various temples. It happened that Jia Qin’s mother, Mrs Zhou, who lived in the back street, had been considering how to obtain some charge, however small, for her son from Jia Zheng, so that he might make a little money to spend. Hearing of this matter, she came by sedan-chair to ask Xi-feng’s help. As she was not generally given to putting on airs, Xi-feng agreed. Having thought out what to say, she reported to Lady Wang:

‘We really mustn’t send these young monks and Taoists away. Her Highness may come out at any time and want them to perform their services. If we scatter them, it will only mean more trouble when they’re needed again. I think we should simply send them to our family temple, the Temple of the Iron Threshold. All we need do is send someone there once a month with a few taels for firewood and rice. The moment they’re wanted, we can go and fetch them. No trouble at all.’
Lady Wang heard her out and consulted Jia Zheng.

segments.text: ‘That reminds me,’ Jia Zheng said with a smile. ‘Yes, that is what we shall do.’
He sent for Jia Lian at once. Jia Lian was having a meal with Xi-feng when the summons came. Not knowing what it was about, he left his meal and was going off when Xi-feng caught hold of him.
‘Wait a moment and listen,’ she said, smiling. ‘If it’s anything else, I have nothing to say. But if it’s about the little monks, you must do as I tell you.’
She coached him in what he was to say.
‘I know nothing about it,’ Jia Lian said with a laugh. ‘If you’re so clever, go and tell him yourself.’
Xi-feng stiffened her neck, laid down her chopsticks and looked at him with a smile that was not quite a smile.
‘Do you mean that, or are you joking?’

segments.text: Jia Lian laughed.

‘Yun, the son of Fifth Sister-in-law over by the west gallery, has asked me two or three times to find him something to manage. I agreed and told him to wait. At last something comes along, and you snatch it away.’

‘Don’t worry,’ said Xi-feng, smiling. ‘Her Highness has said she wants a great many more pines and cypresses planted in the north-east corner of the garden, and flowers and other plants below the tower. When that work comes up, I promise Yun shall have charge of it.’
‘Very well, if that’s how it is. Only last night I wanted to try things a different way, and you made such a fuss about it.’
Xi-feng gave a snort of laughter, spat at him, lowered her head and went on with her meal.

segments.text: Jia Lian had already gone off laughing. When he reached the front and saw Jia Zheng, it was indeed about the young monks. He followed Xi-feng’s plan.
‘Qin seems to have come on remarkably well lately. Why not leave this in his charge? We can simply let him draw the monthly allowance at the same rate as when they were here.’

Jia Zheng had never paid much attention to such matters, and agreed to Jia Lian’s proposal. Back in their room, Jia Lian told Xi-feng, who immediately sent word to Mrs Zhou. Jia Qin came to see the couple and could not thank them enough.

segments.text: Jia Qin picked up a piece at random and tossed it to the men at the scales for their tea. He told a page to carry the money home and went to consult his mother. He promptly hired a large male donkey for himself to ride and several carts. At a side gate of the Rong mansion he called out the twenty-four young clerics, seated them in the carts, and set off straight for the Temple of the Iron Threshold outside the city. segments.text: Let us return to Jia Yuan-chun. After arranging the Prospect Garden poems in the palace, she suddenly thought of the garden’s lovely scenery. Now that her visit was over, Jia Zheng would surely lock it up with reverent care and dare not let anyone disturb it. How desolate it would be! She had several sisters and cousins at home who could write both poetry and rhyme-prose. Why not tell them to live there, so that the girls need not languish in neglect, nor the flowers and willows lose their charm? Then she thought of Bao-yu. He had grown up among the girls, unlike his brothers and cousins. If she did not include him, he might feel lonely and become unhappy, which would only worry Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang. The best thing would be to tell him to live in the garden too. Having settled this in her mind, she sent the eunuch Xia Shou-zhong to the Rong mansion with an edict: Bao-chai and the other girls were to be free to live in the garden, with no prohibitions or locked gates to keep them out, and Bao-yu was to accompany them there to pursue his studies.

segments.text: Jia Zheng and Lady Wang received the edict. After Xia Shou-zhong had left, they informed Grandmother Jia and sent people into the garden to clean and put the rooms in order, hanging curtains and setting up beds with their bed-hangings. The others heard the news calmly enough, but Bao-yu was beside himself with delight. He was discussing arrangements with Grandmother Jia, wanting this and asking for that, when a maid suddenly came in.
‘His Lordship is asking for Bao-yu.’

To Bao-yu it was like a thunderclap. His pleasure vanished at once; his face changed colour. Clutching Grandmother Jia, he writhed like a twisted sweet and would sooner have died than go. She had to comfort him.

‘My precious boy, go along. I’m here. He daren’t ill-treat you. Besides, you wrote that fine piece. Her Highness has told you to live in the garden, and I expect he has a few instructions for you, just to keep you out of mischief. Whatever he says, answer him nicely. That’s all you need do.’

segments.text: As she soothed him, she called for two old nurses.
‘Take Bao-yu over carefully. Don’t let his father frighten him.’

The nurses promised. Bao-yu had no choice but to go, dragging himself along in steps scarcely three cun long. Jia Zheng happened to be in Lady Wang’s room discussing household matters. Golden, Cai-yun, Cai-xia, Xiu-luan, Xiu-feng and the other maids were standing under the eaves of the verandah. At the sight of Bao-yu they all smiled behind pursed lips. Golden caught hold of him.
‘I’ve just put scented rouge on my lips,’ she whispered with a smile. ‘Do you feel like tasting it now?’
Cai-yun pushed her away, laughing.
‘He’s worried enough already, and you’re still teasing him! Go in quickly, while His Lordship is in a good mood.’

segments.text: Bao-yu edged through the doorway. Jia Zheng and Lady Wang were in the inner room. Aunt Zhao raised the curtain and Bao-yu bowed as he went in. His parents sat facing one another on the kang, talking. Below them stood a row of chairs occupied by Ying-chun, Tan-chun, Xi-chun and Jia Huan. When he entered, only Tan-chun, Xi-chun and Jia Huan got up.

segments.text: Jia Zheng looked up. Before him stood Bao-yu, graceful and radiant, his beauty arresting. He glanced at Jia Huan, with his mean appearance and slovenly manners, and suddenly thought of Jia Zhu. Then he looked again at Lady Wang. This was the only son of her own she had left, and she had always cherished him like a treasure. His own beard was already turning grey. These thoughts together melted away eight or nine tenths of his usual dislike of Bao-yu and wish to punish him. After a long pause he said:

‘Her Highness says you spend your days running about outside and are growing ever more idle. You are now to be kept under supervision, studying and practising your writing in the garden with your sisters. Apply yourself properly. If you fail again to behave as you should, you had better look out!’
Bao-yu answered, ‘Yes, sir,’ several times in quick succession. Lady Wang drew him down to sit beside her. The other three sat down again.

segments.text: Lady Wang stroked the back of Bao-yu’s neck.
‘Have you finished the pills you were given the other day?’
‘There’s one left.’
‘Have ten more fetched tomorrow. Every night at bedtime, let Aroma see that you take your medicine before you go to sleep.’
‘Ever since you gave the order, Mother, Aroma has remembered every evening and made sure I took it.’
‘Who is Aroma?’ Jia Zheng asked.
‘A maid,’ said Lady Wang.
‘Any ordinary name would do for a maid. Who had the perverse fancy of calling her that?’
Seeing his displeasure, Lady Wang tried to shield Bao-yu.
‘Her Old Ladyship named her.’
‘How would Her Old Ladyship know such a phrase? It must have been Bao-yu.’
Seeing that there was no concealing it, Bao-yu rose to reply.

‘In my reading I remembered a line by an old poet: “the flowers’ aroma steals upon one, telling of the warmth of day”. Since the maid’s surname is Hua, “flower”, the name came to me and I gave it to her.’
Lady Wang hurried to say, ‘Bao-yu, change it when you get back.

segments.text: There’s no need for you to be angry over such a little thing, sir.’
‘There’s no harm in it, after all. Why change it? It simply shows that Bao-yu neglects his proper work and devotes his efforts to florid verses and amorous compositions.’
Then he snapped out, ‘You wicked little beast! Why are you still here?’
‘Go along,’ Lady Wang said quickly. ‘Her Old Ladyship is probably waiting for you to eat.’
Bao-yu answered obediently and withdrew slowly. Once outside he grinned at Golden, stuck out his tongue and was off like a wisp of smoke, taking the two nurses with him.

segments.text: At the entrance to the passage hall he found Aroma leaning against the doorway. Seeing him return safe and sound, she broke into smiles.
‘What did he want you for?’
‘Nothing much. He was only afraid I’d get into mischief in the garden and wanted to give me some instructions.’
Talking as they went, he returned to Grandmother Jia and reported what had happened. Lin Dai-yu was there, and he asked her:
‘Where would you like to live?’
She had been turning that very question over in her mind. At his question she smiled.
‘I think Naiad’s House would be nice. I love those few stems of bamboo screening the winding balustrade. It’s more secluded than anywhere else.’
Bao-yu clapped his hands and laughed.
‘Exactly what I thought! I was going to tell you to live there. I’ll take the House of Green Delights. Then we’ll be close to each other, and both our places will be quiet and secluded.’
While they were discussing it, a messenger from Jia Zheng came to tell Grandmother Jia:
‘The twenty-second of the second month is an auspicious day for the young master and young ladies to move in.

segments.text: People will be sent in over the next few days to allot the rooms and put them in order.’

Xue Bao-chai was assigned Allspice Court, Lin Dai-yu Naiad’s House, Jia Ying-chun the Brocade-adorned Tower, Tan-chun Autumn Studio, Xi-chun Knotweed Breeze Pavilion, Li Wan Sweet-rice Village, and Bao-yu the House of Green Delights. Each residence was given two additional old nurses and four maids, not counting its occupant’s own wet nurses and personal maids, and there were also servants specifically responsible for cleaning and tidying. On the twenty-second they all moved in. At once the flowers seemed to beckon to embroidered sashes, and the willows brushed scented breezes: the garden was no longer as lonely as before.

segments.text: But enough of these details. Once Bao-yu was living in the garden, he was completely content and could think of nothing else to want. He spent every day with the girls and maids: reading, writing, playing the qin or chess, painting or composing poems. They traced patterns of luan-birds and embroidered phoenixes, played games with grasses and put flowers in their hair, hummed and sang softly, made riddles out of the parts of characters and guessed the number of counters in a closed hand. There was nothing they did not try, and he was very happy. He wrote several poems about the occasions of his daily life. They were not particularly good, but the feelings and scenes were true. segments.text: Some worldly flatterers of the time, seeing that these poems were by a twelve- or thirteen-year-old young master of the Rong mansion, copied them out and praised them everywhere. There were also frivolous young men who took a fancy to the sensuous, seductive lines, wrote them on fans and walls, and recited and applauded them at every opportunity. People consequently began to come asking Bao-yu for poems and specimens of his calligraphy, commissioning paintings and requesting inscriptions. More pleased with himself than ever, he spent whole days on these extraneous pursuits.

segments.text: Who would have thought that vexation could spring from such tranquillity? One day Bao-yu suddenly grew dissatisfied. Nothing was right, neither this nor that; indoors or out, he was always miserable. Most of the people in the garden were young girls, still in a world of unawakened, carefree innocence. They sat or lay down without reserve, laughed without a thought behind it: how could they know what was on Bao-yu’s mind? In his discontent he lost the inclination to stay in the garden and spent his time idling about outside, still in a daze. Seeing him like this, Tealeaf wanted to cheer him up. But every amusement he thought of was something Bao-yu had already tired of, and would give him no pleasure. There was just one thing Bao-yu had never seen. Having thought of it, Tealeaf went to a bookshop and bought a great many novels old and new, unofficial lives of Flying Swallow, He-de, Wu Ze-tian and Noble Consort Yang, and scripts of romance plays. He tempted Bao-yu to read them. Bao-yu had never seen books of this kind, and the moment he did, he felt he had found a treasure. Tealeaf warned him not to take them into the garden.
‘If anyone finds out, I’ll get more than I bargained for.’

But how could Bao-yu bear not to take them in? After much hesitation, he selected a few sets with the more subtle, carefully wrought writing, took them into the garden and put them above his bed, to read in secret when no one was there.

segments.text: The coarse and over-explicit ones he hid in the outer study. One day, in the middle of the third month, he took a set of The Western Chamber after breakfast and sat on a rock beneath the peach trees by the Drenched Blossoms sluice-bridge. He opened it and began to savour it from the beginning. He had just reached ‘The falling red gathers in ranks’ when a gust of wind blew down most of the peach blossom from the branches, covering him, his book and the ground. He was about to shake it off, but feared that feet would trample it. Instead he gathered the petals in the front of his clothes, went to the pool and shook them into it. They floated and drifted on the water, and at last passed out through the Drenched Blossoms sluice.

segments.text: When he returned, a great many blossoms were still on the ground. As he stood wondering what to do, a voice behind him said:
‘What are you doing here?’
He turned and saw Lin Dai-yu. She carried a flower hoe over her shoulder, with a bag for blossoms hanging from it, and held a blossom broom in her hand.
‘Good, good!’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Come and sweep these up and put them in the water. I’ve just put a great many in there.’

‘The water’s no good,’ said Dai-yu. ‘It looks clean here, but once it flows out where people live, all their filthy, stinking refuse is tipped into it, and the flowers will be ruined just the same. I have a grave for flowers in that corner. We can sweep them up, put them in this silk bag and bury them in the earth. In time they’ll simply turn to earth themselves. Isn’t that cleaner?’
Bao-yu was delighted.
‘Let me put down my book and help you.’
‘What book?’
At the question Bao-yu tried frantically to hide it.
‘Only the Doctrine of the Mean and the Great Learning.’
Dai-yu laughed. ‘You’re trying your tricks on me again.

segments.text: You’d do much better to let me see it now.’

‘Dear cousin, I’m not afraid where you’re concerned. But once you’ve read it, whatever you do, don’t tell anyone else. It really is a wonderful book! You’ll forget all about eating once you’ve started.’

He handed it to her as he spoke. Dai-yu put down her flower-gathering things and took the book. She read from the beginning, enjoying it more and more, and in less time than it would have taken to eat a meal she had finished all sixteen scenes. The words startled her with their beauty and seemed to leave a lingering fragrance in her mouth. Even when she had finished, she remained lost in thought, silently committing the lines to memory.

segments.text: I’ll tell Uncle and Aunt.’
At the word ‘insult’, the rims of her eyes had already reddened. She turned to go. Bao-yu panicked and hurried in front of her to block her way.

‘Dear cousin, please forgive me just this once! I was wrong to say it. If I meant to insult you, may I fall into the pool tomorrow and be swallowed by a scabby-headed giant turtle and turn into a great big tortoise myself. And one day, when you’ve become a “Lady of the First Rank” and fall ill and die in your old age, I’ll go to your grave and carry your memorial stone on my back for the rest of my life.’
Dai-yu gave a sudden snort of laughter. Rubbing her eyes, she laughed and said:
‘So you can be frightened into this state too, yet still you keep talking nonsense. Pah! You’re just “a seedling that never flowers, a silver-looking spearhead made of pewter”.’
‘And what about that?’ Bao-yu said with a laugh. ‘I can go and tell on you too.’
‘You say you can remember anything after one reading,’ Dai-yu said, smiling. ‘Can’t I take in ten lines at a glance?’
Bao-yu put away the book.
‘Let’s get on and bury the flowers,’ he said with a smile. ‘No more of that.’

segments.text: They gathered the fallen blossoms and had just finished burying them when Aroma came up.

‘I’ve looked everywhere, and at last I’ve tracked you down here! The Elder Master is unwell. The young ladies have all gone over to ask after him, and Her Old Ladyship wants you sent over too. Come back and change your clothes.’

Bao-yu quickly picked up the book, said goodbye to Dai-yu and went back with Aroma to change. We may leave them there. Dai-yu, seeing Bao-yu go and hearing that the other girls were all out too, felt lonely. She was about to return to her room. As she passed the corner of the wall of Pear-tree Court, she heard the clear, lingering notes of a flute and a voice singing with tender turns of melody. She knew it was the twelve girls rehearsing their plays. She had never much cared for the theatre and, paying little attention, walked on. Then two lines drifted into her ears, so distinctly that she missed not a word:

‘So vivid purple, lovely red have blossomed everywhere,
Yet all are given over to broken wells and crumbling walls.’

segments.text: The words stirred a deep, lingering feeling in Dai-yu. She stopped and listened closely. The singing went on:

‘In this fine hour, before this lovely scene, what can I do?
Whose courtyard has the joys to gladden the heart?’

At these two lines she could not help nodding and sighing to herself. ‘So there is fine writing in plays too,’ she thought. ‘What a pity people only watch the performance. They may never appreciate what is in the words.’ Then she regretted letting her thoughts wander and missing the song. She listened again:

‘Only for you, my flower-fair love,
And these years that flow like water…’

At these two lines her heart stirred and her senses reeled. Then came ‘You pity yourself in your secluded chamber’ and other lines. More entranced than ever, as if intoxicated, she could no longer stand. She sank on to a rock in the artificial hill and slowly savoured those eight Chinese characters, ‘my flower-fair love, these years that flow like water’. Suddenly she remembered a line she had recently seen in an old poem: ‘Water flows, flowers fade; neither has a heart.’ Then there was the lyric, ‘Water flows, flowers fall, spring is gone: heaven and the world below.’ And from The Western Chamber, which she had just read, came ‘Flowers fall, and the water flows red; ten thousand idle sorrows.’ All returned to her at once and gathered together in her mind.

segments.text: Now, as Lin Dai-yu’s thoughts of love grew ever more entangled and held her fast, someone suddenly clapped her on the back.
‘What are you doing here all by yourself?’
Dai-yu gave quite a start. She turned to find that it was Caltrop.
‘You silly girl! What a fright you gave me. Where have you just come from?’

Caltrop giggled. ‘I came to look for our young lady, but I can’t find her anywhere. Your Nightingale is looking for you too. She says Mrs Lian has sent you some sort of tea. Come along. Let’s go back to your rooms and sit down.’

As she spoke, she took Dai-yu by the hand and led her back to the Naiad’s House. Sure enough, Xi-feng had sent two little jars of new tea of the kind reserved for imperial use. Dai-yu and Caltrop sat down.

segments.text: What serious business could they have had to discuss? They merely remarked on how well this piece was embroidered and how fine the stitches were in that, played a game of chess and read a few lines of a book. Then Caltrop left, and we need say no more of them.

Let us return to Bao-yu. Aroma had found him and brought him back to his room, where Faithful was indeed reclining on the bed, examining Aroma’s needlework. When she saw him she said, ‘Where have you been? Her Old Ladyship is waiting for you. She wants you to go over and ask after the Elder Master. Hurry up and change your clothes so you can go.’
Aroma went into the inner room to fetch his clothes.

segments.text: Bao-yu sat on the edge of the bed and slipped off his shoes. While he was waiting for his boots, he looked round at Faithful. She wore a pale-pink silk-damask jacket, a dark-blue satin waistcoat and a white silk-crêpe sash. With her face turned away, she had bent her head over the needlework; round her neck she wore a flowered collar. Bao-yu brought his face close to her neck to smell the scented oil, stroking her all the while. Her skin was as white and smooth as Aroma’s. He clambered on to her like a monkey and said with an importunate grin, ‘Dear sister, spare me a taste of the rouge on your lips.’ As he spoke, he clung to her like a sticky twist of sugar.

segments.text: ‘Aroma, come out and look at him!’ Faithful cried. ‘You’ve been with him all your life, and you never tell him off. He’s still just the same.’
Aroma came out with his clothes in her arms.
‘Whatever I say, you won’t change,’ she told Bao-yu. ‘What am I to do with you? If you go on like this, it will be impossible to stay here.’

As she spoke, she urged him into his clothes. He went with Faithful to the front to see Grandmother Jia. Having paid his respects, he came outside, where his attendants and horses were ready. He was just about to mount when Jia Lian came back from his own visit to ask after his father and was dismounting. Meeting face to face, the two exchanged a few words. Then someone stepped forward from one side.
‘My respects to you, Uncle Bao.’

Bao-yu looked at him. He was a tall, slender young man with a long face, no more than eighteen or nineteen, and decidedly gentle and handsome in appearance. He looked very familiar, yet Bao-yu could not remember which branch of the family he belonged to or what his name was.
‘Why are you staring like that?’ Jia Lian asked with a laugh. ‘Don’t you even recognise him?

segments.text: ‘He’s Yun, the son of our Fifth Sister-in-law who lives in the rear lane.’
‘Of course, of course!’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘How could I have forgotten?’
He asked after the young man’s mother and what business had brought him there.
‘I came to have a word with Second Uncle,’ Jia Yun replied, pointing to Jia Lian.
‘You’ve grown even better-looking than before,’ said Bao-yu with a smile. ‘You look quite like a son of mine.’

segments.text: ‘Have you no shame?’ Jia Lian laughed. ‘He’s four or five years older than you, and you’re making him your son!’
‘How old are you now?’ Bao-yu asked, smiling.
‘Eighteen,’ Jia Yun replied.

segments.text: Jia Yun was a particularly quick-witted, perceptive young fellow. Hearing Bao-yu speak in this way, he smiled.

‘As the saying goes, “A grandfather in a cradle, a grandson leaning on a stick.” I may be older, but however high the mountain, it cannot rise above the sun. These past few years, since my father died, I’ve had no one to look after me or guide me. If you don’t think your nephew too stupid, Uncle Bao, it would be my good fortune to have you take me for your son.’
‘Do you hear that?’ Jia Lian laughed. ‘Taking a son isn’t something you can easily get out of!’ With that he went inside.

‘Come and see me tomorrow, if you have time,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Don’t go skulking about with those others. I haven’t a moment just now. Come to the study tomorrow and we’ll have a chat. I’ll take you into the garden to amuse ourselves.’
He took hold of the saddle and mounted, and rode over to Jia She’s quarters surrounded by his pages.

segments.text: On seeing Jia She, he found that his uncle had merely caught a slight chill. First he delivered Grandmother Jia’s enquiries, then paid his own respects. Jia She rose to give his reply to Grandmother Jia before calling someone in.
‘Take the young master inside to sit with Her Ladyship.’
Bao-yu withdrew and went round to the back, into the principal room.

segments.text: When Lady Xing saw him, she first rose to ask after Grandmother Jia; only then did Bao-yu pay his own respects. She drew him up on to the kang to sit beside her, asked after the others and ordered tea. Before he had finished a cup, Jia Cong came in to greet him.

‘Where did this monkey spring from?’ Lady Xing said. ‘Has that nurse of yours dropped dead? Can’t she tidy you up? Look at your eyebrows and mouth, all black with dirt! Is that how a schoolboy from a respectable family ought to look?’

segments.text: While she was speaking, the young uncle and nephew, Jia Huan and Jia Lan, arrived together. After they had paid their respects, Lady Xing told them to sit on chairs. Jia Huan saw Bao-yu sharing Lady Xing’s cushion on the kang while she fondled and caressed him in every possible way, and already felt thoroughly out of sorts. Before long he gave Jia Lan a look to say he wanted to leave. Jia Lan had to comply, and they rose together to take their leave. Seeing that they were going, Bao-yu stood up too, intending to go back with them.
‘Stay where you are,’ Lady Xing said with a smile. ‘I still have something to say to you.’
Bao-yu could only sit down again. Lady Xing turned to the other two.
‘When you get back, each of you give your mother my regards. All those aunts and sisters of yours are here, making my head spin, so I shan’t keep you to dinner today.’
Jia Huan and Jia Lan assented and went home.

segments.text: ‘Are all the girls over here, then?’ Bao-yu asked with a smile. ‘How is it I haven’t seen them?’
‘They sat here for a while, then went to one of the rooms at the back. I don’t know which.’
‘You said you had something to tell me, Aunt. What was it?’
‘Nothing at all,’ Lady Xing said, laughing. ‘I only wanted you to wait and have dinner with the girls before you went. And I have something amusing for you to take back and play with.’

As aunt and nephew talked, dinnertime came round before they knew it. Tables and chairs were set out, cups and dishes arranged, and Lady Xing and the young people ate. Afterwards Bao-yu went to take his leave of Jia She and returned home with the girls. They paid their respects to Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang and the others, then went to their own rooms to rest. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: Meanwhile Jia Yun had gone in to see Jia Lian and ask whether there was any work available.

‘Something did come up the other day,’ Jia Lian told him, ‘but your aunt begged me so persistently that I gave it to Jia Qin. She has promised me that, as there are still several places in the garden where flowers and trees have to be planted, you shall certainly have the job when that work comes up.’
Jia Yun listened, then after a pause said, ‘In that case, I’ll wait. You needn’t mention to Aunt that I came to ask today, Uncle. There will be time enough when the job comes up.’

‘Why should I mention it? As though I had time for such idle talk! I have to go to Xingyi at the fifth watch tomorrow, and must manage to get back the same day. Go and wait for now. Come for news after the first watch has begun the day after tomorrow. If you come earlier I shan’t have time to see you.’

segments.text: With that he went back to change his clothes. Jia Yun left the Rong mansion to go home, thinking as he walked. Having hit upon a plan, he went straight to the house of his mother’s brother, Bu Shi-ren.
Bu Shi-ren kept a shop selling aromatics and had only just returned from it when Jia Yun unexpectedly came in. They exchanged greetings, and he asked what had brought his nephew there at that hour.

‘There’s something I need your help with, Uncle. I have a piece of business that calls for some bingpian and musk. Do be a good uncle and let me have four taels’ weight of each on credit. I’ll bring you the full payment in the eighth month.’
Bu Shi-ren gave a cold laugh.

‘Don’t speak to me of credit again. Only the other day, one of the men at our shop let a relation have several taels’ worth of goods on credit, and the money still hasn’t been paid. We all had to make up the loss. So we drew up an agreement: no more credit for friends or relations. Anyone who breaks it must pay for a feast costing twenty taels of silver. Besides, these goods are in short supply now. Even if you brought cash to buy them at our little second-rate shop, we wouldn’t have that much. We’d have to buy it in from elsewhere.

segments.text: ‘My boy, if your uncle had it, of course he ought to give it to you. I tell your aunt every day that what worries me is your lack of sense. If you had any spirit, you’d go to the senior branch of your family. Even if you couldn’t see the masters themselves, you could swallow your pride, make yourself agreeable to their steward or one of the managers, and get something to take charge of. The other day, when I was going out of the city, I met the fourth young man of your third branch riding a great jackass, with five carts and forty or fifty monks and Taoists on their way to the family temple. There’s a capable fellow for you! He got the job, didn’t he?’
Unable to bear any more of this harangue, Jia Yun stood up to leave.
‘Why such a hurry?’ Bu Shi-ren said. ‘Stay and eat before you go.’

He had scarcely finished when his wife said, ‘You’ve lost your senses again. Haven’t I just told you there’s no rice? I bought half a catty of flour to make you some noodles, and here you are putting on airs of plenty! Are you keeping your nephew here to go hungry?’

segments.text: ‘Buy another half-catty to add to it, then,’ said Bu Shi-ren.
His wife called to their daughter. ‘Yin-jie, go across the way and ask Mrs Wang whether she can lend us twenty or thirty cash. We’ll send it back tomorrow.’
While the couple were talking, Jia Yun had already said several times, ‘Please don’t trouble yourselves,’ and vanished.

We shall leave the Bu couple and follow Jia Yun, who, stung by his uncle’s treatment, went straight back the way he had come. Troubled at heart, he walked on with his head down, thinking, and unexpectedly ran headlong into a drunken man. He had quite a fright.
‘Damn your mother!’ the drunk swore. ‘Are you blind, barging into me?’

Jia Yun tried to dodge away, but the man had already caught hold of him. Looking into his face, he recognised his next-door neighbour, Ni Er. This Ni Er was a ruffian who lent money at exorbitant interest, took a cut of the gambling dens’ takings and made a business of brawling, bullying and drinking. He was now on his way back, drunk, from collecting interest at a debtor’s house. Jia Yun’s collision had put him in a vile temper, and he raised his fist to strike.

segments.text: ‘Old Er, don’t hit me!’ the other cried. ‘It was my fault for bumping into you.’

Recognising a familiar voice, Ni Er opened his drunken eyes and saw Jia Yun. He hastily let go and, swaying on his feet, said with a laugh, ‘Why, it’s Second Master Jia! I deserve to die! I deserve to die! Where are you off to now?’
‘Don’t ask. I’ve just had another snub, for no reason at all.’

‘Never mind, never mind. If someone’s treated you badly, tell me and I’ll settle it for you. In all these streets and alleys, whoever he may be, if he offends a neighbour of mine, of Drunken Vajra Ni Er, I’ll see his household scattered to the winds!’
‘Don’t get angry yet, Old Er. Let me tell you what happened.’
He told him the whole business with Bu Shi-ren. Ni Er was furious.
‘If he weren’t your uncle, I’d have some names to call him! It makes my blood boil. Well, don’t you worry. I have a few taels on me. Whatever you need, take them and buy it.

segments.text: ‘There’s just one thing. We’ve been neighbours all these years, and everyone knows I lend money, but you’ve never once asked me for any. Is it that you despise me as a ruffian and think it beneath your dignity? Or are you afraid I’d be hard to deal with and charge too much interest? If it’s the interest you’re afraid of, I won’t charge any on this, and there’s no need for a written agreement. But if you think it beneath you, I wouldn’t presume to lend it. We can each go our own way.’
As he spoke, he actually drew a roll of silver out of his shoulder-bag.
