segments.text: Jia Yun thought to himself, ‘Ruffian and scoundrel though Ni Er is, he treats different people differently, and has quite a name for generosity and honour. If I refuse his kindness today, he may feel slighted and make trouble. I’d better borrow it and pay him back double another day.’
Having made up his mind, he smiled.

‘Old Er, you really are a fine fellow. Don’t suppose I’ve never thought of asking you. But all the people you mix with are bold men who can do things. You wouldn’t take any notice of someone as helpless and useless as me. If I’d asked, would you have lent me anything? Now you’ve been so generous, how could I refuse? I’ll go home and draw up the usual agreement and bring it over.’
Ni Er burst out laughing.

‘You’ve a clever tongue, but I won’t listen to that. If they’re people I call my friends, how could I lend them money and take interest from them? If I lend to someone for the sake of the interest, that isn’t friendship.

segments.text: ‘Enough of this talk. Since you’re willing to take notice of me, here’s a little over fifteen taels and three qian of silver. Take it and buy what you need. If you’re going to write out some bond, give me my silver back now, and let me lend it to people I can expect a return from.’
Taking the silver, Jia Yun smiled. ‘All right, I won’t write one. Why get so worked up?’

‘That’s more like it,’ Ni Er said with a laugh. ‘It’s getting dark. I won’t keep you for tea or wine; I have something to see to over there. You go on home. And do me a favour: take a message to my household. Tell them to shut the doors early and go to bed. I shan’t be coming home. If there’s anything urgent, have my daughter come and find me first thing tomorrow at the horse-dealer Wang Shortlegs’.’

segments.text: With that he staggered away, and we shall leave him there.

Jia Yun found this chance encounter very remarkable. He thought Ni Er was a decent sort after all. Yet he was still afraid it might be drunken generosity: what would he do if the man demanded twice as much tomorrow? He could not make up his mind. Then another thought came to him. ‘Never mind. Once that business comes off, I can pay him back double.’

He went straight to a money shop and had the silver weighed: fifteen taels, three qian, four fen and two li. Finding that Ni Er had told the truth, Jia Yun was more pleased than ever. He put the silver away and went home, first stopping next door to give Ni Er’s wife his message.

His mother was sitting on the kang twisting thread. When she saw him, she asked where he had been all day. Afraid of upsetting her, Jia Yun said nothing about Bu Shi-ren, but told her only that he had been waiting at the Rong mansion for Uncle Lian. Then he asked whether she had eaten.

segments.text: She had, his mother said, and told him where she had left his food. The little maid brought it for him. It was already time to light the lamps. Jia Yun ate, made ready for bed and went to sleep. The night passed without incident.

Early next morning he got up, washed his face and went out through the south gate to buy bingpian and musk at a large aromatics shop. Then he made for the Rong mansion. On learning that Jia Lian had gone out, he went round to the back.

segments.text: At the entrance to Jia Lian’s courtyard he saw several pages sweeping with great long brooms. Just then Zhou Rui’s wife came out through the gate and called to them, ‘Stop sweeping for a moment. Your mistress is coming out.’
Jia Yun hurried forward with a smile. ‘Where is Second Aunt going?’
‘Her Old Ladyship has sent for her,’ Zhou Rui’s wife replied. ‘I suppose it’s to cut out some lengths of cloth.’

segments.text: As they spoke, Xi-feng appeared with a crowd of attendants about her. Jia Yun knew very well that she liked flattery and display. He hastily held his hands close to his sides and stepped smartly forward to pay his respects with the greatest deference. Xi-feng did not even give him a proper look, but walked on, merely asking after his mother.
‘Why doesn’t she come to see us?’
‘She hasn’t been very well. She’s always thinking of you, Aunt, and wanting to come and see you, but she hasn’t been able to.’
‘What a liar you are!’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘If I hadn’t mentioned her, you wouldn’t have told me she was thinking of me.’

‘Would I dare lie to an elder unless I wanted to be struck by lightning?’ Jia Yun asked with a smile. ‘Only last night we were talking about you. Mother was saying how delicately built you are, with so much to do, and how extraordinary your energy must be, to manage everything so thoroughly. Anyone with a little less would have worn herself to a shadow long ago.’
Xi-feng’s face was all smiles. In spite of herself, she stopped walking.
‘And what set the pair of you talking about me behind my back?’
‘There was a reason. I have a friend whose family has a little money and who keeps an aromatics shop.

segments.text: ‘He had bought the rank of assistant prefect, and the other day he was appointed to some place in Yunnan, I don’t know where. He’s taking his whole household with him and closing the shop here. So he went through his accounts and stock, paid what he owed, sold off what he could cheaply, and shared out the fine, costly goods among his friends and relations. What he gave me was some bingpian and musk.

‘I talked it over with my mother. If I tried to sell it on, I couldn’t get the original price. Besides, who would pay all that silver for it, and what would they want it for? Even a very wealthy household would be doing well to use a few fen or qian. As for giving it away, I don’t know anyone whose station calls for such things. They’d only sell it for half a coin when it was worth a whole one. That was what made me think of you, Aunt. In past years I’ve seen you spend great packets of silver on these things. Even leaving aside what Her Imperial Highness will need in the palace this year, you’re bound to use ten times the usual amount of aromatics for the Dragon Boat Festival alone.

segments.text: ‘So the more I thought about it, the more I felt that giving it to you was the only fitting way to show my respect and not let it go to waste.’

As he spoke, he held up a brocade-covered box. Xi-feng was just at the point of preparing gifts for the Dragon Boat Festival and buying aromatics and medicinal ingredients. Jia Yun’s unexpected offering, together with his long speech, left her both flattered and delighted.
‘Take it from Master Yun,’ she told Felicity, ‘and carry it home to Patience.’

Hearing the talk come round to the point he wanted, Jia Yun ventured a little further and deliberately asked, ‘So Uncle has mentioned me?’

segments.text: Xi-feng was just about to tell him about the work he was to be given when she checked herself. ‘If I tell him now,’ she thought, ‘he’ll think I can’t see a present without snatching at it, promising him a job merely for this little bit of perfume. I won’t mention it today.’

She therefore kept back every word about putting him in charge of the flower- and tree-planting, made a couple of indifferent remarks and went on to Grandmother Jia’s. Jia Yun could hardly raise the matter himself and had to withdraw.

segments.text: When he had seen Bao-yu the day before, he had been told to wait for him in the outer study. So, after his meal, Jia Yun came back to Patterned Snow Studio, the study outside the ceremonial gate of Grandmother Jia’s quarters. He found the two pages Tealeaf and Chu-yao playing Chinese chess and quarrelling over the capture of a chariot. Four or five others, Yin-quan, Sao-hua, Tiao-yun and Ban-he among them, were up at the eaves, taking little sparrows from their nests for amusement.

segments.text: Jia Yun entered the courtyard and stamped his foot.
‘You mischievous monkeys! Here I am.’
Only when the pages saw him coming did they scatter. Jia Yun went into the room, sat down on a chair and asked, ‘Hasn’t Master Bao come out yet?’
‘He hasn’t been out at all today,’ said Tealeaf. ‘What is it you want, sir? I’ll go and find out for you.’
With that he went off.

When he looked for the other pages, they had all gone off to play. He was growing thoroughly bored when a soft young voice called ‘Brother!’ from the doorway.

segments.text: Jia Yun looked out and saw a maid of sixteen or seventeen, delicately made and neat in appearance. At the sight of him she drew back and slipped out of view. Just then Tealeaf came along. Seeing the girl at the door, he said, ‘Good, good! I couldn’t find anyone to take a message.’
Jia Yun too had seen Tealeaf and hurried out to ask what had happened.

‘I’ve been waiting all day and no one’s come by,’ Tealeaf said. ‘This girl belongs to Master Bao’s rooms. Be a good girl and take a message in: say that the Second Master from the rear lane has come.’

Only then did the girl realise that this was a young gentleman of the family. No longer avoiding him as she had at first, she fixed Jia Yun with a couple of very intent looks. She heard him say, ‘Never mind lanes, rear or front. Just say it’s Yun.’
After a pause the girl gave a cool little laugh.
‘If you ask me, sir, you’d better go home. Whatever you have to say can wait until tomorrow. If I have a chance this evening, I’ll tell him.’
‘What do you mean by that?’ Tealeaf asked.
‘He didn’t have his midday sleep today, so naturally he’ll have his evening meal early.

segments.text: ‘And he won’t be coming out here tonight. Are we to keep the gentleman waiting hungry just for our amusement? He’d do better to go home and come back tomorrow. Even if someone comes along later and offers to take a message, it’s no use. They’ll say yes readily enough, but do you suppose they’ll take it?’

Jia Yun found the girl’s speech direct and charming. He wanted to ask her name, but since she belonged to Bao-yu’s rooms, he felt it would not be proper. He could only say, ‘You’re quite right. I’ll come again tomorrow.’
He started out.
‘I’ll make some tea,’ said Tealeaf. ‘Have a cup before you go, sir.’
‘No tea, thank you. I still have something to do,’ Jia Yun said, looking back as he walked. While he spoke, his eyes sought the girl, who was still standing there.

segments.text: Jia Yun went straight home. When he reached the main gate the next day, he happened to meet Xi-feng setting out to pay her respects in the other quarters. She had just got into her carriage. Seeing him, she had someone call him over and said with a smile through the window, ‘Yun, you’ve a nerve, trying your tricks on me! I thought you were giving me a present, but it turns out you want something. Your uncle told me yesterday that you’d been asking him for a job.’

‘Please don’t mention my asking Uncle, Aunt,’ Jia Yun said with a smile. ‘I was regretting it only yesterday. If I’d known how it would turn out, I’d have come to you from the start and it would all have been settled by now. Who could have thought Uncle wouldn’t be able to manage it?’
‘No wonder you came looking for me yesterday, then, when you’d got nowhere with him,’ Xi-feng said, laughing.

‘You misjudge my wish to honour you, Aunt. I never meant anything of the kind. If I had, wouldn’t I have asked you yesterday? But now that you know about it, I shall have to give up on Uncle and beg you to show me a little kindness.’

segments.text: Xi-feng gave a cold laugh.

‘What can I say if you insist on going the long way round? If you’d told me at the start, what couldn’t have been done? Such a little matter, and it’s been held up all this time. There are still flowers to be planted in the garden, and I couldn’t think of anyone for it. If you’d come earlier, wouldn’t it all have been settled?’
‘In that case, Aunt, give me the job tomorrow,’ Jia Yun said, smiling.

After a pause Xi-feng said, ‘On second thoughts, I don’t think this one would do. Wait until that big order for fireworks, lanterns and candles comes up in the first month of next year. I’ll give you that instead.’

segments.text: ‘I shall be back as soon as I’ve eaten. Come for the money a little after noon, and go in to plant the trees the day after tomorrow.’

She ordered the driver to start, and her scented carriage went straight on its way. Beside himself with delight, Jia Yun went to Patterned Snow Studio to ask for Bao-yu, only to learn that he had gone to the Prince of Beijing’s mansion early that morning. Jia Yun sat idly until midday. On hearing that Xi-feng had returned, he wrote out a requisition and went to collect an authorisation tally.

segments.text: Outside the courtyard he sent in his name. Sunshine came out, took only the requisition and carried it in. The amount of silver and the month and year were endorsed on it, and it was handed to Jia Yun together with the tally. He took them and saw that the approved amount was two hundred taels. Unable to contain his delight, he turned and went straight to the silver treasury, handed them to the man who received the tallies and requisitions, and collected the money.
When he went home and told his mother, both were naturally delighted. At the fifth watch next morning, Jia Yun first sought out Ni Er and repaid the exact sum he had borrowed.

segments.text: Seeing that Jia Yun now had money, Ni Er accepted the repayment in full, and we need say no more of him. Jia Yun then took another fifty taels and went out through the west gate to the gardener Fang Chun’s house to buy trees. We shall leave him there.

Now let us return to Bao-yu. On the day he met Jia Yun, he had told him to come and talk the following day. But it had been merely the talk of a young gentleman accustomed to wealth and privilege. Why would he keep it in mind? He had promptly forgotten it. This evening, on returning from the Prince of Beijing’s mansion, he paid his respects to Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang and the others, then went back into the garden, changed his clothes and prepared to take a bath.

segments.text: Aroma had been asked over by Xue Bao-chai to make ornamental knots. Ripple and Emerald had gone to hurry along the hot water. Sandal had been fetched home for her mother’s birthday, and Musk was at home recovering from illness. There were still a few maids who did the rough work and answered calls, but, thinking they were unlikely to be wanted, they had all gone out to find companions to play with. So it happened that for this brief interval Bao-yu was alone in the room. As luck would have it, he wanted tea. Only after he had called two or three times did two or three old women come in. At the sight of them, he hurriedly waved them away.
‘Never mind, never mind. I don’t need you.’

segments.text: The old women had to withdraw. With no maids about, Bao-yu could only get up himself, take a bowl and go to the teapot to pour some tea.
‘Careful you don’t scald your hand, sir. Let me pour it,’ a voice behind him said.
As she spoke, she came forward and took the bowl from him. Bao-yu gave a start.
‘Where were you? You appeared so suddenly you gave me a fright.’
Handing him the tea, the maid replied, ‘I was in the back courtyard. I’ve just come through the rear door of the inner room. Didn’t you hear my footsteps?’

segments.text: As he drank, Bao-yu looked the girl over carefully. Her clothes were neither new nor particularly old, but she had a head of thick black hair coiled into a bun, a long face and a slender, delicate figure. She was decidedly pretty and neat. Having looked at her, Bao-yu smiled and asked, ‘Do you belong to my rooms too?’

segments.text: ‘Yes,’ the maid replied.
‘If you belong here, how is it I don’t know you?’
The girl gave a cool laugh.
‘There are plenty you don’t know, not just me. I never serve tea or water, or bring this and carry that. I don’t do any of the work you can see, so how would you know me?’
‘Why don’t you do the work I can see?’

‘That’s not easy for me to say. But there is one thing I ought to tell you, sir. Someone called Yun came to see you yesterday. I thought you wouldn’t have time, so I told Tealeaf to tell him to come early today. I didn’t expect you to go off to the Prince of Beijing’s instead.’

segments.text: Ripple and Emerald were complaining to one another.
‘You’ve wet my skirt!’
‘And you’ve trodden on my shoe!’

Suddenly someone came out to take the water. They looked and saw that it was none other than Crimson. Both were astonished. Setting down the water, they hurried into the room and looked all about, but there was nobody there except Bao-yu. This made them thoroughly uneasy. They could only prepare the things for his bath. When he had taken off his clothes, they came out, pulling the door shut behind them, and went to the room on the other side to find Crimson and ask what she had been saying in his room just now.

‘When have I been in his room?’ Crimson said. ‘My handkerchief had gone missing, and I went round to the back to look for it. Then the young master wanted tea, and when he called, not one of you sisters was there. So I went in. I’d only just poured the tea when you came.’

segments.text: At this Ripple spat straight in her face.

‘Shameless little slut! We told you to go and hurry the water along, and you said you had something to do. You made us go instead, while you waited to seize this fine opportunity. Edging your way in, bit by bit, and here you are! Do you think we can’t keep up with you? Take a look in the mirror and see whether you’re fit to serve tea and water!’
‘Tomorrow I’ll tell the others,’ Emerald said. ‘Whenever there’s tea or water wanted, or anything to be carried in or out, none of us need stir. Let her do it all.’
‘In that case,’ said Ripple, ‘we might as well all go away and leave her alone in his rooms.’
They were still keeping up this barrage, one after the other, when an old woman came in with a message from Xi-feng.

‘Someone will be bringing gardeners in to plant trees tomorrow. You’re to be more careful. Don’t leave your jackets and skirts hanging out to dry all over the place. That whole stretch along the artificial hill is being screened off with hangings. Don’t go running about where you please.’
‘Do you know who’s bringing the workmen in to supervise them?’ Ripple asked.
‘Someone called Master Yun, from the rear lane.’
Neither Ripple nor Emerald knew him, and they went on asking all sorts of other questions.

segments.text: Crimson, however, understood at once: it was the young man she had seen in the outer study yesterday.

Her surname was Lin and her childhood name Hong-yu, ‘red jade’. But because the ‘yu’, or ‘jade’, encroached on the names of Lin Dai-yu and Bao-yu, everyone had dropped that part and called her simply Crimson. Her family had served the Rong mansion for generations, and her parents now managed the houses and land in various places. She was only sixteen. When servants were being assigned to Prospect Garden, she had been sent to the House of Green Delights, where life was quiet and secluded enough. But then came the order for people to move into the garden, and Bao-yu happened to be given that very house.

Inexperienced girl though she was, Crimson had a certain prettiness and an earnest, foolish longing to rise in the world. Time and again she wanted to show what she could do in front of Bao-yu. But all the people about him had sharp tongues and ready claws. Where could she find a place among them? Today, unexpectedly, she had at last had a little opening, only to meet this spiteful attack from Ripple and the others. Already half her hopes had turned to ashes.

segments.text: She was brooding over it when the old woman’s mention of Jia Yun stirred something in her heart. Still troubled, she returned to her room and lay on the bed thinking it over in secret, turning this way and that without knowing what to do.
Suddenly a low voice called outside the window, ‘Crimson, I’ve found your handkerchief. I have it here.’
She hurried out to look. It was none other than Jia Yun. Her fair face coloured with bashfulness.
‘Where did you find it, sir?’
‘Come here and I’ll tell you,’ Jia Yun said with a smile, reaching out to take hold of her as he spoke.
Crimson turned quickly to run, but caught her foot on the threshold and fell.
To learn what really happened, you must read the next chapter.

segments.text: Now Crimson, her mind wandering and her thoughts entangled in love, had drifted off to sleep. She met Jia Yun, who tried to take hold of her; turning to run, she tripped over the threshold and fell. The fright woke her, and only then did she realise it had been a dream. She tossed and turned after that, unable to sleep all night. At daybreak she got up. Several of the other maids came to fetch her to sweep the rooms and floors and carry water for washing. Without stopping to wash her face or comb her hair properly, she twisted up her hair anyhow before the mirror, washed her hands, tied a cloth round her waist and went to clean the rooms.

Bao-yu, meanwhile, had noticed Crimson the day before and had not forgotten her. He could have called for her by name to wait on him, but for two things: first, he was afraid of hurting Aroma and the others; and second, he did not yet know what sort of girl Crimson was. If she turned out well, all would be well; if she did not, it would be awkward to send her back.

segments.text: These thoughts made him restless. He too rose early without washing or combing his hair, and sat lost in thought. Presently he lowered the window, and through its gauze screen could see clearly outside. Several maids were sweeping the courtyard, all of them rouged and powdered, with flowers and willow sprigs in their hair, but the girl from yesterday was nowhere to be seen. He slipped his shoes on and sauntered out, pretending to look at the flowers, glancing here and peering there. Raising his eyes, he thought he saw someone leaning against the railing beneath the covered walk at the south-west corner. Annoyingly, a crab-apple tree in front of him blocked the view. He moved a step farther and looked more closely. Sure enough, there was yesterday’s girl, lost in thought. He wanted to go up to her, but could find no good way of doing so. While he hesitated, Emerald came to hurry him in to wash his face, and he had to go. We may leave him there.

segments.text: Crimson was still standing in her reverie when she saw Aroma beckon and had to go over to her.
‘Our watering can still hasn’t been put in order and brought back,’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘Go to Miss Lin’s and borrow theirs for us.’

Crimson agreed and set off for Naiad’s House. Just as she was crossing Green Haze Bridge, she looked up and saw screens stretched all along the upper slope. Only then did she remember that workmen were planting trees there that day. Turning to look, she saw a cluster of men digging in the distance, with Jia Yun seated on a rock of the artificial hill. She wanted to go over, but dared not. Dispiritedly she went on to Naiad’s House, fetched the watering can and returned, then lay down listlessly in her room.

segments.text: The others supposed she was merely feeling a little unwell and paid no attention. A day soon passed. The next day was the birthday of Wang Zi-teng’s wife, who had sent invitations to Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang. Grandmother Jia was not feeling well, so Lady Wang decided not to go either. Aunt Xue went, however, with Xi-feng, the Jia girls, Bao-chai and Bao-yu. They did not return until evening.

segments.text: As it happened, when Jia Huan came home from school, Lady Wang had told him to copy out the Vajra Mantra and recite it. He was now sitting on her kang, ordering the lamps to be lit and making a great show of his copying. One moment he called to Cai-yun to pour him a cup of tea, the next to Silver to trim a candle; then he complained that Golden was standing in his light. The maids, who had always disliked him, took no notice. Only Cai-xia was still on good terms with him. She poured a cup of tea and handed it to him, and, seeing Lady Wang occupied in conversation, spoke to him quietly.
‘Do behave yourself. Why must you make everyone dislike you?’
‘I know all about it,’ said Jia Huan. ‘Don’t try to fool me. You’re friendly with Bao-yu now and won’t have anything to do with me. I’ve seen it for myself.’
Cai-xia bit her lip and poked him in the forehead.
‘Ungrateful thing! You’re like the dog that bit Lü Dong-bin: you don’t know a kind heart when you find one.’

segments.text: They were still talking when Xi-feng came in and paid her respects to Lady Wang, who began asking her all about the party: which ladies had been there, whether the plays were good, what the food had been like. They had exchanged only a few words when Bao-yu arrived. He came in and greeted Lady Wang with a few impeccably proper remarks, then had his brow-band removed, his robe taken off and his boots pulled away, and tumbled headlong into her arms. Lady Wang stroked and caressed his face and body, while he clung round her neck and chattered on.

‘My child, you’ve had too much wine again. Your face is burning,’ she said. ‘And still you keep wriggling about! You’ll make the wine go to your head in a moment. Won’t you lie quietly over there for a little while?’

She called for a pillow. At this Bao-yu slipped out of her arms and lay down behind her, then called Cai-xia to pat him. He joked and talked to her, but she answered coolly and scarcely attended to him; her eyes kept straying towards Jia Huan.

segments.text: Bao-yu took her hand and smiled.
‘Dear sister, do pay me a little attention too.’
As he spoke he kept hold of her hand, but Cai-xia pulled it away, refusing him.
‘Go on like that and I’ll shout.’

segments.text: Jia Huan could hear their teasing. He had long hated Bao-yu, and now the sight of him playing with Cai-xia made the malice within him harder than ever to contain. He dared not speak out, but had often plotted against him in secret, without finding a chance to act. Now that Bao-yu was so close, he decided to blind him with hot oil. Deliberately making it look like an accident, he gave the candle-lamp, brimming with oily liquid, a push straight at Bao-yu’s face.

Bao-yu cried out, startling everyone in the room. They hurriedly moved the standing lamp over from the floor and brought three or four more lights from the inner and outer rooms. In their light they saw oil all over his face and head. Frantic with distress and anger, Lady Wang ordered the maids to wipe him clean, while scolding Jia Huan. Xi-feng sprang up on to the kang to help attend to Bao-yu.
‘Third Brother’s still such a flustered chicken,’ she said, smiling. ‘I’ve always said you’re no good in grand company. Aunt Zhao ought to teach you better now and then.’
This reminded Lady Wang. She stopped scolding Jia Huan and called Aunt Zhao over instead.
‘You’ve brought this black-hearted, ill-bred little wretch into the world, and you won’t even keep him in order!

segments.text: ‘Time after time I’ve let things pass, and now you’ve grown so pleased with yourselves that you keep going further!’

Aunt Zhao had long harboured jealousy and resentment against both Xi-feng and Bao-yu, but had never dared show it. Now Jia Huan had caused fresh trouble and brought this abuse down on her. Not only must she swallow it in silence: she had to go and help tend Bao-yu as well. A line of blisters had risen on his left cheek; fortunately his eyes were quite untouched. At the sight, Lady Wang’s heart ached. Afraid, too, of what she could possibly say when Grandmother Jia asked about it next day, she turned in her agitation to rebuke Aunt Zhao once more. Then she comforted Bao-yu and ordered medicine to draw out the poison and reduce the swelling to be brought and applied.
‘It hurts a little, but it’s nothing serious,’ Bao-yu said. ‘If Grandmother asks tomorrow, just say I burnt myself.’

‘Even if we say that, she’ll still scold us for not watching you properly and letting you get burnt,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘There’s bound to be a scene whatever happens. You can say what you please tomorrow.’

segments.text: Lady Wang ordered them to take Bao-yu carefully back to his rooms. Aroma and the others were thrown into a panic when they saw him. Dai-yu had felt out of sorts all day with Bao-yu away and no one to talk to. That evening she had already sent two or three times to ask whether he was back. Now at last he was, only to have been burnt. She hurried over and found him looking in a mirror, the whole left side of his face covered with medicine. Thinking the burn must be very serious, she hastened up, asking how it had happened and wanting to see. Bao-yu quickly covered his face and waved her away. He would not let her look, knowing how fastidious she was about cleanliness and how she disliked the sight of such things.
Dai-yu knew her own fastidiousness well enough, and understood that he was afraid she would find it dirty.
‘Let me see where you’ve burnt yourself,’ she said with a smile. ‘What is there to hide?’
As she spoke she came closer and, forcibly turning his head by the neck, took a look and asked how badly it hurt.

segments.text: ‘Not very much. A day or two’s rest will put it right,’ said Bao-yu.

Dai-yu sat for a while, then returned unhappily to her own rooms. Nothing more need be said of that night. Next day Bao-yu went to see Grandmother Jia. Although he declared that he had burnt himself and that no one else was to blame, she duly scolded his attendants all the same.

Another day passed, and Mother Ma, to whom Bao-yu had been entrusted as a godson for spiritual protection, came to pay her respects at the Rong mansion. The sight of him gave her a great start. She asked what had happened, and when told of the burn, nodded and sighed for a while, traced a figure with her finger on his face, and muttered prayers over him.
‘It’s certain to get better. This is only a passing stroke of misfortune.’
Then she turned to Grandmother Jia.

‘Your Old Ladyship, our venerable living Bodhisattva, can have no notion of the terrible things described in the Buddhist scriptures. From the moment a child is born into the family of a prince or a great minister, there are mischievous little demons following him unseen. Whenever they get a chance they give him a twist or a pinch, knock his bowl from his hand as he eats, or trip him up as he walks. That is why so many children in great families never live to grow up.’
‘Is there no Buddhist remedy for it?’ Grandmother Jia asked at once.
‘That’s easy enough,’ said Mother Ma. ‘You need only do more good works on his behalf, to bring him a good return.

segments.text: ‘The scriptures also tell of the Bodhisattva of Great All-Illuminating Light in the West, whose special charge is to shine into the darkness where evil spirits lurk. Any devout man or woman who makes offerings with a sincere heart can secure lasting health and peace for their children and grandchildren, with no more harm from frights, evil spirits or possessing ghosts.’
‘But how does one make offerings to this Bodhisattva?’ asked Grandmother Jia.

‘It costs very little. Besides the incense and candles, one need only provide a few catties of fragrant oil every day to keep a great votive lamp burning. The votive lamp is the Bodhisattva’s own manifested image, and must never be allowed to go out, day or night.’
‘How much oil does it take for a day and a night? Tell me plainly, so that I too can earn this merit.’
At this Mother Ma smiled.

‘There’s no fixed amount. Our benefactors, those living Bodhisattvas, give just as their hearts move them. Several princely consorts and titled ladies make such offerings at our temple. The dowager consort of the Prince of Nan’an’s household has made a great vow and gives generously: forty-eight catties of oil and one catty of wick-rushes every day. Her votive lamp is only a little smaller than a vat. The titled wife of the Marquis of Jintian gives on a somewhat smaller scale, only twenty-four catties of oil a day. Others give five catties, or three, or one. There is no fixed quantity.

segments.text: ‘Poor people in small households cannot afford so much. Even if they give only four taels of oil or half a catty, we still have to light a lamp for them.’
Grandmother Jia nodded thoughtfully.

‘There’s another thing,’ Mother Ma went on. ‘For one’s parents or honoured elders, it does no harm to give more. But when Your Old Ladyship is giving for Bao-yu, too much might be a bad thing. The young gentleman might not be able to bear it, and his blessings would be diminished instead. Besides, there’s no need to spend the household money so freely. If you wish to make an offering, seven catties at the most, or five at the least, will do perfectly well.’
‘In that case,’ said Grandmother Jia, ‘settle it at five catties a day. You can come and draw the whole month’s allowance at once.’
‘Amitabha, merciful great Bodhisattva!’ Mother Ma intoned.
Grandmother Jia then called in a servant and gave further instructions.
‘From now on, whenever Bao-yu goes out, give his pages a few strings of cash to take with them, so that he can give alms to any monks, Taoists or poor people he meets.’
Mother Ma sat a little longer, then wandered about paying her respects in the other courtyards and apartments.

segments.text: Presently she reached Aunt Zhao’s room. After their greetings, Aunt Zhao told a little maid to pour her some tea. Mother Ma noticed a heap of odd scraps and offcuts of silk and satin on the kang, where Aunt Zhao was pasting shoes together.
‘Just when I’ve run out of material for shoe uppers!’ she said. ‘If you have any bits of satin, Mrs Zhao, whatever the colour, do let me have enough for a pair.’

‘Look through it yourself,’ Aunt Zhao sighed. ‘Is there a single decent piece there? Anything decent never reaches my hands. That’s all there is, good or bad. If you don’t mind it, choose a couple of pieces.’
Mother Ma duly chose two pieces and tucked them into her sleeve.

Aunt Zhao sighed.
‘Amitabha! If only I had a little more to spare, I’d make offerings regularly. The will is there, but the means are not.’

segments.text: ‘You’d think they’d got a living dragon, not just Bao-yu. Still, he’s a child, and he has looks people like; if the grown-ups want to make more of him, I can put up with that. It’s this one I can’t stomach.’
She held up two fingers.
Mother Ma understood.
‘Mrs Lian?’
Aunt Zhao waved her hands in alarm, went to the door, lifted the curtain and looked out. Only when she had made sure there was no one about did she return and whisper:
‘Terrible, terrible! As for that woman, if she doesn’t carry every bit of this family’s property off to her own people, you can call me what you like.’
Mother Ma sounded her out.
‘You don’t have to tell me. Can’t we all see it? What amazes me is that you put up with it and let her do as she pleases. Very fine, I must say.’
‘Mother, what can we do but let her? Who would dare do anything to her?’
Mother Ma gave a snort. After a long pause she said:
‘Not that I’d want to say anything sinful, but you’re a helpless lot!

segments.text: ‘You can hardly blame anyone else. If you daren’t act openly, you could have found some way of dealing with her in secret. Why wait till things have come to this?’
Aunt Zhao found sense in these words and was secretly delighted.
‘What could one do in secret? I’ve had the thought myself, only I don’t know anyone with the skill. If you could show me a way, I’d reward you handsomely.’
Seeing that they had come to an understanding, Mother Ma deliberately drew back.
‘Amitabha! Don’t ask me. What do I know of such things? A sin, a sin!’

segments.text: ‘There you go again,’ said Aunt Zhao. ‘You’re always so ready to help people in distress. Surely you won’t stand by and watch them hound my boy and me to death? Or are you afraid I won’t reward you?’
Mother Ma smiled.

‘If you say I can’t bear to see the two of you ill-treated, that’s fair enough. But when you talk of rewarding me, you’ve got your sums wrong. Even supposing I did want a reward from you, what have you got that could tempt me?’
Aunt Zhao could hear her yielding.

‘How can someone as sharp as you suddenly turn so foolish? If your method really works and you finish those two off, surely this property will all be my Huan’s one day. What could you ask for then that you wouldn’t get?’
Mother Ma lowered her head. After a long pause she said:
‘Once it’s done, with nothing in writing, why should you bother about me?’
‘That’s easily settled.

segments.text: ‘I haven’t much in hand just now, but I’ve saved a few taels here and there, and I have some clothes and hairpins. Take something on account. For the rest, I’ll give you a written promise to pay, with any guarantor you like. When the time comes, you’ll get the full amount.’
‘You really mean that?’ asked Mother Ma.
‘How could I lie about such a thing?’

segments.text: She called in an old woman she trusted and whispered a few words in her ear. The woman went out and soon returned with a bond made out for five hundred taels. Aunt Zhao put her handprint on it, then went to the cupboard, took out her private savings and showed them to Mother Ma.
‘Take this first for incense and candles and the expenses of the offerings. Will that do?’

At the sight of the heap of shining silver and the bond, Mother Ma agreed to everything without a further thought. She reached first for the silver, snatched it up and tucked it away, then secured the bond. Next she rummaged for some time inside her waistband, bringing out ten paper-cut ghosts with blue faces and white hair, and two paper figures. She handed them to Aunt Zhao and gave her instructions in a whisper.

‘Write the eight characters of their birth dates and hours on these two paper figures. Hide each figure, with five of the ghosts, in that person’s bed, and that’s all you have to do. I’ll perform the rites at home. They’re bound to work.

segments.text: ‘Above all, be careful, and don’t be afraid!’
They were still talking when one of Lady Wang’s maids came looking for Mother Ma.
‘Are you in here, ma’am? Her Ladyship is waiting for you.’
The two parted, and we may leave them there.

segments.text: Since Bao-yu had burnt his face and stopped going out, Dai-yu had often been able to sit and talk with him. One day, after a meal, she read a couple of passages, but found no pleasure in them. She did some needlework with Nightingale and Snowgoose, but that only made her more restless. After leaning in the doorway for a while in thought, she wandered out to look at the tender bamboo shoots newly thrusting up below the steps, and before she knew it had passed through the courtyard gate. In the garden she could see no one in any direction: only the brightness of flowers and the shadows of willows, with birds calling and water murmuring in the stream.

She strolled towards the House of Green Delights. Several maids were dipping up water and clustering in the covered walk to watch a thrush take its bath. Hearing laughter indoors, she went in and found Li Gong-cai, Xi-feng and Bao-chai all there.
‘Here’s another one!’ they said, laughing as she entered.
‘Everyone’s here today,’ Dai-yu said with a smile. ‘Who sent out the invitations?’
‘Where were you the other day when I sent a maid with two jars of tea for you?’ asked Xi-feng.
‘Oh, of course! I quite forgot. Thank you, thank you.’
‘Have you tried it? Did you like it?’
Before Xi-feng had finished, Bao-yu put in:
‘It ought to be all right, but I didn’t think much of it myself. I don’t know how the others found it.’
‘The flavour’s light,’ said Bao-chai, ‘but the colour isn’t very good.’
‘It came as tribute from Siam,’ said Xi-feng.

segments.text: ‘I didn’t find it very interesting either. It’s not as good as the tea I drink every day.’
‘I liked it,’ said Dai-yu. ‘I don’t know what sort of tastes you all have.’
‘If you really like it, take mine as well,’ said Bao-yu.
‘I have more, if you like it,’ Xi-feng said with a smile.
‘Really? Then I’ll send a maid to fetch it.’
‘No need. I’ll have someone bring it over. There’s something else I shall be asking you to do for me tomorrow. I’ll send that along at the same time.’
‘Do you hear that?’ Dai-yu said, laughing. ‘You only have to drink a little of their tea and they start giving you orders.’
‘I ask you a favour, and you come out with all this nonsense about tea and water!’ Xi-feng laughed. ‘Since you’ve accepted our family’s tea, why haven’t you come into the family as a bride?’
Everyone burst out laughing.

‘Our Second Sister-in-law really does have a way of making jokes.’
‘Making jokes!’ said Dai-yu. ‘Nothing but cheap, spiteful chatter to make people hate her.’
She gave a little spit of contempt.

segments.text: ‘Don’t be absurd!’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘What would you lack if you married into our family?’
She pointed to Bao-yu.
‘Look at him. Are his looks beneath you? His family? His standing? His wealth? Where’s the disgrace to anyone?’
Dai-yu rose to leave.
‘Little Pin-pin’s cross!’ Bao-chai called. ‘Come back and sit down. Going away will spoil it all.’
She rose to catch hold of her. They had just reached the doorway when Aunt Zhao and Aunt Zhou came in to see Bao-yu.

segments.text: Li Gong-cai, Bao-chai, Bao-yu and the others invited the two women to sit. Xi-feng alone went on laughing and talking with Dai-yu, without so much as looking directly at them. Bao-chai was about to speak when a maid from Lady Wang’s rooms appeared.
‘Your uncle’s wife is here. Her Ladyship asks the ladies and young ladies to come out.’
Li Gong-cai immediately called to Xi-feng and the others to go with her. Aunt Zhao and Aunt Zhou hastily took their leave of Bao-yu too.
‘I can’t come out,’ Bao-yu said. ‘Whatever you do, don’t let my aunt come in here.’
Then he added:
‘Cousin Dai-yu, stay a moment. There’s something I want to say.’
Xi-feng turned back, smiling at Dai-yu.
‘Someone wants a word with you.’
She gave Dai-yu a push into the room and went off with Li Wan.

segments.text: Bao-yu took hold of Dai-yu’s sleeve and could do nothing but grin. There was something in his heart, but he could not get it out. Dai-yu’s face grew redder in spite of herself, and she struggled to leave.
Suddenly Bao-yu gave a cry.
‘Oh, my head! What a pain!’
‘Serves you right. Amitabha!’ said Dai-yu.
‘I’m dying!’ he shouted.

He sprang three or four chi off the ground and began yelling and raving wildly. Dai-yu and the maids were terrified, and hurried to tell Lady Wang, Grandmother Jia and the others. Wang Zi-teng’s wife was there too. By the time they all arrived together, Bao-yu was brandishing knives and sticks, threatening to kill himself and throwing everything into turmoil. Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang shook so violently that their clothes trembled. Crying ‘My child!’ and ‘My own flesh!’, they broke into loud sobs.

The whole household was alarmed. Jia She, Lady Xing, Jia Zhen, Jia Zheng, Jia Lian, Jia Rong, Jia Yun, Jia Ping, Aunt Xue and Xue Pan, together with Zhou Rui’s wife and all the other married women-servants and maids, high and low, from the inner and outer quarters, came into the garden to see what was wrong.

segments.text: The garden was instantly a tangle of confusion. While everyone was at a loss, Xi-feng came slashing her way in with a gleaming steel knife. Any chicken she saw she killed, any dog she saw she killed; when she saw a person she tried to kill them too. The panic grew worse. Zhou Rui’s wife quickly brought several strong, bold women to seize her. They wrested the knife away and carried her back to her rooms. Patience, Felicity and the others wept as though heaven and earth were falling apart. Jia Zheng and the rest were now in a quandary: whichever of the two they attended to, they could not leave the other.

segments.text: The others’ agitation need hardly be described. Xue Pan alone was ten times busier than anyone else. He was afraid Aunt Xue would be knocked down in the crush, afraid Bao-chai would be seen, afraid Caltrop would be subjected to some indignity, for he knew that Jia Zhen and his like devoted their energies to women. He had more than he could manage. Then he caught a glimpse of Dai-yu’s graceful, delicate figure, and at once went weak with desire.

Everyone was talking at once. Some urged them to fetch a ritual exorcist to send the evil spirits away; others wanted a female spirit medium to perform a spirit dance; still others recommended Adept Zhang of the Jade Emperor Pavilion. The clamour of conflicting suggestions was endless. They tried every sort of medical treatment and prayer, consulted diviners and appealed to the gods, all without effect. It was close to sunset when Wang Zi-teng’s wife took her leave. Wang Zi-teng himself came the following day to ask after them.

segments.text: Then came people from the young Marquis Shi’s household, Lady Xing’s brothers and all the other relations. Some brought talisman water, others recommended monks and Taoists, but nothing did any good. Bao-yu and his cousin’s wife grew steadily more confused and lost all awareness of their surroundings. They lay in bed, their bodies hot as live coals, saying every kind of wild thing. By night the older women, the married servants and the maids dared not go near them. Both were therefore carried into Lady Wang’s principal apartments, and Jia Yun was put in charge of the pages who took turns keeping watch at night. Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang, Lady Xing, Aunt Xue and the others would not move an inch away, but sat round them weeping helplessly.

segments.text: Jia She and Jia Zheng were afraid that Grandmother Jia would ruin her health with crying. The lamps burnt night and day, the whole household was in distress, and neither man knew what more to do. Jia She still went everywhere in search of monks and Taoists. Jia Zheng, bitterly discouraged by their failure, tried to stop him.
‘Our children’s lot is Heaven’s decree. Human effort cannot force it. Their illness came without warning, and every treatment has failed. It seems Heaven means it to be so. We can only let them go.’

Jia She paid no attention and continued his frantic efforts, but to no avail. Three days passed. Xi-feng and Bao-yu lay in bed with scarcely a breath left in them. Everyone in the household was alarmed and said there was no hope. In haste they prepared the clothes and shoes in which the two were to be laid out. Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang, Jia Lian, Patience and Aroma wept more bitterly than anyone, forgetting food and sleep and declaring that they could not go on living. Aunt Zhao, Jia Huan and their like, of course, had what they wished for.

segments.text: On the morning of the fourth day, Grandmother Jia and the others were weeping round Bao-yu when he opened his eyes.
‘From now on I shan’t be in your house any more. Get everything ready and send me on my way.’
To Grandmother Jia it was as though her heart and liver had been torn out. Aunt Zhao, standing beside her, offered consolation.

‘Your Old Ladyship mustn’t grieve too much. The young gentleman can’t be saved now. Better dress him properly and let him go back sooner, so that he needn’t suffer so much. If you keep clinging to him and his last breath won’t leave him, he’ll suffer and have no peace in the other world either.’

segments.text: Before she had finished, Grandmother Jia spat in her face.

‘Rotten-tongued, good-for-nothing old woman! Who asked you to come chattering here? How do you know he’s suffering and has no peace in the other world? How do you know he can’t be saved? What do you stand to gain by wishing him dead? Don’t dream of it! If he dies, I’ll have your lives for his. Haven’t you always been egging them on to force him to write and study, till you’ve frightened the courage out of him? Doesn’t he run from his father like a mouse from a cat? Haven’t you strumpets been behind it all? Now you’ve driven him to death and got your wish. Which of you do you think I’ll spare?’

She wept as she cursed. Hearing this, Jia Zheng was more wretched than ever. He ordered Aunt Zhao away and came forward himself to soothe his mother as gently as he could. Just then someone came to report:
‘Both coffins are ready, sir. Will you come out and look at them?’
To Grandmother Jia this was oil on the fire.
‘Who has been making coffins?’ she cried, and kept shouting for the coffin-makers to be dragged in and beaten to death.

segments.text: While the turmoil was at its height and no one could bring it to an end, the faint tapping of a wooden fish prayer-block was heard, followed by a chanted invocation:

‘Homage to the Bodhisattva Who Releases Karmic Wrongs! Are your loved ones afflicted, your household in ruin? Has danger befallen you, or have evil spirits taken possession? We are skilled in curing all such troubles.’

Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang could not wait a moment after hearing this. They ordered someone to hurry out and bring the visitors in. Jia Zheng felt ill at ease, but how could he oppose his mother? Besides, he wondered how the words could be heard so clearly this far inside the house. Finding it strange himself, he sent to have them admitted. When everyone looked up, they saw a scabby-headed monk and a lame Taoist. What did the monk look like?

segments.text: ‘There are indeed two people under an evil influence,’ said Jia Zheng. ‘What talisman water have you to offer?’
The Taoist smiled.
‘You have a rare treasure in your own house. Why ask us for talisman water?’
Jia Zheng sensed a meaning in this and was stirred.
‘My son was born with a piece of precious jade, and the inscription says that it can dispel evil spirits. Yet it seems to have no power at all.’

‘You have no idea of that object’s wondrous uses, sir,’ said the monk. ‘It has now been beguiled by sensual pleasures, wealth and gain, and so has lost its power. Bring it out for us to recite over. That should put things right.’

segments.text: Having recited these lines, he stroked and handled the jade for a while, uttered some wild words, then handed it to Jia Zheng.

‘Its power has returned. It must not be profaned. Hang it from the lintel of the bedchamber and put both patients in that one room. Except for their own wives and mothers, no women must be allowed to intrude upon them. After thirty-three days, I guarantee they will be well, their illness gone and their former health restored.’

He turned to leave as he spoke. Jia Zheng hurried after them, still trying to speak, inviting the two to sit down for tea and wishing to offer a gift of thanks, but they were already gone. Grandmother Jia and the others kept sending people after them. There was not a trace to be found.

segments.text: They could only do as they had been told. Both patients were placed in Lady Wang’s bedchamber, with the jade suspended above the door. Lady Wang kept watch herself and would let no one else in. By evening the two actually began to come round and said they were hungry. Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang were as delighted as if they had found a treasure. Rice water was quickly cooked and given to them; their strength gradually returned and the evil influence began to recede. Only then did the household breathe freely again.

segments.text: Li Gong-cai, the three Jia girls, Bao-chai, Dai-yu, Patience, Aroma and the others were waiting for news in the outer room. When word came that the patients had taken rice water and regained their senses, Dai-yu was the first to speak.
‘Amitabha!’
Bao-chai turned and looked at her for a long while, then gave a sudden little laugh. No one understood.
‘Why are you laughing all of a sudden, Cousin Bao-chai?’ asked Xi-chun.

‘I was thinking how much busier the Buddha is than any of us,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘He has to expound the scriptures and preach the Law, and bring salvation to all living beings. Then Bao-yu and Cousin Feng fall ill, and with all the incense burnt and vows to be fulfilled, he has to grant blessings and avert calamity. Now they’re only just a little better, and he has Miss Lin’s marriage to arrange as well. Isn’t it funny how busy he is?’
Dai-yu blushed in spite of herself and spat in contempt.
‘You’re all wicked, every one of you! Heaven knows what deaths you’ll die. Instead of learning from decent people, you can only copy Cousin Feng’s cheap talk and rotten tongue.’
She flung aside the door-curtain and went out.

segments.text: After thirty-three days of convalescence, Bao-yu was strong again, and even the scars on his face had healed smooth. He returned to Prospect Garden, of which we need say no more. Now, during his illness Jia Yun had brought the household pages to keep watch, remaining there day and night. Crimson and the other maids were also attending Bao-yu, and after seeing one another for so many days they had gradually grown familiar. Crimson noticed a handkerchief in Jia Yun’s hand which looked very like the one she had lost. She wanted to ask him about it, but could hardly bring herself to do so. Then the monk and the Taoist unexpectedly arrived; none of the men was needed any longer, and Jia Yun went back to his tree-planting. She tried to put the matter out of her mind, but could not. She wanted to go and ask, yet feared that people would grow suspicious. While she was wavering, unable to settle to anything, a voice suddenly called outside the window.
‘Sister, are you in?’
Crimson looked out through a hole in the window-paper. It was Melilot, a little maid from the same courtyard.
‘I’m here. Come in.’
Melilot ran in, sat down on the bed and said with a smile, ‘What luck I’ve had!

segments.text: ‘I was washing things in the courtyard just now when Master Bao said some tea was to be sent to Miss Lin. Sister Hua gave it to me to take. Money had just come from Her Old Ladyship for Miss Lin, and she was sharing it out among her maids. When she saw me, she scooped up two handfuls for me too. I don’t know how much there is.

segments.text: ‘Will you keep it for me?’
She opened her handkerchief and poured out the money. Crimson counted it carefully, five by five and ten by ten, and put it away for her.
‘How have you really been feeling lately?’ Melilot asked. ‘If you ask me, you ought to go home for a couple of days and have a doctor see you. A couple of doses of medicine would soon put you right.’
‘What nonsense! There’s nothing wrong with me. Why should I go home?’
‘I’ve thought of something. Miss Lin is delicate and always taking medicine. Ask her for some. It would do just as well.’
‘Don’t be silly! You can’t take any medicine that happens to come along.’
‘But you can’t go on like this, hardly bothering to eat or drink. What will become of you?’
‘What does it matter? Better to die soon and have done with it!’
‘Why say things like that when there’s nothing the matter?’

segments.text: ‘What do you know of what’s on my mind?’ said Crimson.
Melilot nodded and thought for a moment.

‘Well, I can’t blame you. It’s hard to find a footing here. Take yesterday. Her Old Ladyship said everyone who’d looked after Master Bao through all those days of illness had worked hard. Now that he was well and the vows had all been fulfilled at the different temples, she wanted the people attending him rewarded according to their grades. They count us as too young to qualify, and I don’t complain of that. But why shouldn’t you be included? That’s what I can’t stomach. If Aroma got ten shares, I wouldn’t grudge her a thing. She deserves them. In all conscience, who would dare compare herself with her? Quite apart from all the care and trouble she takes, we couldn’t compete with her even if she didn’t. What makes me angry is Skybright, Mackerel and that lot, all reckoned among the best. They trade on their parents’ standing, and everyone makes up to them. Don’t you think it’s maddening?’
‘They aren’t worth getting angry about,’ said Crimson.

segments.text: ‘As the saying goes, “Though you build an awning a thousand li long, every feast must end.” Who stays with anyone all their life? Another three or five years, and we shall all be off about our own affairs. Who will care about anyone else then?’
These few words touched Melilot in spite of herself. Her eyes reddened, but she was ashamed to burst into tears for no apparent reason and forced a smile.
‘What you say is true. Only yesterday Master Bao was talking about how he would do up his rooms and have his clothes made, as though there were hundreds of years of fretting ahead of him.’

segments.text: Crimson gave a couple of cold little laughs and was about to speak when a little maid, whose hair had not yet been allowed to grow, came in carrying embroidery patterns and two sheets of paper.
‘Here are two patterns for you to trace.’
She flung them down beside Crimson, turned and ran.
‘Whose are they?’ Crimson called after her. ‘Can’t you wait to finish speaking before you run off? Is someone keeping steamed buns for you? Are you afraid they’ll get cold?’
‘Sister Mackerel’s!’ came the reply from outside the window, followed by a thudding of running feet.
Crimson threw the patterns aside in a temper and searched the drawer for a brush. After a long hunt she had found nothing but worn-out ones.
‘Where did I put that new brush the other day? Why can’t I remember?’
She fell into a reverie as she spoke, then after a moment smiled.
‘Of course. Oriole took it the other evening.’

segments.text: ‘Go and fetch it for me,’ she told Melilot.
‘Sister Hua’s waiting for me to help her lift a chest. You’ll have to go yourself.’
‘She’s waiting for you, and here you sit chattering? If I hadn’t asked you to fetch the brush, she wouldn’t be waiting for you at all, I suppose. You little wretch!’

She went out herself, left the House of Green Delights and headed straight for Bao-chai’s courtyard. Near the Drenched Blossoms Pavilion she saw Bao-yu’s nurse, Nurse Li, coming towards her. Crimson stopped and asked with a smile, ‘Where have you been, Granny Li? What brings you this way?’
Nurse Li stopped and clapped her hands.

‘Just think! Now he’s taken a fancy to that tree-planting Cloud or Rain or whatever the boy’s called, and he’s made me go and fetch him. If they hear of it up at the main house, there’ll be trouble again.’
‘And you really did as he asked and went to fetch him?’ Crimson asked, smiling.
‘What else could I do?’

‘He’s no fool. Why shouldn’t he come?’
‘Well, if he is coming, you ought to have brought him with you. It won’t do to have him wandering about on his own, stumbling in anywhere.’

segments.text: ‘Have I the time to walk about with him? I’ve told him, and now I’ll send a little maid or one of the old women to bring him in. That will do.’
With that Nurse Li went on her way, leaning on her stick. Crimson stood lost in thought and made no move to fetch the brush. Presently a little maid came running up.
‘What are you doing here, Sister Lin?’ she asked, seeing Crimson standing there.
Crimson looked up and recognised Zhui-er.
‘Where are you off to?’
‘They’ve told me to bring Master Yun in.’

She ran on. Crimson had just reached the gateway by Wasp-waist Bridge when she saw Zhui-er leading Jia Yun towards her. As he walked, Jia Yun let his eyes sweep over Crimson. Crimson pretended to be talking to Zhui-er, but she too stole a glance at Jia Yun. Their eyes met. Crimson blushed involuntarily, turned away and went towards Allspice Court.

segments.text: We shall leave her there. Jia Yun followed Zhui-er by a winding route to the House of Green Delights. She went in first to announce him, then came back to lead him inside. Looking about the courtyard, Jia Yun saw a few ornamental rocks and some plantains; over there, beneath a pine, two cranes were preening their feathers. Cages of every kind hung along a covered walk, filled with rare and beautiful birds.

segments.text: At the far end stood a small projecting building of five rooms, its screens all carved in fresh designs. Above them hung a tablet inscribed in four large characters, ‘Delight in Red and Joy in Green’.
‘So that is why they call it the House of Green Delights,’ Jia Yun thought. ‘Those are the words on the tablet.’
Just then a laughing voice came through the gauze window.
‘Come in, come in! How could I have forgotten you for two or three months?’

Recognising Bao-yu’s voice, Jia Yun hurried into the room. He looked up to find gold and colour shining everywhere, patterns and inscriptions dazzling his eyes, but no sign of Bao-yu. Turning his head, he saw a large full-length mirror to his left. Two maids of about the same age, fifteen or sixteen, came out from behind it.
‘Please take a seat in the inner room, Master Yun.’

Not daring even to look them straight in the face, Jia Yun hastily assented. He passed through another green-gauze screen. There was a small bed decorated with filled-in lacquer, hung with scarlet curtains patterned with scattered flowers in gold. Bao-yu, in his everyday clothes with his slippers loosely on, was reclining on the bed with a book. At the sight of Jia Yun he tossed it aside and rose, all smiles.

segments.text: Jia Yun hurried forward to pay his respects. Bao-yu invited him to sit, and he took a chair lower down the room.
‘When I saw you that month, I told you to come to the study,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Then one thing happened after another, and I forgot all about you.’
‘It was only my bad luck,’ Jia Yun replied, smiling. ‘And then you fell ill, Uncle. Are you quite well again now?’
‘Quite well. I hear you worked hard for several days.’
‘It was no more than my duty. Your recovery is a blessing for our whole family.’

As they spoke, a maid brought him tea. Jia Yun went on talking to Bao-yu, but glanced sideways at her: a slender figure, a longish face, a silvery-pink jacket, a dark satin waistcoat and a finely pleated skirt of white damask. It was none other than Aroma. During Bao-yu’s illness, Jia Yun had spent two days in the inner quarters and learnt the names and faces of half the people of consequence there.

segments.text: He also knew that Aroma’s position in Bao-yu’s rooms was different from the others’. Seeing her bring him tea, with Bao-yu sitting beside him, he rose hastily, smiling.
‘Sister, why should you pour tea for me? I’m no guest here in my uncle’s rooms. Let me pour it myself.’
‘Just sit down,’ Bao-yu said. ‘Must you stand on ceremony even with the maids?’
‘You may say so, Uncle, but how could I take liberties with the young ladies who serve you?’
As he spoke he sat down to drink his tea.

segments.text: Bao-yu chatted with him about things of no importance: whose actors were good, whose garden was fine, who had pretty maids, who gave sumptuous dinners, who owned rare curiosities and who had unusual treasures. Jia Yun could only follow his lead. After a time, seeing that Bao-yu was growing listless, he rose to take his leave. Bao-yu made no great effort to keep him, merely saying, ‘Come whenever you have time.’ He told the little maid Zhui-er to show him out again.

segments.text: Once they had left the House of Green Delights, Jia Yun looked about and saw no one near. He began to slacken his pace, drawing Zhui-er into conversation with one question after another.
‘How old are you? What’s your name? What work do your parents do? How many years have you been in Uncle Bao’s rooms? How much do you get a month? How many girls are there in his rooms altogether?’
Zhui-er answered each question in turn.
‘That girl you were speaking to just now,’ Jia Yun went on, ‘is she called Crimson?’
‘Yes, she’s called Crimson,’ said Zhui-er with a smile.

segments.text: ‘Why do you ask about her?’
‘She was asking you about a handkerchief just now. I happen to have picked one up.’
Zhui-er smiled.

‘She’s asked me several times whether I’ve seen her handkerchief. As if I had time to bother about such things! Today she asked again, and said she’d give me something if I found it for her. That was just now, at the gate of Allspice Court. You heard her yourself, Master Yun. I’m not making it up. Do give it to me, dear Master Yun, if you’ve found it. I want to see what she gives me in return.’

segments.text: Now, when Jia Yun had come into the garden to plant trees the previous month, he had picked up a gauze handkerchief. He knew that someone in the garden must have dropped it, but had no idea who, and so had not dared to do anything rash. Hearing Crimson ask Zhui-er about it, he knew at last that it was hers, and felt delighted at his good fortune. With Zhui-er pressing him for it, he quickly formed a plan. He took a handkerchief of his own from his sleeve and said to her with a smile, ‘You can have it. But if she gives you a reward, you mustn’t keep it from me.’
Zhui-er agreed readily, took the handkerchief, escorted Jia Yun out and returned to look for Crimson. Of that, no more for the present.
After sending Jia Yun away, Bao-yu lay back listlessly on the bed and seemed to be drifting off. Aroma came over, sat on the edge of the bed and gave him a push.
‘Going to sleep again? It’s so dull in here. Why don’t you go out for a walk?’
Bao-yu took her hand and smiled.
‘I want to, but I can’t bear to leave you.’
‘Come along, get up!’ she said, smiling, and pulled him to his feet.

segments.text: ‘But where am I to go? Everything is so tiresome.’
‘You’ll feel better once you’re out. Drooping about like this only makes you more bored and restless.’

Still listless, Bao-yu could only do as she said. He drifted out of the room, played with the birds along the covered walk for a while, then went outside the courtyard and watched the goldfish in the Drenched Blossoms stream. Suddenly two young deer came darting down the slope like arrows. Bao-yu was wondering what could be the matter when Jia Lan appeared behind them with a little bow. Seeing Bao-yu ahead of him, he stopped and smiled.
‘You’re at home, Second Uncle! I thought you’d gone out.’
‘Up to mischief again? What do you want to shoot them for? They’ve done nothing to you.’
‘I’m not studying just now. What else is there to do? I’m practising riding and shooting.’
‘When you fall and knock your teeth out, perhaps you’ll stop practising.’

segments.text: As he spoke, Bao-yu let his feet carry him on until he reached a courtyard gate. The bamboos rose thick as phoenix tails, murmuring softly like dragons. Looking up, he saw the three characters for ‘Naiad’s House’ on the tablet above the gate. He wandered in. Bamboo blinds hung to the ground, and not a human voice disturbed the stillness. At the window he caught a faint fragrance stealing through the green gauze. He put his face close and peered inside. Suddenly a long, soft sigh reached him, followed by the words:
‘“Day after day, thoughts of love leave me drowsy and dazed.”’
Something stirred and tingled in Bao-yu’s heart. Looking again, he saw Dai-yu stretching herself on the bed.

‘Why “Day after day, thoughts of love leave me drowsy and dazed”?’ he asked from outside, laughing. As he spoke, he lifted the door-curtain and came in. Dai-yu realised that she had let herself go. She blushed, hid her face in her sleeve and turned towards the wall, pretending to be asleep.

segments.text: Bao-yu had just come over to turn her towards him when Dai-yu’s nurse and two old women followed him in.
‘Your cousin is asleep. Please come back when she wakes.’
They had scarcely spoken when Dai-yu turned and sat up.
‘Who’s asleep?’ she asked, smiling.
Seeing her up, the women smiled too.
‘We thought you were asleep, miss.’
Then they called to Nightingale, ‘Your young lady’s awake. Come and attend to her,’ and went away.

segments.text: Sitting on the bed, Dai-yu raised a hand to smooth the hair at her temples and smiled at Bao-yu.
‘What do you mean by coming in when I’m asleep?’
The sight of her starry eyes still faintly misted with drowsiness and her fragrant cheeks flushed pink had already set his senses reeling. He sank sideways into a chair.
‘What were you saying just now?’ he asked with a smile.
‘I wasn’t saying anything.’
‘You’ll get a flick on the forehead! I heard every word.’

segments.text: As they were speaking, Nightingale came in.
‘Nightingale, pour me a bowl of your best tea,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
‘Where would we get good tea? If it’s good tea you want, you’ll have to wait until Aroma comes.’
‘Don’t mind him,’ Dai-yu said. ‘Fetch some water for me first.’
‘He’s a guest,’ Nightingale said, smiling. ‘Naturally I must pour his tea before I fetch your water.’
She went to pour the tea.
‘Good girl,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.

‘“If I shared the lovers’ bed-curtains with your loving mistress,
How could I bear to fold the quilt and make the bed?”’
Dai-yu’s face fell at once.
‘Cousin Bao, what did you say?’
‘I didn’t say anything,’ he replied, still smiling.
Dai-yu began to cry.

‘So this is the latest fashion! You hear coarse talk outside and come and repeat it to me. You read filthy books and use them to make fun of me. I’ve become something for you gentlemen to amuse yourselves with.’
Still crying, she got off the bed and made for the door. Bao-yu panicked, not knowing what to do, and hurried after her.
‘Dear cousin, I deserved to die for saying it. Don’t tell on me.

segments.text: ‘If I ever dare do it again, may a boil grow on my mouth and my tongue rot away.’
At that moment Aroma came in.
‘Come back and get dressed at once. The Master wants you.’
Bao-yu felt as though a thunderbolt had burst over his head. He forgot everything else and hurried back to dress. Leaving the garden, he found Tealeaf waiting at the inner gate.
‘What’s it about?’ he asked.
‘Come along, sir. You have to go and see him anyway. You’ll find out when you get there.’
As he spoke, Tealeaf urged Bao-yu on.

segments.text: They passed the great hall, Bao-yu still full of misgivings. Suddenly a burst of loud laughter came from the corner of a wall. He turned, and Xue Pan jumped out, clapping his hands.
‘If I hadn’t said Uncle wanted you, how could I have got you out so quickly?’

Tealeaf knelt down, laughing too. Bao-yu stood bewildered for some time before he understood that Xue Pan had tricked him into coming out. Xue Pan hurriedly bowed and clasped his hands in apology, begging him not to punish the boy.
‘I made him do it.’
There was nothing Bao-yu could do. He could only smile and ask, ‘Trick me if you like, but why bring my father into it? I shall tell Aunt and let her judge whether that’s a proper thing to do.’
‘My dear cousin, all I wanted was to get you out quickly. I forgot that I shouldn’t mention him. Another day you can trick me and bring my father into it. Then we’ll be even.’
‘Oh, oh, now you’re worse than ever!’ said Bao-yu. Then he turned to Tealeaf. ‘You treacherous little bastard! What are you still kneeling for?’
Tealeaf quickly kowtowed and got up.

segments.text: ‘I wouldn’t have disturbed you for anything less,’ Xue Pan said, ‘but tomorrow, the third of the fifth month, is my birthday. And who should turn up but Cheng Ri-xing from the antiques trade? Heaven knows where he found them, but he brought me fresh lotus roots this thick and this long, floury and crisp, watermelons this big, a fresh sturgeon this long, and a Siamese pig this size, smoked with aromatic cypress, a tribute gift from Siam. Tell me those aren’t four rarities! The fish and the pig are only hard to get because they cost so much. But how he managed to grow lotus roots and melons like that, I can’t imagine. I gave some to Mother at once, and hurried some over to your grandmother and my uncle and aunt. Now I’ve kept a little for myself, but I was afraid of using up my good fortune by eating it all alone. I thought and thought, and apart from me you’re the only person worthy of eating it. So I’ve specially asked you over. And by good luck the boy who sings has just arrived. How about spending the day enjoying ourselves?’

segments.text: After tea, Xue Pan ordered the wine brought in. He had scarcely finished speaking before the pages were bustling about in all directions, and only after a good deal of activity was everything ready and everyone seated. Bao-yu found the melons and lotus roots as remarkable as promised.
‘My birthday present hasn’t even reached you, and here I am enjoying your hospitality already,’ he said with a smile.
‘So you are! What are you giving me tomorrow?’
‘What have I to give? Money, food, clothes, any of those things, none of them is really mine. Only a piece of my own calligraphy or a picture I’ve painted would count as something of my own.’

segments.text: Xue Pan laughed.

‘Speaking of pictures, you’ve reminded me. Yesterday I saw an erotic painting at someone’s house, really beautifully done. There was a lot of writing on it too. I didn’t look closely at that, just at the signature. It was painted by “Geng Huang”. Absolutely marvellous!’

Bao-yu was puzzled. He had seen a fair number of old and new paintings and works of calligraphy, but where had this ‘Geng Huang’ come from? After thinking for some time, he suddenly began to laugh. He asked for a brush and wrote two characters on his palm.
‘Are you sure you read “Geng Huang” correctly?’
‘Of course I did!’
Bao-yu opened his hand for him to see.
‘Could it have been these two characters? They aren’t very different from “Geng Huang”.’
They all looked. The characters were ‘Tang Yin’.
‘Those must have been the characters,’ they said, laughing. ‘Perhaps your eyes were playing tricks on you for a moment.’
Xue Pan felt rather foolish, but laughed it off.
‘Who knows whether he’s “Sugar Silver” or “Fruit Silver”?’

segments.text: As they were speaking, a page announced that Mr Feng had arrived. Bao-yu knew this must be Feng Zi-ying, the son of Feng Tang, General of Divine Valour. Xue Pan and the others all called out, ‘Show him in!’ Before they had finished, Feng Zi-ying was already coming in, laughing and talking as he walked. Everyone rose from the table to offer him a seat.
‘Very nice!’ Feng Zi-ying said with a laugh.

segments.text: ‘No more going out, then? Just enjoying yourselves at home!’
Bao-yu and Xue Pan both smiled.
‘We haven’t seen you for ages. Is your honoured father keeping well?’
‘Thanks to your good wishes, my father is well enough. My mother caught a chill recently and has been unwell for a couple of days.’
Noticing some bruises on his face, Xue Pan asked with a laugh, ‘Who have you been fighting this time? You’re sporting a fine signboard!’
‘Ever since I injured Commandant Qiu’s son that time, I’ve made a point of not losing my temper,’ Feng Zi-ying replied, smiling. ‘Why should I be fighting again?

segments.text: ‘This mark on my face came from a hare-hawk catching me with its wing when we were out hunting on Iron-net Mountain the other day.’
‘When was that?’ Bao-yu asked.
‘We left on the twenty-eighth of the third month and only came back the day before yesterday.’
‘No wonder I didn’t see you at Mr Shen’s dinner the other day, on the third or fourth. I meant to ask about you, but somehow forgot. Did you go on your own, or was your honoured father there too?’

‘It was because Father was going that I had no choice but to go. Do you think I’ve gone mad with idleness? Why go looking for hardship when the few of us could be drinking wine and listening to songs? This time there was great good fortune in the midst of great misfortune.’
Seeing that he had finished his tea, Xue Pan and the rest urged him to join them at the table and tell his story at leisure. Feng Zi-ying stood up.
‘By rights I should stay and drink a few cups with you. But there’s something of the greatest importance I have to report to Father in person when I get back. I really can’t accept.’
Neither Xue Pan nor Bao-yu nor anyone else would hear of it. They caught hold of him and would not let him go.

segments.text: ‘This is extraordinary!’ Feng Zi-ying said with a laugh. ‘In all the years we’ve known one another, when have you ever treated me like this? I truly can’t stay. If you insist on my drinking, bring me a large cup and I’ll have two.’
They had to agree. Xue Pan held the wine-pot and Bao-yu the cups, and two large beakers were filled. Feng Zi-ying remained standing and drained them straight off.
‘At least finish telling us about this “good fortune in misfortune” before you go,’ Bao-yu said.
‘There’s no time to do it justice today. I mean to give a party specially, so that I can invite you over and tell you all about it. Besides, I have a favour to ask.’
Taking their hands in farewell, he made for the door.

segments.text: ‘Now you’ve got us all worked up, you can’t just leave it there,’ Xue Pan said. ‘When are you going to invite us? Tell us, and save us wondering.’
‘Ten days at most. Eight at the least.’
As he spoke, Feng Zi-ying went out, mounted his horse and rode away. The others returned to their places, drank a while longer and then dispersed.

When Bao-yu returned to the garden, Aroma, who thought he had gone to see Jia Zheng, was still worrying about what might have happened to him. Seeing him come home tipsy, she asked what had happened, and he told her everything.
‘Here was I waiting with my heart in my mouth, while you were off enjoying yourself. You might at least have sent someone with a message.’
‘I meant to send word. But when Mr Feng came, it went clean out of my head.’

segments.text: They were still talking when Bao-chai came in with a smile.
‘You’ve been enjoying rare delicacies without us.’
‘They came from your family,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Naturally you had the first taste.’
Bao-chai shook her head and smiled.

‘My brother did specially invite me to eat some yesterday. I wouldn’t, and told him to keep them for guests and presents. I know my lot in life is too humble, my share of good fortune too small, to deserve such food.’
A maid brought tea, and she drank it while they chatted. We need say no more of that.

segments.text: Now Dai-yu, having heard that Jia Zheng had summoned Bao-yu and finding him gone all day, had also been anxious on his behalf. After supper, when she heard that he was back, she wanted to go and ask him what had happened. She strolled over, saw Bao-chai enter his courtyard and followed. At the Drenched Blossoms Bridge she came upon all kinds of waterfowl bathing in the pool. She could not tell what they were called, but their brilliant markings were so beautiful that she stopped to watch them for a while. When she went on to the House of Green Delights, she found the courtyard gate shut and knocked.

segments.text: Unfortunately, Skybright had just quarrelled with Emerald and was in a bad temper. Bao-chai’s arrival had given her someone else to be angry with, and she was grumbling in the courtyard.
‘Whether she has anything to come for or not, she’s always here, sitting on and on, keeping us from our sleep till all hours!’
When she heard another knock at the gate, she grew angrier still. Without asking who it was, she called out, ‘We’ve all gone to bed. Come back tomorrow!’

Dai-yu knew the maids’ ways. They were used to playing together, and she thought perhaps the girl inside had failed to recognise her voice and was refusing to open because she took her for another maid. She therefore raised her voice.
‘It’s me. Aren’t you going to open the gate?’
But Skybright still did not recognise her.
