segments.text: ‘I don’t care who you are,’ she snapped. ‘Master Bao’s orders are that no one is to be let in!’
Dai-yu stood outside, stunned with anger. She was about to call out and challenge her, but thought better of provoking a quarrel.

‘They say my aunt’s house is as good as my own, but I am a guest here all the same. Both my parents are dead. I have no one to turn to and depend on their household for a home. If I really lose my temper, I shall only make myself ridiculous.’

At these thoughts her tears began to fall. She could neither bring herself to go away nor bear to stay. While she stood there uncertain, laughter and voices came from within. She listened: they were Bao-yu’s and Bao-chai’s. Angrier than ever, she turned the matter over in her mind until she suddenly remembered what had happened that morning.

‘He must be angry because I threatened to tell on him. But I never did tell! You might have found that out before taking such a grudge against me. You won’t let me in today, but can you avoid seeing me tomorrow?’

The more she thought, the more she grieved. Heedless of the cold dew on the moss and the chill wind along the flower-path, she stood alone in the shadow of the flowers at a corner of the wall and began to sob bitterly.

segments.text: Now Dai-yu was still weeping when she heard the courtyard gate open and saw Bao-chai come out, with Bao-yu, Aroma and a whole party seeing her off. She was about to go up and question Bao-yu, but feared that asking him in front of everyone would embarrass him and make things awkward. She slipped aside and let Bao-chai pass. Only after Bao-yu and the others had gone back in and shut the gate did she come out again. Still looking towards it, she shed a few more tears. At last, feeling the futility of it, she turned and went home, where she listlessly removed what remained of her make-up.

segments.text: Nightingale and Snowgoose were well acquainted with Dai-yu’s ways. She would sit idle and dejected, frowning or sighing; and when nothing whatever seemed to have happened, for no reason that anyone could discover, her tears would begin again and scarcely ever dry. At first people had tried to comfort her, fearing that she missed her parents or her home, or had suffered some slight. They had done what they could to soothe and reassure her. But as month followed month and year followed year, and she was still the same, they grew accustomed to it and ceased to take much notice. So now no one troubled her. They left her to sit in her misery and went to bed themselves. Dai-yu leaned against the bed-rail, her arms clasped round her knees and her eyes full of tears, as motionless as an image carved in wood or moulded in clay. She sat like this until well into the second watch before at last going to sleep. Nothing further happened that night.

segments.text: The next day was the twenty-sixth of the fourth month. As it happened, the solar term Grain in Ear began that day in the wei hour. An old custom required offerings of every kind to be set out on this day to honour the Flower God and bid him farewell. Once Grain in Ear had come, it was said, summer had arrived, the flowers would all shed their petals, and the Flower God must relinquish his office. He therefore needed a proper send-off. The custom was particularly favoured among the women, and everyone in Prospect Garden was up early. Some of the girls wove petals and willow twigs into miniature sedan chairs and horses; others folded figured silks, brocades and gauzes into standards, pennons and banners, all fastened with coloured thread. These things hung from every tree and every flowering spray. Embroidered ribbons fluttered throughout the garden, and the flower-laden branches tossed and swayed. As for the girls themselves, so beautifully were they dressed that peach blossom blushed and apricot blossom yielded, swallows envied them and orioles were put to shame. There was no describing it all.

segments.text: Bao-chai, Ying-chun, Tan-chun, Xi-chun, Li Wan and Xi-feng were amusing themselves in the garden, together with Qiao-jie, Da-jie, Caltrop and all the maids. Only Dai-yu was missing.
‘Where is Cousin Lin?’ Ying-chun asked. ‘What a lazy girl! Surely she can’t still be asleep?’
‘Wait here,’ said Bao-chai. ‘I’ll go and pester her into coming.’
Leaving the others, she went straight towards Naiad’s House.

segments.text: On the way she met Wen-guan and the other eleven girls of the troupe coming to join them. They greeted her and chatted for a while. Bao-chai turned and pointed.
‘They’re all over there. Go and find them. I’m just fetching Miss Lin, and then I’ll come.’

She continued along the winding path towards Naiad’s House. Suddenly she looked up and saw Bao-yu go in. She stopped, lowered her head and considered. Bao-yu and Dai-yu had grown up together. As cousins they often took little heed of what might be thought of their intimacy, and passed from teasing and laughter to pleasure or anger without warning. Besides, Dai-yu was always prone to suspicion and sulks. If she herself went in after him now, it would put Bao-yu in an awkward position and make Dai-yu suspicious. No, she had better turn back. Having made up her mind, she did so.

segments.text: She was just going to find the other girls when she caught sight of a pair of jade-pale butterflies ahead, each as large as a round fan. One rose while the other dipped, dancing into the wind, a delightful sight. Wanting to catch them for fun, Bao-chai took a fan from her sleeve and went down on to the grass after them. Up and down, to and fro they flew, threading the flowers and passing the willows, until they seemed about to cross the water. They drew Bao-chai after them, stepping softly all the way to Dripping Emerald Pavilion in the middle of the pond. Fragrant sweat was streaming from her and she was panting in little breaths. She had lost all desire to catch the butterflies and was about to turn back when she heard voices whispering inside the pavilion. It stood over the water, approached on all four sides by covered walks and winding bridges, and its carved lattice windows were covered with paper.

segments.text: Hearing the voices from outside, Bao-chai stopped and listened closely.
‘Look at this handkerchief. If it really is the one you lost, take it. If not, it must go back to Master Yun.’
Another voice answered:
‘Of course it’s mine! Give it here.’
‘And what will you give me for finding it? You don’t expect me to do it for nothing, do you?’
‘I’ve promised you a reward. Of course I shan’t cheat you.’
‘You must reward me for finding it and bringing it to you. But what about the person who picked it up? Aren’t you going to give him anything?’

segments.text: The other replied:
‘Don’t talk nonsense. He’s a gentleman. If he finds something of mine, naturally he ought to give it back. What should I give him a reward for?’
‘But what am I to tell him if you don’t? Besides, he said over and over that I wasn’t to give it to you unless there was something for him.’
After a pause came the answer:
‘Very well. Take this one of mine and give it to him as his reward. But what if you tell anyone? You must swear you won’t.’

segments.text: Bao-chai was alarmed to hear this.

‘No wonder fornicators and thieves have always had their wits about them!’ she thought. ‘Once they open the windows and find me here, won’t they be ashamed! And that voice sounded very like Crimson from Bao-yu’s rooms. She’s always been conceited and ambitious, a thoroughly crafty, difficult creature. Now I’ve heard her secret, she may turn on me in desperation. A desperate man rebels, a cornered dog will leap a wall. She might make trouble, and I should find myself in a very awkward position. Even if I hurry away, I don’t suppose I can escape in time. I shall have to try the golden cicada’s trick of slipping out of its shell.’
Before she had finished thinking, she heard a creak. Deliberately making her footsteps louder, she called out with a laugh:
‘Little Pin-pin, let’s see where you can hide!’
She made a show of hurrying after someone. Crimson and Zhui-er inside had only just pushed a window open. At the sight of Bao-chai calling out and running past, both stood dumbfounded.

segments.text: Bao-chai turned to them with a smile.
‘Where have you hidden Miss Lin?’
‘We haven’t seen her,’ said Zhui-er.

‘I saw her from the other side of the stream just now, crouching here and playing with the water. I meant to creep up and give her a fright, but before I could reach her she saw me, slipped round to the east and disappeared. I wonder if she’s hidden herself in here.’
As she spoke, she went in and made a pretence of looking round. Then she came straight out and walked away, saying:
‘She must have crawled into one of the grottoes again. A snake might give her a bite for her pains!’

segments.text: ‘Miss Lin was crouching here. She must have heard us!’
Zhui-er too was silent for a long while.
‘What are we to do?’ Crimson asked again.
‘Even if she did hear, what’s it to anyone?’ said Zhui-er. ‘Let everyone mind their own business, and that’s the end of it.’
‘It wouldn’t be so bad if Miss Bao had heard,’ said Crimson. ‘But Miss Lin has such a sharp tongue, and nothing escapes her. If she’s heard us and lets something slip, what shall we do then?’
They were still talking when Wen-guan, Caltrop, Chess, Scribe and the others came up to the pavilion. The two girls had to drop the subject and join in their laughter and chatter.

segments.text: Just then they saw Xi-feng standing on the slope, beckoning. Crimson hastily left the others and ran over to her.
‘What can I do for you, ma’am?’ she asked with a smile.
Xi-feng looked her over. Seeing a neat, pretty girl who knew how to speak, she smiled too.

‘My maids haven’t come into the garden with me today. I’ve just remembered something and want to send someone out, but I don’t know whether you’re capable of it. Can you give a message without leaving anything out?’
‘Just tell me what to say, ma’am. If I leave anything out and spoil your business, you may punish me as you please.’
‘Which young lady do you serve?’ Xi-feng asked, smiling. ‘If I send you off and she comes looking for you, I shall know what to tell her.’
‘I’m in Master Bao’s rooms.’
‘Oh!’ Xi-feng laughed.

segments.text: ‘So you’re one of Bao-yu’s girls! No wonder. Very well. Go to my rooms and tell Sister Patience that there’s a roll of silver on the table in the outer room, underneath the stand holding the Ru-ware plate. It’s a hundred and sixty taels, the embroiderers’ wages. When Zhang Cai’s wife comes to collect it, have her watch while it’s weighed, then give it to her to take away. And there’s a little purse further inside, by the head of the bed. Bring that to me.’

segments.text: Crimson set off at once. When she returned, Xi-feng was no longer on the slope. She saw Chess coming out of a grotto and standing there tying her skirt, and hurried over.
‘Sister, do you know where Mrs Lian has gone?’
‘I didn’t notice,’ said Chess.
Crimson turned and looked about. Over by the pond, Tan-chun and Bao-chai were watching the fish. She went up and asked with a deferential smile:
‘Can you tell me where Mrs Lian has gone, young ladies?’
‘Try your eldest mistress’s courtyard,’ said Tan-chun.

Crimson went on towards Sweet-rice Village. Coming straight towards her were Skybright, Mackerel, Emerald, Purple Silk, Musk, Scribe, Picture, Oriole and a crowd of others. The moment Skybright saw her, she said:
‘Just you go on running wild! The courtyard flowers aren’t watered, the birds aren’t fed, the tea stove isn’t lit, and you’re out here strolling about.’
‘Master Bao said yesterday that the flowers weren’t to be watered today,’ Crimson answered. ‘Every other day is enough.

segments.text: ‘You might first ask whether I’ve been strolling,’ Crimson said. ‘Mrs Lian sent me with a message and told me to fetch something.’
She held up the purse for them to see. At this they fell silent, and everyone went their separate ways. Skybright gave a cold laugh.

‘So that’s it! She’s flown up to a higher branch and thinks we’re beneath her now. She may have managed half a word, but does the mistress even know her name yet? And look how pleased she is with herself! Running an errand once or twice is nothing. She’ll still have to do as she’s told afterwards. If she’s so clever, let her leave this garden today and stay on her high branch for good. Then we’ll see!’
Still talking, she went on her way.

segments.text: It was no use arguing. Crimson swallowed her anger and went to find Xi-feng. Sure enough, when she reached Li Wan’s rooms, Xi-feng was there talking to her. Crimson went up to report.

segments.text: ‘And what did she tell him, to suit my wishes?’ Xi-feng asked with a smile.
Crimson replied:

‘Sister Patience said, “Our mistress sends her greetings to the mistress here. Our Second Master has been away from home. Although there has been a delay of two days, the mistress need have no worries. When the Fifth Mistress is better, our mistress will come with the Fifth Mistress to visit the mistress here. The Fifth Mistress sent someone the other day to say that the uncle’s wife had sent word, asking after the mistress and also asking the married daughter of this house for two Wondrous All-Purpose Longevity Pills. If any can be had, the mistress need only send someone to bring them to our mistress. When someone goes that way tomorrow, they can take them along to the uncle’s wife over there.”’

segments.text: Before she had quite finished, Li Wan exclaimed:
‘Oh dear! I can’t make head or tail of all that. Nothing but mistresses and masters!’
‘No wonder you can’t,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘There are four or five households involved.’
She turned back to Crimson with a smile.

‘Good girl! Well done for getting it all straight. You’re not like those others, twisting and squirming and buzzing like mosquitoes. You’ve no idea, sister-in-law: apart from the few people I always have at hand, I dread having to speak to anyone nowadays. They have to stretch every sentence out and chop it into two or three bits, weighing each word, putting on airs, humming and hawing. They make me burn with impatience, and they haven’t the least idea! Our Patience used to do it too. I asked her, “Must you buzz like a mosquito to be a beauty?” It took several tellings before she improved.’

segments.text: Li Gong-cai laughed.
‘Of course, they should all be brazen, down-at-heel rogues like you!’
‘Now this girl is good,’ Xi-feng went on. ‘She hasn’t said much on either of these two occasions, but you can hear how briskly she gets to the point.’
She smiled at Crimson.
‘You shall come and wait on me tomorrow. I’ll take you for my daughter. With a little training from me, you’ll make something of yourself.’
Crimson burst out laughing.

‘What are you laughing at?’ Xi-feng demanded. ‘You think I’m young, only a few years older than you, and here I am setting up as your mother? Don’t flatter yourself! Just ask about. There are people far older than you begging to call me Mother, and I won’t give them the time of day. I’m doing you an honour!’
‘That isn’t what I’m laughing at, ma’am,’ Crimson said, smiling. ‘You’ve got the generations wrong. My mother is your daughter, and now you want me for a daughter too.’
‘Who is your mother?’
‘You mean you don’t know her?’ Li Gong-cai asked with a laugh.

segments.text: ‘She’s Lin Zhi-xiao’s daughter.’
Xi-feng was astonished.
‘Oh! So she’s his girl!’
Then she laughed.

‘You couldn’t get a sound out of Lin Zhi-xiao or his wife with an awl. I’m always saying what a well-matched pair they are, one deaf as heaven and the other dumb as earth. Who would have expected them to produce such a clever girl? How old are you?’

segments.text: ‘Seventeen,’ Crimson replied.
Asked her name, she said:
‘It used to be Hong-yu, “red jade”, but because the jade was the same as Master Bao’s, they only call me Crimson now.’
Xi-feng frowned and turned her head aside.
‘What a nuisance! You’d think jade had done someone some good. Jade for you, jade for me!’
Then she went on:

‘If she’s so willing to come with me, what was her mother about? I told her, “Lai Da’s wife has so much on her hands these days, I don’t suppose she knows who’s who in this household. Pick me out two good maids, will you?” She agreed readily enough. But instead of choosing anyone, she sent this girl somewhere else. Would it have been so dreadful to put her with me?’
‘Now you’re being suspicious again,’ Li Wan said with a laugh.

segments.text: ‘The girl came in before you asked her mother. How can you blame her?’
‘In that case, I’ll speak to Bao-yu tomorrow,’ said Xi-feng. ‘He can get someone else and this girl shall come with me. Though I don’t know whether she wants to.’
Crimson smiled.

‘It isn’t for us to say what we want or don’t want. But if I waited on you, ma’am, I could learn to judge people’s looks and moods, how to behave indoors and out, with those above me and below me, and gain some knowledge of affairs both great and small.’
Just then one of Lady Wang’s maids came to fetch Xi-feng, who took her leave of Li Gong-cai. Crimson returned to the House of Green Delights. We may leave her there.

segments.text: Let us now return to Dai-yu. Having slept so poorly, she rose late the next morning. When she heard that all the girls were in the garden holding a farewell gathering for the flowers, she was afraid they would laugh at her for being foolish and lazy. She hurried to wash and dress and came out. She had just reached the courtyard when Bao-yu entered, smiling.
‘My dear cousin, did you tell on me yesterday? You kept me worrying all night.’
Dai-yu turned and called to Nightingale:

‘Tidy the room and lower one of the gauze window panels. When the big swallow comes back, let down the curtain and hold it with the lion-shaped weight. Once you’ve lit the incense, put the cover on the burner.’

Still speaking, she walked on towards the gate. Bao-yu supposed that she was still upset about what had happened at midday yesterday. He knew nothing of the affair that evening, and went on bowing and making apologetic gestures. Dai-yu would not so much as look him in the face. She went out on her own and straight off to find the other girls. Bao-yu was bewildered.
‘From the way she’s behaving,’ he thought, ‘it doesn’t seem to be yesterday’s business. But I came back late yesterday and didn’t see her. I can’t have offended her in any other way.’

segments.text: Thinking this, he could not help hurrying after her. Bao-chai and Tan-chun were over there watching the cranes. When Dai-yu arrived, the three stood talking together. Presently Tan-chun saw Bao-yu and smiled.
‘Brother Bao, how are you? I haven’t seen you for three whole days.’
‘And how are you, sister?’ he asked with a smile. ‘I was only asking our eldest sister-in-law about you the other day.’
‘Come over here, brother. I want a word with you.’
He followed her to a pomegranate tree.
‘Has Father sent for you at all these last few days?’ she asked.
‘No,’ Bao-yu said, smiling.
‘I thought I heard yesterday that he’d called you out.’
‘Someone must have got it wrong. He hasn’t sent for me.’
Tan-chun smiled again.

‘I’ve saved another ten-odd strings of cash these last few months. Take it, and next time you go out, bring me back some good calligraphy or paintings, or some nice little things, light and delicate.’

segments.text: ‘I wander all over, inside the city and out, through great arcades and little temples,’ Bao-yu said, ‘and I’ve never found anything really novel and finely made. It’s all antiques in gold, jade, bronze or porcelain that there’s nowhere to put, or else silks, food and clothes.’

‘Who wants those?’ said Tan-chun. ‘Something like the little willow basket you bought last time, or the incense box hollowed out of a whole bamboo root, or the little clay stove. Those are just the things. I loved them more than I can say, but everyone else took a fancy to them too and carried them off as if they were treasures.’
‘Oh, so that’s what you want!’ Bao-yu laughed. ‘Those cost next to nothing. Give the boys five hundred cash and they’ll bring you a cartload.’

segments.text: Bao-yu laughed.

‘Talking of shoes reminds me of something. I was wearing them that day and happened to meet Father. He didn’t like the look of them at all and asked who had made them. I didn’t dare breathe a word about my Third Sister. I said they were a present from my uncle’s wife for my birthday the other day. When he heard they were from my uncle’s wife, he couldn’t very well object, though after a while he did say, “What’s the point? A waste of labour and good silk, making things like that.” When I came back I told Aroma. She said that was nothing: Aunt Zhao was furious and full of complaints. “Her own brother goes about with his shoes and stockings hanging off him, and no one sees! Yet she has time to make things like these!”’
Tan-chun’s face darkened at once.
‘How can anyone talk such utter nonsense!

segments.text: ‘If I happen to have nothing to do and make a pair of shoes now and then, I shall give them to whichever brother I please. Who has any right to stop me? She’s getting angry for nothing.’
Bao-yu nodded, smiling.
‘You don’t understand. Naturally, she’s thinking of something else.’
Tan-chun grew angrier still and turned her head away.

‘Now you’re talking nonsense too! Of course she’s thinking of something else, but it’s all mean, underhand notions. Let her think as she likes. I recognise Father and Mother, and no one else. As for my sisters and brothers, I’m fond of whoever is fond of me. All this talk of being born to a concubine means nothing to me. I know I ought not to speak of her like this, but there’s no excuse for such stupidity! And here’s another absurdity. The last time I gave you that money to bring me back those little things, she saw me a couple of days afterwards and began saying how she had no money and how hard things were. I paid no attention.

segments.text: ‘But later, when the maids had gone out, she began complaining. Why did I give you my savings to spend instead of giving them to Huan? It made me want to laugh and lose my temper all at once. I went out and joined Mother.’
While they were talking, Bao-chai called over with a laugh:
‘When you’ve finished, come back! Now we can see who’s brother and sister. You leave everyone else behind to talk secrets.

segments.text: ‘We mustn’t hear so much as a word!’

Only then did Tan-chun and Bao-yu return, laughing. Finding Dai-yu gone, Bao-yu knew that she had slipped off somewhere to avoid him. After thinking it over, he decided he might as well wait a couple of days for her anger to subside before going to see her. Then he looked down and saw fallen balsam and pomegranate blossoms, with flowers of every other kind, lying layer upon layer like brocade over the ground. He sighed.
‘She’s so angry, she hasn’t even come to gather the flowers. I’ll take them over for her and ask her about it tomorrow.’
Just then Bao-chai called them to go out with her.
‘I’ll come in a moment,’ said Bao-yu.

He waited until the two girls were far away, then gathered the blossoms in the fold of his robe. Over hills and across streams, through trees and among flowers he went, straight to the place where he and Dai-yu had buried the peach blossom that day. He was nearly at the flowers’ grave, though not yet round the slope, when he heard sobbing on the other side. Between her sobs someone was pouring out her grief, weeping most bitterly.

segments.text: ‘I wonder whose maid that is,’ Bao-yu thought. ‘She must have been badly treated and come here to cry.’
He stopped where he stood and listened. This was what he heard her lament:

segments.text: Dai-yu was still grieving when she suddenly heard sobbing on the slope above her. “Everyone laughs at me for being a little foolish,” she thought. “Can there be another fool here?” She looked up and saw Bao-yu.
‘Pah! I wondered who it was. So it’s that heartless wretch who’ll die before his time…’
No sooner had she said ‘die before his time’ than she covered her mouth, gave a long sigh, turned and left.

segments.text: Bao-yu wept for a while longer. Then, looking up and finding Dai-yu gone, he knew she must have seen him and slipped away. He too felt dispirited. Getting up and shaking the earth from his clothes, he went down the hill to find the path back to the House of Green Delights. As chance would have it, Dai-yu was walking just ahead. He hurried after her.
‘Wait a moment. I know you won’t speak to me. I only want to say one thing, and after that I’ll leave you alone.’
Dai-yu looked back. Seeing who it was, she would have ignored him, but there was something behind that ‘one thing’ and ‘leave you alone’. She could not help stopping.
‘If you have one thing to say, please say it.’
‘Suppose it’s two things?’ Bao-yu asked with a smile. ‘Will you listen?’
At that Dai-yu turned and walked away.
‘If it was to come to this,’ he sighed behind her, ‘why did we ever begin?’
She could not help stopping again.
‘Begin what? Come to what?’
‘When you first came here,’ he said with a sigh, ‘wasn’t I the one who played with you and made you laugh?

segments.text: ‘you hold them in your heart, while going three days without a word to me, four without seeing me. I haven’t a brother or sister of my very own. There are two, of course, but you know they have a different mother. I’m an only child, just as you are, and I thought perhaps you felt as I did. But it seems I’ve troubled myself for nothing, and now I have no one to hear my grievance!’

Tears began to fall as he spoke. Hearing his words and seeing him like this, Dai-yu felt more than half her anger die away. She too shed tears, looking down without a word. Seeing her so, Bao-yu went on:

‘I know I’m no good now. But however bad I am, I would never knowingly do anything wrong to you. If I did go a little wrong, you could explain it to me and warn me not to do it again. You could scold me, or hit me a couple of times. I wouldn’t lose heart. Instead, you simply won’t speak to me. I can’t make any sense of it. I’m quite beside myself and don’t know what to do.

segments.text: ‘Even if I died, I’d be a wronged ghost. No prayers of the holiest Buddhist or Taoist could deliver me. You would still have to explain the reason before I could be born again!’
At these words, last night’s affair seemed to slip far from Dai-yu’s mind.
‘If that’s how you feel, why wouldn’t you let the maids open the door when I came yesterday?’
‘Where did you get that idea?’ Bao-yu asked in astonishment. ‘If I ever did such a thing, may I drop dead this instant!’
‘Pah! Talking about death first thing in the morning, without a thought for ill luck! If you did, you did; if you didn’t, you didn’t. Why swear an oath?’
‘I truly never saw you come. Cousin Bao-chai sat for a little while, and then she left.’
Dai-yu thought a moment, then smiled.
‘Of course. Your maids were probably too lazy to stir. They can be surly enough.’
‘That must be it. When I go back I’ll find out who it was and give them a good talking-to.’
‘Those young ladies of yours could certainly do with one, though I suppose it isn’t my place to say so.

segments.text: While they were talking, a maid came to call them to eat, and they both went to the front. Seeing Dai-yu, Lady Wang asked:
‘My dear, has Doctor Bao’s medicine done you any good?’
‘It’s much the same. Grandmother still wants me to take Doctor Wang’s medicine.’

‘You don’t understand, Mother,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Cousin Lin’s trouble is internal. She was born delicate, so she can’t stand the least wind or cold. A couple of doses of a decoction will put that right. Once the wind and cold have been driven out, pills are better.’
‘The doctor mentioned some pills the other day,’ said Lady Wang, ‘but I’ve forgotten the name.’
‘I know what those pills are. He only wants her to take ginseng pills to nourish the blood.’
‘No, not those.’
‘Eight-Treasure Mother-Benefiting Pills? Left-Restoring? Right-Restoring? Or else Maiwei Dihuang Pills?’

segments.text: ‘None of those,’ said Lady Wang. ‘All I remember is that there was a “Vajra” in it somewhere.’
Bao-yu spread his hands and laughed.
‘I’ve never heard of any Vajra Pills. If there are Vajra Pills, there must be Bodhisattva Powder too!’
Everyone in the room laughed.
‘Perhaps it was Heavenly King Heart-Nourishing Pills,’ Bao-chai suggested with a small smile.
‘That was the name,’ Lady Wang said, laughing. ‘How muddled I’ve become!’
‘You’re not muddled, Mother. It’s all those Vajras and Bodhisattvas ordering you about that have muddled you.’
‘Making fun of your own mother, you shameless thing! You’re asking for another beating from your father.’
‘My father would never beat me for that,’ said Bao-yu, laughing.
‘Well, if those are the pills,’ Lady Wang continued, ‘we’ll send out for some tomorrow.’

‘None of them are any use,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Give me three hundred and sixty taels, Mother, and I’ll have a batch of pills made up for Cousin Lin. I guarantee she’ll be better before she’s finished them.’
‘Poppycock!

segments.text: ‘What medicine could cost so much?’

‘I mean it,’ said Bao-yu, laughing. ‘My prescription is different from other people’s. The ingredients have such strange names that I can’t explain them all at once. Human placenta from a first pregnancy, human-shaped ginseng with its leaves: three hundred and sixty taels wouldn’t cover those alone. He-shou-wu as big as a tortoise, the core of fuling from the roots of a thousand-year-old pine, things like that don’t even count as rarities. They’re just among the ordinary ingredients. As for the chief ingredient, you’d get a fright if I told you. Cousin Xue begged me for a year or two before I let him have the prescription. Then he spent another two or three years collecting the ingredients, and over a thousand taels, before he could have it made up. If you don’t believe me, ask Cousin Bao-chai.’
Bao-chai shook her hand at him, laughing.
‘I know nothing about it. I’ve never even heard of it. Don’t make Aunt ask me.’
‘That’s our Bao-chai,’ said Lady Wang with a smile. ‘A good child who doesn’t tell lies.’
Bao-yu, who had been standing in the middle of the room, spun round and clapped his hands.
‘But I’m telling the truth, and you say I’m lying!’
As he spoke, he turned again and saw Dai-yu sitting behind Bao-chai, suppressing a smile and drawing a finger down her cheek to shame him.

segments.text: Xi-feng had been in the inner room watching the servants set up the table. Hearing this, she came out with a smile.

‘Cousin Bao isn’t lying. There is such a thing. The other day Cousin Xue came to me himself to ask for pearls. I asked what he wanted them for, and he said he was having medicine made up. He was grumbling too: if only he’d never started! Who could have known it would be such a business? I asked what medicine it was, and he said it was Cousin Bao’s prescription. He named any number of ingredients, but I had no time to listen. He said he could have bought a few pearls himself, only these had to have been worn on someone’s head, so he’d come to me. “If you haven’t any loose ones, cousin,” he said, “ones on a flower ornament will do. Take them off, and I’ll choose some good ones and have them threaded for you afterwards.” There was nothing for it: I took two pearl flowers apart there and then and gave him the pearls. He also took a piece of scarlet gauze for imperial use, three chi long, to sift the powder after grinding it in a mortar.’
At every sentence Bao-yu invoked the Buddha.
‘Here’s the sun shining inside the house!’
When Xi-feng had finished, he went on:
‘You see, Mother, even that was only making do.

segments.text: ‘Strictly according to the prescription, the pearls and precious stones ought to come from an ancient tomb: you need the ornaments rich people were buried in long ago. But who could go digging up graves for that nowadays? So ornaments worn by living people can be used instead.’

‘Amitabha!’ said Lady Wang. ‘How easy it is to squander money when you don’t keep house! Even if there were such things in a tomb, the people have been dead for hundreds of years. Digging up bodies and stealing bones now, no medicine made of that would do any good!’
‘Did you hear?’ Bao-yu said to Dai-yu. ‘Surely Cousin Xi-feng isn’t joining me in telling lies?’
His face was turned to Dai-yu, but his eyes glanced at Bao-chai.
Dai-yu caught Lady Wang’s arm.
‘Listen to him, Aunt. Cousin Bao-chai won’t back up his lie, so he takes it out on me.’
‘You do bully your cousin, Bao-yu,’ Lady Wang agreed.

‘You don’t understand, Mother,’ said Bao-yu with a smile. ‘Even when Cousin Bao-chai was living at home, she didn’t know about Cousin Xue’s affairs. Now that she’s living in the garden, naturally she knows still less.

segments.text: ‘Cousin Lin was making faces at me behind my back just now. She thought I was lying.’

At that moment a maid came from Grandmother Jia’s to fetch Bao-yu and Dai-yu to eat. Without calling Bao-yu, Dai-yu rose, took the maid by the hand and made to leave. The maid suggested waiting for him.
‘He isn’t eating. Let’s go. I’m going on ahead.’
And out she went.
‘I’ll eat with you today, Mother,’ said Bao-yu.
‘No, no. I’m keeping a vegetarian fast today. Go and have your own meal.’
‘I’ll keep the fast with you.’
Telling the maid to go, he ran ahead and sat down at the table.
‘You girls go on with your meal,’ Lady Wang said to Bao-chai and the others, smiling. ‘Let him be.’
‘Do go,’ said Bao-chai with a smile. ‘Whether you eat there or not, at least walk over with Miss Lin. She’s very upset.’
‘Never mind her. She’ll be all right in a little while.’
When he had finished eating, however, Bao-yu was afraid Grandmother Jia might be worrying about him. He was also worrying about Dai-yu himself. He hurriedly called for tea to rinse his mouth.

segments.text: Tan-chun and Xi-chun laughed.
‘Second Brother, what keeps you in such a hurry all day? Even eating and drinking tea have to be done in a rush.’
‘Let him finish quickly and go to Cousin Lin,’ said Bao-chai with a smile. ‘What good is he doing, hanging about here?’

Bao-yu drank his tea and went out, making straight for the western courtyard. As he passed Xi-feng’s gate he saw her with one foot planted on the threshold, picking her teeth with an ear-scoop and watching ten or so pages move flowerpots.

segments.text: ‘Just the person I want,’ she called with a smile. ‘Come in. Come in and write a few words for me.’
Bao-yu had to follow her. Once they were inside, she called for brush, inkstone and paper.
‘Forty bolts of scarlet figured satin,’ she dictated. ‘Forty bolts of satin with python designs. One hundred bolts of gauze for imperial use, in various colours. Four gold neck-rings.’
‘What is this supposed to be?’ Bao-yu asked. ‘It isn’t an account, and it isn’t a list of presents. How am I to write it?’
‘Just put it down. So long as I understand it, that’s all that matters.’

segments.text: Bao-yu could only write as he was told. As Xi-feng put the paper away, she smiled.

‘There’s something else I wanted to ask you. I don’t know whether you’ll agree. You have a maid called Crimson. I’ve been meaning to ask you for her, to work for me, but never got round to it. Seeing you today reminded me.’
‘I’ve more than enough people in my rooms. If you like any of them, cousin, take her. Why ask me?’
‘In that case I’ll send someone to fetch her.’
‘Do.’
He was already going when Xi-feng called him back.
‘Come here. There’s one more thing.’
‘Grandmother’s asking for me. Whatever it is can wait till I come back.’
He went on to Grandmother Jia’s, where he found everyone had finished eating.
‘What delicacies did you have with your mother?’ she asked.
‘No delicacies, but I ate an extra bowl of rice. Where’s Cousin Lin?’
‘In the inner room.’

Dai-yu paid no attention and went on cutting.

‘What are you making, Cousin Lin?’

segments.text: Seeing Dai-yu cutting out the cloth, she smiled.
‘You grow cleverer every day. You can even cut things out now.’
‘Only telling lies to take people in,’ Dai-yu said with a smile.
‘Here’s something to make you laugh,’ said Bao-chai. ‘Just now, when I said I knew nothing about that medicine, Cousin Bao took offence.’
‘Never mind him,’ said Dai-yu. ‘He’ll be all right in a little while.’
‘Grandmother wants to play dominoes,’ Bao-yu told Bao-chai, ‘and there aren’t enough people. Why don’t you go and play?’
‘Did you think I came here to play dominoes?’ she asked with a smile, and went out.
‘You had better go,’ said Dai-yu. ‘There’s a tiger in here. Mind it doesn’t eat you!’

segments.text: She went on cutting. Seeing that she would take no notice of him, Bao-yu could only try another smile.
‘Why don’t you go out for a little walk? You can do that later.’
Still she ignored him. He asked the maids who had told her to cut it out.
‘Whoever told me to,’ Dai-yu answered when she heard him questioning them, ‘it’s no concern of yours, Master Bao.’
He was about to reply when someone came in to say that a caller outside had brought an invitation. Bao-yu slipped out at once.
‘Amitabha!’ Dai-yu called after him. ‘I might as well be dead by the time you come back.’

Outside, Tealeaf told him that Mr Feng had sent to invite him. Remembering yesterday’s conversation, Bao-yu told him to fetch his going-out clothes and went to the study. Tealeaf hurried straight to the inner gate to wait for someone. An old woman came out, and he went up to her.
‘Master Bao’s in the study waiting for his going-out clothes. Would you be so kind as to take a message in?’

segments.text: ‘A fine business! Master Bao lives in the garden now, and all his people are there, but you come running here to have a message taken in!’
‘Quite right to scold me,’ said Tealeaf with a laugh. ‘I’ve lost my wits.’

He went straight to the inner gate on the east. The page on duty was down by the paved walk playing ball. Tealeaf explained what was wanted. The boy ran in and, after some time, brought out a bundle and handed it to him. Back in the study Bao-yu changed his clothes, ordered his horse and set off with only four pages: Tealeaf, Chu-yao, Shuang-rui and Shuang-shou.

segments.text: They went straight to Feng Zi-ying’s house. Someone announced Bao-yu, and Feng came out to welcome him in. Xue Pan had been waiting there for some time. There were also a number of boy singers, Jiang Yu-han, an actor who played young female roles, and Nuageuse, a courtesan from the Budding Grove. Once the introductions were over, they drank tea.
Raising his cup, Bao-yu said with a smile, ‘That fortunate and unfortunate business you spoke of the other day has been on my mind day and night. The moment I heard your invitation today, I came.’

‘You cousins are an honest pair,’ Feng Zi-ying said, laughing. ‘That was only a pretext. I truly wanted to have you both here for a drink, but I was afraid you’d find excuses, so I said that to tempt you. And today you came the moment I asked! Who would have thought you’d take it all as true?’
They all laughed. The wine was brought in, and they took their places.

segments.text: ‘Very sensible,’ said Feng Zi-ying, Jiang Yu-han and the rest.
Bao-yu lifted the beaker and drank it dry in one draught.

‘We each have to give a girl’s grief, care, delight and joy, and explain the reason for each. When you’ve finished, you drink the cup required by the game. For the song round, you sing one of the latest fashionable songs. For the closing quotation, you take your cue from something on the table: it can be an old poem, an old couplet, something from the Four Books or the Five Classics, or a familiar saying.’
Before he had finished, Xue Pan stood up and interrupted.
‘I’m not playing. Leave me out. You’re only trying to make a fool of me!’
Nuageuse stood up too and pushed him back into his seat.

‘What are you afraid of?’ she asked, laughing. ‘You drink every day, and yet you can’t even do as well as I can? I’m going to have a turn too. If you get it right, well and good. If you don’t, you only have to drink a few cups. They won’t kill you. But if you break the rules now, you’ll have to drink ten large beakers and go and pour for everyone else, won’t you?’
They all clapped and applauded her.

segments.text: ‘Those all make sense,’ the others said.
Only Xue Pan lifted his chin and shook his head.
‘No good. He should drink a forfeit.’
‘Why should he?’ they asked.
‘I couldn’t understand a word of it. Why shouldn’t he?’
Nuageuse gave him a pinch and laughed.
‘Keep quiet and think of your own lines. If you can’t say them when your turn comes, you’ll have to drink again.’
She took up her pipa to accompany Bao-yu, who sang:

segments.text: ‘Here I go,’ said Xue Pan. ‘A girl’s grief…’
Nothing more came, though they waited a long while.
‘Grief over what?’ Feng Zi-ying asked with a laugh. ‘Out with it!’
Xue Pan’s eyes bulged like bells in his anxiety. He stared for a long time before managing:
‘A girl’s grief…’

He coughed twice and tried again:
‘

‘A forfeit! A forfeit!’ they roared with laughter. ‘That’s even more absurd. We could just forgive the first one.’
They were about to pour the wine when Bao-yu said with a smile, ‘So long as it rhymes.’
‘The master of the game has allowed it,’ Xue Pan said. ‘What are you making a fuss for?’
At that they desisted.
‘The next two will be even harder,’ Nuageuse said with a laugh. ‘Let me do them for you.’

‘Nonsense! Do you really think I haven’t any good ones? Listen!’

segments.text: The company accepted it, and his turn was done. But Xue Pan jumped up again and shouted:
‘Outrageous! Outrageous! A forfeit! There’s no precious treasure on this table. What are you doing reciting about one?’
Jiang Yu-han looked blank.
‘What precious treasure?’
‘Still denying it? Say it again.’
Jiang Yu-han could only repeat the line.
‘If Aroma isn’t a precious treasure, what is she?’ Xue Pan demanded. ‘Don’t believe me? Ask him.’
He pointed to Bao-yu.
Bao-yu grew embarrassed.
‘Cousin Xue, how much should you drink for that?’
‘A forfeit, a forfeit!’ Xue Pan agreed, and lifted his cup and drained it.
Feng Zi-ying and Jiang Yu-han did not understand, so Nuageuse explained. Jiang Yu-han rose at once to apologise.
‘No blame where there was no knowledge,’ the others said.

segments.text: A little later Bao-yu left the table to relieve himself, and Jiang Yu-han followed. As they stood beneath the eaves of the verandah, Jiang apologised again. Bao-yu was so taken by his gentle, enchanting manner that he could not bear to part with him. He held his hand tightly.

‘Come and see us whenever you’re free. And there’s something else I wanted to ask. There’s someone in your company called Bijou. Where is he? His fame has spread everywhere, and I alone have never had the good fortune to meet him.’
‘That’s my nickname,’ Jiang Yu-han said with a smile.
Bao-yu stamped his foot in delight and laughed.
‘What luck! What luck!

segments.text: ‘Your reputation is well deserved. It’s our first meeting today. What can I do to mark it?’
After thinking a moment, he took his fan from his sleeve, unfastened its open-ring jade pendant and handed it to Bijou.
‘A poor little thing, but let it stand for the friendship we’ve made today.’

segments.text: Bijou accepted it with a smile.
‘How can I deserve a reward when I’ve done nothing to earn it? Well, I have a rare thing here. I only put it on this morning. It’s quite new, and may serve as a small token of my affection.’
He lifted his robe, untied the scarlet sash that fastened his underclothes and handed it to Bao-yu.

‘This sash was sent as tribute by the queen of Qianxiang. If you wear it in summer, it scents your skin and leaves no sweat-stains. The Prince of Beijing gave it to me yesterday, and I put it on for the first time today. I would never give it to anyone else. Will you take off the one you’re wearing, Master Bao, and let me have that to tie round myself?’
Overjoyed, Bao-yu accepted it at once, untied his own pine-pollen-green sash and handed it to Bijou. They had just tied them on when a great shout rang out.
‘Caught you!’

segments.text: ‘Quick, let me see what you’ve got.’
‘Nothing,’ they both said.
Xue Pan would not let them go. Only when Feng Zi-ying came out were they released, and they returned to their places and went on drinking. The party did not break up until evening.
Back in the garden, Bao-yu took off his outer clothes and drank some tea. Aroma noticed that the pendant was missing from his fan.
‘What happened to it?’
‘I lost it on horseback.’
At bedtime she saw the sash round his waist, scarlet as a drop of blood, and guessed most of the story.
‘Now you’ve got a fine new one to hold your trousers up, give me mine back.’
Only then did Bao-yu remember that the sash had belonged to Aroma, and that he ought not to have given it away. He regretted it, but could not bring himself to say so. He could only smile.
‘I’ll give you another.’
Aroma nodded and sighed.
‘I knew you’d been up to that sort of thing again. You had no business giving my things to those scoundrels. Really, there’s no accounting for you. You never think.’
She would have said more, but was afraid of upsetting him with so much wine in him, and had to go to sleep too. Nothing more need be said of the night.

segments.text: She had only just woken at daybreak when Bao-yu said with a smile:
‘There were thieves about in the night, and you never knew. Look at your trousers.’
Aroma looked down. The sash Bao-yu had worn the day before was now tied round her own waist. Knowing he must have changed it in the night, she hastily tugged it off.
‘I don’t want the thing. Take it away this instant!’

Bao-yu had to coax and persuade her for some time. With no help for it, she tied it round her waist. But afterwards, when he had gone out, she took it off after all, flung it into an empty chest and tied on another of her own.

segments.text: Bao-yu paid no attention to this. He asked whether anything had happened the day before.
‘Mrs Lian sent for Crimson,’ Aroma told him. ‘She wanted to wait until you came back, but I thought there was no need, so I took it on myself to send her.’
‘Quite right. I knew about it already. There was no need to wait for me.’

‘Yesterday Her Highness sent Eunuch Xia out with a hundred and twenty taels,’ Aroma went on. ‘She wants a three-day Taoist offering rite for peace at the Temple of Pure Emptiness, from the first to the third, with plays and offerings. Mr Zhen is to lead all the gentlemen in kneeling before the incense and worshipping the Buddha. She also sent Dragon Boat Festival gifts.’

She called a little maid to bring out the presents received the day before. There were two fine palace fans, two strings of red musk-scented beads, two lengths of phoenix-tail gauze and a furong bamboo mat. Bao-yu was delighted.
‘Did everyone else get the same?’
‘Her Old Ladyship had a scented ruyi and an agate pillow as well.

segments.text: ‘What’s the reason for that?’ Bao-yu asked, smiling. ‘Why aren’t Miss Lin’s the same as mine, instead of Cousin Bao-chai’s? Could they have been handed out wrongly?’

‘Every share had a label on it when they came out yesterday,’ said Aroma. ‘How could there be a mistake? Yours were in Her Old Ladyship’s rooms. I went and fetched them. Her Old Ladyship says you’re to go into the Palace on your own tomorrow, at the fifth watch, to give thanks.’
‘Of course I must go.’
Then he called Purple Silk.
‘Take these to Miss Lin. Tell her they came for me yesterday, and she can keep whatever she likes.’
Purple Silk took them away as she was told, but soon came back.
‘Miss Lin says she had some yesterday too, and you’re to keep these, Master Bao.’

segments.text: Dai-yu had long since put aside what had troubled her about Bao-yu the day before. Now her thoughts were on today’s grievance.
‘I haven’t the good fortune to bear such favours. I’m not like Miss Bao, with all that gold and jade. I’m only a creature of grass and trees.’
The words ‘gold and jade’ set Bao-yu’s heart stirring with doubt.
‘Whatever other people say about gold and jade, if I have any such thought myself, may Heaven destroy me and earth swallow me, and may I never be born human again in ten thousand lifetimes!’
Dai-yu knew from this that she had aroused his suspicions. She hastened to smile again.
‘How silly! Why swear an oath over nothing? What do I care about your gold and jade?’
‘It’s hard to tell you what’s in my heart,’ said Bao-yu. ‘One day you’ll understand. After Grandmother, Father and Mother, you come fourth. If there’s anyone fifth, I’ll swear another oath.’
‘You needn’t swear. I know very well that you have room in your heart for your younger cousin. Only when an elder cousin appears, you forget the younger one.’
‘That’s your own suspicion. I never do.’
‘Then when that girl Bao-chai wouldn’t back up your lie yesterday, why did you question me?

segments.text: ‘If it had been me, there’s no knowing how you’d have behaved.’

Just then they saw Bao-chai coming from the other direction and moved away. She saw them quite clearly, but pretended not to, and went past with her head lowered. She sat for a while at Lady Wang’s, then went to Grandmother Jia’s, where she found Bao-yu.

Bao-chai’s mother had once told Lady Wang and the others that her golden locket had been given by a monk, and that when the time came she must marry someone who had jade. Because of this Bao-chai always kept her distance from Bao-yu. Yesterday’s gifts from Yuan-chun, when she alone had received the same as he, had made her feel still more awkward. Fortunately Bao-yu was so bound up with Dai-yu, with his every thought fixed on her, that he paid no attention to the matter.
Now, however, he suddenly asked with a smile:
‘Cousin Bao-chai, may I see your red musk-scented beads?’
As it happened, she was wearing a string round her left wrist. Since he had asked, she had to slip them off.

segments.text: Bao-chai’s flesh was full and smooth, and the beads would not come off easily. Watching that soft, snow-white arm, Bao-yu felt a stirring of desire.
“If only that arm belonged to Cousin Lin,” he thought, “I might at least get to touch it. Why must it belong to her?”

He was regretting his lack of the good fortune to touch it when the business of ‘gold and jade’ suddenly came back to him. He looked again at Bao-chai: a face like a silver basin, eyes like glistening apricots, lips red without rouge, brows dark without paint. Hers was a different kind of charm and grace from Dai-yu’s. He stared, quite lost, and even forgot to take the beads when she slipped them off and held them out.
Seeing his abstraction, Bao-chai grew embarrassed herself. She put down the beads and was turning to go when she saw Dai-yu with one foot on the threshold, biting her handkerchief and smiling.
‘You can’t stand the wind,’ Bao-chai said. ‘Why are you standing in the draught again?’
‘I was in the room,’ Dai-yu said with a smile. ‘Then I heard a cry in the sky and came out to look. It was only a silly goose.’
‘Where’s the silly goose?

‘As soon as I came out, it went “honk!” and flew away.’

segments.text: Bao-yu was still staring vacantly when Dai-yu flung her handkerchief at him. It struck him squarely in the eye and gave him quite a fright. He asked who had done it.
‘Oh, I wouldn’t dare!’ said Dai-yu, shaking her head and smiling. ‘My hand slipped. Cousin Bao wanted to see a silly goose, so I was pointing one out to her. I didn’t mean to let go.’
Bao-yu rubbed his eye. He wanted to say something, but could find nothing he could very well say.

segments.text: Presently Xi-feng arrived. Speaking of the offering service to be held at the Temple of Pure Emptiness on the first day of the month, she invited Bao-chai, Bao-yu, Dai-yu and the others to go and see the plays.
‘No, no, it will be dreadfully hot,’ said Bao-chai with a smile. ‘What play could they put on that we haven’t seen? I shan’t go.’

‘It’s cool there,’ said Xi-feng, ‘and there are galleries on either side. If we’re going, I’ll send people over a few days beforehand, turn all those Taoists out, have the galleries swept clean and the curtains hung, and see that not a single idler is let into the temple. Then it will be pleasant. I’ve already told Her Ladyship. If none of you go, I’m going. I’ve been shut up till I’m sick of it these last few days. Whenever there’s a play at home, I never get to sit and watch it in peace.’

segments.text: Grandmother Jia heard this and smiled.
‘In that case, I’ll go with you.’
‘If you come too, Grandmother, that will be splendid!’ said Xi-feng, laughing. ‘Only I shan’t have my ease after all.’
‘Tomorrow I shall sit in the gallery facing the stage, and you can sit in one at the side. You needn’t come over to me and stand on ceremony. Will that do?’

segments.text: ‘Now that is kind of you, Grandmother!’ said Xi-feng with a smile.
Grandmother Jia turned to Bao-chai.
‘You must come too, and bring your mother. These long days, you do nothing but sleep if you stay at home.’
Bao-chai could only agree.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia sent someone to invite Aunt Xue and to tell Lady Wang on the way that she meant to take the girls with her. Lady Wang had already said she would not go, partly because she was unwell and partly because she was expecting someone to come from Yuan-chun. When she heard what Grandmother Jia now proposed, she smiled.
‘She’s as fond of an outing as ever.’
She sent word into the Garden: ‘Anyone who would like an outing may go with Her Old Ladyship on the first.’

When the news spread, the others took it calmly enough, but the maids, who never got beyond the threshold from one day to the next, all longed to go. Even where a mistress was disinclined, her maids used every argument to persuade her, until Li Gong-cai and the rest had all said they were coming. Grandmother Jia was more delighted than ever. She had already sent people ahead to clean and make the arrangements, of which we need say no more.

segments.text: On the first, carriages crowded before the Rong mansion, with men and horses clustered all about. Those responsible for the procession had learnt that the service was an act of piety on behalf of Her Highness, and that Grandmother Jia was going in person to offer incense. Besides being the first day of the month, it was the season of the Dragon Boat Festival. Every item of equipment was therefore supplied in full ceremonial style, quite unlike an ordinary outing.

Before long Grandmother Jia and the others came out. She took a great sedan chair with eight bearers. Li Wan, Xi-feng and Aunt Xue each had a four-bearer chair. Bao-chai and Dai-yu shared a carriage with a kingfisher-green canopy, pearl tassels and eight treasures; Ying-chun, Tan-chun and Xi-chun rode together in another, with vermilion wheels and an ornate canopy.

After them came Grandmother Jia’s maids Faithful, Parrot, Amber and Pearl; Dai-yu’s maids Nightingale, Snowgoose and Chun-xian; Bao-chai’s maids Oriole and Wen-xing; Ying-chun’s maids Chess and Xiu-ju; Tan-chun’s maids Scribe and Ebony; Xi-chun’s maids Picture and Cai-ping; Aunt Xue’s maids Tong-xi and Tong-gui, together with Caltrop and Caltrop’s own maid Zhen-er; Li Wan’s maids Su-yun and Bi-yue; and Xi-feng’s maids Patience, Felicity and Crimson. Golden and Cai-yun, two of Lady Wang’s maids, also wanted to go with Xi-feng. The wet-nurse, holding Da-jie and bringing Qiao-jie along, rode in a separate carriage with two more maids. Add the elderly nurses and wet-nurses from all the apartments, and the married women of the household accompanying them, and their carriages filled the whole street in a solid mass.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia’s chair and those of the other ladies were already far away while the people at the gate were still getting into their carriages. Here someone was saying, ‘I’m not sitting with you!’ and another, ‘You’re squashing our mistress’s bundle!’ From one carriage came ‘You’ve crushed my flowers!’ and from another, ‘You’ve snapped my fan!’ Their shrill chatter, laughter and joking never stopped.

segments.text: Zhou Rui’s wife walked up and down among them.
‘Girls, you’re in the street! People will laugh at you.’

Only after she had said it twice did they grow a little quieter. The full ceremonial escort at the head of the procession had meanwhile drawn up at the Temple of Pure Emptiness. Bao-yu rode on horseback in front of Grandmother Jia’s chair. People stood on either side of the street to watch.

segments.text: As they approached the temple, bells and drums rang out. Taoist Master Zhang, robed and bearing incense, was waiting by the roadside at the head of his fellow Taoists to welcome them. Just inside the main gate, Grandmother Jia looked out of her chair and saw the clay images of the great marshal guarding the gate, Thousand-li Eye, Wind-following Ear, the local Earth God and the City God of the district. She ordered the bearers to stop. Jia Zhen came up with the younger men of the family to greet her.

Knowing that Faithful and the other maids were still too far behind to help Grandmother Jia out, Xi-feng got out of her own chair and hurried forward to support her. A young Taoist of twelve or thirteen happened to be there with his snuffers and their holder, tending the candlewicks. He was trying to find a chance to slip away and hide when he ran straight into Xi-feng. Up went her hand. She struck him across the face so hard that he tumbled over.
‘You fucking wild-bull bastard! Where are you blundering?’

The young Taoist scrambled up and tried to run again, without stopping to pick up the snuffers. Just then Bao-chai and the others were getting out of their carriage, surrounded by an impenetrable throng of serving-women. Seeing a little Taoist come tumbling out, they all shouted, ‘Catch him, catch him, catch him!

segments.text: ‘Hit him, hit him, hit him!’
‘What is it?’ Grandmother Jia asked at once. Jia Zhen hurried out to see. Xi-feng came up and took Grandmother Jia’s arm.
‘A little Taoist who trims the candles. He didn’t get out of the way in time, and now he’s darting about among us.’

‘Bring the child here at once,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Don’t frighten him. Children from humble homes are always petted and spoilt. How should he ever have seen such a great procession? Poor little thing, if you frighten him, think how his mother and father would feel.’

She told Jia Zhen to fetch him gently. Jia Zhen had no choice but to bring the boy over. Still holding the snuffers in one hand, the child knelt on the ground, trembling all over. Grandmother Jia told Jia Zhen to help him up and reassure him, and asked him his age. The child could not get a word out.
‘Poor little thing!’ she said again. ‘Zhen, take him away now. Give him some money to buy fruit, and don’t let anyone ill-treat him.’
Jia Zhen assented and led him away.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia now took the party through the successive courts, worshipping and looking about her as they went. Outside, the pages had just seen the ladies pass through the second gate when Jia Zhen appeared with the little Taoist. He called for someone to take the child away, give him a few hundred cash and see that no one ill-treated him. One of the servants hurried up and led him off.

segments.text: Standing on the steps, Jia Zhen asked, ‘Where’s the steward?’
The pages below shouted together, ‘Fetch the steward!’
Lin Zhi-xiao came running up, straightening his hat with one hand.

‘There’s plenty of room here,’ said Jia Zhen, ‘but I hadn’t expected so many people today. Take the men you need into your courtyard, and send the ones you don’t need into the other one. Pick out a few more of the young pages and station them at this second gate and the two side gates to fetch things and carry messages. Do you understand? All the young ladies and married ladies are here today. Not a single person with no business here is to get through.’
Lin Zhi-xiao hastened to say that he understood, and added several respectful yeses.
‘Off you go,’ said Jia Zhen. ‘And why haven’t I seen Rong?’
He had scarcely finished speaking when Jia Rong came running out of the bell tower.
‘Look at him! I haven’t even dared complain of the heat, and he’s already gone off to cool himself!’
He shouted to the servants to spit on him.

segments.text: The pages knew Jia Zhen’s temper too well to disobey. One came forward and spat in Jia Rong’s face.
‘Ask him!’ said Jia Zhen.
‘The Master doesn’t mind the heat yet,’ the page said to Jia Rong. ‘What makes you think you can go off to cool yourself first?’

Jia Rong stood with his hands lowered, not daring to utter a word. When Jia Yun, Jia Ping, Jia Qin and the others heard this, they were not the only ones thrown into alarm: even Jia Huang, Jia Bin and Jia Qiong bestirred themselves, edging forward one by one from the foot of the wall.

‘What are you standing there for?’ Jia Zhen said to his son. ‘Get on a horse and go home. Tell your mother and your wife that Her Old Ladyship and the young ladies are all here, and they’re to come at once to attend them.’
Jia Rong hurried out, calling over and over for a horse.
‘What were they all doing earlier?’ he grumbled. ‘Now he has to pick on me!’
He turned on the pages. ‘Are your hands tied? Can’t you even bring a horse?’
He was tempted to send a page on the errand, but feared that questions afterwards would expose him. There was nothing for it but to ride home himself. We need not follow him.

segments.text: Jia Zhen was about to go back inside when he noticed Taoist Master Zhang waiting beside him with a deferential smile.

‘By rights I ought to be inside attending Her Old Ladyship. I’m hardly an outsider. But the weather is hot and all the young ladies have come out today. I would not venture in without your instructions, sir. I thought I would wait here, in case Her Old Ladyship should ask for me or wish to visit any part of the temple.’

Jia Zhen knew that Zhang had originally entered religion as a substitute for the Duke of Rong; that the late emperor had himself addressed him as ‘Immortal of the Great Illusion’; that he now held the seal of the Taoist Registry; and that the present emperor had bestowed on him the title ‘Adept of Completion’. Princes, dukes and provincial commanders all called him ‘the Immortal’. He was not a man Jia Zhen would dare slight. Besides, he was a frequent visitor to both mansions and had met all the ladies and girls. Hearing this speech, Jia Zhen smiled.
‘Why talk like that among ourselves? Another word and I’ll pull that beard of yours out! Come along in with me.’

segments.text: Master Zhang laughed heartily and followed him in. Jia Zhen bent respectfully towards Grandmother Jia, smiling.
‘Grandfather Zhang has come to pay his respects.’
‘Help him over,’ she said at once.
Jia Zhen hurried back to support him. Master Zhang began with a great laugh.

‘Buddha of Boundless Life! Has our venerable lady been enjoying blessings, long life, peace and health? And all the ladies and young ladies, have you been enjoying good fortune? It’s some time since I came to pay my respects, and Your Old Ladyship looks better than ever.’
‘And how are you, old immortal?’ Grandmother Jia asked with a smile.

‘By the blessings of Your Old Ladyship’s boundless good fortune and long life, this humble Taoist is still quite well. But it is the young master I have been thinking about. Has he been keeping well? On the twenty-sixth of the fourth month, not long ago, we celebrated the sacred birthday of the Great King Who Covers the Sky here. There were few visitors and everything was very clean. I thought of inviting him over to look about, but they said he wasn’t at home. How was that?’
‘He really wasn’t at home,’ said Grandmother Jia, turning to call Bao-yu.
He had just come back from relieving himself and hurried forward.
‘Are you well, Grandfather Zhang?’
Master Zhang embraced him, returned his greeting and smiled at Grandmother Jia.
‘The young master is filling out splendidly.’

segments.text: ‘He looks well enough outside,’ said Grandmother Jia, ‘but he’s weak within. And his father keeps driving him at his books. He’s positively driven the child into an illness.’

‘Just lately I’ve seen the young master’s calligraphy and poems in several houses,’ said Master Zhang, ‘and they were remarkably good. Why does His Lordship still complain that he isn’t fond enough of studying? To my humble mind, that ought to be enough.’
Then he sighed.
‘When I look at the young master’s face and figure, the way he speaks and moves, it is as though the old Duke had been cast in the very same mould!’
Tears ran from his eyes. Grandmother Jia too could not keep the tears from streaming down her face.
‘That’s just it. Of all these sons and grandsons I’ve brought up, not one looks like the old Duke. Only my Yu takes after his grandfather.’

segments.text: Master Zhang turned to Jia Zhen.
‘The gentlemen of your generation never saw the old Duke, of course. I dare say even the Elder Master and the Second Master can scarcely remember what he looked like.’
Then he gave another hearty laugh.

‘I saw a young lady in someone’s house the other day. She is fifteen this year, and a very fine-looking girl. It occurred to me that it must be time to look for a match for the young master. In looks, intelligence, family standing and means, I should say she would suit. But I don’t know Your Old Ladyship’s wishes, and would not presume. Only when I have your instructions would I venture to speak to the family.’

‘A monk told us some time ago that the child’s destiny forbids an early marriage,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Let him grow a little older before we decide. You may keep an eye out meanwhile. Never mind the family’s standing or wealth. If you find a girl whose looks are good enough for him, let me know. If her family is poor, all we need do is give them a few taels of silver.

segments.text: ‘It’s good looks and a good disposition that are hard to find.’
When she had finished, Xi-feng spoke up with a smile.

‘Grandfather Zhang, you haven’t renewed our little girl’s amulet of religious dedication. Yet the other day you had the face to send and ask me for some gosling-yellow satin! I was afraid your old face wouldn’t stand it if I refused.’
Master Zhang burst out laughing.

‘There now! My eyes are going. I hadn’t noticed you were here, ma’am, and never thanked you. The amulet has been ready for some time. I meant to send it over the other day, but then Her Highness’s service came unexpectedly and drove it clean out of my head. It’s still being kept before the Buddha. I’ll fetch it.’

He hurried to the great hall and soon came back carrying the amulet on a tea tray draped with a scripture cloth of scarlet satin patterned with pythons. Da-jie’s wet-nurse took the amulet. Master Zhang was about to take Da-jie in his arms when Xi-feng said, laughing:
‘You might just have brought it in your hand. What did you want a tray for?’
‘Hands aren’t always clean. How could I carry it in my hand?

segments.text: ‘A tray is cleaner.’
‘Well, you gave me quite a fright, bringing out that tray,’ said Xi-feng. ‘I didn’t think you were bringing us an amulet. I thought you’d come to collect alms!’

‘You monkey, you monkey!’ Grandmother Jia said, turning to her. ‘Aren’t you afraid of going down to the hell where they cut out your tongue?’

segments.text: ‘He and I don’t mind,’ said Xi-feng, laughing. ‘Isn’t he always telling me I ought to store up hidden merit, or I’ll die young if I leave it too late?’
Master Zhang laughed too.

‘My tray is to serve two purposes, but neither is collecting alms. I should like to ask the young master to take off his jade, so that I may carry it out on the tray for the brethren who have come from far away, and my disciples and their disciples, to admire.’
‘If that’s all,’ said Grandmother Jia, ‘why should you run about at your age? Take him along to show them, then send him back. Wouldn’t that save trouble?’

‘Your Old Ladyship doesn’t realise. I may be over eighty, but thanks to your blessings I’m still quite strong. Besides, there are a great many people outside and the smell is unpleasant. In this hot weather the young master would not be used to it. If he were upset by the foul air, that would be paying far too dear for it.’

segments.text: Grandmother Jia told Bao-yu to take off the Spiritual Jade and put it on the tray. With the greatest care Master Zhang laid it on the python-patterned cloth and carried it out. Grandmother Jia and the others looked about the temple a little longer, then went towards the upper galleries. Jia Zhen came to report that Grandfather Zhang had brought the jade back. Even as he spoke, Master Zhang approached with the tray, smiling.

‘Thanks to me, they have all had a sight of the young master’s jade. It truly is a rarity. They had no gifts worthy of the occasion, but these are the ritual objects they use in transmitting the Way, and each was eager to offer his as a token of respect and good wishes. Even if the young master thinks little of them, he can keep them in his room to play with, or give them away as rewards.’

Grandmother Jia looked into the tray. There were gold arc-shaped pendants and open-ring jade pendants, pieces with auspicious designs for ‘May all things go as you wish’ or ‘Peace year after year’, strung with pearls and gems, carved in jade or worked in gold. There must have been thirty to fifty of them altogether.

segments.text: ‘Now you’re being foolish too,’ she said. ‘Where do people who have renounced the world find the means for such things? There’s no need for this. We can’t accept them.’

‘They only wish to show their respect,’ Master Zhang said with a smile. ‘I could hardly stop them. If Your Old Ladyship refuses, they will think how little account you make of me, as though I had never belonged to your household.’
At this, Grandmother Jia told someone to receive the gifts.

‘Grandmother,’ said Bao-yu with a smile, ‘after what Grandfather Zhang has said, we can’t refuse. But I have no use for them. Why not have the pages carry them out with me, and I’ll give them to poor people?’
‘That’s a good idea,’ said Grandmother Jia, smiling.
Master Zhang hastened to stop him.

‘Your wish to do good is admirable, young master, but even if these things aren’t great rarities, they are objects of some value. Giving them to beggars would do the beggars no good, and would only waste the things themselves. If you want to give alms to the poor, why not give them money?’
Bao-yu accordingly told the servants to put the gifts away, and decided to distribute money that evening instead.

segments.text: Master Zhang now withdrew. Grandmother Jia and the others went upstairs and settled in the gallery facing the stage. Xi-feng and her party took the eastern gallery, while the maids occupied the western one and took turns attending their mistresses. Presently Jia Zhen came to report.
‘Lots have been drawn before the deity to choose the plays. The first is The Tale of the White Serpent.’
‘What happens in The Tale of the White Serpent?’ Grandmother Jia asked.
‘The story of Han Gaozu slaying the serpent at the beginning of his rise. The second is A Bedful of Official Tablets.’
Grandmother Jia smiled.
‘That comes second, does it? Very well. If the gods and Buddhas wish it so, we must let it be.’
She asked what the third was.
‘A Dream of the Southern Bough,’ said Jia Zhen.

Grandmother Jia said nothing. Jia Zhen withdrew to make the arrangements outside for submitting the ritual memorials and petitions, burning paper money and provisions, and beginning the plays. We need say no more of that.

segments.text: Up in the gallery, Bao-yu sat beside Grandmother Jia. He had a little maid bring the tray of gifts, put his own jade back on, and sifted through the other things, picking them out one by one to show her. Catching sight of a qilin of pure gold with kingfisher-feather inlay, Grandmother Jia took it up.
‘That’s like one I’ve seen some child wearing. Whose was it?’
‘Cousin Shi has one,’ said Bao-chai with a smile. ‘Only hers is smaller.’
‘Of course, our little Yun has one.’
‘She so often comes to stay with us,’ said Bao-yu, ‘yet I’ve never noticed it.’
‘Cousin Bao is observant,’ said Tan-chun, laughing. ‘She remembers everything.’
Dai-yu gave a cold little laugh.
‘With other things there are limits. It’s only the things people wear that she notices so particularly.’
Bao-chai turned away, pretending not to have heard. On learning that Shi Xiang-yun had such an ornament, Bao-yu quickly took the qilin and tucked it inside his robe.

segments.text: Then it occurred to him that someone might notice how he had kept the thing as soon as he heard Xiang-yun had one. His hand still inside his robe, he glanced about him. No one seemed to be paying much attention, except Dai-yu, who was watching him and nodding as though in admiration. Feeling embarrassed, he brought it out again and smiled at her.
‘It’s rather a pretty little thing. I’ll keep it for you, and when we get home I’ll thread a cord through it for you to wear.’
Dai-yu turned her head away.
‘I don’t want it.’

segments.text: ‘If you really don’t want it,’ said Bao-yu with a smile, ‘I shall have to keep it myself.’

He put it away again. He was just about to speak when the wives of Jia Zhen and Jia Rong arrived, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law. After they had exchanged greetings with everyone, Grandmother Jia said:
‘What have you come for? I only came out for a look about because I had nothing to do.’

Before she had finished, someone announced that people had come from General Feng’s household. Feng Zi-ying’s family, hearing that the Jias were holding an offering service at the temple, had hastily prepared pigs and sheep, incense and candles, money for tea and other gifts, and sent them over. Xi-feng hurried from her gallery into Grandmother Jia’s and clapped her hands.

‘Oh dear! I never thought of this. I thought we women were just coming out for an outing, and now people think we’ve set up some grand altar of fasting and offerings, and are sending presents. It’s all Grandmother’s doing! Now we shall have to get packets of reward money ready as well.’

segments.text: She had scarcely spoken when two stewards’ wives from the Feng household came upstairs. Before they had gone, gifts arrived from Vice-Minister Zhao. One household followed another. Hearing that the Jias were holding an offering service and their womenfolk were at the temple, relatives near and far, close friends and families of longstanding acquaintance all sent presents. Grandmother Jia began to regret having come.
‘It’s not as though we were holding some important observance. We only came out for an outing. I never thought about presents. We’ve put everyone to trouble for nothing.’
Though they spent the day watching plays, they went home in the afternoon, and the next day she felt disinclined to go again.
‘Even building a wall means disturbing the earth,’ said Xi-feng. ‘We’ve stirred everyone up already. We may as well go out again today and enjoy ourselves.’

But there were two things on Grandmother Jia’s mind. First, ever since Master Zhang had raised the question of finding Bao-yu a wife the day before, the boy had been unhappy. On coming home he had lost his temper and complained that Zhang had proposed a match for him, saying over and over that he would never see him again. No one else knew why. Second, Dai-yu had come home suffering from the heat. For these two reasons, Grandmother Jia firmly refused to go.

segments.text: Bao-yu had been deeply troubled by Master Zhang’s talk of a match the day before. Now, hearing Dai-yu say this, he thought: ‘I could forgive anyone else for not knowing what is in my heart. But now even she is making fun of me.’ His distress grew a hundred times worse than usual. Before anyone else he could never have flown into such a rage. But from Dai-yu these words were altogether different from the same words spoken by another. His face darkened at once.
‘All the time I’ve known you has been wasted. Enough, enough!’
Dai-yu gave two cold little laughs.
‘I know it’s been wasted. How could I compare with someone who has something to match yours?’
Bao-yu came right up to her and demanded, ‘Are you deliberately wishing Heaven to punish me and Earth to destroy me?’
For a moment Dai-yu could make no sense of this.
‘Only yesterday I swore it several times over this very thing,’ he went on. ‘And today you condemn me to it again.

segments.text: ‘If Heaven punishes me and Earth destroys me, what good will that do you?’
Only now did Dai-yu remember what he had said the day before. She had indeed spoken wrongly this time. Agitated and ashamed, she answered in a trembling voice:

‘If I deliberately wished any such thing on you, may Heaven punish me and Earth destroy me too! Why must you do this? I know what it is. When Master Zhang proposed that match yesterday, you were afraid it would spoil your splendid marriage. You’re angry about it, and you’ve come to take it out on me.’

segments.text: Now Bao-yu had been born with a certain disreputable weakness: he was a fool for love. He and Dai-yu had grown up in daily intimacy, their feelings answering each other’s. As he began to understand something of the world, and read those improper books and unorthodox tales, he found that none of the accomplished girls he saw in the homes of relatives or friends could begin to compare with Dai-yu. He had therefore long cherished a feeling he could not put into words. In his happiness or his anger, he tried every possible indirect means of sounding her out. Dai-yu, as it happened, had something of the same foolishness, and she too used feigned feelings to test his. You hide your true heart and show me something false; I hide my true heart and show you something false. When two such pretences meet, something real must come of it in the end. In all the little complications between them, a quarrel now and then was scarcely to be avoided.

At this very moment, Bao-yu was thinking: ‘I can forgive others for not knowing my heart. But can you really not see that in my heart and in my eyes there is only you? Instead of sharing my unhappiness, you make fun of me and shut my mouth with such words.

segments.text: ‘All the time you are in my heart, it counts for nothing. There is no place for me in yours.’

That was what he felt, but he could not say it. Dai-yu was thinking: ‘Of course there is a place for me in your heart. People may talk about “gold matching jade”, but surely you wouldn’t value that absurd tale more than me? When I keep bringing up “gold and jade”, you need only remain perfectly calm, as though you hadn’t heard. Then I would know you valued me and had no thought of that at all. Why do you get so agitated the moment I mention it? It must be because “gold and jade” is always in your mind. When I bring it up, you’re afraid I will begin to suspect, so you make a show of being upset, deliberately trying to deceive me.’

segments.text: Thus the two of them, who had begun with one heart, put out so many branches and leaves that they made two hearts of it instead. Bao-yu went on thinking: ‘I don’t mind what happens to me, so long as you have your wish. I would willingly die for you this instant. Whether you know it or not makes no difference. Only let me follow my own heart. That would show you were close to me, not far away.’

Dai-yu meanwhile was thinking: ‘You need only look after yourself. If you are well, I shall be well too. Why should you let yourself suffer for my sake? Don’t you realise that when you suffer, I suffer? You are the one who won’t let me come close. You are deliberately making me keep my distance.’
