segments.text: Both wished for closeness, yet each made it seem that distance was intended. These thoughts were part of the two young people’s habitual secret feelings, and it would be difficult to recount them all. Let us return to what could be seen.

Dai-yu’s words ‘splendid marriage’ were more than Bao-yu could bear. He choked on his anger and could not get a word out. In a fit of temper he tore the Spiritual Jade from his neck, clenched his teeth and hurled it to the ground with all his strength.
‘Wretched bit of rubbish! I’ll smash you and have done with it!’
But the jade was extraordinarily hard. The throw had not done it the slightest harm. Seeing it unbroken, Bao-yu turned to look for something to smash it with. Dai-yu had already begun to cry.
‘Why must you do this? Throwing and smashing a dumb thing that can’t answer! If you want to smash something, you’d better smash me.’
As the quarrel went on, Nightingale, Snowgoose and the others hurried over to calm them.

segments.text: Then, seeing Bao-yu hammering at the jade with all his might, they tried to snatch it away, but could not. This was worse than any of their previous quarrels. They had no choice but to fetch Aroma, who came in haste and finally managed to take it from him.
‘I’m smashing my own things,’ Bao-yu said with a cold laugh. ‘What has it to do with any of you?’

segments.text: His face had turned yellow with rage, his whole expression distorted. Aroma had never seen him so angry. She took his hand and spoke with a smile.
‘You may have quarrelled with your cousin, but there’s no need to smash this. If you broke it, how could she bear the feeling of it, or face anyone afterwards?’

As Dai-yu wept, she heard Aroma put into words exactly what was in her own heart. So Bao-yu did not understand her as well as Aroma did! Her grief redoubled, and she sobbed more bitterly than ever. In her distress she could no longer keep down the xiangru decoction she had just taken to relieve the effects of the heat. With a retch she brought it all up. Nightingale hurried forward to catch it in a handkerchief, which Dai-yu soaked through in mouthful after mouthful. Snowgoose came to pat her back.

‘However upset you are, miss, you must take some care of yourself,’ said Nightingale. ‘You had only just taken your medicine and begun to feel better. Now you’ve quarrelled with Master Bao and brought it all up again. If it brings on an illness, how could Master Bao bear it?’
Nightingale had put into words exactly what was in Bao-yu’s heart. So Dai-yu did not understand him as well as Nightingale did!

segments.text: He saw Dai-yu, her face flushed and her head throbbing, gasping as she cried, tears and sweat running together. She was terribly frail. Now he regretted arguing with her. Look at the state she was in, and he could not suffer it in her place. At the thought, his own tears began to fall.

Aroma, standing beside him as they both wept, felt her heart ache too. His hand was icy in hers. She wanted to tell him not to cry, but feared that some grievance might remain pent up in him; and she also feared slighting Dai-yu. Better that they should all have a cry and let it go. She began to weep as well. Nightingale cleaned up the vomited medicine, then took a fan and gently fanned Dai-yu. Seeing the other three utterly silent, each weeping alone, she too was overcome and wiped her eyes with her handkerchief. The four of them wept facing one another without a word.

segments.text: After a while Aroma forced a smile and said to Bao-yu:
‘If nothing else, one look at the tassel on this jade ought to stop you quarrelling with Miss Lin.’

At these words Dai-yu rushed over, heedless of her illness, and snatched it away. She snatched up a pair of scissors and began to cut the tassel. Before Aroma and Nightingale could take it from her, she had cut it into several pieces.
‘All my work was wasted too,’ she cried. ‘He doesn’t want it. There’ll be someone else to make him a better one.’
Aroma hastily took the jade.
‘Why do this? It was my fault for saying too much.’
‘Go on cutting,’ Bao-yu said to Dai-yu. ‘I shan’t wear it anyway. It doesn’t matter.’

segments.text: While all this was going on inside, the old serving-women had seen Dai-yu weeping and vomiting, and Bao-yu smashing his jade. They did not know where it would end. Afraid they might be held responsible, they went together to the front of the house to tell Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang, and so clear themselves of blame. Seeing them make such an urgent business of their report, the two ladies feared that some great calamity had occurred, and hurried into the Garden to see the young cousins.

In her alarm, Aroma blamed Nightingale for troubling Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship. Nightingale, supposing Aroma had gone to tell them, blamed her in turn. When Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang came in, neither Bao-yu nor Dai-yu had anything to say; questioned, neither could give a reason for the quarrel. The blame was therefore shifted to Aroma and Nightingale.
‘Why haven’t you taken proper care of them? Here they are making all this trouble, and neither of you doing anything!’
The two maids received a thorough scolding and lecture.

segments.text: Neither could say a word in her defence. They could only listen. At last Grandmother Jia took Bao-yu away, and peace was restored.

A day passed, and on the third, Xue Pan’s birthday, his family gave a feast with plays and invited the Jias. Bao-yu had not seen Dai-yu since offending her, and was full of remorse. Listless and dispirited, he had no heart for plays. He pleaded illness and did not go. Dai-yu had merely suffered a little from the sultry heat two days before, and was not seriously ill. Hearing that he was not going, she thought: ‘He loves wine and plays, yet today he won’t go. It must be because he was so angry yesterday. Or perhaps, seeing that I’m not going, he has no heart for it either. But whatever happened yesterday, I should never, never have cut the tassel on his jade. He certainly won’t wear it again now, until I make him another.’
She deeply regretted what she had done.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia, seeing how angry they both were, had thought that if they met at the plays that day, it would all blow over. Instead, neither would go. Distracted, the old lady began to complain.

‘What sins must this old wretch have committed in another life, to be saddled with two such thoughtless little tormentors! Not a day passes but they give me something to worry about. It’s just as the saying goes: “Those who owe each other grief are bound to meet.” Once I’ve closed my eyes and breathed my last, these two tormentors can turn heaven upside down for all I care. What I don’t see won’t trouble me. But no, this last breath won’t leave me!’

segments.text: As she complained, she too began to weep. Her words reached Bao-yu and Dai-yu. Neither of them, as it happened, had ever heard the saying ‘Those who owe each other grief are bound to meet’. Now the words had suddenly come to them. Each lowered their head and pondered their meaning as though in Chan meditation; each found tears falling unawares. Though they had not met, one shed tears into the breeze at the Naiad’s House while the other sighed long before the moon at the House of Green Delights. Were they not two people apart, whose feelings sprang from a single heart?

segments.text: Aroma tried to reason with Bao-yu.

‘No matter how you look at it, the fault is all yours. When the pages at home quarrel with their sisters, or a husband and wife fall out, you hear about it and scold the pages for being fools who can’t understand a girl’s feelings. Now you’re doing the very same thing. Tomorrow is the fifth, the great festival. If you two still behave like enemies, Her Old Ladyship will be angrier than ever, and no one will have any peace. Take my advice. Swallow your pride and make a proper apology, so that everyone can be as they were before. It would be better in every way.’

segments.text: Now Dai-yu regretted her quarrel with Bao-yu, but could hardly go and seek him out. Day and night she was miserable, as though something had gone missing. Nightingale guessed what was on her mind and tried to reason with her.

‘If you ask me, miss, you were a little too hasty the other day. Other people may not know Master Bao’s temper, but surely we do. It isn’t just once or twice that there’s been trouble over that jade.’
‘Pah!’ said Dai-yu. ‘So you’re taking his side and finding fault with me! What was hasty about me?’

‘Why did you have to cut the tassel off, when there was nothing wrong with it?’ Nightingale asked, smiling. ‘That makes him three parts in the wrong and you seven. As I see it, he’s always good to you. It’s only because you’re so easily offended, and so often put him in the wrong for nothing, that things have come to this.’

segments.text: Dai-yu was about to answer when someone called at the courtyard gate. Nightingale listened for a moment and smiled.
‘That’s Master Bao’s voice. He must have come to apologise.’
‘Don’t open the gate!’ said Dai-yu.
‘There you go again, miss. It’s such a hot day, with the sun beating down like that. What if he falls ill out there in the sun?’

segments.text: As she spoke she went out to open the gate. It was indeed Bao-yu. She let him in with a smile.
‘I thought Master Bao was never going to darken our door again. And here you are!’
‘You make so much of the tiniest thing,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Why on earth shouldn’t I come? Even if I died, my ghost would come a hundred times a day. Is Cousin Lin quite well again?’
‘Her illness is better. Her temper isn’t, though.’

segments.text: ‘I know what’s troubling her,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.

He went in as he spoke and found Dai-yu on her bed, crying again. She had not been crying before; but when she heard he had come, her heart ached in spite of herself, and the tears began to roll down, beyond her power to stop them.

‘Are you quite well again, cousin?’
Dai-yu went on wiping her tears, without answering. Bao-yu edged himself on to the side of the bed and smiled.
‘I know you’re not angry with me.

segments.text: ‘Only if I stay away, other people will think we’ve quarrelled again. And if we wait for them to come and make peace between us, won’t that make us seem like strangers? You’d better beat me or scold me now, just as you please. Only don’t refuse to speak to me.’

He called her ‘dear cousin’ tens of thousands of times. Dai-yu had meant never to have anything more to do with him. But now, when he said that letting other people know of their quarrel would make them seem like strangers, she could see once again that he felt himself closer to her than anyone else. Unable to hold back her tears, she said:
‘You needn’t coax me. From now on, I shan’t presume to be close to you any more, Master Bao. You can think of me as gone.’
‘Where would you go?’ Bao-yu asked with a smile.
‘Home.’
‘I’ll go with you,’ he said, still smiling.
‘I’ll die.’
‘If you die, I’ll become a monk!’

segments.text: Dai-yu’s expression hardened at once.

‘You must have a death wish yourself, talking such nonsense! You’ve several sisters of your own, older and younger. If they all died one day, how many bodies have you got to turn into monks? I shall tell people what you’ve said and let them judge.’

segments.text: Bao-yu knew he had spoken rashly. It was too late to regret it now. His face flushed deep red, and he hung his head, not daring to make a sound. Fortunately no one else was in the room. Dai-yu stared hard at him for a long while, too angry to utter a word. When she saw his face swelling purple with the strain, she clenched her teeth, jabbed him hard in the forehead with one finger and gave a little snort.
‘You, you—’ she said through her teeth.

She had scarcely got the two words out before she sighed again and took up her handkerchief to wipe her eyes. Bao-yu’s heart was already full of things he could not say, and now he had blundered and was bitterly sorry. The poke in the forehead, her attempt to speak, the words that would not come, her sighing and weeping: all this moved him too, until tears rolled down his own face. He meant to wipe them away with his handkerchief, only to find he had forgotten it again, and used his sleeve instead. Though she was crying, Dai-yu noticed at once. He was wearing a brand-new mauve gauze robe, and there he was wiping his tears on it! Still wiping her own eyes, she turned, took a fine silk handkerchief lying beside her pillow and flung it into his lap. Without a word, she covered her face and went on crying.

segments.text: Bao-yu hastily caught the handkerchief and wiped his tears. He edged a little closer, took one of Dai-yu’s hands and smiled.
‘I’m torn to pieces inside, and still you cry! Come, let’s go to Grandmother together.’
Dai-yu flung his hand away.
‘Who wants you pawing at them? You’re growing older every day, and still you’re so shameless, without the least idea how to behave.’

segments.text: Before she had finished, a voice called, ‘All right again!’
Both of them jumped. Turning round, they saw Xi-feng come bounding in, laughing.

‘Grandmother’s been blaming heaven and earth, insisting I come and see whether you’ve made it up. I told her there was no need. Give them three days, I said, and they’ll make it up by themselves. She scolded me and said I was lazy. Well, here I am, and it’s just as I told her. I can’t see what the two of you ever have to quarrel about. Friends for three days, enemies for two! The older you get, the more childish you become. Here you are holding hands and crying. Why were you a pair of fighting cocks yesterday? Come along to Grandmother and set the poor old lady’s mind at rest.’
She took Dai-yu by the hand and started off. Dai-yu turned to call her maids, but not one was there.
‘What do you want them for?’ said Xi-feng. ‘I’m here to wait on you.’
Talking all the while, she pulled her away.

segments.text: Bao-yu followed them out through the garden gate. When they reached Grandmother Jia, Xi-feng said, laughing:

‘I told you no one need trouble about them: they’d make it up themselves. But you wouldn’t believe me, Grandmother. You insisted I go and mediate. And when I got there to make peace, what did I find but the two of them already apologising to each other! Smiling at each other, pouring out their feelings, like “a hawk with its claws round a kite’s feet”. Each had the other hooked. What need was there for me to make peace?’
Everyone in the room laughed.

segments.text: Bao-chai was there too. Dai-yu sat down beside Grandmother Jia without a word. Bao-yu, having nothing to say, turned to Bao-chai with a smile.

‘It was Cousin Xue’s birthday, and I had to be ill just then. I had no other present to give him, and couldn’t even go and kowtow. He didn’t know I was ill. He must have thought I was lazy and making excuses. If he’s cross with me later, you’ll explain for me, won’t you, cousin?’

‘What a fuss!’ Bao-chai said, smiling. ‘Even if you’d wanted to come, we couldn’t have put you to the trouble, much less when you were ill. You cousins see each other every day. Making a point of such things would only put you on a formal footing.’

segments.text: ‘As long as you understand, cousin, that’s all right,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Why aren’t you watching the plays?’
‘I can’t stand the heat. I watched two scenes and was terribly hot. I wanted to go, but the guests wouldn’t leave, so I had to make the excuse that I wasn’t feeling well and come away.’
Hearing this, Bao-yu could not help looking awkward. He tried to cover his embarrassment with another smiling remark.
‘No wonder they compare you to Noble Consort Yang. You’re plump and afraid of the heat too.’
Bao-chai was furious, but could hardly act on it. After a moment’s thought her face reddened. She gave two cold little laughs.
‘I may be like Noble Consort Yang, but I haven’t a fine elder or younger brother to play Yang Guo-zhong!’
Just then the little maid Indigo, who had lost her fan, came up to Bao-chai with a smile.
‘I’m sure you’ve hidden it, Miss Bao. Do be kind and give it back.’
Bao-chai pointed at her.
‘Mind what you’re saying! If I’d been playing with you, you might have cause to suspect me.

Indigo ran off at this. Bao-yu knew he had blundered again. With so many people present, he was even more embarrassed than he had been with Dai-yu. He quickly turned away and tried to make conversation with somebody else.

segments.text: Dai-yu had been thoroughly pleased to hear Bao-yu tease Bao-chai and was just about to join in and have a laugh at her expense. But Indigo’s search for her fan had brought those two retorts from Bao-chai, and Dai-yu changed what she was going to say.
‘Cousin Bao,’ she asked, smiling, ‘which two scenes did you see?’
Bao-chai had noticed the look of satisfaction on Dai-yu’s face: Bao-yu’s teasing must have been just what she wanted to hear. Now this sudden question came. Bao-chai smiled.
‘I saw Li Kui scold Song Jiang and then apologise to him.’
‘You know everything, past and present,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘How can you not know the name of that play, instead of telling us all that? It’s called Bearing Thorns to Beg Pardon.’

‘So it’s called Bearing Thorns to Beg Pardon!’ Bao-chai said, smiling. ‘You know everything, past and present, so of course you know about bearing thorns to beg pardon. I know nothing about bearing thorns to beg pardon!’
Before she had finished, Bao-yu and Dai-yu, whose consciences were uneasy, had already blushed scarlet.

segments.text: Xi-feng understood little of these matters, but a glance at the three of them was enough to tell her what was meant. She too smiled and asked the company:
‘Who’s been eating raw ginger in this sweltering weather?’
No one understood.
‘No one’s been eating raw ginger,’ they said.

segments.text: Xi-feng deliberately put her hand to her cheek and looked surprised.
‘If no one’s been eating raw ginger, why is there such a sting?’

This made Bao-yu and Dai-yu feel more uncomfortable still. Bao-chai was about to say something else, but Bao-yu looked so thoroughly abashed, so altered, that she could not go on. She brought it to an end with a smile. None of the others had understood what the four of them were saying, so they let it pass.

segments.text: Presently Bao-chai and Xi-feng left. Dai-yu turned to Bao-yu with a smile.
‘Now you’ve had a taste of someone fiercer than I am. Did you think everyone was as slow-witted and tongue-tied as me, letting people say whatever they please?’

Bao-yu was already feeling foolish because Bao-chai had taken his words amiss. Dai-yu’s question only made him more irritable. He wanted to retort, but was afraid that she too would take it amiss. He had to swallow his anger and went straight out, listless and dejected.

segments.text: It was the height of summer, the morning meal was over, and the long day had left most of the household, masters and servants alike, drowsy and tired. Bao-yu wandered with his hands behind his back. Wherever he went, not a sound was to be heard. Leaving Grandmother Jia’s rooms, he went west through a passage hall to Xi-feng’s courtyard. When he reached the gate he found it shut. He knew her regular custom in hot weather was to rest at midday for a double-hour. It would not do to go in, so he passed through a corner gate and entered Lady Wang’s principal room. Several maids were nodding over the needlework in their hands. In the inner room Lady Wang was asleep on a summer couch, with Golden seated beside her patting her legs. Golden too was swaying drowsily, her eyes half closed.

segments.text: Bao-yu went softly up to her and took off one of her dangling earrings. Golden opened her eyes and saw who it was.
‘As sleepy as all that?’ he whispered with a smile.

She smiled with her lips pressed together, waved him away and closed her eyes again. The sight of her made him unwilling to leave. He quietly craned his neck to make sure Lady Wang’s eyes were shut, then reached into the purse at his side, took out some Fragrant Snow Mouth-Moistening Pills and slipped them into Golden’s mouth. Without opening her eyes, she simply held them there. Bao-yu came closer, took her hand and whispered, smiling:
‘Tomorrow I’ll ask Mother to give you to me. Then we can be together.’
Golden did not answer.
‘Or I’ll ask as soon as Mother wakes up,’ he went on.
Golden opened her eyes, gave him a push and smiled.
‘What’s the hurry? “A golden hairpin may fall down a well, but what’s yours will still be yours.” Don’t you even understand that saying?

segments.text: ‘I’ll tell you something worth your while. Go to the little courtyard to the east and catch Huan and Cai-yun together.’
‘Let him do as he pleases,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘I only want to stay with you.’
Lady Wang suddenly rolled over and sat up. She struck Golden across the face, then pointed at her and scolded:
‘You filthy little whore! It’s you who teach decent young gentlemen to misbehave.’
The moment Bao-yu saw his mother sit up, he had fled like a wisp of smoke.

segments.text: Golden dropped to her knees, weeping.

‘I’ll never dare do it again. Beat me or scold me as you please, Your Ladyship. Only don’t send me away, and I shall count it heaven’s own mercy. I’ve been with you for ten years and more. If I’m driven out now, how can I ever face anyone again?’

Lady Wang was indeed a kind, generous and compassionate woman, and had never once struck any of her maids. But now she had suddenly seen Golden behave with a shamelessness of the very kind she had most detested all her life. Unable to contain her anger, she had struck her once and scolded her. For all Golden’s pleading, she would not keep her. In the end she sent for Golden’s mother, old Mrs Bai, to take her away. Golden went out in shame and humiliation. We need say no more of her for the present.

segments.text: To return to Bao-yu: when he saw Lady Wang wake, he had hurried off into Prospect Garden in discomfiture. The blazing sun was overhead; the shadows of the trees spread over the ground. Cicadas filled his ears, but no human voice disturbed the stillness. He had just reached a rose trellis when he heard someone sob. Puzzled, he stopped and listened carefully. There was indeed someone on the far side of the trellis. It was the fifth month, when the roses were thick with leaves and blossom. Bao-yu quietly peered through a gap in the fence. A girl was crouching beneath the flowers, scratching at the earth with a hairpin, the kind used to fasten up the hair, while tears ran silently down her face.

segments.text: ‘Can this be another foolish girl come to bury flowers like Little Pin-pin?’ Bao-yu wondered. Then he sighed to himself. ‘If she really is burying flowers, it’s Dong Shi copying a beauty’s frown. Not only is there nothing new in it: it’s positively tiresome.’

He was about to call out, ‘You needn’t copy Miss Lin!’ Fortunately, before the words had left his mouth, he looked again. The girl’s face was unfamiliar. She was not a maid, but seemed to be one of the twelve girls learning to act, though he could not tell which sort of role she played: male, female, painted-face or clown. He quickly put out his tongue and covered his mouth.
‘Luckily I didn’t blurt it out. Both times before, speaking too soon was what made Pin-pin angry and Bao-chai take offence. If I offend these girls as well, I’ll feel more foolish than ever.’

segments.text: As he thought this, he was vexed that he could not recognise her. He looked more closely. Her brows drew together like spring hills, her eyes narrowed like autumn water; her face was delicate, her waist slender, and her graceful, swaying figure was very like Dai-yu’s. Already he could not bear to leave her and simply gazed, entranced. Though she was scratching the ground with her golden hairpin, she was not digging a hole to bury flowers. She was tracing a character in the earth. Bao-yu followed the hairpin up and down, watching each upright, each cross-stroke, dot and hook. He counted: eighteen strokes. Then he used his finger to trace them on his palm in the same order, trying to make out the character. When he had finished, he thought a moment and recognised it: ‘qiang’, the character for rose. ‘She must want to write a poem or a song,’ he thought. ‘Perhaps the sight of these flowers has moved her and a couple of lines have come to her. Afraid of forgetting them in the excitement, she may be writing in the earth while she works them out. Let’s see what she writes next.’ He went on thinking and watching. The girl was still tracing away, but whatever she wrote, it was always ‘qiang’.

segments.text: ‘She looks so frail. How can her heart bear such suffering? If only I could take some of it from you!’

In the dog days the weather was changeable: a single cloud could bring rain. Suddenly a cool breeze passed, and a shower came swishing down. Bao-yu saw the water dripping from the girl’s head; her gauze clothes were soaked in an instant.
‘Rain now!’ he thought. ‘How can a girl so delicate stand the shock of a sudden downpour?’
He could not help calling out:
‘Stop writing! Look, it’s pouring. You’re wet through.’

Startled, the girl looked up. Someone outside the flowers was telling her to stop writing because it was raining hard. Bao-yu had a handsome, delicate face; moreover, the profusion of flowers and leaves hid him above and below, leaving only half his face visible. The girl took him for a maid, never imagining it was Bao-yu.
‘Thank you for reminding me, sister,’ she said with a smile. ‘But have you something to shelter you out there?’
Her words brought him to his senses. He gave a cry. Only then did he realise he was cold all over.

segments.text: He looked down and saw that he too was soaked through. ‘Oh dear!’ he said, and ran all the way back to the House of Green Delights, still worrying that the girl had nowhere to shelter from the rain.

The next day was the Dragon Boat Festival. Wen-guan and the other girls, twelve in all, had been given leave from their lessons and had come to amuse themselves about the garden. Two of them, Bao-guan, who played young men, and Yu-guan, who played principal female roles, happened to be at the House of Green Delights, joking with Aroma, when the downpour trapped them there. They had all blocked the drain so that water collected in the courtyard. Some caught waterfowl and others herded them in: green-headed ducks, brightly patterned mandarin ducks, and richly coloured mandarin ducks. They stitched their wings together and let them loose in the courtyard to play, shutting the gate. Aroma and the others were laughing under the covered walk.

segments.text: Finding the gate shut, Bao-yu knocked, but everyone inside was laughing too much to hear. He called for a long while and hammered on the gate till it boomed before they finally heard him. They reckoned Bao-yu could not possibly be coming back just then.
‘Who’s knocking at this hour?’ Aroma called, laughing. ‘There’s no one to let you in.’
‘It’s me!’ said Bao-yu.
‘That sounds like Miss Bao,’ said Musk.
‘Nonsense!’ said Skybright. ‘What would Miss Bao be coming here for now?’
‘Let me peep through the crack,’ said Aroma. ‘If it’s someone we can let in, I’ll open it. If not, they can stay in the rain.’

She went along the covered walk to the gate and looked out. There was Bao-yu, as bedraggled as a chicken caught in the rain. She was at once alarmed and amused. Hastily opening the gate, she doubled up with laughter and clapped her hands.
‘What are you doing running about in rain like this? How were we to know it was you, sir?’

Bao-yu was seething. He had set his heart on giving whoever opened the gate a few kicks. When it opened, he did not look properly to see who was there, still taking it for one of the little maids. He raised his foot and kicked her in the ribs.

segments.text: Aroma cried out. Bao-yu went on scolding:
‘You low little creatures! I’ve let you get away with so much that you’ve grown pleased with yourselves. You’re not afraid of me at all. Now you even make a joke of me!’
As he spoke, he looked down and saw that it was Aroma who was crying. Only then did he realise he had kicked the wrong person. He hastily put on a smile.
‘Oh! It was you who came! Where did I catch you?’

segments.text: Aroma had never even been harshly spoken to. Now, without warning, Bao-yu had lost his temper and kicked her, in front of so many people. Shame, anger and pain left her not knowing where to put herself. She wanted to do something, but reckoned that he probably had not meant to kick her. She had to master herself.
‘You didn’t catch me,’ she said. ‘Go and change your clothes.’
Bao-yu went into his room and began to undress, saying with a smile:
‘In all my life, this is the first time I’ve lost my temper and hit anyone. And to think it had to be you!’
Aroma bore the pain as she helped him change. She too smiled.

‘I’m always the one to begin things, so naturally I should come first, whether it’s something big or small, good or bad. Only don’t let hitting me give you a taste for it, so that you start hitting other people tomorrow.’
‘I didn’t mean it just now,’ said Bao-yu.
‘Who said you meant it? Opening and shutting the gate is usually those little maids’ business.

segments.text: By now the rain had stopped, and Bao-guan and Yu-guan had already gone. The pain under Aroma’s ribs made her feel wretched; she could scarcely eat her evening meal. When she undressed to bathe that night, she saw a bruise as big as a bowl on her side. It frightened her, but she did not like to make it known. Presently she went to bed. The pain followed her into her dreams, and she could not help moaning in her sleep.

Although Bao-yu said he had not meant it, the sight of Aroma so listless kept him from sleeping peacefully either. Hearing her cry out in the night, he knew he must have kicked her hard. He got out of bed and quietly brought a lamp to look at her. Just as he reached her bedside, she coughed twice and spat out a mouthful of phlegm. With another moan she opened her eyes. The sight of Bao-yu startled her.
‘What are you doing?’
‘You were crying out in your sleep. I must have kicked you hard. Let me have a look.’
‘My head’s swimming, and there’s a rank, sweet taste in my throat. Shine the lamp on the floor.’
Bao-yu did as she asked. On the floor lay a mouthful of fresh blood.

segments.text: Now, when Aroma saw the fresh blood she had spat on the floor, her heart sank. She remembered a saying she had often heard: ‘When the young spit blood, their days are numbered. Even if they live long, they will be invalids for life.’ At the thought of it, all her customary dreams of winning distinction and having something to be proud of in years to come turned to ashes. Tears fell from her eyes.
The sight of her crying wrung Bao-yu’s heart too.
‘How do you feel inside?’ he asked.
‘Perfectly well. How should I feel?’ Aroma forced a smile.
Bao-yu wanted to call someone at once to warm rice wine and fetch Shanyangxue Lidong Pills. Aroma caught his hand.

‘It’s easy enough for you to make a fuss,’ she said, smiling, ‘but think how many people you’ll wake. They’ll only blame me for making so much of myself. Nobody knows anything about it, and you’ll let everyone know. That won’t do either of us any good. The sensible thing is to send a page to ask Doctor Wang tomorrow and get me a little medicine. That will soon put me right. Wouldn’t it be better if not a soul knew?’
Bao-yu saw the sense of this and had to give way. He poured some tea from the table and brought it for her to rinse her mouth.

Having asked how it had happened and established that it was simply an injury, Wang Ji-ren named a pill and explained how to take it and how to apply it.

segments.text: Bao-yu remembered the directions, returned to the Garden and treated her accordingly. Of that we need say no more.

This was the Dragon Boat Festival. Sweet flag and mugwort adorned the doors, and tiger charms were tied about people’s arms. At noon Lady Wang gave a feast, inviting Aunt Xue and her daughter and the others to celebrate. Bao-yu noticed that Bao-chai was cool towards him and did not speak to him; he knew it was because of what had happened the day before. Lady Wang, seeing his listlessness, assumed he was ashamed over yesterday’s affair with Golden, and took even less notice of him. Dai-yu thought his languor came of having offended Bao-chai. This made her unhappy, and her own manner grew languid too. Lady Wang had told Xi-feng about Bao-yu and Golden the previous evening. Knowing how displeased she was, Xi-feng did not dare to laugh and joke, but took her cue from Lady Wang’s face, which made things cooler still. Ying-chun and her sisters, seeing everyone else so dispirited, lost their spirits too. They all sat for a little while, then dispersed.

segments.text: Dai-yu was by nature fonder of dispersals than of gatherings. There was a certain reason in her thinking. ‘Whenever people come together, they must part,’ she would say. ‘If they are happy together, won’t it be cold and lonely when they part? And loneliness brings sorrow. Better, then, not to come together at all. Flowers, for instance: we love them when they open, but when they fade they only add to our sadness. Better if they never opened.’

segments.text: Thus, what others found joyful she found sad. Bao-yu, by contrast, wanted everyone always to be together, dreading the sorrow that parting might bring. He wanted flowers always in bloom, dreading the loss of pleasure when they faded. Only when the feast was over and the flowers had fallen did he yield to what could not be helped, for all his thousand griefs. So when today’s dispirited party broke up, Dai-yu thought nothing of it. It was Bao-yu who went back to his room in low spirits, sighing again and again.
Unfortunately, as Skybright came to help him change, she let a fan slip from her hand. It fell to the floor and its ribs broke.
‘Clumsy fool! Clumsy fool!’ Bao-yu sighed. ‘What will become of you? When you have a household of your own to manage, will you still be attending to one thing and forgetting the next?’
Skybright laughed coldly.

‘Master Bao’s temper has grown very grand lately. Nothing we do is right. First you hit Aroma, and now it’s our turn to be found fault with. Kick us or beat us, as you please. Dropping a fan is an everyday thing.

segments.text: ‘In the old days goodness knows how many glass jars and agate bowls like those got broken, and we never heard an angry word. Now all this over one fan! Why bother? If you don’t like us, send us away and choose better ones to wait on you. Wouldn’t it be nicer to part on good terms?’
Bao-yu was trembling all over with anger.
‘Don’t be in such a hurry. The day for parting will come!’

segments.text: Aroma had already heard them from the other side of the room and hurried over.
‘What’s happened now?’ she asked Bao-yu. ‘There, just as I said: I’ve only to be away a moment and something happens.’
Skybright gave another cold laugh.

‘Since you know so well what to say, sister, you should have come sooner and saved the master from losing his temper. From the beginning of time you’re the only one who has ever waited on him. The rest of us never have. It was because you waited on him so well that you got a kick in the chest yesterday. Heaven knows what punishment is waiting tomorrow for those of us who don’t know how!’
Aroma was angry and ashamed. She was about to retort, but Bao-yu’s face had already turned yellow with rage. Swallowing her own anger, she gave Skybright a little push.
‘Be a good girl and go out for a walk. It’s our fault.’
‘Our’ could only mean herself and Bao-yu. This made Skybright more bitter still. She gave several cold little laughs.
‘I wonder who this “our” can be. Don’t make me blush for you!

segments.text: ‘Do you think I don’t know what you’ve been up to behind everyone’s backs? What right have you to talk of “our”? You haven’t even managed to become an acknowledged concubine. You’re no different from me. Where does “our” come in?’
Aroma’s face flushed purple with shame. Thinking it over, she saw that she had chosen the wrong words.
‘If you resent her,’ Bao-yu put in, ‘one day I’ll see that she is promoted, just to spite you.’
Aroma quickly caught his hand.
‘She’s a silly girl. Why argue with her? Besides, you’re usually so forbearing. You’ve let far worse things pass. What’s the matter today?’
‘Oh yes, I’m a silly girl,’ said Skybright with a cold laugh. ‘How could I be fit to speak to?’

‘Are you quarrelling with me, miss, or with Master Bao?’ Aroma asked. ‘If it’s me you’re angry with, tell me. There’s no need to shout about it in front of him. If it’s him you’re angry with, you shouldn’t shout till the whole world knows.

segments.text: ‘I only came in to settle things and persuade you both to take care of yourselves, and you’ve turned on me. You don’t seem to be angry with me, and you don’t seem to be angry with him. What are all these thrusts and jabs meant to achieve? I’ll say no more. Have it your own way.’
She started out.
‘There’s no need to be angry,’ Bao-yu told Skybright. ‘I’ve guessed what’s on your mind. You’re growing up now. Shall I tell Mother to send you away?’
This wounded Skybright afresh.
‘Why should I go?’ she said bitterly. ‘If you’ve taken a dislike to me, you needn’t think you can find some trick to get rid of me.’
‘When have I ever had to put up with such quarrelling?’ said Bao-yu.

segments.text: ‘You must want to leave. I’d better tell Mother and let her send you away.’
He stood up to go. Aroma hurried back and barred his way.
‘Where are you going?’ she asked with a smile.
‘To tell Mother.’

‘What nonsense! Won’t you be ashamed if you really go and tell her? Even if Skybright truly wants to leave, wait until everyone has cooled down. There’ll be time enough to mention it to Her Ladyship in an ordinary conversation. If you rush off now as though it were some urgent business, won’t she grow suspicious?’
‘She won’t suspect anything. I’ll tell her plainly that Skybright’s making a fuss because she wants to go.’

‘When did I ever make a fuss about going?’ Skybright cried through her tears. ‘First you lose your temper, then you try to pin things on me! Go and tell her, then. I’ll dash my brains out before I leave this door.’
‘How strange! You won’t go, and yet you make all this fuss. I can’t stand the noise. You’d better go and have done with it.’
He was determined to tell his mother.

segments.text: Seeing that she could not stop him, Aroma sank to her knees. Emerald, Ripple, Musk and the other maids had been listening outside in complete silence throughout the quarrel. When they heard Aroma kneel and beg him, they all came in and knelt too. Bao-yu hastily raised Aroma, sighed, and sat down on the bed. He told the others to get up and go.
‘What am I to do?’ he said to Aroma. ‘I could wear my heart to pieces and nobody would know.’
Tears began to fall. Seeing him cry, Aroma cried too.

segments.text: Skybright stood crying beside them and was about to speak when Dai-yu came in. She went out instead.
‘Why are you all crying on a festival day?’ Dai-yu asked with a smile. ‘Surely you haven’t been quarrelling over who gets the rice dumplings?’
Bao-yu and Aroma both gave a sudden little laugh.
‘Second Cousin won’t tell me,’ Dai-yu went on, ‘but I’ll find out if I ask you.’

segments.text: She patted Aroma’s shoulder.
‘Do tell me, dear sister-in-law,’ she said, smiling. ‘You two must have had a quarrel. Tell your little sister, and I’ll make peace between you.’
Aroma pushed her away.
‘Miss Lin, what are you playing at? I’m only a maid, and you will keep talking nonsense.’
‘You may call yourself a maid. I treat you as my sister-in-law.’
‘Why must you give people something to say against her?’ Bao-yu asked. ‘They gossip quite enough already. She doesn’t need you to help them.’
‘Miss Lin, you don’t know what’s on my mind,’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘If only I could draw my last breath and have done with it.’
‘If you died, I don’t know about anyone else,’ said Dai-yu, smiling, ‘but I should be the first to cry myself to death.’
‘If you died, I’d become a monk,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.

Dai-yu held up two fingers and smiled with her lips pressed together.
‘That’s twice you’ve become a monk. From now on I shall keep count.’

segments.text: Bao-yu knew she was referring to what he had said the other day. He merely smiled and let it pass. Presently, after Dai-yu had gone, someone came to say that Master Xue wished to see him, and he had to go. It turned out to be a drinking party. Unable to decline, he stayed until the company broke up.

By the time he returned that evening he was a little drunk. He made his unsteady way into his courtyard, where a couch and pillow had already been set out for enjoying the cool air. Someone lay asleep on the couch. Thinking it was Aroma, he sat on the edge and nudged her.
‘Is the pain any better?’
The girl rolled over and sat up.
‘Why must you start on me again?’
He looked: it was not Aroma but Skybright. He pulled her down to sit beside him.

‘You’re getting more and more spoilt,’ he said, smiling. ‘This morning you dropped a fan, and I said only a word or two, but you had all that to say to me. Never mind what you said to me: Aroma came to make peace out of kindness, and you dragged her into it too. Think it over. Was that right?’
‘It’s terribly hot,’ said Skybright. ‘Why all this pulling and tugging?

segments.text: ‘What would it look like if someone saw us? I’m not fit to sit here, anyway.’
‘If you know you’re not fit to sit here,’ Bao-yu said, smiling, ‘why were you lying here?’
Skybright had no answer. She gave a little snort of laughter.
‘It was all right until you came. Now you’re here, I’m not fit for it. Get up and let me go and bathe. Aroma and Musk have had their baths. I’ll call them out.’
‘I’ve been drinking quite a lot again,’ said Bao-yu, ‘and I need a wash too. Since you haven’t had yours, bring some water and let’s bathe together.’
Skybright waved her hand and laughed.

‘No, no! I wouldn’t dare get involved with you, sir. I remember when Emerald helped you bathe: it took two or three whole double-hours. Who knows what you were doing? We couldn’t very well go in. When you’d finished, we went to look. There was water right up the bed legs and pools of it even on the mat. Heaven knows how you managed it. We laughed for days. I haven’t the time to clear up after you. You needn’t bathe with me.

segments.text: ‘It’s cooler today, anyway. You had a bath earlier, and there’s no need for another. I’ll fetch a basin of water so you can wash your face and comb your hair. Faithful has just sent over a lot of fruit. It’s all cooling in the crystal jar. I’ll get them to serve you some.’
‘In that case you’re not to bathe either,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Just wash your hands and bring out the fruit for us to eat.’
‘I’m so clumsy I even drop fans and break them,’ Skybright said, smiling. ‘How could I be fit to serve fruit? Suppose I broke a plate as well. That would be dreadful.’

segments.text: ‘Break it if you like,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Things are only there for people to use. You like one thing and I like another; everyone has a different nature. A fan, for instance, is meant for fanning, but if you want to tear it up for fun, you can do that too. Only you mustn’t take your temper out on it. Cups and plates are meant to hold things, but if you enjoy the crash, you can even smash them on purpose. Only don’t take your temper out on them. That’s what it means to care for things.’

segments.text: ‘If that’s so,’ Skybright said, laughing, ‘give me a fan to tear. I like tearing them best.’
With a smile Bao-yu handed her one. She took it and, sure enough, ripped it in two. There came several more ripping sounds.
‘That sounds good!’ Bao-yu laughed beside her. ‘Tear it louder!’
Just then Musk came up.
‘Do spare yourselves a few sins,’ she said with a smile.
Bao-yu ran over, snatched the fan out of her hand and gave it to Skybright. Skybright tore that into several pieces too, and both of them laughed aloud.
‘What’s the meaning of this?’ said Musk. ‘Making sport with my things?’
‘Open the fan-box and choose another,’ Bao-yu said, laughing. ‘It’s nothing so precious.’
‘In that case, why not bring out the whole box and let her tear as many as she likes?’
‘Go and fetch it, then.’
‘I won’t commit that sin.

Skybright leant against the couch, laughing.
‘I’m tired too. I’ll tear some more tomorrow.’
‘As the ancients said,’ Bao-yu laughed, ‘“A thousand gold pieces cannot buy a smile.”

segments.text: ‘How much could a few fans be worth?’
He called for Aroma as he spoke. She had just changed her clothes and came out. The little maid Melilot gathered up the torn fans, and they all enjoyed the evening air. We need not dwell on it.

At noon next day Lady Wang, Bao-chai, Dai-yu and the other girls were sitting in Grandmother Jia’s room when someone announced, ‘Miss Shi has arrived.’ Soon Shi Xiang-yun indeed appeared in the courtyard, followed by a crowd of maids and serving-women. Bao-chai, Dai-yu and the others hurried to the foot of the steps to meet her. There is no need to describe the affection of young cousins reunited after a month apart. They went inside and exchanged all the proper greetings.
‘It’s hot,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Take off some of those outer clothes.’
Xiang-yun stood up at once to do so.
‘Why did you put all those things on?’ Lady Wang asked with a smile.
‘Second Aunt made me,’ Xiang-yun said, laughing. ‘Who wants to wear all this?’
‘You don’t know her, Aunt,’ Bao-chai put in with a smile. ‘She likes wearing other people’s clothes even better.

segments.text: ‘Do you remember when she was staying here in the third or fourth month last year? She put on Cousin Bao’s robe and boots and tied his brow-band on too. At first glance you’d have thought it was him, except for the two earrings. She stood behind that chair, and Grandmother kept calling, “Bao-yu, come here! The tassels on that lantern will shake dust into your eyes.” She only laughed and wouldn’t come. In the end none of us could keep from laughing, and Grandmother laughed too. “Well,” she said, “you look very handsome as a boy!”’

‘That’s nothing,’ Dai-yu said. ‘What about when we brought her here in the first month the year before last? She hadn’t been with us two days when it began to snow. I think Grandmother and Aunt had just come back from paying their respects to the ancestral portraits. Grandmother’s brand-new scarlet broadcloth cloak was lying there. The moment no one was looking, she put it on. It was far too big and far too long, so she tied a sash round the waist and went into the back courtyard to make a snowman with the maids. She fell headlong by the ditch and covered herself in mud and water.’
At these memories everyone laughed.

segments.text: ‘Nurse Zhou,’ Bao-chai asked the nurse with a smile, ‘is your young lady still as mischievous as ever?’
Nurse Zhou laughed too.

‘I don’t mind the mischief,’ Ying-chun said, smiling. ‘It’s the talking I object to. Even when she’s lying in bed, she goes on chattering, laughing for a bit and then talking again. Where does she find so much to say?’
‘I expect she’s better now,’ said Lady Wang. ‘A family came to look her over the other day. She’ll soon have a mother-in-law. Can she still behave like that?’
‘Are you staying today,’ Grandmother Jia asked, ‘or going home?’

segments.text: ‘Didn’t Your Old Ladyship see we’d brought her clothes?’ Nurse Zhou replied with a smile. ‘Of course she’s staying a couple of days.’
‘Is Cousin Bao-yu out?’ Xiang-yun asked.
‘She never thinks of anyone but Cousin Bao,’ Bao-chai said, laughing. ‘What a pair of innocents they are! You see, she hasn’t grown out of her mischief.’
‘You’re all growing up now,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘You must stop using childhood names.’

segments.text: She had scarcely spoken when Bao-yu appeared.
‘Cousin Yun’s here!’ he said, smiling. ‘Why didn’t you come when we sent for you the other day?’
‘Grandmother has just been telling this one off,’ said Lady Wang, ‘and here he comes calling her by name as well.’
‘Your cousin has something nice,’ Dai-yu told Xiang-yun. ‘He’s been waiting for you.’
‘What is it?’
‘Don’t believe her,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘It’s only a few days since I saw you, and you’ve grown taller still.’

‘Thank you for thinking of her,’ said Bao-yu.
‘I’ve brought her something nice.’
She took out a handkerchief tied in a knot.
‘What is it?’ Bao-yu asked. ‘You’d have done better to bring her a couple of those red-veined stone rings you sent the other day.’

segments.text: ‘And what do you call these?’ Xiang-yun said, laughing, and untied the bundle.
They looked. Sure enough, there were four of the same red-veined stone rings she had sent before.

‘Just look at the way her mind works,’ Dai-yu said, laughing. ‘When you sent ours the other day, wouldn’t it have saved trouble to send hers too? Now you’ve gone to all the bother of bringing them yourself. I thought it must be something new and wonderful, and here it’s only the same thing. You really are a silly girl.’

‘You’re the silly one!’ Xiang-yun replied with a smile. ‘Let me explain, and everyone can judge which of us is silly. When I send things to you, the messenger needn’t say a word. They’re brought in, and anyone can see they’re meant for the young ladies. But if I sent things for the maids as well, I’d first have to explain to him that this one was for one maid and that one for another. If he understood, well and good. But suppose he were a bit stupid and couldn’t remember the maids’ names? He’d mix everything up and talk such nonsense that even your presents would get muddled.

segments.text: ‘It would be all right if I sent a woman who knew them. But the other day I happened to send a page. How could I start telling him the maids’ names? Since I was coming anyway, wasn’t it simpler to bring their things myself?’
She laid out the four rings.
‘One for Sister Aroma, one for Sister Faithful, one for Sister Golden, and one for Sister Patience. Four different people. Could a page really remember all that so clearly?’
‘Quite clear, indeed!’ they all said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘Still as good at talking as ever,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘You’ll never give way to anyone.’
Dai-yu laughed coldly.
‘She needn’t be good at talking. Her gold qilin can talk for her.’

She rose and went out. Fortunately the others had not heard. Only Bao-chai pressed her lips together in a smile. Bao-yu, who had heard, was regretting his own ill-chosen words when he caught sight of Bao-chai’s smile and could not help smiling too. Seeing him smile, Bao-chai quickly got up and went to find Dai-yu and talk to her.

segments.text: ‘Have some tea and a rest,’ Grandmother Jia told Xiang-yun, ‘then go and see your cousins’ wives. It’s cool in the Garden too. Go and walk there with the girls.’

Xiang-yun agreed. She wrapped up three of the rings, rested a little, then rose to visit Xi-feng and the others. Her nurses and maids followed. She spent a while laughing and talking at Xi-feng’s, then went into Prospect Garden. After visiting Li Gong-cai and sitting with her briefly, she set off for the House of Green Delights to find Aroma.

segments.text: She turned to her attendants.
‘You needn’t follow me. Go and see your friends and relations. Kingfisher can stay and look after me.’
Off they went to find their aunts and sisters-in-law, and soon only Xiang-yun and Kingfisher remained.
‘Why aren’t these lotuses in flower yet?’ Kingfisher asked.
‘It isn’t time.’
‘Are they the same as the ones in our pond, with petals in tiers?’
‘Theirs aren’t as good as ours.’
‘They have a pomegranate tree over there with four or five branches all covered in them, one tier rising out of another. It’s a wonder they can grow like that.’
‘Flowers and plants are just like people,’ Xiang-yun said. ‘If their vital energy flows strongly, they grow well.’
Kingfisher turned her face away.
‘I don’t believe that. If they’re like people, why have I never seen anyone with another head growing on top of their head?’
Xiang-yun could not help laughing.
‘I tell you not to talk, but you will.

segments.text: ‘How is anyone supposed to answer that? Everything between heaven and earth is born of the two vital energies, yin and yang. Whether it’s upright or perverse, strange or monstrous, all its countless transformations come from yin and yang working with or against each other. Many things only seem strange because people seldom see them. The principle is the same in the end.’
‘So ever since heaven and earth were made, right down to now, it’s all been yins and yangs?’ asked Kingfisher.

‘Silly creature!’ Xiang-yun laughed. ‘The more you talk, the more you talk through your backside. What do you mean, “all yins and yangs”? Do you think there’s a separate thing called a yin-and-yang? “Yin” and “yang” are two words for what is really one. When yang reaches its limit it becomes yin, and when yin reaches its limit it becomes yang. It isn’t that yin comes to an end and a new yang is born, or yang comes to an end and a new yin is born.’
‘You’ve muddled me completely! What is this yin-and-yang, without shape or shadow? Just tell me, miss: what does it look like?’
‘How could yin and yang have a shape? They’re simply vital energy. Things take form when they receive it.

segments.text: ‘Heaven, for example, is yang, and earth is yin. Water is yin and fire is yang. The sun is yang and the moon is yin.’
‘Yes, yes!’ Kingfisher said, smiling. ‘Now I understand. No wonder everyone calls the sun the “Great Yang”, and fortune-tellers call the moon the “Great Yin”. That’s the reason.’
‘Amitabha!’ Xiang-yun said, laughing. ‘You’ve understood at last.’

segments.text: ‘I can see how big things like that have yin and yang,’ said Kingfisher, ‘but surely mosquitoes and fleas and midges, flowers and grass, tiles and bricks don’t have them too?’
‘How could anything not have yin and yang?’ said Xiang-yun. ‘Even a leaf has them. The upper side, facing the sun, is yang; the lower side, turned away in the shade, is yin.’
Kingfisher nodded and smiled.
‘So that’s how it is. Now I understand.

segments.text: ‘But what about the fans in our hands? Which part is yang and which is yin?’
‘This front side is yang, and the back is yin.’

Kingfisher smiled and nodded again. She wanted to ask about a few more things, but could not think of any. Suddenly she looked down and saw the gold qilin hanging from Xiang-yun’s palace sash. She lifted it.
‘Miss, does this have yin and yang too?’
‘Among birds and beasts, the male is yang and the female is yin; the dam is yin, the sire is yang. Of course it does!’
‘Is this one male, then, or female?’
‘Even I don’t know that.’
‘Never mind that, then. But if everything has yin and yang, how is it that we people don’t?’
Xiang-yun spat towards her face.
‘Shameless creature! Walk on properly. Your questions get better and better!’
Kingfisher laughed.
‘Why shouldn’t you tell me that?

segments.text: ‘I know anyway. There’s no need to make it hard for me.’
‘What do you know?’ Xiang-yun asked, laughing.
‘You’re yang, miss, and I’m yin.’
Xiang-yun pressed her handkerchief to her mouth and laughed aloud.
‘There, I’ve got it right,’ said Kingfisher. ‘That’s why you’re laughing so much.’
‘Quite right. Quite right.’

segments.text: ‘The rule with people is that masters are yang and servants are yin. Do you think I don’t understand even that great principle?’
‘You understand very well,’ Xiang-yun said, laughing.
They walked on as they talked. Just as they reached the rose trellis, Xiang-yun said, ‘Look, someone’s dropped a piece of jewellery. It’s shining there, all gold.’
Kingfisher hurried over, picked it up and closed her hand round it.
‘Now we can tell yin from yang,’ she said, smiling.
First she examined Shi Xiang-yun’s qilin. Xiang-yun wanted to see what she had found, but Kingfisher would not open her hand.
‘It’s a treasure, miss. You mustn’t look. Where can it have come from? How strange! I’ve never seen anyone here with one of these.’
‘Give it to me and let me see,’ Xiang-yun said with a smile.
Kingfisher opened her hand.
‘There you are!’

Xiang-yun looked. It was a splendidly worked gold qilin, larger and more richly ornamented than her own. She took it in her palm and said nothing. While she stood lost in thought, Bao-yu came towards them.
‘What are you two doing out here in the sun?’ he asked with a smile.

segments.text: ‘Why haven’t you gone to find Aroma?’
Xiang-yun quickly hid the qilin.
‘We were just going. Let’s go together.’

They went into the House of Green Delights. Aroma was leaning on the railing by the steps to catch the breeze. Seeing Xiang-yun, she hurried down to meet her. Hand in hand, they smiled and exchanged news of all the time they had been apart.
When they had gone in and sat down, Bao-yu said with a smile, ‘You should have come sooner. I’ve got something nice, and I’ve been waiting especially for you.’
He began feeling about inside his clothes. After a long search he exclaimed, ‘Oh!’ and asked Aroma, ‘Did you put that thing away?’
‘What thing?’
‘The qilin I got the other day.’
‘You carry it about with you every day. Why ask me?’
Bao-yu clapped his hands.
‘Then it’s lost! Where am I to look for it?’
He was about to get up and search for it himself. Only now did Xiang-yun realise it was he who had dropped it.
‘When did you get a qilin?’ she asked with a smile.
‘It took some getting hold of the other day. I’ve no idea when I lost it. What a fool I am!’
‘Fortunately it’s only a plaything, and look at the state you’re in!’
She opened her hand.
‘Have a look. Is this it?’
At the sight of it Bao-yu was overjoyed, and began to say…
To learn what followed, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: Now, Bao-yu was delighted to see the qilin. He reached for it.
‘Thank goodness you found it!’ he said, smiling. ‘Where was it?’
‘Luckily it was only this,’ Shi Xiang-yun said with a smile. ‘Suppose you lost your official seal one day. Would you let that pass too?’
‘Losing a seal would be nothing. If I lost this, I’d deserve to die.’
Aroma poured Xiang-yun some tea.
‘Miss,’ she said with a smile, ‘I hear congratulations were in order the other day.’
Xiang-yun blushed and drank her tea without answering.
‘Shy now, are we?’ Aroma went on. ‘Do you remember what you used to say to me at night ten years ago, when we were staying in the heated room on the west side?

segments.text: ‘You weren’t shy then. Why are you shy now?’

‘You can talk!’ Xiang-yun said, smiling. ‘We were such friends in those days. Then the lady of our household died, and I went home for a while. Why did they have to send you to wait on Second Cousin? When I came back, you didn’t treat me as you used to.’
‘You can talk too,’ Aroma said with a smile.

segments.text: ‘It used to be “sister” this and “sister” that, coaxing me to comb your hair and wash your face, make you this and do that for you. Now you’re grown up, you put on a young lady’s airs. If you act the young lady, how can I dare to be familiar?’

‘Amitabha! What an injustice! What a wicked accusation!’ Xiang-yun cried. ‘May I drop dead this minute if I’m like that. Just look: in all this heat, the moment I arrive I have to hurry over to see you first. Ask Kingfisher if you don’t believe me. When I’m at home, when does an hour pass without my talking of you?’
Before she had finished, Aroma and Bao-yu hastened to soothe her.
‘You’re taking a joke seriously again! Still as quick-tempered as ever.’
‘You don’t say how your words choke a person. You only say they’re quick-tempered.’
As she spoke she opened her handkerchief and gave Aroma the ring. Aroma thanked her warmly.

‘I’ve already had one of those you sent the young ladies the other day,’ she said, smiling. ‘Now you’ve brought me another yourself. That proves you haven’t forgotten me. This alone is enough to show it.

segments.text: ‘A ring isn’t worth much, but it shows your heart is true.’
‘Who gave you one?’ Xiang-yun asked.
‘Miss Bao.’

‘I thought it would have been Cousin Lin,’ Xiang-yun said with a smile. ‘So it was Cousin Bao-chai. At home I’m always thinking that none of the other cousins can compare with her. What a pity we weren’t born of the same mother. If only I had a sister like her, it wouldn’t matter even if I had no parents.’

segments.text: Her eyes reddened as she spoke.
‘There, there, there!’ said Bao-yu. ‘Don’t talk about that.’
‘Why shouldn’t I? I know your sore point. You’re afraid your Cousin Lin will hear and be cross with me for praising Cousin Bao. Isn’t that it?’
Aroma gave a little snort of laughter.
‘Miss Yun, the older you grow, the more plainly you speak your mind.’
‘I’ve always said how hard it is to talk to you girls,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘And I was right.’
‘My dear cousin,’ said Xiang-yun, ‘do stop saying things to turn my stomach.

segments.text: ‘You can talk well enough in front of us. Once you see your Cousin Lin, goodness knows what happens to you.’
‘Enough joking,’ said Aroma. ‘There’s something I really must ask you to do for me.’
‘What is it?’
‘There’s a pair of shoes to make; the inner soles are cut out. I haven’t been well these last two days and can’t do them. If you have time, could you do them for me?’

‘Well, this is strange!’ Xiang-yun said, laughing. ‘Apart from all the clever people you have here, there are the sewing women and the people who do the cutting. Why ask me? Whoever you asked to do your work, would they have the nerve to refuse?’
‘You’re being silly again,’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘Don’t you know we never let those sewing women do the work for this room?’
Now Xiang-yun knew the shoes were Bao-yu’s.
‘In that case I’ll do them for you,’ she said, smiling. ‘Only on one condition: I’ll do yours, but I won’t do anyone else’s.’
‘There you go again,’ Aroma laughed. ‘Who am I, to trouble you to make my shoes?

segments.text: ‘To tell you the truth, they aren’t mine. Never mind whose they are. I’ll be grateful to you all the same.’
‘Well, goodness knows how many things of yours I’ve made already,’ said Xiang-yun. ‘You must know why I won’t do these today.’
‘I really don’t.’
Xiang-yun laughed coldly.

‘I heard the fan-case I made was taken out to compare with someone else’s work, and then cut up in a fit of temper. I heard about it long ago. You needn’t hide it from me. And now you want me to make something else. I’ve become your servant, have I?’

segments.text: ‘I didn’t know you’d made it,’ Bao-yu put in hastily, with a smile.

‘He really didn’t know,’ Aroma said, smiling too. ‘It was a story I told him. I said there was a girl outside who was wonderfully good at needlework, that she embroidered the most extraordinary flowers, and that I’d had her bring a fan-case for us to see how good it was. He believed me and took it out to show to everyone. Somehow he offended Miss Lin again, and she cut it in two. When he came back, he was still asking me to hurry and have another made. Only then did I tell him you had done it. You should have seen how sorry he was.’
‘Stranger still!’ said Xiang-yun. ‘Miss Lin had no reason to be angry. Since she knows how to cut, let her do the sewing.’

‘She won’t do it,’ said Aroma. ‘Even as things are, Her Old Ladyship worries about her overdoing it. The doctor says she needs quiet and rest. Who would trouble her to sew? Last year it took her a whole year to make one scent-bag. Half this year has gone, and we haven’t seen her pick up a needle yet.’

segments.text: While they were talking, someone came to report, ‘The gentleman from Xinglong Street is here. The master wants Master Bao to come out and meet him.’

Bao-yu knew this meant Jia Yu-cun had come, and was thoroughly displeased. Aroma hurried to fetch his clothes. As he pulled on his boots, he grumbled, ‘Why isn’t it enough for Father to sit with him? He has to see me every time.’
‘Of course your father sends for you,’ Xiang-yun said, smiling as she fanned herself. ‘You’re so good at receiving guests.’
‘It isn’t Father. It’s the man himself who always asks to see me.’
‘An accomplished host never lacks for visitors,’ Xiang-yun said with a smile. ‘You must have some qualities that impress him, or he wouldn’t be so eager to see you.’
‘Enough, enough! I wouldn’t dare call myself accomplished. I’m the most common of common people, and I’ve no wish to associate with these men.’

‘Still the same temper,’ Xiang-yun said, smiling. ‘You’re growing up now. Even if you don’t want to study and take the examinations for juren and jinshi, you ought to see more of these men in office and talk about the business of an official career and public affairs. You’d learn how to deal with the world, and have some friends in years to come.

segments.text: ‘What do you mean by spending the whole year here, always mixing with us?’
‘Miss,’ Bao-yu replied, ‘please go and sit with one of the other girls. I’m afraid my room might sully someone so learned in public affairs.’
‘Miss Yun, please don’t talk like that,’ said Aroma. ‘Miss Bao once said the same thing. He didn’t care how humiliated she might feel: he gave a snort, got to his feet and walked away.

segments.text: ‘I felt dreadful. I thought she must be angry. But afterwards she was just the same as ever. Such self-control, and such a generous heart! Yet this one here has grown distant towards her instead. If you sulked and wouldn’t speak to Miss Lin, think how many apologies you’d have to make!’
‘Has Miss Lin ever talked that damned nonsense?’ Bao-yu asked. ‘If she had, I’d have grown distant towards her long ago.’
Aroma and Xiang-yun both nodded, smiling.
‘Oh yes, damned nonsense, of course.’

segments.text: Dai-yu, meanwhile, knew that Xiang-yun was there and that Bao-yu had hurried over too. They must be talking about the qilin. She reflected that in the romances and unofficial histories Bao-yu had lately acquired, clever young men and beautiful girls were usually brought together by little trinkets: mandarin ducks or phoenixes, jade rings or gold pendants, handkerchiefs of merfolk silk or luan-bird sashes. Some small thing always united them for life. Now that Bao-yu too had a qilin, she feared it might make an opening for some romantic affair between him and Shi Xiang-yun. So she slipped over quietly, to see what the two of them had in mind and act as the occasion required.
Unexpectedly, just as she arrived, she heard Xiang-yun speaking of public affairs, and Bao-yu saying, ‘Cousin Lin doesn’t talk that damned nonsense. If she did, I’d grow distant towards her too.’
At these words Dai-yu felt joy and alarm, and both grieved and sighed.

segments.text: Her joy was that her judgment had proved sound. She had always thought he understood her, and he did. Her alarm was that he should speak so warmly of her in front of others, laying bare his private feelings with such intimacy, without the least concern for what people might suspect. Her sigh was for this: since you understand me, surely I may understand you too. If we understand each other, why should there be all this talk of gold and jade? And if gold and jade must be spoken of, it ought to be you and I. Why must a Bao-chai come into it?

segments.text: Her grief was that her parents had died so early. However deeply words might be engraved upon her heart and bones, she had no one to speak for her. Besides, of late she had often felt dazed and absent-minded; her illness was gradually taking hold. The doctors even said her qi was weak and her blood deficient, and feared a wasting illness might develop. Though we understand each other, I fear I may not be able to stay long. Even if you understand me, what can you do about my ill-starred life?
At this thought tears rolled down her face. She considered going in to see them, but it seemed pointless now. Wiping her tears, she turned to go back.

segments.text: Bao-yu hurried into his clothes and came out. Suddenly he saw Dai-yu walking slowly ahead of him, apparently wiping away tears. He hastened to catch up.
‘Where are you going, cousin?’ he asked with a smile. ‘Why are you crying again? Who’s offended you this time?’
Dai-yu turned and saw who it was. She forced a smile.
‘I’m perfectly well. When have I been crying?’
‘Look at you!’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘The tears aren’t dry on your eyes yet, and you’re still telling lies.’
As he spoke he could not help raising his hand to wipe them away. Dai-yu quickly stepped back.
‘Are you courting death again? What do you mean by pawing at me like that?’
Bao-yu smiled.
‘Talking to you, I forgot myself. My hand moved before I knew it. I couldn’t stop to think about life and death.’
‘Your dying wouldn’t matter much. But what would become of the gold you left behind, and that qilin of yours?’
This upset Bao-yu again. He stepped towards her.
‘Still saying that! Are you trying to curse me or drive me mad?’
Only then did Dai-yu recall what had happened the other day. Regretting her rash words, she hastily smiled.
‘Don’t get upset. I spoke wrongly.

segments.text: ‘It’s nothing to get so worked up about. The veins are standing out, and your face is covered in sweat.’
She could not help coming closer and raising her hand to wipe his face. Bao-yu looked at her for a long while before he spoke: only three Chinese characters, ‘Rest easy.’
Dai-yu stared for a long time.
‘What have I to be uneasy about? I don’t understand. Tell me what you mean by easy and uneasy.’
Bao-yu sighed.
‘Do you really not understand? Have I been wrong in all the thought I’ve given you? If I can’t even understand what you mean, it’s no wonder you’re angry with me every day.’
‘I really don’t understand this talk of resting easy or not resting easy.’
Bao-yu nodded and sighed.

‘My dear cousin, don’t deceive me. If you truly don’t understand, then not only has all my feeling for you been wasted, but I’ve failed all the feeling you’ve shown me too. It’s because you never rest easy that you’ve made yourself so ill.

segments.text: ‘If only you could set your mind at rest a little, your illness wouldn’t grow worse day after day.’

To Dai-yu the words were like a thunderclap and a flash of lightning. As she considered them, they seemed more heartfelt even than if they had been drawn from her own innermost being. Ten thousand things filled her heart that she longed to say, yet she could not utter so much as half a word. She only gazed at him. Bao-yu too had ten thousand things in his heart, with no idea which to begin with. He gazed at Dai-yu in turn.
They stood looking at each other for a long while. Then Dai-yu gave a single cough, tears rolled from both eyes, and she turned to leave. Bao-yu hurried forward and caught her.
‘My dear cousin, stay just a moment. Let me say one thing before you go.’
Wiping her tears, Dai-yu pushed his hand away.
‘What is there to say? I’ve known what you would say for a long time!’
She went straight on without even turning her head.

segments.text: Bao-yu stood there in a daze. In his haste to leave he had forgotten his fan. Afraid he would be hot, Aroma had hurried after him with one, and on looking up had seen him standing with Dai-yu. Now Dai-yu had gone, but he had not moved. Aroma came up to him.
‘You went off without a fan. Luckily I noticed and hurried after you with it.’
Bao-yu was lost in thought. Though he saw Aroma speaking to him, he did not recognise who she was. He seized her hand.

‘My dear cousin, I’ve never dared speak of what’s in my heart. Today I’ll be bold and say it, and die content! I too have made myself ill over you, but I daren’t tell anyone. I can only hide it. I’m afraid my illness won’t get better until yours does. Even in sleep and dreams I can’t forget you!’
Aroma was frightened out of her wits.
‘Heaven and all the bodhisattvas! You’ll be the death of me!’ she cried.

segments.text: After he had gone, Aroma thought over what he had said. It must have been on Dai-yu’s account. If things were like this, some disgraceful affair in the future could scarcely be avoided. The thought was frightening. She stood in a daze, tears falling, while she silently considered how to prevent such a shameful calamity.
While she was still pondering what to do, Bao-chai came towards her.
‘What are you dreaming about in this blazing sun?’ she asked with a smile.
Aroma quickly smiled back.
‘There were two sparrows fighting over there. They were rather amusing, and I got caught up in watching them.’

‘Where was Cousin Bao hurrying off to, all dressed?’ Bao-chai asked. ‘I saw him just now and was going to stop him and ask. But his talk gets more and more incoherent, so I didn’t call him. I let him go.’
‘The master sent for him.’

segments.text: ‘Oh dear!’ Bao-chai exclaimed. ‘Why send for him in this glaring heat? I hope he hasn’t remembered something and lost his temper, and called him out to give him a lecture.’
‘No, not that,’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘I think a guest wants to see him.’
‘What a tiresome guest!’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘Why go running about on such a hot day instead of staying at home in the cool?’
‘You should tell him so,’ Aroma said, smiling.

segments.text: ‘What’s Yun doing at your place?’ Bao-chai asked.
‘We were just chatting,’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘You know that pair of shoes I pasted up the other day? I’m going to have her sew them.’

At this Bao-chai looked in both directions. Seeing no one passing, she said with a smile, ‘You’re such a sensible person. How can you suddenly forget to consider someone else’s circumstances? From the way Yun has seemed lately, and things I’ve picked up here and there, she has no say in anything at home. Her family thinks it spends too much, so they don’t employ sewing women. Most ordinary things have to be made by the women and girls themselves. Why else, on these last few visits, would she tell me how tired she is at home as soon as we’re alone? When I ask another question or two about their daily life, her eyes redden. She mumbles and hesitates, wanting to speak and not quite daring.

segments.text: ‘When I think of her situation, it must be the misery of having lost her parents so young. I can’t help feeling sad when I look at her.’
Aroma clapped her hands.

‘Of course! Of course! No wonder, when I asked her last month to tie me ten butterfly knots, it took her so long to send them. She even said, “They’re roughly done. Use them somewhere they’ll do for now. If you want them neat and even, wait till I come to stay, and I’ll make them properly.” Now you’ve told me this, Miss Bao, I see she must have felt she couldn’t refuse. Who knows how late into the night she had to work at home to do them? How thoughtless I’ve been! If I’d known, I’d never have troubled her.’
‘Last time she told me she worked until the third watch at home,’ said Bao-chai. ‘And if she does even a little for someone else, the ladies of her family are displeased.’
‘And our stubborn, contrary young master won’t let the household sewing women do a single thing, large or small,’ said Aroma.

segments.text: ‘I can’t manage all of it.’
‘Why pay any attention to him?’ Bao-chai asked with a smile. ‘Have someone do it and say it was you.’
‘He wouldn’t believe it,’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘He can tell. There’s nothing for it: I shall just have to wear myself out a little at a time.’
‘Don’t worry. How would it be if I did some for you?’
‘If you really would, that would be a blessing for me. I’ll bring it over myself this evening.’

segments.text: She had scarcely finished when an old woman came hurrying up.
‘Who could have thought it! Miss Golden’s thrown herself down a well and died, just like that!’
Aroma gave a start.
‘Which Golden?’ she asked quickly.

segments.text: ‘Just now someone was drawing water from the well in the south-eastern corner and saw a body. They hurried to call people to haul it out, and there she was. Her family are still rushing about trying to bring her back to life. What’s the use?’
‘How strange,’ Bao-chai said.
Aroma nodded and sighed at the news. Remembering their sisterly closeness, she began to cry. Bao-chai hurried to Lady Wang to offer comfort. Aroma went back to her own quarters; we leave her there.

‘Where have you come from?’ Lady Wang asked.
‘From the Garden.’
‘Did you see your Cousin Bao there?’
‘Yes, I saw him just now.

segments.text: ‘He had dressed and gone out. I don’t know where he was going.’
Lady Wang nodded.
‘Have you heard this extraordinary thing?’ she said through her tears. ‘Golden has suddenly thrown herself down a well and died!’
‘Why should she throw herself down a well, just like that?’ Bao-chai asked. ‘How strange.’

‘She broke something of mine the other day. I lost my temper, hit her a few times and sent her away. I only meant to leave her to fret for a couple of days and then have her back. Who could have known she was so proud-spirited that she would throw herself down a well? Isn’t it my sin?’
Bao-chai sighed.

‘You’re kind-hearted, Aunt, so naturally you think that. But I don’t believe she threw herself down in anger. Most likely, after she went home, she was playing about by the well and slipped and fell. She’d been so used to being kept in order here that, once she was out, naturally she’d want to wander about and amuse herself. Surely no one could take offence to that degree! Even if she did, she was only a foolish girl, and not worth regretting.’
Lady Wang nodded and sighed.
‘You may say that, but my mind is still uneasy.’
‘You needn’t keep dwelling on it, Aunt,’ Bao-chai said with a sigh. ‘If you feel so badly, give a few more taels of silver towards her funeral. That will fulfil your duty to her as her mistress.’
‘I’ve just given her mother fifty taels,’ said Lady Wang. ‘I also meant to give her two sets of your cousins’ new clothes to be buried in.

segments.text: ‘But Feng says there happen to be no newly made clothes, except the two sets for your Cousin Lin’s birthday. That child has always been so sensitive, and she has trouble enough with her health. After saying the clothes were for her birthday, how could we use them to dress someone for burial? It would be unlucky. So I’ve told the tailors to hurry and make two sets. With another maid, a few taels would have been enough. But although Golden was a maid, she had always been almost a daughter to me.’
As she spoke, the tears fell again.

Taking in their words and expressions, Bao-chai understood most of it. She saw that the clothes were properly handed over, and Lady Wang called Golden’s mother to take them away.
