segments.text: Now Lady Wang called Golden’s mother forward and gave her several hairpins and rings in person. She also ordered several groups of monks to be invited to recite scriptures in rites for the release of the dead. The mother kowtowed her thanks and withdrew.

Bao-yu had heard the news on returning from his meeting with Yu-cun. Realising that Golden had killed herself in shame and anger, he had been stricken to the heart. When he came in and Lady Wang scolded and admonished him, he could find nothing to say. Bao-chai’s arrival gave him a chance to leave. He had no idea where to go. With his hands behind his back and his head bent, he walked slowly on, sighing as he went, until his wandering steps brought him to the hall. He had just rounded the screen-door when someone coming in from the other direction collided with him full on.
‘Stand still!’ the man shouted.
Bao-yu started and looked up. It was none other than his father. He caught his breath, then could only stand to one side with his hands hanging down.

‘What is the matter with you?’ Jia Zheng asked. ‘Why are you moping about with your head down, sighing? When Yu-cun came just now and wanted to see you, you took an age to answer the summons. And when you did come, there was nothing spirited or easy about your conversation. You were as listless and drooping as ever.

segments.text: ‘Your face is full of longing and discontent, and now here you are sighing again. Haven’t you enough of everything? Aren’t you comfortable enough? What can you possibly have to behave like this about?’

For all his usual quickness of tongue, Bao-yu could think only of his grief for Golden. He wished he could die that very moment and follow her. He heard none of what his father was saying, but stood staring blankly.

segments.text: Jia Zheng had not been angry to begin with, but the boy’s frightened manner and unaccustomed failure to answer now began to irritate him. He was about to speak again when a servant came to report that someone from the Prince of Zhongshun’s mansion wished to see him.

Jia Zheng was puzzled. He had never had dealings with the prince’s household: why should they send someone today? Still wondering, he ordered the visitor to be shown in at once and hurried out. Finding that it was the prince’s chief secretary, he hastened to welcome him into the hall, where he had him seated and served with tea.
Before they could exchange civilities, the chief secretary began:

‘I should not have presumed to intrude upon your distinguished household on my own account. I come at the prince’s command, with a favour to ask. For His Highness’s sake, may I venture to ask you to help us? His Highness will appreciate it, and we who serve him shall be endlessly grateful too.’
Unable to make anything of this, Jia Zheng rose with a courteous smile.
‘Since you come at the prince’s command, sir, may I ask what instructions you bring? Pray explain, so that I may carry them out.’
The chief secretary gave a cold laugh.
‘There is nothing to carry out. One word from you will settle it.

segments.text: ‘We have an actor in our household who plays young female roles, a certain Bijou. He has always lived quite contentedly at the mansion, but now he has been away for three to five days. We have looked everywhere and can find no trace of him, so we have been making enquiries in all quarters. Eight people out of ten in this city say that lately he has become very close to that son of yours who was born with the jade in his mouth. Once we heard this, we reported it to the prince: yours is not a house like any other, where we might simply walk in and demand him. His Highness said, “If it were any other actor, I should not mind losing a hundred of them. But Bijou is so ready with an answer, so discreet and dependable, so entirely to this old man’s liking, that I simply cannot do without him.” That is why we ask you to instruct your son to let Bijou return. His Highness’s earnest wishes will be satisfied, and we shall be spared all the trouble of searching for him.’
He ended with a prompt bow.

segments.text: Shocked and furious, Jia Zheng sent for Bao-yu at once. Bao-yu hurried in, not knowing why he was wanted.

‘You damned wretch!’ Jia Zheng demanded. ‘It is bad enough that you do no studying at home. Must you go out and commit these lawless outrages as well? Bijou is in attendance on the Prince of Zhongshun himself. What are you, you miserable nobody, to lure him away for no reason and bring this trouble down on me?’
Bao-yu was terrified.
‘I truly know nothing about it,’ he answered hurriedly. ‘I don’t even know what “Bijou” means. How can there be any question of my “luring him away”?’
He began to cry. Before Jia Zheng could speak, the chief secretary gave another cold laugh.
‘There is no need to conceal it, young sir. Whether you are hiding him here or know where he is, tell us now and spare us the trouble. We should certainly be grateful.’
Bao-yu repeated that he knew nothing about it.
‘It may only be a false rumour.’
‘We have evidence,’ the chief secretary said with a cold laugh. ‘Why go on denying it?

segments.text: ‘Must I bring it out before your father? Wouldn’t that be rather awkward for you? If you don’t know the man, how did his scarlet sash come to be round your waist?’
Bao-yu was thunderstruck. He stared, speechless.
How had the man found that out? If he knew something so secret, there was probably little else Bao-yu could hide from him. Better send him away before he brought up anything more.

‘Since you know all about him, sir,’ he said, ‘how is it you haven’t heard of such an important thing as his buying a house? I’ve heard that out in the eastern suburbs, twenty li from the city, there’s a place called Zitan Fort, or something of the sort. He has bought a few mu of land and a few rooms there. Perhaps that is where he is.’
The chief secretary smiled.
‘Then that must be the place. I shall go and look. If we find him, all well and good. If not, I shall have to come and consult you again.’
With that, he hurried away.

segments.text: By now Jia Zheng’s eyes were staring and his mouth was twisted with rage. As he escorted the chief secretary out, he turned to order Bao-yu:
‘Don’t move! I have questions to ask you when I get back.’
He saw the official all the way out. He had only just turned back when he caught sight of Jia Huan rushing about with several pages. He shouted to the pages:
‘Beat him! Beat him!’
At the sight of his father, Jia Huan went limp with fear and stopped at once with his head lowered.
‘What are you running about for?’ Jia Zheng demanded. ‘Where have the people in charge of you gone wandering off to, leaving you to gallop about like a wild horse?’
He ordered the servants who accompanied Jia Huan to school to be fetched. Seeing how angry his father was, Jia Huan seized his chance.

‘I wasn’t running before. Only, as I was passing the well, there was a maid drowned in it. I saw her head, this big, and her body, this thick, all swollen up. It was so frightening that I ran over here.’
Alarmed and bewildered, Jia Zheng asked:
‘Who would jump into a well for no reason?

segments.text: ‘Nothing like this has ever happened in our family. From our ancestors’ time we have always treated our servants kindly and leniently. I suppose I have neglected household affairs these past few years, and naturally the people in charge have taken the opportunity to oppress and extort until they have brought about this waste of a life. If outsiders hear of it, where will our ancestors’ honour be?’

He shouted for Jia Lian, Lai Da and Lai Xing to be summoned at once. The pages answered and were about to go when Jia Huan hurried forward, caught the skirt of his father’s robe and knelt close against his knees.
‘Don’t be angry, Father. No one knows a thing about it except the people in Her Ladyship’s rooms. I heard my mother say…’
He broke off and looked round in every direction. Jia Zheng understood, and glanced at the pages. Taking the hint, they all drew back to either side and behind him.
Jia Huan then whispered:

‘My mother told me that the other day, in Her Ladyship’s room, my elder brother Bao-yu seized her maid Golden and tried to rape her. When he couldn’t, he beat her. Golden was so angry that she threw herself into the well and died.’
Before he had finished, Jia Zheng’s face had turned the colour of gold paper with fury.
‘Bring Bao-yu here at once!’ he roared.

segments.text: He strode towards the study farther inside, shouting as he went:

‘If anyone tries to reason with me today, I shall hand over my cap and girdle of office, the household property, everything, and let him live with Bao-yu! Sinner that I am, I shall shave off these few troublesome hairs at my temples and find some peaceful place to end my days. At least I shall be free of the guilt of disgracing my ancestors and begetting a rebellious son.’

The gentlemen who were his guests and the servants knew from his manner that Bao-yu was once more the cause. In dismay, biting their fingers and tongues, they hastily withdrew. Jia Zheng sat bolt upright in his chair, panting, his face streaked with tears. His orders came one upon another:
‘Fetch Bao-yu! Bring a heavy cudgel! Get a rope and tie him up! Shut every gate! If anyone takes word to the women’s quarters, beat him to death on the spot!’
The pages could only answer in chorus. Several went to find Bao-yu.

segments.text: When Jia Zheng had ordered him not to move, Bao-yu had known that things were likely to go badly for him. He could not have guessed how much more Jia Huan had added. He was pacing helplessly round the hall, longing for someone to carry a message inside, but there was no one to be seen. Even Tealeaf was nowhere about.
As he watched and waited, an old woman servant came out. He rushed to catch hold of her as though he had found a treasure.
‘Go in quickly and tell them! The Master’s going to beat me! Hurry, hurry! It’s urgent, urgent!’

In his agitation Bao-yu could not speak clearly, and the old woman happened to be deaf. She made out nothing of his message. His cry of ‘Urgent!’ (yaojin) reached her as ‘Jump in the well!’ (tiaojing).
‘Let her jump in the well if she wants to,’ she said with a smile. ‘What have you to be frightened of, Master Bao?’
Realising that she was deaf, Bao-yu said desperately:
‘Go out and fetch my page, then!’
‘What is there left to settle?’ she answered. ‘It was all settled long ago.

segments.text: ‘Her Ladyship has given clothes and money too. How can you say it isn’t settled?’
Bao-yu stamped in desperation. Before he could think where else to turn, Jia Zheng’s pages arrived and forced him out.

At the sight of him Jia Zheng’s eyes turned dark red. He had no time now to question the boy about the charges: consorting with actors outside, exchanging private gifts, neglecting his studies at home and violating his mother’s maid. He merely shouted:
‘Gag him! Beat him to death!’

Not daring to disobey, the pages pressed Bao-yu down on a bench and struck him ten or so times with a heavy paddle. Even this was too gentle for Jia Zheng. He kicked the man wielding it aside, seized it himself and, with his teeth clenched, brought it down with all his strength thirty or forty times.
Seeing that the beating was taking an ominous turn, the gentlemen hurried forward to wrest the paddle away and plead with him. Jia Zheng would not listen.
‘Ask him what he has done! Ask yourselves whether it can be forgiven! You are the very people who have let him grow so rotten, and even now you come to intercede.

segments.text: ‘Will you wait until you have brought him to murder his sovereign and his father before you stop pleading for him?’

The men recoiled at these words. Knowing that he was beside himself with rage, they hurried out again and could only find someone to take word inside. Lady Wang did not dare to tell Grandmother Jia first. She hastily put on her clothes and hurried straight to the study without stopping to consider who might be there. The gentlemen and pages scarcely had time to scramble out of her way.

segments.text: Lady Wang’s entrance was like oil poured on Jia Zheng’s fire. The paddle came down harder and faster than ever. The two pages holding Bao-yu hastily let go and moved away, but by now he could no longer stir. Jia Zheng was about to strike again when Lady Wang seized the paddle and held it in her arms.
‘Enough! Enough!’ he cried. ‘You will not be satisfied until you have driven me to my death today!’

segments.text: Jia Zheng gave a cold laugh.

‘Don’t bring that up. I have already failed in my duty as a son by raising this unworthy wretch. Yet whenever I try to discipline him, everyone comes to his defence. I had better strangle him outright today and put an end to any trouble he may cause in future!’
He called for a rope to strangle the boy. Lady Wang hurriedly threw her arms round him, weeping.

‘It is right for you to discipline your son, but you must have some regard for me as your wife. I am nearly fifty now, and this wretched child is all I have. If you are determined to punish him so harshly, I dare not plead too much. But if you insist on his death today, aren’t you deliberately trying to put an end to me? If you must strangle him, fetch the rope and strangle me first. Then strangle him. Neither of us will dare bear you any resentment, and at least we shall have each other to depend on in the world below.’
With that she flung herself over Bao-yu’s body and wept aloud.

segments.text: At these words Jia Zheng gave a deep sigh and sat down, tears falling like rain.

Lady Wang held Bao-yu in her arms. His face was white, his breathing faint, and the green gauze drawers he wore were covered in bloodstains. Unable to bear it, she untied his sash to look. From buttocks to shins he was bruised blue and purple; here the skin was whole, there broken. Not a single patch was unhurt. She burst into loud sobs.
‘My poor, ill-fated child!’
The cry brought Jia Zhu suddenly to mind. She called his name through her tears.
‘If only you were alive, I wouldn’t care if I lost a hundred like him!’

Hearing that Lady Wang had gone out, Li Gong-cai, Wang Xi-feng, Ying-chun and her sisters had already come from the inner quarters. The others could bear to hear Lady Wang crying out Jia Zhu’s name, but Gong-cai could not contain herself and began to weep aloud too. At the sound, Jia Zheng’s tears rolled down in great drops.

segments.text: While the scene was still at its height, a maid came to announce:
‘Her Old Ladyship is here.’
She had not finished when a quavering voice could be heard outside the window:
‘Kill me first, then kill him! Wouldn’t that settle everything?’

At his mother’s arrival Jia Zheng was overcome with distress and alarm, and hurried out to meet her. She was coming towards him, leaning on a maid and panting for breath. He bowed before her with a placating smile.
‘What has upset you so, Mother, that you should come out yourself in this dreadful heat? If you had anything to say, you need only have sent for me and given me your instructions.’
Grandmother Jia stopped and caught her breath. Then she spoke sharply:
‘Oh, it is me you are speaking to! I do have instructions to give, but the pity is that in all my life I have never raised a good son. Who am I to give them to?’
Dismayed by her words, Jia Zheng fell to his knees.
‘In disciplining my son,’ he said tearfully, ‘I am only trying to bring honour to our ancestors. How can I bear to hear you speak like this, Mother?’
Grandmother Jia spat in contempt.
‘You can’t bear a single word from me, but Bao-yu is supposed to bear those murderous blows of yours?

segments.text: ‘You say disciplining your son brings honour to our ancestors. Is this how your father disciplined you?’
Tears began to roll down her face. Jia Zheng once more attempted a smile.
‘Please don’t grieve, Mother. It was only that I lost my temper for a moment. I shall never beat him again.’
Grandmother Jia gave a cold laugh.

‘There is no need to take that sulky tone with me. He is your son. I have no business interfering, whether you beat him or not. I suppose you are tired of the lot of us. We had better leave you as soon as we can, and then we shall all have some peace.’
She ordered the chairs and horses to be made ready.
‘Your wife, Bao-yu and I are going back to Nanjing this instant!’
The household servants could only murmur assent, without doing anything. Grandmother Jia called to Lady Wang:

‘There is no need for you to cry either. Bao-yu is still young, so you feel for him. When he grows up and becomes some grand official, he may not even remember that you are his mother. You had better not feel for him now. It may save you some vexation later.’
Jia Zheng hastily knocked his head on the ground and wept.
‘When you speak like this, Mother, you leave me nowhere to stand.’
Grandmother Jia laughed coldly.
‘You have plainly left me nowhere to stand, and now you make it all about yourself!

segments.text: ‘Once we have gone back, you can have your peace of mind. Then we shall see who comes to give you leave to beat him.’
As she spoke she kept ordering the luggage, carriage and chairs to be got ready at once for their return. Jia Zheng went on kowtowing, desperately imploring her forgiveness and admitting his fault.

Even as she spoke, Grandmother Jia was anxious about Bao-yu, and hurried in to see him. This beating was nothing like the others. In grief and anger she too took him in her arms and wept without stopping. Only after Lady Wang, Xi-feng and the others had comforted her for some time did she gradually grow calmer.
Maids and married women servants came forward to help Bao-yu to his feet. Xi-feng rounded on them.
‘Stupid creatures! Open your eyes and look at him! Beaten like this, and you expect him to walk with your help? Go in this instant and fetch that long cane-seated bench!’
They hurried in and brought it out, lifted Bao-yu onto it, then followed Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang and the others into the inner quarters and carried him to Grandmother Jia’s room.

segments.text: Seeing that Grandmother Jia’s anger had not quite subsided, Jia Zheng dared not go about his own affairs and followed them in. He looked at Bao-yu. He had indeed beaten him too severely. Then he looked at Lady Wang. Over and over she was calling, ‘My child! My own flesh and blood!’

‘If you had died young in Zhu’s place, and he had been left alive, your father would have been spared this anger, and I wouldn’t have wasted half a lifetime worrying. If anything happens to you now, and you leave me behind, who will I have to depend on?’
After a torrent of reproaches, she went back to weeping over her ‘good-for-nothing child’.

segments.text: Jia Zheng’s spirit sank as he listened. He regretted having struck so cruelly and brought the boy to this pass. He first tried to soothe Grandmother Jia, but she said through her tears:
‘Why don’t you go? What are you still doing here? Are you not satisfied yet? Must you watch him die before you will leave?’
Only then did Jia Zheng withdraw.

segments.text: By this time Aunt Xue, Bao-chai, Caltrop, Aroma and Shi Xiang-yun were all there too. Aroma’s heart was full of grief and resentment, but she could not give it free expression. Everyone was crowded round Bao-yu, some giving him water, others fanning him, and she could find no way to help. She decided instead to go out to the inner gate and have the pages fetch Tealeaf, whom she questioned closely.
‘Everything was perfectly all right just now. Why did the beating start? And why didn’t you come and warn us sooner?’
‘That’s just it! I wasn’t there,’ Tealeaf said in agitation. ‘I only heard when the beating was half over. I hurried to find out why. It was over Bijou and Sister Golden.’
‘How did the Master come to hear about them?’

‘The Bijou business was most likely Master Xue’s doing. He’s always jealous and couldn’t find any way of getting his own back, so I suppose he stirred up someone outside to come and set the Master against him. As for Golden, it was Master Huan who told him. I heard that from the Master’s own servants.’
Both explanations fitted what Aroma knew, and she was largely convinced that they were true.

segments.text: She went back to find everyone still tending Bao-yu. When everything had been seen to, Grandmother Jia ordered them to carry him carefully to his own room. They answered and, with many hands helping, hurried him to the House of Green Delights and laid him comfortably on his own bed. There was another long spell of bustle before they gradually dispersed. Only then could Aroma come forward to tend him with care and ask what had really happened.
To hear that, you must listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: Now that Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang and the others had gone, Aroma came and sat beside Bao-yu. With tears in her eyes she asked, ‘How did they come to beat you like this?’
‘It was only about those things,’ Bao-yu sighed. ‘What’s the use of asking? It hurts terribly below the waist. Have a look and see where I’m injured.’

Aroma gently slipped her hands under him and began pulling down his undergarment. At the slightest movement Bao-yu clenched his teeth and cried out, and she hastily stopped. Only after three or four such attempts did she get it down. The upper part of his legs was black and blue, with hard, swollen welts four fingers wide. Aroma clenched her own teeth.

‘Dear heaven! How could he bring himself to hit so hard? If you’d listened to a single word I said, it would never have come to this. Thank goodness your bones and sinews aren’t damaged. What should we have done if you’d been crippled?’

segments.text: As she spoke, the maids announced, ‘Miss Bao is here.’ There was no time to put his undergarment back on, so Aroma covered him with a lined gauze coverlet. Bao-chai came in carrying a single medicinal pill in her hand.
‘Grind this up with wine tonight and put it on him,’ she told Aroma. ‘Once it disperses the heat-toxin in the stagnant blood, he should soon be better.’
She handed it to Aroma and asked, ‘Are you feeling any better now?’
Bao-yu thanked her, said he was, and asked her to sit down. Seeing that he could open his eyes and speak, quite unlike before, Bao-chai felt much reassured. She nodded and sighed.
‘If only you’d listened to advice sooner, this need never have happened. It isn’t just Grandmother and Aunt who are distressed. Even we feel the pain when we see you.’

She hastily swallowed the rest of what she had begun to say. Regretting her haste, she blushed and lowered her head. To Bao-yu those words were full of tenderness and intimacy, with a world of meaning behind them. Seeing her suddenly break off, blush and hang her head, doing nothing but finger her sash, in a confusion of shy embarrassment beyond description, he felt his heart fill with delight. His pain had long since flown beyond the clouds, and he thought:
‘I’ve only had a few blows, and already each of them shows such pity and grief for me. How lovely to see, how touching, how worthy of affection and respect!

segments.text: ‘If some calamity were really to kill me, who knows how deeply they would mourn? If this is how they feel, I could die this very moment. To have such feelings from them would leave me nothing to regret, even if everything I might have achieved in life went pouring down the river. If I couldn’t be content in the world of shadows then, I should be a very foolish ghost indeed.’
As he thought this, he heard Bao-chai ask Aroma, ‘What suddenly made him so angry that he began to beat him?’

Aroma repeated what Tealeaf had told her. Bao-yu had known nothing of Jia Huan’s words until she spoke of them now. When she brought Xue Pan into it as well, he feared Bao-chai would take it to heart and hastily stopped her.
‘Cousin Xue has never been like that. You mustn’t go guessing at random.’
Bao-chai knew he had interrupted Aroma for fear of hurting her feelings. She thought to herself:
‘Beaten to this state, with more pain than he can bear, and still he is so considerate, so afraid of giving offence. He really does take thought for us.

Of course he stopped Aroma because he was afraid I’d take it to heart. But does he suppose I don’t know how my brother indulges his every whim and desire, without a thought for the consequences?

segments.text: ‘The uproar he made over Qin Zhong that time! He is bound to be worse now than he was then.’

She smiled and said, ‘There’s no need to blame this person or that. As I see it, Cousin Bao’s own conduct is at fault. His father is angry because he chooses to associate with such people. Even if my brother spoke carelessly and happened to mention him, he can’t have meant to stir up trouble. For one thing, it was only the truth; for another, he never considers these little precautions against giving people the wrong idea. Miss Aroma, you’ve grown up knowing someone as considerate as Cousin Bao. You’ve never met a man who fears neither heaven nor earth and says whatever comes into his head.’

As soon as Bao-yu had cut her short, Aroma had realised how rash she had been to mention Xue Pan. Already afraid of having embarrassed Bao-chai, she now felt so ashamed that she could say nothing. Bao-yu, meanwhile, found in Bao-chai’s words both high-minded good sense and a release from his own misgivings, and felt even happier than before.

segments.text: He was just about to speak when Bao-chai rose.
‘I’ll come and see you again tomorrow. Take good care of yourself. I brought some medicine and gave it to Aroma just now. Put it on tonight and you’re sure to be better.’
She went out, and Aroma hurried after her to see her beyond the courtyard.
‘You’ve been so thoughtful, miss. When Master Bao is better, he’ll come himself to thank you.’

Bao-chai turned back with a smile. ‘There’s nothing to thank me for. Just persuade him to rest quietly and keep from filling his head with foolish fancies. Don’t disturb Grandmother, Aunt or any of the others about it. If word should reach his father, he might do nothing at the time, but when something brings it to mind later, there’s sure to be trouble.’
With that she went away.

Bao-yu lay silently on the bed, but the pain in his buttocks was like needles probing and knives gouging, with a burning heat like fire. At the slightest turn he could not help crying out.

segments.text: Bao-yu lay in a drowsy stupor. He saw Jiang Yu-han come in and tell him how the Prince of Zhongshun’s household had seized him. Then Golden appeared, weeping as she told him how she had thrown herself into the well for his sake. Half dreaming, half awake, Bao-yu paid little heed. Suddenly he felt someone shaking him and dimly heard a sound of grief. He started out of his dream and opened his eyes. It was none other than Dai-yu.
Still afraid that he was dreaming, he hastily raised himself to examine her face. Her eyes were swollen like peaches, her whole face shining with tears. If it was not Dai-yu, who else could it be?

segments.text: He wanted to look longer, but the pain below his waist was more than he could bear. Unable to hold himself up, he cried out and fell back. Then he sighed.

‘What did you come running here for? The sun may have gone down, but the heat hasn’t left the ground. Walking back and forth, you’ll make yourself ill with it again. I’ve been beaten, but it doesn’t hurt. I’m only putting this on to fool them, so they’ll spread the story outside and Father will hear. It’s all a pretence. You mustn’t take it seriously.’

Dai-yu was not weeping aloud. Yet this silent weeping, which stifled her breath and choked her throat, was all the more terrible. At his words a thousand things rose in her heart, but she could not utter them. Only after a long while did she manage to say between sobs, ‘Do change your ways from now on!’
Bao-yu gave a long sigh. ‘Rest easy. Don’t say such things. Even if I died for these people, I should do it willingly!’
He had scarcely finished when someone outside the courtyard announced, ‘Mrs Lian is here.’ Knowing that Xi-feng had come, Dai-yu hurriedly stood up.
‘I’ll go out through the back courtyard. I’ll come again later.’

segments.text: Bao-yu caught her by the hand. ‘How strange! Why have you suddenly become afraid of her?’
Dai-yu stamped her foot in agitation and whispered, ‘Look at my eyes! She’ll only make fun of me for her own amusement.’
He let go at once. In two or three quick steps Dai-yu was round the bed and out through the back courtyard. Xi-feng had already entered from the front.
‘Are you any better?’ she asked Bao-yu. ‘If there’s anything you’d like to eat, send someone to my rooms for it.’
Aunt Xue came next, and presently Grandmother Jia sent someone as well.

segments.text: By lamplighting time Bao-yu had taken only two mouthfuls of soup before sinking into a heavy sleep. Then Zhou Rui’s wife, Wu Xin-deng’s wife and Zheng Hao-shi’s wife, older women who often came to the house, arrived, having heard of his beating. Aroma hurried out to meet them.
‘You’re a moment too late, aunties,’ she said softly, smiling. ‘Master Bao has only just fallen asleep.’
She took them to sit in the other room and poured tea for them. They sat quietly for a little while, then told her, ‘When Master Bao wakes, tell him we came.’

segments.text: Aroma promised and saw them out. She was just turning back when an old woman arrived from Lady Wang, saying that Her Ladyship wanted one of Master Bao’s attendants. Aroma thought for a moment, then went back and quietly told Skybright, Musk, Sandal, Ripple and the others:
‘Her Ladyship has sent for someone. Stay in the room and take good care of things. I’ll be back as soon as I can.’
She went straight out of the garden with the old woman to the main apartments. Lady Wang was sitting on a couch for keeping cool, fanning herself with a palm-leaf fan.
‘Any of them would have done,’ she said when Aroma appeared. ‘Now you’ve left him too. Who’s waiting on him?’

Aroma hastily answered with a respectful smile. ‘Master Bao has just settled into a sound sleep. Those four or five girls have improved now and know how to look after him. Please don’t worry, ma’am. I was afraid you might have some instructions, and if I sent one of them she might not understand properly and cause a delay.’
‘There’s nothing in particular. I only wanted to ask how bad his pain is now.’
‘I’ve put on the medicine Miss Bao brought. He’s better than he was.

segments.text: ‘Before, he was in too much pain to lie still. Now he’s sleeping soundly. That shows he must be better.’
‘Has he had anything to eat?’ Lady Wang asked.

‘He took two mouthfuls of the bowl of soup Her Old Ladyship sent. He kept saying he was thirsty and wanted some sour-plum drink. I thought sour plums were astringent. He’d only just been beaten and hadn’t been allowed to cry out, so all that distress was bound to leave heat-toxin and heated blood pent up in his heart. If he drank that and it trapped them there, what should we do if he developed a serious illness?

segments.text: ‘So I talked to him for ages and finally persuaded him not to have it. I only mixed him a drink with the rose syrup preserved in sugar. He had half a bowl, then said he was tired of it, that it didn’t taste sweet and fragrant any more.’

‘Oh dear, you should have come and told me sooner,’ said Lady Wang. ‘Someone sent me two bottles of essence the other day. I meant to give him some, but I was afraid he’d waste it, so I didn’t. If he’s tired of that rose syrup, take him two bottles of this.

segments.text: ‘When he needs more, I can come and get it. That will do just as well.’

Cai-yun went away and, after some time, brought back two bottles and handed them to Aroma. They were little glass bottles, about three cun high, with screw-on silver caps. One pale-yellow paper label read ‘Osmanthus Essence’, the other ‘Rose Essence’.
‘What precious stuff!’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘How much can a tiny bottle like this hold?’
‘It’s made for presentation to the throne,’ Lady Wang said. ‘Didn’t you see the pale-yellow labels? Keep it safe for him, and don’t let him waste it.’

segments.text: Aroma promised and was about to go when Lady Wang called her back.
‘Wait. I’ve remembered something I wanted to ask you.’

Aroma hurried back. Seeing that there was no one else in the room, Lady Wang asked, ‘I seem to have heard that Bao-yu was beaten today because Huan said something to his father. Have you heard anything about that? If you have, tell me. I shan’t make a fuss and let people know it came from you.’
‘I haven’t heard that,’ said Aroma. ‘It was because Master Bao had been keeping an actor to himself, and the people came to His Lordship to demand him back. That’s why he was beaten.’
Lady Wang shook her head. ‘That was part of it. There was another reason too.’
‘I really don’t know of any other reason. But let me be bold enough to say something foolish to you today, ma’am. To be fair…’
She broke off and swallowed the rest.
‘Go on,’ said Lady Wang.
Aroma smiled. ‘If you won’t be angry, ma’am, I’ll say it.’
‘Why should I be angry? Say what you have to say.’
‘To be fair, Master Bao does need a lesson or two from His Lordship.

segments.text: ‘When have I not known how to discipline a son? When Master Zhu was alive, how did I bring him up? Can I have forgotten how to bring up a son now? There is a reason for it. I think to myself that I’m nearly fifty, with only this one left. He’s frail, and his grandmother treasures him so. If I were too strict, and anything happened to him, or his grandmother made herself ill with anger, the whole household would be in an uproar. Wouldn’t that make things worse? That’s how I’ve let him become so spoilt. I keep talking till my mouth is worn out: advising him, reasoning with him, scolding in anger, crying. He’s good at the time, but afterwards it’s as though nothing had been said. He won’t stop until he’s suffered for it. But if they beat him beyond recovery, who will I have to depend on?’
As she spoke, her tears began to fall.

segments.text: Lady Wang’s grief touched Aroma’s heart, and she too began to weep.

‘You bore him, ma’am. How could you not feel for him? Even for us servants, it would be a blessing if we could serve him and all come through safely. If things go on like this, we can’t even hope for that. What day, what hour passes without my trying to advise him? But nothing I say will bring him to his senses. Then those people are so ready to seek his company, so it isn’t entirely his fault. In the end, it’s always we who are in the wrong for trying to reason with him. Now you’ve brought it up, ma’am, there’s something else that’s been troubling me. I’ve often wanted to come and ask what you think should be done. Only I was afraid you might suspect me. Then it wouldn’t just be that I’d wasted my breath. There’d be nowhere left to bury me.’

Hearing that there was something behind this, Lady Wang hastily asked, ‘My child, tell me whatever is on your mind. Lately I’ve heard everyone praising you, both openly and in private. I thought it was simply that you took good care of Bao-yu and were pleasant to the others. Those little virtues were why I began treating you on the same footing as the senior concubines.

segments.text: ‘But what you’ve just said is sound good sense, exactly what I’ve been thinking. Tell me whatever you have to say. Only don’t let anyone else know.’
‘I have nothing else to say, ma’am. I only wanted your instructions: couldn’t some way be found to have Master Bao move out of the garden again?’
Lady Wang was startled. She caught Aroma’s hand.
‘Has Bao-yu been up to something with someone?’

‘Please don’t suspect anything, ma’am!’ Aroma answered hastily. ‘There’s been nothing of the kind. It’s only my humble opinion. Master Bao is growing up now, and so are the young ladies in the garden. Miss Lin and Miss Bao are his cousins, one his father’s sister’s daughter and the other his mother’s sister’s daughter. Cousins they may be, but there is still the distinction between a boy and girls. Living together day and night isn’t fitting. One can’t help worrying, and it doesn’t look right to outsiders either. These are family matters. As the saying goes, “In quiet times, think of what may go wrong.” So much of the senseless trouble in the world starts with something done quite innocently. Someone with a suspicious mind sees it, takes it as deliberate, and talks it into something bad.

segments.text: ‘We simply must guard against it beforehand. You know Master Bao’s usual ways, ma’am. He does so love playing about among us girls. If we aren’t careful, and something goes a little wrong sooner or later, whether it’s true or not, there are so many people and so many tongues. What restraint do those malicious mouths ever show? When they’re pleased, they make him out better than a bodhisattva; when they aren’t, they make him worse than a beast. If people speak well of Master Bao in future, it means no more than that we all go on our way and nothing happens. But if anyone says one bad word, never mind us: even being ground to pieces for our countless offences would be a small thing. Wouldn’t his reputation and character be ruined for the rest of his life? And how could you face His Lordship? There’s another saying: “A gentleman guards against trouble before it comes.” Better to take precautions now.

segments.text: ‘You have so much to attend to, ma’am. Naturally you can’t think of everything at once. It would be one thing if we hadn’t thought of it; but having thought of it, we’d be all the more to blame if we didn’t tell you plainly. Lately it’s kept me anxious day and night, and I haven’t been able to speak of it to anyone. Only the lamp knows.’
These words struck Lady Wang like thunder and lightning, bringing Golden’s affair directly to mind. Her gratitude and affection for Aroma knew no bounds. She hastily smiled.

‘My child, to think you have such judgement, and can consider everything so thoroughly! Of course I’ve thought of it too, but things kept happening and I forgot. What you’ve said today has reminded me. You’ve taken such pains to protect the name and standing of both my son and me. Truly, I never knew how good you were.

segments.text: ‘Well, go back now. I shall decide what to do. But there’s one thing more. Now that you’ve spoken like this, I’m entrusting him to you. Whatever happens, watch over him. In protecting him, you’ll be protecting me. I certainly shan’t let you go unrewarded.’

segments.text: Aroma promised over and over, and left. When she got back Bao-yu had just woken, and she told him about the essences. Delighted, he immediately had some mixed for him to try. It was indeed wonderfully fragrant. But he was thinking of Dai-yu and longing to send someone to her. Afraid of Aroma, he devised a way round her and first sent her to borrow a book from Bao-chai.

segments.text: Once Aroma had gone, Bao-yu called Skybright.
‘Go to Miss Lin’s and see what she’s doing. If she asks about me, tell her I’m better.’
‘What am I to go there for, out of the blue?’ said Skybright. ‘You must at least give me a message, so it looks like an errand.’
‘There’s nothing to say.’
‘Then give me something to take, or something to fetch. Otherwise how am I to strike up a conversation when I get there?’
Bao-yu thought for a moment, then reached for two handkerchiefs and tossed them to her with a smile.
‘Very well. Say I sent you to give her these.’
‘That’s stranger still! What would she want with these two handkerchiefs, neither new nor worn out? She’ll only be cross again and say you’re making fun of her.’
‘Don’t worry,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘She’ll understand.’

segments.text: Skybright had no choice but to take the handkerchiefs to Naiad’s House. Chun-xian was hanging handkerchiefs over the railing to dry. Seeing her come in, she hastily waved a hand.
‘She’s gone to bed.’
Skybright went inside. The room was quite dark, with no lamp lit. Dai-yu was already in bed and asked who was there.
‘Skybright,’ she answered quickly.
‘What is it?’
‘Master Bao has sent you some handkerchiefs, miss.’
Dai-yu was puzzled. Why should he send her handkerchiefs?
‘Who gave them to him?’ she asked. ‘They must be very fine ones. Tell him to keep them for someone else. I’ve no use for them just now.’
Skybright smiled. ‘They aren’t new. Just old ones he uses every day.’

segments.text: This puzzled Dai-yu still more. She searched her mind carefully, and after a little thought suddenly understood.
‘Put them down and go,’ she said at once.
Skybright could only set them down and leave. All the way back she turned the matter over, unable to make out what it meant.

segments.text: Now that Dai-yu had divined the meaning of the handkerchiefs, her whole being was swept away. Bao-yu had taken such pains because he understood the pains of her heart: that made her glad. Yet she did not know what would come of those feelings: that made her grieve. To send two old handkerchiefs out of the blue! If it were not for his understanding of her deepest feelings, the mere sight of them would make her laugh. Then she thought of his having someone bring them to her in secret, and was afraid. And when she considered her own constant weeping, it seemed so pointless that she felt ashamed. Turning these thoughts this way and that, she suddenly felt all her inward parts blaze with heat. Her lingering feelings would not release her. She called for a lamp, quite forgetting questions of propriety and suspicion, ground ink at the desk, dipped her brush, and wrote swiftly on the two old handkerchiefs:

segments.text: Dai-yu was about to write more when she felt her whole body grow hot and her face begin to burn. She went to the dressing table, lifted the brocade cover from the mirror and looked. Her cheeks were crimson. Admiring herself, she thought her colour put peach blossom to shame, not knowing that illness was taking root in that very moment. Presently she went to bed, still holding the handkerchiefs and pondering them. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: When Aroma went to see Bao-chai, she found that Bao-chai was not in the garden: she had gone to her mother’s. Aroma returned empty-handed. Bao-chai did not come back until the second watch. Knowing Xue Pan’s nature as she did, she had already half suspected that he had prompted someone to inform against Bao-yu. Hearing Aroma say it too had made her all the more convinced.

segments.text: But Aroma’s information came from Tealeaf, and Tealeaf had merely guessed in private. With no facts to go on, he had settled it in his own mind that Xue Pan was responsible. Xue Pan owed it all to his usual reputation. This time he had actually done nothing of the kind, yet people fastened the charge on him so firmly that he could scarcely open his mouth to defend himself.
That day he came home after drinking outside and went to see his mother. Bao-chai was there. After a little idle talk, he asked, ‘I hear Cousin Bao has had a hard time of it. What was it about?’
Aunt Xue was already upset over this. At his question she clenched her teeth.
‘You good-for-nothing! It’s all your doing, and you still have the face to ask!’
Xue Pan was taken aback. ‘What have I done?’ he asked hastily.
‘Still playing the fool! Everyone knows you told on him, and you’re still denying it.’
‘If everyone said I’d killed someone, would you believe that too?’
‘Even your sister knows you told. Surely you don’t think she’d falsely accuse you?’
Bao-chai hastened to intervene. ‘Mother, Brother, please stop shouting. If we’re calm about it, we can get to the rights and wrongs.’
Then she turned to Xue Pan. ‘Whether you told or not, it’s over now. There’s no need to argue it out and turn a little matter into a big one.

segments.text: ‘All I ask is that from now on you spend less time making trouble outside and interfering in other people’s affairs. You all go roaming about together every day, and you’re so heedless. If nothing happens afterwards, well and good. But if something does happen, everyone will suspect you, even if you had nothing to do with it. Never mind anyone else: I should be the first to suspect you.’

Xue Pan was a blunt man who spoke his mind, and he had never been able to bear this sort of veiled insinuation. Now Bao-chai was telling him to stop roaming about, while his mother accused him of wagging his tongue and causing Bao-yu’s beating. He was already jumping with agitation, protesting his innocence with oaths staked on his own life.

segments.text: ‘Who’s fastening this filth on me?’ he cursed. ‘I’ll knock the teeth out of the bastard! It’s plain enough: Bao-yu’s been beaten, and they’re trying to curry favour by using me as a screen. Is Bao-yu the King of Heaven? His father gives him a beating, and the whole family has to make a commotion for days! That time he’d misbehaved and Uncle gave him a couple of blows, Grandmother somehow found out afterwards, said it was Cousin Zhen’s doing, and sent for him and scolded him for nothing. Now they’re dragging me in as well! Let them. I’m not afraid. I might as well go in and beat Bao-yu to death, then pay for his life with mine. That will settle it for everyone.’
Shouting as he went, he seized a door-bar and started off. Aunt Xue caught hold of him in alarm.
‘You wicked wretch! Are you trying to get yourself killed? Who are you going to hit? Hit me first!’

Xue Pan’s eyes bulged like bronze bells. ‘What do you want of me? You won’t let me go, and you won’t stop accusing me for nothing! As long as Bao-yu lives, I shall have to bear the blame. Better if we all died and had some peace.’
Bao-chai hurried forward to reason with him too. ‘Do try to be patient.

segments.text: ‘Mother is so distressed, and instead of trying to comfort her you make all this fuss. Even if it weren’t Mother, even if it were someone else trying to reason with you, it would be for your own good. But it only seems to make you lose your temper.’
‘Now you talk like that!’ said Xue Pan. ‘You started it all!’
‘You blame me for speaking, but never blame your own heedless behaviour.’

‘You’re always blaming me for being heedless. Why don’t you blame Bao-yu for the way he goes about inviting trouble? Never mind anything else. Take that business with Bijou the other day. We’d met him ten times or so, and I’d never said a single affectionate word to him. How was it that Bao-yu met him, didn’t even know his name yet, and gave him his sash? Are you going to blame that on my tongue as well?’
‘Why bring that up again?’ Aunt Xue and Bao-chai cried in agitation. ‘That’s exactly what he was beaten for! It must have been you who told.’
‘You’ll be the death of me with this!

segments.text: ‘I’m not angry at being accused of telling. What angers me is the whole world being turned upside down over one Bao-yu.’
‘Who’s made a commotion?’ said Bao-chai. ‘You’re the one who started brandishing weapons, and now you blame everyone else.’

Everything Bao-chai said was reasonable, and Xue Pan could find no answer. She was even harder to answer than his mother. He wanted to find something that would silence her, so that no one would dare contradict him again. Still in the heat of his anger, he gave no thought to the weight of his words.

‘My dear sister, there’s no need to quarrel with me. I’ve known what you were thinking for a long time. Mother told me once that this gold of yours could only be properly matched with someone who had jade. You took it to heart, and when you saw Bao-yu had that wretched thing, naturally you began taking his side at every turn.’
Before he had finished, Bao-chai was stunned with anger. She caught hold of Aunt Xue and cried, ‘Mother, listen to what Brother’s saying!’
Seeing his sister weep, Xue Pan knew he had been rash. But in a huff he went off to his own room and to bed, and we shall leave him there.

segments.text: Aunt Xue was trembling all over with anger, but tried to comfort Bao-chai.
‘You know that wretch has never talked sense. Tomorrow I’ll make him apologise to you.’

Bao-chai’s heart was full of hurt and indignation. She wanted to give way to it, yet feared distressing her mother. There was nothing for it but to take leave of her in tears and return to her own rooms, where she wept the whole night. Next morning she had no heart to wash or dress her hair. She made herself ready anyhow and came out to see her mother. By chance she met Dai-yu standing alone in the shade of some flowers. Dai-yu asked where she was going.
‘Home,’ Bao-chai said, and walked on as she spoke. Dai-yu saw how listless she looked as she went, and the traces of tears round her eyes, so unlike her usual self. Smiling, she called after her:
‘Take care of yourself too, cousin. Even two vats full of tears won’t cure the wounds from a beating!’
To learn how Bao-chai answered, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: Now Bao-chai had heard Dai-yu’s cutting remark quite clearly, but her thoughts were with her mother and brother. Without turning round, she walked straight on. Dai-yu remained in the shade of the flowers, looking from afar towards the House of Green Delights. Li Gong-cai, Ying-chun, Tan-chun, Xi-chun and all sorts of other people had been to see Bao-yu and gone away again, group after group, until all had dispersed. Only Xi-feng had not appeared. Dai-yu wondered:

‘Why hasn’t she come to see him? Even if she were tied up with something, surely she would come and make a little show of herself to please Grandmother and Aunt. There must be a reason why she hasn’t come by this time.’

Still puzzling, she looked up again and saw another bright cluster of people approaching the House of Green Delights. Looking closely, she made out Grandmother Jia leaning on Xi-feng’s hand, with Lady Xing and Lady Wang behind, followed by Aunt Zhou and the maids and married servants. They all went into the courtyard.

segments.text: Dai-yu nodded involuntarily. Thinking how fortunate people were who had parents, she soon had tears running down her face again. A little later she saw Bao-chai, Aunt Xue and their party enter too. Suddenly Nightingale came up behind her.
‘Come and take your medicine, miss. The boiled water’s gone cold again.’
‘What do you want of me?’ said Dai-yu. ‘Always hurrying me! What business is it of yours whether I take it or not?’

Nightingale smiled. ‘Your cough has only just got a little better, and already you won’t take your medicine. It may be the fifth month, with the weather so hot, but you still ought to take care. You’ve been standing in this damp place all morning. It’s time you went back and rested.’
These words made Dai-yu realise that her legs were a little sore. She stood blankly for a while, then slowly made her way back to Naiad’s House, leaning on Nightingale.

segments.text: Inside the courtyard gate, the ground was patterned with uneven bamboo shadows and patches of moss, some dark, some light. They brought to mind two lines from The Western Chamber:

‘Does anyone pass through this secluded place?
Cold, pale dew lies scattered on the green moss.’

She sighed inwardly. ‘Shuang-wen, Shuang-wen, you were indeed ill-fated. Yet even in your misfortune you had your widowed mother and your young brother. Today I, Lin Dai-yu, have neither widowed mother nor young brother. The ancients said that beauties are ill-fated. But I am no beauty. Why should my fate be harder even than Shuang-wen’s?’
She walked on, absorbed in these thoughts. Suddenly the parrot on the verandah saw her and swooped down with a squawk, giving her a start.
‘You wretched thing! You’ve flapped dust all over my head again.’
The parrot flew back to its perch and called, ‘Snowgoose! Quick, lift the curtain! Miss is here!’

segments.text: Dai-yu stopped and tapped the perch with her hand. ‘Has it had fresh food and water?’
The parrot gave a long sigh, remarkably like Dai-yu’s own customary sighs, and began to recite:
Dai-yu and Nightingale both laughed.
‘Those are all lines you’re always reciting, miss,’ said Nightingale. ‘How clever of it to remember them!’

Dai-yu had the perch taken down and hung on a hook outside the round window. Then she went indoors and sat just inside it. After she had taken her medicine, she watched the bamboo shadows outside fall across the gauze. The room was filled with a moist green shade, and the tables and sleeping mats seemed to breathe coolness. With nothing to relieve her low spirits, she amused herself by teasing the parrot through the window gauze, and taught it to recite some of her favourite poems and lyrics. Let us leave her there for the moment.

segments.text: When Bao-chai had reached home earlier, she had found her mother dressing her hair.
‘What have you come running here for so early?’ Aunt Xue asked as soon as she saw her.
‘I wanted to see how you were, Mother. After I left yesterday, did he come back and make more trouble?’

She sat down beside her mother as she spoke, and could not help beginning to cry. At the sight of her tears, Aunt Xue could no longer hold back her own. She wept for a while, then tried to comfort her.
‘My child, don’t grieve. Wait till I deal with him. If anything happened to you, who should I have left to depend on?’
Xue Pan heard from outside and hurried in. Facing Bao-chai, he made one bow after another, now to one side, now to the other.

‘Dear sister, forgive me this once! I’d been drinking yesterday, and I came home late. I must have run into spirits on the road. I hadn’t come to my senses when I got home. Heaven knows what nonsense I talked; I don’t even know myself. No wonder you’re angry.’
Bao-chai had been crying with her face covered. Now she could not help finding this funny. She raised her head and spat on the ground.
‘There’s no need for all this play-acting.

segments.text: ‘I know how tired you are of Mother and me. You’re trying every way you can to drive us away, so you can have peace of mind.’
‘Where do you get that from?’ Xue Pan asked hastily, smiling. ‘You leave me no ground to stand on! You’ve never been one to take things amiss and twist words like this.’
Aunt Xue broke in. ‘You can hear your sister twisting words well enough. What about those things you said last night? Were they right and proper? You really must have lost your senses!’
‘Don’t be angry, Mother. And don’t be upset, sister. From now on I won’t go drinking and roaming about with them again. How’s that?’
‘Now you’re coming to your senses!’ Bao-chai said with a smile.
‘If you could stick to that,’ said Aunt Xue, ‘dragons would lay eggs.’
‘If I ever go out with them again, sister, and you hear of it, spit on me! Call me a beast, say I’m not human. How’s that?

segments.text: ‘Why should you both have to worry every day over me alone? It might be forgivable to make Mother angry, but if I keep making my sister worry about me too, I’m less than human. Now Father’s gone, instead of being more dutiful to Mother and more loving to my sister, I make one angry and the other unhappy. I really am worse than a beast.’
As he spoke, tears began rolling from his eyes in spite of himself. Aunt Xue had stopped crying, but his words stirred her grief again.

segments.text: ‘Call Caltrop to pour some tea for my sister.’
‘I don’t want tea,’ said Bao-chai. ‘Once Mother’s washed her hands, we’ll go over.’
‘Let me see your neck circlet,’ said Xue Pan. ‘Perhaps it’s time to have it brightened up.’
‘It’s shining gold already. What would be the use?’
‘You ought to have some more clothes now too. Tell me what colours and patterns you’d like.’
‘I haven’t even worn all the clothes I have. What do I want more for?’
Presently Aunt Xue changed her clothes and took Bao-chai by the hand and went in. Only then did Xue Pan go out.

segments.text: Aunt Xue and Bao-chai came into the garden to visit Bao-yu. At the House of Green Delights, the many maids and older women standing in the porches and covered walkways showed them that Grandmother Jia and the others were there. Mother and daughter went inside and exchanged greetings with everyone. Bao-yu was lying on the couch. When Aunt Xue asked if he was better, he tried hastily to raise himself.
‘Better,’ he answered. ‘But I can’t bear putting you and my cousin to so much trouble, Aunt.’
Aunt Xue helped him lie down again. ‘Whatever you’d like, just tell me.’
‘When I think of anything, I’ll be sure to ask you for it,’ he said with a smile.
Lady Wang asked too, ‘What would you like to eat? We can send it over later.’

segments.text: ‘Of all things, he has to want that.’
Grandmother Jia at once called repeatedly for someone to have it made.
‘Don’t be in such a hurry, Grannie dear,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘Let me think who put the moulds away.’
She turned and told an old woman to ask the kitchen steward for them. After some time the woman returned.
‘The kitchen steward says all four sets of soup moulds were handed back.’
Xi-feng considered. ‘I remember who they went to. Most likely they’re in the tea room.’
She sent to ask the tea-room steward, but they had not received them either. In the end they were brought by the person in charge of the gold and silver utensils.

segments.text: Aunt Xue took them first to have a look. It was a little box holding four sets of silver moulds, each over a chi long and a cun square, with hollows chiselled in them the size of beans. There were chrysanthemums, plum blossoms, lotus seed-pods, water-chestnuts, thirty or forty shapes altogether, all most delicately made. She smiled at Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang.
‘Your household really has thought of everything. Even a bowl of soup has all these patterns! If you hadn’t told me, I could have looked at this and never known what it was for.’

Xi-feng answered with a laugh before anyone else could speak. ‘You wouldn’t know about these, Aunt. They thought them up last year when they were preparing the food. They press some sort of dough into the moulds and borrow a little fragrance from fresh lotus leaves. It all depends on a good broth. There’s really nothing in it. Who would eat it every day? They made it once to show what it was like. Whatever made him think of it today?’
She took the box and handed it to a woman, telling her to have the kitchen take several chickens at once, add the other ingredients and make ten or so bowls.

segments.text: ‘What do we want so much for?’ asked Lady Wang.

‘There’s a reason,’ Xi-feng replied, smiling. ‘We don’t often make this at home. Now Cousin Bao has thought of it, it wouldn’t seem quite right to make it just for him, while Grandmother, Aunt and you had none. Better make enough for everyone while we’re about it, and let me look good on the strength of it too.’

segments.text: ‘You monkey!’ Grandmother Jia laughed. ‘How clever you are! Winning people over with the household’s money.’
Everyone laughed, and Xi-feng hastened to join in.
‘Never mind that. I can still afford this little treat for you.’
She turned to the woman. ‘Tell the kitchen to put in whatever it needs and make it properly. They can collect the money from my account.’
The woman assented and went away.

segments.text: Bao-chai smiled from her place beside them. ‘In the years I’ve been here, I’ve watched carefully. However clever Feng is, she’ll never be cleverer than Grandmother.’

‘I’m old now,’ Grandmother Jia answered. ‘What cleverness have I left? When I was little Feng’s age, I could do even better than she can. She may not be up to what we were, but she’s not bad, and she’s far ahead of your aunt. Poor thing, your aunt hardly speaks, like a block of wood. That never showed her to advantage before her parents-in-law. Feng has such a pleasing tongue. How can you blame people for loving her?’
‘Does that mean you don’t love people who don’t talk much?’ Bao-yu asked with a smile.
‘Quiet people have their own ways of being lovable. And those with pleasing tongues have faults of their own that can make them less likeable than the quiet ones.’

segments.text: ‘That’s what I thought,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘My elder sister-in-law doesn’t talk much, but you treat her just the same as Cousin Feng. If only the good talkers were lovable, Cousin Feng and Cousin Lin would be the only ones among all these sisters and cousins worth loving.’

‘Speaking of the girls,’ said Grandmother Jia, ‘I’m not saying this to flatter Mrs Xue to her face, but it’s the plain truth: beginning with the four girls of our own family, not one of them can compare with Bao-chai.’
‘Now you’re being partial, Your Old Ladyship,’ Aunt Xue said quickly, smiling.
Lady Wang hastened to add, with a smile, ‘She often tells me in private how good Bao-chai is. That’s no empty compliment.’

Bao-yu had been leading Grandmother Jia on in the hope of hearing Dai-yu praised. To hear her praise Bao-chai instead was quite unexpected. He looked at Bao-chai and smiled, but she had already turned away to talk to Aroma.

segments.text: Someone came to announce the meal. Grandmother Jia rose, told Bao-yu to take good care of himself, and gave the maids another round of instructions. Then, supported by Xi-feng and inviting Aunt Xue to go before her, she went out with the others. She asked whether the soup was ready yet, then said to Aunt Xue and the rest:
‘Whatever you’d like to eat, just tell me. I know how to make Feng get it for us.’
Aunt Xue smiled. ‘You do enjoy teasing her, Your Old Ladyship. She’s always finding things to offer you, and in the end you can eat so little of them.’
‘Don’t say that, Aunt,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘Our dear old Grannie only objects to human flesh because it’s sour. If she didn’t, she’d have eaten me up long ago.’

segments.text: Before she had finished, Grandmother Jia and everyone else burst out laughing. Even Bao-yu, in his room, could not hold back his laughter.
‘That tongue of Mrs Lian’s really is terrifying!’ Aroma said with a smile.
Bao-yu smiled and reached for her hand. ‘You’ve been standing all this time. Aren’t you tired?’
As he spoke he drew her down to sit beside him.

segments.text: ‘You’ve forgotten again,’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘While Miss Bao’s still in the courtyard, ask her if Oriole can come and knot a few cords for you.’
‘Good thing you reminded me!’ Bao-yu said with a smile. He lifted his head and called through the window:
‘Cousin Bao! Could Oriole come after dinner and make me a few knotted cords? Would she have time?’
Bao-chai turned back. ‘Of course she would. I’ll send her over in a little while.’
Grandmother Jia and the others had not quite heard. They stopped to ask Bao-chai, and only understood when she explained.
‘Good child,’ said Grandmother Jia, ‘do send her to make a few for your cousin. If that leaves you with no one to wait on you, I’ve plenty of idle maids. Take whichever you like.’
Aunt Xue, Bao-chai and the others laughed. ‘We’ll just send her to do it. What is there for her to attend to? She does nothing all day but idle and play.’

segments.text: Talking as they went, they started forward again and came upon Shi Xiang-yun, Patience, Caltrop and the others picking balsam flowers beside the rocks. Seeing them approach, the girls came to meet them. Presently they were outside the garden. Afraid Grandmother Jia might be tired, Lady Wang asked her to sit in the main apartments. Grandmother Jia’s legs were indeed sore, and she nodded her agreement. Lady Wang sent a maid ahead at once to have the seats made ready.

Aunt Zhao was pleading illness, so only Aunt Zhou was there with the married servants and maids, busily lifting curtains, setting backrests upright and spreading cushions. Grandmother Jia came in on Xi-feng’s arm and sat down with Aunt Xue, each in her proper place as hostess and guest.

‘Let the younger daughters-in-law wait on us,’ Grandmother Jia told Lady Wang. ‘Sit there yourself, so we can talk.’

segments.text: Only then did Lady Wang sit down on a small stool. She told Xi-feng, ‘Have Her Old Ladyship’s dinner served here, and bring some extra dishes.’

Xi-feng assented and went out to send word to Grandmother Jia’s apartments. The women there passed the message outside, and the maids all hurried over. Lady Wang then sent for the girls. After a good deal of fetching, only Tan-chun and Xi-chun came. Ying-chun was feeling unwell and would not eat. As for Dai-yu, it went without saying: ordinarily she could manage only five meals out of ten, and no one paid much heed any more.
Presently the food arrived and the tables were set in place. Xi-feng stood holding a bundle of ivory chopsticks wrapped in a towel.
‘Grandmother and Aunt needn’t stand on ceremony,’ she said, smiling. ‘Just leave it all to me.’
‘This is how we do things,’ Grandmother Jia told Aunt Xue with a smile.

segments.text: Presently the lotus-leaf soup arrived. Grandmother Jia inspected it. Lady Wang turned, saw Silver nearby and told her to take some to Bao-yu.
‘She can’t carry it all by herself,’ said Xi-feng.
Just then Oriole and Xi-er came in. Knowing they had finished their meal, Bao-chai told Oriole, ‘Cousin Bao has just asked you to make some knotted cords. You two can go together.’
Oriole assented and went out with Silver.
‘It’s such a long way, and so hot,’ said Oriole. ‘How are we going to carry it?’
‘Don’t worry. I have a way,’ Silver said with a smile.

She called an older serving-woman, had the soup, food and other things put into a food-box, and told her to carry it behind them. The two girls went empty-handed. Only when they were inside the gate of the House of Green Delights did Silver take it from her and go with Oriole into Bao-yu’s room. Aroma, Musk and Ripple were laughing and joking with him. At the sight of the two newcomers, they all hurried to get up.
‘How did you two happen to come at just the same time?’ they asked with smiles, taking the things from them as they spoke.

segments.text: Silver sat on a stool, but Oriole did not venture to sit. Aroma quickly brought her a footstool, and still she would not sit down.

Bao-yu had been delighted to see Oriole. But suddenly seeing Silver too, he thought of her elder sister Golden and felt both grief and shame. He forgot Oriole for the moment and began speaking to Silver. Aroma, afraid Oriole would be embarrassed at being neglected, and seeing that she would not sit down, took her out to the other room for tea and a talk.

segments.text: Musk and the others brought bowls and chopsticks and prepared to serve the meal. But Bao-yu would not eat.
‘Is your mother well?’ he asked Silver.
Her face was full of anger. She would not look him in the eye, and only after a long time did she say one word: ‘Yes.’
Bao-yu felt rebuffed. After another long pause, he could only put on a smile and ask, ‘Who sent you to bring me this?’
‘The mistresses, of course!’

Seeing her still so mournful and sullen, Bao-yu knew it was because of Golden. He wanted to humble himself and coax her round, but with so many people there he could not bring himself to do it. By every pretext he could devise, he sent them all out, then again smiled and asked her all sorts of questions. At first Silver remained displeased, but however bitterly she spoke, he showed no temper at all and remained gentle and kind. She began to feel embarrassed herself, and a little warmth came into her face.
‘Dear sister,’ Bao-yu begged with a smile, ‘bring me the soup and let me taste it.’
‘I’ve never fed anyone. Wait till they come back.’
‘I’m not asking you to feed me.

segments.text: ‘I can’t walk, that’s all. If you hand it to me and I drink it, you can go back sooner, report that you’ve done your errand, and have your dinner. If I keep wasting time, won’t you be starved? If you can’t be bothered to move, I’ll have to bear the pain and get it myself.’
He began struggling to get off the bed, unable to keep from crying out. At this Silver could no longer keep her seat.
‘Lie down! What sins did you commit in some former life, to have them catch up with you here and now? And you expect me to think anything of you!’

‘Dear sister,’ Bao-yu said, smiling, ‘if you’re angry, be as angry as you like here. But do look more pleasant when you see Grandmother and Mother. If you still look like this, you’ll be scolded again.’

segments.text: ‘Drink it, drink it!’ said Silver. ‘Don’t try your sweet talk on me. I don’t believe a word of it.’
She urged him to take two mouthfuls. Then Bao-yu deliberately said, ‘It isn’t nice. I don’t want any more.’
‘Amitabha! If this isn’t nice, what is?’
‘It has no taste at all. If you don’t believe me, try it yourself.’
In sheer defiance, Silver did taste it.
‘Now it’s delicious,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
Only then did Silver understand that he had tricked her into taking a mouthful.
‘You said it wasn’t nice. Even if you say it is now, I shan’t let you have any.’
Bao-yu went on smiling and pleading for it, but she would not give it to him. She called the others to serve his meal.

segments.text: The maids had only just come in when someone announced, ‘Two women from Second Master Fu’s household have come to pay their respects. They would like to see Master Bao.’

Bao-yu knew they were servants of the assistant prefect Fu Shi. Fu Shi was a protégé of Jia Zheng’s, and for years had owed his success to the Jia family’s name and influence. Jia Zheng thought highly of him, and treated him differently from his other protégés. His household often sent people over.

Now Bao-yu ordinarily detested stupid men and foolish women. Why should he ask to see these two old women today? There was a reason. He had heard that Fu Shi had a younger sister named Fu Qiu-fang, a jewel of a young lady, whom people often praised for both talent and beauty. He had never seen her himself, but his distant thoughts and admiration were full of sincere respect. Afraid that refusing to admit the servants would slight Fu Qiu-fang, he hastened to have them shown in.

Fu Shi had come up in the world only recently. Because Qiu-fang had some beauty and exceptional intelligence, he had set his heart on using his sister to make a marriage alliance with a great and noble family. He would not readily promise her to anyone, and so had delayed until now.

segments.text: Fu Qiu-fang was now twenty-three and still unbetrothed. But the great and noble families thought Fu Shi a shabby scholar of little family standing, and would not seek the match. He had his own purposes in cultivating the Jia family too.

The two women he had sent today happened to be particularly ignorant. Told that Bao-yu would see them, they came in, paid their respects and had barely exchanged a few words. Silver stopped teasing Bao-yu as soon as she saw strangers arrive. Holding the soup in her hands, she listened intently. Bao-yu was equally intent on talking to the women. As he ate, he reached for the soup. Both were looking at the visitors, and he put out his hand too sharply and upset the bowl, spilling the hot soup over his hand.
Silver was not scalded, but she jumped and then hastily laughed. ‘Whatever are you doing!’
The maids hurried forward in alarm to take the bowl. Bao-yu did not even notice that his own hand was scalded. He kept asking Silver, ‘Where did it burn you? Does it hurt?’
Silver and all the others laughed.

segments.text: ‘You’re the one who’s scalded,’ Silver said, ‘and you keep asking me!’

Only then did Bao-yu notice his own burn. Everyone hurried to clear up. He ate no more, washed his hands, took some tea and spoke a little longer with the two women. Then they took their leave. Skybright and the others saw them as far as the bridge before returning.
Once no one was near, the women talked as they walked.
‘No wonder people say their Bao-yu is all fine looks and muddle inside, good to look at but no use for anything,’ one said with a laugh. ‘He really is a bit of a fool.

segments.text: ‘Scalding his own hand and asking someone else whether it hurts! What is that if not foolishness?’

The other laughed too. ‘The last time I came, I heard plenty of people in his own household complaining. He certainly is foolish. There he was in a downpour, soaked like a bedraggled chicken, and telling other people, “It’s raining. Quick, get under cover!” Isn’t that funny?

segments.text: ‘And he hasn’t an ounce of spirit. He even puts up with those little maids’ tempers. When he’s taking care of things, even a loose end of thread is precious. When he’s wasting them, he doesn’t care if they’re worth a thousand or ten thousand.’
Talking all the way, the women left the garden, said goodbye to the others and went home. Of them we need say no more.
Once they had gone, Aroma brought Oriole back and asked Bao-yu what kind of cords he wanted knotted.
‘I was so busy talking, I forgot you,’ he told Oriole with a smile. ‘There’s nothing else I wanted you for, just to make me a few knotted cords.’
‘For holding what?’ asked Oriole.
‘Never mind what they hold. Make me a few of every kind.’
Oriole clapped her hands and laughed. ‘Goodness! If that’s what you want, I shan’t finish in ten years.’

segments.text: ‘Dear sister, you’ve nothing to do just now,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Make them all for me.’
‘How could she finish them all at once?’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘Choose a couple you need most for now.’
‘What would those be?’ asked Oriole. ‘Fans, scented pendants and sashes, I suppose.’
‘Sashes will do,’ said Bao-yu.
‘What colour is the sash?’
‘Scarlet.’
‘Scarlet needs a black cord to look well. Or dark blue: that will keep the colour from being too strong.’
‘What goes with pine-pollen green?’
‘Peach-pink.’
Bao-yu smiled. ‘That would be lovely and bright. I’d like something soft and elegant with a touch of brightness too.’
‘Spring green and willow yellow are my favourites.’
‘Very well. Make a peach-pink one, and a spring-green one too.’
‘What pattern?’
‘How many patterns are there?’
‘Incense Stick, Upturned Stool, Elephant’s Eye, Paired Diamonds, Linked Rings, Plum Blossom and Willow Leaf.’
‘What was the pattern you made for the Third Miss the other day?’

segments.text: ‘That was Clustered-Heart Plum Blossom.’
‘That’s the one I like,’ said Bao-yu, and asked Aroma to bring the thread. She had just fetched it when an old woman called outside the window, ‘The young ladies’ dinner is ready.’
‘Go and eat,’ Bao-yu said. ‘Be quick and come back.’
‘How can we go with a guest here?’ Aroma asked with a smile.

segments.text: Oriole smiled as she sorted the thread. ‘What makes you talk like that? Go and eat, then come back.’
Only then did Aroma and the others go, leaving two little maids to answer calls. Bao-yu watched Oriole knotting the cord and chatted with her.
‘How old are you now?’
‘Sixteen,’ she answered, her hands still working.
‘What is your surname?’

segments.text: ‘Huang.’
Bao-yu smiled. ‘Then your surname and your name go perfectly together. Huang means yellow: you really are a yellow oriole.’
Oriole laughed. ‘My name used to have two Chinese characters: Golden Oriole. Miss thought it was awkward to say, so she just called me Oriole, and now everyone does.’
‘Cousin Bao must be fond of you. When she marries, you’ll be going with her, of course.’
Oriole smiled with closed lips.
‘I’m always saying to Aroma,’ Bao-yu went on, smiling, ‘I wonder what lucky man will have the joy of both of you one day, mistress and maid.’
‘You don’t even know the qualities our miss has that no one else in the world possesses,’ Oriole said with a smile. ‘Her looks are the least of it.’
Her sweet simplicity, her gentle ways and the entrancing sound of her talk and laughter had already quite overcome Bao-yu. How much more so when she brought up Bao-chai!
‘What qualities?’ he asked. ‘Dear sister, tell me all about them.’
‘I’ll tell you, but you mustn’t go and tell her.’
‘Of course not,’ Bao-yu said, smiling.
Just then a voice outside asked, ‘Why is it so quiet here?’
They both turned. It was none other than Bao-chai.

segments.text: Bao-yu hastily asked her to sit. She did so, and asked Oriole, ‘What are you making?’ As she spoke she looked at the work in her hands. It was only half done.
‘What’s so interesting about that?’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘You’d do better to knot a cover for the jade.’
The suggestion reminded Bao-yu at once. He clapped his hands and smiled.
‘You’re right, cousin! I’d forgotten. But what colour would go well with it?’

‘Mixed colours certainly won’t do. Scarlet would clash, yellow wouldn’t show to advantage, and black would be too dark. Let me think of a way. Bring the gold thread, put it with black pearl-thread, twist them together strand by strand, and knot the cover with that. Then it will look well.’

segments.text: ‘There’ll be things to embarrass you much more than this before long.’

Aroma heard the implication. She knew Bao-chai was not one to make light, cutting jokes at other people’s expense, and now remembered what Lady Wang had meant the other day. She said no more about it, but showed Bao-yu the dishes.
‘I’ll wash my hands and come back for the thread.’

segments.text: With that she went straight out. After eating and washing her hands, she came back and took out the gold thread for Oriole to use. By this time Bao-chai had already gone: Xue Pan had sent someone to ask her over.
Bao-yu was watching the knotting when two maids arrived from Lady Xing with two kinds of fruit for him.
‘Can you walk yet?’ they asked. ‘If you can, you’re to come over tomorrow for a little change. Her Ladyship is very concerned about you.’
‘If I can walk, I shall certainly go and pay my respects to her,’ Bao-yu answered at once. ‘The pain is better than it was. Please tell her not to worry.’

He asked the two maids to sit and called Ripple, telling her to take half the fruit they had just brought to Miss Lin. Ripple assented and was about to go when Dai-yu’s voice was heard in the courtyard.
‘Ask her in at once!’ Bao-yu called.
To learn what followed, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: After returning from Lady Wang’s, Grandmother Jia was naturally delighted to see Bao-yu improving day by day. Afraid that Jia Zheng might send for him again, she summoned the head of his personal pages.

‘In future, if your master wants Bao-yu to meet visitors or entertain guests, don’t come in with the message. Tell him I have said this: first, the beating was too severe, and he will need several months of proper nursing before he can get about; second, his stars are unfavourable. Now that offerings have been made to them, he must see no outsiders. He is not to go beyond the inner gate until the eighth month is over.’
The head page received her instructions and withdrew.
