segments.text: Grandmother Jia also sent for Nurse Li, Aroma and the others and told them to pass this on to Bao-yu, so that he need not worry. Bao-yu had always been reluctant to converse with gentlemen and officials, and particularly detested the ceremonial hats and robes, the visits of congratulation and condolence, and all such comings and goings. This pronouncement suited him better still. Not only did he shut out relatives and friends alike; even his morning and evening attendance on his elders was left very much to his own convenience. He spent his days wandering or lying about the garden, merely calling on Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang early each morning before coming back. Yet he was often perfectly willing to run errands for the maids, and so passed his time in ample leisure. If Bao-chai or anyone like her took an opportunity to offer him guidance, he would grow angry instead.

‘A girl as pure and unspoilt as that, and now she too must learn to fish for fame and buy herself a reputation, joining those traitors to the country, those office-hungry ghosts! It all began with the ancients making trouble for no reason, setting up their doctrines and fine phrases to instruct the filthy bearded creatures who came after them. And I have the misfortune to live when even the jewelled chambers of girls have caught the infection. What a betrayal of all the finest spirit of heaven and earth that went into making them!’
The calamity thus spread to the ancients: apart from the Four Books, he actually burnt the other books.

segments.text: Seeing him behave so wildly, the others gave up talking to him about these serious matters. Dai-yu alone had never, from childhood onwards, urged him to make a career or a name for himself, and for this he held her in profound esteem.

But enough of that. To return to Wang Xi-feng: since Golden’s death, several families of servants had suddenly taken to bringing her little offerings, calling to pay their respects and flattering her. She was puzzled, unable to make out what they meant by it. After yet another gift arrived, she asked Patience with a smile that evening, when they were alone, ‘Those families don’t usually have much to do with me. Why have they suddenly become so friendly?’

Patience gave a cold laugh. ‘Can’t you work even that out, ma’am? My guess is that their daughters are all maids in Her Ladyship’s rooms. There are four senior girls there who get a tael of silver a month; the rest only get a few hundred cash. Now Golden’s dead, they must be after that nice little one-tael opening.’

segments.text: Xi-feng laughed. ‘Of course! Of course! You’ve put me on to it. What a greedy lot they are. They’ve made plenty of money, and none of the hard jobs ever comes their way. They might be satisfied with putting up a daughter to cover their own obligations, but no, they must have this as well. Very well, then. It isn’t often their money finds its way to me, and they’ve asked for it themselves. Whatever they send, I’ll take. I know what I’m going to do.’

segments.text: Having settled that to her satisfaction, Xi-feng let the matter drag on until the families had sent all the gifts she thought sufficient. Only then did she find an opportunity to speak to Lady Wang. One day at noon, Aunt Xue and her daughter, Dai-yu and the others were having something to eat in Lady Wang’s room, and Xi-feng took her chance.
‘Since Silver’s elder sister died, ma’am, you’ve been one maid short. If there’s a girl you think suitable, please let me know, so that we can arrange the monthly payments for next month.’
Lady Wang considered. ‘As far as I’m concerned, what is all this about a fixed number? Why must there be four or five? Enough to do the work is enough. We might simply do without another.’

‘In principle, ma’am, you’re quite right,’ said Xi-feng, smiling. ‘But it’s the old allowance. Even other households have two girls on that rate, and here you would be, not taking your full number. Besides, saving one tael won’t make much difference.’
Lady Wang thought again. ‘Very well. Draw the allowance as usual, but don’t fill the place. Give the tael to her younger sister Silver.

segments.text: ‘Her sister served me all that time and came to no good end. There is only the younger one left with me now. Letting her have a double share would hardly be excessive.’
Xi-feng assented, then turned to look for Silver. ‘Congratulations! Congratulations!’ she said, smiling.
Silver came forward and kowtowed.
‘There was something I meant to ask you,’ Lady Wang went on. ‘How much do Aunt Zhao and Aunt Zhou receive each month now?’
‘The fixed allowance, ma’am, two taels each. Aunt Zhao has another two taels for Huan, making four altogether, with four strings of cash besides.’

segments.text: ‘And are they given the full amount?’
Xi-feng thought this a strange question. ‘Of course they are!’ she said quickly.
‘The other day I thought I heard someone complaining that a string of cash was missing. Why was that?’

Xi-feng hastened to explain, smiling. ‘The concubines’ maids used to receive a string each every month. Last year the men outside discussed it and decided to halve the allowance for each maid in those households, making it five hundred cash a head. Each concubine has two maids, so that is where the missing string comes from. They can’t blame me for it. I’d be glad to give it to them, but if the men outside hold it back, am I supposed to make up the difference? The money only passes through my hands. What comes in goes out; I have no say in it. I did ask two or three times for those allowances to be restored, but they said that was all there was under that heading, and there wasn’t much more I could say. As things are, I pay them every month without so much as a day’s delay. When they used to draw it from outside, was there ever a month without a fuss? Did they ever once get it smoothly?’
Lady Wang let the matter drop. After a while she asked, ‘How many maids on one tael are there in the old lady’s rooms?’
‘Eight,’ said Xi-feng.

segments.text: ‘Only seven are actually there now. The eighth is Aroma.’
‘Exactly,’ said Lady Wang. ‘Bao-yu has no one-tael maid of his own. Aroma is still reckoned as belonging to the old lady’s household.’

‘Aroma was always the old lady’s maid,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘She was only given to Bao-yu to use. Her tael still comes out of the old lady’s allowance for maids. It simply wouldn’t do to cut it now on the grounds that she belongs to Bao-yu. If we gave the old lady another maid, then we could discontinue Aroma’s allowance there. If we don’t discontinue it, we ought to add a maid on the same rate to Huan’s rooms, to keep things fair and even. As for the seven senior maids, Skybright, Musk and the others, at one string a month each, and the eight little maids, Melilot and the rest, at five hundred cash each, that was the old lady’s own decision. Who can get angry or resentful about that?’
‘Listen to Feng!’ Aunt Xue laughed. ‘Like a cartload of walnuts tipping out. And her accounts are so clear, her reasoning so fair!’

‘Not a thing. Only wouldn’t it be less tiring if you said it a little more slowly?’
Xi-feng was about to laugh, but checked herself and waited for Lady Wang’s instructions.

segments.text: After thinking for some time, Lady Wang said to Xi-feng, ‘Tomorrow choose a good maid and send her to the old lady in Aroma’s place, and discontinue Aroma’s allowance there. Take two taels of silver and one string of cash out of my own twenty-tael monthly allowance and give them to Aroma. From now on, whatever Aunt Zhao and Aunt Zhou receive, Aroma is to receive too. Only her share must all come out of mine. There is no need to draw on the household funds.’
Xi-feng agreed to each instruction, then gave Aunt Xue a smiling nudge. ‘You heard that, Aunt! What did I always tell you? Today it’s come true.’
‘It should have been done long ago,’ Aunt Xue said.

segments.text: ‘Her looks go without saying. But that open, capable way she has, and the firmness and determination beneath her pleasant manner with people: those are rare qualities.’

‘You have no idea how good that child Aroma is,’ Lady Wang said, her eyes filling. ‘Ten times better than my Bao-yu! If he is truly blessed, and can have her to look after him all his life, that will be enough.’
‘If that’s how you feel, why not have her bridal face-threading done and openly install her in his rooms?’ Xi-feng asked.

segments.text: Some time passed after this. Seeing that there was nothing more to be said, Xi-feng withdrew. She had barely reached the verandah when she found several married servants with household duties waiting to report to her.
‘What have you been discussing all this time, ma’am?’ they asked, smiling. ‘You must be terribly hot.’

Xi-feng rolled her sleeves up several times and stood with a foot on the threshold of the side gate. ‘There’s a cool draught through here. I’ll catch a little of it before I go.’ Then she told them, ‘You wonder what kept me talking so long? Her Ladyship remembered things from two hundred years ago and wanted to ask me about them. Could I refuse to answer?’

She gave a cold laugh. ‘From now on I really will do a few spiteful things. Let them complain to Her Ladyship; I’m not afraid. Their hearts must be clogged with grease, the filthy low creatures! May their tongues rot, may they die a wretched death! They can stop their damned dreaming. There are days ahead when the whole lot will be cut off.

segments.text: Meanwhile, Lady Wang and the others finished their watermelon, chatted a little longer and dispersed. Bao-chai, Dai-yu and the rest returned to the garden. Bao-chai invited Dai-yu to go with her to Lotus Pavilion, but Dai-yu said she wanted a bath at once, so they parted. Walking on alone, Bao-chai went into the House of Green Delights on her way, hoping a little conversation with Bao-yu would dispel the afternoon drowsiness. To her surprise, the courtyard was utterly still. Even the two cranes beneath the plantains were asleep. She followed the covered walk to the rooms. On the bed in the outer room the maids lay asleep, sprawling in every direction. Passing the ornamental lattice partition, she entered Bao-yu’s room. He was asleep on his bed, with Aroma sitting beside him at her needlework. A fly-whisk with rhinoceros-horn mounts lay nearby.
Bao-chai went up and whispered with a smile, ‘You do take such care! There can’t be any flies or mosquitoes in here. What do you need a whisk for?’
Aroma, taken unawares, looked up with a start. Seeing Bao-chai, she hastily laid down her sewing and rose, whispering with a smile, ‘Oh, miss, I didn’t know you’d come in. You startled me.

segments.text: ‘You wouldn’t know, miss, but although there aren’t any flies or mosquitoes, there’s a sort of tiny insect that gets through the holes in the gauze. You can’t even see it. Once you’re asleep it bites, and it’s just like being nipped by an ant.’

‘No wonder,’ said Bao-chai. ‘The water is so close behind the house, and there are all those scented flowers, and the rooms are fragrant too. Those insects grow in the hearts of flowers. They come flocking wherever they smell a scent.’

As she spoke, she looked at Aroma’s sewing. It was a stomach-cover of white figured silk lined with red, embroidered with mandarin ducks playing among lotuses: red flowers, green leaves and ducks in many colours.

segments.text: ‘Oh, what lovely bright work!’ said Bao-chai. ‘Who is it for, to be worth so much trouble?’
Aroma pursed her lips towards the bed.
‘At his age, does he still wear one?’ Bao-chai asked, smiling.

Aroma smiled. ‘He wouldn’t wear one before. That’s why I’ve taken such pains to make it beautiful: when he sees it, he won’t be able to resist. In this hot weather he’s so careless when he goes to sleep. If I can coax him into wearing it, we needn’t worry so much if he isn’t properly covered at night. You think I’ve spent time on this? You haven’t seen the one he’s wearing now.’
‘What patience you have!’
‘I’ve been at it a long time today, with my head down. My neck’s terribly stiff.’ Aroma smiled. ‘Be a dear, miss, and sit here a moment. I’ll just go out and stretch my legs.’

She went. Bao-chai was so absorbed in examining the work that, without thinking, she lowered herself into the very place Aroma had just left. Finding the embroidery really delightful, she could not help picking up the needle and putting in a few stitches for her.

segments.text: Now Dai-yu had met Shi Xiang-yun, who proposed that they go and congratulate Aroma. They came into the silent courtyard, and Xiang-yun turned aside to look for Aroma in the side rooms. Dai-yu went to the window and looked through its gauze. Bao-yu, in a silvery-pink gauze tunic, lay at ease on the bed, while Bao-chai sat beside him sewing, with the fly-whisk at her side. At the sight, Dai-yu quickly drew back out of view and pressed a hand over her mouth to keep from laughing. She beckoned to Xiang-yun. Seeing her like this, Xiang-yun supposed there must be something new to see and hurried over for a look. She too was about to laugh, but suddenly remembered how kindly Bao-chai always treated her, and covered her mouth. Knowing Dai-yu’s merciless tongue, she was afraid she would make some cutting joke, so quickly drew her away.
‘Come on. I’ve just remembered Aroma said she was going to the pond at midday to wash some clothes. She must have gone there. Let’s go and find her.’
Dai-yu understood perfectly. She gave a couple of dry laughs, but had to go with her.

segments.text: She had not finished speaking when someone arrived from Xi-feng to summon Aroma.
‘That’s what it’s about,’ said Bao-chai, smiling.

Aroma had to wake two of the maids. She left the House of Green Delights with Bao-chai, then went on to Xi-feng’s. Sure enough, Xi-feng told her about the new arrangement and directed her to kowtow to Lady Wang, but said she need not go to Grandmother Jia. Aroma was quite embarrassed. She hurried back after seeing Lady Wang and found Bao-yu awake. When he asked why she had been sent for, she gave him only a vague answer. Not until the house was quiet that night did she tell him.

Beside himself with delight, he said, smiling, ‘Now let’s see whether you go home! You went home once, and when you came back you said your brother wanted to buy you out. You said you had no settled place here, and what would it all come to in the end? You frightened me with all those cold, heartless words, as though we were strangers. From now on, I’d like to see who dares take you away.’

segments.text: Aroma gave a cold laugh. ‘You’d better not talk like that. From now on I belong to Her Ladyship. If I want to leave, I don’t even have to tell you. I need only ask her, and go.’
‘Even supposing I behaved badly and you asked Mother’s leave and went,’ Bao-yu said, smiling, ‘once people heard you’d left because I was no good, you wouldn’t be very happy about it either.’

Aroma smiled. ‘Why shouldn’t I be? If you turned thief and robber, would I have to follow you? And if there were nothing else, there would still be death. Live a hundred years, you have to die all the same. Once the breath is gone, you neither hear nor see any more, and that’s that.’

segments.text: Bao-yu hurriedly put a hand over her mouth. ‘Enough, enough! Don’t say things like that.’

Aroma knew his peculiar nature well. He disliked flattering, auspicious talk as hollow and untrue, yet such unreserved truths made him sorrowful. Regretting her rashness, she quickly smiled and turned the conversation, asking him only about the things he most enjoyed discussing. First came spring breezes and autumn moons, then the soft bloom of powder and the lustre of rouge, then the goodness of girls. When the talk came round to girls dying, Aroma hurriedly stopped herself. Bao-yu was in full flow. Seeing her fall silent, he smiled.

‘Who doesn’t die? What matters is to die well. Those filthy bearded creatures know only this: a civil official dies remonstrating with his sovereign, a soldier dies in battle. These, they say, are the two deaths by which a man wins honour and keeps his integrity. How much better not to die at all! There has to be a benighted ruler before the official can remonstrate. He thinks only of winning a name, throws away his life, and where does that leave his sovereign? There has to be a war before the soldier can fight. He throws away his life, thinking only of the glory he will win in battle, and where does that leave his country?

segments.text: ‘Neither is a proper death.’
‘Loyal ministers and good generals only die when they have no choice,’ Aroma said.

‘The generals merely rely on hot-blooded courage. They have no plans, no strategy. They lose their lives through their own incompetence. Is that having no choice? The civil officials are worse still. They have read a couple of lines and let them foul their minds. Let the court show the slightest fault and they babble out their advice, thinking only of a reputation for loyalty and sacrifice. Up comes a surge of that filthy spirit, and they rush to their deaths. Is that having no choice? They ought to know that the sovereign receives his mandate from Heaven. If he were neither wise nor benevolent, Heaven and earth would never entrust all those weighty affairs to him. Clearly, those who die like that are buying a reputation; they know nothing of the greater duty. Take me, now. If I were truly fortunate, this would be the time for me to die, while all of you are here. If the tears you shed for me could flow into a great river, float my body away and carry it somewhere lonely, where not even a crow or sparrow ever came, and I could dissolve on the wind and never be born human again, then I should have died at the right time.’
Faced with this sudden outpouring of wild talk, Aroma said she was sleepy and paid him no more attention.

segments.text: Only then did Bao-yu close his eyes and go to sleep. By the next day the matter had been put aside.

One day, tired of wandering everywhere, Bao-yu thought of the songs in The Peony Pavilion. He read them through twice, but still felt unsatisfied. Having heard that Ling-guan, who played young female roles among the twelve girls at Pear-tree Court, sang them better than anyone, he made a point of going out through the side gate to find her. Bao-guan and Yu-guan were in the courtyard. When they saw him, both smilingly offered him a seat.
‘Where is Ling-guan?’ he asked.
‘In her room,’ they told him.
He hurried in. Ling-guan was lying alone against a pillow. When he entered, she did not stir.

segments.text: Bao-yu was so used to playing with the other girls that he assumed Ling-guan would be just like them. He went over and sat beside her, then coaxed her with a smile to get up and sing the suite beginning ‘Gossamer drifts in the clear air’. To his surprise, the moment he sat down she raised herself and moved away.
‘My voice is hoarse,’ she said gravely. ‘When Her Imperial Highness sent for us the other day, I didn’t even sing for her.’

Now that she was sitting upright, Bao-yu looked more closely and recognised the girl who had been tracing ‘qiang’ beneath the roses. He had never been shunned like this before. Flushing with embarrassment at her reception, he could only leave. Bao-guan and the others, puzzled, asked what had happened. He told them and was going out when Bao-guan said, ‘Wait just a little. When Master Qiang comes, if he asks her to sing, she certainly will.’

segments.text: Puzzled by this, Bao-yu asked, ‘Where has Qiang gone?’
‘He’s just gone out. Ling-guan must want something again, and he’s off finding a way to get it for her.’

Bao-yu thought this remarkable. He had been standing there only a little while when Jia Qiang came in from outside, carrying a birdcage with a miniature stage fastened to it and a bird inside. He was hurrying eagerly in to find Ling-guan, but had to stop when he saw Bao-yu.
‘What sort of bird is it?’ Bao-yu asked. ‘Can it carry flags and run about a stage?’
‘A Jade-crowned Golden Bean,’ said Jia Qiang, smiling.
‘What did you pay for it?’
‘One tael and eight qian of silver.’
As he spoke, he invited Bao-yu to sit down, then went into Ling-guan’s room.

segments.text: Bao-yu had now lost all interest in hearing songs. He wanted to see how Jia Qiang and Ling-guan behaved together. Jia Qiang went in smiling.
‘Get up and look at this toy.’
Ling-guan sat up and asked what it was.
‘I’ve bought you a bird to play with, so you won’t be bored every day with nothing to cheer you up. I’ll show you how it works.’
With a little grain he coaxed the bird to scamper about the stage, carrying masks and flags in its beak.
‘How amusing!’ the other girls all laughed.
Ling-guan alone gave a couple of cold laughs and lay down again in a temper. Jia Qiang kept smiling ingratiatingly and asking whether she liked it.

‘Your family brings perfectly good people here and shuts them up in this prison to learn that wretched trade. Isn’t that enough? Now you must get a bird and make it do exactly the same thing. You’ve plainly brought it here to mimic us and make fun of us, and then you ask me if I like it!’
Jia Qiang was alarmed. He hastily swore oaths on his own life.

segments.text: ‘What scented grease got into my head today?’ he went on. ‘I spent a tael or two on it to amuse you. I never thought of that. All right, all right! I’ll set it free, and may that spare you illness and misfortune.’
He did indeed release the bird, then pulled the cage to pieces.

But Ling-guan went on. ‘A bird may not be a person, but it too has an old bird waiting in its nest. How could you have the heart to catch it and make it do that wretched work? I coughed up two mouthfuls of blood today. Her Ladyship sent for the doctor to see me, and instead of asking him properly about it for me, you bring this thing here to make fun of me. No one cares about me, no one looks after me, and I have to be ill as well!’
She began to cry.

‘I asked the doctor last night,’ Jia Qiang said hurriedly. ‘He said it wasn’t serious. He said you were to take two doses of medicine and he’d see you again the day after tomorrow. How was I to know you’d bring up blood again today? I’ll go and fetch him now.’

segments.text: He was about to go when Ling-guan called him back.
‘Stop! The sun’s vicious out there now. If you go storming off to fetch him, I won’t see him when he comes.’

Jia Qiang had to stop where he was. Bao-yu watched, spellbound. Only now did he understand the deeper meaning of her tracing ‘qiang’. Unable to remain, he slipped away. Jia Qiang’s whole attention was on Ling-guan, and he did not see him out. The other girls did that instead.

segments.text: Weighing it all over in his mind, Bao-yu returned in a daze to the House of Green Delights, where Dai-yu and Aroma were sitting talking. As soon as he came in he gave Aroma a long sigh.

‘What I said last night was wrong. No wonder Father says I see the sky through a tube and measure the sea with a ladle. Last night I said your tears would all be for my burial. That was wrong. I can’t have them all. From now on, each of us can only have our own share of tears.’
To Aroma, last night’s talk had been mere nonsense, already forgotten. She had not expected him to bring it up again.
‘You really are a little mad,’ she said with a laugh.

Bao-yu made no reply. From then on, he understood profoundly that each person had an allotted share in the bonds of love. Yet he would often grieve in secret: ‘Who will be there one day to shed tears at my burial?’

segments.text: These were things Bao-yu carried in his heart, and we must not presume to guess too freely at them. Dai-yu, seeing him in this state, knew that he had fallen under some new spell somewhere, but could hardly question him closely.
‘I’ve just heard from Aunt Wang that tomorrow is Aunt Xue’s birthday,’ she said. ‘She asked me to find out, if I came this way, whether you’re going. Send someone to the front to let her know.’

‘I didn’t even go to Uncle She’s birthday last time. If I go to this one, what if I meet someone? I’m not going to any of them. It’s so hot, and there would be all that dressing up. Aunt Xue won’t necessarily be offended if I don’t go.’

‘What a thing to say!’ Aroma put in quickly. ‘It isn’t the same as your elder uncle. She lives so close, and she’s your aunt. If you don’t go, won’t she start wondering? If you’re afraid of the heat, go first thing in the morning, kowtow to her, have a cup of tea and come back. Wouldn’t that be the proper thing?’

segments.text: Before Bao-yu could answer, Dai-yu smiled. ‘You ought to go, if only for the sake of someone who chases mosquitoes away for you.’
Bao-yu did not understand. ‘What do you mean, chases mosquitoes?’
Aroma told him how, while he was asleep the day before with no one to sit beside him, Miss Bao had stayed for a little while.
‘That was wrong of me,’ Bao-yu said at once. ‘How could I lie there asleep? It was disrespectful to her.’ Then he added, ‘I shall certainly go tomorrow.’

segments.text: Presently Bao-chai hurried over, and parting became harder than ever. Bao-chai, though, understood that if Xiang-yun’s servants reported this to her aunt, she might suffer for it when she got home, so she urged her to go. They all saw her to the inner gate. A moment later she turned and called him close, then whispered, ‘Even if the old lady forgets about me, you must keep reminding her to send for me.’

segments.text: That year Jia Zheng was again appointed to a provincial educational commission, and chose the twentieth of the eighth month for his departure. On that day he paid his respects at the ancestral shrine and took leave of Grandmother Jia before setting out. Bao-yu and the other young men of the family accompanied him as far as the Pavilion of Parting Tears. Once Jia Zheng had left, there was much outside the household that we cannot record. We shall speak only of Bao-yu, wandering through the garden day after day as the whim took him, truly wasting his time and adding empty days to his years. One day, when he was at a loose end, Ebony came in with a sheet of floral notepaper for him.
‘Of course! I’d forgotten,’ Bao-yu said. ‘I was just saying I must go and see Third Sister, and here you are. Is she any better?’
‘She’s quite well now,’ said Ebony. ‘She isn’t taking medicine today. It was only a slight chill.’
Bao-yu unfolded the paper and read:

segments.text: The other evening, when the rain had newly cleared and the moonlight shone as though washed clean, I could not bear to go to bed and lose so rare a prospect. Though the water-clock had marked the third watch, I still lingered by the paulownia railings. Unprepared for the assault of wind and dew, I fell ill, unfit even to gather firewood. Yesterday you honoured me with a visit and affectionate counsel, then sent your maid repeatedly to inquire after me, besides bestowing fresh lychees and a specimen of Zhen-qing’s calligraphy. How deep your sympathy, how generous your care!

Now, in the quiet hours spent leaning at my desk or resting on my bed, I have been thinking of the men of former times. Even amid the assaults and rivalries of fame and profit, they would set aside a little plot of hills and water, summon friends from afar and welcome those nearby, throw away their carriage-pins or cling to their shafts to detain them, intent on gathering two or three kindred spirits there. They would raise a platform for letters or found a society of poets. What began in a passing impulse became a delightful story for all time.

Though your sister has no talent, I too am fortunate enough to dwell among rocks and springs, and I admire the accomplishments of Xue and Lin. It is a pity that these wind-swept courts and moonlit pavilions have yet to entertain a gathering of poets. With apricot blossom before our curtains and peach blossom beside the stream, perhaps we too might send the wine-cup flying as we sing. Who says that the great talents of the Lotus Society must be confined to bearded men? Let the elegant gatherings of East Mountain yield a place to us who wear rouge and powder. If you will come rowing through the snow, your sister will sweep the fallen flowers to receive you. Respectfully submitted.

segments.text: Ever since Heaven bestowed upon me the favour of being received as your son, I have thought day and night of some way to show my filial devotion, yet have found no opportunity. While buying flowers and plants recently, thanks to the good fortune you confer upon me, I became acquainted with many gardeners and came to know many celebrated gardens. By chance I saw a rare variety of white begonia. I tried every means, but could obtain only two pots. If you regard me as your own son, pray keep them for your enjoyment. The weather being hot, I fear that a visit might inconvenience the young ladies in the garden, and so I dare not present myself. I respectfully send this letter and bow to wish you well.

segments.text: Bao-yu smiled when he had read it.
‘Has he come alone? Is anyone with him?’
‘There are two pots of flowers as well,’ the woman replied.
‘Go out and say I’ve read his note. It was thoughtful of him to remember me. Just have the flowers brought to my rooms.’
He went on with Ebony to Autumn Studio, where Bao-chai, Dai-yu, Ying-chun and Xi-chun were already gathered.
‘Here’s another!’ they all said, smiling as he entered.

‘At least I’m not entirely commonplace,’ Tan-chun said with a laugh. ‘The idea happened to occur to me, so I wrote a few notes to see what would happen. Who would have thought a single summons would bring everyone?’
‘It’s a pity we’ve left it so late,’ Bao-yu said. ‘We ought to have had a society long ago.’
‘Form as many societies as you please,’ said Dai-yu, ‘but don’t count me in. I wouldn’t dare.’
‘If you wouldn’t dare, who would?’ Ying-chun laughed.
‘This is a serious undertaking,’ Bao-yu said. ‘We must all put our hearts into it, instead of each insisting on giving way to the next.

segments.text: Whatever ideas you have, say them, and we’ll discuss them together. Cousin Bao-chai, you suggest something. Cousin Dai-yu, let’s hear from you too.’
‘What’s the hurry?’ said Bao-chai. ‘We aren’t all here yet.’
Before she had finished, Li Wan came in, smiling.

‘How elegant! If you’re founding a poetry society, I nominate myself to preside. I had the very same idea back in the spring, but then I thought: I can’t write poetry, so why should I meddle? I forgot about it and never said anything. Since Third Sister is so keen, I’ll help her set it going.’

‘If we really are to have a poetry society,’ Dai-yu said, ‘we’re all venerable poets now. We must first get rid of these “sister” and “brother-in-law” and “sister-in-law” names. They’re far too commonplace.’

‘Exactly,’ said Li Wan. ‘Why don’t we each choose a literary name? It would be much more elegant to address one another that way. I’ve decided on the Old Farmer of Sweet-rice Village. No one else may have it.’
‘I’ll be the Recluse of Autumn Studio,’ Tan-chun said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘Recluse, master of this or that: they aren’t really suitable, and they’re cumbersome,’ Bao-yu said. ‘There are plenty of paulownias and plantains here. Why not name yourself after one of those?’
‘I have it!’ Tan-chun laughed. ‘I’m fondest of the plantains. I’ll call myself the Guest beneath the Plantain.’
Everyone found this pleasingly original.
‘Quick, take her away and stew her flesh to eat with our wine,’ Dai-yu said with a laugh.
No one understood.
‘There’s an old story of “a deer covered with plantain leaves”,’ she explained. ‘If she calls herself the Guest beneath the Plantain, isn’t she a deer? Hurry up and make us some dried venison.’
They all burst out laughing.
‘Don’t be so quick with your clever insults,’ Tan-chun laughed back. ‘I’ve already thought of a lovely name that suits you perfectly.’
She turned to the others.

‘In ancient times E-huang and Nü-ying wept on the bamboos and stained them with their tears. That’s why the spotted kind is also called the bamboo of the Xiang Princesses. Now she lives at Naiad’s House, and she’s so fond of crying that, one day, when she’s pining for our brother-in-law Lin, all her bamboos will be spotted too.

segments.text: From now on we need only call her the Naiad.’
They all clapped and applauded the name. Lin Dai-yu lowered her head and said nothing.
‘I thought of a good one for our eldest Miss Xue long ago,’ Li Wan said, smiling. ‘It has just three characters too.’
Xi-chun and Ying-chun both asked what it was.
‘I’m conferring on her the title of Lady of Allspice. What do you think?’
‘An excellent title,’ said Tan-chun with a laugh.
‘What about me?’ asked Bao-yu. ‘You must think of one for me too.’
‘You have one already,’ Bao-chai said, smiling. ‘Busy over Nothing. Those three characters suit you perfectly.’
‘You can keep your old name, King of Flowers of the Crimson Grotto,’ said Li Wan.

segments.text: Bao-yu laughed.
‘That was something I did when I was little. Why bring it up now?’
‘You have more than enough names,’ said Tan-chun. ‘Why do you need another? Whatever we choose to call you, just answer to it.’

‘I’d better give you one after all,’ Bao-chai said. ‘It’s the most commonplace name imaginable, but it suits you very well. Wealth and honour are hard enough to come by, and so is leisure. You can hardly ever have both, yet you’ve managed it. We might as well call you the Gentleman of Wealth and Leisure.’
‘I’m not worthy of it, not worthy of it,’ Bao-yu laughed. ‘Call me whatever you like.’
‘What names shall we give Second Sister and Fourth Sister?’ Li Wan asked.
‘We can hardly write poetry,’ said Ying-chun. ‘What would we want names for?’
‘Even so, you ought to have them,’ said Tan-chun.
‘She lives at Amaryllis Eyot, so let her be Amaryllis,’ Bao-chai said. ‘Fourth Sister is at Lotus Pavilion. We can simply call her Lotus Pavilion.’

segments.text: ‘That will do very well,’ said Li Wan. ‘But I am the eldest here, so you must all do as I suggest. I guarantee you’ll like it. There are seven of us founding this society, and Second Sister, Fourth Sister and I can’t write poetry. You must excuse the three of us and give us each some other duty.’
‘We’ve chosen names, and you’re still calling us the old ones!’ Tan-chun laughed. ‘We might as well never have bothered. We ought to make a rule fining anyone who gets it wrong.’

‘Let’s establish the society before we settle the fines,’ said Li Wan. ‘I have plenty of room. We’ll meet at my place. Though I can’t write poetry, if all these poets will tolerate an unlettered visitor, I’ll be your hostess, and some of their elegance will rub off on me.

segments.text: If you elect me president, I naturally can’t manage by myself. I shall need two vice-presidents, and will invite the two learned scholars Amaryllis and Lotus Pavilion: one to set the subjects and rhymes, the other to make fair copies and oversee the proceedings. Nor must it be an absolute rule that the three of us never write anything. If the subject and rhymes happen to be easy, we can each try a poem. But you four must be obliged to write. On those terms we can begin. If you won’t agree, I wouldn’t dare to follow in such illustrious company.’

Ying-chun and Xi-chun were not naturally inclined to poetry, and with Bao-chai and Dai-yu there to outshine them, this proposal suited them perfectly. Both declared it excellent. Tan-chun and the others understood their feelings, and, seeing how pleased they were, could scarcely press them. They had to agree.
‘Very well, then,’ Tan-chun said with a laugh. ‘But I can’t help finding it funny. Here I’ve thought of this perfectly good idea, only to put the three of you in charge of me!’
‘In that case, let’s go to Sweet-rice Village,’ Bao-yu said.
‘Always in a hurry,’ said Li Wan. ‘Today we’re only discussing it. Wait till I invite you.’
‘We ought to decide how often to meet,’ Bao-chai said.
‘Too often, and it would stop being fun,’ said Tan-chun.

segments.text: ‘Two or three times a month would be enough.’
Bao-chai nodded.

‘Twice a month will do. We should fix the dates and meet whatever the weather. Besides those two days, if anyone feels inspired to hold an extra meeting, we can go to their place or they can bring it here. That would give us plenty of freedom and make it more enjoyable.’
Everyone thought this an even better suggestion.

segments.text: ‘Only, since the idea was mine,’ said Tan-chun, ‘I must be hostess the first time. Otherwise all my enthusiasm will have come to nothing.’
‘Then why not hold the first meeting tomorrow?’ Li Wan asked.
‘Today is better than tomorrow. This very moment will do perfectly. You set the subject, Amaryllis can choose the rhymes, and Lotus Pavilion can supervise.’
‘If you ask me,’ said Ying-chun, ‘we needn’t leave the subject and rhymes to any one person. Drawing lots would be fairer.’
‘As I was coming over,’ Li Wan said, ‘I saw them carrying in two pots of white begonias. They were lovely flowers. Why not write about those?’

segments.text: ‘We haven’t even admired them yet, and we’re to write poems already?’ said Ying-chun.

‘They’re only white begonias,’ said Bao-chai. ‘Why must we see them before we write? The poems and rhyme-prose of the ancients were simply ways of giving expression to their thoughts and feelings. If they had all waited to see things for themselves, we wouldn’t have so many poems now.’
‘In that case, let me choose the rhymes,’ said Ying-chun.

She went to the bookcase, took down a volume of poetry and opened it at random. The poem she found happened to be a regulated poem of eight seven-character lines. She passed it to the others to see: they would all have to write in that form. Closing the book, she said to a little maid:
‘Say any word that comes into your head.’
The girl was leaning against the door and said, ‘Door.’
‘Then it will be mén, “door”,’ Ying-chun laughed. ‘The thirteenth rhyme group, yuan. And the first rhyme-word must be mén.’

She called for the box of rhyme-tokens, pulled out the drawer for the thirteenth group and told the same little maid to pick four tokens at random. The girl took out pén, “pot”; hún, “soul”; hén, “trace”; and hūn, “dusk”.

segments.text: ‘Pot and door will be rather difficult,’ Bao-yu said.

Scribe laid out four identical sets of paper and brushes, and they all fell silent to think. Dai-yu alone stroked the paulownia, gazed at the autumn scene, or laughed and joked with the maids. Ying-chun told a maid to light a stick of Sweet-dream incense. These sticks were only about three cun long and as thin as a rush wick; they burnt quickly and so provided the time limit. Anyone who had not finished when the incense burnt out would be fined.
Tan-chun was the first to have her poem ready. She wrote it down herself, made some alterations, and handed it to Ying-chun.
‘Have you got yours, Lady of Allspice?’ she asked Bao-chai.
‘I have, but it isn’t good.’
Bao-yu paced up and down the covered walk with his hands behind his back.
‘Listen, they’ve both finished,’ he said to Dai-yu.
‘Never mind me.’
Seeing that Bao-chai had already made her fair copy, Bao-yu cried:
‘This is terrible! There’s only one cun of incense left, and I’ve only got four lines.’

segments.text: He turned to Dai-yu again.
‘The incense is almost finished. Why do you keep crouching on that damp ground?’
She paid him no attention.
‘I can’t worry about you now,’ he said. ‘Good or bad, I’d better write mine out.’
He went to the table and began.

segments.text: ‘The Young Master of Green Delights comes last,’ said Li Wan. ‘Do you accept that?’
‘Mine wasn’t good to begin with,’ Bao-yu answered. ‘It’s the fairest possible judgement.’
Then he smiled.
‘Only, Allspice’s and the Naiad’s might bear a little more consideration.’
‘You asked me to judge, and it’s no business of yours,’ said Li Wan. ‘One more word from anyone, and there’ll be a fine.’
Bao-yu had to give in.

‘From now on,’ Li Wan continued, ‘I fix the second and sixteenth of every month as our meeting days. The subjects and rhymes will be for me to decide. In between, if you feel like it, choose other days and hold extra meetings. I won’t interfere, even if you meet every day of the month.

segments.text: Only, on the second and sixteenth you must come to me.’
‘But we must give the society a name,’ Bao-yu said.

‘A commonplace one won’t do,’ said Tan-chun, ‘and neither will something so original that it’s odd and far-fetched. Since we happen to have begun with poems on begonias, let’s call it the Begonia Society. It may be commonplace, but as there really was such an occasion, that needn’t matter.’
They discussed it a little longer, took some wine and fruit, then dispersed, some to their own rooms, others to see Grandmother Jia or Lady Wang. We have nothing further to relate of them just now.

Aroma had seen Bao-yu hurry off with Ebony after reading the note, without knowing what it was about. Later she saw the women from the rear gate bring in two pots of begonias. She asked where they came from, and the old woman told her what had happened with Bao-yu. Aroma had the pots set in place and invited the women to sit in the servants’ room. She went to her own room, weighed out six qian of silver and wrapped it up. Then she brought this, together with three hundred cash, to the two women.
‘The silver is for the lads who carried the flowers. Buy yourselves some wine with the cash.’

segments.text: The women got up, beaming, with a thousand thanks and protests that they could not possibly take it. Only when Aroma insisted and refused to take it back did they accept.
‘Are there any lads on duty outside the back gate?’ Aroma asked.
‘There are four every day,’ they hastened to reply, ‘kept there to run errands for the inner rooms. What would you like done, miss? We’ll tell them.’

‘What errand would I have?’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘Master Bao wants to send someone to the young marquis’s house today with some things for Miss Shi. Since you happen to be here, tell the lads at the back gate to hire a carriage as you go out. Come here for the money afterwards. Don’t let them go blundering about at the front.’
The women agreed and went off.

segments.text: They looked at one another, but none could remember. After a while Skybright laughed.
‘It went to Miss Tan-chun with the lychees. It hasn’t come back yet.’
‘We have plenty of ordinary dishes for sending things,’ said Aroma. ‘Why did it have to be that one?’

‘I said exactly the same thing,’ Skybright answered. ‘He said the fresh lychees would look prettier on it. When I took them over, Miss Tan-chun thought so too, and asked us to leave the dish with them. That’s why I didn’t bring it back. Look, those two “linked-pearl” vases from the very top shelf haven’t come back either.’

‘Talking of the vases reminds me of something funny,’ Ripple said, laughing. ‘When Master Bao has a fit of filial devotion, he gives twice the proper measure. The other day he saw the osmanthus in the garden and cut two sprays, meaning to put them in a vase for himself. Then it suddenly struck him that these were fresh flowers, just opened in our own garden, and he couldn’t presume to enjoy them first. He insisted on taking that pair of vases down, filled them with water and arranged the flowers himself, then had someone carry them while he went in person to present one to Her Old Ladyship and one to Her Ladyship.

segments.text: His fit of filial devotion brought good fortune even to the person who went with him. It happened to be my turn to carry them that day. Her Old Ladyship was so delighted she didn’t know what to do. She told everyone she saw, “It’s Bao-yu who really thinks of me. He remembers me even over a spray of flowers. And people complain that I’m too fond of him!” You know she hardly ever speaks to me ordinarily. I don’t seem to take her fancy. But that day she actually told someone to give me a few hundred cash. She said I was a poor little thing, so slight and delicate. A piece of good fortune I’d never have dreamt of! A few hundred cash is nothing; being singled out like that is another matter. When we got to Her Ladyship’s, she was going through her boxes with Mrs Lian, Aunt Zhao, Aunt Zhou and quite a number of others. They were looking for the brightly coloured clothes she used to wear when she was young. I didn’t know who they were for.

segments.text: As soon as she saw the flowers, she stopped looking for clothes and came to admire them. And with Mrs Lian there to join in, praising Master Bao’s devotion and how well he knew what was proper, there were two cartloads of compliments, true or not. Before all those people, Her Ladyship felt it reflected credit on her and silenced every critic. She was more pleased than ever, and gave me two of the garments that were ready to hand. The clothes themselves were nothing: we get clothes every year anyway. But it isn’t every day you get such a lucky chance.’
‘Pah! You little fool, you’ve never seen anything!’ Skybright said with a laugh. ‘The best were given to someone else. You only got the leftovers, and you think it was an honour!’
‘Whoever the good ones went to, it was still a kindness from Her Ladyship,’ said Ripple.

‘I wouldn’t have taken them,’ Skybright said. ‘If they’d been left over from someone elsewhere, well and good. But when we all belong to this room, is one of us any better than another? Give her the good ones and me the leavings? I’d rather have nothing. Even if I offended Her Ladyship, I wouldn’t swallow an insult like that.’
‘Who here got them?’ Ripple asked quickly.

segments.text: ‘I was ill for a few days and went home, so I don’t know. Be a good sister and tell me.’
‘If I told you, would you take yours back to Her Ladyship now?’ Skybright asked.
‘Don’t be silly,’ Ripple laughed. ‘I only want to hear, for the fun of it. Even if they were left over from a dog in this room, I’d be grateful to Her Ladyship. The rest is no concern of mine.’
The others all laughed.
‘What a neat way of abusing her! They did go to that spotted foreign lapdog.’
‘You foul-mouthed creatures,’ Aroma said, laughing. ‘The moment you have nothing to do, you make me the butt of your jokes. Heaven knows what deaths you’ll all die!’
‘So it was you, Sister!’ said Ripple. ‘I truly didn’t know. Let me beg your pardon.’
‘Stop your nonsense,’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘What matters is that one of you should fetch the dish.’
‘We ought to fetch the vases when there’s a moment, too,’ said Musk. ‘The one at Her Old Ladyship’s is all right, but there are too many people handling things in Her Ladyship’s rooms.

segments.text: The others might leave it alone, but if Aunt Zhao’s lot see something from here, they’ll never rest till they’ve spitefully damaged it. Her Ladyship doesn’t pay much attention to such things. Better bring it back soon.’
Skybright threw down her needlework.
‘You’re right about that. I’ll go and fetch it.’
‘Let me get it,’ said Ripple. ‘You go for your dish.’
‘No, I insist on going,’ Skybright laughed. ‘You’ve had all the lucky chances. Can’t I have one for once?’
‘All that’s happened is that Ripple got some clothes once,’ Musk said with a laugh. ‘Why should they happen to be sorting clothes again today, just when you turn up?’
Skybright gave a cold laugh.
‘Even if I don’t find them sorting clothes, Her Ladyship may notice how conscientious I am and spare two taels a month for me out of her allowance. Who knows?’
Then she laughed again.
‘Don’t play your little tricks with me. There’s nothing I don’t know about.’
And out she ran.

segments.text: Ripple went out with her and made her own way to Tan-chun’s, where she collected the dish. Aroma had the gifts ready. She called an elderly woman who served in their quarters, old Nurse Song.
‘Go and wash and comb your hair properly, then come back in your outdoor clothes. I’m sending you to Miss Shi with some things.’
‘Just give them to me and tell me what to say, miss,’ the old woman replied. ‘Then I can get ready and go straight off.’

Aroma brought over two small filigree boxes. She opened the first, which held two kinds of fresh produce, red water-caltrops and gorgon fruit. In the other was a dish of cakes made from the new chestnut flour and steamed with osmanthus sugar. She went on:

‘Say: “These are all from this year’s crop in our own garden. Master Bao sends them for you to try. The other day you admired this agate dish, so please keep it for your enjoyment. In the silk bundle is the needlework you asked me to do last time. Please excuse its roughness and make do with it.”

segments.text: Give her our respects and Master Bao’s good wishes. That’s all.’
‘Might Master Bao have anything else to say?’ Nurse Song asked. ‘You’d better ask him, miss, or we may find we’ve forgotten something afterwards.’
‘Did you see him at Miss Tan-chun’s just now?’ Aroma asked Ripple.
‘They’re all there talking about founding some poetry society, and writing poems,’ Ripple answered. ‘I don’t suppose he has any message. You can go.’
The old woman took the things out and went to change. Aroma reminded her:
‘Go by the back gate. There’ll be a lad and a carriage waiting.’
Nurse Song left, and we need say no more of her for the moment.

segments.text: When Bao-yu returned, he first hurried to admire the begonias, then went into his room and told Aroma about the poetry society. Aroma in turn told him that she had sent Nurse Song to Shi Xiang-yun with the gifts. Bao-yu clapped his hands.
‘We forgot her! I knew there was something on my mind, but I couldn’t think what. Thank goodness you reminded me. I must invite her. What pleasure would there be in a poetry society without her?’

‘It isn’t anything urgent, only an amusement,’ Aroma urged. ‘She hasn’t your freedom, and she can’t decide things for herself at home. If you tell her, she’ll want to come and may not be allowed. If she can’t, she’ll keep fretting about it. You’ll only make her unhappy for nothing.’
‘That doesn’t matter,’ said Bao-yu. ‘I’ll ask Grandmother to send for her.’
As they were speaking, Nurse Song returned. She delivered Xiang-yun’s thanks and her message to Aroma for all the trouble she had taken, then added:
‘She asked what Master Bao was doing. I said you and the young ladies were founding some poetry society and writing poems.

segments.text: Early next morning he went back to Grandmother Jia’s to urge her to send for Xiang-yun. It was not until the afternoon that she arrived, and only then did he feel at ease. As soon as they met he told her the whole story and was about to show her the poems, but Li Wan and the others stopped him.

‘Don’t show her the poems yet. Tell her the rhymes first. Since she’s late, her first penalty must be to write a poem matching them. If it’s good, we’ll admit her to the society. If it isn’t, she must pay a further penalty by entertaining us before we consider it.’

‘You forgot to invite me,’ said Shi Xiang-yun. ‘I ought to be fining you! Give me the rhymes. I may have no talent, but I shall have to do my best and make a fool of myself. If you’ll let me join, I’ll even sweep the floor and burn the incense.’

Her good humour delighted them more than ever. They all wondered reproachfully how they could have forgotten her the day before, and hurried to tell her the rhymes. Xiang-yun was too eager to pause over polishing and revising. She went on talking to everyone, but in her mind the answering poems were already complete. She wrote them out with whatever brush and paper came to hand, then said with a smile:
‘I’ve written two to match your rhymes. I don’t know whether they’re good or bad. I’ve only done as I was told.’
She handed them over.

segments.text: They marvelled as they read, praising each successive line.
‘Now those really do begonia poems justice,’ they all said. ‘We truly deserve to have a Begonia Society.’
‘Will you fine me by making me hostess tomorrow?’ Shi Xiang-yun asked. ‘May I be the first to invite an extra meeting?’
‘Better still!’ they replied.

They then showed her the previous day’s poems and discussed them together. In the evening Bao-chai invited Xiang-yun to spend the night at Allspice Court. By lamplight Xiang-yun planned how to entertain the society and choose its themes.

segments.text: Bao-chai listened to her for a long time, but none of her plans would do.

‘If you call a meeting, you have to be the hostess,’ she told her. ‘It may only be an amusement, but you must think it through. It has to be manageable for you and give no offence to anyone, or there’ll be no pleasure in it. You can’t decide things for yourself at home. You only have those few strings of cash each month, and they scarcely cover your own expenses. If you start spending on something as unnecessary as this and your aunt hears of it, she’ll have still more to complain of. Besides, even if you spent it all, it wouldn’t pay for entertaining us.

segments.text: You can hardly go home and ask for more on that account. Or were you going to ask for money here?’
At these words Xiang-yun saw the difficulty and began to hesitate.

‘I’ve already thought of a way,’ Bao-chai went on. ‘There’s a man at our pawnshop whose family’s fields produce exceptionally fine, fat crabs. He sent us several catties the other day. More than half the people here, from Grandmother down to those in the garden, are fond of crabs. Aunt was saying just the other day that she meant to invite Grandmother into the garden to admire the osmanthus and eat crabs, but she’s had other things to do and hasn’t invited her yet. For now, say nothing about the poetry society. Simply invite everyone. When they’ve gone, we can write as much poetry as we please. I’ll speak to my brother and ask for several baskets of the biggest, fattest crabs, fetch a few jars of good wine from the shop, and provide dishes of fruit for four or five tables. That would save trouble and make a lively party for everyone.’
Xiang-yun was deeply grateful and impressed. She warmly praised Bao-chai for thinking of everything.

segments.text: ‘I’m speaking entirely for your sake,’ Bao-chai added with a smile. ‘You mustn’t take offence and think I’m looking down on you, or all our affection will have been wasted. If you won’t take it amiss, I can tell them to make the arrangements.’

‘Dear cousin, now you’re the one taking things the wrong way!’ Xiang-yun laughed. ‘However foolish I may be, I’d scarcely be human if I couldn’t tell kindness from unkindness. If I didn’t look on you as my own elder sister, I wouldn’t have told you all those private troubles at home last time.’
Bao-chai called an old woman servant.
‘Go out and tell my brother to send several baskets of big crabs like the ones we had the other day. We’re inviting Her Old Ladyship and my aunt to admire the osmanthus tomorrow after the meal.

segments.text: Tell him he must be sure not to forget. I’ve already given the invitations today.’
The old woman went out to deliver the message and returned. There is nothing further to say of her.
Bao-chai turned again to Xiang-yun.

‘The themes shouldn’t be too ingeniously novel, either. Think of those odd, far-fetched subjects in the old poets, and those impossibly difficult rhymes. If the subject is over-elaborate and the rhymes too hard, there can never be a good poem. It only shows a petty spirit. Certainly poetry must avoid hackneyed phrases, but it mustn’t strain too hard after the unfamiliar. The first thing is a fresh conception; the words will then be fresh of themselves. After all, none of this amounts to very much. Spinning and needlework are our proper occupations. In an idle moment, reading a few chapters of something truly useful to us would be a better way to spend our time.’
Xiang-yun merely assented. Then she smiled.
‘I was thinking: yesterday they wrote about begonias. What if we write about chrysanthemums now?’
‘Chrysanthemums suit the season,’ said Bao-chai, ‘but so many people have written about them already.’
‘That’s what I thought. I’m afraid of being trite.’
Bao-chai considered.

‘I have it. Let the chrysanthemums be the guests and the human beings the hosts. We’ll devise several titles, each of two characters: one for the thing itself and one of broader application. The concrete word will be ju, “chrysanthemum”; the other we’ll take from the general-purpose category.

segments.text: That way we shall both celebrate the chrysanthemum and describe what people do. No one has done it before, so we can’t be trite. Each subject will embrace both scene and object, and be fresh without being petty.’
‘That’s very good,’ said Xiang-yun, smiling. ‘But what sort of broader words should we use? Think of one to show me.’
Bao-chai thought for a moment and smiled.
‘Chrysanthemum Dreams would do.’
‘How good!’ Xiang-yun laughed. ‘I have one too. Would Chrysanthemum Shadows do?’
‘Well enough, though people have written that one before. If we have a number of subjects, it can go in among them. I’ve thought of another.’
‘Tell me quickly.’
‘What about Questioning Chrysanthemums?’
Xiang-yun slapped the table in delight.
‘I’ve got another too. What about Seeking Chrysanthemums?’
Bao-chai found that interesting as well.
‘We might as well think of ten. Let’s write them down and go on.’
They ground ink and dipped a brush. Xiang-yun wrote while Bao-chai dictated, and before long they had made up ten.

‘Ten don’t quite make a set. Let’s make it twelve and have it complete, like an album of paintings and calligraphy.’

segments.text: ‘Now that we’ve gone this far,’ she said, ‘we might as well put them in order.’
‘Better still,’ said Xiang-yun. ‘We shall have a whole chrysanthemum album.’

‘First comes Remembering Chrysanthemums,’ Bao-chai began. ‘Since remembering them doesn’t bring them to us, we seek them: Seeking Chrysanthemums comes second. Once found, they are planted: Planting Chrysanthemums is third. When they flower abundantly, we sit before them and admire them: Facing Chrysanthemums is fourth. Still not content with sitting before them, we cut some and set them in a vase to enjoy: Chrysanthemums in a Vase comes fifth. But with the flowers in their vase and no poem about them, even they seem to lack colour. So the sixth is Singing of Chrysanthemums. Once they have entered verse, we must let brush and ink do their part as well: Painting Chrysanthemums is seventh. After all this busy devotion, we still don’t know exactly what is so wonderful about them, and cannot help asking: Questioning Chrysanthemums is eighth. If the chrysanthemums could answer, we should be beside ourselves with delight: Wearing Chrysanthemums is ninth. That exhausts what people do, but not what we can write about the flowers. Chrysanthemum Shadows and Chrysanthemum Dreams follow as the tenth and eleventh. The last leaf will be Fading Chrysanthemums, gathering up all the splendour of the earlier themes.

segments.text: There we have the lovely sights and occupations of all three autumn months.’
Xiang-yun copied the subjects in the order Bao-chai had given, read them through once more, and asked:
‘What rhymes shall we prescribe?’

‘I’ve never liked prescribing rhymes,’ Bao-chai replied. ‘If there’s a good poem to be written, why bind it hand and foot with a rhyme? Let’s not copy that petty school. We’ll set the subjects and leave the rhymes free. The whole point is to enjoy the good lines that may occur to us, not to make things difficult for anyone.’
‘Quite right,’ said Xiang-yun. ‘Everyone’s poetry will be the better for it. But there are only five of us. Surely we aren’t each to write twelve poems on these twelve subjects?’
‘That would be asking far too much,’ Bao-chai said.

segments.text: ‘Make a fair copy of the titles and put them on the wall tomorrow. All the poems must be regulated verse of eight seven-character lines. Once they’ve seen the list, everyone can choose whichever subject they like. Anyone who feels equal to all twelve may write them all; anyone who can’t manage even one needn’t write one. Let talent and speed take the honours. Once all twelve subjects have been covered, no one may come along afterwards with another poem. We’ll simply fine the latecomer.’
‘That will do,’ said Xiang-yun.
With their plans settled, the two put out the lamp and went to bed. To learn what happened, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: Bao-chai and Xiang-yun had settled their plans; nothing more need be said of that night. Next day Xiang-yun invited Grandmother Jia and the others to admire the osmanthus.
‘She is so keen,’ they all said, ‘we must let her entertain us.’
At noon Grandmother Jia duly came into the garden with Lady Wang and Xi-feng, having invited Aunt Xue and the others to join them.
‘Where shall we go?’ she asked.
‘Wherever you would like, Mother,’ said Lady Wang.

‘Everything is laid out at Lotus Pavilion,’ said Xi-feng. ‘The two osmanthus trees below the slope are flowering beautifully, and the water is so clear and green. Sitting in the pavilion out over the water, we shall have an open view all round. Even looking at the water will freshen our eyes.’

segments.text: ‘Quite right,’ said Grandmother Jia, and led them towards Lotus Pavilion.

The pavilion stood in the pool, with windows on all four sides. Winding covered walks to left and right crossed the water to the banks, and a zigzag bamboo bridge made a secluded approach from behind. As they stepped on to this bridge, Xi-feng hurried forward to support Grandmother Jia.
‘Step out boldly, Grannie. There’s nothing to worry about. Bamboo bridges always creak and crack like this.’

Once inside, they saw two bamboo tables set beyond the balustrade. One held cups, chopsticks and the wine service; on the other were a tea whisk, tea bowls and all the other tea things. Two or three maids were fanning a little stove to boil the tea, while several others tended another stove for warming the wine.
‘How thoughtful, to have arranged for tea,’ Grandmother Jia said delightedly. ‘And both the place and all the things are so clean.’
‘Cousin Bao-chai helped me get them ready,’ Xiang-yun said with a smile.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia looked up at the nameboard, then turned to Aunt Xue.

‘When I was little, we had a pavilion just like this at home. It was called Rosy-cloud Pavilion, or something of the sort. I was about their age then, and my sisters and I used to go there to play every day. Once I lost my footing and fell in. I very nearly drowned. They got me out at last, but I struck my head on a wooden peg and cut it open. That hollow at my temple, about the size of a fingertip, is where it was injured. Everyone was afraid of my having been in the water, and afraid I might have caught a chill as well. They all said I wouldn’t live. But here I am.’
Before anyone else could speak, Xi-feng put in, laughing, ‘If you hadn’t lived, who would be enjoying all these blessings now?

segments.text: ‘That only shows what a store of long life and good fortune you had from the very beginning, Grannie. The spirits arranged for that hollow to be knocked into your head to hold it all. The God of Longevity had a hollow in his forehead to begin with too. It was only after he had filled it with ten thousand blessings and ten thousand years of life that it bulged out into a bump.’
Before she had finished, Grandmother Jia and the others were helpless with laughter.
‘You monkey! You’re spoilt beyond bearing,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Now you’ve taken to making fun of me. I could tear that glib mouth of yours!’
‘I was afraid the crabs might leave you with a chill inside,’ said Xi-feng. ‘I thought I’d make you laugh and cheer you up. When you’re in good spirits, another crab or two won’t hurt you.’
‘Then you shall stay with me day and night from now on,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘I shall have a good laugh often and keep my spirits up. You shan’t go home.’
‘It’s because you’re so fond of her that she’s grown so spoilt,’ Lady Wang said, smiling. ‘Say that, and tomorrow she’ll be more disrespectful than ever.’
‘I like her as she is,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Besides, she’s not a child who doesn’t know where to draw the line.

segments.text: ‘When we’re at home with no outsiders, this is how the women of a family ought to be together. So long as she observes the proper courtesies, that is enough. Why make her stand about like an attendant to a god?’

They went on into the pavilion. Tea was served, and Xi-feng busied herself arranging tables and calling for cups and chopsticks. At the table in the place of honour sat Grandmother Jia, Aunt Xue, Bao-chai, Dai-yu and Bao-yu. Xiang-yun, Lady Wang, Ying-chun, Tan-chun and Xi-chun sat at the table on the east. The table by the door to the west was for Li Wan and Xi-feng, but their seats were left empty. Neither ventured to sit; they attended to Grandmother Jia’s and Lady Wang’s tables instead.
‘Don’t bring too many crabs at once,’ Xi-feng instructed. ‘Keep them in the steamer. Bring ten, and when we’ve eaten those, bring some more.’
She called for water, washed her hands, and stood beside Grandmother Jia to pick out crab meat. The first portion she offered to Aunt Xue.
‘I enjoy it more when I break them open myself,’ Aunt Xue said. ‘You needn’t serve me.’

segments.text: Xi-feng gave it to Grandmother Jia instead. Her second portion went to Bao-yu.
‘Bring the wine good and hot,’ she said, and sent the little maids for mung-bean meal scented with chrysanthemum leaves and osmanthus flowers, to have ready for washing their hands.

After eating one crab with the company, Xiang-yun left her seat to see to her guests. She went outside and told the servants to take a plateful each to Aunt Zhao and Aunt Zhou. Xi-feng came over to her.
‘You’re not used to looking after a party. Go and eat. I’ll see to things for you now, and have mine when everyone has gone.’
Xiang-yun would not agree. She ordered two more tables to be set in the covered walk and invited Faithful, Amber, Cai-xia, Cai-yun and Patience to sit down there.
‘If you’re staying here to wait on them, Mrs Lian,’ Faithful said to Xi-feng with a smile, ‘we shall go and eat.’
‘Go along, all of you. Leave everything to me.’

Xiang-yun returned to her seat. Xi-feng and Li Wan also ate a little for form’s sake, but Xi-feng was soon up and busy again. Presently she came out into the covered walk. Faithful and the others, who were thoroughly enjoying their meal, rose when they saw her.
‘What have you come out again for, ma’am?

segments.text: ‘Do let us enjoy ourselves for a moment.’
‘You little baggage, Faithful! You get worse and worse,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘Here I am doing your work for you, and instead of being grateful, you complain. Pour me a cup of wine at once.’
Faithful laughed and filled a cup, holding it to Xi-feng’s lips. Xi-feng tipped back her head and drank it. Patience had already picked a shellful of roe for her.
‘Plenty of ginger and vinegar,’ said Xi-feng.
She ate it, then smiled at them. ‘Sit down and eat, all of you. I’m going now.’
‘What a cheek, coming to eat our food!’ said Faithful.
‘Don’t you play your tricks on me. Do you know your Master Lian has taken a fancy to you? He means to ask Grandmother for you as his little second wife.’
‘Pah! What a thing for a mistress to say! If I don’t smear these fishy hands all over your face, my name’s not Faithful.’
She ran at her with her hands out.
‘Dear Faithful, let me off just this once,’ Xi-feng pleaded.
‘If Faithful did go to him, would Patience let her off?’ Amber said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘Look at her. She hasn’t eaten two crabs, but she’s swallowed a whole dish of vinegar. And we’re to think she doesn’t know how to be jealous!’
Patience was just breaking open a crab full of roe. At this mockery she thrust it towards Amber’s face.
‘You little gossiping baggage!’ she scolded, laughing.

Amber laughed too and dodged aside. Patience missed her, stumbled forward, and smeared it neatly across Xi-feng’s cheek. Xi-feng, who was still teasing Faithful, gave a startled ‘Oh!’ Everyone burst out laughing. Xi-feng herself could not help laughing as she swore at Patience.
‘You damned whore! Have you eaten your eyes out? Smearing your mother like that!’

‘Bless the Buddha,’ said Faithful. ‘Retribution!’
Hearing the noise, Grandmother Jia kept calling from her table, ‘What have you seen that’s so funny? Tell us, so that we can laugh too.’

‘Have pity on the poor thing,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Give her a few little legs and belly-flaps to eat, and have done with it.’

segments.text: Only when Grandmother Jia had finished did everyone else leave their seats. They all washed their hands and spent a little time enjoying themselves, some admiring the flowers, others dabbling in the water and watching the fish. Lady Wang said to Grandmother Jia:
‘It’s windy here, and you’ve just been eating crabs. Hadn’t you better go back to your room for a rest? If you feel like it, we can come again tomorrow.’
‘Yes, indeed,’ said Grandmother Jia, smiling. ‘I thought you were all enjoying yourselves, and I was afraid I should spoil your pleasure if I went. Since you say so, let us go.’
She turned to Xiang-yun. ‘Don’t let your Cousin Bao-yu or your Cousin Dai-yu eat too much.’

segments.text: Xiang-yun promised.
‘And neither of you two must eat too much either,’ Grandmother Jia added to her and Bao-chai. ‘They taste good, but they’re not very good for you. Too many will give you a stomach-ache.’
They both readily agreed and saw her out of the garden. When they returned, they ordered the remains of the meal to be cleared and the tables laid afresh.

‘We needn’t have them laid,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Let’s write our poems. Put the big round table in the middle, with all the food and wine on it. There’s no need for fixed places. Anyone who wants something can go and eat. Wouldn’t it be more comfortable to sit wherever we please?’
‘Much better,’ said Bao-chai.
‘That’s all very well,’ said Xiang-yun, ‘but there are other people to think of.’

She had another table laid, with hot crabs, and invited Aroma, Nightingale, Chess, Scribe, Picture, Oriole, Ebony and the others to sit down together. Two patterned felt rugs were spread under the osmanthus trees on the slope for the waiting women and little maids. They were told to sit down and eat and drink as much as they liked, and come when they were called.

segments.text: Xiang-yun took out the list of subjects and pinned it to the wall with a needle. They all examined it.
‘Novel enough, certainly. But I’m afraid we shan’t be able to write anything.’
Xiang-yun explained why they had not prescribed a rhyme. Bao-yu approved.
‘That’s how it ought to be. I dislike being given a rhyme too.’

Dai-yu, who drank very little and was eating no more crab, had an embroidered stool brought to the balustrade and sat down with a fishing rod. Bao-chai played for a while with a sprig of osmanthus, then leaned over the window ledge, picking off the little flowers and dropping them on to the water. Fish rose, their mouths working at the surface. Xiang-yun would lose herself in thought for a moment, then urge Aroma and her companions to help themselves, or call to the people on the slope to eat their fill. Tan-chun, Li Wan and Xi-chun stood in the shade of a weeping willow, watching the gulls and egrets. Ying-chun sat alone in the shadow of the flowers, threading jasmine blossoms with a needle. Bao-yu watched Dai-yu fishing for a while, leaned down beside Bao-chai for a word or two of banter, then went to see how Aroma and the others were getting on with their crabs, and drank a little wine with them.

segments.text: Aroma picked out a shellful of meat for him too.

Dai-yu put down her fishing rod and came over to the table. She picked up the blackened-silver wine pot with its plum-blossom design and chose a tiny banana-leaf cup of begonia-pink translucent stone. Seeing that she wanted wine, a maid hurried over to pour it.
‘Go on with your meal,’ Dai-yu said. ‘Let me pour my own. It’s more fun.’
She filled the cup halfway, but saw that it was rice wine.
‘I’ve had a little crab and I feel a slight pain at the pit of my stomach. I need a sip of spirits, really hot.’

‘There are spirits,’ Bao-yu said at once, and ordered a pot of the wine steeped with silk-tree flowers to be heated. Dai-yu took only one sip and put it down. Bao-chai came over, took another cup and had a sip too. Then she dipped a brush in ink, went to the wall and marked the first subject, ‘Remembering Chrysanthemums’, adding the character Heng beneath it.
‘Dear Cousin, I’ve already got four lines for the second one,’ Bao-yu said hastily. ‘Let me have that.’
‘I’ve only just managed one poem, and you’re in such a hurry already!’ said Bao-chai, smiling.
Without a word, Dai-yu took the brush, marked the eighth subject, ‘Questioning Chrysanthemums’, and then the eleventh, ‘Chrysanthemum Dreams’, adding the character Xiao.

segments.text: Bao-yu took the brush too, marked the second subject, ‘Seeking Chrysanthemums’, and added Jiang. Tan-chun came to look.
‘No one’s taken “Wearing Chrysanthemums”. I’ll do that.’
She pointed at Bao-yu, smiling. ‘It has just been proclaimed that no words about women’s chambers are allowed. You’d better be careful.’
Just then Xiang-yun came over and marked the fourth and fifth subjects, ‘Facing Chrysanthemums’ and ‘Chrysanthemums in a Vase’, adding the character Xiang.
‘You ought to have a pen-name too,’ said Tan-chun.
‘There are several halls and pavilions at home,’ Xiang-yun said, ‘but I don’t live in any of them. There would be no fun in borrowing their names.’
‘Grandmother was just saying your family had a waterside pavilion called Rosy-cloud Pavilion,’ said Bao-chai. ‘Surely that belongs to you. It may be gone now, but you’re still one of its old owners.’
They all agreed. Before Xiang-yun could do anything, Bao-yu struck out Xiang for her and wrote Xia instead.

segments.text: They praised each poem as they read it, never tiring of complimenting one another.

‘Let me judge impartially,’ Li Wan said, smiling. ‘Taken as a whole, each of you has some striking lines. My impartial verdict today is: “Singing of Chrysanthemums” first, “Questioning Chrysanthemums” second, and “Chrysanthemum Dreams” third. The subjects are fresh, the poems fresh, and the conception fresher still. You mustn’t be angry if I name Naiad the winner. After those come “Wearing Chrysanthemums”, “Facing Chrysanthemums”, “Chrysanthemums in a Vase”, “Painting Chrysanthemums” and “Remembering Chrysanthemums”.’
Bao-yu clapped his hands delightedly. ‘Exactly! Perfectly fair!’
‘Mine isn’t good either,’ said Dai-yu. ‘It is rather too finely wrought.’
‘But the artfulness works,’ said Li Wan. ‘There’s no sign of anything laboured or piled up.’
‘To my mind,’ said Dai-yu, ‘the finest line of all is “In the cold garden at sunset, I recall old wanderings”. It applies the colour from the reverse side.

segments.text: ‘“I put my book aside and face one spray of autumn” is already marvellous. It has said everything about having chrysanthemums in a vase; there is nowhere else to go. So the poem turns back and thinks of them before they were picked and brought indoors. That takes the thought so much deeper.’
‘True,’ said Li Wan, smiling. ‘But your line about “fragrance held between my teeth” is a match for it.’
‘For steadiness of touch, it is still Lady of Allspice,’ said Tan-chun. ‘“Autumn has left no trace” and “in dreams I know them” bring the remembering out beautifully.’
‘And your “coolly wets my short temple-locks” and “scents my kudzu headcloth” leave nothing unsaid about wearing chrysanthemums,’ Bao-chai replied with a smile.
‘“With whom do you withdraw?” and “why do you bloom so late?”’ said Xiang-yun. ‘You really have questioned the chrysanthemums until they have no answer left.’

‘As for your “bareheaded … I sit” and “clasping my knees and chanting”,’ Li Wan said, laughing, ‘you won’t leave them alone for a moment. If chrysanthemums had feelings, they would certainly be sick of you.’
They all laughed.

‘I’ve failed the examination again,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Aren’t “who grows them”, “where is their autumn”, “I come far in waxed clogs” and “my cool chant never ends” all about seeking them? And aren’t “last night’s rain” and “this morning’s frost” about planting them?

segments.text: ‘My only grievance is that they can’t compete with “With fragrance held between my teeth, I chant to the moon”, “Clasping my knees and chanting in the cool, clear scent”, “short temple-locks”, “kudzu headcloth”, “the gold is faint”, “their green hangs tattered”, “autumn has left no trace” and “in dreams I know them”.’
‘When I have a little leisure,’ he added, ‘I’ll write all twelve by myself.’
‘Yours are good too,’ said Li Wan. ‘Only not quite so fresh and ingenious as those particular lines.’

segments.text: When they had finished, they all declared it the finest possible poem on eating crabs. It took real talent to put a large meaning into such a little subject, though the satire on the world was rather too savage.
As they spoke, Patience came back into the garden. What had brought her? To find out, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: When the others saw Patience arrive, they all asked, ‘What is your mistress doing? Why hasn’t she come back?’

‘How could she find the time?’ Patience said, smiling. ‘She says she didn’t get a proper chance to eat, and now she can’t come, so she’s sent me to ask whether there are any crabs left. I’m to take a few home for her.’
‘There are plenty,’ said Xiang-yun, and quickly had someone fetch ten of the very largest.
‘Make more of them the round-bellied ones,’ Patience said.
They tried to draw her down to sit with them, but she refused.
‘I insist,’ said Li Wan, laughing. She pulled Patience down beside her, took up a cup of wine and held it to her lips. Patience hurriedly drank a mouthful and was about to leave.
‘I won’t let you go,’ Li Wan said. ‘Plainly no one counts but Feng. You won’t listen to me.’ Then she told the older women, ‘Take the box over first. Say I’m keeping Patience here.’
Presently the woman returned with the box. ‘Mrs Lian says you and the young ladies mustn’t laugh at her for asking for something to eat, ma’am.

segments.text: ‘In this box are water-caltrop flour cakes and chicken-fat rolls that have just come from her uncle’s wife. They’re for you and the young ladies.’
Then she turned to Patience. ‘She says she sends you on an errand and you get so fond of the company you won’t come back. She advises you to have one cup less.’
‘And what will she do to me if I have one more?’ Patience said with a laugh, and went on drinking and eating crabs.

Li Wan put an arm round her and smiled. ‘What a pity, with such a pretty, respectable face, to have no better fortune than service in someone’s rooms. Who that didn’t know you wouldn’t take you for a mistress of the house?’
