segments.text: Eating and drinking with Bao-chai, Xiang-yun and the others, Patience turned her head and laughed. ‘Please don’t keep feeling me, ma’am. It tickles!’
‘Oh! What’s this hard thing?’ Li Wan asked.
‘Keys.’

‘What keys? So afraid the precious private things might be stolen that you have to keep the keys on you! I’m always joking with people: when the Tang Monk goes to fetch the scriptures, there’s a white horse to carry him; when Liu Zhi-yuan sets out to win an empire, there’s a melon spirit to bring him a helmet and armour; and where there’s Feng, there’s you. You’re your mistress’s master key. What do you need these keys for?’
‘You’ve had some wine, ma’am, and now you’re making fun of me,’ Patience said, laughing.

‘But it’s true,’ said Bao-chai with a smile. ‘When we have nothing else to do and start talking about people, we always say you few girls are each one in a hundred. The best of it is that each of you has her own particular virtues.’
‘There’s a providence in little things as well as great,’ said Li Wan.

‘Only yesterday Grandmother said she was better than we are,’ Xi-chun said, smiling.
‘She really is a good one,’ said Patience. ‘We can’t compare with her.’
‘Cai-xia in Mother’s rooms is a quiet, honest girl,’ Bao-yu said.

‘Indeed she is,’ said Tan-chun. ‘She may look simple, but she knows what’s what. Mother is like a Buddha and doesn’t pay attention to things, but Cai-xia knows them all. segments.text: ‘Then you’re fortunate, and so is Feng,’ said Li Wan. ‘When Master Zhu was alive, didn’t he have two girls too? Do you think I’m the sort of woman who couldn’t tolerate them? Yet day after day they were unhappy. So when he died, I sent them both away while they were still young. If even one had been willing to stay, I would have had someone to help me.’
Tears fell as she spoke.
‘Why make yourself sad again?’ the others said. ‘We had better break up.’
They washed their hands and agreed to go together to pay their respects to Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang.

segments.text: The older women and maids swept the pavilion and cleared away the cups and dishes. Aroma walked towards the front with Patience, inviting her to come into her room for a little while and have another cup of tea.
‘No more tea. Another time,’ Patience said, and was about to go out when Aroma called her back.
‘Why hasn’t this month’s money been paid yet? Even the old lady and Her Ladyship haven’t had theirs.’
Patience quickly turned and came close to her. Only when she had made sure no one was nearby did she whisper, ‘Don’t ask. It will be paid in a few days, anyway.’
Aroma laughed. ‘What can it be, to frighten you like that?’

Patience told her in a whisper. ‘Our mistress drew this month’s money long ago and lent it out. She’s waiting for interest to come in from elsewhere, and when she has enough together she’ll pay everyone. I’m only telling you because it’s you. You mustn’t tell a soul.’
‘Is she still short of money?’ said Aroma. ‘Will she never have enough? Why burden herself with all that worry?’
‘That’s what I say,’ Patience answered with a laugh.

segments.text: ‘Over these last few years she’s made several hundred taels out of this one lot of money. Then she never needs to spend her own household-expense allowance or monthly money, so she puts the little sums together, eight or ten taels at a time, and lends those out. The interest on her private money alone comes to over a thousand taels in less than a year.’
Aroma laughed. ‘So mistress and maid make interest on our money, while we’re fooled into sitting here waiting!’
‘What an ungrateful thing to say. Surely you aren’t short of money?’
‘I’m not. But then I have nowhere to spend it. I only keep it ready for our young gentleman.’
‘If you ever need money urgently, I have a few taels. Take those first, and I’ll deduct them from yours when it comes.’
‘I don’t need any now. If something comes up and I haven’t enough, I’ll send someone to fetch it.’

segments.text: Everyone stood up as Patience came in. Grannie Liu knew her standing from the last visit and hurriedly hopped down to greet her.

‘How are you, miss? Everyone at home sends their respects. I meant to come and pay my respects to Madam and see you long ago, but we’ve been busy on the farm. This year, at last, we’ve managed to harvest two shi of grain more than usual, and we’ve had plenty of fruit and vegetables too. These are the first pickings. We wouldn’t sell them. We saved the very best for Madam and you young ladies to taste. You must get tired of delicacies from the hills and seas every day. These will give you a little taste of the countryside. It’s our poor way of showing we think of you.’
‘Thank you for taking so much trouble,’ Patience said at once.

segments.text: ‘No wonder!’ Patience said with a laugh. ‘I wasn’t going to have any, but Mrs Zhu and the young ladies kept hold of me and forced it on me. I had to drink two cups, and my face went red.’
‘I was thinking I’d like some,’ Zhang Cai’s wife said, laughing, ‘but no one invited me. Next time someone asks you, miss, take me along.’
They all laughed.
‘I saw those crabs this morning,’ Zhou Rui’s wife said. ‘Only two or three would make a catty. Three great baskets like that must have held seventy or eighty catties.’
‘Even that might not be enough for everyone, high and low,’ said Zhou Rui’s wife.

segments.text: ‘Ten catties, five qian. Five fives, two taels and five; three fives are fifteen. Then add the wine and the other dishes, and that’s more than twenty taels altogether. Bless the Buddha! The cost of that one meal would keep us country people for a year.’
‘I suppose you’ve seen our mistress?’ Patience asked.
‘Yes. She told us to wait.’ Grannie Liu looked out at the sky. ‘It’s getting late. We ought to go, or we’ll be in a fix if we can’t get out of the city.’
‘That’s true,’ said Zhou Rui’s wife. ‘I’ll go and see for you.’
She went straight off and returned after some time, smiling.
‘Your luck has come in, Grannie. You’ve taken the fancy of two people at once.’
Patience and the others asked what she meant.
‘Mrs Lian is with the old lady,’ Zhou Rui’s wife explained, smiling. ‘I only meant to tell her quietly, “Grannie Liu wants to go home. She’s afraid she’ll be too late to get out of the city.”

segments.text: ‘Mrs Lian said, “She’s come such a long way, and taken all the trouble of carrying those heavy things here. If it’s late, let her stay the night and go tomorrow.” Doesn’t that show you’ve taken her fancy? And that isn’t all. The old lady happened to hear and asked who Grannie Liu was. Mrs Lian explained, and the old lady said, “I was just wishing for someone really old to talk to. Ask her to come and see me.” Isn’t that a blessing from heaven you never expected?’
She urged Grannie Liu to get down and come along.
‘How can I go before her looking like this?’ Grannie Liu asked. ‘Be a good sister and say I’ve gone.’

‘Do go,’ Patience said quickly. ‘It doesn’t matter. Our old lady is the kindest of people to the old and poor. She isn’t like those blustering, deceitful creatures. You must be frightened of going before someone so grand. Mrs Zhou and I will take you.’
Together with Zhou Rui’s wife, she led Grannie Liu towards Grandmother Jia’s rooms.

segments.text: The pages on duty at the inner gate all stood when they saw Patience come out. Two ran forward after her, calling, ‘Miss!’
‘What is it now?’ she asked.
One of the pages smiled. ‘It’s getting late, and my mother’s ill. She’s waiting for me to fetch a doctor. Please, miss, could I have half a day off?’

‘What a fine lot you are! You’ve arranged it all between you, one asking for leave every day, never going to our mistress, only pestering me. Zhu-er went off the other day, and of course the master wanted him. He couldn’t be found, so I had to answer for it, and was accused of showing favouritism into the bargain. Now here you are.’
‘His mother really is ill,’ Zhou Rui’s wife said. ‘Do answer for him, miss, and let him go.’

‘Be here first thing tomorrow,’ Patience said. ‘Listen: I have work for you. Just you try sleeping till the sun’s on your backside before you come! And on your way, take a message to Wang-er. Say it’s from our mistress. Ask him about the rest of that interest.

segments.text: ‘If he doesn’t bring it in tomorrow, she doesn’t want it at all. He might as well have it to spend himself.’

The page agreed with delight and went off. Patience and the others reached Grandmother Jia’s rooms, where the girls from Prospect Garden were keeping her company. Grannie Liu walked in to find the room full of pearls and jade, a bright flutter of finery, without knowing who anyone was. She saw an old lady reclining on a couch, with a beautiful maid all wrapped in gauze and silk, sitting behind her and massaging her legs. Xi-feng stood beside them, talking and laughing. Grannie Liu knew then that this must be Grandmother Jia. She hurried forward with an ingratiating smile and curtseyed several times.
‘My respects to our venerable Star of Longevity!’

segments.text: Grandmother Jia raised herself a little to return the greeting and told Zhou Rui’s wife to bring a chair for her. Ban-er was still too shy with strangers to offer any greeting.
‘My old relation, how old are you this year?’ Grandmother Jia asked.
Grannie Liu quickly stood up. ‘Seventy-five.’
‘At her age, still so strong!’ Grandmother Jia said to the others. ‘She’s several years older than I am.

segments.text: ‘When I’m that old, heaven knows how little I’ll be able to move.’
‘We were born to work, Your Old Ladyship,’ Grannie Liu said with a smile, ‘and you were born to enjoy good fortune. If we lived as you do, there’d be no one to do the farm work.’
‘Are your eyes and teeth still good?’
‘Yes, they’re still good, except that this year a back tooth on the left has started to wobble.’

‘I’m old and none of me is any use now,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘My eyes are dim, my ears are deaf and my memory’s gone. I can’t even remember old relations like you. When relations call, I don’t see them, for fear they’ll laugh at me. I eat a little of whatever I can chew, have a sleep, and when I’m bored I joke for a while with these grandchildren. That’s all.’
‘That’s just your good fortune, Your Old Ladyship,’ Grannie Liu said, smiling. ‘We couldn’t do that if we wanted to.’
‘Good fortune? I’m only an old good-for-nothing.’
This made everyone laugh.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia went on with a smile. ‘Feng tells me you’ve brought a great many pumpkins and vegetables. I’ve told her to have them prepared at once. I’ve been longing for vegetables freshly picked from the ground. What they buy outside never tastes as good as what you grow in your fields.’
‘It’s a little taste of the country,’ Grannie Liu said, smiling, ‘something fresh for a change. We’d like fish and meat, only we can’t afford them.’

‘Now we’ve met as relations, you mustn’t go away with nothing,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Unless you dislike it here, stay a day or two before going home. We have a garden too, and fruit in it. You can try some tomorrow, and take some home. Then you’ll have made a proper visit to your relations.’
Seeing how pleased Grandmother Jia was, Xi-feng quickly added her invitation. ‘Our place may not be as large as your farmyard, but we do have a couple of empty rooms.

segments.text: ‘Stay two days and tell our old lady some of the news and stories from your part of the world.’
‘Don’t tease her, Feng,’ Grandmother Jia said with a laugh. ‘She’s a plain country person. How is she to stand up to your jokes?’

She told someone to bring a handful of fruit for Ban-er, but with so many people there he was afraid to eat. She then had some money given to him and told the little pages to take him outside to play. After drinking her tea, Grannie Liu told Grandmother Jia some of the things she had seen and heard in the country, and the old lady became more and more interested. While they were talking, Xi-feng sent to invite Grannie Liu to supper. Grandmother Jia chose several dishes from her own meal and had them sent over for Grannie Liu to eat.

segments.text: Seeing how much Grannie Liu had pleased Grandmother Jia, Xi-feng sent her back after supper. Faithful promptly told an older woman to take her for a bath, and herself chose a couple of everyday garments for her to change into. Grannie Liu had never known such treatment. She hurriedly changed, came out and sat before Grandmother Jia’s couch, searching her mind for more things to say. Bao-yu and the girls were all sitting there too. Having never heard anything of the kind, they found her tales more entertaining than the stories told by the blind professional storytellers. Country woman though she was, Grannie Liu had some natural shrewdness. She was old, moreover, and experienced in the ways of the world. Seeing, first, how much Grandmother Jia enjoyed it, and then how eagerly the young people listened, she invented things to tell them even when she had nothing left to say.

‘In our village we grow grain and vegetables, year in, year out, spring, summer, autumn and winter, wind or rain. When do we ever have time to sit down? The edge of a field is our wayside resting-pavilion every day. There’s no end to the strange things we see.

segments.text: ‘Last winter, for instance, it snowed for days on end, till the snow lay three or four chi deep on the ground. I was up early one morning. Before I’d left my room I heard a rustling outside in the firewood. Someone must be stealing it, I thought. I put my eye to a hole in the window, and it wasn’t anyone from our village.’
‘A traveller feeling cold, I expect,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Seeing firewood ready to hand, they might well take a little to make a fire.’

‘But it wasn’t a traveller, either,’ said Grannie Liu, smiling. ‘That’s what was so strange. Who do you think it was, venerable Star of Longevity? A lovely young girl of seventeen or eighteen, with her hair combed smooth and shining, in a scarlet jacket and a white figured-silk skirt—’
She had reached this point when a commotion broke out outside. Someone said, ‘It’s nothing. Don’t frighten the old lady.’
Grandmother Jia and the others quickly asked what was happening.
‘There was a fire in the stables in the south courtyard,’ a maid reported. ‘It’s nothing to worry about. It’s already been brought under control.’
Grandmother Jia was very easily frightened. She rose at once, leaning on someone for support, and went out on to the verandah to look. The glow of the fire was still bright in the south-east.

segments.text: Frightened, Grandmother Jia invoked the Buddha and hurriedly sent someone to burn incense before the God of Fire. Lady Wang and the others hastened over to ask after her and assure her that the fire was already dying down.
‘Please go back inside, Your Old Ladyship.’
Grandmother Jia would not lead them back in until she had watched the last of the glow disappear. Bao-yu was meanwhile eager to question Grannie Liu.
‘Why was that girl taking firewood in the deep snow? What if the cold had made her ill?’
‘It was all that talk of taking firewood that brought on the fire,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘And you’re still asking! No more of that. Tell us something else.’
Disappointed though he was, Bao-yu had to give up. Grannie Liu thought up another tale.
‘In the village east of ours there’s an old grannie in her nineties.

segments.text: ‘Every day she eats vegetarian food and prays to the Buddha. Well, she so moved the Bodhisattva Guanyin that one night Guanyin came to her in a dream and said, “You are so devout! Your family line was to have died out, but I have now petitioned the Jade Emperor, and you are to have a grandson.” You see, the old grannie had only one son, and that son had only one son of his own. They’d managed to bring him up to seventeen or eighteen, and then he died. They cried something dreadful. But afterwards another boy really was born. He’s only thirteen or fourteen this year, white as a ball of snow and ever so clever. So you see, those gods and Buddhas really do exist.’
This whole story answered exactly to what was in Grandmother Jia’s and Lady Wang’s hearts. Even Lady Wang listened spellbound.

segments.text: Bao-yu was still preoccupied with the story about the firewood, brooding over it and turning it over in his mind. Tan-chun asked him, ‘After all the hospitality Xiang-yun gave us yesterday, shall we discuss another poetry meeting when we get back? We could repay her hospitality with a dinner and invite Grandmother to admire the chrysanthemums as well.’

‘Grandmother has already said she wants to give a dinner in return for Xiang-yun’s,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘We’re to keep them company. It will be soon enough for us to give ours after we’ve eaten hers.’
‘It will only get colder as time goes on. Grandmother may not feel like it then.’
‘But Grandmother likes rain and snow.

Dai-yu quickly smiled. ‘Writing poems in the snow? I think we’d do better to get a bundle of firewood and go pulling sticks out of it in the snow. That would be much more fun.’
Bao-chai and the others laughed. Bao-yu gave Dai-yu a look and said nothing.

segments.text: When they broke up, Bao-yu made sure to take Grannie Liu aside and question her closely about who the girl was. Grannie Liu had to invent an answer.
‘She’s the one they worship in a little shrine on the field ridge north of our village. Not a god or a Buddha. There was once a gentleman called…’
She began trying to think of a name.
‘It doesn’t matter what he was called,’ Bao-yu said. ‘Don’t trouble to think of it. Just tell me what happened.’
‘This gentleman had no son, only a daughter called Ming-yu. She was educated and could read, and her father and mother loved her like a precious jewel.

segments.text: ‘Sadly, when Miss Ming-yu was seventeen, she fell ill and died.’
Bao-yu stamped his foot in grief and asked what happened next.

‘Her father and mother missed her so much that they built this shrine and had a statue made of Miss Ming-yu. They appointed someone to burn incense and tend the fire. But years and years have gone by. The people are gone, the temple is falling down, and the statue has turned into a spirit.’
‘Not turned into a spirit,’ Bao-yu said quickly. ‘People like her are, as a rule, alive even after they die.’

‘Bless the Buddha! So that’s it. If you hadn’t told us, young master, we’d all have thought she’d turned into a spirit. She often takes human shape and goes wandering through the villages and along the roads by the inns. The girl taking firewood that I told you about was her. The people in our village have been discussing whether to smash the statue and pull down the temple.’
‘You mustn’t do that! It would be a great sin to pull down the temple.’
‘Lucky you told me, young master. I’ll tell them when I go home tomorrow.’

‘Our old lady and my mother are both good people,’ Bao-yu said. ‘Everyone in the family, old and young, is fond of doing good and giving alms. They particularly like repairing temples and making images of the gods.

When you’ve collected enough, you can rebuild the temple and refurbish the clay image, and we’ll give you money every month to keep the incense burning. Wouldn’t that be a good thing?’
‘If you did that, the young lady would bring me a blessing too. I’d have a few coins to spend.’
Bao-yu asked the names of the place and village, how far away they were and in which direction. Grannie Liu made it all up as she went along.

segments.text: Bao-yu believed every word. Back in his room, he spent the night planning it all. Early next morning he came out, gave Tealeaf several hundred cash and sent him first to look the place over carefully, following the place names and directions Grannie Liu had given. They would decide what to do when he returned. After Tealeaf had gone, Bao-yu waited and waited, but there was no sign of him. He grew as frantic as an ant on a hot pan. At last, when the sun was setting, Tealeaf came back in high spirits.
‘Was there a temple?’ Bao-yu asked at once.

‘You hadn’t heard her properly, sir,’ Tealeaf said with a smile. ‘You gave me a fine search. The place names and directions weren’t as you said, so I spent all day looking. I didn’t find a ruined temple till I got to a field ridge to the north-east.’
Bao-yu’s face lit up with joy. ‘Grannie Liu is old. She could easily have remembered it wrong for a moment. Tell me what you saw.’

segments.text: Bao-yu hurried in on hearing this. Amber was standing by the screen.
‘Do go at once. They’re waiting to speak to you.’
He went to the principal rooms and found Grandmother Jia discussing a return party for Xiang-yun with Lady Wang and the girls.

‘I have an idea,’ he said. ‘Since there won’t be any outside guests, why have a set number of dishes? Choose a few of the things each of us likes best and have those made. And instead of laying tables for a banquet, put a tall little table in front of each person, with one or two of their favourite dishes, a compartmented box of assorted things, and a wine pot to pour for themselves. Wouldn’t that make a change?’
Grandmother Jia approved and sent word to the kitchen at once.
‘Tomorrow, just make the things we like best. Pack a box for each person as well. We’ll have breakfast in the garden too.’
While they were still discussing it, the lamps were lit. Nothing more need be said of that night.

segments.text: To their delight, next morning dawned clear and bright. Li Wan was up before daybreak, supervising the older women and maids as they swept away fallen leaves, wiped tables and chairs, and set out the tea and wine services. Felicity came in with Grannie Liu and Ban-er.
‘How busy you are, Mrs Zhu!’
‘I told you yesterday you wouldn’t get away,’ Li Wan said to Grannie Liu with a smile, ‘but you were in such a hurry to go.’
‘Her Old Ladyship kept me,’ Grannie Liu said, laughing. ‘She said I was to have a day’s fun too.’
Felicity produced several keys of different sizes.

‘Our mistress says there may not be enough tall tables out here. She thought we might open the upper rooms and bring down the ones stored there, just for the day. She ought to have come herself, but she’s talking to Her Ladyship. Would you open up and have them carried down, ma’am?’

segments.text: Li Wan told Su-yun to take the keys and sent an older woman to fetch some of the pages from the inner gate. Standing below Prospect Tower, she looked up while someone went to open Brocade-adorned Pavilion, and the tables were carried down one by one. Pages, older women and maids all lent a hand. More than twenty were brought down.
‘Take care,’ said Li Wan. ‘Don’t rush about as though devils were after you. Mind you don’t knock the carved edges.’
She turned to Grannie Liu with a smile. ‘Why don’t you go up and have a look too, Grannie?’

Grannie Liu had been longing for the invitation. Taking Ban-er with her, she climbed the stairs and went inside. Screens, tables, chairs and lanterns of every size were stacked there in a dense mass. She did not know much about them, but their colours dazzled her, and each had something wonderful about it. With several invocations of the Buddha, she came back to the others. The doors were locked, and they all went down.

segments.text: As she spoke, Bi-yue brought forward a large green-jade platter shaped like a lotus leaf, full of chrysanthemum sprays in different colours. Grandmother Jia chose a large red flower and put it in her hair. Turning, she caught sight of Grannie Liu.
‘Come and have a flower too!’
Before she had finished, Xi-feng caught hold of Grannie Liu.
‘Let me dress you up.’
She stuck the whole platterful of flowers all over her head, this way and that. Grandmother Jia and the others laughed uncontrollably.
‘I wonder what blessings this old head has earned,’ Grannie Liu said, laughing, ‘to be made so grand today.’

segments.text: Talking and laughing, they reached Drenched Blossoms Pavilion. The maids brought a large brocade cushion and spread it on the bench along the balustrade. Grandmother Jia sat down against a pillar and asked Grannie Liu to sit beside her.
‘Do you like the garden?’
Grannie Liu invoked the Buddha.

‘At New Year, we country folk come into town to buy pictures to put up. When we have a spare moment, we’re always saying, “How could we ever go and walk about inside a picture?” We know it’s only a made-up thing. Where could there be a real place like that? But now I’ve come into your garden and seen it, why, it’s ten times better than the pictures. If only someone would paint this very garden for me to take home and show them! It would do me good even after I’m dead.’
Grandmother Jia pointed to Xi-chun with a smile.
‘Look at my little granddaughter here. She can paint. How would it be if I asked her to paint one for you?’
Grannie Liu was so pleased that she hurried over and took Xi-chun’s hand.
‘My dear young lady, at your age, and with such good looks, to be so clever too! You must be an immortal born into this world.’

segments.text: After a short rest, Grandmother Jia naturally took Grannie Liu to see the sights. They went first to Naiad’s House. Inside the gate, bamboos stood close on either side of a narrow, winding pebble path, and green moss covered the ground. Grannie Liu left the path free for Grandmother Jia and the others and walked on the earth instead. Amber caught her arm.
‘Come up on the path, Grannie. Mind you don’t slip on that moss.’
‘Never fear. We’re used to walking on such things. You young ladies keep to the path. It would be a pity to dirty those embroidered shoes.’
Talking to them, she paid no attention to her feet, and sure enough, she slipped and came down with a thump. They all clapped their hands and laughed.
‘You little baggages!’ Grandmother Jia scolded, laughing too. ‘Help her up, instead of standing there laughing.’
But Grannie Liu had already scrambled to her feet and was laughing herself.
‘No sooner was the boast out of my mouth than I was slapped for it.’
‘Have you hurt your back?’ Grandmother Jia asked.

segments.text: ‘Let the girls give it a rub.’
‘As if I were such a delicate creature! There isn’t a day I don’t fall down a couple of times. If I had to have it rubbed every time, there’d be no end to it.’
Nightingale had already raised the bamboo blind, and Grandmother Jia and the others went in and sat down. Dai-yu herself brought Grandmother Jia a covered bowl of tea on a small tray.
‘We shan’t have tea,’ Lady Wang said. ‘You needn’t pour any for us, dear.’

Dai-yu told a maid to move the chair she usually sat in by the window to a lower place, and invited Lady Wang to sit there. Grannie Liu noticed the brushes and inkstone on the table beneath the window, and the shelves stacked full of books.
‘This must be one of the young gentlemen’s studies.’
‘It is my granddaughter’s room,’ Grandmother Jia said, pointing to Dai-yu. ‘My daughter’s child.’
Grannie Liu looked Dai-yu carefully up and down.
‘It’s nothing like a young lady’s chamber. It’s better than the finest study.’
‘Where has Bao-yu got to?’ Grandmother Jia asked.
‘On one of the boats in the pool,’ the maids replied.
‘Who has got boats ready?’
‘When we opened the upper rooms for the tables,’ Li Wan said quickly, ‘I thought you might like a ride, so I had them made ready.’
Grandmother Jia was about to answer when someone announced Aunt Xue. They were just rising as she came in. Taking her seat, she said with a smile:
‘You’re in fine spirits today, coming out so early.’
‘I was just saying we must fine anyone who came late,’ Grandmother Jia replied. ‘And here you are, the late one!’

segments.text: After a little talk and laughter, Grandmother Jia noticed that the window gauze had faded.

‘This gauze looks pretty when it’s first put up,’ she said to Lady Wang, ‘but it loses its fresh green after a time. There are no peach or apricot trees in this courtyard, and the bamboo is green already. More green gauze on the windows is quite the wrong thing. I remember we used to have four or five colours of window gauze. Have hers changed tomorrow.’

‘When I opened the storeroom yesterday,’ Xi-feng put in, ‘I saw quite a few bolts of silvery-pink cicada-wing gauze in the big wooden chests. Some had sprays of flowers on them, some flowing clouds and ten thousand blessings, some a hundred butterflies among flowers. Such fresh colours, and the gauze so light and soft! I’d never seen anything like it. I took out two bolts. I thought they would make two lovely padded gauze quilts.’
‘Pah!’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘Everyone says there is nothing you haven’t handled or seen, and you don’t even know what this gauze is. You’ll be boasting again tomorrow, no doubt.’
Aunt Xue and the others laughed.
‘However much she has handled and seen, how could she presume to compare with you?

segments.text: ‘No wonder she took it for cicada-wing gauze. It does look a little like it. Anyone who didn’t know would call it that. Its proper name is Soft Mist Gauze.’
‘What a pretty name,’ said Xi-feng. ‘But I’ve grown to this age and seen hundreds of kinds of gauze and silk, and I’ve never heard of it.’

‘And how long have you lived?’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘You’ve seen a few odds and ends that were lying about for want of a place to put them, and now you’re boasting. Soft Mist Gauze comes in only four colours: clear-sky blue after rain, olive-yellow, pine green, and silvery-pink. Make it into bed-curtains or cover window frames with it, and from a distance it looks like mist. That is why it is called Soft Mist Gauze. The silvery-pink is also called Rosy-cloud Gauze. Even the gauze officially supplied to the Palace nowadays is not so soft and substantial, so light and closely woven.’

segments.text: ‘Never mind Xi-feng not having seen it,’ said Aunt Xue with a smile. ‘I’ve never even heard of it.’
While they were talking, Xi-feng had already had a bolt brought in.

‘That is it,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘At first we used it only on window frames. Later we tried making quilts and bed-curtains with it, and it did very well. Find a few bolts tomorrow, and use the silvery-pink on her windows.’
Xi-feng agreed. Everyone looked at it and admired it. Grannie Liu kept peering at it, murmuring prayers to the Buddha.
‘We couldn’t hope to have clothes made of this, and you put it on the windows! Isn’t it a waste?’
‘It doesn’t look well as clothes,’ said Grandmother Jia.
Xi-feng pulled out the front of the padded scarlet gauze jacket she was wearing and showed it to Grandmother Jia and Aunt Xue.
‘Look at my jacket.’
‘That is very fine too,’ they both said. ‘It’s made in the Palace workshops for use at court nowadays, but it still isn’t as good as this.’
‘This thin stuff!’ said Xi-feng. ‘And they call it made in the Palace workshops for use at court. It isn’t even as good as what they used to make for officials.’
‘Look again,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘There may be some blue too.

segments.text: ‘Those cupboards are bigger and taller than a whole room in our house. No wonder there’s a ladder in the back courtyard. I thought, “They don’t go on to the roof to dry things, so what do they want a ladder for?” Then I realised it must be for putting things in and out of the top cupboards. How else could anyone reach them? And now I see this little room, and it’s even more beautifully arranged than the big ones. Everything in it is so pretty, and I don’t know what any of it is called. The more I look, the less I want to leave.’
‘There are better things still,’ said Xi-feng. ‘I’ll take you to see them all.’
They left Naiad’s House.

segments.text: In the distance they could see a group of people poling boats on the pool.
‘Since they’ve got the boats ready, let’s have a ride,’ said Grandmother Jia.

They set off towards Amaryllis Eyot and the knotweed shallows. Before they reached the pool, they met several older women carrying large boxes, all alike, decorated in colours, fine wirework and incised gold. Xi-feng asked Lady Wang where breakfast should be laid.
‘Ask Grandmother. Wherever she would like.’
Grandmother Jia turned round.
‘Your third sister’s would be a good place. Take the people there and set it out. We’ll come round by boat.’
Xi-feng went back with Tan-chun, Li Wan, Faithful, Amber and the people carrying the food. Taking a short cut to Autumn Studio, they arranged the tables in its Dawn-green Hall.
‘We’re always saying how the gentlemen outside have a hanger-on to amuse them when they eat and drink,’ Faithful said, laughing. ‘Today we’ve got a female hanger-on of our own.’
Li Wan, who was a kind-hearted person, did not understand her.

segments.text: Xi-feng knew very well that she meant Grannie Liu.
‘Then we’ll have some fun with her today,’ she said, laughing too.
The two of them put their heads together and made their plans.
‘You never do a good deed,’ Li Wan protested with a smile. ‘You’re not children any more, and you’re still so mischievous. Mind Grandmother doesn’t scold you.’
‘It has nothing to do with you,’ said Faithful, laughing. ‘I’ll take responsibility.’

segments.text: Grandmother Jia and the others arrived as they spoke, and sat down wherever they pleased. The maids first brought two trays of tea, which everyone drank. Xi-feng, holding a bundle of ebony chopsticks with three silver mounts, wrapped in a Western-cloth napkin, counted the places and laid them out.
‘Bring that little nanmu table over,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Let Cousin Liu sit close beside me.’
It was brought at once. Xi-feng gave Faithful a look, and Faithful took Grannie Liu outside. She whispered a string of instructions to her, ending:
‘That’s the rule in our household. If you get it wrong, we shall laugh at you.’

With everything settled, they returned to their seats. Aunt Xue had eaten before coming, so she sat aside drinking tea. Grandmother Jia had Bao-yu, Xiang-yun, Dai-yu and Bao-chai at her table; Lady Wang sat with Ying-chun and her two sisters; Grannie Liu had a table beside Grandmother Jia. At meals Grandmother Jia usually had little maids standing by with a rinsing bowl, fly-whisk, towels and handkerchiefs.

segments.text: Faithful no longer did that work, but today she deliberately took the fly-whisk and began to use it. Knowing that she meant to play a trick on Grannie Liu, the maids withdrew and left her to it. As she stood waiting, Faithful whispered to Grannie Liu:
‘Don’t forget.’
‘You can trust me, miss.’

Once seated, Grannie Liu picked up her chopsticks. They were heavy and awkward in her hand. Xi-feng and Faithful had agreed to give her, alone of all the company, an old-fashioned square-sided pair of ivory chopsticks mounted in gold.
‘These rakes are heavier than our iron shovel,’ Grannie Liu said. ‘How am I to wrestle with them?’
Everyone laughed.

segments.text: A married servant came in and stood in the middle of the room with a food box. A maid lifted the lid. There were two bowls of food inside. Li Wan set one on Grandmother Jia’s table. Xi-feng deliberately chose a bowl of pigeons’ eggs for Grannie Liu.
As Grandmother Jia invited everyone to begin, Grannie Liu stood up and called out:

‘Old Liu, old Liu, eats as much as a cow;
Won’t lift her head till she’s eaten a whole old sow.’

Then she puffed out her cheeks and said nothing. At first they stared. Then the whole company, high and low, burst into laughter. Xiang-yun could not contain herself and sprayed out a mouthful of rice. Dai-yu laughed until her breath caught and she lay over the table gasping. Bao-yu rolled into Grandmother Jia’s arms, and she held him, laughing and crying, ‘My darling!’ Lady Wang pointed at Xi-feng, unable to get a word out. Aunt Xue lost control too and sprayed her tea all over Tan-chun’s skirt. Tan-chun tipped her rice bowl on to Ying-chun. Xi-chun left her seat and pulled at her nurse, begging her to rub her aching stomach.

segments.text: Not one of the attendants could keep from doubling up. Some escaped outside to squat and laugh; others fought down their laughter to come and help the girls change their clothes. Only Xi-feng and Faithful kept straight faces and continued urging Grannie Liu to eat. She picked up her chopsticks, which refused to obey her.
‘Even the chickens here are pretty. And such neat little eggs they lay! Lovely little things. I’ll shove one down.’
They had only just stopped laughing, and now they began again. Tears ran down Grandmother Jia’s face while Amber patted her back.
‘That imp Xi-feng must be behind this,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Don’t believe what she tells you.’
Grannie Liu was still admiring the little eggs and preparing to shove one down.
‘They’re a tael of silver each,’ Xi-feng told her, smiling. ‘Taste one quickly. They won’t be good once they’re cold.’

Grannie Liu reached out with her chopsticks, but could not get hold of one. After a long struggle all round the bowl, she finally managed to trap one. She had just stretched out her neck to eat it when it slipped away, rolled off the table and fell to the ground. She put down her chopsticks and was about to pick it up herself, but one of the attendants had already retrieved it and taken it away.

segments.text: ‘A tael of silver!’ Grannie Liu sighed. ‘Gone, and it didn’t even make a sound.’
No one had any thought of eating now; they were all watching her and laughing.
‘Why have you brought out those chopsticks?’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘We’re not entertaining guests at a grand banquet. This is all Xi-feng’s doing. Change them at once.’

The attendants had not prepared the ivory chopsticks: Xi-feng and Faithful had brought them. At Grandmother Jia’s words they hurried to take them away and substituted a silver-mounted ebony pair like everyone else’s.
‘Gold ones gone, silver ones come,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘Neither sits in the hand like ours.’
‘If there’s poison in the food,’ Xi-feng said, ‘the silver will detect it when you put them in.’
‘If there’s poison in this food, ours must be pure arsenic.

segments.text: When the meal was over, Grandmother Jia and the others went into Tan-chun’s bedroom to chat. The tables were cleared and another meal was laid out. Watching Li Wan and Xi-feng sit down opposite one another to eat, Grannie Liu sighed.
‘Never mind anything else, it’s the way you do things here that I admire. No wonder they say good manners come from great houses.’
‘You mustn’t take it to heart,’ Xi-feng said quickly, smiling. ‘We were only having a little fun just now.’
Before she had finished, Faithful came in.
‘Don’t be angry, Grannie,’ she said with a smile. ‘I owe you an apology.’

‘What are you saying, miss? We were coaxing Her Old Ladyship into a good laugh. What was there to be angry about? When you gave me my instructions, I understood at once. It was only to give everyone a bit of fun. If I’d been angry inside, I wouldn’t have said it.’
Faithful scolded the servants. ‘Why hasn’t anyone poured Grannie some tea?’
‘That woman brought me some just now,’ Grannie Liu said hastily. ‘I’ve had it. You ought to have your meal too, miss.’
Xi-feng caught hold of Faithful.
‘Sit down and eat with us. It will save them making a fuss again later.’
Faithful sat down.

segments.text: The older women brought another bowl and pair of chopsticks, and the three finished their meal.
‘You all eat such a little bit, and then you’ve done,’ Grannie Liu said, smiling. ‘I wonder you don’t go hungry. No wonder a puff of wind would blow you over.’
‘There’s plenty left today,’ Faithful asked. ‘Where has it all gone?’
‘It hasn’t been shared out yet,’ the women told her. ‘We’re keeping it here to give them all their portions together.’
‘They can’t eat all this. Choose two dishes and send them to Patience in Mrs Lian’s rooms.’
‘She’s had her meal already,’ said Xi-feng. ‘There’s no need.’
‘Then she can feed your cat with them.’
The women quickly chose two dishes, put them in a box and sent them off.
‘Where has Su-yun gone?’ Faithful asked.
‘They’re all eating here together,’ said Li Wan. ‘What do you want her for now?’
‘That’s all right, then.’
‘Aroma isn’t here,’ Xi-feng said. ‘You might have a couple of dishes sent to her.’
Faithful did so, then asked the older women, ‘Have the compartmented boxes been filled for the drinking party later?’
‘They’ll probably be a little while yet.’
‘Hurry them up.’
The women agreed.

segments.text: Xi-feng and the others went into Tan-chun’s room, where the older and younger women were talking and laughing. Tan-chun liked space and openness: the three bays of her room had never been partitioned. A large rosewood table with a marble top stood in the middle, piled with copybooks of famous calligraphers’ work, dozens of fine inkstones and brush pots of every kind. The brushes in the large brush holder stood thick as a wood. To one side was a Ru-ware flower vase as big as a dou grain measure, filled with white ‘Crystal Ball’ chrysanthemums. segments.text: A large tripod vessel stood on the table. To the left, on a red sandalwood stand, a great dish of Daguan ware held dozens of large, delicately formed, tender-yellow finger citrons. To the right, a white-jade chime carved as paired fish hung from a stand in foreign lacquer, with a little mallet beside it. Ban-er, becoming rather more at home, reached for the mallet to strike it, but the maids hurried to stop him. Then he wanted to eat a finger citron. Tan-chun chose one for him.
‘You can play with it,’ she said, ‘but you can’t eat it.’
Her couch was on the east. The bed, raised on a platform, had spring-green gauze curtains embroidered on both sides with flowers and insects. Ban-er ran over to look.
‘Here’s a bush-cricket! Here’s a grasshopper!’
Grannie Liu slapped him.
‘You nasty little wretch, making a filthy nuisance of yourself! We let you in to look, and now you’re getting above yourself.’
Ban-er began to cry, and only when everyone intervened did she stop. Grandmother Jia looked for a while through the gauze window into the back courtyard.
‘The parasol trees under the eaves of the back veranda have come on well too. Only they’re a little thin.’
As they spoke, a gust of wind brought the faint sound of drums and music.

segments.text: ‘Whose wedding is that?’ Grandmother Jia asked. ‘We must be quite close to the street here.’
‘We couldn’t hear anything from the street,’ Lady Wang and the others replied, smiling. ‘It’s our dozen or so girls practising their music.’
‘If they’re practising, why not have them in here?’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘They can have an outing too, and we shall enjoy it.’
Xi-feng sent for them at once and ordered long tables to be set out and covered with red felt.

‘Set them up out over the water at Lotus Pavilion,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘It will sound better over the water. Later we’ll have our wine below Brocade-adorned Pavilion. There’s plenty of room, and it’s near enough to hear.’
Everyone agreed it was a good place. Grandmother Jia smiled at Aunt Xue.

‘Let us go. These girls don’t much like people sitting about in their rooms. They’re afraid we shall make them dirty. We mustn’t be so lacking in tact. Let’s go for our boat ride, then have our wine.’
They all rose to leave.
‘What a thing to say!’ Tan-chun protested, laughing. ‘We can hardly get you and Aunt to come and sit with us, however much we beg.’
‘My third girl is very good,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘It’s only the two Jades who are such nuisances.

segments.text: ‘When we’ve had too much wine, we’ll go and make a disturbance in their rooms on purpose.’

They all laughed and went out together. A short walk brought them to Leafy Islet, where the boatwomen chosen from Suzhou had already brought up two tang-wood pleasure boats. Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang, Aunt Xue, Grannie Liu, Faithful and Silver were helped into the first, with Li Wan following. Xi-feng got in too and stood in the bow, determined to try her hand at poling.
‘This is no game,’ Grandmother Jia called from the cabin. ‘It may not be a river, but it’s deep enough. Come in here at once.’
‘What is there to be afraid of? Don’t worry, Grannie.’

With one push of the pole, Xi-feng sent the boat away from the bank. Out in the middle of the pool, with so many people in the little boat, Xi-feng felt it rocking alarmingly. She hastily handed the pole to a boatwoman and crouched down. Ying-chun, her sisters and the others, with Bao-yu, boarded the second boat and followed. The remaining nurses and maids walked along the bank beside them.
‘Those ragged lotus leaves are hateful,’ Bao-yu said. ‘Why haven’t they sent someone to pull them out?’
‘These last few days we haven’t given the garden a moment’s peace,’ Bao-chai said, smiling. ‘We’re out here every day. When would there be time to send anyone to tidy it?’
‘I dislike Li Yi-shan’s poetry more than anyone’s,’ Dai-yu said. ‘The only line I like is this: “Leave the withered lotus; listen to the rain.”

segments.text: ‘And you won’t leave even that.’
‘It is a fine line,’ Bao-yu said. ‘We won’t have them pulled out in future.’
They had reached the vine-shaded creek below Flowering Inlets. Its gloom struck cold to the bone, and the withered grass and dying water-caltrops on both banks deepened the feeling of autumn.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia noticed a spacious, airy building on the bank.
‘Isn’t that Miss Xue’s place?’
‘Yes,’ they told her.

She had the boat brought to shore, and they went up the cloud-stepping stone stairway into Allspice Court. An unusual fragrance met them. The strange plants and fairy-like vines grew greener as the weather grew colder. They were all in fruit, hung with lovely clusters like little coral beads. But inside, the rooms were like a cave of snow, without a single ornament. On the table stood only a coarse Ding-ware vase containing a few sprays of chrysanthemums, two books, a tea caddy and tea cups. Plain blue gauze curtains hung round the bed, and the quilt and bedding were very simple.

‘The child is far too unassuming,’ Grandmother Jia sighed. ‘If you had no ornaments, why didn’t you ask your aunt for some? I haven’t attended to it either; it never occurred to me. Of course, you must have left your own things at home and not brought them with you.’

‘You might have sent your cousin a few pretty things. How mean of you!’
‘She doesn’t want them,’ Lady Wang and Xi-feng protested, smiling. ‘We did send some, and she sent them all back.’
‘She doesn’t bother much with such things at home either,’ Aunt Xue said with a smile.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia shook her head.

‘It won’t do. She may save herself some trouble, but suppose a relation calls: it wouldn’t look right. Besides, it’s unlucky for young girls to have such bare rooms. Old women like us ought to be living in the stables, then! Listen to the descriptions of young ladies’ chambers in books and plays. You can’t imagine how exquisite they are. Our girls may not presume to rival those young ladies, but they needn’t fall so far below the proper standard. When the things are there already, why not put them out? If she really likes simplicity, a few less would do. I used to be the best of anyone at arranging a room. Now I’m old, I haven’t the leisure or the inclination. These girls are learning to do it quite well. Vulgarity is the danger: even fine things can be spoilt by the way you set them out. I don’t think theirs are vulgar. Now let me arrange yours for you. I promise it will be both handsome and simple.

segments.text: ‘There are two things among my private possessions that I’ve kept all this time without letting Bao-yu see them. If he’d set eyes on them, they would have been gone.’
She called Faithful over and gave her instructions herself.

‘The miniature rock landscape, the little gauze table-screen, and that tripod of smoky-black translucent stone: those three on this table will be enough. Bring the white damask bed-curtains with the ink paintings and calligraphy too, and change these curtains.’

Faithful agreed, then said with a smile, ‘Those things are in one of the chests upstairs in the east building, goodness knows which. We shall have to take our time looking. Perhaps we could bring them tomorrow.’
‘Tomorrow or the day after will do. Only don’t forget.’
After sitting a little longer, Grandmother Jia came out, and they went straight to the space below Brocade-adorned Pavilion.

segments.text: Wen-guan and the others came to pay their respects and asked what pieces they should rehearse.
‘Choose a few you’re not so familiar with,’ Grandmother Jia told them.

They withdrew to Lotus Pavilion, and we shall leave them there. Meanwhile Xi-feng and her helpers had finished setting everything out. At the upper end stood a couch on either side, each spread with brocade cushions and furong bamboo mats, with two carved-lacquer tables before it. There were tables shaped like begonia blossoms, plum blossoms, lotus leaves and mallow flowers, square ones and round ones, in a variety of shapes. On one table stood an incense burner, a vase and a compartmented food box; the other was left clear for the dishes each person liked. The two upper couches and their four tables were for Grandmother Jia and Aunt Xue. Below them, Lady Wang had a chair and two tables; everyone else had a chair and one table.

segments.text: Each person had a blackened-silver wine pot with Western chasing, to pour for themselves, and an enamel cup with assorted designs. Once everyone was seated, Grandmother Jia said with a smile:
‘Let’s have a couple of cups first. We ought to play a drinking game today. It will be more fun.’
‘You will know some good games, of course,’ Aunt Xue and the others replied, laughing. ‘How could we keep up? You mean to get us all drunk. Let us just drink a couple of extra cups and have done.’
‘You’ve become modest today too,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘You must be tired of me now I’m old.’
‘It isn’t modesty,’ said Aunt Xue. ‘I’m afraid I won’t be able to answer, and then I shall look a fool.’

Aunt Xue nodded and laughed. ‘Very well, I submit to the rules. But you must drink a cup to start the game, ma’am.’
‘Of course,’ Grandmother Jia said, and drank one.

segments.text: Xi-feng brought Faithful over.
‘If she is in the game, there can be no question of her standing,’ said Lady Wang.
She turned to a little maid. ‘Bring a chair and put it with your two mistresses.’
Faithful half protested, half accepted, thanked them for the seat and sat down. After drinking a cup of wine herself, she said with a smile:
‘The rules of a drinking game are as binding as military orders. High or low, it makes no difference. I alone am in command. Anyone who disobeys me will be punished.’
‘Certainly,’ Lady Wang and the others said, laughing. ‘Tell us quickly.’
Before Faithful could begin, Grannie Liu got up and waved her hands.
‘Don’t play such tricks on me. I’m going home.’
‘That won’t do at all,’ they all laughed.
‘Bring her back to her place!’ Faithful ordered the little maids.
Laughing too, the girls did pull her back into her seat.
‘Spare me!’ Grannie Liu kept crying.
‘Anyone who says another word will be fined a whole pot.’
Grannie Liu fell silent.

segments.text: ‘Now I shall call out hands of dominoes,’ said Faithful. ‘We’ll begin with Her Old Ladyship and go round in order, ending with Grannie Liu. ‘That’s a good game,’ they said. ‘Begin.’

segments.text: Now Grannie Liu held out both hands to show them, and said, ‘The flower falls and a big pumpkin grows.’ The whole company roared with laughter. She drank the cup required by the game, then continued her joking.

‘To tell you the truth, I’m clumsy with my hands and feet, and I’ve had wine as well. I might let this porcelain cup slip and break it. If you have a wooden one, bring it for me. Then if I drop it on the ground, no harm will be done.’
They laughed again. Xi-feng promptly took her up.

‘If you really want a wooden one, I’ll have it fetched. But there’s one thing I must tell you first. Wooden cups aren’t like porcelain ones. They come in sets, and you have to drink your way through the whole set.’

Grannie Liu considered this. ‘I was only making a joke to amuse them. Who would have thought they really had such things? I’ve been to feasts at the big houses of country gentlemen often enough, and I’ve seen gold cups and silver cups, but I’ve never heard of wooden ones.

segments.text: ‘Oh, I know! They must be those little wooden bowls children use. She’s only trying to coax a couple more bowls of wine into me. Never mind. This wine tastes like honey-water, anyway. A little more won’t hurt.’
Having thought it over, she said, ‘Bring them here, and then we’ll see.’
Xi-feng told Felicity, ‘In the inner room at the front there’s a set of ten bamboo-root cups on the bookshelf. Fetch them.’
Felicity had answered and was just going when Faithful laughed.

‘I know those ten cups of yours. They’re still quite small. Besides, you said wood just now. It won’t look very well if you produce bamboo root instead. Why not fetch our big set of ten, hollowed out of solid boxwood root, and give her ten good doses?’
‘Better still!’ said Xi-feng, laughing.

Faithful did send someone for them. At the sight, Grannie Liu was both startled and delighted. What startled her was the row of ten cups, diminishing in size: the largest was quite as big as a small basin, and even the tenth and smallest was twice the size of the cup she was holding. What delighted her was the extraordinary carving, all landscapes, trees and figures, with cursive writing and seal impressions besides.

segments.text: ‘Just bring me the little one,’ she said hastily. ‘What do I want with so many?’

‘You can’t drink out of only one of these,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘Nobody in our family can hold that much, so no one dares use them. But you asked for them, Grannie, and now we’ve gone to all this trouble to find them, you must drink from each in turn.’
‘Oh, I daren’t!’ cried Grannie Liu in alarm. ‘My dear Madam, have mercy on me!’
Grandmother Jia, Aunt Xue and Lady Wang knew that at her age she could not stand it.
‘A joke is a joke,’ they hastily interposed, smiling. ‘She mustn’t drink too much. Just this first cup will do.’
‘Blessed Buddha!’ said Grannie Liu. ‘Let me go on drinking from the little cup. Put this big one away for me, and I’ll take it home and drink it at my leisure.’
This set them all laughing again. Faithful could do nothing but have a large cup filled to the brim. Grannie Liu held it in both hands to drink.
‘Slowly,’ Grandmother Jia and Aunt Xue both warned her. ‘Don’t choke.’
Aunt Xue also told Xi-feng to give her something to eat.

segments.text: ‘What would you like, Grannie?’ Xi-feng asked, smiling. ‘Tell me the name and I’ll pick it up and feed you.’
‘What do I know about the names? Everything’s good.’
‘Give her some of the aubergine relish,’ said Grandmother Jia, smiling.
Xi-feng obediently picked some up and put it into Grannie Liu’s mouth.
‘You eat aubergines every day,’ she said with a laugh. ‘Now try ours and see whether we make them taste nice.’
‘Don’t you fool me!’ Grannie Liu laughed. ‘If aubergines could taste like this, we needn’t grow grain any more. We’d grow nothing but aubergines.’

segments.text: ‘It really is aubergine,’ they all said, laughing. ‘We aren’t fooling you now.’
‘Is it really?’ Grannie Liu asked in astonishment. ‘Then I’ve been eating all this time for nothing. Give me a little more, Madam. I’ll chew this mouthful carefully.’
Xi-feng put some more into her mouth. After chewing it for a long time, Grannie Liu laughed.
‘There’s a bit of an aubergine flavour, but it still doesn’t seem like aubergine. Tell me how you make it, and I’ll make some to eat myself.’

‘There’s nothing difficult about it,’ said Xi-feng, smiling. ‘You pare the skin off freshly picked aubergines, keeping only the flesh, cut it into little dice and fry it in chicken fat. Then take chicken breast, fragrant mushrooms, fresh bamboo shoots, ordinary mushrooms, five-spice dried bean curd and dried fruits and nuts of all kinds. Dice those too, simmer them in chicken stock until it has cooked away, finish with sesame oil and mix in some wine-lees sauce. Put it all in a porcelain jar and seal it tight. When you want to eat it, take some out and mix in stir-fried chicken pieces. That’s all.’
Grannie Liu shook her head and stuck out her tongue.
‘Merciful Buddha!

segments.text: ‘You’d need ten or so chickens just to go with it. No wonder it tastes like that!’
Talking and laughing, she slowly finished the wine, but went on examining the cup with great interest.
‘You haven’t had enough fun yet,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘Have another cup!’
‘Oh, no!’ Grannie Liu said quickly. ‘That would be the death of me. I’m only admiring the pattern. How ever did they make it?’
‘Now you’ve finished the wine,’ Faithful asked with a smile, ‘what wood is the cup made of, after all?’

segments.text: ‘No wonder you don’t know, miss,’ Grannie Liu said, laughing. ‘Living behind golden gates and embroidered curtains, how would you know one wood from another? We spend our lives with trees for neighbours. When we’re sleepy, we lay our heads on them; when we’re tired, we lean against them; when the crops fail and we’re hungry, we even eat them. We see them every day, hear them every day and talk about them every day. So I can tell good from bad and true from false. Let me have a look.’
As she spoke, she studied it closely for some time.

‘A family like yours would never have any of the cheap stuff. You wouldn’t keep wood that was easy to come by. Now, judging by the weight of this cup, it certainly isn’t poplar. It must be yellow pine.’
The whole company burst out laughing.

segments.text: An older serving-woman came up to Grandmother Jia.
‘The girls are all at Lotus Pavilion, ma’am. They ask whether they should begin playing or wait a little longer.’
‘Why, I’d quite forgotten them!’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘Tell them to begin.’

The woman answered and went away. Soon the lingering notes of flutes and pipes rose with the sound of mouth-organs and transverse flutes. The breeze was fresh and the air clear. Coming through the trees and over the water, the music could not but lift the spirits and open the heart. Bao-yu was the first to give way to it. He took up his wine pot, poured a cup and drained it in one mouthful. He poured another and was about to drink when Lady Wang, who also wanted some, told a servant to bring her warm wine instead. Bao-yu quickly carried his own cup over and held it to her lips. She took two sips from his hand. When the warm wine arrived, Bao-yu returned to his seat. Lady Wang took up the warmed pot and rose from the table. Everyone else rose too, including Aunt Xue. Grandmother Jia at once told Li Wan and Xi-feng to take the pot from her.
‘Let your aunt sit down. Then everyone can be comfortable.’
At this, Lady Wang handed the pot to Xi-feng and sat down again.

segments.text: ‘Let everyone have a couple of cups,’ Grandmother Jia said, smiling. ‘This really is a pleasant day.’
She raised her cup to Aunt Xue, then turned to Xiang-yun and Bao-chai.
‘You two girls must have a cup as well. Your younger cousin may not be much of a drinker, but don’t let her off.’

As she spoke, she emptied her own cup. Xiang-yun, Bao-chai and Dai-yu all drained theirs too. Between the music and the wine, Grannie Liu was so delighted that she began waving her arms and tapping her feet. Bao-yu left his seat and went over to Dai-yu.
‘Look at Grannie Liu!’ he said, laughing.
‘In ancient times,’ Dai-yu replied with a smile, ‘when the sages’ music sounded, all the beasts danced. Today we have only one cow.’
The girls all laughed.

segments.text: Presently the music stopped. Aunt Xue rose from the table.
‘I think we’ve all had enough wine,’ she said, smiling. ‘Let’s take a stroll before we sit down again.’

Grandmother Jia had been wanting a walk herself. They all rose and followed her out to enjoy the garden. Wishing to give Grannie Liu some diversion, Grandmother Jia took her by the hand and wandered for a while among the trees in front of the rockery, telling her what this tree was, what that rock was, and what those flowers were. Grannie Liu took it all in, then said to Grandmother Jia:
‘Who would have thought it? In town it isn’t just the people who are grand. Even the birds are grand. Once a bird comes here to you, it turns handsome and learns to talk as well.’
No one understood. They asked which birds had turned handsome and learnt to talk.

They all began to laugh.

segments.text: The maids came to ask them to have some refreshments.
‘After those cups of wine I’m not hungry,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Still, bring them here, and everyone can have a little as they please.’

The maids brought two small tables and two little food-boxes. When these were opened, each contained two kinds of food. In one were lotus-root-starch cakes with osmanthus sugar, and pine-kernel rolls made with goose fat. In the other were little dumplings about a cun across. Grandmother Jia asked what the filling was, and the serving-women quickly answered that it was crab.
‘All that grease!’ she said with a frown. ‘Who could eat such things?’

The other kind, little pastries in assorted shapes fried in butter, did not please her either. She invited Aunt Xue to help herself, but Aunt Xue took only one cake. Grandmother Jia chose a roll, took no more than a taste and handed the remaining half to a maid. Grannie Liu, struck by the delicate openwork of the little pastries, picked one in the shape of a peony.
‘The cleverest girls where we live couldn’t cut a thing like this out of paper,’ she said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘I want to eat it, but I can’t bear to. I ought to wrap some up and take them home for the girls to copy their patterns.’
Everyone laughed.
‘I’ll give you a jarful when you go home,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘For now, eat that one while it’s hot.’

segments.text: The others chose a piece or two of whatever they liked and had done. Grannie Liu had never eaten such things before, and they were so daintily made that they scarcely seemed to make a heap on the dishes. By the time she and Ban-er had tried a little of each, half a dishful was gone. Xi-feng had the rest gathered onto two dishes and into a compartmented box, and sent to Wen-guan and the others. Just then the nurse brought Da-jie in her arms, and everyone amused the child for a while. Da-jie had been playing with a large pomelo. When she caught sight of the finger citron Ban-er was holding, she wanted that instead. A maid coaxed her, saying she would fetch it, but Da-jie could not wait and began to cry. Everyone hurried to give Ban-er the pomelo and coax the citron from him. Only when Da-jie had it did she stop. Ban-er had been playing with the citron for some time and now had both hands full of fruit to eat. The pomelo, so round and fragrant, seemed even more fun. He went off kicking it about like a ball and wanted the citron no longer. After tea, Grandmother Jia and the others took Grannie Liu on to Green Bower Hermitage.

segments.text: Adamantina hurried out to welcome them. In the courtyard they found the flowers and trees flourishing.
‘You can tell these are people devoted to religious practice,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘With nothing else to do, they are always tending things. It looks even better than anywhere else.’
As she spoke, she made her way towards the eastern meditation hall. Adamantina smilingly invited them further in.

‘We’ve just been eating meat and drinking wine,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘You have the Bodhisattva in there. It would be a sin to offend him. We’ll sit here. Bring us some of your good tea, and we’ll leave after a cup.’

Adamantina hurried to brew it. Bao-yu watched closely to see how she went about things. She herself carried a little begonia-shaped tea tray of carved lacquer, picked out in gold with cloud-dragons offering long life. On it stood a small lidded cup in five-colour Chenghua ware, which she presented to Grandmother Jia.
‘I don’t drink Lu’an tea,’ said Grandmother Jia.
‘I know,’ Adamantina answered with a smile. ‘This is Old Man’s Eyebrows.’
Grandmother Jia took it and asked what water she had used.
‘Rainwater collected and kept from last year,’ Adamantina replied, smiling.
Grandmother Jia drank half the cup, then smilingly passed it to Grannie Liu.
‘Try this tea.’
Grannie Liu swallowed the rest in one gulp.
‘It’s good enough,’ she said, laughing, ‘but a little weak. It would be better if you boiled it up stronger.’
Grandmother Jia and the others all laughed.

segments.text: The rest were served in matching thin-bodied white lidded bowls from the imperial kilns. Adamantina tugged at the fronts of Bao-chai’s and Dai-yu’s clothes, and the two followed her out. Bao-yu quietly came after them. She invited them into a side room, where Bao-chai sat on the couch and Dai-yu on Adamantina’s rush meditation cushion. Adamantina herself fanned the little stove until the water boiled, then made a separate pot of tea. Bao-yu came in, smiling.
‘So you’re having private tea all to yourselves!’
‘Here you are again, cadging tea,’ the two girls said, laughing. ‘There’s none for you.’
Adamantina was just going to fetch cups when the old woman who served at the hermitage came in with the cups from the other room.
‘Don’t put that Chenghua cup away,’ Adamantina told her at once. ‘Leave it outside.’

Bao-yu understood: because Grannie Liu had drunk from it, she thought it dirty and would not have it. Then he saw her bring out two other cups. One had a single handle at the side, and was engraved with the three characters for ‘Banpao cup’ in clerical script. On the back was a line of small regular characters: ‘A treasured plaything of Wang Kai of the Jin’; and another line of small characters read, ‘Seen in the imperial treasury by Su Shi of Meishan, in the fourth month of the fifth year of Yuanfeng of the Song.’

segments.text: Adamantina filled the Banpao cup and handed it to Bao-chai. The other was shaped like a small begging-bowl and likewise bore three engraved characters, this time in the drooping-pearl style of seal script: ‘Xingxi bowl’. Adamantina filled it for Dai-yu. For Bao-yu she used the green-jade cup she herself had been drinking from every day.
‘They say that “in worldly matters all are equal”,’ Bao-yu said, laughing. ‘But those two get such rare old treasures, and I get a common vessel.’

segments.text: ‘A common vessel?’ said Adamantina. ‘I don’t mean to boast, but I doubt whether your whole house could produce another common vessel like this.’

‘As the saying goes, “Follow the customs of the place you’re in”,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Once we come here to you, gold, jade, pearls and jewels must naturally all be dismissed as common things.’
Adamantina was delighted at this. She found an enormous beaker carved from a single bamboo root as a coiling dragon, with nine bends, ten rings and a hundred and twenty joints.
‘This is the only one left,’ she said, laughing. ‘Could you drink this whole beaker?’
‘Yes, I could!’ Bao-yu answered eagerly, delighted.

‘Even if you could, I haven’t that much tea to waste,’ Adamantina said with a laugh. ‘Haven’t you heard? “One cup is for savouring; two make you a dolt merely quenching his thirst; three are for watering cattle and mules.” What would drinking this whole beaker make you?’
Bao-chai, Dai-yu and Bao-yu all laughed.

segments.text: Adamantina took the pot and poured only about a cupful into the great beaker. Bao-yu sipped it carefully. It did indeed seem incomparably light and delicate, and he could not praise it enough.
‘You have those two to thank for the tea you’ve had today,’ Adamantina said seriously. ‘If you came by yourself, I wouldn’t give you any.’
‘I know that very well,’ Bao-yu answered with a smile. ‘I don’t owe you any thanks. I need only thank them.’
‘Then you understand,’ said Adamantina.
Dai-yu asked, ‘Is this last year’s rainwater too?’
Adamantina gave a cold laugh.

‘Someone like you, and such a philistine! You can’t even tell the water by its taste. This is snow I collected from plum blossoms five years ago, when I was living at Panxiang Temple at Xuanmu. All I gathered filled that one ghost-face-blue flower jar. I could never bear to use it, so I buried it underground and only opened it this summer. I’ve used it once before. This is the second time. How can you not taste the difference? How could rainwater kept over from last year be as light and delicate as this? How could one drink it?’
Knowing her eccentric disposition, Dai-yu thought it best neither to say much more nor to sit much longer. When she had finished her tea, she asked Bao-chai to leave with her.

segments.text: Bao-yu spoke to Adamantina with a conciliatory smile.
‘That teacup may be dirty, but wouldn’t it be a pity simply to throw it away? Why not give it to the poor old woman? She could sell it and have something to live on. Would that do, do you think?’
Adamantina considered, then nodded.

‘Very well. Luckily I’ve never drunk from it myself. If I had used it, I would sooner smash it than give it to her. If you want her to have it, I shan’t interfere. I’ll give it to you. Only take it away quickly.’
‘Of course,’ said Bao-yu. ‘You couldn’t go talking to her and handing things back and forth. Then you would be dirtied too. Just leave it to me.’
Adamantina told someone to bring it and give it to him. Bao-yu took it.
‘When we’ve gone,’ he added, ‘shall I send a few of the boys to fetch some buckets of water from the stream to wash the ground?’
‘That would be better still,’ Adamantina said, smiling. ‘Only tell them to leave the water by the wall outside the hermitage gate. They mustn’t come in.’
‘Of course not.’
He slipped the cup into his sleeve, then gave it to a little maid from Grandmother Jia’s rooms to hold.
‘When Grannie Liu goes home tomorrow, give her this to take with her.’
By the time he had made this clear, Grandmother Jia had come out and was ready to leave.

segments.text: Adamantina made little effort to keep them. She saw them through the hermitage gate, then turned back and shut it. We shall say no more of her. Grandmother Jia, feeling tired, told Lady Wang and Ying-chun and her sisters to keep Aunt Xue company over some more wine, while she went to rest at Sweet-rice Village. Xi-feng at once sent for the little bamboo chair. Grandmother Jia sat down in it, and two serving-women lifted it and carried her off, surrounded by Xi-feng, Li Wan and a crowd of maids and older women. We shall leave them there. Aunt Xue now took her leave too. Lady Wang dismissed Wen-guan and the others, and had the compartmented food-boxes distributed among the maids. She herself took the opportunity to rest, reclining informally on the couch where Grandmother Jia had been sitting. She told a little maid to lower the blind, then to massage her legs.
‘If there’s any word from Her Old Ladyship, call me.’
With that, she too fell asleep where she lay.

segments.text: Bao-yu, Xiang-yun and the others watched the maids set the food-boxes on the rocks. Some sat on the rocks, some on the grass, some leaned against trees, and some settled by the water. It was a lively gathering. Presently Faithful came to take Grannie Liu round the garden, and everyone hurried after them to enjoy the fun. When they reached the archway bearing the words ‘Villa for the Family Visit’, Grannie Liu exclaimed:
‘Oh, my! There’s a great temple here too!’
She dropped to the ground and kowtowed. They doubled up with laughter.
‘What are you laughing at? I know all the characters on that arch. We have plenty of temples like this where I come from, with just such archways. The writing is the name of the temple.’
‘Then tell us which temple this is,’ they said, laughing.

segments.text: Grannie Liu looked up and pointed to the inscription.
‘Aren’t those the four characters for “Precious Hall of the Jade Emperor”?’

They laughed, clapping their hands and stamping their feet, and were ready to tease her further when a sudden rumbling began in Grannie Liu’s belly. She hastily caught hold of a little maid, asked for two sheets of paper and started undoing her clothes. Still laughing, everyone cried out:
‘You can’t do that here!’
They quickly told an older serving-woman to take her off towards the north-east. Having shown her where to go, the woman was glad to slip away and rest.

segments.text: Grannie Liu had drunk some wine, and rice wine did not agree with her constitution. Moreover, she had eaten a great deal of rich food, then drunk several bowls of tea to quench her thirst. A thorough bout of diarrhoea was the result. She had to squat for a long time before she was finished. Coming out of the privy, she felt the wine take hold in the breeze. At her age, too, rising suddenly after squatting so long made her eyes swim and her head spin. She could no longer make out the way.

When she reached a building, she could find no door. After searching for some time, she noticed a stretch of bamboo trellis.
‘They have bean frames here too,’ she thought.

segments.text: Still thinking this, she followed the flower trellis until she found a moon gate and went through. Suddenly a narrow pool lay before her, only seven or eight chi wide, with stone banks and clear green water flowing away to one side. A slab of white stone spanned it. Grannie Liu crossed the slab, followed the pebble walk round two bends and came to a door. She went in, and there, facing her, was a girl coming to meet her with a broad smile.
‘You girls left me behind,’ Grannie Liu said at once, smiling. ‘I’ve had to knock my head about finding my way here.’
The girl made no answer. Grannie Liu hurried forward to take her hand. Thump! She struck the wooden partition and gave her head a painful knock. Looking closely, she saw that it was a painting.
‘So paintings can stand right out, as alive as that!’ she thought.
She went on looking and thinking, then felt it with her hand. It was perfectly flat all over. She nodded and gave two sighs of wonder.

segments.text: Only when she turned round did she find a small doorway hung with a soft spring-green curtain scattered with flowers. Grannie Liu lifted it and went in. Looking up, she saw that the walls on every side were all intricate openwork, with qin, swords, vases and incense burners set against them, brocade coverings and gauze screens, glittering gold and gleaming pearls. Even the bricks beneath her feet were green and carved with flowers. Her eyes were more dazzled than ever. She looked for a door to get out, but where was there a door? Bookshelves on her left, a screen on her right. At last she found a doorway behind the screen and turned through it, only to see her daughter’s mother-in-law coming in from outside to meet her. Grannie Liu was astonished.
‘You must have wondered why I hadn’t come home these last few days. Fancy your finding your way here! Which of the young ladies brought you in?’
Her fellow grandmother merely smiled, without answering.
‘You’ve seen so little of the world!’ Grannie Liu said with a laugh. ‘The moment you saw the lovely flowers in this garden, you couldn’t rest till you’d stuck them all over your head.’
Still the other woman said nothing. Suddenly a thought struck her.
‘I’ve often heard that very rich families have a thing called a dressing-mirror. Could that be me in the mirror?’
She put out a hand to feel it and looked more closely. So it was: the mirror was set in the middle of a purple sandalwood partition, carved in openwork on all four sides.

segments.text: ‘But if this blocks the way, how am I to get out?’ she said, feeling about with her hands as she spoke.

The mirror had a Western mechanism by which it could be opened and closed. As Grannie Liu groped about, she happened to press with just the right force in just the right place. The catch sprang, the mirror swung aside and a doorway appeared. Astonished and delighted, she stepped through. There before her was a bed with the most exquisite hangings. By now she was thoroughly tipsy and tired from walking. She plumped herself down on the bed, meaning only to rest for a moment. But she could not help herself: she swayed backwards and forwards, her eyes grew dim, and, rolling onto her side, she fell fast asleep on the bed.

segments.text: Meanwhile the others had waited in vain for her return. Ban-er, finding his grandmother gone, began to cry in distress.
‘Surely she hasn’t fallen into the privy?’ they said, laughing. ‘Send someone to look, quickly.’
Two serving-women were sent, but came back saying she was not there. They searched everywhere without finding her. Aroma thought over the paths she might have taken.

‘She must be drunk and have lost her way, and gone down this path into our back courtyard. If she went through the flower trellis and in at the back door, she might bump her head, but at least the little maids would know. If she missed the trellis and went further south-west, it would be all right if she found a way out; if not, she could wander round for a good long time. I’d better go and see.’
Thinking this, she went back and called out as she entered the House of Green Delights. But the little maids who should have been in the rooms had slipped off to play.

segments.text: Aroma went straight indoors. As she turned past the lattice partition with its varied patterns, she heard thunderous snoring. She hurried in. The room smelt of wine and farts. Looking round, she saw Grannie Liu sprawled on her back across the bed, arms and legs flung wide. Aroma was badly startled. She rushed over and shook her awake with all her might. Grannie Liu opened her eyes in alarm. At the sight of Aroma she scrambled up.
‘I’ve done wrong, miss! But I haven’t dirtied the bed or the curtains.’

As she spoke, she brushed at them with her hand. Afraid of attracting attention and letting Bao-yu hear of it, Aroma waved at her to be quiet. She quickly put three or four handfuls of Baihe incense into the tripod burner and replaced its cover. After tidying a little, relieved that there had been no vomiting, she said with a quiet smile:
‘It’s all right. I’m here. Come out with me.’
Grannie Liu followed her into the little maids’ room. Aroma told her to sit down.
‘Just say you were drunk and lay down on the rockery stones for a nap.’
Grannie Liu agreed and said she understood.

segments.text: Aroma gave her two bowls of tea. Only then did she feel sober again.
‘Which young lady’s bedroom is this, so beautiful?’ she asked. ‘It was like being in a heavenly palace.’
Aroma smiled a little.
‘That? It’s Master Bao’s bedroom.’

Grannie Liu was too frightened to say a word. Aroma took her out by the front. When they met the others, she merely said she had found her asleep on the grass and brought her back. Nobody pursued the matter, and that was that.

Feeling languid, she would not eat, but returned to her own rooms to rest in the little open bamboo carrying-chair. She told Xi-feng and the others to have their supper, and only then did the women go back into the garden.
