segments.text: The girls went back into the garden, ate their meal and dispersed. There is nothing more to tell of them for the moment.
Grannie Liu first took Ban-er to see Xi-feng.

‘We really must go home early tomorrow. It’s only been two or three days, but in that little while I’ve seen and tasted and heard things I never knew of in all my life. Her Old Ladyship and you, Madam, and all the young ladies, even the girls in each of the apartments, have been so kind to a poor old woman. When I get home I’ve nothing to repay you with. All I can do is buy some good incense and pray to the Buddha for you every day, that you may all live to a hundred. That will be my way of showing what I feel.’

‘Don’t be too pleased with yourself,’ said Xi-feng, smiling. ‘It’s all because of you that Her Old Ladyship has caught a chill. She’s lying down, saying she feels unwell. And our Da-jie has caught cold too. She’s got a fever.’
Grannie Liu sighed in concern.
‘Her Old Ladyship’s getting on in years. She’s not used to so much exertion.’
‘She’s never enjoyed herself as much as she did yesterday,’ said Xi-feng.

segments.text: ‘She often goes into the garden, but usually she just sits in one or two places and comes back. Yesterday, because you were here and she wanted to show you round, she walked over more than half of it. Da-jie went looking for me, and Her Ladyship gave her a piece of cake. Who would have thought that eating it out in the wind would bring on a fever?’

‘The little miss doesn’t often go into the garden, I expect,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘It’s a strange place to her, and little ones oughtn’t to go into strange places. She’s not like our children. Once they can walk, there isn’t a graveyard they won’t run about in. For one thing, the wind may have struck her. Then again, she’s so pure herself, and her eyes are pure too: she may have come upon some spirit. If you ask me, you ought to look it up in the book about spirits. She may have been troubled by one.’

segments.text: This reminded Xi-feng of something. She told Patience to fetch The Jade Casket Almanac and sent for Sunshine to read it. He turned over the pages for a while, then read out:

‘“The twenty-fifth day of the eighth month. The sick person has encountered a flower spirit in the south-east. Take forty sheets of paper money in five colours and go forty paces to the south-east to send it away. Most auspicious.”’
‘Exactly!’ said Xi-feng, laughing. ‘What else would you find in the garden but a flower spirit? I expect Her Old Ladyship met one too.’

She ordered two sets of paper money to be brought and summoned two people, one to send the evil spirits away for Grandmother Jia and the other for Da-jie. Sure enough, the child was soon sleeping peacefully.
‘There’s no denying that you older people have seen more of life,’ said Xi-feng with a smile. ‘My Da-jie is always falling ill. I don’t know why.’

‘That does happen,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘Children brought up in rich households are generally too delicate. Naturally they can’t bear the least little hardship. And a child can’t stand having too much honour paid to her, either.

segments.text: ‘Love her a little less, Madam, and she’ll be all right.’

‘There’s something in that too. Now I think of it, she hasn’t got a name yet. You give her one. First, she can borrow a little of your long life; and then, you’re country people and, don’t be offended, you do have a harder time of it. A name given her by someone poor might just keep her troubles down.’
Grannie Liu thought for a moment, then smiled.
‘When was she born?’
‘That’s just it. Her birthday’s an unlucky one. It happens to be the seventh day of the seventh month.’

‘Why, that’s just right!’ Grannie Liu said eagerly. ‘Call her Qiao-ge. It’s what they call fighting poison with poison, or fire with fire. You must use my name for her, Madam. She’ll live to a hundred, I’m sure. Later on, when she’s grown up and everyone has a family and a livelihood of their own, if things should ever go against her, her troubles will turn to blessings and bad luck to good. It will all come from that word “Qiao”.’
Xi-feng was naturally delighted. She thanked her warmly, then said with a smile:
‘Let’s only pray she fulfils your words.’
She called Patience and told her:
‘We’ve things to do tomorrow and may not have a moment to spare.

segments.text: ‘While you have time, get Grannie’s presents ready, so that she can leave comfortably first thing in the morning.’
‘You mustn’t go to any more expense,’ Grannie Liu protested. ‘I’ve been a trouble to you for several days already. If I take things away as well, I shall feel worse than ever.’
‘There’s nothing much,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Only ordinary things. Good or bad, take them with you. They’ll give the neighbours something to look at. You’ll have something to show for your trip to town.’
Patience came over.
‘Come and have a look in here, Grannie.’

segments.text: Grannie Liu hurried after her into the next room. Half the kang was piled with things. Patience picked them up one by one to show her.

‘Here’s the bolt of blue-green gauze you asked for yesterday. Mrs Lian has added a piece of pale-blue solid-ground gauze for the lining. Here are two lengths of pongee, good for jackets or skirts. There are two bolts of silk in this bundle, so you can have new clothes for the New Year. This box has all sorts of pastries made in the palace, some you’ve tasted and some you haven’t. Take them home and put them out on plates when you have visitors. They’re rather better than the ones you can buy there. These are the two sacks you brought the fruit and vegetables in yesterday. This one now has two dou of non-glutinous rice from the imperial fields. You won’t find better for making porridge. The other has fruit from the garden and all sorts of dried fruit. This packet is eight taels of silver. All those are from Mrs Lian. These two packets have fifty taels each, a hundred altogether. They’re from Her Ladyship. She says you’re to use the money to set up a little business or buy a few mu of land, so that you won’t have to depend on relations and friends any more.’
Then she lowered her voice and smiled.
‘These two jackets and two skirts, the four head-cloths and this packet of embroidery thread are from me, Grannie.

segments.text: ‘The clothes aren’t new, but I haven’t worn them very much. If they’re not good enough for you, I wouldn’t presume.’

Every time Patience named an article, Grannie Liu invoked the Buddha. She had done so several thousand times already. Now, finding that Patience too was giving her all these things, and speaking so modestly about it, she invoked him again in her eagerness to reply.

‘What are you saying, miss? Me turn up my nose at such lovely things! Even if I had the money, I couldn’t buy things like these. Only I’m so ashamed. It doesn’t seem right to take them, but if I don’t, I’m throwing your kindness back in your face.’

‘Don’t talk as though we were strangers,’ Patience said, smiling. ‘I wouldn’t do this if I didn’t think of you as one of us. Take them without worrying. I’m going to ask you for something too. At New Year, just bring us some of your dried vegetables: those dried huitiaocai greens, cowpeas, flat beans, aubergines, strips of gourd, a little of each. Everyone here likes them, from the highest to the lowest. That will do. Nothing else at all. Don’t go to any unnecessary trouble.’
Grannie Liu promised, thanking her over and over again.

segments.text: ‘Now you just go and get your sleep,’ said Patience. ‘I’ll pack everything properly and leave it here. First thing tomorrow I’ll have the boys hire a cart and load it up. There’s nothing at all for you to worry about.’

Grannie Liu’s gratitude knew no bounds. She went back to thank Xi-feng again and again and take her leave, then spent the night in Grandmother Jia’s quarters. Early next morning she washed and combed her hair and was ready to say goodbye. As Grandmother Jia was unwell, everyone came to enquire after her, and someone was sent out to summon a doctor. Presently a serving-woman announced his arrival. The old nurses asked Grandmother Jia to sit behind the curtain.
‘I’m an old woman now,’ she said. ‘I could be the mother of any fellow like that. Am I to be afraid of him? Don’t draw the curtain. Let him examine me as I am.’
The women brought a small table, laid a little cushion on it and sent word for the doctor to be admitted.

segments.text: Soon Jia Zhen, Jia Lian and Jia Rong appeared, bringing Doctor Wang with them. He did not venture on to the central path but kept to the side and followed Jia Zhen up to the steps. Two women were already holding up the portière; two more led the way inside. Bao-yu too came out to meet him.

Grandmother Jia sat upright on a couch in a jacket of pearl-curled lambskin faced with blue-green crinkled silk. Four little maids, still too young to wear their hair long, stood to either side with fly-whisks, a rinsing-bowl and other articles. Five or six old nurses were ranged on either hand like outspread wings. Behind the green gauze screen he could dimly make out a crowd of figures in red and green, wearing jewelled hairpins and pearls. Doctor Wang dared not raise his eyes. He stepped forward at once and paid his respects.
Seeing his sixth-rank robes, Grandmother Jia knew that he was an imperial physician, and greeted him with a smile.
‘How are you, Doctor?’
Then she asked Jia Zhen, ‘What is this gentleman’s surname?’
‘Wang,’ Jia Zhen and the others hastened to reply.
‘Wang Jun-xiao, who used to be head of the Imperial Medical Academy, was very good at taking pulses.’
The doctor bent low, his head bowed, and replied with a smile:
‘He was my paternal grandfather’s younger brother, Your Old Ladyship.’

Doctor Wang sat with one knee bent under him and, his head tilted, felt her pulse for some time. He then examined the other wrist, half rose with his head bowed and withdrew.

segments.text: ‘Thank you for your trouble,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Zhen, take him out and see that he has some tea.’
Jia Zhen, Jia Lian and the others replied with repeated assurances of obedience and escorted Doctor Wang to the outer study.

‘Her Old Ladyship has nothing else the matter with her,’ he said. ‘She has merely caught a little chill. There is really no need for medicine. Somewhat plainer food and a little extra warmth will put her right. I’ll leave a prescription here. If she feels like taking it, have one dose prepared according to the prescription. If she can’t be bothered, never mind.’
He drank his tea and wrote the prescription. Just as he was about to leave, the wet-nurse appeared carrying Da-jie.
‘Have a look at us too, Doctor,’ she said, smiling.
He rose at once. Leaving the child in her nurse’s arms, he supported her hand with his left and felt her pulse with his right. Then he touched her head and asked her to put out her tongue.

‘The little lady will scold me again for saying so,’ he said with a smile, ‘but all she needs is to be left quietly alone and go without a couple of meals. There’s no need for a decoction. I’ll send some pills over. Grind them up in ginger broth for her at bedtime and let her take it. That will do.’
With that he took his leave.

segments.text: Seeing that there was nothing more to be done, Grannie Liu came forward to take her leave of Grandmother Jia.
‘Come again when you have time,’ said Grandmother Jia. She called Faithful. ‘See Grannie Liu safely out, and look after her properly. I’m not well enough to see you off myself.’
Grannie Liu thanked her, said goodbye once more and went out with Faithful. In the servants’ room Faithful pointed to a bundle on the kang.

‘These are some clothes of Her Old Ladyship’s, given her on birthdays and festivals in past years. She never wears clothes other people have made for her, but it seems a pity to leave them lying there. They’ve never been worn, not even once. Yesterday she told me to get out two sets for you to take away. Give them to someone, or wear them yourselves at home. Don’t laugh at them. This box has the little pastries you asked for. And this packet has the medicines you spoke about the other day: Meihua Dianshe Pills, Zijin Tablets, Huoluo Pills and Cuisheng Baoming Pills. Each kind is wrapped in its own prescription, and they’re all inside the same bundle. Here are two purses for you as well. Keep them for fun.’
She loosened the drawstrings and took out two little silver pieces with brush, ingot and ruyi motifs to show her.
‘You can have the purses,’ she added with a smile, ‘but leave these for me.’
Grannie Liu was already overjoyed and had invoked the Buddha several thousand times more. On hearing this she said:
‘Of course, miss. You keep them.’
Seeing that she had taken it seriously, Faithful put them back into the purses and laughed.
‘I’m only teasing you. I’ve plenty.

segments.text: ‘What good did I do in some former life, to be treated like this today?’
She took the cup.
‘The clothes you changed into when I had you take a bath the other day were mine,’ said Faithful. ‘If you don’t mind them, I have a few more you can have.’

Grannie Liu thanked her eagerly again. Faithful did indeed fetch two more garments and pack them for her. Grannie Liu wanted to go into the garden to thank Bao-yu and the girls and say goodbye, and to call on Lady Wang too.
‘There’s no need,’ said Faithful. ‘They aren’t seeing anyone just now. I’ll tell them for you later. Come again when you have time.’
She summoned an old serving-woman.
‘Get two boys from the inner gate to help Grannie carry her things out.’

The woman agreed and went with Grannie Liu to Xi-feng’s quarters to collect the rest. At the side gate she had the boys carry everything outside and saw Grannie Liu right into the cart. There we may leave her.

segments.text: After breakfast Bao-chai and the others had again enquired after Grandmother Jia and were returning to the garden. Where the paths divided, Bao-chai called to Dai-yu:
‘Come with me, Little Pin-pin. There’s something I want to ask you.’
Dai-yu went with her to Allspice Court. Once they were in the room, Bao-chai sat down and smiled.
‘On your knees. I’m going to question you.’
Dai-yu had no idea why.
‘Look at Bao-chai! She’s gone mad!’ she said, laughing. ‘What do you want to question me about?’

segments.text: Bao-chai gave a little scoffing laugh.
‘A fine young lady you are! Such a nicely sheltered girl! What are these things that come out of your mouth? You’d better confess.’
Still bewildered, Dai-yu kept laughing, though she was beginning to feel uneasy.
‘What have I ever said? You’re only trying to find something against me. Tell me what it is, then.’
‘Still playing the innocent!’ said Bao-chai with a smile. ‘What was it you said in the drinking game yesterday? I can’t imagine where you found it.’

Dai-yu thought back. Only then did she remember her carelessness of the previous day, when she had quoted those two lines from The Peony Pavilion and The Western Chamber. She blushed, went over and put her arms round Bao-chai.
‘Dear cousin,’ she said, smiling, ‘I didn’t realise. They just slipped out. You must teach me better. I won’t say them again.’

segments.text: ‘I don’t know them either,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘They sounded so strange when you said them that I wanted you to explain.’
‘Dear cousin, don’t tell anyone. I’ll never say them again.’

Seeing her scarlet with embarrassment and begging so earnestly, Bao-chai would not press her any further. She drew her down to sit and have some tea, then began to speak to her gently and without haste.

‘What sort of person do you think I am? I was naughty too. When I was seven or eight I was quite a handful. We’re a reading family, after all. My grandfather liked collecting books. There were a great many of us in the household then, boys and girls all together, and none of us wanted to read the proper books. Some of the boys liked poetry and some liked lyrics. We had everything: The Western Chamber, The Lute, A Hundred Yuan Plays, all those sorts of books. They read them on the sly, keeping it from us, and we read them on the sly, keeping it from them. Then the grown-ups found out. There were beatings and scoldings, and books were burnt, and only then did we give them up.

segments.text: ‘That’s why girls like us are better off not knowing how to read. Even a man is better off without books if they don’t teach him how to behave, let alone you or me. Writing poems and practising calligraphy aren’t really our business. For that matter, they aren’t really a man’s business either. A man should read to learn sound principles, help the state and govern the people. That would be something. But you don’t hear of men like that nowadays. Reading only makes them worse. The books do them harm, and it’s a pity, but they abuse the books as well. They’d be better off farming or trading. At least they wouldn’t do much damage that way.

Dai-yu sat with her head lowered over her tea. In her heart she acknowledged the force of what Bao-chai said, and could only answer, ‘Yes.’
Just then Su-yun came in.
‘My mistress asks if you two young ladies will come and discuss something important.

segments.text: Li Wan smiled when she saw them.
‘Our society has hardly begun, and already someone’s trying to wriggle out. Our fourth young lady wants a year’s leave.’
‘It’s all because of what Grandmother said yesterday,’ said Dai-yu, laughing. ‘Asking her to paint the garden! Of course she jumped at the chance to take leave.’
‘You can’t blame Grandmother,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘It all came from something Grannie Liu said.’
‘Of course!’ Dai-yu put in at once. ‘All because of something she said. What sort of grannie is she, anyway? Just call her Mother Locust and be done with it.’
Everyone laughed.

‘When Xi-feng has finished with a subject, you’d think there could be nothing left to say,’ said Bao-chai, smiling. ‘Luckily she can’t read and doesn’t know much about books, so hers are only ordinary street jokes. But there’s Little Pin-pin with that wicked tongue of hers. She uses the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals: takes the essence of a vulgar joke, cuts away the excess, gives it a polish and finds a comparison. Every phrase tells.

segments.text: ‘Those three characters, “Mother Locust”, bring back the whole scene yesterday. How she thinks of them so quickly!’
‘Your commentary is quite a match for either of them,’ the others said, laughing.
‘I asked you here to decide how much leave we should give her,’ said Li Wan. ‘I offered a month, but she says it isn’t enough. What do you think?’

‘A year isn’t too much, if you look at it properly,’ said Dai-yu. ‘It took a year just to build this garden. Naturally it will take two to paint it. There’s the ink to grind, and the brush to dip, and the paper to spread out, and the colours to put on, and then there’s…’
By now they all knew she was teasing Xi-chun, and broke in, laughing:
‘What else is there?’
Dai-yu could no longer keep from laughing herself.
‘Then there’s painting it all, ever so slowly, just as it is. That must take two years!’
They clapped their hands and laughed without stopping.
‘That last bit is the best,’ said Bao-chai. ‘“Then there’s painting it all, ever so slowly.”

‘It’s all your praise that makes her so pleased with herself,’ Xi-chun said. ‘Now even I’m something for her to make fun of.’
Dai-yu promptly took her hand, laughing.
‘Tell me, are you only painting the garden, or are you putting all of us in too?’

‘It was only going to be the garden,’ said Xi-chun. ‘But yesterday Grandmother said that with no one in it, it would look like a plan of a house. ‘The figures are easy enough,’ Dai-yu said. ‘It’s the insects you’re no good at.’
‘What nonsense!’ said Li Wan. ‘Where would insects come into this?

segments.text: ‘A bird or two, perhaps, to fill it out.’
‘You can leave out the other insects,’ Dai-yu said with a laugh, ‘but if yesterday’s Mother Locust isn’t in it, won’t the record be incomplete?’
They all laughed again. Dai-yu held both hands to her chest, laughing as she spoke.
‘Do hurry up and paint it. I’ve even got the inscription ready. We’ll give it a name: “Taking the Locust to a Feast”.’

This sent them into still louder laughter. They rocked backwards and forwards, until suddenly there was a thump. Something had fallen. They looked round in alarm and saw what had happened. Xiang-yun had been leaning with her whole weight over the back of a chair, laughing. The chair had not been standing squarely, and, before she knew it, their weight had shifted the wrong way. Both she and the chair had tipped sideways to the east. Luckily the wooden partition stopped them from reaching the floor. At the sight, the others laughed harder than ever. Bao-yu hurried to help her up, and only then did the laughter gradually subside.

Bao-yu gave Dai-yu a look. She understood and went into the inner room, lifted the mirror-cover and looked at herself. The hair at her temples was a little loose. She quickly opened Li Wan’s toilet-box, took out the small smoothing-brush and passed it over her hair a couple of times before the mirror. Having put everything back, she came out and pointed at Li Wan.
‘You’re supposed to lead us in our sewing and teach us how to behave. Instead you call us here to make a great noisy game of everything.’
‘Just listen to her!’ Li Wan said, laughing.

segments.text: Dai-yu was already blushing. She caught hold of Bao-chai.
‘Let’s give her a year’s leave.’

‘Listen to me,’ said Bao-chai. ‘I have a fair proposal. Our Lotus Pavilion girl can paint, but only a few freehand strokes. To make a picture of this garden, you need someone who already has a few landscapes composed in their mind. The garden itself is like a painting. The rocks and trees, the towers and houses, near and far, crowded or spread apart, are neither too many nor too few. They are just right as they are. But if you simply copy it all on to paper, it’s bound not to come off. You have to consider the space on the paper, what is near and what is far, how much to put in and how little, what is principal and what is secondary. Where something needs adding, add it; where something needs taking away, take it away; what should be hidden must be hidden, and what should show must show. Once you have a first sketch, you must look it over and weigh everything up before you have a proper design.

‘Then, secondly, all those towers and houses have to be drawn with ruled lines. One moment’s carelessness, and the railings lean, the pillars fall, the doors and windows turn upside down and the steps come apart. You might even have a table squeezed into a wall or a flowerpot sitting on a curtain. Then your picture really would be a joke.

segments.text: ‘Thirdly, when you put in the figures, you must think about their spacing and their different heights too. The folds of clothes, the ribbons on skirts, fingers and feet are especially important. One careless stroke, and you’ve given someone a swollen hand or a twisted leg. Getting the face coloured and the hair drawn is a small matter by comparison. I think the whole thing is very difficult. A year’s leave is too much, but a month is too little. Let’s give her six months and appoint Cousin Bao to help. Not because he knows enough to teach her to paint: that would only make matters worse. But whenever there’s something she doesn’t understand, or can’t decide where to put, he can take it outside and ask those gentlemen who know how to paint. That will make it easier.’

segments.text: Bao-yu was the first to respond, delighted.
‘Exactly! Zhan Zi-liang is excellent at finely drawn buildings, and no one can touch Cheng Ri-xing for beautiful women. I’ll go and ask them now.’
‘I call you Busy over Nothing,’ said Bao-chai. ‘The moment I mention it, you’re off to ask. Wait till we’ve settled everything. What are you going to paint on, to begin with?’
‘We have Snow-wave paper. It’s large and takes ink well.’
Bao-chai gave a scoffing laugh.

‘Didn’t I say you were no use? Snow-wave paper is for calligraphy, or freehand painting, or Southern School landscapes, if you know how to do them. It takes ink and stands up to texture strokes. But use it for this, and it won’t take the colours properly; it’s hard to lay a wash on, too. You’ll get a poor painting and waste good paper. I’ll tell you what to do.

segments.text: ‘When the garden was being built, there was a detailed plan. It was only drawn by the workmen, but the placing and direction of everything are right. Ask Aunt Wang for it. Then ask Xi-feng for a piece of heavy silk the same size as the paper and have one of the gentlemen size it with alum. Get him to make a sketch from the plan, leaving things out and adding things where necessary, and put in the figures. You’ll have to let them mix the blues and greens and prepare the gold and silver paint too. You’ll also need to light a separate brazier, ready for melting the glue, drawing off the glue solution and washing brushes. Then you’ll need a large oil-painted work-table, with felt spread over it. You haven’t all the dishes or brushes you need either. You must get a fresh set of everything.’

‘When have I ever had all those painting things?’ said Xi-chun. ‘I just paint with whatever writing-brush comes to hand. Even for colours, I only have ochre, Guangdong indigo, gamboge and rouge, those four. Apart from that, there are two colour brushes, and that’s all.’
‘You should have said so before.

segments.text: ‘I still have some of those things,’ Bao-chai went on. ‘Only you had no use for them, and they’d have lain idle if I’d given them to you. I’ve been keeping them for you, and now that you need them I can let you have some. But you should save them for painting fans. It would be a pity to use them up on a picture as large as this. Today I’ll make you a list. Take it to Grandmother and ask for what’s on it. You probably don’t know everything that’s needed. I’ll dictate and Cousin Bao can write.’

Bao-yu had already got brush and inkstone ready. Afraid he might not remember everything clearly, he had meant to write it down. At Bao-chai’s words he took up his brush with delight and listened attentively.
She dictated:

‘Four No. 1 flat brushes; four No. 2 flat brushes; four No. 3 flat brushes; four large wash brushes; four medium wash brushes; four small wash brushes; ten large southern crab-claw brushes; ten small crab-claw brushes; ten beard-and-eyebrow brushes; twenty large colour brushes; twenty small colour brushes; ten brushes for painting faces; twenty willow-twig brushes; four taels of arrowhead vermilion; four taels of southern ochre; four taels of mineral yellow; four taels of mineral blue; four taels of mineral green; four taels of bamboo-cast gamboge; eight taels of Guangdong indigo; four boxes of shell white; ten sheets of rouge; two hundred packets of dachi gold leaf; two hundred packets of qingjin painting colour; four taels of Guangyun glue; four taels of purified alum.

‘What do you know about it?’ Bao-chai said, laughing too.

segments.text: As she spoke she came over, pressed Dai-yu down on the kang and made to pinch her cheeks. Dai-yu laughed and begged for mercy.
‘Dear cousin, let me off! Little Pin-pin is young. She talks away without knowing what she ought to say. You’re older, you must teach me. If you won’t forgive me, who else can I ask?’
The others had no idea that there was more in this than they knew.
‘She sounds so pitiful,’ they laughed. ‘Even our hearts are melting. Do let her off.’
Bao-chai had only been playing. But when she heard Dai-yu bring in their earlier conversation about her indiscriminate reading, she could hardly go on rough-and-tumbling with her. She let her up.
‘You really are like an elder sister,’ Dai-yu said, smiling. ‘If it were me, I’d never let anyone off.’
Bao-chai pointed at her with a smile.
‘No wonder Grandmother dotes on you and everyone loves your cleverness. I’m growing very fond of you myself today. Come here and let me smooth your hair.’

Dai-yu obediently turned round, and Bao-chai smoothed it up with her hand. Watching beside them, Bao-yu thought this lovelier still. He could not help regretting that he had made Dai-yu brush back the hair at her temples earlier. He should have left it loose for Bao-chai to smooth now.

‘Now that it’s written, take it to Grandmother tomorrow. If we have the things in the house, well and good. If not, get some money and buy them. I’ll help you mix the colours.’
Bao-yu hastily put the list away.

segments.text: They talked of this and that for a while longer. After the evening meal they went to enquire after Grandmother Jia again. There had been nothing seriously wrong with her, only tiredness and a slight chill. After a day of keeping warm and resting, and one dose of medicine to disperse the chill, she was well again by evening.
To learn what happened on the following day, listen to the next chapter.

segments.text: Now Lady Wang saw that Grandmother Jia had merely caught a little chill that day in Prospect Garden. It was no serious illness: the doctor had been called, and two doses of medicine had put her right. Relieved, Lady Wang sent for Xi-feng and told her to prepare the things that were to be sent to Jia Zheng. While they were discussing this, a messenger came to summon them to Grandmother Jia. Lady Wang at once took Xi-feng over with her.

segments.text: ‘Are you feeling a little better now?’ Lady Wang asked again.
‘Much better today. I tasted the young pheasant broth you sent just now. It had quite a flavour. I ate two pieces of the meat as well, and felt all the better for it.’
‘That was Xi-feng’s offering to you,’ said Lady Wang, smiling. ‘She has a truly devoted heart. You haven’t wasted all the affection you’ve lavished on her.’
Grandmother Jia smiled and nodded.

‘It was good of her to think of it. If there’s any uncooked meat left, have another couple of pieces fried for me, nice and salty. They’ll give some flavour to my porridge. Good as that broth is, it doesn’t go with thin rice porridge.’

segments.text: Xi-feng promptly assented and sent someone to the kitchen with the order. Grandmother Jia turned back to Lady Wang with a smile.

‘This is all I sent for you about. The second is Feng’s birthday. The last two years I’d been meaning well beforehand to give her a birthday party, but each time some important business came up just as the day arrived, and it was allowed to pass. This year everyone is here, and I don’t suppose anything will happen. Let us all have a proper day’s enjoyment.’
‘I was thinking about it too,’ said Lady Wang. ‘Since you feel inclined, why don’t we settle it now?’

‘Whenever we’ve had a birthday before, no matter whose it was, we’ve all sent separate presents. It’s become rather commonplace, and somehow it makes us seem like strangers. I’ve thought of a new way today. It will be more friendly, and we can have a little fun out of it too.’

‘I thought we might copy the small households and each put in a share,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Whatever it comes to, that’s what we’ll spend. Wouldn’t that be fun?’

Zhen’s wife from the other mansion was to come too, along with Lai Da’s wife and the other married servants of standing who had charge of household affairs.

segments.text: Seeing Grandmother Jia in such good spirits, the maids and older women caught her excitement. They hurried off in different directions, some to invite, some to pass the word. In less time than it took to eat a meal, old and young, high and low, were crowded thickly into the room. Only Aunt Xue sat facing Grandmother Jia. Lady Xing and Lady Wang occupied the two chairs by the door. Five or six of the girls, including Bao-chai, sat on the kang; Bao-yu sat nestled in front of his grandmother. The floor was packed with people standing. Grandmother Jia promptly ordered a few small stools to be brought for Lai Da’s mother and several other elderly servants of standing. It was the Jia family’s custom to accord old servants who had attended the parents of the present generation greater consideration than the younger masters and mistresses. Thus You-shi and Xi-feng remained standing, while the three or four old women, including Lai Da’s mother, begged leave to sit and took the little stools.

segments.text: Smiling, Grandmother Jia repeated her proposal. Who among them would refuse to join in the fun? Besides, some were fond of Xi-feng and quite willing to do it; others were afraid of her and eager for a chance to ingratiate themselves. All could afford it. At the first mention, therefore, they cheerfully agreed.
‘I’ll give twenty taels,’ Grandmother Jia began.
‘I shall follow your example,’ said Aunt Xue, smiling. ‘Twenty taels from me too.’
‘We daren’t put ourselves on a level with you,’ said Lady Xing and Lady Wang. ‘We must come a step lower. Sixteen taels each will do.’

segments.text: ‘Then we must come a step lower still,’ You-shi and Li Wan said with a smile. ‘Twelve taels each.’
‘You’re a widow without a livelihood,’ Grandmother Jia hastily told Li Wan. ‘How could we drag you into paying for this? I’ll pay your share.’

‘Don’t get carried away, Grannie,’ Xi-feng said quickly, laughing. ‘Do the accounts before you take on anything more. You’ve already got two other shares to pay, and now you’re taking on another twelve taels for my elder sister-in-law. You’re enjoying saying it now; in a little while you’ll think it over and feel the pinch. Afterwards you’ll be saying, “All that money spent on Feng!”

segments.text: ‘Then you’ll think of some clever trick to wheedle three or four shares out of me to make it up on the quiet, and I shan’t know what’s happened.’
Everyone laughed.
‘Well, what would you have me do?’ Grandmother Jia asked, laughing too.

‘My birthday hasn’t come yet, and already I’ve had so much honour I’m quite uncomfortable with it. I’m not being asked to part with a single cash, and I feel dreadful putting all these people to such trouble. Why don’t I pay my elder sister-in-law’s share? Then on the day I shall only have to eat a little more, and I shall have had all the good of it.’
Lady Xing and the others thought this quite right, and Grandmother Jia consented.

‘There’s one other thing,’ Xi-feng went on, smiling. ‘Our Old Ancestress is giving twenty taels for herself, as well as Cousin Lin’s share and Brother Bao’s. Aunt is giving twenty for herself and Cousin Bao-chai’s share too. That’s fair enough. But our two ladies are only giving sixteen taels apiece, and neither is paying for anyone else. Their own shares are smaller to begin with. That doesn’t seem altogether fair. Our Old Ancestress is being done out of her money!’
‘My Feng is the one who takes my part!’ Grandmother Jia said at once, laughing. ‘Quite right!

segments.text: ‘If it hadn’t been for you, they’d have taken me in again.’
‘Just give the two children to the two ladies, one apiece,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Whatever contribution is fixed, let each lady pay one of their shares.’
‘That’s perfectly fair,’ Grandmother Jia said quickly. ‘We’ll do that.’
Lai Da’s mother rose hastily, smiling.

‘Well, this is turning things upside down! I feel indignant on Their Ladyships’ behalf. A son’s wife on one side, a brother’s daughter on the other, and instead of taking her mother-in-law’s and aunt’s part, she sides with someone else! The daughter-in-law has become a stranger, and the brother’s daughter has turned into an outsider’s niece.’
Grandmother Jia and all the others burst out laughing.
‘If the young mistresses give twelve taels,’ Lai Da’s mother went on, ‘then we ought to come a step below them.’
‘That won’t do,’ said Grandmother Jia.

segments.text: ‘You ought to be a step lower, it’s true, but I know you few are all rich women. Your rank may be lower, but you have more money than they do. You must pay the same as they do.’
The old women hastened to agree.
‘The girls need only make a token contribution,’ Grandmother Jia continued. ‘Let each give one month’s allowance.’
She turned and called Faithful.
‘You get a few of your people together too. Talk it over and bring your contributions.’
Faithful assented. Before long she returned with Patience, Aroma, Cai-xia and several younger maids. Some gave two taels, some one.
‘Aren’t you giving your mistress a birthday celebration yourself?’ Grandmother Jia asked Patience. ‘Why are you joining in this?’
‘I’ve made my own little arrangement for her separately,’ Patience replied with a smile. ‘This is the general fund, and I ought to give a share to that too.’
‘Now that is a good girl,’ said Grandmother Jia.
‘That’s everyone, high and low,’ Xi-feng said, smiling. ‘There are still the two aunts, though. We ought to ask if they want to contribute.

‘They’ll give two taels each.’

segments.text: ‘Bring the brushes and inkstone,’ Grandmother Jia said happily. ‘Let us work out exactly how much there is.’
You-shi meanwhile was scolding Xi-feng under her breath.
‘You insatiable little bitch! All these mothers-in-law and aunts putting up money for your birthday, and you’re still not satisfied. Why drag those two poor miserable creatures into it?’

‘Don’t talk nonsense,’ Xi-feng murmured back with a smile. ‘I’ll settle with you when we get out of here. Why should they be miserable? If they have any money, they’ll only pour it away on someone else. Better to make them contribute to our fun.’
By now the calculation was finished. They had collected more than a hundred and fifty taels in all.
‘A day’s plays and feasting won’t use all that,’ said Grandmother Jia.
‘With no outside guests and not many tables, it will pay for two or three days,’ said You-shi.

‘Let Feng say which troupe is best, and send for them,’ said Grandmother Jia.
‘We know our own troupe’s performances by heart,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Why don’t we spend a little and have an outside company for a change?’
‘I’m putting Zhen’s wife in charge of this,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Feng is not to have a single thing to worry about. It will only count if she can enjoy a whole day.’
You-shi assented. They talked a little longer, then, seeing that Grandmother Jia was tired, gradually took their leave.

segments.text: ‘You little creature, what a run of luck you’re having!’ You-shi said, laughing. ‘I wondered what business they were sending for us about, and it was nothing but this. As if paying weren’t enough, I’m to have all the worry too. How are you going to thank me?’
‘Don’t talk such rubbish. I didn’t send for you. What have I to thank you for? Afraid of a little trouble, are you? Go straight back to the old lady and ask her to appoint someone else.’
‘Just look how pleased with herself she is! I advise you to keep a little in reserve. Fill it too full and it spills over.’
They talked a while longer before parting.

segments.text: The silver was sent to the Ning mansion the next day. You-shi had only just risen and was washing and doing her hair. She asked who had brought it.
‘Mrs Lin,’ the maids replied.
You-shi told them to call her in. A maid went to the servants’ rooms and fetched Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife. You-shi had her sit on the footstool and, busy with her toilette, asked:
‘How much is there in this packet?’
‘This is the money from those of us below stairs. We put it together and brought it over first. Her Old Ladyship’s and Their Ladyships’ shares aren’t here yet.’
Just then the maids announced that Her Ladyship and Aunt Xue at the other mansion had sent people with their contributions.

‘Little hussies!’ You-shi scolded, laughing. ‘You remember every word that doesn’t matter. Yesterday the old lady happened to be in good spirits and deliberately chose to play at pooling our pennies like some small household. You’ve remembered that, and now it comes out of your mouths as solemn business! Hurry up and bring it in. See that the people have tea before you send them away.’
The maids assented and promptly brought in two packets. Bao-chai’s and Dai-yu’s shares were included.

‘And what about your elder mistress’s?’
‘When you go over, ma’am, you’ll find the money is all being paid out through Mrs Lian. It’s all included.’

segments.text: By now You-shi had finished dressing and ordered her carriage. Presently she reached the Rong mansion and went first to Xi-feng, who had already sealed up the silver and was just about to send it off.
‘Is it all there?’ You-shi asked.
‘Every bit. Hurry up and take it away. If it gets lost, I’m not responsible.’
‘I don’t quite trust you. I’d better count it in front of you.’
She did indeed count it against the list. Only Li Wan’s contribution was missing.
‘I knew you were up to some damned trick! Where’s your elder sister-in-law’s money?’
‘Isn’t there enough for you there?’ Xi-feng said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘One share short won’t matter. If you run short, I’ll give it to you then.’
‘You made a fine show in front of everyone yesterday, and today you’re trying to wriggle out of it with me. I won’t have it. I’ll simply go and ask the old lady.’
‘So that’s how hard you can be! Next time anything comes up, I’ll insist on every item being just so, and don’t you complain.’
‘So you can be frightened too! If it weren’t for all the attention you usually pay me, I certainly wouldn’t let you off.’
As she spoke, You-shi took out Patience’s contribution.
‘Patience, come here. Put your money away. If there isn’t enough, I’ll make up your share.’
Patience understood her meaning.
‘Please use it for now, ma’am. If there’s any left over, giving it to me afterwards will come to the same thing.’
‘Is your mistress the only one allowed to play tricks? Mayn’t I do a kindness?’
Patience had no choice but to take it.
‘Your mistress is so particular over every penny,’ You-shi went on. ‘What does she mean to do with all this money she gets together?

segments.text: ‘If she can’t spend it, she can take it into her coffin to spend there.’

Still talking, she set off for Grandmother Jia’s. She paid her respects and exchanged a few words, then went into Faithful’s room to discuss the arrangements. On how best to please Grandmother Jia, she deferred entirely to Faithful’s advice. They settled everything between them. As she was leaving, You-shi gave Faithful back her two taels as well.
‘We shan’t be able to spend even what we have.’

She went straight out and called on Lady Wang for a little talk. When Lady Wang went into the prayer room, she returned Cai-yun’s contribution too. Xi-feng was not there, so she presently gave Aunt Zhou and Aunt Zhao their money back as well. Neither dared accept it at first.
‘You poor things, where would you find money to spare? If Feng hears of it, I’ll answer for it.’
At that, they accepted with a thousand thanks. You-shi went straight out, got into her carriage and returned home. Of that we need say no more.

segments.text: In the blink of an eye it was the second day of the ninth month. Everyone in the Garden had heard that You-shi had arranged a splendid entertainment. There were to be not only plays but acrobatic performances and storytellers, men and women alike. They were all preparing for a day of fun.

‘Today is a regular meeting day of our society,’ Li Wan reminded the girls. ‘Don’t forget. Bao-yu hasn’t come either. I suppose he’s so taken up with the excitement that he’s thrown all our quiet refinements aside.’

‘He really has gone out. They say a friend has died, and he’s gone to pay a visit of condolence.’
‘Certainly not,’ said Tan-chun. ‘Whatever it is, there is no reason for him to go out today. Tell Aroma to come. I’ll ask her.’
Even as she spoke, Aroma appeared. Li Wan and the others all began:

‘Whatever business he had today, he ought not to have gone out. First, it’s Mrs Lian’s birthday. The old lady is making such an occasion of it, and everyone in both households is joining in. Yet off he goes! And second, this is the first regular meeting of our society. He hasn’t asked for leave. He’s simply gone off on his own!’

‘He told me last night,’ Aroma said with a sigh. ‘He had something important to do at the Prince of Beijing’s first thing this morning, and he’d come straight back. I tried to persuade him not to go, but he wouldn’t listen. Then this morning he asked for plain clothes. Perhaps some favourite concubine in the Prince’s household has died. I really don’t know.’
‘If that’s the case, he ought to go,’ said Li Wan and the others. ‘But he should have come back by now.’
They began discussing it among themselves.
‘Let us get on with our poems, and fine him when he comes back.’
They had hardly said this when a messenger arrived from Grandmother Jia to fetch them, and they all went to the front of the mansion.

segments.text: Aroma explained Bao-yu’s absence. Grandmother Jia was displeased and sent someone to bring him back.
Bao-yu, as it happened, had a private matter on his mind. The day before, he had instructed Tealeaf:

‘I’m going out early tomorrow. Have two horses ready and wait at the back gate. No one else is to come. Tell Li Gui I’ve gone to the Prince of Beijing’s. If anyone wants to look for me, he’s to stop them. There’s no need to come looking. He need only say they’ve kept me there and I shall certainly be back soon.’

Tealeaf could make nothing of it, but had to pass on the message as instructed. Sure enough, early that morning he was waiting with two horses at the back gate of the Garden. At daybreak Bao-yu came through the side gate, dressed from head to foot in plain clothes. Without a word he swung himself into the saddle, bent forward and went jolting off along the street. Tealeaf could only mount and whip his horse to catch up.
‘Where are we going?’ he called urgently from behind.
‘Where does this road lead?’ Bao-yu asked.
‘It’s the main road out of the north gate. There’s nothing but lonely country beyond. Nothing to amuse you there.’
Bao-yu nodded.
‘A lonely place is just what I want.’
He gave his horse another cut. Already it had rounded two corners and passed out through the city gate.

segments.text: More at a loss than ever, Tealeaf could only keep close behind. They rode seven or eight li without stopping. As the houses grew fewer, Bao-yu at last reined in and looked back.
‘Is there anywhere here that sells incense?’
‘There’s incense to be had. What sort do you want?’
‘Other kinds won’t do,’ Bao-yu said after thinking. ‘It must be sandalwood, yun and jiang.’
‘Those three will be hard to find,’ Tealeaf said, smiling.
Bao-yu was at a loss. Seeing his difficulty, Tealeaf asked:
‘What do you want it for? I’ve often seen loose incense in that little sachet of yours, Master Bao. Why don’t you have a look?’

This reminded Bao-yu. Reaching back, he pulled a sachet from his robe and felt inside. There were indeed two tiny fragments of chensu incense. He was delighted, though he thought it rather lacking in reverence. On second thoughts, something he had carried on his own person was better than anything bought. He then asked about an incense burner and charcoal.

‘Now that is out of the question,’ said Tealeaf. ‘Where would you find those in the middle of the country? If you wanted all these things, why didn’t you say so before? We could have brought them so easily.’

segments.text: ‘Idiot! If I could have brought them, we shouldn’t have had to tear off as if our lives depended on it.’
Tealeaf thought for a while, then smiled.

‘I’ve an idea, Master Bao. I don’t know what you’ll think of it. I don’t suppose this is all you’ll want. There may be other things as well, and we can’t go on like this. Another two li along this road brings us to the Water Spirit Convent.’

segments.text: ‘The Water Spirit Convent is here?’ Bao-yu asked eagerly. ‘Better still! Let us go.’
He urged his horse on, looking back at Tealeaf as he rode.
‘The nun from there often visits us. If we go and ask to borrow an incense burner, she’s sure to agree.’

‘We support their worship, of course she will. But even if it were a temple where nobody knew us, they wouldn’t dare refuse. There’s just one thing: I’ve always noticed you disliked this convent more than any other. How have you taken such a fancy to it today?’

‘What I’ve always hated is the way ignorant people go worshipping gods and building temples without knowing why. Some rich old fellow, or some rich foolish woman, hears of a god and builds a temple to worship it in, without even knowing who the god is. They hear something out of an unofficial history or a storybook and take it for truth. This Water Spirit Convent, for instance, is called that because it houses the goddess of the Luo River. They don’t realise there never was a goddess of the Luo River in ancient times. Cao Zi-jian made her up. Yet these fools have had a statue made and worship it.

segments.text: ‘Today, though, it suits what is in my heart, so I’m borrowing it for once.’

They were already at the gate. The old nun was so astonished to see Bao-yu that he might have been a living dragon dropped from the sky. She hurried forward to greet him and told an old Taoist to take the horses. Bao-yu went in. He did not bow to the goddess’s image, but studied it admiringly. Clay though it was, it truly had the movement of one ‘light as a startled wild goose, graceful as a swimming dragon’, and the beauty of ‘a lotus rising from green waves, the sun shining on morning clouds’. Tears fell from his eyes before he knew it. The old nun brought him tea.

segments.text: Bao-yu asked to borrow an incense burner. The nun was gone some time and returned with incense, offerings and paper spirit-offerings all ready as well.
‘I don’t need any of those,’ said Bao-yu.
He told Tealeaf to carry the burner into the back garden. There they looked for a clean place to put it, but could find none.
‘What about the platform by that well?’ Tealeaf suggested.

Bao-yu nodded. They went to it together and set the burner down. Tealeaf stood to one side. Bao-yu took out his incense and lit it, made an abbreviated obeisance with tears in his eyes, then turned and told Tealeaf to take the burner away.
Tealeaf said he would, but instead of picking it up he hastily dropped to the ground and kowtowed several times, praying aloud:

‘I, Tealeaf, have served Master Bao these several years. There’s nothing in his heart I don’t know about, except today’s offering. He hasn’t told me about that, and I daren’t ask. I don’t know the name of the spirit receiving it, but I imagine she must be a sister such as the world has only one of and heaven cannot match, a lady of the utmost intelligence and grace. My master cannot put what is in his heart into words, so let me pray for him. If your fragrant soul has feeling, if your sweet spirit knows affection, then though the worlds of the living and the dead divide you, you are kindred hearts. You might still come and see Master Bao from time to time.

segments.text: ‘In the world below, watch over him, so that in his next life he too may be a girl and keep you all company. Never let him be born again as one of these filthy bearded creatures.’
He kowtowed several more times before getting up. Bao-yu had begun to laugh before he finished. He gave him a kick.
‘Stop talking nonsense. Someone will hear and laugh at us.’
Tealeaf rose and picked up the burner. As he walked beside Bao-yu, he said:

‘I’ve told the nun you haven’t eaten yet and asked her to put together whatever she has. Try to eat a little, Master Bao. I know there’s a great feast at home today, with all the excitement that goes with it, and that’s why you’ve come away. A quiet day here will do all that respect requires, anyhow. But going without food simply won’t do.’
‘If I’m not having the plays and the wine,’ Bao-yu said, ‘there’s no reason I shouldn’t have a little plain vegetarian food.’

segments.text: ‘First, Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship can be easy in their minds. Second, you’ve paid your respects here, and that’s all that’s needed. Even if you go home and watch the plays and drink wine, that isn’t something you’ve gone out of your way to do. You’re only keeping your elders company out of filial duty. If you let them worry just for the sake of this, even the spirit you’ve just made an offering to won’t be at peace. What do you think of that, Master Bao?’

‘I can guess what you mean,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘You’re thinking that you’re the only one who came out with me, and you’re afraid of getting the blame when we go back. That’s why you’re persuading me with such grand arguments. I only came to pay my respects before going back to the wine and the plays. I never said I wouldn’t go into the city all day. Now I’ve done what I wished, we can hurry back and put everyone’s mind at rest. Won’t that fulfil both obligations?’

segments.text: ‘Better still,’ said Tealeaf.

They went into the convent hall, where the nun had indeed laid a table with vegetarian dishes. Bao-yu ate a little, without much attention to what it was, and Tealeaf ate too. Then they mounted and took the same road back. From behind, Tealeaf kept warning him:
‘Ride carefully, Master Bao. This horse hasn’t been ridden much. Keep a firm hold of the reins.’

Even as he spoke they were back inside the city. They went in by the rear gate as before and hurried to the House of Green Delights. Aroma and the others were not there, only a few old women left to watch the rooms. At the sight of him their faces broke into smiles.
‘Blessed Buddha, here you are at last! Miss Hua has been frantic. They’re at the feast now. You must hurry over, Master Bao.’
Bao-yu hastily took off his plain clothes and found some fine ones to change into himself. He asked where the feast was being held. The old women told him it was in the large new reception hall.

segments.text: He set off straight for it. Already he could faintly hear singing and pipes. As he reached the far side of the passage-hall, he saw Silver sitting alone beneath the eaves, crying. When she saw him she wiped her tears away.
‘Here comes the phoenix! Hurry in. A little longer and they’d have turned the place upside down.’
‘Guess where I’ve been,’ Bao-yu said with a coaxing smile.

Silver gave no answer, but went on wiping her eyes. Bao-yu hurried into the hall to see Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang and the rest. Everyone really did receive him as though a phoenix had arrived. He hastened to offer Xi-feng his birthday respects. Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang both scolded him for not knowing how to behave.
‘Running off by yourself without a word to anyone! How can we allow that? Do it again, and when your father comes home we shall certainly tell him to beat you.’

They went on to abuse the pages for obeying him in everything, going wherever he chose without reporting it. At the same time they asked where he had been, whether he had eaten anything, and whether anything had frightened him.

segments.text: ‘One of the Prince of Beijing’s favourite concubines died yesterday,’ Bao-yu merely replied. ‘I went to offer my condolences. He was crying so much I couldn’t leave him and come straight back, so I stayed a little longer.’
‘Go out on your own again without telling us first, and I’ll certainly have your father beat you,’ said Grandmother Jia.
Bao-yu assented. She then wanted the pages who had gone with him beaten, but everyone hastened to plead for them.
‘You needn’t worry any more. He’s come back. We can all set our minds at rest and enjoy ourselves.’

It was her earlier anxiety that had made Grandmother Jia so fierce. Now he was back, she was more than happy: how could she still be angry? She let the matter drop. Indeed, fearful that he might feel ill, or had not eaten enough wherever he had been, or had had a fright on the road, she began coaxing him in every possible way. Aroma had already come to attend to him. They all went back to watching the play.

segments.text: While everyone watched The Thorn Hairpin, Bao-yu sat with the girls. When they reached the scene called ‘The Husband’s Offering’, Dai-yu said to Bao-chai:

‘This Wang Shi-peng is quite unreasonable. He could make his offering anywhere. Why must he run all the way to the riverbank? As the saying goes, “The sight of a thing brings the person to mind.” All the water in the world comes from one source. He could scoop a bowlful up anywhere, look at it and cry. That would give his feelings all the expression they needed.’
Bao-chai did not answer.

segments.text: Bao-yu turned round and asked for wine to be warmed so that he could offer Xi-feng a cup. Grandmother Jia had said that this day was to be different from other days: Xi-feng must be allowed a whole day of unrestrained enjoyment. She herself had not felt inclined to sit at a formal feast, but reclined on a couch in the inner room, watching the play with Aunt Xue. A few dishes she happened to fancy had been set on a little table, so that she could eat and talk as she pleased. She had given the food from her own two banquet tables to the senior and junior maids who had no places, and to the women on duty or waiting to be called. They were to sit beneath the eaves outside the window and eat and drink as they liked, without standing on ceremony.

segments.text: Lady Wang and Lady Xing sat at a high table in the main part of the room. The girls occupied several tables outside. Every so often Grandmother Jia would tell You-shi and the others:
‘Put Feng at the head of the table. You must be good hostesses on my behalf. She works so hard all year round.’
You-shi assented, then replied with a smile:
‘She isn’t used to the place of honour. She can’t get comfortable however she sits, and she won’t drink either.’
‘You don’t know how to manage her,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘I’ll go and offer her some myself.’
Xi-feng hurried in, smiling.
‘Don’t believe them, Grannie. I’ve had several cups already.’
Grandmother Jia laughed and told You-shi:
‘Quick, take her out and hold her down in the chair. All of you must take turns offering her wine. If she still won’t drink, I really shall come myself.’
Laughing, You-shi drew Xi-feng outside again and sat her down. She called for a cup and stand, filled the cup with wine and said:
‘All year long you take such pains over the old lady, Her Ladyship and me.

segments.text: ‘I’ve nothing to show my affection for you today but a cup I’ve poured myself. Be a good girl and take a sip from my hand.’
‘If you really mean to honour me,’ Xi-feng said with a laugh, ‘kneel down, and I’ll drink.’

‘Listen to her! She doesn’t know who she is any more! Let me tell you, a chance like today doesn’t come easily. Once it’s over, who knows whether you’ll have another like it? While you can, just swallow a couple of damned cups.’

Xi-feng saw there was no escaping and drank two cups. Next the girls came to offer theirs, and she had to take a sip from each. Seeing Grandmother Jia still in such high spirits, Lai Da’s mother could hardly fail to join in. She brought some of the other old nurses to offer their cups. Xi-feng could not easily refuse them either and had to drink another couple of mouthfuls. When Faithful and the others came in their turn, she truly could take no more.
‘Dear sisters, do let me off!’ she begged. ‘I’ll drink again tomorrow.’
‘So we really count for nothing?’ Faithful said, smiling. ‘Even Her Ladyship shows us some consideration when we’re with her.

segments.text: While no one was watching, Xi-feng left the feast and went round beneath the eaves at the back of the rooms. Patience had been keeping an eye on her and hurried after her. Xi-feng leaned on her arm. They had only just reached the covered passage when they saw a little maid from their own rooms standing there. At the sight of the two of them she turned and ran. Suspicious, Xi-feng called after her. At first the maid pretended not to hear, but when Patience too began calling from behind, she had to come back. Now thoroughly suspicious, Xi-feng hurried into the passage-hall with Patience, called the little maid in after them and shut the lattice doors. She sat on the steps of the little courtyard and ordered the girl to kneel.
‘Fetch two boys from the inner gate,’ she snapped at Patience. ‘Bring ropes and whips, and flog that little bitch to pieces. She has no eyes for her mistress!’
The child was already terrified out of her wits. She wept and kept knocking her forehead on the ground, begging for mercy.
‘I’m not a ghost,’ Xi-feng demanded. ‘When you saw me, why didn’t you stand still and behave properly? What were you running away for?’
‘I didn’t see you coming, ma’am,’ the maid sobbed.

segments.text: ‘I was worried about there being no one in the rooms. That’s why I ran.’

‘If there was no one in the rooms, who told you to come here? Even if you didn’t see me, Patience and I were behind you, calling ourselves hoarse a dozen times. The more we called, the faster you ran. We weren’t far away. Have you gone deaf? And now you’re answering me back!’
She raised her hand and slapped the girl’s face, making her stagger, then struck the other cheek. Both cheeks immediately swelled and turned purple.

segments.text: ‘Was he afraid I might go home? There must be some other reason. Tell me quickly, and I’ll be kind to you from now on. If you don’t tell me every bit of it, I’ll have a knife brought this instant and cut your flesh.’
Reaching back, she pulled a hairpin out of her hair and jabbed wildly at the girl’s mouth. The terrified child dodged and wept, pleading:
‘I’ll tell you, ma’am, but don’t say I told you.’

segments.text: Xi-feng was so furious that her whole body went weak. She rose hastily and went straight home. As she reached the courtyard gate, she saw another little maid peeping out. This one too ducked her head and ran at the sight of her. Xi-feng shouted her name and ordered her to stop. The girl was quick-witted. Seeing she could not escape, she ran out towards Xi-feng instead, smiling.
‘I was just going to tell you, ma’am. How lucky you’ve come.’

segments.text: ‘Tell me what?’
The maid told her what the Second Master was doing at home, repeating what the other girl had said.
‘Pah! What were you doing all this time?’ Xi-feng spat. ‘Now I’ve caught sight of you, you come and wash your hands of it!’
She raised her hand and gave this girl too a slap that sent her stumbling. Then she crept to the window and listened. Inside there was talk and laughter.
‘When will that King Yama of a wife of yours die?’ the woman said with a laugh. ‘What a good thing that would be.’
‘If she died, and I married another, she’d be just the same,’ said Jia Lian. ‘What good would that do?’
‘If she died, you could make Patience your lawful wife. She might be better.’
‘Nowadays she won’t even let me touch Patience,’ Jia Lian said. ‘Patience has a bellyful of grievances too, but she daren’t speak.

segments.text: ‘Why was I fated to have a yaksha for my evil star?’

Xi-feng was shaking all over with rage. Hearing them both praise Patience, she suspected that Patience must have been voicing resentment behind her back as well. The wine surged up more fiercely than ever. Without stopping to think, she turned and struck Patience twice, kicked the door open and rushed in. Allowing no explanations, she seized Bao Er’s wife and began tearing at her and beating her. Then, afraid Jia Lian might get out, she planted herself in the doorway and cursed:

‘You whore! You steal your master for a lover, and you want to kill your mistress too! Patience, come here! You whores and bastards are all tangled on the same vine. All of you can’t bear the sight of me, and to my face you coax and flatter!’
She struck Patience several more times. With nowhere to appeal against this injustice, Patience could only choke and cry with rage.
‘You do these shameless things, and what do you drag me into them for?’ she cried, and began tearing at Bao Er’s wife and beating her too.

segments.text: Jia Lian had also drunk too much. Coming in high spirits, he had not taken proper precautions. The sight of Xi-feng had already left him at his wits’ end; now that Patience was making trouble too, his anger sent the wine to his head. When Xi-feng was beating Bao Er’s wife he had been angry and ashamed, but had hardly been in a position to speak. Seeing Patience join in, he came forward, kicking and cursing her.
‘You little whore! So you’re laying hands on people too!’
Patience lost her nerve and stopped at once.
‘You were talking behind my back,’ she cried. ‘Why did you have to drag me in?’

Seeing her afraid of Jia Lian made Xi-feng angrier still. She rushed up and hit Patience again, insisting that she strike Bao Er’s wife. Driven beyond endurance, Patience ran outside to look for a knife and kill herself. The older women and maids hurried to stop her and tried to reason with her.
When Xi-feng saw that Patience had gone to take her own life, she threw herself head first against Jia Lian’s chest.
‘You’re all in league to harm me! I caught you at it, and now you all turn round and threaten me. Strangle me too, then!’
In a rage, Jia Lian snatched a sword from the wall.
‘No need to kill yourselves. I’ve had enough too. I’ll kill the lot of you and pay with my own life. That’ll finish everything!’
As the uproar grew impossible to settle, You-shi arrived with a crowd of people.
‘What’s all this? You were perfectly all right just now. How did this begin?’
The sight of an audience made Jia Lian use his drinking as an excuse to act still drunker. He swaggered all the more, deliberately making a show of wanting to kill Xi-feng.

segments.text: Once people had come, Xi-feng was no longer so wildly defiant. She left them all and ran weeping towards Grandmother Jia’s. By now the play was over. She rushed up to Grandmother Jia and flung herself into her arms.
‘Save me, Grannie! Master Lian’s going to kill me!’
Grandmother Jia, Lady Xing and Lady Wang hastily asked what had happened.

‘I’d just gone home to change,’ Xi-feng sobbed. ‘I didn’t expect to find him there talking to someone. I thought he must have a visitor, and I was too frightened to go in. I listened outside the window, and it was Bao Er’s wife he was talking to. They were saying how fierce I was, and planning to poison me and make Patience his lawful wife. Of course I was angry, but I didn’t dare quarrel with him. I only gave Patience a couple of blows and asked her why she wanted to harm me. He was ashamed, and then he wanted to kill me.’
Grandmother Jia and the others believed every word.
‘This is beyond everything! Bring that low-bred wretch here at once!’
Before they had finished, Jia Lian came rushing after her, sword in hand, with a crowd of people behind him.

segments.text: Jia Lian was well aware of Grandmother Jia’s habitual indulgence towards them. With that to rely on, even his mother and aunt were no obstacle, and he had come blustering after Xi-feng. Lady Xing and Lady Wang hastily barred his way, furious at the sight of him.
‘You low-bred wretch! You’re getting quite beyond yourself. The old lady is here!’
Jia Lian looked sideways at them through half-closed eyes.
‘It’s the old lady who’s spoilt her. That’s why she behaves like this. She’s even started swearing at me!’
Lady Xing angrily wrested the sword from him, ordering him over and over to get out. Jia Lian went on with his wilful, wheedling, drunken nonsense.
‘I know you have no regard for any of us,’ Grandmother Jia said in anger. ‘Send someone for his father!’
Only then did Jia Lian stagger out. Sulking, he did not go back to his rooms but made for the outer study.

segments.text: Lady Xing and Lady Wang now turned to scolding Xi-feng as well.

‘What is there to make such a fuss about?’ Grandmother Jia said with a laugh. ‘They’re young things, like greedy cats. How can you keep them from doing this sort of thing? People have always gone through it when they’re young. It’s all my fault. I let her have a little too much wine, and then she started on the vinegar of jealousy as well.’
Everyone laughed.
‘Don’t worry,’ Grandmother Jia continued. ‘Tomorrow I’ll have him come and apologise to you. Don’t go back and put him to shame today.’
Then she began scolding Patience.
‘That little hussy! I always thought well of her. Who would have guessed she was so wicked in secret?’

‘Patience has done nothing wrong,’ You-shi and the others said, smiling. ‘Feng took her anger out on her. Husband and wife couldn’t very well beat each other, so they both vented their temper on Patience. The poor girl has been wronged dreadfully, and now you’re scolding her too.’
‘Oh, so that’s it! I thought she didn’t seem the sort to play those sly tricks. In that case, poor child, she’s borne their anger for nothing.’
She called Amber.
‘Go and tell Patience this from me: I know she’s been wronged. Tomorrow I’ll make Feng apologise to her.

‘I wanted to ask you before,’ she said, smiling. ‘But with the elder mistress and all the young ladies inviting you, it wouldn’t have done for me to join in.’
Patience managed a smile in return.
‘Thank you.’ Then she added, ‘Everything was perfectly all right. Who could have expected this? All that anger poured on me for no reason whatever.’

segments.text: ‘Your mistress is usually so good to you,’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘She only lost her temper for a moment.’

‘I’ve nothing to say against her,’ said Patience. ‘It was that whore who brought this on me, and then she had to drag me in to make it more amusing. And as if that weren’t enough, our muddle-headed master turned round and hit me too.’
The injustice of it overcame her again, and the tears fell.
‘Dear sister, don’t be unhappy,’ Bao-yu hastened to say. ‘Let me apologise for the two of them.’
‘What has it to do with you?’ Patience said, smiling.
‘We brothers and sisters are all one,’ Bao-yu replied with a smile. ‘If they offend someone, it’s only right for me to apologise for them.’
He went on:

‘What a pity! Your new clothes are stained too. There are some of your Sister Hua’s clothes here. Why don’t you change, and we’ll spray these with a little distilled spirit and iron them? Do your hair again, too, and wash your face.’

As he spoke, he told the little maids to bring washing water and heat an iron. Patience had often heard it said that Bao-yu had a particular gift for getting on with girls. For his part, knowing her to be Jia Lian’s favourite concubine and Xi-feng’s trusted confidante, Bao-yu had not felt free to become intimate with her. The impossibility of showing her all the attentiveness he wished had often been a regret to him.

segments.text: Now, watching him, Patience quietly considered that what people said was true: he thought of everything. Aroma made a point of opening her chest and taking out two seldom-worn garments for her to change into. Patience hastily took off her own clothes and went to wash her face.

‘You ought to put on a little rouge and powder too,’ Bao-yu urged with a smile. ‘Otherwise it will look as though you’re sulking with Cousin Feng. Besides, it’s her birthday, and Grandmother has sent someone to comfort you.’

Patience thought this reasonable and looked for powder, but could see none. Bao-yu hurried to the dressing-table and lifted the lid of a Xuande-ware porcelain box. Inside was a row of ten powder-filled hosta buds. He picked one up and handed it to Patience.
‘This isn’t lead powder,’ he told her with a smile. ‘It’s made from zi-moli seeds, ground up and mixed with fragrant ingredients.’

segments.text: Patience tipped some into her palm. It was indeed fine in all four respects: light, white, delicately rosy and fragrant. It spread easily and evenly over her face and left the skin soft and lustrous, unlike other powders, which looked bluish and heavy and felt dry and clogging. She then noticed that the rouge was not in sheets. It filled a little white-jade box and looked like a poured ointment.

‘The rouge they sell in the shops is never clean, and the colour is weak,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘This is the best rouge, with the juice squeezed out, washed and settled clear of the dregs, then blended with flower distillate and steamed down. Just pick up a little with a fine hairpin, put it on your palm, mix it with a drop of water and apply it to your lips. What’s left on your hand will be enough for your cheeks.’

Patience followed his directions. The result was remarkably fresh and bright, and a sweet fragrance lay over both cheeks. Bao-yu then used bamboo scissors to cut a twin-flowered autumn orchid from its pot and tucked it into her hair at the temple. Just then a maid arrived from Li Wan to fetch her, and she hurried away.

segments.text: Bao-yu had always deeply regretted that he had never been able to do anything for Patience, especially as she was a girl of the first order, exceptionally clever, handsome and refined, quite unlike those vulgar, stupid, clumsy creatures. Today was Golden’s birthday, and he had been unhappy all day. He had never expected this later disturbance to give him a chance to show Patience even a little of his care. It was a pleasure he had never imagined could fall to him in this life. He lay back on the bed, contented at heart.

Then he thought how Jia Lian knew only how to gratify himself with sexual pleasure, not how to cherish the women about him. He thought too of Patience, with no parents, brothers or sisters, all alone in attendance on Jia Lian and Xi-feng. With Jia Lian so coarse and Xi-feng so overbearing, she had somehow managed to accommodate them both, yet today she had suffered this brutality. Surely, he thought, her lot was even harder than Dai-yu’s. At this he grew sad again, and tears sprang to his eyes. Seeing that Aroma and the others were out of the room, he let himself shed a few bitter tears without restraint.

He got up again. The spirit sprayed on Patience’s clothes was now half dry, so he took the iron, pressed the garments and folded them neatly. Noticing that she had forgotten her handkerchief, which still bore the marks of her tears, he took it to the basin, washed it and hung it up to dry.

segments.text: By turns happy and sad, he sat listlessly for a while, then went to Sweet-rice Village for some conversation. They did not part until after the lamps were lit. Patience stayed the night with Li Wan, while Xi-feng remained with Grandmother Jia. When Jia Lian returned to his rooms that evening, he found them desolate. He could hardly go and fetch the women, so he slept through the night as best he could. On waking next morning, he thought of the previous day’s events, found them thoroughly mortifying, and regretted them bitterly.

Lady Xing, still concerned about his drunkenness the day before, came over early and told him to come with her to Grandmother Jia’s. He had to swallow his shame and go. He knelt before Grandmother Jia.
‘Well? What is it?’ she asked.
‘Yesterday I had too much wine and disturbed Your Old Ladyship,’ Jia Lian said quickly, with an ingratiating smile. ‘I’ve come to receive my punishment.’

‘Pah, you low creature! After pouring that yellow swill down your throat, why couldn’t you lie down like a corpse and keep quiet? Instead, you had to start beating your wife. Feng is always boasting, and she’s as fierce as a tyrant, but yesterday you frightened her pitifully. If I hadn’t been here, and you’d killed her, where would you be now?’
Full of grievances of his own, Jia Lian dared not argue. He could only admit his fault.

segments.text: ‘And aren’t Feng and Patience both beauties?’ Grandmother Jia went on. ‘Still you’re not satisfied! Always sneaking about after something, dragging every filthy, stinking creature into your room. Beating your wife over one of these whores, and beating your own concubine too! A fine son of a great family you are. You’ve slapped your own face. If you have any regard for me, get up. I’ll forgive you. Apologise nicely to your wife and take her home. That will please me. Otherwise you can go straight out. I wouldn’t presume to have you kneeling before me.’

At these words Jia Lian looked at Xi-feng standing nearby. She was not dressed in her finery. Her eyes were swollen from crying; she wore neither rouge nor powder, and her face was sallow. She seemed more appealing and pitiable than usual.
‘Better to apologise,’ he thought. ‘Then we can both be all right again, and it will please the old lady as well.’
Having decided, he smiled.
‘I daren’t disobey you, Grandmother. But it will only spoil her more.’
‘Nonsense!’ Grandmother Jia said with a laugh.

segments.text: ‘I know how well she understands proper behaviour. She would never offend anyone. If she gives you offence in future, I shall certainly see justice done and have her submit to you.’
Jia Lian got up, made Xi-feng a bow and smiled.
‘It was all my fault, after all. Pray forgive me, Mrs Lian.’
The whole room laughed.
‘Feng, no more anger,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘If you’re angry again, I shall be angry too.’

She sent for Patience and told Xi-feng and Jia Lian to comfort her. At the sight of Patience, Jia Lian cast restraint still further aside. As the saying goes, ‘A wife cannot match a concubine, nor a concubine a stolen affair.’ No sooner had Grandmother Jia spoken than he hurried forward.
‘You were badly treated yesterday, my dear. It was all my fault. Your mistress offended you because of me as well. My own apology isn’t enough: I must apologise on her behalf too.’
He made another bow, which set Grandmother Jia laughing. Xi-feng laughed too.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia then told Xi-feng to comfort Patience. Patience quickly came forward and kowtowed to her.
‘To have made you angry on your birthday, ma’am! I deserve to die.’

Xi-feng had already been ashamed and sorry for drinking too much the day before. Forgetting their accustomed affection, she had flown into a temper and, merely on hearing what others said, had humiliated Patience for no reason. Now that the girl behaved like this instead, shame and sorrow overcame her. She hastily pulled her up, and her tears fell.

‘I’ve waited on you all these years,’ Patience said, ‘and you’ve never so much as flicked me with a fingernail. Even when you hit me yesterday, I didn’t blame you. It was all that whore’s doing. No wonder you were angry.’
Her own tears fell too. Grandmother Jia ordered them all three to be taken back to their rooms.
‘If one of them mentions this again, come and tell me at once. I don’t care who it is. I’ll give them a beating with my stick.’

segments.text: ‘That whore wished me dead, and you helped her curse me. Even if I’d been no good for a thousand days, surely there’d been one good day. After wearing myself out, I’m worth less than a whore. What face have I left to go on living like this?’
She began crying again.
‘Still not satisfied?’ said Jia Lian.

segments.text: ‘Think carefully. Who was more in the wrong yesterday? Today, in front of everyone, it was I who went down on my knees, and I who apologised. You’ve had all the credit you could want. Yet here you are, nagging again. Must I kneel down to you before you’ll stop? Insisting on having your own way in everything isn’t such a good thing.’
Xi-feng could find nothing to say. Patience gave a sudden little snort of laughter.
‘So we’re all right again!’ Jia Lian said, laughing too. ‘Upon my word, I don’t know what to do with you.’
