segments.text: They were still talking when a married servant came to report:
‘Bao Er’s wife has hanged herself.’
Jia Lian and Xi-feng were both startled. Xi-feng quickly suppressed her look of alarm and snapped instead:
‘If she’s dead, she’s dead. What is there to make a fuss about?’
Presently Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife came in and told Xi-feng quietly:
‘Bao Er’s wife has hanged herself. Her own family want to bring a complaint.’
‘Splendid!’ Xi-feng said with a laugh. ‘I’ve been longing for a lawsuit.’
‘I’ve just been talking to them with some of the others,’ said Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife. ‘We reasoned with them, threatened them a little and promised them some money. They’ve agreed to leave it.’

‘I haven’t a single cash. And if I had, I wouldn’t give it to them. Let them bring their complaint. You’re not to persuade them, and there’s no need to frighten them either. Just let them go and complain. When they fail, we’ll have them charged with extorting money over a corpse!’
Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife was at a loss. Then she saw Jia Lian signalling to her with his eyes. Understanding him, she went outside to wait.

segments.text: ‘I’ll go out and see what’s happening,’ said Jia Lian.
‘You’re not to give them any money,’ Xi-feng said.

Jia Lian went straight out to consult Lin Zhi-xiao. He sent people to cajole and threaten by turns, and only after two hundred taels had been promised for the funeral was the matter settled. Afraid there might still be trouble, Jia Lian sent a message to Wang Zi-teng and had several constables and coroners’ assistants called in to help with the funeral arrangements.

segments.text: At the sight of this, her relatives would not have dared to argue further even if they had wanted to. They could only swallow their anger and say no more. Jia Lian also told Lin Zhi-xiao to put the two hundred taels into the year’s accounts, spreading it among different expense entries to make the sum up. He privately gave Bao Er some silver as well and consoled him.
‘Another day I’ll find you a good wife.’
With both his standing and his purse improved, what had Bao Er to object to? He went on currying favour with Jia Lian as before. Of that we need say no more.

segments.text: Inside, though Xi-feng was uneasy at heart, she went on pretending to take no notice. When there was no one else in the room, she drew Patience towards her with a smile.
‘I poured too much damned wine down my throat yesterday. Don’t hold it against me. Where did I hit you? Let me see.’
‘You didn’t hit me hard,’ Patience replied.
Just then someone announced that the ladies and girls had all come in. To learn what followed, read the next chapter.

segments.text: Xi-feng was still comforting Patience when the girls came in. She hurriedly offered them seats, and Patience poured the tea.
‘What a full gathering!’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘Anyone would think I’d sent out invitations.’
‘We’ve come on two errands,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘One for me and one for Fourth Sister, with a message from Grandmother thrown in.’
‘What can be so important?’

‘We’ve started a poetry society, and at the very first meeting someone was missing. None of us can bring ourselves to be stern, so it’s all got out of hand. I think we must have you for Censor of the Society, to be perfectly impartial and show no mercy. Then Fourth Sister needs all sorts of things for painting the garden. We told Grandmother, and she said, “There may still be some left from years ago in the rooms beneath the rear storey. Look and see. If there are, bring them out; if not, send someone to buy them.”’
‘I can’t make verses, wet or dry,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘Do you want me there to do the eating?’
‘You needn’t write any, whether you can or not,’ said Tan-chun.

segments.text: ‘And you call yourself our elder sister-in-law!’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘The girls were put in your charge to study, learn their manners and do their sewing. If they misbehave, you’re supposed to put them right. Now they start a poetry society, which can’t cost much, and you wash your hands of them? Grandmother and Lady Wang are different: they’re the old ladies of the family. You have ten taels a month, twice what we get. Then Grandmother and Lady Wang say, “Poor thing, she’s a widow with no livelihood, and a boy to bring up. That won’t be enough,” and add another full ten taels, putting you on the same footing as themselves. You’ve been given garden land too, with your own rents to collect, and when the yearly allowances are divided at New Year, yours is in the very highest class. You and your son, masters and servants all told, don’t make ten people, and your food and clothes still come out of the common household funds. Add it all up and you must have four or five hundred taels a year.

segments.text: ‘Just listen!’ Li Wan said, laughing. ‘One word from me, and off she goes, with two cartloads of penny-pinching market talk, such as you’d hear from some muddy-legged rogue, forever weighing and reckoning to the last fraction. To think that this creature was born a young lady in a great, learned family of high officials, and married into another just as good, yet still behaves like this! If she’d been born a boy in some poor little household, there’s no saying what low tricks and cheap, nasty talk we’d have had. You’ve calculated the whole world into your pocket! And yesterday you actually hit Patience. How could you raise your hand to her? Did you pour all that yellow swill into a dog’s belly? I was so angry, I wanted to come and stand up for Patience. I thought it over for ages. It was your birthday, your precious “day a dog’s tail grows a tip”, which comes round so seldom, and I was afraid of upsetting Grandmother. That was the only reason I didn’t come. I’m still angry, and here you are provoking me again! You’re not fit to pick up Patience’s shoes. You two ought to change places.’
Everyone laughed.

segments.text: ‘Be a dear sister-in-law and take them back to the garden for now,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘I was just going to reckon up the rice accounts when Lady Xing sent for me. I don’t know what she wants this time, but I shall have to go over. And I haven’t yet arranged to have your extra clothes made for the New Year.’
‘I’m not concerned with any of that,’ said Li Wan. ‘Finish my business first, so that I can go and rest without these young ladies worrying me.’

‘Do spare me a moment, dear sister-in-law!’ Xi-feng said quickly, with a laugh. ‘You’ve always been so kind to me. Why should you stop just because of Patience? You used to tell me that however much I had to do, I must look after myself and snatch a rest whenever I could. Now you’re trying to drive me to my death. Besides, it wouldn’t matter if anyone else’s New Year clothes were late, but if theirs were, you’d be responsible. Wouldn’t Grandmother blame you for not concerning yourself with it, when a single word from you was all it needed?

segments.text: ‘I’d rather be blamed myself. How could I let you suffer on my account?’
‘Listen to that!’ Li Wan said, laughing. ‘Isn’t it beautifully put? What a tongue she has! Now tell me, will you take our poetry society in hand or won’t you?’

‘What a question!’ said Xi-feng. ‘If I don’t join and spend a little money, I shall be a rebel against Prospect Garden. How could I expect to get another meal here? I’ll take office first thing tomorrow, dismount and pay my respects to the official seal, and put down fifty taels to begin with. You can take your time spending it on the society’s gatherings. Then, a few days later, you’ll find I write neither poems nor essays and am no more than a common creature after all. Censor or no Censor, once you’ve got the money you’ll turn me out!’
They all laughed again.

‘I’ll open the storerooms in a little while,’ Xi-feng went on, ‘and have everything of the sort brought out for you to look over. Keep whatever you can use. If anything’s missing, I’ll send someone to buy it from your list.

segments.text: ‘I’ll cut out the painting silk straight away. As for the plan, Lady Wang hasn’t got it: it’s still over at Cousin Zhen’s. I’m telling you so you won’t get sent away empty-handed. I’ll have it fetched, and send it out with the silk to the painters, for them to size the silk with alum. Will that do?’
Li Wan nodded, smiling.
‘We shall be obliged to you. If you really do all that, it will do very well. Come, then, let’s go home. We can come back and pester her if she doesn’t send it.’
She rose to leave with the girls.
‘There’s only one person behind all this,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Bao-yu!’
Li Wan turned back with a laugh.
‘We came about him, and I’d quite forgotten! He was the one who missed the first meeting. We’re all too soft-hearted. How do you think we ought to punish him?’
Xi-feng considered.
‘There’s only one thing for it. Make him sweep the floor in every one of your rooms.’

segments.text: ‘That’s a good idea!’ they all said, laughing.
They were just going when a little maid came in supporting Nanny Lai. Xi-feng and the others hurriedly stood up.
‘Sit down, Nanny!’
They all congratulated her. Nanny Lai sat on the edge of the kang and smiled.

‘It’s a happy thing for me, and for my masters and mistresses too. Where would our good fortune have come from without your kindness? Yesterday you sent young Cai with more gifts, ma’am. My grandson kowtowed at the gate towards your rooms to thank you.’
‘When does he leave to take up his post?’ Li Wan asked with a smile.
Nanny Lai sighed.

‘What have I to do with their arrangements? Let them see to it! He came and kowtowed to me at home the other day, and I had no soft words for him. “My boy,” I said, “don’t think being an official entitles you to bully people and ride roughshod over them. You’re thirty this year. Though you were born a servant, the masters were kind enough to give you your freedom the moment you left your mother’s womb. With their good fortune sheltering you above and your parents supporting you below, you’ve learnt your letters and read your books just like a young gentleman. Maids, serving-women and nurses have carried you up to this age as though they were cradling a phoenix.

segments.text: ‘“You don’t even know how to write the two characters for ‘servant’! You know only how to enjoy yourself, not what your grandfather and father suffered. It took two or three generations of endurance to produce a creature like you. All those illnesses and troubles you had as a child: the money spent on you would have made a silver boy your size. When you were twenty, our masters were kind enough to let you purchase official standing. Think of all the sons of respectable families with proper claims to it who are going hungry! You’re a servant’s offspring. Take care you don’t use up your good fortune. Now you’ve enjoyed ten years of ease, and heaven knows what strings you’ve pulled, but you’ve begged the masters to help and got yourself selected for a post. A district or county magistrate may be a minor official, but his responsibilities are great. The magistrate of a district is father and mother to all its people. Unless you behave yourself, do your duty to your country and honour your masters, heaven itself may refuse to tolerate you.”’
‘You worry too much,’ Li Wan and Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘He seems quite all right to us.

segments.text: ‘He used to come in once or twice in earlier years, but we haven’t seen him for several years now, only his name on the lists at New Year and birthdays. The other day he came to pay his respects to Grandmother and Lady Wang, and we saw him in Grandmother’s courtyard in his new official dress. He looked quite imposing, and he’s filled out too. Now that he’s got a post, you ought to be enjoying yourself, not worrying over all this. If he misbehaves, he still has his father to deal with him. All you need do is take your ease. Whenever you’re free, get into your chair and come over for a day’s cards and a good talk with Grandmother. Who would have the face to deny you anything?

‘You don’t know, ma’am.

segments.text: ‘These young people have to be kept under strict control. Strict as we are, they still find chances to get into mischief and make their elders worry. People who know them say they’re naughty children. Those who don’t say they’re using their money and influence to bully others, and even our masters’ name suffers. segments.text: She pointed at Bao-yu.

‘Don’t be offended with me, but nowadays your father only keeps you a little in order, and Grandmother is there in front of you, shielding you. Who didn’t see the beatings your father got from your grandfather when he was a boy? He never was as fearless of heaven and earth as you are. Nor was your elder uncle: naughty as he was, he was never such a confirmed little troublemaker as you. He was beaten every day too. And your Cousin Zhen’s grandfather at the Ning mansion, his temper was like oil poured on a fire! Once he was angry, he forgot all about its being his own son. You’d have thought he was trying a thief. From what I see and hear nowadays, Master Zhen does discipline his son rather as the old master used to, but there’s no rhyme or reason to it.

segments.text: While she was speaking, Lai Da’s wife arrived. Zhou Rui’s wife and Zhang Cai’s wife followed with business to report.
‘The daughter-in-law has come to fetch her mother-in-law,’ Xi-feng said, smiling.
‘Not to fetch her, ma’am. I’ve come to find out whether you ladies and young ladies will honour us.’

‘Dear me, I’m getting foolish!’ Nanny Lai said with a laugh. ‘Instead of saying what I came to say, I’ve been turning over all this stale grain and rotten sesame, the same old stories. As our boy has been selected for a post, our relations and friends want to congratulate him, so we must give a feast at home. I thought, if we gave just one day’s entertainment, whoever we invited, we’d be leaving someone out. Then I thought again: this is glory we never dreamt of, all through our masters’ good fortune. I’d be willing to spend every penny we had on it. So I told his father to give three days’ feasting. On the first day we’ll lay a few tables and have a play in our poor little garden, and invite Her Old Ladyship, Their Ladyships and all the ladies and girls to while away a day with us. There’ll be another play and a few tables in the outer hall, where the masters and young masters can honour us with their presence. On the second day we’ll invite our relations and friends, and on the third our fellow servants from both mansions.

segments.text: ‘Three days of merrymaking, to share a little reflected glory from our masters’ good fortune.’
‘What date is it?’ Li Wan and Xi-feng asked, laughing. ‘We’ll certainly come. Grandmother may even feel like coming too.’
‘We’ve chosen the fourteenth,’ Lai Da’s wife hastened to say. ‘Please come for the sake of our old mistress.’

‘I can’t answer for anyone else, but I shall certainly be there,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Only let me warn you, I’m bringing no present, and I don’t know how to give tips. I shall eat and go, so don’t laugh at me.’
‘What are you saying, ma’am?’ Lai Da’s wife laughed. ‘If you want to give us something, twenty or thirty thousand taels will do.’
‘I’ve just invited Her Old Ladyship,’ Nanny Lai said with a smile, ‘and she says she’ll come too. My old face still counts for something.’
She repeated her invitation before rising to go. Catching sight of Zhou Rui’s wife, she remembered something.
‘There’s one other thing I meant to ask you, ma’am. What has Mrs Zhou’s boy done wrong, for you to dismiss him?’
‘That’s just what I meant to tell your daughter-in-law,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘There’s so much to do that I forgot.

segments.text: ‘Mrs Lai, tell your husband when you get home that neither mansion is to take that boy in. He can go and fend for himself.’
Lai Da’s wife had to assent. Zhou Rui’s wife hurriedly knelt and begged for mercy.
‘Tell me what happened,’ Nanny Lai put in. ‘Let me judge.’

‘On my birthday the other day, before we’d had any wine inside, that boy was drunk already,’ said Xi-feng. ‘My mother’s household sent presents, and instead of attending to things outside, he sat there abusing people and didn’t even send the gifts in. Only when the two women had come inside did he bring them in with the young pages. The pages managed perfectly well, but he dropped the box he was carrying and scattered steamed buns all over the courtyard. When the visitors had gone, I sent Sunshine to reprimand him, and he gave Sunshine a mouthful of abuse. What should I keep a lawless little bastard like that for?’

‘And I was wondering what terrible thing it could be!’ Nanny Lai said, laughing. ‘So that’s all. Listen to me, ma’am. If he’s done wrong, beat him, scold him, make him mend his ways. But you certainly mustn’t turn him out.

segments.text: ‘He isn’t like one of our own household-born servants. He belongs to the servants Lady Wang brought with her when she married. If you dismiss him out of hand, it will reflect badly on Her Ladyship. I say you should teach him a lesson with a few strokes of the board, as a warning for next time, and keep him on. If not for his mother’s sake, then for Her Ladyship’s.’
‘Very well,’ Xi-feng said to Lai Da’s wife. ‘Have him given forty strokes, and forbid him to drink from now on.’

segments.text: Lai Da’s wife assented. Zhou Rui’s wife kowtowed and rose, then would have kowtowed to Nanny Lai as well, but Lai Da’s wife caught hold of her and stopped her. The three of them went away, and Li Wan and the others returned to the garden.

By evening Xi-feng did indeed have a quantity of old painting equipment brought out of storage and sent into the garden. Bao-chai and the others sorted through it, but only half the things were fit for use. They made a fresh list of the other half and sent it to Xi-feng to have replacements bought. We need not dwell on this.

segments.text: One day the silk came back from outside, sized with alum and with the preliminary drawing begun. Bao-yu now went to Xi-chun’s every day to help. Tan-chun, Li Wan, Ying-chun and Bao-chai often sat there too, both to watch the painting and as a convenient way of meeting.

With the weather turning cool and the nights growing longer, Bao-chai went to her mother’s rooms to discuss getting some sewing ready. During the day she paid her respects to Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang twice, and would naturally stay a little while to keep them company as they wished. She also had to find time for a chat with the girls in the garden. There was little leisure by day, so every night she worked at her needle by lamplight and did not go to bed until the third watch.

Every year after the Spring and Autumn Equinoxes Dai-yu suffered a bout of coughing. This autumn, with Grandmother Jia in such good spirits, she had gone on a couple of extra outings and tired herself too much. Her cough had returned over the last few days, and seemed worse than usual. She no longer went out, but stayed in her room to nurse herself. Sometimes she grew lonely and wished one of the girls would come and talk to her to pass the time. Yet when Bao-chai or the others came to visit, scarcely a few words had been exchanged before she felt weary of them.

segments.text: They all made allowances for her illness, and knew that she was naturally frail and could bear very little distress. If she was inattentive to her guests or careless of courtesies, no one judged her harshly.
Bao-chai came to see her that day, and they began to speak of her illness.

‘The physicians who come here are all quite good,’ said Bao-chai, ‘but their medicine never seems to do you any good. Wouldn’t it be better to ask someone more skilful to see you and get you well? To go through this every spring and summer, when you’re neither old nor a little child: what sort of life is it? It can’t go on for ever.’
‘It’s no use,’ said Dai-yu. ‘I know this illness of mine will never get better. Never mind when I’m ill: you have only to look at me on my good days to see that.’
Bao-chai nodded.
‘That’s true enough. The ancients said, “Those who eat grain live.” Yet what you eat never seems to build up your strength, your qi or your blood. That isn’t good either.’
‘“Life and death are ordained; wealth and rank rest with Heaven,”’ Dai-yu said with a sigh. ‘We can’t force these things by our own efforts.

segments.text: ‘This year it seems worse than in former years.’
She had already coughed two or three times while they were talking.

‘I looked at your prescription yesterday,’ said Bao-chai. ‘There seems to be too much ginseng and cinnamon bark. They may replenish qi and strengthen the spirit, but they mustn’t be too heating. I should say the first thing is to calm the liver and strengthen the stomach. Once the liver fire is calmed, it can’t overcome earth; with the stomach’s qi sound, food will be able to nourish you. Every morning, take one tael of the best bird’s nests and five qian of rock sugar, and simmer them into a congee in a small silver saucepan. If you get into the habit of eating that, it will do more than medicine. There’s nothing better for nourishing yin and replenishing qi.’

segments.text: ‘You’ve always been very kind to people,’ Dai-yu said with a sigh, ‘but I’m so suspicious that I thought you were hiding something wicked in your heart. The other day, when you said I shouldn’t read those miscellaneous books and gave me such good advice, I was deeply grateful. I was wrong about you before, and I’ve gone on being wrong all this time. When I think of it, my mother died so early, and I have no brothers or sisters. I’m fifteen this year, yet no one has ever spoken to guide me as you did the other day. No wonder Yun says you’re good. I used to feel quite put out when she praised you, but yesterday I found out for myself. Suppose you’d been the one to say those words: I’d never have let you off so lightly. You took no offence at all, and even advised me as you did. That shows how wrong I was. If I hadn’t seen it the other day, I’d never be telling you this now. About the bird’s-nest congee you suggested: bird’s nests are easy enough to get, but I’m always unwell, and this illness comes back every year without anything very urgent about it.

segments.text: ‘Calling doctors, boiling medicine, ginseng and cinnamon bark: it’s already turned the place upside down. Now if I dream up some new business about cooking bird’s-nest congee, Grandmother, Lady Wang and Cousin Feng may not object, but the women and maids below them are bound to think I’m making too much trouble. Look at the people here. Because Grandmother is especially fond of Bao-yu and Feng, they watch even those two like tigers and gossip behind their backs. What must it be like for me? Besides, I’m not really one of their mistresses. I only came here because I had no one and nowhere else to turn to, and they already resent me enough. Why should I give them more reason to curse me by not knowing my place?’

segments.text: ‘By that reckoning, I’m in the same position,’ said Bao-chai.

‘How can you compare yourself to me? You have your mother and brother. Your family has business interests and land here, and still has a house and land at home. You’re simply staying here rent-free because you’re relations. In everything else, great or small, you don’t cost them a single cash. You can leave whenever you choose. I have nothing at all. Food, clothes, everything I use, down to a blade of grass or a scrap of paper, comes to me just as it does to the daughters of this house. How could those petty people help resenting it?’
‘In the end it can only cost them an extra dowry,’ Bao-chai said, smiling. ‘There’s no need to worry about that yet.’
Dai-yu blushed in spite of herself.
‘Here I am treating you as a serious person and telling you my troubles,’ she said with a laugh, ‘and you make fun of me!’
‘It’s a joke, but it’s true too. Don’t worry. As long as I’m here, I’ll keep you company.

segments.text: ‘If anything hurts or worries you, tell me. Whatever I can put right for you, I will, for as long as I can. I may have a brother, but you know what he’s like. It’s only in having a mother that I’m a little better off than you. We can sympathise with each other’s troubles. You’re an intelligent girl: why give way to “Sima Niu’s lament”? Still, what you said just now is quite right. Better to save trouble than make more. I’ll go home tomorrow and speak to Mother. I think we still have some bird’s nests, and I can send you a few taels. Then your maids can cook them each day, quite easily, without mobilising the whole household.’
‘It’s not the gift that matters,’ Dai-yu said quickly, smiling. ‘It’s your kindness.’
‘That’s hardly worth mentioning. My only fear is that I fail to give everyone the attention I should. I’m afraid you must be tired of me now. I’ll go.’
‘Come back this evening and talk to me a little.’
Bao-chai promised and left. We may leave her there.

segments.text: Dai-yu drank a mouthful or two of thin congee and lay back on her bed. Before the sun had set, the weather unexpectedly changed and rain began to patter down. The lingering autumn rain came softly, with no certainty of cloud or clearing. Evening drew on, dark and heavy beneath the clouds, and the drops striking the bamboo tips made it lonelier still. Knowing that Bao-chai would not be able to come, Dai-yu picked up a book at random by the lamp. It was Miscellaneous Yuefu Pieces, containing poems such as ‘Autumn Chamber Lament’ and ‘Lament for Parting’. She found herself moved, and could not keep her feelings from finding words. She composed a piece ‘In the Manner of a Parting Song’, following the pattern of ‘A Moonlit Night of Flowers on the Spring River’, and gave it the title ‘An Evening of Wind and Rain at the Autumn Window’. segments.text: ‘If I wore it, I’d look like one of those fishermen’s wives in pictures or on the stage.’

Only after the words were out did she realise how little she had considered them. Set beside what she had just called Bao-yu, they were beyond recalling. Her face flushed scarlet with embarrassment, and she bent over the table, coughing without a pause. Bao-yu, however, had not noticed. Seeing the poem on the desk, he picked it up and read it through, then could not help exclaiming over it. Dai-yu heard him, hastily rose, snatched it from him and burnt it at the lamp.
‘I’ve already learnt it by heart,’ he said, smiling. ‘Burning it won’t matter.’
‘I’m much better now,’ said Dai-yu. ‘Thank you for coming several times a day to see me, even in the rain. It’s late, and I want to rest. Please go back for now and come again tomorrow.’

Bao-yu reached inside his clothes and brought out a gold watch the size of a walnut. He glanced at it: the hand showed that it was about the turn from the hour of the Dog to the hour of the Pig. He quickly put it away.
‘You certainly ought to be resting. I’ve kept you occupied all this time again.’
He put on his cape and hat and went out, then turned and came back.
‘If there’s anything you fancy eating, tell me. I can ask Grandmother first thing tomorrow. Won’t I explain it better than the old women?’
‘If I think of anything in the night, I’ll tell you tomorrow morning,’ Dai-yu said with a smile.

Even if you dropped it, it wouldn’t be such a great loss. What’s suddenly given you this taste for “cutting open your belly to hide a pearl”?’

Bao-yu hastily took it. The two older women went ahead with umbrellas and the translucent-panel lantern; two young maids followed behind with umbrellas. Bao-yu handed his lantern to one of the little maids to carry, rested a hand on her shoulder and went off with them.

segments.text: Just then a woman from Allspice Court arrived, also carrying an umbrella and a lantern. She brought a large bundle of the best bird’s nests and a packet of fine white imported sugar in plum-petal flakes like snow.
‘These are better than the ones you can buy,’ she said. ‘Miss Bao-chai says you’re to use these to begin with, and she’ll send more when they’re finished.’
‘Tell her I’m obliged to her for taking such trouble,’ Dai-yu said, and asked the woman to sit outside and have some tea.
‘I won’t have tea, miss,’ the woman said with a smile. ‘I’ve something else to do.’
‘I know how busy you are,’ said Dai-yu, smiling. ‘Now the weather’s cooler and the nights are longer, all the more reason to get an evening party together and have a good long gamble.’

‘To tell you the truth, miss, I’ve done very well this year,’ the woman said with a laugh. ‘There are always a few of us on night duty in the different places, and it wouldn’t do to miss a watch. Better to get together for an evening’s play: we keep the watch and pass the time too. Tonight it’s my turn to host. Now the garden gates are shut, it’s time to begin.’

She told someone to give the woman a few hundred cash to buy wine and keep out the damp.
‘Now I’ve put you to the expense of treating me to wine as well, miss,’ said the woman, smiling.
She kowtowed, collected the money outside and went away under her umbrella.

segments.text: Nightingale put away the bird’s nests, moved the lamp, lowered the curtain and helped Dai-yu to bed. On her pillow, Dai-yu thought gratefully of Bao-chai, then envied her for having a mother and brother. She thought too that, close as she and Bao-yu had always been, their intimacy was still open to suspicion. Outside the window the rain pattered on bamboo tips and withered leaves. A chill stole through the curtains, and tears fell again before she knew it. Only towards the end of the fourth watch did she gradually fall asleep. We may leave her there for the moment. To learn what followed—

segments.text: Only towards the end of the fourth watch did Dai-yu gradually fall asleep. We may leave her there for the moment.
Now Xi-feng, summoned by Lady Xing without knowing why, hurriedly changed her clothes and ornaments and went over in her carriage. Lady Xing sent everyone out of the room and spoke to her quietly.

‘I’ve sent for you about one thing only. There’s a difficult matter your father-in-law has entrusted to me, and I can’t decide what to do, so I wanted to consult you first. He’s taken a fancy to Grandmother’s Faithful and wants her in his rooms. He’s told me to ask Grandmother for her. I think it’s an ordinary enough thing to ask, but I’m afraid she won’t let her go. Can you think of a way?’
‘If you ask me,’ Xi-feng said at once, ‘I wouldn’t invite the rebuff.

segments.text: ‘Grandmother can’t even eat her dinner without Faithful. How could she bear to part with her? Besides, when we’re talking of one thing and another, she often says, “At his age, what does he want with one concubine after another in his rooms, spoiling the poor girls’ lives for nothing? Instead of looking after his health or doing his work properly, he spends his days drinking with his concubines.” Does that sound as though she’s pleased with him, Mother? We ought to be keeping out of the way, and here you are, poking a straw up a tiger’s nose! Please don’t be angry with me, but I daren’t go.

segments.text: ‘It plainly won’t do any good, and it will only make things unpleasant. At his age, when he does something improper, you ought to try to dissuade him. It isn’t as though he were still young and could do these things without its mattering. Now he has a whole crowd of brothers, nephews, sons and grandsons. If he carries on like this, how can he face them?’
Lady Xing gave a cold laugh.

‘Plenty of great families have three or four concubines. Why should ours be the one that can’t? He might not listen even if I did try to dissuade him. However fond Grandmother is of the maid, it won’t be so easy for her to refuse her own grown son, a man with a greying beard and an official post, when he asks to take the girl into his rooms. I only sent for you to talk it over, and the first thing you do is deliver a whole sermon on our faults. As if I’d ever ask you to go! Naturally I’ll speak to her myself. You say I don’t try to dissuade him. Don’t you know his temper? Before I could persuade him of anything, he’d have turned on me.’

segments.text: Xi-feng knew Lady Xing’s foolish, obstinate nature. First came her own safety, which she sought by complying with Jia She in everything; next came the pleasure she took in grasping at money and possessions. She left every household affair, great or small, to Jia She. But wherever money passed through her hands, coming in or going out, she was exceedingly stingy, making his extravagance her excuse: ‘I have to economise where I can, to make up for it.’ She trusted none of the children or servants, and would not listen to a word from any of them. Hearing her now, Xi-feng knew she had grown contrary again and that advice would be wasted. She hastily put on a conciliatory smile.

‘What you say is perfectly right, Mother. How long have I lived? What do I know about the rights and wrongs of things? After all, to a mother or father, never mind a maid: even a priceless living treasure would go to their son before anyone else. How can one believe what’s said behind his back?

segments.text: ‘I really am a fool. When Lian does something wrong, you and Father are so angry you’d like to drag him in and beat him dead on the spot. Yet once you see him, you let it pass, and give him your own favourite things just as before. Naturally Grandmother must be the same towards Father. I say, Grandmother’s in a good mood today. If you want to ask her, do it today. I’ll go ahead and keep her laughing. When you arrive, I’ll find an excuse to slip away, taking the other people out with me, so you can speak to her alone. If she gives you the girl, so much the better. If not, no harm’s done, and no one else will know.’
Lady Xing was pleased again at this, and explained further.

‘My idea is not to ask Grandmother first. If she refuses, that’s the end of it. I mean to have a quiet word with Faithful beforehand. Of course she’ll be shy, but once I explain it carefully, she’ll naturally say nothing, and that will settle it.

segments.text: ‘Then I can speak to Grandmother. Even if she refuses, she won’t be able to hold out against the girl’s own wishes. As the saying goes, “You can’t keep someone who means to leave.” Then it’s bound to come right.’

‘You’re the one with the clever plans, Mother,’ said Xi-feng, smiling. ‘That’s a thousand times surer. Never mind Faithful: who wouldn’t want to better herself and get on in the world? Who would turn down being half a mistress and choose to stay a maid, only to be married off to some serving lad in the end?’
‘Exactly,’ said Lady Xing with a smile. ‘Not only Faithful. Which of the senior maids with duties of their own wouldn’t want it? Go ahead, but don’t let a word slip. I’ll come over after dinner.’

segments.text: ‘Faithful has always been a difficult creature,’ Xi-feng thought. ‘Even so, she might yet agree. If I go first and Mother follows, all will be well if the girl consents. But if she doesn’t, Mother is so suspicious she may think I’ve let the secret out and put her up to making difficulties. Then, finding my warning come true, she’ll turn her mortification into anger and take it out on me. I don’t want that. Better to go over together. Whether the girl agrees or not, she won’t be able to suspect me.’
Having thought it through, she smiled.

‘Just before I came, Aunt sent over two cages of quails. I told them to fry the birds, and meant to have them sent here in time for your dinner. But as I was coming through the main gate, I saw the lads carrying your carriage away. They said a joint had come apart and it was going to be repaired. Why don’t we go over together now in mine?’
Lady Xing sent for her people to help her change.

segments.text: Lady Xing thought this sensible and went by herself to Grandmother Jia’s. After chatting for a while, she left on the pretext of going to Lady Wang’s rooms, went out by the back door and passed Faithful’s bedroom. Faithful was sitting there at her sewing. Seeing Lady Xing, she hastily rose.
‘What are you making?’ Lady Xing asked with a smile. ‘Let me see. Your embroidered flowers get better and better.’

She took the work from Faithful’s hands, looked it over and praised it unceasingly. Then she put it down and surveyed the girl from head to foot. Faithful wore a half-worn lotus-mauve figured-silk jacket, a dark-blue satin waistcoat with piped edges, and a pale-green skirt. She had a wasp waist and slender back, an oval face, glossy black hair, a high nose and a faint scattering of freckles on either cheek. Such scrutiny made her feel awkward, and she wondered at it.
‘What brings Your Ladyship here at such an in-between hour?’ she asked with a smile.
Lady Xing gave a look, and her attendants withdrew.

segments.text: Lady Xing sat down, took Faithful’s hand and smiled.
‘I’ve come especially to congratulate you.’
Faithful already had some inkling of what she meant. In spite of herself she blushed, lowered her head and said nothing. Lady Xing went on:

‘You know your master has no one dependable to attend to him. He thought of buying another girl, but you never know what sort of unclean goings-on the girls from those dealers have been mixed up in, or what’s wrong with them. You buy one, and within two or three days she’s up to all her filthy tricks again. So he wanted to choose a girl born into service in the household and take her into his rooms. But he couldn’t find a good one. Either her looks weren’t right or her disposition wasn’t right; if she had one merit, she lacked another. He’s been quietly looking them over for six months, and of all these girls, you’re the pick. Looks, conduct, gentleness, reliability: you have everything. He means to ask Grandmother for you and take you into his rooms. You’re not like a girl newly bought outside. As soon as you enter, you’ll have your bridal face-threading, and he’ll acknowledge you as his concubine. Think of the honour and respect!

segments.text: ‘And you’re a girl who wants to do well. As the saying goes, “Gold must be paid for with gold.” Who would have thought the master would set such store by you? Now all those high ambitions of yours can be fulfilled, and you’ll stop the mouths of the people who dislike you. Come with me and tell Grandmother!’
She took Faithful’s hand to lead her away. Faithful blushed, pulled her hand away and would not go. Taking this for shyness, Lady Xing said:
‘What is there to be ashamed of? You needn’t say a word. Just come with me.’
Faithful merely kept her head down and did not move. Seeing this, Lady Xing tried again.

‘Surely you don’t mean you’re unwilling? If you really are, you’re a foolish girl indeed. You could be a mistress, and you’d rather be a maid! In two or three years you’ll only be paired off with a serving lad and still be a slave.

segments.text: Faithful kept her head down, still without speaking.
‘You’re usually so quick and forthright,’ Lady Xing went on. ‘Why all this hanging back? If there’s anything you’re not happy about, tell me. I’ll see that everything is just as you wish.’
Still Faithful said nothing. Lady Xing smiled again.

‘It must be that you have your father and mother, and you’re too shy to speak for yourself. You’re waiting for them to ask you. That’s reasonable enough. I’ll go and speak to them and have them ask you. Whatever you want to say, you can tell them.’
With that she went to Xi-feng’s rooms.

segments.text: Xi-feng had long since changed. Finding herself alone with Patience, she had told her what was afoot. Patience too shook her head and smiled.
‘I’m not sure it will come off. From the things she says when we talk in private, I don’t think she’s likely to agree. But we can only wait and see.’

‘Her Ladyship is bound to come here to talk it over,’ said Xi-feng. ‘If the girl agrees, well and good. If she doesn’t, Her Ladyship will have made a fool of herself for nothing, and how will she like that in front of all of you? Tell them to fry the quails, add a few other dishes from whatever there is, and get dinner ready. Then go off somewhere for a stroll. Come back when you think she’s gone.’
Patience passed on these instructions to the older women and went leisurely into the garden, free to do as she pleased.

segments.text: Meanwhile, Faithful saw Lady Xing leave. She must have gone to consult Xi-feng, and someone was bound to come and question her. Better to get out of the way. She found Amber.
‘If Her Old Ladyship asks for me, say I’m not well and haven’t had any breakfast. I’m going for a walk in the garden and shall be back soon.’
Amber agreed. Faithful too went into the garden and wandered from place to place until she happened to meet Patience. Seeing there was no one else about, Patience smiled.
‘Here comes the new concubine!’
Faithful blushed.
‘So you’ve all joined forces to plot against me! Just wait till I have it out with your mistress.’

Patience regretted her slip. She led Faithful under a maple tree, sat with her on a rock and told her outright the whole story, everything that had been said and done from Xi-feng’s going over to her coming back. Her face still red, Faithful gave a cold laugh.

‘We’ve always been friends, you and I. Think of Aroma, Amber, Su-yun, Nightingale, Cai-xia, Silver, Musk and Ebony; Kingfisher, who went away with Miss Shi; Ke-ren and Golden, who are dead; Snowpink, who left. With you and me, that makes a dozen or more. Ever since we were little, what was there we didn’t tell each other?

segments.text: Patience was about to laugh and reply when laughter rang out behind the rockery.
‘What a shameless girl! How can you say such things without your teeth setting on edge?’
Startled, the two of them jumped up and looked behind the rocks. It was none other than Aroma, who came out smiling.
‘What’s happened? Tell me.’
All three sat down on the rock, and Patience told Aroma what had just passed.
‘Really, we’ve no business saying it, but that Elder Master is too lustful. Let a girl be even passably good-looking, and he won’t leave her alone.’
Then Patience said:
‘If you don’t want to go, I can show you a way to settle it without any trouble.’
‘What way?’ asked Faithful. ‘Let me hear it.’
‘Just tell Her Old Ladyship you’ve already been given to Master Lian,’ Patience said with a smile. ‘Then the Elder Master won’t be able to ask for you.’
Faithful spat.
‘You wretch! How can you say that? Wasn’t your mistress talking that same nonsense the other day?

segments.text: ‘And now look how it’s come true!’
‘Neither of those two wants it,’ Aroma said, smiling, ‘so I’ll tell Her Old Ladyship to say she’s already promised you to Bao-yu. That’ll make the Elder Master give it up too.’
Faithful was angry, embarrassed and desperate all at once.

‘You two little bitches! May you both come to a bad end! Here I am in trouble, thinking you’re serious people, telling you about it so you can help me out, and you take turns making fun of me. You think your own futures are all settled, and you’ll both be concubines one day.

segments.text: ‘Well, I don’t believe everything in this world necessarily goes just as we wish. Restrain yourselves a little. Don’t be too pleased with yourselves!’
Seeing how upset she was, they hastily smiled and pleaded with her.
‘Dear sister, don’t take it to heart. We’ve been like real sisters since we were little. It was only a joke, with no one else about. Tell us what you mean to do, so we can stop worrying.’
‘What do I mean to do? I simply won’t go, and that’s all.’
Patience shook her head.

‘You may not want to go, but that doesn’t mean he’ll let the matter drop. You know his temper. You belong to Her Old Ladyship’s rooms, so he daren’t do anything to you now, but can you stay with her for ever? You’ll have to leave one day.

segments.text: ‘If you fall into his hands then, it’ll be worse.’
Faithful gave a cold laugh.

‘As long as Her Old Ladyship lives, I won’t leave her. If she dies, he’ll have three years’ mourning to observe, whatever else happens. A man can’t start taking concubines the moment his mother dies! Who knows what things will be like in three years? I’ll think about it then. Even if I’m driven into the last corner, I can cut off my hair and become a nun. Failing that, there’s still death. What if I never marry a man as long as I live? So much the cleaner!’
‘The little minx really has no shame!’ Patience and Aroma said, laughing. ‘Now she’ll say anything that comes into her head.’

‘Things have come to this,’ said Faithful. ‘What does it matter if I’m shameless for a moment? If you don’t believe me, wait and see. Her Ladyship just said she was going to find my father and mother. Let her go and look in Nanjing!’

And you still have your brother and sister-in-law here. It’s a pity you were born into service in this household, instead of being here on your own like the two of us.’
‘What if I was born here? “If an ox won’t drink, must you force its head down?” If I don’t agree, is he going to kill my father and mother?’

segments.text: As they spoke, they saw Faithful’s sister-in-law coming towards them.
‘She couldn’t find your parents straight away,’ said Aroma, ‘so she must have spoken to your sister-in-law.’
‘That whore is a camel-dealer through nine kingdoms,’ said Faithful. ‘Could she hear of this without running to curry favour?’
Before the words were out, her sister-in-law was standing before them.
‘Nowhere I haven’t looked, and here you are, miss!’ she said, smiling. ‘Come with me. I want a word with you.’
Patience and Aroma hurriedly offered her a seat.
‘Please stay where you are, girls. I only came to have a word with our young lady.’
Aroma and Patience pretended to know nothing.
‘What’s so urgent?’ they asked with smiles. ‘We’re guessing riddles, with slaps as forfeits. Let us finish this one before she goes.’
‘What is it?’ Faithful asked. ‘Say it here.’
‘Come with me and I’ll tell you over there,’ her sister-in-law said, smiling. ‘They’re fine words, anyway.’
‘Is it what the Elder Lady told you?’
‘If you know already, miss, why make it difficult for me?

segments.text: ‘“Fine words”, indeed! Emperor Huizong’s hawks and Zhao Zi-ang’s horses: those are fine pictures. “Happy news”! First-rate pox with the pustules full of pus: that’s happy news too. No wonder you’re always envying families whose girls have become concubines, and who all use her position to throw their weight about. The whole family turns concubine! You’ve watched till your eyes are red with envy, and now you want to shove me into the firepit too. If I win favour, you’ll swagger about outside and promote yourselves to “Her Ladyship’s brother” without being asked. If I lose favour and come to grief, you’ll pull your filthy turtle necks into your shells and leave me to live or die as I can.’
She was weeping as she spoke, and Patience and Aroma held her back and tried to soothe her. Her sister-in-law could not bear the humiliation.
‘Whether you want it or not, you can say so decently. There’s no call to drag everyone else into it. As they say, “Don’t talk of shortness in front of a dwarf.”

segments.text: ‘And neither of us has a mother or father or brothers in this household using us to throw their weight about. She knows who she’s abusing. We have no reason to take it to heart.’

‘She’s ashamed because I’ve cursed her,’ said Faithful. ‘She’s nothing to cover her face with, so now she’s trying to set you two against me. Luckily you both have some sense. I was so angry I didn’t make distinctions, and she seized the opening.’
Her sister-in-law knew she had made herself unwelcome and went off in a huff.

segments.text: Faithful was so angry that she went on cursing, and it took Patience and Aroma some time to quieten her. Then Patience asked Aroma:
‘What were you hiding there for? We never saw you.’

‘I went to Fourth Miss’s rooms to look for our Master Bao,’ said Aroma. ‘But I was just too late. They said he’d gone home. I wondered why I hadn’t met him, and thought I’d try Miss Lin’s. Then I met one of her people, who said he hadn’t been there either. I was wondering whether he’d left the garden when you came along. I ducked out of sight, and you never noticed me. Then she came too. I slipped from behind the tree to the back of the rockery, and I saw you two come over to talk. Who would have thought your four eyes could miss me?’

segments.text: She had scarcely finished when someone laughed behind them.
‘Their four eyes missed you? Your six eyes all missed me!’
All three jumped and turned round. It was none other than Bao-yu, coming towards them. Aroma was the first to laugh.
‘You’ve given me a fine search! Where have you been?’

‘I was coming out of Fourth Sister’s when I saw you ahead,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘I knew you were looking for me, so I hid to tease you. I watched you go past with your head down, go into the courtyard and come out again, asking everyone you met. I was laughing away, waiting for you to come close enough for me to give you a fright. Then I saw you skulking about too and knew you were going to play the same trick on someone else. I peeped round to see who it was, and there were these two, so I circled round behind you. When you came out, I took your hiding-place.’
‘Let’s look behind us again,’ Patience said, laughing. ‘Who knows? We might find two more.’
‘There are no more this time,’ Bao-yu said with a laugh.
Faithful knew by now that Bao-yu had heard everything. She simply lay forward over the rock and pretended to be asleep.

segments.text: Bao-yu nudged her, smiling.
‘This rock is cold. Wouldn’t it be better to go back to the rooms and sleep?’

He drew her up as he spoke, and quickly invited Patience to come home with him for tea. Patience and Aroma both urged Faithful to come, and at last she rose. All four went to the House of Green Delights. Having heard everything they had said, Bao-yu was naturally unhappy. He lay silently on his bed and left the three of them to talk and laugh in the outer room.

segments.text: Meanwhile, Lady Xing had asked Xi-feng about Faithful’s parents.

‘Her father is called Jin Cai,’ Xi-feng told her. ‘He and his wife both look after the house in Nanjing. They hardly ever come up to the capital. Her brother, Jin Wen-xiang, is the buyer for Grandmother’s rooms, and her sister-in-law is in charge of Grandmother’s laundry.’

Lady Xing sent for Jin Wen-xiang’s wife and explained everything carefully. Naturally Mrs Jin was delighted. She set off eagerly to find Faithful, expecting everything to be settled as soon as she spoke. Instead, Faithful had given her a tongue-lashing, and Aroma and Patience had added a few words of their own. She came back angry and humiliated.
‘It’s no use,’ she told Lady Xing. ‘She gave me a round of abuse.’
With Xi-feng there, she dared not mention Patience, but said only:
‘Aroma helped her attack me too. They said all sorts of ungrateful things I couldn’t repeat to Your Ladyship. You and the master had better buy someone else.

‘Why didn’t you slap her face and send her back?’ Xi-feng broke in. ‘The moment I leave the house, off she goes wandering! I come home and can’t find so much as her shadow.

segments.text: ‘She must have helped them say something too!’
‘Miss Patience wasn’t actually there,’ said Mrs Jin. ‘I thought I saw her at a distance, but I couldn’t be sure. It was only a guess.’
Xi-feng sent someone to fetch her.
‘Go and drag her here this minute. Tell her I’m home and Her Ladyship is here too. Ask her to come and lend a hand!’
Felicity hurried forward.

‘Miss Lin sent people over with written invitations three or four times before she went, ma’am. I went to call her as soon as you came in, but Miss Lin said, “Tell your mistress I need her for something.”’
Only then did Xi-feng let it drop, though she still made a show of saying:
‘Every day she needs her! What can there be to do?’

‘There are other people looking after the house in Nanjing. It isn’t just that one family. Have Jin Cai brought up here at once.’

segments.text: ‘The last letter from Nanjing said Jin Cai had phlegm clouding his mind,’ Jia Lian replied. ‘They’d even given him money for a coffin. I don’t know whether he’s dead or alive by now. Even if he’s alive, he’s lost all awareness, so bringing him here would be no use. His wife is deaf too.’
Jia She roared at him and cursed.
‘You vile, low-bred bastard! You know everything, don’t you? Get out of here!’

Frightened, Jia Lian withdrew. Presently Jia She sent for Jin Wen-xiang. Jia Lian remained in attendance in the outer study, afraid either to go home or to face his father. He could only wait and listen. Before long Jin Wen-xiang arrived. The pages took him straight through the inner gate, and it was not until enough time had passed for five or six meals that he came out and left.

segments.text: For the moment Jia Lian dared not ask what had happened. After a while he learnt that Jia She had gone to sleep, and only then came home. Not until Xi-feng told him that evening did he understand.

Faithful did not sleep all night. Next day her brother asked Grandmother Jia for permission to take her home for a visit. Grandmother Jia agreed and told her to go. Faithful wanted to refuse, but feared making her mistress suspicious, and reluctantly went out. Her brother had no choice but to repeat Jia She’s words, promising how honoured she would be and how she would manage affairs as a concubine. Faithful set her teeth and would not consent. Unable to do anything with her, he had to report back to Jia She, who flew into a rage.

‘I’ll tell you what to do. Have your wife tell her this, in my very words: “Since ancient times the moon goddess has loved a young man.” She must think I’m too old. I suppose she’s hankering after the young masters, most likely Bao-yu, though Lian may come into it too. If that’s what she has in mind, tell her to give up the idea now. Once she’s refused to come to me, who else will dare take her?

segments.text: ‘That’s one thing. The other is that she thinks, because the old lady’s fond of her, she’ll be married outside one day as someone’s proper wife. Tell her to think carefully. Whoever she marries, she won’t easily get out of my clutches. Unless she dies, or never marries a man all her life, I won’t admit defeat. Otherwise, she’d better change her mind now. She’ll find there are plenty of advantages.’
To every sentence Jin Wen-xiang answered, ‘Yes, sir.’

‘Don’t try to deceive me,’ Jia She said. ‘Tomorrow I’ll send your mistress over again to question Faithful. If you’ve told her and she refuses, you won’t be to blame. But if she agrees when she’s asked, look out for your head!’

segments.text: Jin Wen-xiang hastily agreed over and over again and went home. He did not even wait to tell his wife and have her pass it on, but delivered the message to Faithful face to face. She was so angry that she could find nothing to say. After thinking for a moment, she said:
‘Even if I were willing to go, you’d have to take me to tell Her Old Ladyship first.’
Her brother and sister-in-law supposed she had thought better of it and were overjoyed. Her sister-in-law took her straight up to see Grandmother Jia.

segments.text: As it happened, Lady Wang, Aunt Xue, Li Wan, Xi-feng, Bao-chai and the other girls were all with Grandmother Jia, along with several of the married women of standing who supervised work in the outer household. They were keeping her entertained. Faithful was delighted beyond measure. She pulled her sister-in-law with her and knelt before Grandmother Jia. Weeping as she spoke, she told how Lady Xing had come to her, what her sister-in-law had said in the garden, and what her brother had said that day.

‘Because I wouldn’t agree, the Elder Master went so far as to say I was in love with Bao-yu, or else waiting to be married outside. Even if I went up to heaven, I’d never get out of his clutches all my life. He’d have his revenge in the end. Well, my mind is made up. Here, before everyone, I say that all my life, never mind “Bao-yu”, even if it were “Bao-jin” or “Bao-yin”, “Bao the Heavenly King” or “Bao the Emperor”, I will not marry, whatever happens. Even if Your Old Ladyship forced me, I’d cut my own throat rather than obey! If I’m fortunate, I’ll die before you. If I’m not, if I’m destined to beg my bread, once I’ve served you to the end of your life, I still won’t go with my parents or my brother. I’ll either seek death or cut off my hair and become a nun.

segments.text: ‘If I’m not speaking from my heart, if I’m only putting you off with words until I can contrive something else, let Heaven and Earth, ghosts and spirits, the sun and the moon look into my throat! Let boils grow out of it and rot until I melt into a puddle of putrid paste here before you!’

She had slipped a pair of scissors into her sleeve before coming in. As she spoke, she loosened her hair with her left hand and cut into it with her right. The women and maids rushed to hold her back, but she had already cut off half a lock. They looked: fortunately she had so much hair that the scissors had not gone right through it. They hurriedly pinned it up for her again.
Grandmother Jia was trembling all over with rage. She could only repeat:
‘She’s the one dependable person I have left, and now they want to scheme her away from me too!’
Seeing Lady Wang beside her, she turned on her.

‘So you’ve all been deceiving me! So dutiful on the outside, and plotting against me in secret. If I have anything nice, you want it; if I have anyone good, you want her too. I’ve only this one little maid left. Naturally, when you see how well I treat her, you can’t bear it. Get her away, and then you can do what you like with me!’
Lady Wang hastily stood up, not daring to answer a word.

segments.text: Seeing that Lady Wang too had come under blame, Aunt Xue found it awkward to intervene. At the first words of Faithful’s story, Li Wan had already taken the girls outside. Tan-chun was thoughtful. She considered that, unjustly treated as Lady Wang was, she could not dare defend herself. Aunt Xue was her own sister, so naturally she could not speak for her either. It would be awkward for Bao-chai to defend her aunt; Li Wan, Xi-feng and Bao-yu would none of them dare. This was just the moment when one of the girls was needed. Ying-chun was too meek, Xi-chun too young. So Tan-chun listened for a while outside the window, then went in and spoke to Grandmother Jia with a conciliatory smile.

‘What has this to do with Mother, Grandmother? Think about it. If an elder brother wants to take someone into his rooms, how is his younger brother’s wife to know? Even if she does know, she must pretend she doesn’t.’
Before she had quite finished, Grandmother Jia smiled.

‘Of course! I really am old and muddle-headed. Don’t laugh at me, Aunt Xue. Your sister is most dutiful to me, not like my elder daughter-in-law, who thinks of nothing but being afraid of her husband and only goes through the motions with her mother-in-law. I have treated her unfairly.’

segments.text: Aunt Xue merely answered, ‘Yes,’ then added:
‘It’s not unheard of for an old lady to be partial to her younger son’s wife.’
‘I’m not partial!’ said Grandmother Jia. Then she went on, ‘Bao-yu, I blamed your mother unjustly. Why didn’t you remind me? Why stand there watching her suffer?’

‘Was I to take Mother’s side against Uncle and Aunt?’ Bao-yu asked with a smile. ‘There was only one lot of blame to go round. If Mother was here and wouldn’t take it, who was she to pass it on to? I’d have said it was my fault, but you wouldn’t have believed me.’
‘There’s sense in that too,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘Go and kneel to your mother. Tell her, “Please don’t feel hurt, Mother. Grandmother is getting old. Bear with her for Bao-yu’s sake.”’
Bao-yu hurried over and knelt, about to speak, but Lady Wang quickly drew him up, smiling.
‘Get up, get up! You certainly mustn’t. Surely you aren’t going to apologise to me for your grandmother!’
Bao-yu rose at once. Grandmother Jia smiled again.
‘Xi-feng didn’t remind me either.’
‘Here I am, not blaming you,’ Xi-feng said, laughing, ‘and you turn round and find fault with me?’

segments.text: Grandmother Jia and all the others laughed.
‘Now that is strange! Let’s hear what I’ve done wrong.’

‘Who told you to bring people up so well?’ said Xi-feng. ‘You make them as fresh and tender as young spring onions. How can you blame anyone for wanting them? Luckily I’m your granddaughter-in-law. If I were your grandson, I’d have asked for her long ago. Would I have waited till now?’
‘So it’s my fault, is it?’ Grandmother Jia asked, laughing.
‘Of course it’s your fault, Grandmother.’
‘Very well, I don’t want her either. Take her away with you!’
‘Wait till I’ve earned enough merit in this life to be born a man in the next,’ Xi-feng said. ‘Then I’ll ask for her.’
‘Take her and put her in Lian’s rooms,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘See whether that shameless father-in-law of yours still wants her then!’
‘Lian isn’t good enough for her,’ said Xi-feng. ‘He’s only fit to muddle along with Patience and me, a pair of burnt rolls.’
Everyone laughed. Then a maid announced:
‘The Elder Lady is here.’
Lady Wang hurried out to meet her.

segments.text: When Lady Wang heard that Lady Xing had come, she hurried out to meet her. Lady Xing still did not know that Grandmother Jia had heard about Faithful; she had come to find out how matters stood. She was barely inside the courtyard gate when several old women quietly told her, and only then did she learn the truth. She would have turned back, but those inside already knew she was there, and Lady Wang was coming out to welcome her. She had no choice but to go in. First she paid her respects to Grandmother Jia, who would not say a word to her. She herself felt ashamed and sorry. Xi-feng had already found a pretext to withdraw. Faithful, too, had gone back to her room to nurse her anger. Aunt Xue, Lady Wang and the others, afraid of adding to Lady Xing’s embarrassment, gradually withdrew as well. Lady Xing did not yet dare leave.

segments.text: When no one else was left, Grandmother Jia spoke.

‘I hear you have come matchmaking for your husband. You certainly observe the Three Obediences and Four Virtues, but there is such a thing as being too virtuous a wife! You have sons and grandsons all about you now, yet you are still afraid of him. You can’t so much as say a word or two to restrain him. You let him carry on just as he pleases.’
Lady Xing’s face was scarlet.
‘I’ve tried several times, but he won’t listen. There’s nothing you don’t know about him, Mother. I really had no choice.’

‘If he forced you to murder someone, would you do that too? Think for a moment. Your sister-in-law is an unassuming soul, and she is always ailing. What is there in this whole household that she doesn’t have to worry about? Your daughter-in-law helps her, certainly, but she is at one job after another all day, dropping the rake to take up the broom. I’ve cut down my own demands in every way. If there are things those two fail to see to, Faithful is a careful girl and gives a little thought to my affairs. Whatever I ought to have, she goes and gets it. Whatever needs adding, she finds a moment to tell them so.

segments.text: ‘If Faithful didn’t do that, with everything those two have to look after, indoors and out, great and small, how could they help overlooking a thing or two? Am I to start worrying about things myself at my age? Or to spend my days making out lists of what to ask you for? Of all the people who have come and gone in these rooms, she is the only one left with a few years behind her and some knowledge of my habits and my temper. And then the masters and mistresses all like her. She doesn’t trade on my favour to ask this lady for clothes and that young mistress for money. That is why, these past few years, whatever the business, everyone has trusted what she said, from your sister-in-law and your daughter-in-law down to the least of the servants. I’m not the only one who depends on her. She saves them both a great deal of worry too. With someone like her here, even if my daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law forget something, I don’t have to go without it, and there is nothing to make me angry. Now, if she goes, whom are you going to find to look after me? You might find me a perfect pearl of a girl, but if she couldn’t say what was needed she would be no use.

segments.text: Then she called for a servant.
‘Ask Aunt Xue and the girls to come and talk to me. We were just enjoying ourselves. Why has everyone gone?’
The maids answered at once and went off. Everyone hurried back, except Aunt Xue, who said to the maid:
‘I’ve only just come away. What am I to go back for? Tell her I’ve gone to sleep.’
‘My dear, dear lady, my honoured ancestress! Her Old Ladyship is angry. If you don’t come, there’ll be no end to it. Do come, for our sakes. If you’re tired, I’ll carry you on my back.’
‘You little imp! What are you so frightened of? She’ll scold you a little and that will be the end of it.’
Nevertheless, she had to go back with the little maid. Grandmother Jia hastened to offer her a seat, then said with a smile:
‘Let’s play cards. Aunt Xue is out of practice too. We’ll sit together and not let Xi-feng get the better of us.’
‘Quite right,’ said Aunt Xue, smiling. ‘You must keep an eye on my hand for me.

segments.text: ‘Will it be just the four of us, or shall we have someone else?’
‘There are only four,’ said Lady Wang with a smile.
‘Another would make it livelier,’ said Xi-feng.
‘Call Faithful,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Let her sit next to me, below me. Aunt Xue’s eyes are growing dim. She can look after both our hands.’
Xi-feng sighed and turned to Tan-chun.
‘You girls can all read and write. Why don’t you learn to tell fortunes?’
‘What an extraordinary idea! Instead of putting your mind to winning a little money from Grandmother, you start thinking about fortune-telling.’
‘I want to find out how much I’m destined to lose today. Win, indeed! Look at them. I haven’t even taken the field, and they’ve laid ambushes on either side.’

segments.text: Grandmother Jia and Aunt Xue both laughed. Presently Faithful came and sat next to Grandmother Jia, with Xi-feng next below her. A red felt cloth was spread out, the cards were shuffled, the order of the first draw was decided, and the five players took up their hands. They had been playing for a while when Faithful saw that Grandmother Jia’s hand was ready, needing only the two-circle card to complete it. She gave Xi-feng a secret signal. It was Xi-feng’s turn to play a card. Deliberately, she hesitated for some time, then said with a smile:
‘Aunt must be holding back the card I need. But unless I play this one, I can’t hold out any longer.’

‘I shall check afterwards.’
‘Check all you like. Play yours first and let me see what it is.’
Xi-feng laid it down in front of her. Aunt Xue saw that it was the two-circle card and smiled.
‘I’ve no use for it, but I’m afraid it will complete Grandmother’s hand.’
‘Oh, I’ve played the wrong one!’ Xi-feng said quickly, smiling.
Grandmother Jia had already thrown her cards down with a laugh.
‘Don’t you dare take it back! Who told you to make a mistake?’
‘You see why I wanted my fortune told! I play the card myself, and then blame it on an ambush!’

‘Exactly. You ought to give yourself a slap on the mouth and ask yourself why.’ Grandmother Jia turned to Aunt Xue with a smile. ‘It’s not that I’m mean and want to win money. It’s the good luck of winning.’
‘Of course it is. Who could be fool enough to say you wanted the money?’
Xi-feng had been counting out her cash. At this, she hurriedly threaded the coins back onto their string and smiled at the others.
‘That puts me in my place.

segments.text: Patience put the money down where she had been told, joined in the laughter for a while, then went back. At the courtyard gate she met Jia Lian, who asked her:
‘Where is Her Ladyship? Father has sent me to fetch her.’

‘With Grandmother,’ Patience answered quickly, smiling. ‘She’s been standing there all this time and hasn’t moved. You’d better leave well alone. Grandmother has been angry for half the day. It’s only just easing off, after all the trouble Mrs Lian has taken to amuse her.’

‘I’ll simply say I’ve come for Grandmother’s instructions: is she going to Lai Da’s on the fourteenth, so that we can get the sedan ready? I can fetch Mother and help to amuse her at the same time. Why not?’
‘If you ask me, you’d better not go. Everyone in the family has been in the wrong, even Lady Wang and Bao-yu. Now you want to go and take your turn too.’

‘It’s all over now. Surely she won’t start again? Besides, it has nothing to do with me. And Father told me himself to fetch Mother. If I send someone else and he hears of it, he’s in just the mood to seize on that and take it out on me.’
He went off as he spoke.

segments.text: Meanwhile, the card-playing went on for half the day and ended only when it was time for supper. The next day or two passed without event. Before long it was the fourteenth. Lai Da’s wife came before daylight to renew her invitation. Grandmother Jia was in good spirits and took Lady Wang, Aunt Xue, Bao-yu, the girls and the others to spend half the day in Lai Da’s garden. Though it could not rival Prospect Garden, it was spacious and very well kept. Among its springs and rocks, trees and groves, halls, towers and pavilions, there were several sights to astonish the eye.

In the outer hall were Xue Pan, Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Jia Rong and a few of their nearer clansmen. The more distant relations had not come, nor had Jia She. The Lai family had also invited several serving officials and young men from established families to keep them company. One of these was Liu Xiang-lian. Ever since their previous meeting, Xue Pan had been unable to forget him. He had learnt that Xiang-lian was particularly fond of amateur acting, playing both male and female leads in romantic pieces. He had misunderstood this and wrongly taken him for a young man available for amorous favours. He had been eager to get to know him, only regretting that there was no one to introduce them. To meet him by chance today seemed more than he could have wished for.

Liu Xiang-lian came of an established family. He had made nothing of his studies, and both his parents had died while he was young. By nature frank and chivalrous, careless of trifles, he was passionately fond of spear-play and swordsmanship. Gambling, drinking, visiting the pleasure quarters, playing the flute or the zheng: there was nothing he would not do.

segments.text: As he was young and handsome as well, people who did not know his background mistook him for a professional actor. Lai Da’s son, Lai Shang-rong, was an old friend of his and had invited him to help entertain the guests that day. Once the wine had gone round, the others were tolerable enough, but Xue Pan alone reverted to his old ways. Xiang-lian had long since grown displeased and wanted to slip away at the first opportunity and have done with it. Lai Shang-rong, however, would not let him go on any account.

‘Master Bao has just spoken to me again,’ he said. ‘You saw one another when he came in, but there were too many people about for him to talk. He told me to ask you not to leave when the party breaks up. He still has something to say to you. If you insist on going, let me call him out. You two can see each other before you go, and then it will be nothing to do with me.’

He told the pages to find an old woman in the inner quarters and quietly ask her to bring Master Bao out. In less time than it takes to drink a cup of tea, Bao-yu appeared. Lai Shang-rong smiled at him.
‘My dear uncle, I leave him in your hands. I must go and see to the guests.’
He went straight off.

segments.text: Bao-yu drew Liu Xiang-lian into a small study beside the hall. They sat down, and he asked whether Xiang-lian had been to Qin Zhong’s grave lately.

‘Of course I have. The other day several of us went hawking. We were only two li from his grave when I remembered how much rain we’d had this summer and began to fear the mound wouldn’t hold. I slipped away from the others to look. Sure enough, a little more of it had given way. When I got home I managed to get together a few hundred cash. Early on the third day I went out and hired two men to put it right.’

‘That explains it,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Last month there were lotus seedpods in the pond in Prospect Garden. I picked ten and sent Tealeaf out to place them as an offering on his grave. When he came back I asked whether the rain had washed it away. He said not only had it not been washed away, it looked more freshly made than on his last visit. I thought some of his friends must have built it up again. How I hate being shut up at home every day, unable to decide the smallest thing for myself! I can’t make a move without someone knowing about it. If one person doesn’t stop me, another talks me out of it. I can say what I like, but I can’t do anything.

segments.text: ‘Even when I have money, I’m not allowed to spend it as I choose.’

‘There’s no need for you to worry about this,’ said Xiang-lian. ‘I’m out and about. It’s enough that you remember him. The first day of the tenth month will soon be here, and I’ve already put aside the money for visiting his grave. You know I’m as poor as can be. There’s nothing saved up at home, and if a few coins do come my way, they’re gone as soon as I get them. Better put this much aside while I can than find myself empty-handed when the day comes.’
‘That was just what I wanted to send Tealeaf to find you about. But you’re hardly ever at home. I know you drift about day after day, with no fixed place to be found.’
‘You needn’t look for me on that account either. Each of us can do what he can. In fact, I mean to go away before long, wander about for three or five years and then come back.’
‘Why?’ Bao-yu asked at once.
Liu Xiang-lian gave a cold laugh.
‘You don’t know what’s on my mind. You’ll understand when the time comes. For now, I must say goodbye.’
‘We so seldom meet. Why not stay till the party ends tonight and leave together?’
‘That esteemed cousin of yours, your aunt’s son, is still the same. If I stay, there may be trouble. Better for me to keep out of his way.’
Bao-yu thought for a moment.
‘In that case, you had better avoid him.

Liu Xiang-lian rose to go.
‘Go back inside, all of you. There’s no need to see me out.’

segments.text: He left the study as he spoke. He had scarcely reached the main gate when he found Xue Pan shouting there:
‘Who let little Liu go?’

Liu Xiang-lian’s anger flared. He longed to kill him with a single punch, but then reflected that a drunken brawl would put Lai Shang-rong in an awkward position. He forced himself, again and again, to hold back. Suddenly Xue Pan saw him coming. Delighted as though he had found a treasure, he lurched forward, caught hold of him and smiled.
‘Brother, where have you been?’
‘Out for a stroll. I’ll be back.’

‘My dear brother, all the pleasure goes when you do. Do stay a little. Be kind to me. Whatever important business you have, leave it to your big brother. There’s no hurry. With a brother like me, it’s easy enough for you to get office or make your fortune.’
At this intolerable behaviour, Xiang-lian felt both anger and shame. A plan occurred to him. Drawing Xue Pan aside where no one could see them, he smiled.
‘Do you really care for me, or are you only pretending?’
Xue Pan was almost beside himself with delight. He gave him a sidelong look and hurriedly answered with a smile:
‘Dear brother, how can you ask me such a thing?

segments.text: ‘If I’m pretending, may I drop dead before your eyes!’

‘In that case, this is not the place. We’ll sit a little longer. Then I’ll go first and you can follow me out to my lodgings. We can spend the whole night drinking on our own. I’ve two splendid boys there too, who’ve never been out into the world. You needn’t bring a single servant. There will be people ready to wait on you when you get there.’
The joy of hearing this half sobered Xue Pan.
‘Do you mean it?’
‘What! I offer you my true affection, and you don’t believe me!’
‘I’m no fool,’ Xue Pan said hastily, smiling. ‘Of course I believe you! But I don’t know the place. If you go first, where am I to find you?’
‘My lodgings are outside the north gate. Can you bear to leave home and spend a night outside the city?’
‘With you, what do I need a home for?’
‘Then I’ll wait for you on the bridge outside the north gate.

segments.text: ‘Let’s go back to the table and have some wine. Wait until you see I’ve left before you follow. Then they won’t notice.’

Xue Pan readily agreed. The two went back to their places and drank for a while. Xue Pan could scarcely contain himself. He kept looking at Xiang-lian, growing more delighted the more he thought about it. Pot after pot, without anyone urging him, he drank and drank again, until, before he knew it, he was very nearly dead drunk.

segments.text: Xiang-lian rose and went out, slipping away when no one was watching. Outside the gate he told his page Xing-nu:
‘Go home ahead of me. I’m just going outside the city and then I’ll be back.’

With that he mounted his horse, rode straight through the north gate and waited on the bridge for Xue Pan. In less time than it takes to eat a meal, he saw Xue Pan riding towards him in the distance on a large horse, mouth open and eyes staring, his head turning this way and that like a rattle-drum. When he reached Xiang-lian’s horse, he was so intent on looking far ahead that he took no notice of what was close at hand and rode straight past. Half amused and half enraged, Xiang-lian gave his horse its head and followed.

segments.text: As Xue Pan looked ahead, houses and people grew fewer and fewer. He wheeled his horse round to search again. To his surprise, as soon as he turned he saw Xiang-lian. It was like finding a rare treasure.
‘I knew you would never break your word!’ he said with a smile.
‘Hurry on,’ Xiang-lian answered, smiling. ‘If anyone sees us and follows, it will be awkward.’
He set off at a gallop, and Xue Pan followed close behind.

segments.text: Seeing that there was hardly anyone ahead and that a stretch of reed marsh lay nearby, Xiang-lian dismounted and tied his horse to a tree. He smiled at Xue Pan.
‘Get down. Let’s swear an oath first. If either of us changes his mind later, or tells anyone, let the oath fall on him.’
‘A very good idea,’ said Xue Pan, smiling.
He hurriedly dismounted, tied his horse to a tree as well, then knelt.
‘If in time I change my mind, or tell anyone, may Heaven destroy me and Earth annihilate me!’

He had not finished when there came a thud. Something like an iron hammer struck the back of his neck. Everything went black, golden stars burst before his eyes, and he fell helplessly to the ground. Xiang-lian stepped up to look at him. Knowing that he was a clumsy fellow unused to being beaten, he used only three-tenths of his strength to give him several slaps across the face. In an instant the face was a fruit stall of colours. At first Xue Pan tried to struggle up, but two jabs from the toe of Xiang-lian’s boot knocked him down again.
‘It was supposed to be something we both wanted! If you didn’t want it, you only had to say so. Why trick me out here to beat me?’
As he spoke, he poured out a stream of abuse.
