segments.text: ‘You blind fool! Take a good look at who Master Liu is! Instead of begging for mercy, you insult me! There’s no point in beating you to death. I’ll just teach you what I can do.’
He fetched his riding-whip and struck Xue Pan thirty or forty times, from his back down to his shins. More than half sobered now, Xue Pan could not bear the pain, and cries of ‘Ow! Ow!’ escaped him.
‘So that’s all you amount to!’ Xiang-lian said with a cold laugh. ‘I thought you weren’t afraid of a beating.’
As he spoke he lifted Xue Pan’s left leg and dragged him a few paces into the mire among the reeds, rolling him in muddy water from head to foot.
‘Do you know who I am now?’
Xue Pan did not answer. He lay face down, groaning. Xiang-lian threw down the whip and hammered him several times with his fists. Xue Pan rolled about and screamed.
‘My ribs are broken! I know you’re a respectable gentleman. I listened to what other people said and got it wrong.’
‘Leave other people out of it. Tell me what you have to say now.’
‘There’s nothing I can say now.

‘Ow! My dear elder brother!’
Xiang-lian punched him twice more in succession.

segments.text: ‘Ow!’ Xue Pan cried hastily. ‘Good master, spare this blind fool who had no eyes to see! From now on I shall respect you and fear you.’
‘Drink a couple of mouthfuls of that water,’ said Xiang-lian.
Xue Pan frowned as he heard him.
‘That water is filthy. How could I swallow it?’
Xiang-lian raised his fist and struck.
‘I’ll drink! I’ll drink!’
Xue Pan had no choice but to bend his head down among the roots of the reeds and take a mouthful. Before he could swallow, he retched and brought up everything he had just eaten.
‘You filthy thing! Eat it all up, and I’ll let you off.’
Xue Pan knocked his head to the ground again and again.
‘Please earn yourself some unseen merit and spare me! I couldn’t eat that if you killed me.’
‘You’re stinking me out!’ said Xiang-lian.
He left Xue Pan where he was, led out his horse, found his stirrup and rode away. Only when Xue Pan saw that he had gone did he begin to feel safe. He bitterly regretted having mistaken the man.

segments.text: He tried to struggle up, but the pain all over his body was unbearable.
Meanwhile, Jia Zhen and the others had suddenly missed the pair of them from the feast and searched everywhere without finding them. Someone said:
‘I think they went out through the north gate.’

Xue Pan’s pages lived in fear of him. He had forbidden them to follow, so who dared go looking for him? In the end Jia Zhen grew uneasy and sent Jia Rong out with the pages. Asking their way and following his trail, they went straight through the north gate. More than two li beyond the bridge, they suddenly saw Xue Pan’s horse tied up beside a reed-filled hollow.
‘Good!’ they all said. ‘Where there’s a horse, there must be a man.’

They went up to the horse together and heard someone groaning among the reeds. Hurrying over, they found Xue Pan with his clothes in shreds and his face swollen and cut, rolled in mud from head to foot, inside his clothes and out, like a muddy pig. Jia Rong had already guessed nine-tenths of what had happened. He hastily dismounted and had the others help Xue Pan out.
‘Uncle Xue,’ he said, laughing, ‘you make advances every day. Today you’ve made them all the way into a reed pit!

segments.text: ‘The Dragon King must have fallen for your charms too and wanted you for a son-in-law. You must have run into his horns.’

Xue Pan was so ashamed that he wished he could crawl into a crack in the earth. As for climbing onto a horse, that was out of the question. Jia Rong had to send someone to the settlement outside the city gate to hire a small sedan. Xue Pan got in, and they all went back into the city. Jia Rong still wanted to have him carried to the feast at the Lais’, but Xue Pan pleaded with him in every way, and told him not to tell anyone. Only then did Jia Rong agree to let him go home by himself. He returned to the Lais’ to report to Jia Zhen and describe the state in which he had found him. Jia Zhen, too, knew that Xiang-lian had given him the beating.
‘It will do him good to come off the worse for once,’ he said, laughing.
When the party broke up that evening, he went to enquire after Xue Pan, but Xue Pan was nursing himself in his bedroom and pleaded illness to avoid seeing him.

segments.text: When Grandmother Jia and the others returned and went to their separate homes, Aunt Xue and Bao-chai found Caltrop with her eyes swollen from crying. Having learnt the reason, they hurried to see Xue Pan. Though there were marks of injury on his face and body, neither his sinews nor his bones had been damaged. Aunt Xue was torn between distress and fury. She scolded Xue Pan, then cursed Liu Xiang-lian. She wanted to tell Lady Wang and send men to find and seize Xiang-lian. Bao-chai hurried to dissuade her.

‘It’s nothing so very serious. They were drinking together, and it’s common enough for people to fall out over wine. If one of them is drunk, he may get a few extra blows. Besides, everyone knows how lawless our family is. You only feel this way because you’re distressed about him, Mother. It will be easy enough to get satisfaction. In three or five days, when Brother is better and can go out, Cousin Zhen, Cousin Lian and the rest won’t simply let it drop. They will naturally give a dinner and invite the man, and he can admit his fault and apologise to Brother in front of them all. But if you make a great affair of it now and tell everyone, you’ll only seem partial and overindulgent: you let him make trouble and provoke people, and then, the one time he happens to get the worse of it, you raise an army, using your relations’ influence to bully ordinary people.’
‘My child,’ said Aunt Xue, ‘you really have thought it through. I was too angry to think clearly.’
‘This is just what he needs,’ Bao-chai said with a smile.

segments.text: ‘He isn’t afraid of you and he won’t listen to anyone. He grows more unbridled every day. After two or three lessons like this, he may stop.’

Xue Pan lay on the kang cursing Liu Xiang-lian bitterly. He ordered the pages to tear down Xiang-lian’s house, beat him to death and take him to court. Aunt Xue stopped them. She merely said that Liu Xiang-lian had got carried away in his cups, and now that he was sober he was full of remorse and had fled for fear of punishment. Xue Pan heard her account.
To learn the truth of the matter—

segments.text: Only after hearing this did Xue Pan’s anger begin to subside. Three or five days later the pain was gone, but the marks remained. Ashamed to face his friends and relations, he stayed at home pretending to be ill. Before long it was the tenth month. Some of the men from the shops were settling their annual accounts before going home, and the family naturally gave a farewell dinner for them. Among them was Zhang De-hui, a man over sixty who had worked in the Xue family’s pawnshop from his youth and managed its business. He had two or three thousand taels of his own to live on. He too was going home that year and would not return until the following spring.

‘Paper goods and aromatics have been scarce this year,’ he remarked. ‘They’re sure to be dear next year. I’ll send my eldest boy up first to look after the pawnshop. Then, on my way back before the Dragon Boat Festival, I’ll buy some paper goods, incense and fans to sell here. Even after duties and expenses, there should be several times the outlay in profit.’

Xue Pan considered this. ‘Since that beating I can hardly face anyone. I’ve been wanting to hide for six months or a year, but there’s nowhere to go. I can’t keep pretending to be ill for ever. Besides, I’ve grown to this age without learning either letters or arms. They say I’m in business, but I’ve never so much as handled a silver balance or an abacus. I know nothing of places or customs, roads or distances. Why not get a little capital together and spend a year travelling with Zhang De-hui?

segments.text: That evening Xue Pan told his mother. Aunt Xue was pleased, but she was afraid he would get into trouble away from home; losing the capital was the least of her worries. She would not let him go.

‘At least if you stay with me I can feel a little easier. There’s no need for you to do this business. We aren’t waiting for those few hundred taels to live on. Keeping out of mischief at home would be worth more than the money.’
But Xue Pan had decided, and would not listen.

‘Every day you say I know nothing of the world. I don’t understand this, I won’t learn that. Now I’ve made up my mind to give up all those things that don’t matter, become a man, do something and learn business, you won’t let me! What am I supposed to do? I’m not a girl. How long are you going to keep me shut up at home? Besides, Zhang De-hui is a respectable old man. Our families have known each other for generations. What can go wrong if I go with him? Even if I do go astray for a moment, he’ll speak to me and put me right.

With that, he went off to bed in a sulk.

segments.text: After hearing him out, Aunt Xue consulted Bao-chai.

‘If he really wants to get some experience of proper business,’ Bao-chai said with a smile, ‘that is a good thing. Of course, he talks very well at home. Once he’s away, his old habits may return, and then it will be harder still to restrain him. But we can’t worry about everything. If he truly changes, it will be a blessing for the rest of his life. If he doesn’t, Mother, there’s nothing else you can do. We must do our part and leave the rest to Heaven. He’s a grown man. If we’re always afraid he doesn’t know the ways of the world and can’t go anywhere or do anything, we can keep him shut up this year, but next year he’ll be just the same. Since what he proposes is perfectly proper, reckon on losing eight hundred or a thousand taels, and let him have a try. There will be the shop men to help him, after all. They would hardly have the face to cheat him. Besides, once he’s away there will be no one to egg him on and no one for him to fall back on. Out there, why should anybody be afraid of anybody else? If he has money, he eats; if he hasn’t, he goes hungry. With nobody to turn to, he may even give less trouble than he does at home.’

segments.text: Aunt Xue thought for a while.
‘You’re right. If a little money will teach him some sense, it will be well spent.’

With that settled, the night passed without further incident. Next day Aunt Xue sent for Zhang De-hui and had Xue Pan entertain him with food and wine in the study. She herself stood in the rear gallery, speaking through the window and entrusting her son to his care with a thousand injunctions. Zhang De-hui promised everything. After the meal, as he took his leave, he added:
‘The fourteenth is an excellent day for starting a journey. If the young master packs at once and hires the mules, we can set off early that morning.’

Xue Pan was delighted and told his mother. For the next several days Aunt Xue, Bao-chai, Caltrop and two elderly nurses were busy with his travelling things. To go with him they chose an old servant who was his wet-nurse’s husband, two longstanding servants familiar with the world, and the two pages who usually attended him: six people in all, master and servants. Three large carts were hired solely for their luggage and equipment, and four mules for the long journey.

segments.text: Xue Pan himself was to ride a large iron-grey pacing mule kept by the family, with a saddle-horse in reserve. Once everything was ready, Aunt Xue and Bao-chai spent night after night advising and cautioning him; we need not set down all they said. On the thirteenth he went first to take leave of his uncle, then called on everyone at the Jia mansion. Jia Zhen and the others naturally insisted on farewell entertainments, which need not detain us either. Early on the fourteenth Aunt Xue, Bao-chai and the others went with him right out beyond the ceremonial gate. Mother and daughter watched him go, four eyes full of tears, before turning back.

segments.text: Aunt Xue had brought only four or five servant families to the capital, with two or three old nurses and young maids. Now that Xue Pan had taken his party away, only one or two men remained in the outer quarters. That very day she went to the study and had all its ornaments, curios, curtains and hangings brought into the inner rooms and put away. The wives of two of the men who had gone were told to sleep in the inner quarters too. She also told Caltrop to put her own room thoroughly in order.
‘Lock the door and come and sleep in my room at night.’

‘Since you have all these people to keep you company, Mother,’ said Bao-chai, ‘why not let Caltrop come and keep me company? It’s so empty in the Garden, and the nights are getting long. I do needlework every evening. Surely another person would make it all the better.’

‘Of course!’ Aunt Xue said, smiling. ‘I’d forgotten. She ought to go with you. I was only saying to your brother the other day that Wen-xing is too young and can’t get anything straight, and Oriole isn’t enough to look after you alone. I meant to buy another maid for you.’

segments.text: ‘You never know what you’re getting when you buy one,’ said Bao-chai. ‘If we make a bad choice, the money is the least of it. We shall only have made trouble for ourselves. Better inquire at our leisure. If we find someone whose background we know, then we can buy her.’
As she spoke, she told Caltrop to pack her bedding and toilet-box, and had an old nurse and Zhen-er take them to Allspice Court. Then she and Caltrop went back into the Garden together.

segments.text: ‘I was going to ask your mother myself,’ said Caltrop, ‘whether I might keep you company while the master was away. But I was afraid she might take it amiss and think I only wanted to play in the Garden. I never expected you to ask!’

‘I know you’ve been longing to be here for more than a day or two,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘You simply haven’t had the leisure. Even when you came every day, you were always in such a hurry that it was no pleasure. So I thought we might take the opportunity and let you stay a whole year. I shall have another companion, and you’ll have your wish.’
‘Dear miss,’ Caltrop said, smiling, ‘while I have the chance, do teach me to write poems.’

‘You’ve won Long and now you want Shu!’ Bao-chai laughed. ‘On your first day here, I advise you to go out by the eastern side gate and call on everyone, beginning with Grandmother. Pay your respects all round. There’s no need to make a special announcement that you’ve moved into the Garden. If anyone asks, just mention that I brought you in to keep me company. That will do.

‘I’ve brought her in to keep me company today,’ Bao-chai told Patience, smiling. ‘I was just going to let your mistress know.’

segments.text: ‘Oh, miss, what are you saying?’ Patience laughed. ‘I don’t know how to answer you.’

‘It’s only proper. An inn has its proprietor and a temple its abbot. It’s a small matter, but someone ought to be told. Even the people who keep watch at night should know there are two more here, so that they can attend to the doors and gates. Tell her when you go back, will you? Then I needn’t send anyone.’
Patience agreed, and turned to Caltrop with a smile.
‘Now you’re here, aren’t you going to call on your neighbours?’
‘I was just sending her,’ said Bao-chai.
‘You needn’t come to our place yet,’ Patience told her. ‘The Second Master is ill at home.’
Caltrop assented and left, beginning her round at Grandmother Jia’s. We need say no more of that.

segments.text: As soon as Caltrop had gone, Patience caught Bao-chai by the arm.
‘Have you heard our news, miss?’
‘No. These last few days I’ve been busy getting my brother off. I know nothing of what’s happened here. I haven’t even seen the girls for the past two days.’
‘The Elder Master’s beaten the Second Master till he can’t move,’ said Patience with a little laugh. ‘Surely you’ve heard that?’
‘I thought I heard something this morning, but I wasn’t sure. I was just going to see your mistress when you came. What was he beaten for this time?’
Patience cursed through clenched teeth.

‘It’s all that Jia Yu-cun, Rain-village or Wind-village or whatever he calls himself! A stray bastard picked up Heaven knows where, and too tough to starve. We haven’t known him ten years, and look at all the trouble he’s made! This spring the Elder Master saw some old fans somewhere. When he came home, all the fine fans in his own collection were no good any more. He immediately had people searching everywhere.

segments.text: ‘And there was this wretched man who didn’t know what was good for him, nicknamed Stony. He was too poor to buy food, but he had twenty old fans, and he’d sooner die than let one of them go outside his door. The Second Master called in no end of favours before he managed to meet him. After a great deal of persuasion the man invited him to his house, sat him down and let him have a quick look at them. The Second Master said they were beyond anything: mottled Xiangfei bamboo, palm bamboo, milu and jade bamboo, all with genuine paintings and calligraphy by the old masters. He told the Elder Master, who ordered him to buy them, whatever the price. But that Stony said, “I’ll starve or freeze to death first. I wouldn’t sell them for a thousand taels apiece!” There was nothing the Elder Master could do, so he cursed the Second Master every day for being useless. The man had already been offered five hundred taels, the silver to be weighed out before the fans were handed over. Still he wouldn’t sell. “If you want my fans,” he said, “you must take my life first!” Tell me, miss, what could anyone do?

segments.text: ‘Then that conscienceless Yu-cun heard of it and thought up a scheme. He falsely charged the man with owing money to the government, had him taken to the yamen, and said his property must be sold to make up the arrears. He confiscated the fans, put an official valuation on them and sent them here. Whether Stony is alive or dead now, I don’t know. The Elder Master took the fans and asked the Second Master, “How did he manage to get them, then?” All the Second Master said was, “Ruining a man and his household over such a little thing is no great feat!”

segments.text: ‘That made the Elder Master angry. He said the Second Master was trying to silence him with an insolent answer. That was the main thing. There have been a few smaller things these last few days too, but I can’t remember them clearly. They all came together, and he started beating him. He wasn’t held down and beaten with a board or a stick. He was standing up, and I don’t know what the Elder Master hit him with, just struck out at him anyhow. There are two cuts on his face. We heard your mother had some pills to put on injuries from a beating. Do find me one quickly, miss.’
Bao-chai at once sent Oriole to ask for one and gave it to Patience.
‘In that case, give them my regards. I shan’t go over.’
Patience promised and went away. We may leave her there.

segments.text: ‘Now that I’m here and have some time to myself,’ Caltrop said with a smile, ‘you must teach me to write poems. It would be such good fortune for me!’
‘If you want to write poems, you must take me as your teacher,’ Dai-yu smiled. ‘I don’t know much, but I can probably teach you the rudiments.’
‘If you mean it, I shall. Only you mustn’t get tired of me!’

‘What’s so difficult that you need to study it? There’s an opening, a development, a turn and a conclusion. The middle sections, development and turn, make two pairs of matching lines. Level tones answer oblique tones, grammatical words answer substantive words, and substantive words grammatical ones. If you really have an extraordinary line, you can even disregard the matching of tones and words.’

‘No wonder!’ Caltrop said, smiling. ‘I often get hold of an old book of poems and steal a little time to read one or two. Some lines match perfectly, and some don’t. Then I’ve heard the rule, “One, three, five may go free; two, four, six must be clear.” In old poems some keep to it, but others go wrong even at two, four and six. It has puzzled me every day.

segments.text: ‘If the feeling and thought are true, it will be good of itself, even without ornament in the words. That is what is meant by “not letting words harm the meaning”.’
‘I love those lines by Lu Fang-weng,’ Caltrop said, smiling. ‘“Thick curtains left unrolled keep fragrance long; / The old inkstone’s slight hollow holds more ink.” There’s such pleasure in them!’

‘You must never take poems like that as your model. Because you don’t yet understand poetry, you like what is obvious and easy. Once you fall into that manner, you’ll never learn your way out. Now listen to me. If you truly want to learn, I have The Collected Works of Wang Mo-jie. Read a hundred of his five-character regulated poems first. Study them carefully until you know them through and through. Then read a hundred or two of old Du’s seven-character regulated poems, and after that a hundred or two of Li Qing-lian’s seven-character quatrains. Once those three have given you a foundation, you can look at Tao Yuan-ming, Ying Yang, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao and the others. You’re so intelligent and quick that in less than a year you’ll be an old hand at poetry, never fear!’
‘In that case, dear miss, do get me the book,’ Caltrop said with a smile. ‘Even if I only take it back and read a few poems tonight, that will be something.’
Dai-yu told Nightingale to bring Wang You-cheng’s five-character regulated poems and handed them to Caltrop.
‘The ones with red circles are my selections. Read every one of them.

segments.text: ‘Have you begun to get a taste of them?’
‘A little, though I don’t know whether I’m right. Let me tell you.’
‘It’s only by discussing and examining them that you can improve,’ Dai-yu smiled. ‘Go on. I’m listening.’

‘It seems to me,’ Caltrop said, smiling, ‘that what is good in poetry is something you can’t put into words, yet when you think about it, it is perfectly true to life. There are things that seem unreasonable, but when you think them over they have both sense and feeling.’
‘There’s something in that. But where did you find it?’

‘In his “On the Frontier”, there’s the couplet: “Across the great desert, solitary smoke is straight; / Above the long river, the setting sun is round.” How can smoke be straight? And of course the sun is round. “Straight” seems unreasonable, and “round” too ordinary. But if I close the book and think, it’s as though I can see the scene. And if I try to find two other words to replace them, I can’t.

segments.text: ‘Then there’s “The sun sets: rivers and lakes are white; / The tide comes: earth and sky are blue-green.” “White” and “blue-green” seem unreasonable too. Yet when I think about it, only those two words can describe it fully. Saying them feels like having an olive weighing thousands of catties in my mouth. And “At the ferry landing, sunset remains; / From the village, solitary smoke rises.” “Remains” and “rises”: how did he ever think of them? The year we came to the capital, we moored one evening. There was nobody on the bank, only a few trees. Some families far away were cooking supper, and the smoke was a deep blue-green, going straight up to join the clouds. When I read those two lines last night, I seemed to be back there again.’

segments.text: While she was speaking, Bao-yu and Tan-chun arrived and sat down to listen to her discussion of poetry.

‘If that’s how it is,’ Bao-yu said with a smile, ‘you needn’t read any more poems. Understanding doesn’t depend on quantity. From what you’ve said about those two lines, you’ve already found the heart of it.’
‘You like his “solitary smoke rises”,’ said Dai-yu, smiling, ‘but you don’t know that he adapted that line from an earlier poet. Let me show you. This one is even plainer and more effortless.’
She found Tao Yuan-ming’s lines, ‘Dim, the distant village; / Lingering, the smoke above its houses,’ and passed them to Caltrop. Caltrop read them, nodding and sighing in admiration.
‘So “rises” was developed out of those two characters for “lingering”!’ she said with a smile.

segments.text: Bao-yu laughed aloud.
‘You’ve got it! No more explanations. More study will only muddle you. Start writing. It’s sure to be good.’
‘Tomorrow I’ll send you an invitation to join the society,’ Tan-chun said, smiling.
‘Why tease me, miss? I only envy you all and want to learn for fun.’
‘Who isn’t doing it for fun?’ Tan-chun and Dai-yu both laughed. ‘Do you think we’re serious poets? If we set up as proper poets outside this Garden, people would laugh their teeth out!’

‘That’s giving yourselves up as hopeless,’ said Bao-yu. ‘The other day I was discussing the painting with the gentlemen outside. When they heard we’d formed a poetry society, they begged me to show them our work. I wrote out a few poems for them, and every one of them was sincerely impressed. They’ve copied them out and had them printed.’

segments.text: ‘Is that really true?’ Tan-chun and Dai-yu asked at once.
‘If I’m lying, I’m that parrot on its perch,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
‘You’re quite impossible!’ they both said. ‘Never mind whether they’re any good as poems. Even if they were, you shouldn’t let our writing circulate outside.’
‘What is there to be afraid of? If the women of earlier times hadn’t let their writing circulate, nobody would know of them now.’
Just then Xi-chun’s maid Picture arrived to fetch him, and Bao-yu left. Caltrop again pressed Dai-yu to exchange the book for Du’s regulated poems, and begged her and Tan-chun:
‘Give me a subject to try my hand at. When I’ve cobbled something together, you can correct it.’
‘The moon was beautiful last night,’ Dai-yu said. ‘I meant to try a poem myself but never managed it. You write one instead. Use whichever rhymes you like from the fourteenth rhyme group, han.’

segments.text: Caltrop went back in silence. This time she did not even go indoors, but stayed beneath the trees by the pond, now sitting on a rock in a trance, now squatting to scratch at the earth. People passing by were astonished. Li Wan, Bao-chai, Tan-chun, Bao-yu and the others heard about it and stood some way off on the hillside watching her. She frowned for a while, then smiled to herself.

‘She’ll certainly go mad,’ Bao-chai said, laughing. ‘Last night she kept muttering and mumbling until the fifth watch before she went to sleep. It was light again in less time than it takes to eat a meal. I heard her get up, hurry through her hairdressing and go off to Pin-pin. Then she came back and spent the whole day in a daze. She wrote one poem and it wasn’t good, so now of course she’s writing another.’

‘This is just what they mean by “a place of fine spirit produces people of talent”,’ Bao-yu smiled. ‘Heaven never gives anyone feeling and intelligence for nothing. We’re always lamenting that someone like her should have become so commonplace. Who would have thought this day would come? It shows how just Heaven and earth are.’
‘If you worked as hard as she does,’ Bao-chai said, smiling, ‘what could you fail to learn?’

segments.text: ‘This scarcely seems a poem on the moon,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘Add “light” after “moon” and it might do. Look: every line is about moonlight. Never mind. Poetry begins in nonsense. Give it a few more days and you’ll improve.’
Caltrop had thought this poem wonderful. Their comments dispirited her, but she would not give up and began thinking again.

segments.text: While the girls chatted and laughed, she went out to stroll beneath the bamboo in front of the steps, racking her heart and mind. She heard nothing else, saw nothing else. Presently Tan-chun called through the window with a laugh:
‘Miss Caltrop, take a little leisure!’
Caltrop answered in a daze, ‘“Leisure”, xian, belongs to the fifteenth rhyme group, shan. You’ve used the wrong rhyme.’
They all burst out laughing.
‘She really is possessed by poetry,’ said Bao-chai. ‘And it’s all Pin-pin’s doing!’
‘The Sage says, “Never tire of teaching others”,’ Dai-yu replied, smiling. ‘She came and asked me. How could I refuse to tell her?’
‘Let’s pull her over to Fourth Sister’s,’ Li Wan said with a smile. ‘Get her to look at the painting and bring her back to her senses.’

segments.text: They did indeed come out and pull her along, past Lotus Pavilion to Warm Fragrance Retreat. Xi-chun was tired and lay on her bed having an afternoon nap. The painting silk stood against the wall, covered with gauze. They woke her and lifted the covering to look. Only three tenths of the painting was done. Caltrop noticed several beautiful women in it and pointed, smiling.
‘This one is my mistress, and that one is Miss Lin.’
‘Everyone who can write poetry is in the picture,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘Hurry up and learn!’
They stayed there joking for a while.

segments.text: After they had all dispersed, Caltrop’s mind was still full of poetry. That evening she sat staring at the lamp. After the third watch she lay down, but her eyes stayed wide open; only at the fifth watch did she drift off to sleep. When daylight came, Bao-chai woke and listened. Caltrop was sleeping quietly.
‘She’s been tossing about all night,’ she thought. ‘I wonder whether she managed a poem. She’s tired now. I won’t wake her.’
Just then Caltrop laughed in her sleep.
‘Now I have it! Surely this one must be good?’
Bao-chai did not know whether to sigh or laugh. She quickly woke her.
‘What have you found? Such devotion could reach the immortals. Before you learn to write poetry, you’ll have made yourself ill.’

As she spoke, Bao-chai washed and dressed, then joined the other girls to go to Grandmother Jia’s. Caltrop’s determination to learn poetry had gathered all her vital energies into one purpose. What she could not compose by day had suddenly come to her in eight lines in a dream. As soon as she had washed and dressed, she hurried to write them down. Unable to judge whether they were good or bad, she took them off to Dai-yu again.

Caltrop could not quite believe them. Suspecting that they were only humouring her, she kept questioning Dai-yu, Bao-chai and the others.

segments.text: As they were talking, several little maids and older women hurried up, all smiles.
‘A whole lot of young ladies and married ladies have come. We don’t know any of them. Come quickly, all of you, and meet your relations!’
‘What sort of announcement is that?’ Li Wan laughed. ‘Tell us properly. Whose relations are they?’

‘Your two younger sisters have both come, ma’am. And there’s another young lady they say is Miss Xue’s younger sister, and a gentleman they say is Master Xue’s brother. I’m going to fetch Aunt Xue now. You and the young ladies had better go ahead.’
With that, they went straight on.
‘Can Xue Ke and his sister have arrived?’ Bao-chai said with a smile.

segments.text: Lady Xing’s elder brother and his wife had brought their daughter Xiu-yan to the capital to seek Lady Xing’s help. Xi-feng’s elder brother Wang Ren had happened to be travelling there too, so the two families, connected by marriage, had joined forces on the journey. When they moored halfway, they met the widow of Li Wan’s younger uncle, also bound for the capital with her two daughters, the elder named Li Wen and the younger Li Qi. In conversation they established that they too were related, and the three families continued together. Then Xue Pan’s younger paternal cousin Xue Ke followed with his sister. Years before, while their father was in the capital, he had betrothed his daughter Xue Bao-qin to the son of Academician Mei. Xue Ke was about to bring his own sister up for the marriage when he heard that Wang Ren was going, and hurried after him with her. So they had all arrived together that day to visit or seek shelter with their respective relations.

segments.text: Greetings and introductions followed. Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang were delighted.
‘No wonder the lamp-wick kept crackling and forming flowers last night,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘This is what it foretold!’

She asked after their families, inspected the presents they had brought and ordered food and wine so that they could stay to eat. Xi-feng, needless to say, was busier than ever. Li Wan and Bao-chai naturally had much to say to the aunt and cousins from whom they had been parted. Dai-yu was pleased at first. Then she thought how everyone had their own relations, while she alone was solitary, with no family of her own, and went away to shed tears. Bao-yu understood her feelings well and spent a long time comforting her before she stopped.

segments.text: Then he hurried back to the House of Green Delights and addressed Aroma, Musk, Skybright and the others with a smile.

‘Why aren’t you going to look at them? Who would have thought it? Cousin Bao-chai’s own brother is what he is, but this cousin of theirs is quite different in looks and manners. He’s much more like her own brother. And there’s something more extraordinary. You’re always saying Bao-chai is a perfect beauty. Now look at her younger cousin, and Sister-in-law’s two cousins as well. I can’t even describe them! Heaven, Heaven, how much pure essence and lovely spirit you must have, to make such extraordinary people! I’ve been a frog at the bottom of a well. I was always saying the girls we had here were unique. Who knew we needn’t even look far afield? Here on our own doorstep, each new one surpasses the last. I’ve learnt something more today.

segments.text: ‘Can there possibly be still more, beyond these?’
As he spoke he laughed and sighed to himself. Seeing another of his infatuations coming on, Aroma refused to go and look. Skybright and the others had already been and come back, giggling.
‘Do go and see them! There’s Lady Xing’s niece, Miss Bao-chai’s cousin and Mrs Zhu’s two cousins. Like four fresh water-onions in a bunch!’

segments.text: Before they had finished, Tan-chun came in smiling to find Bao-yu.
‘Our poetry society is going to flourish now.’
‘Exactly!’ Bao-yu smiled. ‘You had the happy thought of starting it, and the spirits have sent all these people here. There’s only one thing: have they ever learnt to write poetry?’
‘I’ve just asked them all. They’re modest about it, but from what I can see, every one of them can. Even if they couldn’t, it wouldn’t be difficult. Look at Caltrop.’
‘They say Miss Xue’s younger cousin is even more beautiful,’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘What do you think, Third Miss?’
‘It’s true. To my mind, neither her elder cousin nor any of the rest of us can compare with her.’
Aroma was astonished.
‘That is strange!’ she laughed. ‘How could anyone be more beautiful? I must go and see.’
‘Grandmother was so enchanted the moment she saw her that she’s already made Mother adopt her as a daughter.

segments.text: ‘Grandmother means to keep her here. It was all settled just now.’
‘Really?’ Bao-yu asked eagerly, delighted.
‘When have I ever lied?’ Tan-chun said, then laughed. ‘Now she’s found such a lovely granddaughter, she’s forgotten this grandson.’
‘That doesn’t matter,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Girls ought to have more affection. It’s only right. Tomorrow’s the sixteenth. Isn’t it time our society met?’
‘Lin has only just got up again, and now Second Sister is ill. Someone always seems to be missing.’
‘Second Sister hardly ever writes poetry. What does it matter if she isn’t there?’

‘Why not wait a few days, let the newcomers get to know us and invite them too? Sister-in-law and Cousin Bao-chai naturally aren’t thinking about poetry just now. Besides, Xiang-yun isn’t here, and Pin-pin has only just recovered. It doesn’t suit anybody. Wait till Yun comes, the new girls feel at home, Pin-pin is quite well, Sister-in-law and Bao-chai have their minds free and Caltrop has improved. Then we could invite a full gathering. Wouldn’t that be better?

segments.text: The brother and sister went together to Grandmother Jia’s. Sure enough, Lady Wang had adopted Bao-qin as her daughter. Grandmother Jia was so fond of her that she would not even let her stay in the Garden: at night she slept in Grandmother’s quarters. Xue Ke settled into Xue Pan’s study.
‘There’s no need for your niece to go home either,’ Grandmother Jia told Lady Xing. ‘Let her stay in the Garden for a few days and enjoy herself before she goes.’

Lady Xing’s brother and sister-in-law were badly off. They had come to the capital relying on her to find them a house and help with their expenses. How could they be anything but pleased? Lady Xing entrusted Xiu-yan to Xi-feng. Xi-feng considered the many girls in the Garden and their different temperaments. It would be inconvenient to establish a separate household for the newcomer. The best plan was to put her with Ying-chun. If Xing Xiu-yan found anything unsatisfactory later, even if Lady Xing heard of it, Xi-feng could not be held responsible. Thereafter, leaving out the days Xiu-yan spent at her parents’ home, whenever she had stayed a full month in Prospect Garden, Xi-feng sent her an allowance equal to Ying-chun’s.

segments.text: Prospect Garden was now livelier than ever. There was Li Wan at their head, then Ying-chun, Tan-chun, Xi-chun, Bao-chai, Dai-yu, Xiang-yun, Li Wen, Li Qi, Bao-qin and Xing Xiu-yan; with Xi-feng and Bao-yu, thirteen in all. As for their ages, apart from Li Wan, the eldest, the other twelve were no more than fifteen, sixteen or seventeen. Three might have been born in the same year, or five might be of one age; two might share a month and day, another two the same hour and moment. For the most part only the month or hour separated them. Even they could not sort it all out precisely. They simply called one another younger brother, elder brother, elder sister or younger sister as it happened.

segments.text: Caltrop’s whole heart was now set on poetry, but she dared not pester Bao-chai too much. Xiang-yun’s arrival was exactly what she needed. Xiang-yun loved talking; how could she resist when Caltrop asked her about poetry? Her enthusiasm grew, and they talked away at length, day and night.

‘I really can’t stand the noise any longer,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘Girls treating poetry as their serious business! If learned people heard you, they would laugh at you for neglecting your proper duties. I haven’t finished dealing with one Caltrop, and now I have a whole sack of chatter like you as well. What is it you keep saying? The brooding depth of Du of the Board of Works, the spare elegance of Wei of Suzhou, the gorgeous luxuriance of Wen Ba-cha, the hidden obscurities of Li Yi-shan. You don’t recognise two poets right under your noses. Why talk about all those dead men?’
‘Which two?’ Xiang-yun asked at once, laughing. ‘Dear cousin, do tell me.’

Xiang-yun and Caltrop both laughed. Just then Bao-qin arrived wearing a cloak of some unknown substance, brilliant in gold and emerald green.
‘Where did that come from?’ Bao-chai asked at once.
‘Because it was sleeting, Grandmother found it for me,’ Bao-qin said with a smile.
Caltrop came closer to look.
‘No wonder it’s so beautiful. It’s woven from peacock feathers.’

segments.text: ‘She never dreamt she would come here now, and once here, find Grandmother so fond of her.’

‘When you aren’t with Grandmother, come into the Garden,’ Xiang-yun told Bao-qin. ‘In those two places you can play, laugh, eat and drink as much as you like. When you go to Lady Wang’s, if she’s in, stay and talk to her as long as you please. But if she isn’t there, don’t go in. The people in those rooms are full of nasty suspicions. They all want to do us harm.’
Bao-chai, Bao-qin, Caltrop, Oriole and the others laughed.

‘Call you thoughtless, and you turn out to have thought of everything,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘But for all your thoughtfulness, your tongue is much too plain. Our Qin is rather like you. You’re always saying you want me for your own elder sister. Today I’ll make you take her for your own younger one.’
Xiang-yun looked at Bao-qin for a long while, then smiled.
‘She’s the only one who ought to wear that cloak. It really wouldn’t suit anyone else.’
Just then Amber came in, smiling.
‘Grandmother says Miss Bao-chai mustn’t keep Miss Qin on too tight a rein.

segments.text: ‘Nothing that comes out of that mouth has any foundation.’

Bao-yu knew Dai-yu’s touchiness well. He had not yet heard what had recently passed between her and Bao-chai, and had been afraid Grandmother’s affection for Bao-qin would upset her. Now, after Xiang-yun’s remark and Bao-chai’s answer, he studied Dai-yu’s expression and manner. They were indeed different from before and bore out Bao-chai’s words. He felt troubled and unhappy.
‘Those two were never such good friends,’ he thought. ‘Now they seem ten times closer than anyone else.’

Presently Dai-yu went after Bao-qin, calling her ‘little sister’ without using her name at all, just as though they were sisters by birth. Bao-qin was young and warm-hearted, naturally clever, and had read and written since childhood. After two days in the Jia household she already had a general notion of its people. She saw that none of the girls was a frivolous, painted beauty, and that they all got on well with her elder cousin; she would not be less friendly in return. Dai-yu struck her as exceptional even among them, and she showed her particular affection and respect. Bao-yu could only watch in silent wonder.

segments.text: After a while Bao-chai and her cousin went to Aunt Xue’s, Xiang-yun went to Grandmother Jia’s, and Dai-yu returned to her room to rest. Bao-yu came to find her.

‘I’ve read The Western Chamber,’ he said with a smile, ‘and there were a few lines I understood well enough to quote as a joke. You were angry with me for it. Now I think of it, there’s one line I don’t understand. I’ll recite it, and you can explain it to me.’
Dai-yu knew at once that there was something behind this.
‘Recite it, then. Let me hear.’
‘There’s a wonderful line in “The Quarrel over the Letter”,’ Bao-yu smiled. ‘“When was it that Meng Guang received Liang Hong’s tray?”

segments.text: ‘That’s the finest line. Those five characters, “Meng Guang received Liang Hong’s tray”, are only a familiar allusion. But what a delightful question he makes with the three little grammatical characters, “When was it that”! When was it that she received it? Do tell me.’
Dai-yu could not help laughing too.
‘A very good question. His question is good, and so is yours.’
‘You used to suspect me. Now you’ve nothing left to say, and I’m the one left out.’
‘Who knew she really was so good?’ Dai-yu said with a smile. ‘I always thought she was hiding some treachery.’

Beginning with her mistake in the drinking game, she told Bao-yu everything in detail, including the bird’s nests Bao-chai had sent and their conversation during her illness. Only then did he understand.
‘I thought so!’ he laughed. ‘I kept wondering, “When was it that Meng Guang received Liang Hong’s tray?” So she received it when “children don’t know how to guard their tongues”.’
Dai-yu began talking of Bao-qin again. Remembering that she had no sisters herself, she could not help crying once more.

segments.text: ‘You’re making yourself miserable again,’ Bao-yu said, hastening to comfort her. ‘Look how much thinner you are this year than last. Yet you still won’t take care of yourself. Every day, when everything is perfectly all right, you have to find something to grieve over and cry for a while before you consider the day’s work done.’
Dai-yu wiped her tears.
‘Lately my heart keeps aching, but I seem to have fewer tears than last year. The ache goes on and on, but there aren’t many tears.’
‘That’s only a fancy you have from crying so much. How could tears grow fewer?’

segments.text: While they were talking, a little maid from Bao-yu’s rooms brought his broadcloth cloak.
‘Mrs Zhu has just sent word that, as it’s snowing, she wants to discuss inviting everyone to write poetry tomorrow.’

Before she had finished, Li Wan’s maid arrived to fetch Dai-yu. Bao-yu invited Dai-yu to go with him to Sweet-rice Village. Dai-yu changed into small boots of red xiang-yang sheepskin, with cloud-shaped work ornamented in gold thread. Over her clothes she put a crane cloak faced with scarlet yusha gauze and lined with white fox fur, fastened with a blue-and-gold sash shot with green, with double rings and a fourfold ruyi knot. She covered her head with a snow hood, and the two set out through the snow together. The other girls were all there, uniformly wrapped in scarlet broadcloth or feather-satin cloaks. Only Li Wan wore a dark-blue duoluo woollen jacket opening down the front, while Bao-chai had a lotus-blue crane cloak of fanba cloth made with imported yarn, its rich patterned ground bearing dou-patterning and flowers. Xing Xiu-yan was still in her ordinary, worn clothes, with nothing to protect her from the snow. Presently Xiang-yun arrived in a lustrous outer coat Grandmother Jia had given her, with sable-head fur outside and thick black-and-grey squirrel fur inside. On her head was a Zhaojun hood of scarlet broadcloth, lined with goose-yellow gold-patterned cloth with cloud-shaped work; she had also wrapped a large sable neck-wrap about her neck.

segments.text: ‘Look, here comes Monkey!’ Dai-yu laughed first. ‘She has a snow cloak like the rest of us, but she’s deliberately dressed herself up as a little Tartar imp.’
‘Look at what I’m wearing underneath,’ Xiang-yun said with a smile, taking off the coat as she spoke.

Under it was a half-worn short ermine jacket, autumn-fragrance in colour, fitted and narrow-sleeved, with an overlapping front and matching-colour triple bands at collar and cuffs. Dragons in five colours were embroidered on it with couched gold work. Beneath that was a very short zhezi garment of pink figured satin and fox-flank fur. A five-coloured palace sash with long tassels was drawn tightly round her waist in a butterfly bow. She too wore small doe-skin boots. The clothes showed off still more her wasp waist and ape’s back, her crane’s poise and mantis-like figure.

‘These five are exempt. Of our own people, Second Sister is ill, so she’s exempt, and Fourth Sister has asked to be excused, so she is too. Send me your four shares. I’ll take charge of the whole thing; five or six taels altogether will be quite enough.’

‘I’ve already decided,’ Li Wan said with a smile. ‘You’ll find out when the time comes tomorrow.’
They chatted a little longer, then went to Grandmother Jia’s. Nothing more need be said of that day.

segments.text: Bao-yu had been so full of the party that he slept badly all night, and next morning he scrambled up at daybreak. Drawing back the bed-curtain, he saw a dazzling brightness at the windows, though the doors and windows were still closed. He began to worry, grumbling that it must have cleared and the sun was already out. He hurried to lift the inner window-screen and looked through the glass. It was not sunlight at all. Heavy snow had fallen all night and lay more than a chi deep; above, it was still as though someone were rubbing cotton and tearing wadding from the sky. Bao-yu was delighted. He called the servants up at once, washed his face and rinsed his mouth, and put on only an aubergine-coloured duoluo woollen jacket lined with fox fur, with a little sea-dragon-fur over-jacket whose shoulders spread like an eagle’s wings. He belted himself, put on a jade-needle rain cape and a golden-vine hat, stepped into shatang-wood clogs and hurried towards Reed Snow Lodge. Outside his courtyard he looked about him. Everything was one colour; far away stood the green pines and emerald bamboo. He felt as if he had been put inside a glass box. He went down to the foot of the hill and had just turned along its base when a cold fragrance brushed his nose.

What a delight! Bao-yu stopped and admired them closely for a while before going on. On the narrow-waisted plank bridge he saw someone approaching under an umbrella: the person Li Wan had sent to invite Xi-feng.

segments.text: At Reed Snow Lodge the maids and older women were sweeping the snow away to open a path. The lodge stood on a strip of riverbank between the hill and the water: a row of several rooms, with thatched eaves, earthen walls, a hibiscus hedge and bamboo windows. One had only to push open a window to fish. Reeds surrounded it on every side. A winding path led away through them to the bamboo bridge at Lotus Pavilion. Seeing him arrive in cape and hat, the servants laughed.
‘We were just saying all we lacked was a fisherman. Now the picture’s complete! The young ladies aren’t coming until after breakfast. You’re in far too much of a hurry.’

Bao-yu had to turn back. At Drenched Blossoms Pavilion he saw Tan-chun coming from Autumn Studio, wrapped in a scarlet broadcloth cloak and wearing a Guanyin hood. She leaned on a little maid’s arm, while a woman behind held an oiled umbrella of blue silk over her. Knowing she was going to Grandmother Jia’s, Bao-yu waited at the pavilion until she reached him, and they left the Garden together. Bao-qin was in the inner room, washing and changing.

segments.text: Presently all the girls arrived. Bao-yu kept saying he was hungry and calling for breakfast. At last it was served. The first dish was lamb steamed in cow’s milk.
‘This is medicine for old people like us,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘It never saw daylight. It’s a pity you children can’t eat it. There’s fresh venison today as well. Wait for that.’
They agreed, but Bao-yu could not wait. He poured tea over a bowl of rice and hurriedly swallowed it with some minced pheasant and pickled melon.
‘I know you have something on today,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘You can’t even spare time to eat.’
She ordered them to keep the venison for his supper. Only when Xi-feng hastily assured her there was more did she leave the matter alone. Xiang-yun whispered a plan to Bao-yu.
‘Since there’s fresh venison, why don’t we ask for a piece and take it into the Garden to cook ourselves? Something to play with and something to eat.’
Bao-yu needed no second bidding. He did indeed ask Xi-feng for a piece and had a woman carry it into the Garden.

segments.text: When the party broke up, everyone went into the Garden and on to Reed Snow Lodge to hear Li Wan announce the subject and rhymes. Only Xiang-yun and Bao-yu were missing.
‘Those two must never be allowed together,’ said Dai-yu. ‘Whenever they are, there’s no end to their schemes. I’m sure they’re plotting what to do with that venison.’
Just then Aunt Li came to see the fun.

‘That young gentleman with the jade and the young lady wearing a gold qilin,’ she said to Li Wan, ‘such clean, delicate-looking children, and neither of them short of food: why are they discussing eating raw meat? They’ve been talking it over quite seriously. I can’t believe meat can be eaten raw.’
‘How dreadful!’ they all laughed. ‘Bring them here at once!’
‘I knew it was Yun’s doing,’ Dai-yu said with a smile. ‘My divination never fails.’

segments.text: Li Wan and the others hurried out to find them.

‘If you two want to eat it raw, I’ll send you to Grandmother’s to do it. You can eat a whole raw deer there for all I care. If you stuff yourselves sick, it won’t be my responsibility. Such heavy snow, such bitter cold, and you have to make trouble for me!’
‘Nothing of the sort,’ Bao-yu laughed. ‘We’re going to roast it.’
‘That’s better.’
The women brought an iron brazier, iron forks and a wire grid.
‘Mind you don’t cut your hands,’ Li Wan warned. ‘There’ll be no crying if you do!’
She went back inside with Tan-chun.

Bao-qin stood nearby smiling in her duck-feather cloak.

‘Try it,’ said Bao-chai. ‘It’s good. Your Cousin Lin is too delicate to digest it, or she would like some too.’

‘Miss Shi won’t let me go. You go back first,’ Patience said.
The maid left. Before long Xi-feng herself appeared, wrapped in a cloak.
‘Eating such good things and never telling me!’ she laughed, joining the group and helping herself.

‘Where could you find another gang of beggars like this?’ Dai-yu laughed. ‘Well, well! Reed Snow Lodge has met its doom today. Yun has utterly disgraced it. I shall weep great tears for Reed Snow Lodge!’

segments.text: When they had finished eating, they washed their hands and rinsed their mouths. As Patience put on her bracelets, she found one missing. They searched in a flurry, right and left, in front and behind, but found no trace of it. Everyone was astonished.
‘I know where that bracelet has gone,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘You go and write your poems. We needn’t look any more. We’ll go back to the front. I guarantee it will turn up within three days.’

segments.text: ‘Better still!’ they all said, laughing.
Bao-chai added the character Feng above the Old Farmer of Sweet-rice Village, and Li Wan explained the subject to her. After thinking for some time, Xi-feng laughed.
‘Don’t make fun of me. I’ve only one plain, ordinary line. What comes after that I haven’t the least idea.’
‘The plainer the better,’ they said, laughing. ‘Give us your line, then go and see to your proper business.’
‘I thought there must be a north wind when it snows,’ said Xi-feng. ‘I heard it blowing all last night, and that gave me a line: “All night the north wind blew hard.” Will that do?’
They exchanged amused glances.
‘It may be plain, but you can’t tell what’s coming next. That’s just how someone who knows about poetry would begin.

segments.text: Xiang-yun had collapsed, helpless with laughter. Watching the three of them compete to get in first, the others had abandoned their own poems and could only laugh. Dai-yu kept pushing Xiang-yun to carry on.
‘So even you run out of talent! Let’s hear what else that tongue of yours can chew over!’
Xiang-yun merely lay in Bao-chai’s arms, laughing without stopping. Bao-chai pushed her upright.
‘If you’re so clever, use up every rhyme in the second group, xiao. Then I’ll admit you’ve beaten me.’
Xiang-yun sat up, laughing. ‘I wasn’t writing poetry at all. I was fighting for my life!’
‘Go on, then,’ they all laughed.
Tan-chun had long since realised that she would get no more lines in and had been writing out what they said.
‘We still haven’t brought it to a close,’ she observed.
At that, Li Wan took it up with a line:

segments.text: ‘Taken line by line, it holds together very well,’ Li Wan said with a smile. ‘Only Bao-yu has failed the examination again.’
‘I’m no good at linking verses,’ he said, laughing. ‘You’ll have to make allowances for me.’

‘We can’t make allowances at every meeting. First the rhymes are too difficult, then you go and get it wrong, then you can’t link verses. Today you must pay a forfeit. I noticed how lovely the red plum blossom was at Green Bower Hermitage. I want a branch for a vase, but Adamantina is such a tiresome person that I won’t have anything to do with her. Your forfeit is to fetch me a branch.’
Everyone agreed that this was both an elegant and an amusing penalty. Bao-yu was delighted to oblige and, accepting it, was about to leave when Xiang-yun and Dai-yu spoke together.
‘It’s terribly cold outside. Have a cup of hot wine before you go.’

segments.text: Xiang-yun had already picked up the wine pot. Dai-yu passed her a large cup, and Xiang-yun filled it to the brim.
‘Once you’ve drunk our wine,’ Xiang-yun said, laughing, ‘your forfeit will be doubled if you don’t bring it back.’
Bao-yu quickly drank the cupful and set off through the snow. Li Wan ordered someone to go with him and take good care of him, but Dai-yu stopped her.
‘No need. Having someone with him would only spoil everything.’
‘Yes,’ Li Wan said, nodding.
She had a maid bring a slender, high-shouldered vase and fill it with water, ready for the plum blossom.
‘When he comes back, we ought to write about red plum blossom,’ she added, smiling.
‘I’ll do the first one,’ Xiang-yun said at once.

‘You certainly shan’t write any more today,’ said Bao-chai. ‘You snatched all the lines for yourself, and there was nothing left for anyone else. That’s no fun. When Bao-yu comes back, we’ll give him another forfeit. He says he can’t link verses; now he can write a poem on his own.’
‘Quite right,’ said Dai-yu, smiling. ‘I have another idea. Some of us didn’t get enough lines in just now. Why not choose the ones who had fewest, and let them write about the red plum blossom?’
‘Exactly,’ said Bao-chai.

‘I have a good subject to set him,’ Xiang-yun said quickly.

segments.text: They asked her what it was.
‘“Calling on Adamantina to Beg Red Plum Blossom”. Wouldn’t that be fun?’

They all agreed that it would. She had hardly finished speaking when Bao-yu came in beaming, a branch of red plum blossom over his shoulder. The maids hurried to take it and put it in the vase. Everyone thanked him with smiles.
‘Enjoy it now,’ said Bao-yu. ‘You’ve no idea how much trouble it cost me.’

Tan-chun had already brought him another cup of warm wine. The maids came forward to take his rain-cape and hat and brush off the snow. Maids from all their rooms had brought more clothes; Aroma too had sent someone with a partly worn jacket of fox-underarm fur. Li Wan had a plate filled with the large steamed taros, and two more with red mandarins, yellow oranges, olives and other fruit, and sent them to Aroma.
Xiang-yun told Bao-yu the subject they had chosen and urged him to begin at once.
‘My dear sisters, let me choose my own rhymes,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Don’t prescribe them.’
‘Write it as you please,’ they all said.

segments.text: As they talked, they admired the plum blossom. The branch stood only about two chi high, but a side bough thrust out across it, some five or six chi long. Smaller branches forked from it: some like coiled hornless dragons, some like stiff earthworms, some single and spare as brushes, others clustered thickly as a wood. The flowers opened in rouge-red, their scent surpassing orchids. Everyone praised them.

segments.text: Dai-yu finished writing. Xiang-yun and the others had only just begun to discuss the poem when several maids ran in.
‘Her Old Ladyship is coming!’
They hurried out to meet her, exclaiming with delight, ‘What a happy thought!’

They could see Grandmother Jia in the distance, wrapped in a great cloak, with a grey-squirrel hood to keep her warm, sitting in a small bamboo chair beneath an oiled blue-silk umbrella. Faithful, Amber and five or six maids in all, each carrying an umbrella, surrounded the chair. Li Wan and the others went forward, but Grandmother Jia had them stopped.
‘Stay where you are.’
When she reached them, she smiled.
‘I’ve come without telling your mother or Feng. There’s no harm in my sitting in this, even with the snow so deep. No need to make them come tramping through it.’

They agreed as they helped her out and took her cloak. On entering the room she exclaimed, smiling, ‘What beautiful plum blossom! You certainly know how to enjoy yourselves. I’ve come to the right place.’
Li Wan had already ordered a large wolfskin rug to be spread in the middle.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia sat down.
‘Go on laughing and eating and drinking,’ she said with a smile. ‘The days are so short now I daren’t take a midday nap. I played cards for a while, then thought of you, and came to join in the fun.’

Li Wan brought her a hand-warmer. Tan-chun fetched a fresh cup and chopsticks, poured warm wine herself and offered it to Grandmother Jia. She took a sip, then asked what was on one of the plates. They hurriedly brought it over and told her it was quail preserved in wine lees.
‘That will do. Tear me off a scrap or two of the leg.’
Li Wan agreed at once, asked for water to wash her hands and tore off the meat herself.
‘Sit down again and talk,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Let me listen.’
She told Li Wan, ‘You sit down too. I want you to behave just as if I weren’t here, or I shall go away.’
Only then did they resume their seats in order, Li Wan moving to the very lowest place. Grandmother Jia asked what they had been doing, and they told her they had been writing poems.

‘This is too much! She’s taking longer than they took to build the garden.’

segments.text: She got back into the bamboo chair. The others clustered round and followed, past Lotus Pavilion and into a narrow passage. At its eastern and western ends were gateways spanning the path, with stone tablets set into both the inner and outer faces of their gatehouses. They entered by the western gate: the tablet outside was carved with ‘Through the Clouds’, the one inside with ‘Across the Moon’. At the middle of the passage they went through the main south-facing entrance, and Grandmother Jia got out of her chair. Xi-chun had already come out to meet her.

An inner covered walk led to Xi-chun’s bedroom. Above its entrance were the three characters ‘Warm Fragrance Retreat’. Several servants lifted the scarlet felt curtain, and warmth and fragrance brushed their faces even before they entered. Grandmother Jia did not sit down, but asked where the painting was.
‘It’s turned cold,’ Xi-chun replied with a smile. ‘The glue has all thickened and set; it won’t flow smoothly. I was afraid the painting would look bad if I went on, so I put it away.’
‘I want it for the New Year,’ Grandmother Jia said, smiling. ‘No making excuses to be lazy. Get it out and hurry on with it.’
Before she had finished, Xi-feng arrived in a purple lambskin jacket, smiling broadly.
‘Our old ancestor slipped away today without a word to anyone. What a search you’ve given me!’
Grandmother Jia was naturally delighted to see her.
‘I was afraid you’d get cold, so I wouldn’t let anyone tell you.

segments.text: ‘I asked the little maids, but they wouldn’t tell me, so I had to come hunting in the garden. I was still wondering about it when two or three nuns arrived, and then I understood. They must have come with the New Year prayer papers, I thought, or to collect their annual allowance and incense money. With so many calls on our old ancestor at the year’s end, she must have gone into hiding from her creditors. I hurried to ask the nuns, and sure enough, I was right. I gave them their annual allowance straight away and sent them off. Now I’ve come to report that the creditors have gone, and you needn’t hide any longer.

segments.text: ‘There’s a beautifully tender pheasant ready. Do come to dinner; leave it any longer and it’ll be tough.’

All through this speech the others were laughing. Without even waiting for Grandmother Jia to answer, Xi-feng ordered the chair brought round. Laughing, Grandmother Jia took her hand and got in again. With everyone about her, she went out through the eastern gate of the passage amid talk and laughter.

All round them lay a world adorned in powder and built in silver. Suddenly they saw Bao-qin in her duck-feather cloak, standing on the slope waiting for them at a distance. Behind her a maid held a vase of red plum blossom.
‘So that’s where our two missing people are,’ they all said, laughing. ‘Waiting for us here! She’s been after plum blossom too.’
Grandmother Jia was delighted.
‘Look at her on that slope,’ she said eagerly, smiling. ‘With her looks, and that cloak, and the plum blossom behind her. What does it remind you of?’
‘Just like the picture by Qiu Shizhou in your room, “Two Beauties”,’ they all said, smiling.
Grandmother Jia shook her head, laughing.
‘Where is there a cloak like this in that picture? And the person in it could never be so lovely!’
Just then, from behind Bao-qin stepped someone in a scarlet broadcloth cloak.

segments.text: ‘Which girl is that?’ Grandmother Jia asked.
‘We’re all here,’ they said, laughing. ‘That’s Bao-yu.’
‘My eyes are getting worse and worse,’ she said with a laugh.
By now they had drawn near, and Bao-yu and Bao-qin it certainly was.

‘I’ve just been to Green Bower Hermitage again,’ Bao-yu told Bao-chai, Dai-yu and the others with a smile. ‘Adamantina is sending each of you a branch of plum blossom. I’ve already had them sent round.’
They all smiled and thanked him for his trouble.

segments.text: Talking as they went, they passed out of the garden gate and returned to Grandmother Jia’s rooms. After dinner they talked and laughed for a while longer. Then Aunt Xue arrived.
‘Such heavy snow! I haven’t come over all day to ask how you were. Haven’t you felt like enjoying yourself today? It’s just the day to admire the snow.’
‘Who says I haven’t enjoyed myself?’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘I went to find the girls and had some fun with them.’

‘Last night I was thinking of borrowing the garden from my sister for the day,’ Aunt Xue said with a smile, ‘and laying on a couple of tables of plain food and wine so that I could invite you to enjoy the snow. But you retired early. My daughter told me you weren’t feeling very cheerful, so I didn’t dare disturb you today.

segments.text: ‘If I’d known, I certainly should have invited you.’
‘This is only the first snow of the tenth month,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘There’ll be plenty more snowy days. It isn’t too late for you to go to that expense.’
‘Indeed,’ said Aunt Xue, smiling. ‘At least you can count the sincerity of my good intentions.’

‘Careful you don’t forget, Aunt,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘Weigh out fifty taels now and let me keep them for you. As soon as it snows, I’ll have the party ready. Then you needn’t worry, and you can’t forget.’

‘In that case, give her the fifty taels to keep,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘We’ll take twenty-five each. When it snows I’ll pretend to be out of spirits, and we’ll let the day slip by. You’ll have still less to worry about, and Feng and I will be that much better off.’
Xi-feng clapped her hands. ‘Perfect! Exactly what I had in mind.’
Everyone laughed.
‘Pah! Shameless creature,’ said Grandmother Jia, laughing. ‘No sooner do I hold out a pole than you climb up it!

Now she reckons it won’t work, so she turns on me to make herself look good, and comes out with all these generous sentiments. Very well, I won’t ask Aunt for any money. segments.text: Grandmother Jia returned to the subject of Bao-qin gathering plum blossom in the snow, saying that the sight had been lovelier than a painting. She went on to ask in detail about the eight characters of Bao-qin’s birth date and time, and about her family’s circumstances. Aunt Xue guessed that she was probably thinking of a match for Bao-yu. She herself would have welcomed it, but Bao-qin was already promised to the Mei family. As Grandmother Jia had said nothing openly, Aunt Xue could not take it upon herself to assume anything. She therefore told her, partly revealing and partly withholding:

‘It’s a pity the child has had so little good fortune. Her father died the year before last. She’s seen a great deal of the world since she was small, though. She went everywhere with her parents, all over the mountains. Her father loved enjoying himself. He had business in different places and took his family along, spending a year travelling about one province, then half the next year in another. They must have covered five or six tenths of the whole country. The year they were here, he promised her to Academician Mei’s son. Then, the very next year, he died, and her mother has a phlegm disorder.’
Xi-feng did not wait for her to finish, but sighed and stamped her foot.
‘What bad luck! I was just going to make a match for her, and now she’s promised to someone already.’
‘Who were you going to match her with?’ Grandmother Jia asked, smiling.
‘Never you mind, old ancestor. I’d made up my mind those two were meant for one another.

segments.text: ‘But now she’s promised, there’s no point saying anything. Better leave it unsaid.’

Grandmother Jia understood what Xi-feng meant. Hearing that Bao-qin was already engaged, she too let the subject drop. They chatted for a while longer, then dispersed. The night passed without anything to relate.

segments.text: Next day the snow had cleared. After the meal, Grandmother Jia again instructed Xi-chun herself.

‘Cold or warm, go on painting. If it really can’t be ready by the New Year, so be it. The most important thing is to put in Qin as she was yesterday, with the maid and the plum blossom, exactly as they looked. Not a brushstroke wrong. Add them as soon as you can.’

‘None of those. I’ve guessed it. It must be a performing monkey.’
‘That’s exactly it,’ Xiang-yun said, laughing.
‘The beginning is all right,’ they said, ‘but how do you explain the last line?’
‘What performing monkey hasn’t had its tail chopped off?’ Xiang-yun replied.

‘What a clever idea!’ they all said. ‘Why not write them out so that we can all read them?’

segments.text: ‘Oh, Cousin Chai! How you do “glue down the bridges before playing the zither”! What an affectation! Granted, those two have no support in the histories. We haven’t read these unofficial tales and don’t know the full story, but surely we’ve seen the two plays? A child of three knows them, let alone us!’
‘That’s quite true,’ said Tan-chun.

‘Besides, she has actually been to the places,’ Li Wan added. ‘There may be no evidence for the two stories, but false tales have been passed from mouth to mouth throughout the ages. People with nothing better to do have even deliberately made these ancient sites to fool others. When I came to the capital that year, for instance, I saw three or four tombs of Lord Guan alone. Everything he did in his lifetime is a matter of record. How can he have so many tombs? Naturally, people in later times admired the kind of man he had been. Some of these stories may well have been made up out of that very admiration. When I looked in the Comprehensive Geography, I found that it wasn’t only Lord Guan who had so many tombs. All sorts of famous people of the past had more than one, and there were still more ancient sites with no evidence behind them.

segments.text: ‘These two stories may have no historical evidence either, but storytellers tell them, they’re acted on the stage, and they’re even explained in the notes to the fortune-sticks people draw. Old and young, men and women, everyone knows them and talks of them in everyday speech. And it isn’t as though we’d been reading the words and songs of The Western Chamber and The Peony Pavilion and had to fear we were reading wicked books. There’s no harm in these at all. Leave them as they are.’
Only then did Bao-chai let the matter drop. They all spent some time guessing, but none of their answers was right.

segments.text: Winter days are short. Before they knew it, it was time to go to the front of the house for the evening meal, and they all went to dinner together. Someone reported to Lady Wang:
‘Aroma’s brother, Hua Zi-fang, has come in to say that their mother is gravely ill and longs to see her daughter. He begs your permission to take Aroma home for a visit.’
‘They are mother and daughter, after all,’ said Lady Wang. ‘How could we refuse to let her go?’
She sent for Xi-feng, told her what had happened and instructed her to make whatever arrangements she thought fit.

segments.text: Xi-feng agreed. Back in her rooms, she sent Zhou Rui’s wife to tell Aroma the news.

‘Send for one of the women who accompany people on visits,’ she added. ‘The two of you are to take two little maids and go with Aroma. Have four older men from outside assigned to the carriages. Order a large carriage for you to ride in with her, and a small one for the maids.’
Zhou Rui’s wife had agreed and was just going when Xi-feng spoke again.

‘Aroma is one for saving trouble. Tell her I said she is to put on some clothes in good, bright colours and take a really big bundle of clothes with her. The wrapper must be a good one too, and she must take a good hand-warmer. Tell her to come and let me see her before she leaves.’
Zhou Rui’s wife agreed and went off.

segments.text: After a while Aroma duly appeared, dressed and ready to go, with the two maids and Zhou Rui’s wife carrying her hand-warmer and bundle of clothes. Xi-feng saw that the gold hairpins and pearl ornaments in her hair looked quite splendid. She then examined her clothes: a peach-pink silk-tapestry jacket with a hundred-boys pattern, lined with ermine; a padded skirt of spring green, worked in couched gold and coloured embroidery; and, over these, a blue satin coat lined with grey squirrel.

‘All three of those were Her Ladyship’s,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘It was very good of her to give them to you. Only the coat is a little too plain, and too cold for this weather. You ought to wear one with a thicker fur.’
‘Her Ladyship only gave me this grey-squirrel one and an ermine one,’ Aroma replied, smiling. ‘She said she would give me one with a thicker fur for the New Year, but I haven’t had it yet.’

‘I have one with a thicker fur,’ said Xi-feng, smiling. ‘I don’t like the way the fur lies any more and was just going to have it altered. Never mind, you can have it to wear first. When Her Ladyship has yours made for the New Year, I’ll have another made for myself. We’ll call that your paying me back.’
The others all laughed. ‘You’re always saying things like that, ma’am.

segments.text: ‘All year round you spend so freely. Who knows how many things you’ve quietly paid for out of your own pocket on Her Ladyship’s behalf? More than anyone could count, and when do you ever settle up with her? Yet now you make us laugh by talking as though you begrudged the least little thing.’

‘How could Her Ladyship think of all these things?’ Xi-feng said, smiling. ‘They’re hardly serious business, after all. Still, however little attention we pay them, the whole family’s dignity is at stake. There’s nothing for it but for me to lose a little myself and see that everyone is properly turned out. I may as well get a good name for it. If they all look like burnt steamed rolls, the first thing people will do is laugh at me for managing the household so well that I’ve turned them into beggars.’
‘Who else has your wisdom, ma’am?’ they all exclaimed admiringly. ‘You think of Her Ladyship above you and care for the servants below.’

As they spoke, Xi-feng told Patience to bring out the dark-blue silk-tapestry coat with eight roundels, lined with sand-fox fur, from the day before, and gave it to Aroma. She then looked at the bundle. It had only a lined wrapper of ink-splashed patterned damask with pale-pink silk inside, and contained just two half-worn garments, a padded jacket and a fur coat.

segments.text: ‘Even one is more than I deserve,’ said Aroma.

‘You take the broadcloth one,’ Patience said, smiling. ‘I brought this other one out at the same time so that someone can take it to Miss Xing. In all that snow yesterday, everyone else had one, broadcloth or yuduan or yusha. A dozen or so scarlet coats against the great expanse of snow: how splendid they looked! Only she had that old felt cloak, and it made her look all the more hunched and shrunken. I did feel sorry for her. Let her have this one now.’
‘My things, and she gives them away on her own authority!’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘As if I couldn’t spend enough by myself, now you’ve come to help me along. Better and better!’

‘It all comes of your constant devotion to Her Ladyship and kindness to the servants,’ the others said, laughing. ‘If you were mean and thought only of your possessions, without a thought for the people beneath you, how would Miss Patience ever dare do such a thing?’
‘That’s why I say she’s the only one who understands even a little of what I feel,’ Xi-feng said, smiling.
Then she gave Aroma further instructions. ‘If your mother gets better, well and good. If she can’t pull through, you must stay there. Send someone to tell me, and I’ll send your bedding over.

She turned to Zhou Rui’s wife. ‘You know our rules, of course. I needn’t tell you.’

‘We know them all,’ Zhou Rui’s wife replied. ‘When we get there, we shall see that their people keep out of the way. If she stays, we shall certainly ask for one or two inner rooms to be set aside for her.’
With that she followed Aroma out, gave orders for lanterns to be made ready, and they drove off to Hua Zi-fang’s house. Of that we need say no more.

segments.text: ‘You must keep a good eye on things yourselves, too. Don’t let Bao-yu get up to any nonsense.’
The two mammas went away. Presently they returned to report, ‘We’ve put Skybright and Musk in his room. The four of us already take turns overseeing the night duty.’
Xi-feng nodded. ‘Make him go to bed early at night and get up early in the morning.’

The old mammas assented and went back to the Garden. Before long, sure enough, Zhou Rui’s wife sent word to Xi-feng that Aroma’s mother had already been laid on her deathbed, and Aroma could not return. Xi-feng reported this to Lady Wang and sent to Prospect Garden for Aroma’s bedding and dressing-case.

segments.text: Bao-yu watched Skybright and Musk put everything in order and send it off. Then the two girls took off what remained of their make-up and changed their skirts and jackets. Skybright settled herself on the warming frame and stayed there.
‘Don’t play the young lady today,’ Musk said, laughing. ‘I advise you to bestir yourself a little.’
‘There’ll be time for me to bestir myself when you’ve all gone. As long as one of you is here, I mean to enjoy it.’
‘There’s a good sister,’ Musk said with a smile. ‘I’ll make the bed. You let down the cover over the long mirror and fasten the catch at the top. You’re taller than I am.’
She went to make Bao-yu’s bed.
Skybright gave an exasperated little sigh, then laughed. ‘I’d only just got warm, and now you have to come bothering me.’

segments.text: Skybright stayed on the warming frame, while Musk slept just outside the warm alcove. After the third watch, Bao-yu called for Aroma in his sleep. He called twice without an answer, then woke and remembered that she was away. He laughed at himself.
Skybright was awake already. Laughing, she called to Musk, ‘Even I’m awake, and she’s right beside him and hasn’t heard a thing. She lies there like a corpse!’
Musk rolled over and yawned. ‘He called for Aroma. What has that to do with me?’ she said with a laugh. Then she asked what he wanted.
Bao-yu wanted tea. Musk got up at once, wearing only her little padded jacket of red silk.
‘Put my jacket round you before you go,’ he said. ‘Mind you don’t catch cold.’

Reaching behind her, Musk took the warm, full-fronted sable-throat jacket he wore when he got up in the night and put it over her shoulders. She stepped down, washed her hands in the basin, then poured a cup of warm water and brought the large rinsing-bowl for Bao-yu to rinse his mouth. Only after that did she take a teacup from the tea-shelf, rinse it first with warm water, pour half a cup from the warm tea-pot and give it to him to drink. She rinsed her own mouth too and drank half a cup herself.

segments.text: ‘Be a good sister and grant me a sip too,’ Skybright said, laughing.
‘You get more shameless by the minute!’ Musk said with a laugh.
‘My dear little sister, tomorrow night you shan’t stir. I’ll wait on you the whole night. How’s that?’

Musk could only help her rinse her mouth too, and pour her half a cup of tea. When she had drunk it, Musk said, laughing, ‘Neither of you is to go to sleep. Keep talking. I’m going out for a little while.’
‘There’s a ghost outside waiting for you,’ Skybright said with a laugh.
‘There’s sure to be a great bright moon,’ said Bao-yu. ‘We’ll keep talking. Off you go.’
As he spoke, he coughed twice.
