segments.text: Musk opened the back door and lifted the felt curtain to look out. The moonlight was indeed beautiful. As soon as she had gone, Skybright decided to give her a fright for fun. Confident that she was stronger than other people and did not feel the cold, she slipped down from the warming frame and followed her out, wearing only her little jacket, without putting anything over it.
‘Mind you don’t get chilled,’ Bao-yu warned her with a smile. ‘It’s no joke.’

segments.text: Skybright merely waved a hand and went out after Musk. The moonlight was like water. Suddenly a light breeze blew, piercing her flesh to the bone and making her hair stand on end.
‘No wonder people say you mustn’t let the wind blow on you when you’re warm,’ she thought. ‘This cold really is fierce.’
She was just about to frighten Musk when Bao-yu called loudly from inside, ‘Skybright’s gone out!’
Skybright hurried back into the room, laughing. ‘As if I could have frightened her to death! Trust you to fuss and flap like an old woman!’

‘It wasn’t really that I thought you’d frighten her too badly,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘First, it’s no good you getting chilled. And then, if she wasn’t expecting you, she might cry out. Suppose she woke the others? They wouldn’t say we’d been having a game. They’d say Aroma had only been away one night and already we were seeing ghosts and spirits. Come and tuck the quilt in on this side for me.’
Skybright came over and tucked it in, then slipped her hand underneath to warm it.
‘What a cold hand!’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘I told you to mind the cold.’
Seeing that her cheeks were as red as rouge, he touched them too. They were icy.

segments.text: ‘Quick, come under the quilt. Come and get warm,’ said Bao-yu.
Before he had finished, the door clacked and Musk came hurrying in, flustered and laughing.

‘I had such a fright! In the shadows behind the rockery, I saw someone crouching. I was just going to cry out, but it was that big ornamental pheasant. It flew up when it saw me and came out into the light, and only then could I see what it was. If I’d screamed without thinking, I’d have had everyone up.’
As she spoke, she washed her hands. Then she laughed again. ‘How is it I never saw Skybright outside? She must have been coming to frighten me.’
‘Here she is, getting warm,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘If I hadn’t called out quickly, you really would have had a fright.’

segments.text: ‘There was no need for me to frighten her,’ said Skybright, laughing. ‘The little hussy had already managed to frighten herself.’
She went back under her own quilt.
‘You don’t mean you went out rigged up as lightly as a trick-rider, just like that?’ said Musk.
‘Just like that,’ Bao-yu said, smiling.
‘Can’t you even choose a decent day to die?’ Musk said. ‘Stand outside a little longer and you’ll have the skin frozen off you.’

She lifted the copper cover from the brazier and used the ash-shovel to bury the glowing charcoal again. She put two pieces of plain incense on it, replaced the cover and went behind the screen to trim the lamp once more. Then she lay down.

‘Go to sleep, girls. There’ll be time to talk tomorrow.’
‘We’d better stop talking,’ Bao-yu whispered with a smile. ‘We’ve set them talking again.’
At last they all went to sleep.

segments.text: When they got up next morning, Skybright did indeed have a stuffy nose and a thick voice, and felt too listless to move.

‘Don’t let anyone know,’ Bao-yu said quickly. ‘If Mother hears, she’ll make you go home to recover. Home may be all very well, but it’s colder there. You’re better off here. Lie down in the inner room, and I’ll have a doctor brought quietly through the back gate to see you.’
‘Even so, you must tell Mrs Zhu,’ Skybright said. ‘Otherwise, when the doctor comes and someone asks, what are you going to say?’
Bao-yu saw that she was right. He called an old mamma and instructed her:

‘Go and tell Mrs Zhu that Skybright has only taken a little chill. It’s nothing serious. Aroma is away, and if Skybright goes home to recover, there’ll be fewer people here than ever. Ask for a doctor to come quietly through the back gate and see her. There’s no need to tell Mother.’
The old mamma was gone some time. When she returned, she said, ‘Mrs Zhu knows. She says if a couple of doses put her right, well and good, but if not, she had better go outside after all.

segments.text: ‘The season is unhealthy just now. It would be bad enough if she gave it to anyone else, but the young ladies’ health is the important thing.’

Skybright was lying in the warm alcove, coughing all the time. At these words she cried out angrily, ‘Have I got the plague, then, that you’re all so afraid of catching it? Once I’ve left here, let’s see you go the rest of your lives without a headache or a fever!’
She actually began to get up. Bao-yu hurried to hold her down, smiling.

‘Don’t be angry. It is her responsibility, after all. She’s afraid Mother will hear and blame her, so she just says it to be on the safe side. You’re always so quick to get angry. No wonder the fire in your liver is so strong now.’

segments.text: As they were talking, word came that the doctor had arrived. Bao-yu went across and hid behind the bookcase. Two or three old mammas from the back gate brought the doctor in. All the maids had withdrawn. Three or four old mammas lowered the scarlet embroidered curtain across the warm alcove, and Skybright put out just one hand. The doctor saw two fingernails on it a full three cun long, still bearing traces of the deep red dye of balsam flowers, and hurriedly turned his head away. One of the old mammas hastened to cover the hand with a handkerchief. Only then did he feel her pulse for a while. He rose and went into the outer room to speak to the mammas.

‘The young lady has taken an external chill, with stagnation within. The season is unhealthy at present; it amounts to a mild cold-induced fever. Fortunately the young lady is always sparing in her diet, and the wind and cold have not affected her severely. Her qi and blood are simply weak by nature, and she has happened to catch a little of what is about. A couple of doses to disperse it should put her right.’
He followed the women out again.

segments.text: Li Wan had already sent word to the people at the back gate and to the maids throughout the Garden to keep out of the way. The doctor had seen the Garden’s scenery, but not a single woman. Outside the gate he sat down in the gatekeepers’ duty room and wrote his prescription.
‘Don’t go yet, sir,’ the old mamma told him. ‘Our young master is a great one for questions. He may have something more to say.’

‘Was that not a young lady just now?’ the doctor asked hurriedly. ‘Was it a young gentleman? The room was just like a lady’s bedchamber, and they lowered the curtain. How could it have been a gentleman?’

The old mamma laughed quietly. ‘My dear sir! No wonder the boys said just now that they’d fetched a new doctor today. You really don’t know anything about our household. The room belongs to our young master. The person in it is his maid, one of the senior girls. What young lady? If it had been a young lady ill in her own bedchamber, do you suppose you’d have got in so easily?’
She took the prescription inside.

segments.text: Bao-yu examined it. It listed zisu, jiegeng, fangfeng, jingjie and other drugs, with zhishi and mahuang further down.

‘Damn him, damn him!’ he said. ‘He treats girls just as he treats us. How can that be right? Whatever stagnation she may have inside, how could she stand zhishi and mahuang? Who fetched him? Send him away at once and get one we know.’

‘We don’t understand whether the medicine’s good or bad,’ the old woman said. ‘It’s easy enough to send the boys for Doctor Wang instead. Only this doctor wasn’t called through the steward’s office, so we shall have to give him something for his chair or horse.’
‘How much?’
‘Too little wouldn’t look well. It ought to be a tael of silver, at least. That’s the proper thing for a household of our standing.’
‘How much do we give Doctor Wang when he comes?’
‘Doctor Wang and Doctor Zhang don’t get money each time they come,’ the woman said, smiling. ‘They’re sent substantial gifts at the four festivals every year. That’s a fixed annual custom.

segments.text: ‘This man is here for the first time. He must have a tael of silver to take away.’
Bao-yu told Musk to fetch the silver.
‘Who knows where Madam Hua has put it?’ said Musk.
‘I’ve often seen her getting money from the little cabinet with mother-of-pearl inlay. Let’s go and look.’

They went to the room where Bao-yu kept his things and opened the inlaid cabinet. The top compartment was full of brushes, ink, fans, incense cakes, purses and sashes of every kind. The lower one held several strings of cash. They opened a drawer and at last found a little winnowing-basket with a few pieces of silver in it. There was a small balance as well. Musk took a piece of silver and picked up the balance.
‘Which mark is one tael?’ she asked Bao-yu.

segments.text: ‘You’re asking me?’ Bao-yu said, laughing. ‘That’s funny. You might have only just come here.’
Musk laughed too and was about to ask someone else.
‘Just pick out a big piece and give him that,’ said Bao-yu. ‘We’re not doing business. Why bother reckoning it up?’
Musk put down the balance, chose a piece and weighed it in her hand.

‘I should think this is about a tael,’ she said with a laugh. ‘Better too much than too little. We don’t want the poor wretch laughing at us. He won’t say we don’t know how to read a balance. He’ll think we’re being mean on purpose.’
The old woman was standing outside on the stone step.

‘That’s a five-tael ingot with half snipped off,’ she said, smiling. ‘There must still be at least two taels in that piece. We haven’t any silver-shears here now. Put it back, miss, and choose a smaller one.’
Musk had already shut the cabinet and come out.
‘Who wants to go looking again?’ she said, laughing. ‘Never mind if it’s a little more. Take it.’
‘Just hurry and tell Tealeaf to fetch Doctor Wang,’ Bao-yu said.
The woman took the silver and went to see to it.

segments.text: ‘When I was ill last year, I had a cold-induced fever and food lying stagnant inside. He saw me, and even then he said I couldn’t stand tiger-and-wolf drugs like mahuang, shigao and zhishi. Beside you, I’m like an old poplar that’s been growing for decades among the graves out in the wilds. You’re like those white begonias Yun brought me in the autumn, just opening into flower. How could you stand medicines that even I can’t bear?’

‘Are poplars the only trees that grow among wild graves?’ Musk and the others asked, laughing. ‘Aren’t there pines and cypresses too? I can’t stand poplars. Such great clumsy trees, with such tiny leaves, and even when there isn’t a breath of wind they keep up that rustling. Fancy choosing one of those to compare yourself to! How low you’ve sunk.’

‘I wouldn’t dare compare myself to pines and cypresses,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Even Confucius said, “Only when the year turns cold do we know that pine and cypress are the last to wither.” That shows how noble those two are. Only someone with no sense of shame would lightly compare himself to them.’

‘The scent of medicine is finer than any scent of flowers or fruit,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Immortals gather herbs and brew them, and lofty scholars and recluses gather and prepare them too. segments.text: ‘That’s a good idea,’ Lady Wang said, smiling. ‘It would be much more convenient in wind or snow. Eating something and then being chilled isn’t good for them. Nor is walking here on an empty stomach, filling it with cold wind, and putting food on top of it. Why not use the five large rooms just inside the back gate of the Garden? There are women on night duty there in any case. We can choose two women cooks to work there and prepare meals just for them. They have their regular allowance of fresh vegetables. They can draw it from the steward’s office, in money or in provisions, as they please. And they can have a share of the pheasants, zhang deer, roe deer and all the other game.’
‘I’ve been thinking the same thing,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Only I was afraid another kitchen would mean more trouble.’

‘No extra trouble at all,’ said Xi-feng. ‘It’s the same allowance. What we add here, we take away there. Even if it did mean a little more trouble, with the girls out in that bitter north wind, the others might manage, but what about Cousin Lin? How could she stand it? Even Cousin Bao couldn’t stand it, let alone the girls.’
‘That’s just it,’ said Grandmother Jia.

‘Fond as I am of her, I do sometimes fear that being so clever may not be a good thing.’

‘You’re wrong there, Grandmother,’ Xi-feng said quickly, laughing. ‘People say that those who are too clever and quick-witted may not live long. segments.text: Concerned about Skybright, Aroma and the rest, Bao-yu returned to the Garden ahead of the others. The scent of medicine filled his room, but no one was there except Skybright, lying alone on the kang, her face burning red. He touched it and found it hot against his hand. Hastily warming his hands at the stove, he put one under the quilt to feel her body. That too was burning.
‘It’s one thing for the others to go,’ he said, ‘but are Musk and Ripple so heartless that they’ve both gone off as well?’

‘I sent Ripple to have her meal. Patience came to fetch Musk just now, and she went out with her. The two of them were being very secretive. I don’t know what they’re talking about. It must be about my staying in here because I’m ill.’

‘Patience isn’t that sort of person. Besides, she didn’t know you were ill, so she can’t have come specially to see you. Most likely she came to talk to Musk, happened to find you ill, and said she’d come to ask after you. That’s an ordinary enough way of being tactful and pleasant. segments.text: ‘We have subjects for our next poetry meeting now,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Narcissi and wintersweet.’
‘No, no!’ Dai-yu laughed. ‘I daren’t write any more poems. Every time I write one, I’m made to pay a forfeit. It’s too humiliating.’
She covered her face with both hands.
‘What’s the need for that?’ Bao-yu laughed. ‘Why make fun of me again? I’m not ashamed, yet here you are hiding your face.’

‘I’ll host the next meeting,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘Four subjects for poems and four for lyrics. Each of us must write four poems and four lyrics. segments.text: ‘When I was eight, I went with my father to the shores of the Western Sea to buy foreign goods. There we came across a girl from the country of Zhenzhen, only fifteen years old. Her face was just like those beauties in Western pictures. She too had yellow hair hanging down, with braids linked together, and her head was covered in jewels: coral, cat’s-eyes and emeralds. Her jacket sleeves were foreign brocade, woven in gold thread with a pattern like mail. She wore a Japanese sword, also mounted in gold and set with jewels. Really, even the beauties in the pictures weren’t as lovely as she was. Someone said she knew Chinese poetry and books, could expound the Five Classics, and could write poems and lyrics. So my father asked an official interpreter to get her to write something for him. What she wrote was a poem of her own.’
They all marvelled at this.
‘Dear Cousin,’ Bao-yu said eagerly, smiling, ‘bring it out and let me see.’
‘It’s put away in Nanjing,’ Bao-qin laughed. ‘How could I fetch it now?’
Bao-yu was bitterly disappointed.
‘I’m not fortunate enough to see such wonders.’
Dai-yu took Bao-qin’s hand with a smile.
‘Don’t try to fool us.

segments.text: ‘I know you’d hardly have left all those things at home when you came here. Naturally you’d have brought them with you. Now you’re making up a story that you haven’t. The others may believe it, but I don’t.’
Bao-qin blushed, lowered her head and smiled without answering.
‘Little Pin-pin is always so good at talking nonsense,’ Bao-chai laughed. ‘What a clever creature you are!’
‘If she’s brought it,’ Dai-yu said, ‘she might as well give us the chance to see something new.’

‘There’s a whole pile of trunks and boxes we haven’t sorted yet,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘Who knows which one it’s in? When we’ve put things in order in a few days, we’ll find it and everyone can see it.’ Then she turned to Bao-qin. ‘If you remember it, why not recite it for us?’
Only then did Bao-qin answer.
‘I remember it was a five-character regulated poem. For a foreign girl, it was quite an achievement.’
‘Don’t start yet,’ said Bao-chai. ‘Let’s send for Yun so that she can hear it too.’

She called Xiao-luo and told her, ‘Go to my rooms and say that a foreign beauty has come here who writes wonderful poetry. Ask our “poetry madwoman” to come and see her, and bring our “poetry simpleton” along as well.’
Xiao-luo went away laughing.

They had scarcely finished when Musk came in.

Bao-yu rose at once and answered, ‘Yes.’
He asked Bao-chai and Bao-qin whether they were going.
‘No,’ said Bao-chai. ‘We just sent our presents yesterday.’
They talked a little longer before parting.

segments.text: Bao-yu let the girls go ahead and stayed behind. Dai-yu called him back.
‘When exactly will Aroma be coming home?’
‘Not until after the funeral, of course.’
Dai-yu had more to say, but did not say it. She was lost in thought for a moment, then said, ‘You’d better go.’
Bao-yu too felt that he had much to tell her, but could not find anything to say. After a moment’s thought he smiled.
‘We’ll talk tomorrow.’
He went down the steps and was about to walk on, his head lowered, when he turned back hastily.
‘The nights are getting longer. How many times do you cough in the night now? How often do you wake?’
‘Last night was better. I only coughed twice. But I only slept for the fourth watch, just that one watch, and couldn’t sleep any more.’
‘There’s something important I meant to say,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘I’ve only just remembered.’
As he spoke he drew closer and lowered his voice.
‘I was thinking about the bird’s nests Cousin Chai sent you…’
Before he could finish, Aunt Zhao came in to see Dai-yu.
‘Have you been well these last two days, Miss?’
Dai-yu knew that she must have come from Tan-chun’s and, passing the door, had stopped to pay a courtesy visit on her way.

segments.text: Next morning, before it was light, Skybright woke Musk.
‘It’s time you woke up. Haven’t you had enough sleep yet? Go out and tell them to get his tea and water ready. I’ll wake him.’
Musk hastily put on her clothes and got up.

‘Let’s wake him first and get his clothes on, then move this warming box away before we let them in. The old nurses have already told us not to let him stay in this room for fear of catching the illness. If they see us all crowded together, they’ll start grumbling again.’
‘That’s what I say too,’ said Skybright.

When they called him, Bao-yu was already awake. He hurriedly got up and put on his clothes. Musk first called in the little maids. Only when everything was in order did she let Ripple, Sandal and the others come in to help him wash and comb his hair.
‘The sky’s overcast again,’ said Musk. ‘It may snow. Wear that set of felt clothes.’
Bao-yu nodded and changed at once. A little maid brought a covered bowl of soup made with Jian lotus seeds and red dates on a small tea tray. He took two sips.

segments.text: Musk brought him a little dish of prepared purple ginger, and he held a piece in his mouth. After giving Skybright more instructions, he went to Grandmother Jia’s. She was not yet up, but on hearing that he was going out she had the door opened and told him to come in. Behind her, Bao-qin was still asleep, her face turned inwards. Grandmother Jia saw that he was wearing a litchi-coloured, arrow-sleeved coat of duoluo cloth with sand-fox fur, and a scarlet broadcloth outer coat with couched gold and coloured embroidery, dark-blue figured-satin edging and rows of tassels.
‘Is it snowing?’ she asked.
‘It’s overcast, but it hasn’t started yet.’
She called Faithful.
‘Give him that Dark-cloud Leopard cloak from yesterday.’

Faithful answered and went to fetch it. When Bao-yu looked, it shone with gold and emerald green, its blue-green lustre flashing; yet it was unlike Bao-qin’s duck-feather cloak. He heard Grandmother Jia say with a smile:
‘This is called peacock-gold cloth. In Russia they twist peacock feathers into thread and weave it. I gave your little cousin the wild-duck one the other day. You may have this.’
Bao-yu made a kowtow and put it on.

segments.text: ‘Go and show it to your mother before you leave,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile.

Bao-yu agreed and came out. Faithful was standing there rubbing her eyes. Ever since her vehement oath that day, she had refused to speak to him, and this had troubled him day and night. Seeing that she was about to avoid him again, he came up to her with a smile.
‘Dear Sister, have a look. Does this suit me?’

Faithful flung her hand aside and went into Grandmother Jia’s room. Bao-yu could only go on to Lady Wang’s and show it to her. Then he returned to the Garden to let Skybright and Musk see it, before going back to Grandmother Jia’s to report.
‘Mother has seen it. She said it would be such a pity to spoil it, and I must wear it carefully and not ruin it.’

segments.text: The old nurses followed him as far as the hall. There his foster-brother Li Gui and five other men, Wang Rong, Zhang Ruo-jin, Zhao Yi-hua, Qian Qi and Zhou Rui, had long been waiting with the four pages Tealeaf, Ban-he, Chu-yao and Sao-hong, carrying bundles of clothes and holding a sitting-cushion, with a white horse fitted with a carved saddle and coloured reins. The old nurses gave the six men further instructions. They hastily answered, ‘Yes, ma’am,’ several times and presented the whip and steadied the stirrup. Bao-yu mounted slowly. Li Gui and Wang Rong held the bit rings, Qian Qi and Zhou Rui led the way, and Zhang Ruo-jin and Zhao Yi-hua kept close behind him on either side.
‘Brother Zhou, Brother Qian,’ Bao-yu said from the saddle, smiling, ‘let’s go out by this side gate. Then I shan’t have to get down again when we pass Father’s study.’
Zhou Rui turned sideways with a smile.
‘The Master’s away, and the study’s kept locked every day. You needn’t dismount, sir.’
‘Even if it’s locked, I ought to get down.’
‘You’re quite right, sir,’ Qian Qi, Li Gui and the others said, laughing.

segments.text: As they spoke, whom should they meet coming in but Lai Da himself. Bao-yu at once reined in, intending to dismount. Lai Da hurried up and held his leg to stop him. Bao-yu stood in the stirrups instead, took his hand with a smile and exchanged a few words with him. Next came a page leading twenty or thirty people with brooms and dustpans. At the sight of Bao-yu they stood against the wall with their hands lowered. Only the page at their head bent one knee and paid his respects. Bao-yu did not know his name and merely smiled and nodded. Not until the horse had passed did the page lead his people away.

Outside the side gate, the servants belonging to Li Gui and the other five men, with several grooms, had some ten horses ready and were waiting. Once through the gate, Li Gui and the others mounted. Leading the way and surrounding Bao-yu, they rode away in a rush. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: Mother Song had no choice but to go and fetch Zhui-er’s mother. The woman packed her daughter’s things, then came to see Skybright and the others.
‘What’s wrong, young ladies? If your little niece has misbehaved, you can teach her. Why send her away? You might at least leave us a little dignity.’
‘Wait till Bao-yu comes and ask him,’ said Skybright. ‘It has nothing to do with us.’
The woman gave a cold laugh.

‘As if I’d dare ask him! What does he ever do without you young ladies arranging it? Even if he agreed, it wouldn’t be much use if you didn’t. Take what you said just now. We may be speaking behind his back, but you called him straight out by his name. You young ladies are allowed to do that. If we did it, we’d be called savages.’
Skybright flushed still more with anger.
‘I called him by his name, did I? Go and tell Her Old Ladyship. Say I’m behaving outrageously and have me sent away too.’
‘Sister,’ Musk broke in, ‘just take your daughter out. If you have anything to say, say it later.

segments.text: ‘Is this a place for you to shout and lecture us on manners? Who have you ever seen teaching us manners? Never mind you: even Grannie Lai and Mrs Lin have to make allowances for us. segments.text: Skybright had caught another draught in the commotion and worked herself into a temper. She felt worse than before and tossed about until the lamps were lit. She had only just grown a little calmer when Bao-yu returned, sighing and stamping his foot as he came in. Musk hurried to ask what was wrong.
‘Grandmother was so pleased to give me this coat today. Who would have thought I’d burn a hole in the rear panel without noticing? Luckily it was late, so neither she nor Mother paid any attention.’
He took it off as he spoke. Musk looked and found a burn hole the size of a fingertip.
‘A spark must have jumped out of your hand-warmer. It’s nothing much. Have someone take it out quietly at once and find a skilled mender to reweave it.’
She wrapped it in a cloth and gave it to an older woman to take out.
‘We must have it back by daybreak. Whatever you do, don’t let Her Old Ladyship or Her Ladyship know.’
The woman was away a long time, but brought it back as it was.
‘We tried not only the skilled menders but tailors, embroiderers and women who do needlework. None of them recognised the stuff, and none dared take it on.’

segments.text: ‘What’s the use of fretting now?’
‘There’s something in that,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
He handed it to her and moved the lamp closer. She examined it carefully for a while.
‘This is woven with peacock-gold thread. If we use peacock-gold thread too, and work it in closely as in darning, perhaps it will pass.’
‘We have peacock thread ready to hand,’ Musk said with a smile, ‘but who here can do that sort of darning except you?’
‘Then I’ll have to risk my life at it.’
‘How can you?’ Bao-yu protested at once. ‘You’ve only just begun to feel better. How could you do any work?’
‘Stop fussing and fretting. I know what I’m doing.’

As she spoke, she sat up, twisted her hair into place and put on some clothes. Her head felt heavy, her body insubstantial; gold stars darted before her eyes. She could hardly hold herself up. Yet if she did not do it, she feared Bao-yu would fret. There was nothing for it but to grit her teeth and force herself on. She told Musk simply to help by twisting the thread. First Skybright took a strand and compared it with the cloth.
‘It isn’t a very close match,’ she said with a smile, ‘but once it’s worked in, it shouldn’t show much.’
‘It’s perfectly good,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Where are we to find a tailor from Russia?’

Skybright first unpicked the lining and fastened a bamboo hoop the size of a teacup’s rim to the back. With a gold knife she scraped all four edges of the hole loose and fluffy. Then she threaded two strands into a needle and, separating warp from weft, worked as she would in darning: first making a ground, then weaving back and forth over it to follow the pattern of the garment.

segments.text: ‘Do go to sleep. If you stay awake another half the night and your eyes are sunken tomorrow, what are we to do?’

Seeing her agitation, Bao-yu lay down as best he could, but still could not sleep. Presently the chiming clock sounded four strokes. The mending was just finished, and Skybright used a small toothbrush to tease out the nap carefully.
‘That’s very good,’ said Musk. ‘Unless someone looks closely, they’ll never see it.’
Bao-yu eagerly asked to look.
‘It really is exactly the same.’
Skybright had had several fits of coughing and had only finished with great difficulty.
‘It’s mended,’ she said, ‘but it still doesn’t look the same. I can’t do any more.’
With a groan, she collapsed helplessly.

segments.text: Now Bao-yu saw that, with the peacock-gold cloak at last mended, Skybright had spent all her strength and was perilously weak. He hurriedly called the little maids to take over patting and massaging her. They worked at this for a while, then settled down to rest. Before there had been time to eat a meal, it was broad daylight. For the moment he would not go out, but ordered them to fetch the doctor at once. Doctor Wang soon arrived. After feeling her pulse, he looked puzzled.

‘She was a little better yesterday. Why is the pulse now so empty and faint, floating and contracting? Has she perhaps eaten too much? If not, she must have overtaxed her mind. The external chill has cleared, but to neglect her recovery after sweating is no trifling matter.’

Still talking, he went out to write a prescription and sent it in. Bao-yu saw that he had reduced the dispersing medicines that drove out the harmful influence, adding instead fuling, dihuang, danggui and other remedies to strengthen the spirit and nourish the blood. He promptly ordered the medicine to be boiled.
‘What are we to do?’ he sighed. ‘If anything should happen to her, it will all be my sin.’
‘Oh, my good master!’ Skybright exclaimed from her pillow. ‘Go and attend to your own affairs!

segments.text: ‘It’s not as though I’ve suddenly got consumption.’

Bao-yu could do nothing but go. That afternoon, however, he said he felt unwell and came home again. Severe though Skybright’s illness was, she was fortunate in having always been one to expend her strength rather than fret her mind. Her food, too, was habitually plain, and she had harmed herself neither by going hungry nor by overeating. The Jia household had a secret remedy of its own: at the slightest cold or cough, whether the sufferer was high or low, complete fasting came first, with medicine and nursing second. Thus, when she had first fallen ill a few days before, she had eaten nothing for two or three days and had been careful to take her medicine and look after herself. Now, after overexerting herself, she was nursed with redoubled care for several days and gradually recovered. As the girls in the Garden were now all eating in their own rooms, cooking and meals were more conveniently managed. Bao-yu could devise all manner of soups and broths to suit her. There is no need to describe them one by one.

segments.text: ‘It’s not me they miss,’ Jia Zhen said with a laugh. ‘New Year’s here again. If it isn’t my presents they’re thinking of, it’s my plays and wine.’

As he spoke he examined the yellow cloth bag. Printed on it in four large characters were the words ‘Imperial Favour Bestowed for Ever’. On the other side was the seal of the Sacrificial Bureau of the Board of Rites, together with a line of small writing:

‘Two shares in all of the perpetual imperial grant for spring sacrifices to Jia Yan, Duke of Ning, and Jia Yuan, Duke of Rong, commuted to a net sum of so many taels of silver. Received in full at this office on such-and-such a day, month and year by Jia Rong, Dragon Guard and candidate for appointment as an imperial guard. Deputy of the Court on duty for the year: so-and-so.’
Below was a flourish of signature in red ink.

segments.text: After his meal, Jia Zhen washed his hands and rinsed his mouth, changed his boots and hat, and ordered Jia Rong to follow him carrying the silver. They reported to Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang, then went over to Jia She and Lady Xing and reported to them before returning home. Jia Zhen took out the silver and ordered the bag to be burnt in the great brazier in the ancestral shrine.

‘Go and ask your Aunt Lian,’ he told Jia Rong, ‘whether she has settled the dates for the New Year feasts in the first month. If she has, have the study make out a clear list. When we send our invitations, we mustn’t clash with theirs. Last year we were careless and invited several of the same families on the same days. Instead of putting it down to carelessness, people might think the two houses had arranged it between them: empty courtesies to save ourselves trouble.’

Jia Rong assented and went over. Soon he returned with the list of feast dates. Jia Zhen read it and ordered it to be given to Lai Sheng, who was to avoid those days when inviting their guests. He was in the hall watching the pages carry folding screens and wipe the tables and the gold and silver sacrificial vessels when a page came up with a formal greeting and a statement of accounts.
‘Steward Wu from Heishan Village has arrived.’

segments.text: Jia Zhen told someone to help him up.

‘Thanks to your blessing, sir, I can still get about,’ Wu Jin-xiao answered, smiling.
‘Your son must be grown up now. You ought to let him make the journey.’

‘To tell you the truth, sir, we’re used to coming. We’d feel cooped up if we didn’t. As for the young ones, don’t they all want to come and see the world at the Emperor’s feet? ‘How many days did it take you?’

‘That explains why you’ve only just arrived. I’ve been looking at your list. You old rogue, you’ve come to do battle with me again this year.’
Wu Jin-xiao hurried two paces forward.
‘If you please, sir, the harvest really was bad this year.

segments.text: ‘The rain began in the third month and went on and on until the eighth. There weren’t five fine days together in all that time. In the ninth month we had hailstones as big as bowls. Over an expanse of nearly thirteen hundred li, people, houses, livestock and crops were struck and damaged by the thousands and tens of thousands. That’s why things are as they are. I wouldn’t dare tell you a lie.’
Jia Zhen frowned.

‘I’d reckoned on your bringing at least five thousand taels of silver. What use is this? You’ve only eight or nine estates left between you now, and this year two have reported drought or flood. Then you come to do battle with me as well! You really mean us to go without a New Year.’

‘Your land has done well enough, sir, compared with some. My brother is only a little over a hundred li from me, yet who would have thought things could be so different? He manages eight estates for the other mansion, several times as much land as you have here. This year he’s only brought this much produce too, and no more than two or three thousand taels of silver extra. They’re short as well.’
‘Exactly,’ said Jia Zhen. ‘I can manage here. We’ve no great exceptional expenses any more, only the cost of keeping the place for a year.

But it’s different in the other mansion. These past few years they’ve had all sorts of new expenses, things they simply can’t avoid paying for, without a single addition to their income or property. They’ve run up a considerable deficit in the last year or two. If we don’t ask you for the money, who are we to ask?’

segments.text: ‘There may be more expenses in that mansion now,’ Wu Jin-xiao said, smiling, ‘but money comes in as well as going out. Surely Her Highness and His Majesty give them rewards?’
Jia Zhen laughed and turned to Jia Rong and the others.
‘Listen to him! Isn’t that a fine thing to say?’
They hastened to laugh.
‘How would you people tucked away in the hills and along the coast know about such things?’ Jia Rong said. ‘Do you suppose Her Highness can hand the Emperor’s treasury over to us?

segments.text: ‘Even if she wished to, she has no say in the matter. Of course there are gifts. At the festivals and appointed seasons they amount to some coloured satins, antiques and curios. Even a gift of money is no more than a hundred taels of gold, worth only a thousand taels of silver. How much of a year’s expenses will that cover? In each of these last two years they’ve had to find several thousand taels more. Think what that first family visit cost, with the Garden to build as well. Work out that one sum, and you’ll see. If there’s another visit in a couple of years, I’m afraid it will leave them penniless.’

‘That’s the trouble with honest country folk,’ Jia Zhen said with a laugh. ‘They see the brightness outside and know nothing of the darkness within. A chime-hammer made of huangbai wood: a fine show outside, bitterness within.’
Jia Rong turned to him with another laugh.
‘But the other mansion really is poor. The other day I heard Aunt Feng and Faithful talking in secret about slipping some of Grandmother’s things out to pawn.’
‘Another of your Aunt Feng’s tricks,’ Jia Zhen said, laughing. ‘They can’t be as poor as that.

segments.text: He then ordered Wu Jin-xiao to be taken out and well looked after; of him we need say no more. Jia Zhen had the offerings for the ancestors set aside from the things just delivered. He took some of each kind and told Jia Rong to send them over to Rong mansion. After keeping what his own household needed, he divided the remainder into shares according to rank and had them piled separately below the terrace. He sent for the younger men of the clan to receive them. Soon Rong mansion too sent over a quantity of sacrificial provisions, as well as gifts for Jia Zhen. After seeing the sacrificial vessels put in order, he slipped his feet into his shoes, threw a thick coat of lynx fur over his shoulders and had a large wolfskin mattress spread in the sun on the stone ledge below a pillar of the hall. With the sun on his back, he idly watched the younger men come to collect their New Year supplies. When he saw Jia Qin among them, he called him over.
‘What are you doing here? Who told you to come?’
Jia Qin stood with his hands at his sides.
‘I heard that you were calling us over to collect things, Uncle, so I came without waiting to be sent for.’
‘These things are meant for those young uncles and cousins of yours who’ve nothing to do and no income.

segments.text: ‘When you had nothing to do a year or two ago, I gave you some too. Now you have a post in the other mansion, looking after the monks and Taoists at the family temple. You have your own monthly allowance, and all the monks’ allowance money passes through your hands as well. To come for this on top of it is altogether too greedy. Look at yourself. Do you look like a man entrusted with money and business? We used to say you had no prospects. What’s become of you now? You look worse than before.’
‘There are a great many mouths at home,’ Jia Qin said, ‘and the expenses are heavy.’
Jia Zhen gave a cold laugh.

‘Still trying to put me off! Do you imagine I don’t know what you get up to at the family temple? Once you’re there, of course, you’re the master. No one dares cross you. You’ve money in your hands, and you’re far enough away from us, so you set yourself up as king and lord it over everyone. Every night you gather a pack of rogues to gamble, and keep women and boys. Now you’ve spent yourself into this state, and you dare come here for provisions! You’ll get no provisions. A thrashing with a water-carrier’s pole is what you’ll get.

segments.text: ‘Once New Year’s over, I shall speak to your Uncle Lian and have you replaced.’

Jia Qin flushed and dared not answer. Someone announced that Prince Shui of the Northern Palace had sent calligraphic couplets and purses. Jia Zhen immediately told Jia Rong to go out and receive the messengers.
‘Just say I’m not at home.’

Jia Rong went. Jia Zhen watched the last of the gifts being collected, then returned to his rooms and ate supper with You-shi. Nothing further happened that night. The next day was busier still; there is no need to describe it all.

segments.text: By the twenty-ninth of the twelfth month, everything was ready. In both mansions the door-gods, couplets and hanging plaques had been replaced, and the peachwood charms freshly oiled. All was bright and new. In Ning mansion every central doorway stood open along the whole route: the main gate, the ceremonial gate, the great hall, the heated chamber, the inner hall, the inner third gate, the inner ceremonial gate and the inner screen-gate, through to the principal hall. Below the steps on either side stood tall vermilion lanterns, all alike, their lights running in two lines like golden dragons. The next day Grandmother Jia and all the women with imperial titles put on court dress according to their ranks. Grandmother Jia took the lead in a great sedan carried by eight men, and they went with their attendants to offer congratulations at court. When the ceremonies and banquet were over, they returned and alighted at the heated chamber in Ning mansion. The younger men who had not accompanied them to court were drawn up before the gate to receive them and led them into the ancestral shrine.

This was Bao-qin’s first visit, and she looked about her with great attention. The shrine occupied a separate courtyard west of Ning mansion. Within a black-painted railing stood a five-bay gateway. Above it hung a plaque bearing the four characters ‘Ancestral Shrine of the Jia Family’, with the inscription beside them: ‘Written by Kong Ji-zong, Duke for the Transmission of Sagehood.’

segments.text: All were in the imperial hand. Inside, incense and candles glowed among brocade hangings and embroidered curtains. The spirit tablets were arranged there, but could not be clearly seen. The members of the Jia family took their places in generational order. Jia Jing presided over the sacrifice, with Jia She assisting. Jia Zhen presented the wine-cup; Jia Lian and Jia Cong presented the silk; Bao-yu carried the incense; Jia Chang and Jia Ling spread the kneeling mats and attended the burning-pit. The blue-robed musicians began to play. There were three offerings of wine, with prostrations and risings, then the sacrificial silk was burnt and wine poured in libation. When the rite was finished, the music ceased and they withdrew.

They crowded round Grandmother Jia and accompanied her to the principal hall. Brocade curtains were raised high before the portraits, painted screens stood about them, and incense and candles shone. High in the centre hung the portraits of the two founding ancestors, the Dukes of Ning and Rong, both in python-pattern robes with jade belts. Several scroll portraits of other ancestors hung on either side. Jia Xing, Jia Zhi and the others formed a line from the inner ceremonial gate to the verandah of the principal hall.

segments.text: Jia Jing and Jia She stood outside the threshold, the women inside it. The menservants and pages all remained beyond the ceremonial gate. As each dish arrived there, Jia Xing, Jia Zhi and the others received it and passed it along the line to Jia Jing on the steps. Jia Rong, as the eldest grandson of the senior branch, alone stood inside the threshold with the women. Whenever Jia Jing brought up a dish, he handed it to Jia Rong, who passed it to his wife. It went on through Xi-feng, You-shi and the others until it reached Lady Wang before the offering-table. She handed it to Grandmother Jia, who then placed it on the table. Lady Xing stood to the west of the table, facing east, and helped Grandmother Jia arrange the offerings. Only when all the dishes, rice, soups, pastries, wine and accompaniments had been passed in did Jia Rong withdraw, descend the steps and take his place at the head of Jia Qin’s generation.

segments.text: Of those whose names contained the ‘wen’ element, Jia Jing stood first; of the next generation, whose names contained ‘jade’, Jia Zhen stood first; and of the next, with the ‘grass’ radical, Jia Rong. The generations were ranged left and right in their prescribed order, the men to the east and the women to the west. They waited until Grandmother Jia had taken up the incense and bowed, then all knelt together. The five-bay hall, the three-bay portico, the verandahs within and without, the steps and the two courtyards below were so packed with bright, flower-like figures that no space remained. Not a bird’s peep could be heard: only the faint chime and tinkle of gold bells and jade pendants swaying, and the rustle and shuffle of boots and shoes as they rose and knelt. When the ceremony was over, Jia Jing, Jia She and the others hurried out to Rong mansion to await Grandmother Jia and pay their respects.

segments.text: The floor of You-shi’s principal room had already been covered from end to end with red felt. In the middle stood a great gilt-enamel brazier with three elephant-trunk feet and a rounded, loach-back rim. The kang facing the entrance had a new scarlet felt covering, with back cushions and bolsters of bright red embroidered in colours with dragons amid clouds upholding the character for longevity. Black foxskin covers were laid over these, and a great white foxskin mattress provided the seat. Grandmother Jia was invited to sit there. Fur mattresses were laid on either side for two or three sisters-in-law of her generation. Lady Xing and the others were seated on another fur-covered little kang at right angles to it, behind a standing screen. Twelve carved-lacquer chairs faced one another in two rows on the floor below, each with matching grey-squirrel covers and cushions and a large copper foot-warmer underneath. Bao-qin and the other girls were given these seats. You-shi herself carried a tray of tea to Grandmother Jia, while Jia Rong’s wife served the other old ladies. You-shi then served Lady Xing and the others, and Jia Rong’s wife the girls. Xi-feng, Li Wan and the rest stood below to attend them. When they had finished their tea, Lady Xing and the others rose first to wait on Grandmother Jia.

segments.text: After her tea and a few words with her old sisters-in-law, Grandmother Jia called for her sedan. Xi-feng hurried forward to help her rise.
‘Your dinner is already prepared, Grandmother,’ You-shi said with a smile. ‘Every year you refuse us the honour of staying to eat before you go home. Are we really so much worse than Feng?’
Xi-feng supported Grandmother Jia on her arm and laughed.
‘Come along, Grandmother. Let’s go home to eat. Never mind her.’

‘You have the ancestors to attend to here,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘You’re busy enough without a fuss over me as well. Besides, every year I don’t stay, you send the dinner over all the same. You might as well send it again. What I can’t eat I can keep for tomorrow. Won’t I get more that way?’
This made everyone laugh. She added to You-shi:
‘Be sure to put trustworthy people in charge of the incense and lights at night. There must be no carelessness about that.’

segments.text: As the sedan emerged, the whole eastern side of the street was lined with the Duke of Ning’s ceremonial insignia, attendants and musical instruments; the western side was similarly lined with those of the Duke of Rong. Passers-by had all been kept back, and no one was allowed through. Soon they reached Rong mansion, where the doors too stood open all the way from the main gate through the principal halls. This time Grandmother Jia did not alight at the heated chamber. They passed the great hall and turned west, taking her to the entrance hall of her own quarters. Everyone escorted her into her principal room. Here too the brocade cushions and embroidered screens were all fresh and new. Pine-and-cypress incense and baihe herb burned in the brazier in the middle of the room.

segments.text: When Grandmother Jia had seated herself, an old nurse announced that the other old ladies had come to pay their respects. She hastily rose to welcome them, but her two or three old sisters-in-law were already entering. They took one another’s arms, laughed and exchanged courtesies. After tea, when the visitors left, Grandmother Jia saw them only as far as the inner ceremonial gate before returning to the chief seat. Jia Jing and Jia She led in the younger men.
‘You have enough trouble all year round,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘There’s no need for bows.’

As she spoke, however, men and women came forward in separate groups, one after another, and all performed their salutations. Folding chairs were set to right and left, and the others took their seats in order of age to receive the greetings of those below them. Then the men and women servants, pages and maids of both mansions paid their respects, arranged by the upper, middle and lower grades of their duties. New Year money, purses and little gold and silver ingots were distributed, and a reunion feast was brought in. Men sat to the east and women to the west. Tusu wine, reunion soup, lucky fruits and wish-fulfilling cakes were served. Grandmother Jia then rose and went into the inner room to change, and only then did the others disperse.

That night incense and offerings were set before the Kitchen God and in every Buddhist shrine. Paper images of Heaven and Earth, with incense and offerings, stood in the courtyard of Lady Wang’s principal rooms. Great transparent horn lanterns were hung high over the main gate of Prospect Garden, with two rows of tall lanterns and lights along all the paths.

segments.text: High and low, everyone was dressed as brightly as a mass of flowers. All night the voices, talk and laughter rang out, and firecrackers and fireworks followed one another without a break. At the fifth watch next morning Grandmother Jia and the others again put on full dress according to rank and went to court with their complete ceremonial retinue, to offer New Year congratulations and celebrate Yuan-chun’s birthday. After the banquet they returned to worship the ancestors once more at Ning mansion, then came home to receive the family’s greetings before changing their clothes and resting. Grandmother Jia saw none of the friends and relations who came with festival greetings. She took her ease, talking only with Aunt Xue and Aunt Li, or playing the counter game and cards with Bao-yu, Bao-qin, Bao-chai, Dai-yu and the other girls. Lady Wang and Xi-feng, meanwhile, were busy every day entertaining New Year guests. The halls and courtyards on their side were full of plays and feasting, with friends and relations coming in an endless stream. Seven or eight busy days passed before it was over.

segments.text: On the evening of the fifteenth, Grandmother Jia ordered several tables of wine and food to be laid in the great reception hall, engaged a troupe of young players and had fine lanterns of every kind hung throughout it. Sons, nephews, grandsons and granddaughters-in-law from both mansions gathered with her for a family feast. Jia Jing never drank wine, so no invitation was sent to him. On the seventeenth, once the ancestral observances were over, he would return outside the city to pursue his cultivation. Even during these few days at home he stayed silently in a quiet room, cut off from all that went on. We need say no more of him. Jia She partook briefly of his mother’s hospitality, then took his leave. Grandmother Jia knew that neither he nor the others would be at ease while he stayed, and let him go. At home he admired the lanterns and drank with his retainers, his ears filled with music and song, his eyes with brocade and embroidery. His unfettered pleasures were naturally rather different from those here.

segments.text: In Grandmother Jia’s reception hall there were ten or so tables. Beside each stood a small stand with a three-piece incense set, burning baihe palace incense bestowed by the Emperor. There were also miniature landscapes, some eight cun long, four or five wide and two or three high, with little rocks dotted among the moss and fresh flowers growing in them. Small trays of foreign lacquer held old-kiln teacups and tiny teapots of assorted designs, in which the finest teas were brewing. The ornamental screens were all of open-carved zitan wood, inset with scarlet gauze bearing openwork embroidery of flowers and poems in cursive script. The woman who had embroidered these screens came from Suzhou. Her name was Hui-niang.

segments.text: She belonged to a scholarly official family and was herself accomplished in painting and calligraphy. Now and then she did a piece or two of needlework for amusement; it was never made for sale. The flower sprays on these screens were all copied from the paintings of famous masters of the Tang, Song, Yuan and Ming dynasties. Their composition and colouring were therefore refined, quite unlike the mere gaudy brilliance of craftsmen’s work. Beside every spray she embroidered in black floss an old poet’s lines on that flower, drawn variously from poems, lyrics, songs or rhapsodies. The hooks and turns of the cursive writing, its light and heavy strokes, its joins and breaks, were indistinguishable from brushwork, nothing like the stiff, disagreeable lettering of commercial embroidery. She did not use her skill for profit. Though her work was known throughout the land, very few possessed any, and many hereditary official and wealthy families had none at all. It had come to be called ‘Hui embroidery’. Lately there had even been common profiteers imitating her stitches and making money from the gullible. But Hui-niang had died young, at eighteen, and now there could never be another piece.

segments.text: Even families that possessed a piece or two treasured them and never put them to use. A band of those gentlemen of the Hanlin Academy who were possessed by the literary demon cherished ‘Hui embroidery’ so deeply that they declared the word ‘embroidery’ inadequate to its wonders. To speak of writing like this as mere embroidery was almost an affront. They discussed it together and decided to suppress the word ‘embroidery’ and substitute ‘patterns’. So now everyone called it ‘Hui patterns’. A genuine example of ‘Hui patterns’ was beyond price.

segments.text: For all the splendour of the Jia family, they had possessed only two or three pieces. Two had been presented to the Emperor the previous year; now only this set of ornamental screens remained, sixteen panels in all. Grandmother Jia valued them as jewels. They were not included among the furnishings brought out for guests, but kept in her own quarters for her pleasure when she was in the mood for a wine party. There were also small old-kiln vases of various kinds, filled with fresh flowers and greenery in arrangements such as ‘Three Friends of Winter’ and ‘Wealth and Honour in the Jade Hall’.

segments.text: The two highest tables were for Aunt Li and Aunt Xue. On the east side Grandmother Jia had a short, low-footed couch with a protective screen open-carved in a kui-dragon pattern, complete with back cushions, bolsters and a fur mattress. On the couch, at one end, stood an exceptionally light and dainty little table of foreign lacquer traced with gold. On it were a teapot, teacup, rinsing-bowl, foreign towel and other such things, as well as a spectacle-case. Grandmother Jia reclined on the couch, laughing and talking with the others, and now and then took up her spectacles to look towards the stage. She smiled at Aunt Xue and Aunt Li.
‘Forgive an old woman. My bones ache. You must allow me to keep you company lying down, though it’s very rude of me.’

She told Amber to sit on the couch and pat her legs with a padded massage club. No dining table had been laid immediately below the couch, only a tall stand bearing an ornamental screen, vases, an incense-burner and the like. A separate, finely made little high table held her wine-cup, spoon and chopsticks. Her dining table was set beside the couch, and she had Bao-qin, Xiang-yun, Dai-yu and Bao-yu sit at it. Every dish and plate of fruit was first held up for her to see. If it pleased her, it was left on the little table for her to taste, then taken away and set before the four young people. They counted simply as sharing Grandmother Jia’s table.

segments.text: From the great beams on either side hung a matching pair of glass lotus lanterns with coloured tassels, linked in threes and clustered in fives. Before each table stood a lacquered stem with a drooping lotus leaf, fitted with a socket holding a coloured candle. These leaves were of chased enamel and turned on movable fittings. They had all been turned outwards, screening the light and directing it towards the stage, so that the play could be seen with particular clarity. Window frames and doors had all been removed, and palace lanterns of every kind with coloured tassels hung in their place. Inside and outside the verandah eaves and under the covered walkways on both sides hung lanterns of horn, glass, embroidered gauze and spun glass; embroidered, painted, built up in relief or cut out; of silk or paper, in every variety. The tables on the verandah were occupied by Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Jia Huan, Jia Cong, Jia Rong, Jia Qin, Jia Yun, Jia Ling, Jia Chang and the others.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia had also sent invitations to the men and women of the wider clan. Some, however, were too old to care for a noisy gathering; some could not conveniently come because no one would be left at home; some were confined by illness and could not come, much as they wished to. Others stayed away out of envy of the rich and shame at their own poverty. There were even some who disliked and feared Xi-feng so much that they refused to come out of spite; and some were shy and awkward, unused to company, and dared not come. Thus, for all the numbers of the clan, the only woman guest was Jia Jun’s mother Lou-shi, who brought Jia Jun with her. Of the men, only Jia Qin, Jia Yun, Jia Chang and Jia Ling came, all four currently working under Xi-feng. Though they were far from all being present, for a small family party the company was quite a lively one.

Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife now arrived with six women servants carrying three kang tables, two women to each table. Every table was covered with a strip of red felt, on which lay new copper cash fresh from the mint, carefully selected for uniform size and threaded on bright red cords.

segments.text: Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife directed them to place two of the tables below Aunt Xue’s and Aunt Li’s seats, and bring the third to Grandmother Jia’s couch.
‘Put it in the middle,’ Grandmother Jia said.

The women knew the procedure well. They set down the tables, untied all the strings of cash, drew out the coloured cords and left the coins in loose heaps. On stage, ‘Meeting in the Tower’, a scene from The Western Tower, was nearing its end. Yu Shu-ye had gone off in a huff, and Wen Bao broke into a comic aside.

‘Off you go in a temper! It so happens that today’s the fifteenth of the first month, and Her Old Ladyship is giving a family feast at Rong mansion. I’ll get on this horse and hurry in to beg some fruit. That’s the important thing!’
This set Grandmother Jia and the others laughing.
‘What a little imp!’ Aunt Xue and the others said. ‘The dear little thing!’
‘He’s only nine,’ said Xi-feng.

segments.text: ‘How cleverly he put that,’ Grandmother Jia said with a laugh. Then she uttered the single word:
‘Reward!’

Three women had already made ready their winnowing baskets. At the word ‘Reward’, they stepped up to the heaps of loose cash and each scooped up a basketful. They came out and called towards the stage:
‘Her Old Ladyship, Aunt Xue and Aunt Li reward Wen Bao with money to buy fruit!’

As they spoke they flung the coins onto the stage, which rang with a great clattering and jingling. Jia Zhen and Jia Lian had already had their pages bring up large winnowing baskets of cash and were keeping them ready out of sight. When they heard Grandmother Jia call for a reward...

segments.text: Now Jia Zhen and Jia Lian had quietly made ready their large winnowing baskets of cash. At Grandmother Jia’s cry of ‘Reward!’ they too hastened to order their pages to scatter the money. The whole stage rang with coins, to Grandmother Jia’s great delight. The two men rose. The pages promptly placed a silver wine-pot, freshly warmed, in Jia Lian’s hands, and he followed Jia Zhen briskly inside. Jia Zhen went first to Aunt Li’s table, bowed and took up her cup, then turned for Jia Lian to fill it. They next went to Aunt Xue’s table and filled her cup too. Both ladies rose hastily, smiling.
‘Do sit down, gentlemen. There’s no need for such ceremony.’

Except for Lady Xing and Lady Wang, everyone had now left their seats and was standing respectfully by with hands lowered. Jia Zhen and Jia Lian came before Grandmother Jia’s couch. As it was so low, they bent their knees and knelt, Jia Zhen in front with the cup, Jia Lian behind with the pot.

‘What are you kneeling down with them for? If you’re so eager, wouldn’t it be better to go and pour everyone a round yourself?’
‘In a little while,’ he whispered back, smiling.
He waited until the two men had finished pouring and risen before he got up himself.

segments.text: The second watch had not yet sounded. They were performing the eight ‘Viewing the Lanterns’ pieces from The Eight Righteous Men. At the height of the excitement, Bao-yu left the table and went towards the door.
‘Where are you going?’ Grandmother Jia called. ‘Those firecrackers outside are fierce. Mind a burning scrap of paper doesn’t fall out of the sky and set you alight.’
‘I’m not going far. I’ll only be out a moment.’
Grandmother Jia told the older women to keep close beside him. Bao-yu went out, but only Musk, Ripple and a few little maids followed him.
‘Why haven’t I seen Aroma?’ Grandmother Jia asked. ‘She’s beginning to give herself airs, sending only the little girls out to wait on him.’

segments.text: Lady Wang hurriedly rose and answered with a smile.
‘Her mother died the other day. She’s in fresh mourning and couldn’t properly come out here.’
Grandmother Jia nodded, then smiled again.

‘When you’re waiting on your master, you can’t make so much of mourning or not mourning. If she were still with me, would she be absent now? It’s all because we’re too easy-going. There are other people to do the work, so we don’t look into these things, and it ends by becoming the rule.’
Xi-feng quickly came forward, smiling.

‘Even if she weren’t in mourning, she would still have to look after the Garden tonight. Lamps, candles and fireworks are the most dangerous things. Once the plays begin here, who in the Garden won’t slip away for a look? She’s careful, and can keep an eye on everything. Then, when we break up and Bao-yu goes back to bed, everything will be ready for him. If she came too, and the others took no trouble, he’d go home to cold bedding, with no tea or hot water ready. Nothing would be as it should. So I told her not to come, but to mind the rooms. Everything will be ready when we leave, we shan’t have to worry here, and she can observe the proper mourning customs as well. Isn’t that three good things at once?

segments.text: ‘If you want her, Grandmother, I’ll send for her at once.’
‘You’re quite right,’ Grandmother Jia said hastily. ‘You’ve thought it out better than I did. Don’t send for her. But when did her mother die? Why didn’t I know?’
‘Aroma came and told you herself the other day,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘Have you forgotten?’
Grandmother Jia thought for a moment and laughed.
‘Now I remember. My memory really is getting poor.’
‘How could you keep all these things in mind?’ they all said, laughing.
Grandmother Jia sighed.

‘I was thinking how she served me when she was a little girl, then served Yun, and was finally given to that demon Bao-yu. She’s had him plaguing her for years. And she isn’t a servant born and bred in our household. She’s had no great favours from us. When her mother died, I meant to give her a few taels to help with the funeral, and then I forgot.’
‘Her Ladyship gave her forty taels the other day,’ said Xi-feng. ‘That will have been enough.’
Grandmother Jia nodded.
‘That’s something, at least.

segments.text: Meanwhile, Bao-yu had gone straight to the Garden. Seeing that he was going back to his rooms, the older women did not follow. They stayed in the tea-room inside the Garden gate to warm themselves at the fire, stealing a little leisure to drink and play cards with the woman in charge of the tea. Bao-yu reached his courtyard. It was brilliantly lit, but not a voice could be heard.
‘Can they all be asleep?’ Musk asked. ‘Let’s creep in and give them a fright.’

They stole on tiptoe past the mirrored partition and peeped in. Aroma and someone else were reclining opposite each other on the heated floor, while two or three old nurses dozed at the far end. Bao-yu thought the pair were asleep too, and was just about to go in when he heard Faithful sigh.

‘You never can tell how things will turn out. With you here by yourself and your parents outside, moving east and west every year with no settled place, you’d have thought you could never be there at the end. Yet this year your mother happened to die here, and you were able to go out and be with her.’
‘Yes,’ Aroma said. ‘I never thought I’d be there at the end for either of my parents.

segments.text: ‘We didn’t know,’ the women said hurriedly, smiling. ‘We’ve got ourselves into trouble on a great holiday! You young ladies must have had a tiring few days.’
They had reached them as they spoke.
‘What are you carrying?’ Musk and Ripple asked.
‘Her Old Ladyship has sent some food for Miss Jin and Miss Hua.’
Ripple laughed.
‘They’re playing The Eight Righteous Men out there, not The Primal Unity Box. Where has “Lady Golden Flower” sprung from?’
‘Lift the lids and let me see,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.

Ripple and Musk hurried forward to open the two boxes. The women holding them quickly squatted down. Bao-yu saw that both boxes were filled with the finest fruit and dishes from the feast. He nodded and walked on. Musk and Ripple dropped the lids back any which way and hastened after him.

‘Those two women are pleasant, and know how to speak to people,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘They’re worn out themselves every day, yet they say it’s you who’ve had a tiring few days. They aren’t the sort to keep boasting of all they do.’
‘The good ones are very good,’ Musk replied. ‘But the ones with no manners really have none.’
‘You understand things,’ he said with a smile. ‘Just make allowances for them as poor, clumsy creatures, and leave it at that.’
Talking thus, they reached the Garden gate.

segments.text: Ripple quickly put a hand into the basin to test the water.
‘You grow more careless as you grow older. Where did you get this cold water?’
‘Look at the weather, miss!’ the little maid said with a smile. ‘I was afraid it would get cold, so I made a point of pouring it boiling hot. And now it’s cold all the same.’
Just then an old woman came along carrying a kettle of boiling water.
‘Be a dear, Mother,’ the little maid said. ‘Come and pour me some.’
‘My dear child, this is for Her Old Ladyship’s tea. You’d better go and fetch your own. It won’t wear your feet out.’
‘I don’t care whose it is,’ Ripple said. ‘Are you refusing us? I’d empty Her Old Ladyship’s teapot for him to wash his hands.’
The old woman turned, saw that it was Ripple, and hastily lifted the kettle to pour.
‘That’s enough. At your age, you ought to have some sense. Who didn’t know it was Her Old Ladyship’s water? Would anyone ask if they weren’t entitled to it?’
‘My eyes are dim,’ the old woman said with a smile. ‘I didn’t recognise you, miss.’
Bao-yu washed his hands. The little maid poured some cleansing paste from the small pot into his hands, and he rubbed it in.

segments.text: Ripple and Musk took advantage of the hot water to wash their hands too, and used the cleansing paste before following Bao-yu inside. He asked for a pot of warm wine and began, as the others had done, with Aunt Li and Aunt Xue. Both urged him to sit down.
‘He’s young. Let him pour,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘But everyone must drain this cup.’
She emptied her own as she spoke. Lady Xing and Lady Wang hastily did the same and urged the two guests to follow suit. Aunt Xue and Aunt Li could only drink theirs too.
‘Pour for all your sisters and cousins as well,’ Grandmother Jia told Bao-yu. ‘Go round them properly. Make every one of them drain her cup.’
He assented and went round them in order. When he reached Dai-yu, however, she would not drink. She picked up her cup and held it to his lips. He emptied it at a draught.
‘Thank you,’ she said, smiling.
He poured her another cup.
‘Bao-yu, don’t drink cold wine,’ Xi-feng said with a laugh. ‘It’ll make your hand shake, and tomorrow you won’t be able to write or draw a bow.’
‘I haven’t had any cold wine,’ he said hastily.
‘I know you haven’t. I was only reminding you.’
Bao-yu finished pouring for everyone inside except Jia Rong’s wife, whose cup was filled by the maids.

segments.text: He went out to the verandah to pour for Jia Zhen and the others, sat with them for a while, then came back in and resumed his own place. Presently soup was served, followed by Lantern Festival dumplings. Grandmother Jia ordered a pause in the plays.
‘The poor children! Give them some piping-hot soup and food before they sing again.’

She also told the servants to take them some of the different fruits, dumplings and other things. When the performance stopped, an older woman brought in two female storytellers who were regular visitors to the household. Two stools were set to one side for them to sit on, and their three-stringed lute and pipa were handed to them. Grandmother Jia asked Aunt Li and Aunt Xue what tale they would like.
‘Anything at all,’ both replied.
‘Have you added any new stories lately?’ she asked the storytellers.
‘We have a new one, set in the last days of the Tang and the Five Dynasties.’
‘What is it called?’
‘The Phoenix Seeks Its Mate.’
‘That’s a good name,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘I wonder how it came by it. Give us an outline first. If it’s good, you can tell it.’

segments.text: ‘Our story tells of a gentleman in the last days of the Tang,’ one began. ‘He came from Jinling, and his name was Wang Zhong. He had served as chief minister under two reigns, and had now retired in his old age to his native place. He had an only son, whose name was Wang Xi-feng.’
Everyone began to laugh.
‘He has our Feng’s name,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing.
A woman servant hurried over and nudged the storyteller.
‘That’s the Second Mistress’s name. Don’t talk nonsense.’
‘Go on, go on,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile.
The storyteller hastily got to her feet, smiling apologetically.
‘We deserve to die! We didn’t know it was your honoured name, ma’am.’

segments.text: ‘Then she catches sight of a good-looking young man, and whether he’s a relation or a friend, she thinks at once of marrying him. segments.text: Xi-feng came forward to pour wine.

‘Enough, enough!’ she said, laughing. ‘The wine’s getting cold. Take a sip to moisten your throat, Grandmother, before you go on picking the lies apart. We’ll call this instalment The Exposure of Tall Tales, set in this very dynasty, this very place, this very year, month, day and hour. But Grandmother has only one mouth and cannot tell two stories at once. Two flowers bloom: let us speak of one branch at a time. Whether the tale be true or false, we shall leave it for the moment, and return to those who were viewing the lanterns and watching the plays. Grandmother, why not let our two honoured guests drink a cup and watch a couple of scenes before taking up yesterday’s tale again?’
She poured as she spoke, laughing, and before she had finished everyone was helpless with laughter. The two storytellers could not stop laughing either.
‘What a tongue you have, ma’am! If you took to storytelling, there’d be no living left for us.’
‘Don’t get too carried away,’ Aunt Xue said, smiling. ‘There are men outside. It isn’t like an ordinary day.’
‘There’s only Cousin Zhen out there,’ Xi-feng said with a laugh. ‘We still count as brother and sister. We’ve played and made mischief together since we were children, all the way up to now.

segments.text: ‘If Your Old Ladyship doesn’t care for the story,’ the storyteller said, ‘perhaps you’d like to hear us play a suite?’
‘Play The General’s Command together,’ said Grandmother Jia.
The two promptly tuned their strings, found the key and began to play. Grandmother Jia asked what watch of the night it was.
‘The third watch,’ the older women hastened to reply.
‘No wonder the cold’s beginning to creep in.’
The maids were already bringing extra clothes and changes of clothing. Lady Wang rose and smiled.
‘Wouldn’t you be better off on the heated floor in the warm inner room? Neither of our two guests is a stranger. We can keep them company.’
‘If that’s so, why don’t we all move in?’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘Wouldn’t we be warmer?’
‘I’m afraid there won’t be room for everyone.’
‘I know what to do. We don’t need all these tables now. Put two or three together, and we can all sit close round them. It’ll be cosier, and warmer too.’
‘That will be much more fun,’ they all said, and rose from their places.

segments.text: The women servants hurried to clear away the remains of the feast. Inside, they set three large tables together in a straight line and laid them with fresh fruit and dishes.
‘No standing on ceremony here,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Just sit where I tell you.’
She gave Aunt Xue and Aunt Li the places of honour at the head, then sat facing west herself, with Bao-qin, Dai-yu and Xiang-yun close beside her on either side.
‘Sit next to your mother,’ she told Bao-yu.

Bao-yu sat between Lady Xing and Lady Wang. Bao-chai and the other girls were on the west side. Below them came Lou-shi with Jia Jun, then You-shi and Li Wan with Jia Lan between them. Jia Rong’s wife sat across the lower end.
‘Zhen, take your younger brothers and go,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘I shall be going to bed myself.’

segments.text: Jia Zhen hastily assented, and they all started to come in again.
‘Off you go!’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘No need to come in. We’ve only just sat down, and now we shall all be getting up again. Go and rest. There’s important business tomorrow.’
Jia Zhen agreed at once, then smiled.
‘We ought to leave Rong here to pour the wine.’
‘So we ought. I’d forgotten him.’

‘Yes, Grandmother,’ Jia Zhen replied, and turned to lead Jia Lian and the rest away. The two were naturally delighted. They ordered people to take Jia Cong and Jia Huang to their respective homes; then Jia Zhen invited Jia Lian to go pleasure-seeking and buy a few smiles. Of that we need say no more.

segments.text: ‘I was just thinking,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile, ‘that for all the people here enjoying themselves, we hadn’t a single complete couple. I’d forgotten Rong. Now we’re complete. Rong, sit beside your wife, and you can have your reunion too.’
A woman servant came to announce that the play was beginning again.

‘We women are just getting into our talk, and now they’re going to make a noise,’ Grandmother Jia said, smiling. ‘Besides, the children must be terribly cold, staying up so late. Never mind. Let them rest for a while. Fetch our own girls and have them sing a couple of scenes on this stage for the others to watch.’

The woman assented and went out. She hurriedly sent someone to Prospect Garden for the girls, while going to the inner gate to summon the pages to attend. The pages went straight to the dressing-room and took out all the adults in the visiting troupe, leaving only the children.

segments.text: Presently the instructor from Pear-tree Court came through the side gate off the covered walk with Wen-guan and the other girls, twelve in all. The older women carried several soft bundles. There had been no time to bring the trunks, so they had guessed at three or five scenes Grandmother Jia might like and bundled up the costumes for them. They led Wen-guan and the rest in to pay their respects; the girls stood with their hands lowered.

‘In the middle of the New Year, and your teacher won’t let you out for a little amusement,’ Grandmother Jia said, smiling. ‘What are you going to sing? Those eight pieces from The Eight Righteous Men have given me a headache. Let’s have something quieter. Now look: Aunt Xue and our kinswoman Mrs Li both have troupes in their own households. Who knows how many fine plays they’ve heard? Their young ladies have seen better plays and heard better singing than our girls have. And these little actors here belong to a troupe kept by a famous connoisseur of the theatre. Children though they are, they’re better than the grown-up troupes. We mustn’t give anyone cause to find fault. We shall have to offer something a little different. Have Parfumée sing Seeking the Dream. Just a light accompaniment of tiqin and pipes. No sheng or dizi at all.’

‘Quite so,’ Wen-guan said with a smile. ‘Of course our plays could never find favour in the eyes of our honoured guests and their young ladies. You can only listen to the way we bring out the words, and hear what our voices are like.’
‘Exactly,’ said Grandmother Jia.
Aunt Li and Aunt Xue laughed in delight.
‘What a quick-witted child! She’s joining you in making fun of us.’
‘Our girls are only for a little amusement at home,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘They don’t go out to earn money, so they’re really rather behind the times.’
Then she added, ‘Have Kui-guan sing Huiming Delivers the Letter. No painted face, either.

segments.text: ‘Just those two scenes, to let them hear something out of the ordinary. And I won’t have you sparing yourselves the least bit of trouble.’
Wen-guan and the others went out, hurriedly dressed and took the stage, first for Seeking the Dream, then for Delivering the Letter. Not a sound came from the audience.
‘It really is remarkable,’ Aunt Xue said with a smile. ‘I’ve watched hundreds of troupes, and I’ve never seen one use pipes for the accompaniment.’

‘Oh, there are some,’ Grandmother Jia replied. ‘Take that passage just now, Clear Skies over the Chu River from The Western Tower. The young male lead often accompanies it on a xiao. But for a whole long sequence like this, it is rare. It all depends on how much trouble the patron cares to take. What’s so extraordinary about it? When I was her age,’ she went on, pointing to Xiang-yun, ‘her grandfather had a troupe of young actors. As luck would have it, a qin-player joined them. When they did Listening to the Qin from The Western Chamber, or Wooing with the Qin from The Jade Hairpin, or Eighteen Songs for the Hu Reed-pipe from The Sequel to the Lute, it was all real. How much better was that than this?’
‘That must have been rarer still,’ they all said.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia called a woman servant and told her to have Wen-guan and the others play the suite Round Lanterns, Full Moon on their wind instruments. The woman went to carry out the order. Jia Rong and his wife now took the wine round together. Seeing Grandmother Jia in such high spirits, Xi-feng smiled.
‘While the storytellers are here, why not have them beat the drum, and we can pass a plum branch? We’ll play “Spring Joy Climbs to the Brows”. How would that be?’
‘A good game,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘Just right for the season and the occasion.’

She promptly ordered a drinking-game drum to be brought, black-lacquered and studded with copper, for the storytellers to play their flourishes on. A spray of red plum blossom was taken from the table.
