segments.text: ‘Whoever has it when the drum stops must drink a cup,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘And ought to say something as well.’

‘Who can be like you, Grandmother, with something ready for every occasion?’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘What about those of us who can’t? It would be no fun for us. I say we ought to have something for learned and simple alike. Let whoever loses tell a joke.’

Everyone knew how good she was at telling jokes, and what an endless store of fresh and funny tales she had. Her proposal delighted not only the people at the table, but every attendant in the room, old and young. The little maids hurried out to fetch their friends.
‘Come and listen! The Second Mistress is going to tell jokes again.’

segments.text: Soon the room was packed with maids. The plays had finished and the music ceased. Grandmother Jia had soup, pastries, fruit and dishes sent to Wen-guan and the others, then gave the word for the drum to begin. The storytellers were old hands at this. Now fast, now slow, they drummed: like the last drops of a water-clock, like bursting beans, like a startled horse careering wildly, like a flash of lightning suddenly gone dark. When the drumming slowed, the plum branch passed slowly; when it quickened, the branch sped from hand to hand. Just as it reached Grandmother Jia, the drum stopped dead. Everyone laughed, and Jia Rong hurried up to pour a cup.
‘Of course the joy must come to you first,’ they said, laughing. ‘Then we can have a little of it through your blessing.’
‘I don’t mind the wine,’ Grandmother Jia said with a laugh. ‘It’s the joke that’s a little difficult.’

segments.text: She began:

‘There was a family with ten sons, and they married ten wives. Only the tenth daughter-in-law was clever and quick. She had a quick mind and a ready tongue, and her parents-in-law loved her best. All day long they said the other nine were unfilial. The nine felt very badly treated, and put their heads together. “We nine are dutiful at heart,” they said. “We just haven’t that little hussy’s clever tongue. Our father-in-law and mother-in-law are old, and they only ever say how good she is. Who can we complain to about such unfairness?” The eldest had an idea. “Tomorrow let’s go to King Yama’s temple, burn incense and put our case to him. We’ll ask why, when he sent us to be born as human beings, he gave that little hussy alone a clever tongue and made the rest of us so dull.” They were all delighted and agreed that it was a very good plan. Next day they went to King Yama’s temple and burnt incense. All nine fell asleep beneath the altar table, and their nine souls waited for King Yama to arrive. They waited and waited, but he never came. Just as they were growing desperate, along came Monkey on his somersault cloud. At the sight of the nine souls he raised his gold-banded staff to strike them. Terrified, they fell on their knees and begged for mercy.

segments.text: ‘Monkey asked what was the matter, and the nine hastened to tell him the whole story. He stamped his foot and sighed. “Lucky you met me! Even if you waited till King Yama came, he wouldn’t know the reason.” When they heard that, they begged him, “Great Sage, have mercy on us, and all will be well!” Monkey laughed. “That’s easy enough. The day the ten of you were sent to be born, I happened to be visiting King Yama. I had a piss on the ground, and your youngest sister-in-law drank it. If you want to be clever and glib-tongued now, there’s plenty more piss. I’ll do you another lot, and you can drink that.”’
When she finished, everyone burst out laughing.

segments.text: ‘Well!’ Xi-feng said with a laugh. ‘Lucky we’re all so slow with our tongues, or we’d have drunk monkey’s piss too.’
You-shi and Lou-shi turned to Li Wan, laughing.
‘Who is it here who’s been drinking monkey’s piss? Don’t pretend it’s nothing to do with you.’
‘It isn’t whether a joke’s good or bad,’ Aunt Xue said with a smile. ‘If it fits the occasion, it makes you laugh.’

The drum began again. The little maids were determined to hear Xi-feng tell a joke, and quietly arranged with the storytellers that a cough should be the signal. Soon the branch had gone round twice and reached Xi-feng. The maids coughed deliberately, and the storytellers stopped.
‘Now we’ve caught her!’ everyone cried, laughing. ‘Quick, drink your wine and tell us a good one. Only don’t make us laugh till our sides ache.’
Xi-feng thought for a moment, then smiled.

‘There was another family keeping the fifteenth of the first month. The whole household was admiring the lanterns and drinking wine, and what a lively party it was! Great-grandmothers-in-law, grandmothers-in-law, mothers-in-law, daughters-in-law, grandsons’ wives, great-grandsons’ wives, grandsons, grand-nephews, great-grandsons, great-great-grandsons, grandsons dribbling on and on, granddaughters, daughters’ daughters, granddaughters related through mothers’ sisters, granddaughters related through fathers’ sisters... Oh my, oh my, what a lively party!’
They were laughing already.
‘Listen to that chatter! Who’s she making fun of now?’
‘If you start on me, I’ll tear your mouth,’ You-shi said with a laugh.
Xi-feng rose and clapped her hands, laughing.
‘Here I am taking all this trouble to tell you a story, and you keep interrupting. I shan’t tell you any more.’
‘Go on, go on,’ Grandmother Jia said, smiling. ‘What happened next?’
Xi-feng thought for a moment.
‘Next, they all sat round together in a room, drank wine all night, and then broke up.’
She said it with a perfectly stern, straight face, and added nothing. They stared at her, still waiting for the rest. It fell utterly flat.

‘I’ll tell you another one about the fifteenth. Some people were carrying a firecracker as big as a house outside the city to let it off. It drew a crowd of over ten thousand who followed to watch. One impatient fellow couldn’t wait, so he secretly touched it off with a stick of incense.

segments.text: ‘There was just a “pfft!” Everyone roared with laughter, and the crowd broke up. The man carrying the firecracker complained that the seller hadn’t bound it tightly enough. It had broken up before they could let it off.’
‘Didn’t the man himself hear it go off?’ Xiang-yun asked.
‘The man was deaf,’ said Xi-feng.
They thought back over the story and all burst out laughing. Then, remembering the first one, which she had never finished, they asked:
‘What happened in the first story? You ought to finish that too.’

‘What a fuss you make! Next day was the sixteenth. New Year was over, the festival was over. I was busy watching everyone clear things away, and couldn’t even keep track of that. How was I to know what happened next?’

segments.text: At this they all began laughing again.
‘They’ve already sounded the fourth watch outside,’ Xi-feng said, laughing. ‘If you ask me, Grandmother’s tired, and it’s time we followed the deaf man’s firecracker and broke up too.’
You-shi and the others held their handkerchiefs over their mouths and rocked backwards and forwards with laughter, pointing at her.
‘This creature really does know how to chatter!’

‘That Feng gets more of a chatterbox every day,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. Then she gave an order. ‘Now she’s mentioned firecrackers, let’s set off our fireworks and clear our heads of the wine.’

Jia Rong hurried out with the pages to set up screens and frames in the courtyard and hang the fireworks in readiness. These had all been sent in as tribute from various places. Though not very large, they were exquisitely made, with every sort of story represented, interspersed with coloured fireworks. Dai-yu’s constitution was delicate, and she could not bear the crackling and banging. Grandmother Jia took her in her arms. Aunt Xue held Xiang-yun.
‘I’m not afraid,’ Xiang-yun said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘She loves nothing better than letting off great big firecrackers herself,’ Bao-chai and the others said with a laugh. ‘As if she’d be frightened of these!’
Lady Wang drew Bao-yu into her arms.
‘Some of us have nobody to love us,’ Xi-feng said, laughing.
‘You have me,’ said You-shi with a smile. ‘I’ll hold you. Aren’t you ashamed, you great baby, wheedling again? One mention of firecrackers, and you’re showing off again today, you bee-dung eater!’
‘When we break up, let’s go and set some off in our Garden,’ Xi-feng said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘I can do it better than the pages.’

As they spoke, one display after another went off outside. There were plenty of smaller fireworks too: ‘Stars All over the Sky’, ‘Nine Dragons Enter the Clouds’, ‘A Clap of Thunder’, ‘Ten Reports Flying Heavenwards’ and others of the kind. When the display was over, the young actors were told to perform a round of Lotus-fall songs. Money was scattered all over the stage, and the children were made to scramble for it to amuse the company. Soup was brought again.
‘It’s a long night,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘I’m beginning to feel hungry.’
‘We have duck-meat porridge ready,’ Xi-feng replied at once.
‘I’d like something plain.’
‘There’s non-glutinous rice porridge cooked with jujubes too,’ Xi-feng said hastily. ‘It was made for the ladies who are keeping a vegetarian fast.’
Grandmother Jia smiled.
‘If it isn’t greasy, it’s sweet.’
‘There’s almond tea as well, only I’m afraid that’s sweet too.’
‘That will do rather better.’
By now the remains of the feast had been cleared away, and all kinds of delicate little dishes had been set out outside.

segments.text: Everyone ate a little, just as they pleased. When they had had tea to rinse their mouths, they finally dispersed. Early on the seventeenth, they went again to Ning mansion to perform the rites, waited while the ancestral shrine was closed and the portraits put away, then returned. That day Aunt Xue’s household was giving its New Year feast. The eighteenth was Lai Da’s turn, the nineteenth Lai Sheng’s at Ning mansion, the twentieth Lin Zhi-xiao’s, the twenty-first Shan Da-liang’s and the twenty-second Wu Xin-deng’s. Grandmother Jia went to some of these houses and not to others. Sometimes she enjoyed herself so much that she stayed until everyone else had gone; sometimes she had had enough and came home after half a day or a short while. As for relatives and friends who invited her or came to dine, she met none of them, fearing the constraint. Lady Xing, Lady Wang and Xi-feng saw to all that. Even Bao-yu went nowhere except to Wang Zi-teng’s, the excuse being that Grandmother Jia had kept him at home to amuse her. It was the servants’ own households, where she could do as she pleased, whose invitations she enjoyed accepting for a little outing.

All the imperial consorts had therefore reduced their meals and laid aside their adornments. Not only could they no longer visit their families, but feasting and entertainments had been suspended too. There was consequently no lantern-riddle gathering at the Rong mansion that year.

segments.text: Scarcely was the New Year bustle over when Xi-feng had a miscarriage. For a month she stayed in her rooms, unable to manage affairs, with two or three imperial physicians prescribing for her every day. Trusting in her strength, she went on planning and calculating even though she did not go out. Whenever something occurred to her, she sent Patience to report it to Lady Wang. Whoever tried to dissuade her, she would not listen.

Lady Wang felt as though she had lost her right arm. How much energy could one person have? She decided important matters herself, but temporarily entrusted all the lesser household business to Li Wan. Li Wan valued goodness more than ability, and inevitably gave the servants too much licence. Lady Wang therefore appointed Tan-chun to deal with matters jointly with her. It was only to be for a month: once Xi-feng had rested and recovered, everything would be handed back to her. But Xi-feng’s constitution was deficient in qi and blood. Young as she was, she had never learnt to look after herself, and her constant determination to outdo others in strength and cleverness had further exhausted her mind and energies. Though it was a miscarriage, it left her seriously depleted. After a month she began to suffer from bleeding as well. She would not speak of it, but the others, seeing how yellow and thin her face had grown, knew that she had not had the rest and care she needed.

segments.text: Lady Wang told her simply to take her medicine and attend to her recovery, and forbade her to concern herself with affairs. Xi-feng herself was afraid that the illness might grow serious and make her a laughing-stock. She therefore hoped to snatch a respite in which to recover, impatient to be her old self again at once. Yet it was not until the eighth or ninth month, after taking medicine and resting all that time, that her strength gradually returned and the bleeding slowly ceased. But that belongs to a later part of the story.

segments.text: For the present, seeing her in this condition, Lady Wang could hardly release Tan-chun and Li Wan from their duties. There were so many people in the Garden that she feared they might not all be properly looked after. She therefore sent specially for Bao-chai and asked her to keep a careful watch everywhere.

‘Those old women are no use. Give them a spare moment and they’re drinking or playing cards. They sleep all day and play cards all night. I know all about it. While Feng was about, they had someone to be afraid of. Now they’ll be taking advantage again. My dear, you’re a sensible girl. Your younger cousins are still children, and I have no time. Will you take a little trouble for me for a day or two and keep an eye on things? If there’s anything I haven’t thought of, come and tell me. Don’t wait until the old lady asks about it and I have nothing to say. If those people misbehave, speak to them freely. If they won’t listen, report it to me. We mustn’t let anything serious happen.’
Bao-chai could only agree.

segments.text: It was the first month of spring. Dai-yu’s cough had returned, and Xiang-yun too, affected by the season’s unhealthy airs, lay ill at Allspice Court, with doctors and medicines coming and going all day. Li Wan and Tan-chun lived some distance apart. Now that they were working together, things were not as they had been in former years, and it was inconvenient for the people who had to come and report to them. They agreed to meet every morning in the small three-bay reception hall south of the Garden gate, transact their business there, and return to their rooms after breakfast, around midday. The hall had originally been set aside for the eunuchs on duty during the Imperial Visit. Since then it had had no use, apart from the old women keeping watch there at night. The weather was now warm; it needed no elaborate fitting-out. A few furnishings would make it ready for the two of them.

The married women responsible for the various household duties came and went in an unending stream to make their reports.

segments.text: When they first heard that Li Wan was to manage things alone, the servants were secretly delighted. She had always been kindly, ready with favours but never with punishments; she would plainly be easier to put off than Xi-feng. Even when Tan-chun was added, they thought her no more than a young, unmarried girl, normally quiet and even-tempered. They paid little heed to her and grew far more slack than they had dared to be under Xi-feng. But after three or four days, when several matters had passed through her hands, they began to discover that Tan-chun was every bit as exacting in detail as Xi-feng. She merely spoke more quietly and had a gentler manner.

It happened that during these days more than a dozen houses of princes, dukes, marquises, earls and hereditary officials, all related to the Rong and Ning households or connected with them by friendship, often of long standing, had promotions or demotions, weddings or funerals to mark. Lady Wang had no leisure from the calls, receptions and farewells of congratulation or condolence. That left no one to see to things in the main house, so the two spent the whole day in the hall.

segments.text: Bao-chai, meanwhile, supervised matters in Lady Wang’s apartments all day and left only when she returned. Every evening, in a pause from her needlework before bed, she took a small sedan-chair and made a round of the Garden with the night-watch attendants. With the three of them managing things in this way, the servants found that they had to be even more careful than when Xi-feng was in charge. Inside and outside alike, they complained among themselves:
‘We’ve only just got rid of one sea-patrolling yaksha, and now we’ve three mountain-guarding Tai Sui gods instead. We can’t even steal a little time at night for a drink and some fun!’

segments.text: One day Lady Wang was going to a banquet at the Marquis of Jinxiang’s. Li Wan and Tan-chun washed and dressed early, attended her departure, then returned to sit in the hall. They had just begun their tea when Wu Xin-deng’s wife came in to report.
‘Aunt Zhao’s brother, Zhao Guo-ji, died yesterday. It was reported to Her Ladyship yesterday. She said she knew, and told us to bring the matter to you, miss, and to Mrs Zhu.’

Having said this, she stood to one side with her hands lowered and said no more. Quite a number of people were there to report on business, all intent on discovering how the two would manage. If they proved competent, everyone would settle down to a proper fear of them. If there were the slightest flaw or impropriety, the servants would not only cease to fear them: once through the inner gate, they would invent any number of stories to make them a laughing-stock. Wu Xin-deng’s wife had already decided on her course. Before Xi-feng she would eagerly have offered suggestions and looked up plenty of precedents for Xi-feng to choose from. Now, despising Li Wan for her honesty and Tan-chun for being a young girl, she said no more than this, to see what ideas they might have of their own.

segments.text: Tan-chun consulted Li Wan. Li Wan thought for a moment.
‘When Aroma’s mother died the other day, I heard she was given forty taels. Allow forty for this case too.’
Wu Xin-deng’s wife promptly said yes, took the authorisation tally and was leaving when Tan-chun called her back.
‘Wait. Come back here.’
The woman had no choice but to return.

‘Don’t draw the silver yet. Let me ask you something. In former years, the old concubines in Grandmother’s apartments belonged to two different classes: some were household-born and some had been brought in from outside. When a relation of a household-born woman died, how much was granted? And how much when it was one of those brought in from outside? Tell us the two rates.’
At this question Wu Xin-deng’s wife suddenly forgot everything. She hurried to put on a smile.
‘It’s hardly an important matter. Whatever you give, who would dare dispute it?’

‘That’s nonsense,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘If you ask me, a hundred would be very nice. But if we don’t follow precedent, it’s not only that you’ll laugh at us. We shan’t be able to face your Second Mistress afterwards.’
‘In that case, I’ll go and look up the old accounts,’ the woman said, smiling. ‘I can’t remember just now.’
‘You’ve been doing this work for years,’ Tan-chun said, still smiling, ‘yet you can’t remember, and come here to make difficulties for us.

Scarlet-faced, Wu Xin-deng’s wife hurried out. The other women put out their tongues. Inside, other business was reported.

segments.text: Presently Mrs Wu returned with the old accounts. Tan-chun found that two household-born women had each received twenty taels, and two who had been brought in from outside had each received forty. There were also two further cases among the latter, one of a hundred taels and one of sixty. Beneath each of these entries the reason was given: in one case, sixty extra taels had been allowed for bringing the parents’ coffins from another province; in the other, twenty extra had been allowed to buy a burial plot. Tan-chun handed the accounts to Li Wan to read.
‘Allow twenty taels,’ she said. ‘Leave the accounts here. We want to look through them carefully.’
Wu Xin-deng’s wife went away.

‘Who do you mean, Aunt?’ Tan-chun asked at once. ‘I don’t understand.

segments.text: ‘Who’s trampling on you? Tell me, and I’ll stand up for you.’
‘You are, miss. Who am I to tell?’
Tan-chun rose hastily.
‘I would not presume to.’
Li Wan rose too and tried to soothe her.

‘Please sit down, both of you, and listen,’ said Aunt Zhao. ‘I’ve spent all these years wearing myself away in these rooms like oil burning in a lamp, and borne you and your brother, and now I’m not even as good as Aroma. What face have I left? Never mind me: you’ve none left either!’
‘So that’s what it is,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘As I said, I wouldn’t presume to break the rules or act against what is right.’
She sat down, opened the accounts for Aunt Zhao to see and read them aloud to her.

‘These are the old rules handed down by our ancestors. Everyone follows them. Am I alone to change them? And it isn’t only Aroma. If Huan takes someone from outside in time to come, she will naturally be treated in the same way as Aroma. This isn’t a question of who stands higher or lower. There’s no question of gaining or losing face.

segments.text: ‘They are Her Ladyship’s servants. I’m acting according to the old rules. If they think the arrangement good, they have our ancestors and Her Ladyship to thank for their kindness. If they call it unfair, they’re foolish and don’t know their good fortune. We can only let them complain. If Her Ladyship gave someone a house as well, what credit would that bring me? If she gave them not a single cash, what discredit would that bring me? With Her Ladyship out, I should think you’d be better resting quietly, Aunt. Why must you keep worrying over things? Her Ladyship is very fond of me, but your constant troublemaking has distressed her time and again. If only I were a man and could go out into the world, I should have left long ago and made something of myself. Then I would have a way of my own. But I’m a girl. I haven’t the liberty to speak even one word out of turn. Her Ladyship understands it all perfectly. She has asked me to look after the household now because she thinks well of me, and before I’ve done a single good thing, you come to humiliate me. If she hears of this and thinks it puts me in a difficult position, she may stop me managing things. That really would be a disgrace, for you as well as for me!’

segments.text: As she spoke, tears began to roll down her cheeks in spite of herself. Aunt Zhao could find nothing else to answer.
‘If Her Ladyship is fond of you, all the more reason to give us a helping hand. You’re so busy winning her affection that you forget us.’

‘How have I forgotten you? What helping hand am I to give? You should each ask yourselves that. What master doesn’t value someone who works hard and is useful? What decent person needs to be pulled along by someone else?’
Li Wan kept trying to pacify Aunt Zhao.
‘Don’t be angry, Aunt. You can’t blame her. Of course she wants to help you. How can she say so openly?’

‘Now you’re being foolish too, Sister-in-law,’ Tan-chun said at once. ‘Who am I to help? Since when do young ladies advance the servants? You should know for yourselves whether they’re good or bad. What has it to do with me?’
‘Who asked you to help other people?’ Aunt Zhao demanded angrily. ‘When you weren’t in charge, I didn’t come asking you. But now what you say goes. One is one and two is two.

A pity she has kindness to spare and nowhere to use it! Don’t worry, miss, it isn’t your money that’s wanted. I was hoping that once you were married you’d give the Zhao family a little extra help. But you haven’t even grown your feathers yet, and already you’ve forgotten your roots and fly only for the highest branches!’
Before she had finished, Tan-chun’s face had turned white with anger. She could scarcely breathe. Sobbing and catching her breath, she demanded:

‘Who is my uncle? My uncle was only just promoted at the New Year to Inspector-General of Nine Provinces. Where has this other uncle sprung from? If that’s what you say, why did Zhao Guo-ji stand up when Huan went out, and follow him to school? Why didn’t he put on an uncle’s airs? What is the point? Who doesn’t know you bore me? Li Wan asked Patience what had brought her.

‘My mistress says that Aunt Zhao’s brother has died,’ Patience replied with a smile. ‘She was afraid the two of you might not know there was a precedent. The ordinary rule allows only twenty taels. But she asks the young lady to decide. Something more could be added.’
Tan-chun had already wiped away her tears.
‘Why add anything for no reason?’ she said at once. ‘Was anyone here carried for twenty-four months before being born?

segments.text: Patience had understood half the situation as soon as she arrived. These words made it clearer still. Seeing Tan-chun’s anger, she dared not treat her with their usual cheerful familiarity, but stood silently to one side, her hands lowered.

Just then Bao-chai came from Lady Wang’s apartments. Tan-chun and the others rose to offer her a seat. Before they could speak, another woman came in on business. As Tan-chun had been crying, three or four little maids brought a washbasin, towels, a hand-mirror and the other things she needed. She was sitting cross-legged on a low wooden couch. The girl with the basin came up to her, knelt on both knees and held it high. Two other little maids bent their knees beside her, holding the towels, mirror, rouge and powder. Seeing that Scribe was not there, Patience hurried forward to turn back Tan-chun’s sleeves and take off her bracelets. She accepted a large towel and spread it over the front of Tan-chun’s clothes. Only then did Tan-chun put her hands into the basin and begin to wash. The woman started her report:
‘Madam, miss, the family school needs to draw Master Huan’s and Master Lan’s school allowances for the year.’
Patience spoke first.
‘What’s your hurry?

Frightened, the woman hastily put on a smile.
‘It was careless of me.’
She hurried out as she spoke.

segments.text: Smoothing powder over her face, Tan-chun gave Patience a cold smile.

‘You came a little too late. There was something else to laugh at. Even Sister Wu, who’s been doing this work so long, came to put us off without first looking things up properly. Luckily we questioned her. She had the face to say she’d forgotten. I asked whether she forgot things and went to look for them afterwards when reporting to your mistress. I shouldn’t think your mistress would have the patience to wait.’

‘If she’d tried that once, she’d have had a couple of tendons in her legs broken long ago,’ Patience replied quickly, smiling. ‘Don’t believe them, miss. They see that Mrs Zhu is a bodhisattva and you’re a modest young lady, so of course they try to shirk and put you off.’
Then she called towards the door:
‘Go on, behave as you please. We’ll have something to say about it when my mistress is well again.’
The women outside all answered with smiles:
‘Miss, you understand things better than anyone. As the saying goes, “Let whoever does the wrong bear the blame.” We wouldn’t dare deceive the young lady.

segments.text: ‘A daughter of the house is an honoured guest. If we really made her angry, we should die without so much as a place to be buried.’
‘It’s as well you understand that,’ said Patience with a cold smile. Then, smiling deferentially at Tan-chun, she went on:

‘You know how much the Second Mistress has to do. How could she keep an eye on all these things? She’s bound to overlook something. As they say, “The onlooker sees clearly.” You’ve been watching quietly these past few years, miss. If there are things that ought to be added or cut which she hasn’t attended to, please make the changes. First, it will benefit Her Ladyship’s affairs; and second, it will be a fitting expression of the kindness you’ve always shown my mistress.’
Before she had finished, Bao-chai and Li Wan both laughed.

‘Clever girl! No wonder Feng is so fond of her. There was nothing to add or cut in the first place, but after hearing that, we shall have to find a thing or two to consider, just to do justice to your speech.’

‘I was bursting with anger, and no one would take the edge off it,’ said Tan-chun, smiling. ‘I was just going to vent it on her mistress when she happened to arrive. Now she’s said all this, I don’t know what to do.’
She called the woman back in and asked:
‘What is this year’s silver for Master Huan and Master Lan at the family school meant to pay for?’
‘Refreshments at school, or paper and brushes,’ the woman replied. ‘Each of them has eight taels to spend in the year.’
‘All the young masters’ expenses are provided for by the monthly allowances drawn in their own rooms,’ said Tan-chun.

‘You’ve delivered your message. Go and see to your own affairs,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘Why busy yourself here?’

‘Why not bring Cousin Bao’s meal here, so that she can eat with us?’ Tan-chun asked.

segments.text: ‘Patience, you’re standing here. You go and ask for it.’
Patience answered at once and went out. The women quickly caught hold of her and whispered with smiles:
‘There’s no need for you to go, miss. We’ve already sent someone.’
As they spoke, they dusted a stone ledge with their handkerchiefs.
‘You must be tired after standing so long, miss. Rest a little here in the sun.’
Patience sat down. Two old women from the tea-room brought a cushion and spread it out.
‘The stone’s cold. This is quite clean. Please make do with it for a little while, miss.’
‘Thank you very much,’ Patience said with a polite smile.
One of them also brought a bowl of fine, freshly brewed tea, saying softly with a smile:
‘This isn’t the tea we ordinarily have. It’s what we serve the young ladies. Have a little to moisten your throat, miss.’
Patience half rose to receive it, then pointed at the women and spoke in a low voice.
‘You’ve gone much too far. She’s a young lady and won’t storm and rage. That’s her sense of dignity, and you take it as a reason to slight her and impose on her.

segments.text: ‘If you really drive her into a fury, the worst they’ll say of her is that she’s rough, and there it ends. You’re the ones who’ll suffer more than you can bear. If she chooses to be wilful, even Her Ladyship has to give way a little, and the Second Mistress daren’t do much about it either. Yet you’re bold enough to think nothing of her. It’s an egg dashing itself against a stone.’
‘We never dared take such liberties,’ they all said hastily. ‘It was Aunt Zhao who made the trouble.’

‘Enough, my good ladies,’ Patience whispered. ‘“When a wall is falling, everyone gives it a push.” Aunt Zhao is certainly muddle-headed, but whenever anything happens, you put all the blame on her. Do you suppose I haven’t learnt in these past few years how little regard you have for anyone, or how cunning you are? If the Second Mistress were the least bit less capable, you ladies would have brought her down long ago. Even as it is, the moment you get an opening you try to make things difficult for her. More than once you’ve had things to say at her expense. Everyone says she’s formidable and you’re all afraid of her. Only I know that in her heart she’s not exactly unafraid of you.

segments.text: Ripple turned, saw Patience and laughed.
‘What are you doing here, mounting an outer guard?’
She came back and sat on Patience’s cushion.
‘What have you come about?’ Patience asked quietly.
‘To ask when we can draw Bao-yu’s monthly allowance and our own.’

‘That’s no great matter. Go straight back and tell Aroma from me not to bring any business here today, whatever it is. Bring one request, and it will be refused. Bring a hundred, and all hundred will be refused.’
‘Why? What’s happened?’ Ripple asked hastily.
Patience and the women all hurried to tell her the reason.

‘They’re looking for some difficult business and someone with standing to make an example of, to overawe everyone else and show them how things are to be done. Why should you be the first to run up against it? If you go in now and they make examples of you, they’ll have the old lady and Her Ladyship to consider. But if they don’t, people will say they favour one over another: that they’re frightened of anyone with the old lady and Her Ladyship behind them and daren’t touch them, but only take the pliable ones by the nose.

segments.text: Bao-chai’s meal arrived next, and Patience hurried in to wait on them. Aunt Zhao had gone by then. The three were eating on the wooden couch, Bao-chai facing south, Tan-chun west and Li Wan east. The women waited quietly under the verandah. Inside, only the maids who were their close personal attendants served them; no one else dared go in unbidden.
‘Let’s all save ourselves trouble,’ the women whispered to one another. ‘No more underhand schemes. Even Mrs Wu has just had a rebuff. What standing have the rest of us?’

They talked quietly as they waited for the meal to end so that they could report. Inside, not a sound could be heard, not even a bowl or chopstick. Presently one maid lifted the curtain high and two others carried out the table. Three girls had been waiting in the tea-room with three basins of water. As soon as the table was out, they went in, and shortly came back with the basins and rinsing-bowls. Only then did Scribe, Su-yun and Oriole enter, each carrying a tea-tray with three covered bowls of tea.

segments.text: Xi-feng asked why she had been away all day. Smiling, Patience told her everything that had happened.
‘Good, good, good!’ Xi-feng laughed. ‘Well done, Third Miss! Didn’t I say she was good? It’s only a pity her luck was poor and she wasn’t born of Her Ladyship.’
‘Now you’re talking foolishly too, ma’am,’ Patience said with a smile. ‘Even if Her Ladyship didn’t bear her, would anyone dare look down on her or treat her differently from the others?’

‘You don’t understand,’ Xi-feng sighed. ‘A son and a daughter may both be born of a concubine, but a girl isn’t in the same position as a man. When it comes to arranging a marriage, there are frivolous people nowadays whose very first question is whether the girl was born of the principal wife or of a concubine. Many won’t have one born of a concubine. Little do they realise that, never mind a concubine’s daughter, even our maids are better than other people’s young ladies. I wonder what unlucky fool will lose his chance by choosing between the two, and what fortunate man who makes no such distinction will win her.’
Then she turned to Patience with a smile.
‘You know how many ways I’ve devised to economise in these past few years. I doubt there’s anyone in the whole household who doesn’t hate me behind my back.

segments.text: ‘I’m riding a tiger now. I may see through a few things, but I can’t simply let up all at once. Besides, more goes out of this household than comes in. Everything, great and small, is still done according to the rules followed when the old lady was in charge, but the income from the estates is no longer what it was. Economise too much, and outsiders laugh at us, the old lady and Her Ladyship have to put up with privations, and the servants complain that we’re mean. But unless we arrange to cut expenses soon, in a few years we shall have used up everything.’
‘That’s just it,’ said Patience. ‘There are still three or four young ladies, two or three young masters, and the old lady. Those great expenses are all ahead of us.’

‘I’ve thought of that too,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘There should be enough. When Bao-yu takes a wife and Cousin Lin marries, neither need draw on the household funds. The old lady has private savings to provide for them. The Second Miss belongs to the Elder Master’s side, so she doesn’t count either. That leaves three or four. Allow ten thousand taels apiece, even at the most extravagant reckoning.

segments.text: ‘Huan’s wedding won’t cost much. Three thousand taels will do; a little saving somewhere or other would cover it. When the old lady’s time comes, all the main things are ready. There will only be odds and ends to pay for, three to five thousand taels at the outside. With a little more economy now, we can make it up by degrees. What worries me is some unexpected business cropping up, a thing or two out of nowhere. That would be disastrous. But leave the future for now. Eat your meal and hurry back to hear what she wants to discuss. This is just the opportunity I need. I’ve been fretting for want of a right arm. There’s Bao-yu, but he isn’t made for this sort of thing. Even if I won him over, he’d be no use. Mrs Zhu is a living Buddha, and no use either. The Second Miss is still less use, and doesn’t belong to this branch of the family in any case. The Fourth Miss is young, and little Lan younger still. As for Huan, he’s a half-frozen kitten with singed fur, only waiting for a hot stove or fire-pit to crawl into. To think that two such utterly different creatures came out of the same mother’s belly! I can’t reconcile myself to it when I think of that.

segments.text: ‘Then there are Cousin Lin and Cousin Bao. They’re both capable, but unfortunately they’re relations staying with us, and one can hardly ask them to manage our household. Besides, one is a paper beauty-lantern that a breath of wind would spoil; the other has made up her mind: “If it’s no affair of mine, I won’t open my mouth. Ask me, and I’ll shake my head and know nothing.” One can hardly press her too far. That leaves only the Third Miss. She has both the brains and the tongue for it, she’s a proper member of our own family, and Her Ladyship is fond of her. The coolness on the surface is all because of that old creature Aunt Zhao and the trouble she makes. In her heart, Her Ladyship feels for her just as she does for Bao-yu. She’s not like Huan, whom it’s truly hard to be fond of. Left to me, he’d have been thrown out long ago. Now that she has ideas of this sort, we ought to work with her and give each other a hand. I shan’t be on my own any more. In all fairness, before Heaven and our own consciences, having someone like her to help will save us some worry and benefit Her Ladyship’s affairs too. And if you look at it from the side of self-interest and scheming, I’ve been too ruthless. It’s time I drew back a little.

segments.text: ‘We should look back a little. If we keep pursuing and squeezing them until they hate us bitterly, they’ll hide knives behind their smiles. Between the two of us, we have only four eyes and two minds. One unguarded moment, and we may come to grief. Let her come forward and take charge while the pressure is on, and people’s old hatred of us will ease for a time. There’s something else. I know how sensible you are, but I’m afraid you may not quite bring yourself round to it, so I’m telling you now. She may be a girl, but she understands every last thing. She’s simply careful what she says. And she knows more of books and writing than I do, which makes her more formidable still. As the saying goes, “To catch the bandits, first catch their chief.” If she means to make a start and set an example, she’s bound to start with me. If she overrules any arrangement of mine, don’t argue. The more respectful you are, and the more you say she’s right to overrule it, the better. Whatever you do, don’t be afraid I’ll lose face and start opposing her. That would spoil everything.’
Before she had finished, Patience laughed.
‘You really do take people for fools. I’ve already done all that, and now you tell me!’
‘I was afraid you had eyes and thoughts for no one but me,’ Xi-feng said with a laugh. ‘That’s why I had to warn you.

‘And I shall say “you”! If you don’t like it, here’s my face. Give it another beating. It’s not as though these cheeks haven’t tasted one before!’

‘You little baggage!’ Xi-feng laughed. ‘How many times are you going to rake that up? You see how ill I am, and still come to provoke me. Come and sit down. No one’s coming, anyway. Let’s get on with eating together.’

segments.text: As she spoke, Felicity came in with two or three other little maids to set up the small kang table. Xi-feng ate only bird’s-nest congee and two small dishes of delicacies; her regular daily dishes had been stopped for the time being. Felicity put Patience’s four regular dishes on the table and served her rice. With one knee bent on the edge of the kang, Patience remained half standing below it as she ate with Xi-feng, then helped her rinse her mouth and wash. When that was done, she gave Felicity a few instructions and went back to Tan-chun. The courtyard was quiet; everyone had dispersed.

‘What I have in mind is simply this,’ she began. ‘Each of us has two taels a month, quite apart from the maids’ monthly allowances.

segments.text: ‘Then someone came the other day to report that our hair oil, rouge and powder cost another two taels a month for each of us. It’s just like those eight taels for the school we were discussing: one allowance on top of another. The matter is small and the money isn’t much, but it still doesn’t seem right. How is it that your mistress never thought of this?’

‘There’s a reason for that, miss,’ Patience answered with a smile. ‘Naturally, the young ladies are entitled to a regular supply of these things. The purchasing steward buys them each month and sends women round to the different apartments to hand them over to us for safekeeping, ready for the young ladies to use. We can hardly each be going about every day with money in our hands, looking for someone to buy hair oil one moment and rouge and powder the next. So the purchasing steward outside draws the whole sum and has the things delivered to us in our different rooms every month.

But I’ve been quietly watching, and a good half of the girls in the different apartments do pay cash for them. I began to wonder whether the purchasing steward was failing to supply them, or supplying them late, or buying rubbish and fobbing us off with things we couldn’t use.’

‘So you’ve noticed it too!’ Tan-chun and Li Wan said, laughing. ‘They don’t fail to supply them. They wouldn’t dare. We use those two taels and have someone’s nurse’s son, or a brother’s son, buy us something fit to use. If we send the household staff, we only get the same thing again.

segments.text: ‘That’s one thing. Then there’s another. You went with us to Lai Da’s before the New Year. How did their little garden compare with ours?’

segments.text: ‘Master Zhu, all fanciful comparisons and fine phrases? Every word of it is true. You’ve had two days’ experience of practical affairs, and already the fumes of profit have gone to your head. Even Master Zhu seems empty and fanciful to you! Wait till you go out and see what there is to be gained and lost in great affairs. You’ll think Confucius emptier still!’

‘Someone as learned as you,’ Tan-chun said, laughing, ‘and you’ve never read the philosophers? Doesn’t the Jizi say, “Those who enter the arena of profit and advancement and move in the sphere of calculation steal the words of Yao and Shun, yet turn their backs on the way of Confucius and Mencius”?’
‘And the next sentence?’ Bao-chai asked with a smile.
‘I’m only quoting the part that suits me. If I recited the next sentence, wouldn’t I be abusing myself?’

‘Nothing in the world is without a use,’ said Bao-chai. ‘And if it has a use, it is worth money. To think that someone as clever as you has never had any experience of these important practical matters! It’s a pity you’ve come to them so late.’
‘You sent for her to discuss business,’ Li Wan said with a laugh, ‘and now you’ve left the business alone and started exchanging learned arguments.’
‘But there’s business in learning,’ said Bao-chai.

segments.text: ‘Apply a little learning to a small affair and you raise it to a higher level. Without learning to lift it, it all sinks into vulgar money-grubbing.’
The three of them were only teasing. After talking and laughing for a while, they returned to their business.
Tan-chun went on:

‘Suppose our garden is only half as large again as theirs. Reckon twice the return, and that gives four hundred taels a year. Of course, to turn it over to someone simply to make money would be petty. That isn’t what a family like ours does. But we could appoint a couple of people to take definite charge of it. With so much of value there, to let everyone go on spoiling it seems a waste of Heaven’s gifts. Why not choose a few of the older women already in the Garden, honest, steady women who know something about gardening, and give them definite charge of its upkeep? We needn’t ask them for rent or taxes. We’d only ask what they could offer us each year.

‘First, there would be people expressly responsible for the Garden. The trees and flowers would improve from year to year, and there would be no need to rush about whenever something had to be done. Second, things wouldn’t be spoilt and their usefulness wasted. Third, the old women could make a little extra for themselves, so that all their year’s hard work here wouldn’t be for nothing. Fourth, we could save the wages of the gardeners, rockery men, sweepers and the rest.

segments.text: ‘Her Ladyship will certainly be pleased if we carry it out. Saving money is the least of it. The chief thing is to have people to keep the place in order, with definite duties, and permission to sell what it produces. Give them authority, make it worth their while, and they’re bound to do their work.’

‘It needed you to propose this, miss,’ said Patience. ‘Even if my mistress had it in mind, she could hardly have brought herself to say it. The young ladies are living in the Garden. Instead of finding more pretty things for them to enjoy, she would be putting people in to supervise it and keep it up, simply to save money. She could never have said that.’
Bao-chai came quickly over, stroked her cheek and laughed.

‘Open your mouth. Let me see what those teeth and that tongue are made of! Ever since this morning, you’ve had a fresh answer for everything. You haven’t flattered the Third Miss, but you haven’t suggested that your mistress lacked the wit to think of any of this, either. Nor have you simply said yes to everything the Third Miss said. Whatever she brings forward, you have an answer ready. Anything she has thought of, your mistress has thought of too. Only there’s always some reason why it couldn’t be done.

segments.text: ‘Now it’s that the young ladies live in the Garden, so it wouldn’t do to put people in charge just to save money. Think what that means. If the Garden really were handed over to someone to make money from, naturally they wouldn’t let anyone pick a single flower or touch a single fruit. They wouldn’t dare interfere with the young ladies’ share, of course, but there would be endless quarrels with the little maids. She thinks of troubles near and far, without either presumption or servility. Even if her mistress weren’t on good terms with us, hearing all that would shame her into being kinder. It would turn ill feeling into friendship.’

‘I was furious this morning,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘When I heard she’d come, I suddenly thought of her mistress and the people she usually sends to deal with things, so ready to throw their weight about. The sight of Patience was enough to make me angry. But there she stood for ages, like a mouse hiding from a cat. I felt sorry for her. Then came all those things she said. Not how well her mistress had treated me, but “It will be a fitting expression of the kindness you’ve always shown my mistress.” That one sentence took all my anger away. I felt ashamed instead, and then I felt hurt.

segments.text: ‘When I thought about it, I’m only a girl who’s managed to leave herself with no one to love or look after her. What kindness have I to offer anyone else?’

As she said it, tears began to fall again. Li Wan and the others were moved by her earnestness. They thought, too, of the slights Aunt Zhao was always casting on her and of how Aunt Zhao had damaged her standing with Lady Wang. They could not help shedding tears themselves, and hurried to comfort her.

‘We’ve a quiet day today. Let’s settle a couple of things that will bring some benefit and put an end to abuses. Then Her Ladyship won’t have trusted us for nothing. Why bring up these unhappy matters again?’
‘I understand it all now,’ Patience said quickly. ‘You need only say who you think suitable, miss. Appoint them, and it’s done.’

‘Even so, we must tell your mistress first,’ said Tan-chun. ‘It’s hardly proper for us to be picking over the little things she’s overlooked. I only do it because she’s a sensible person. If she were muddle-headed, suspicious and jealous, I wouldn’t. It would look as though I were trying to catch her out. How could we go ahead without consulting her?’
‘In that case, I’ll go and tell her,’ Patience said with a smile.
She went away and was some time returning.
‘I said it would be a wasted journey,’ she told them, laughing. ‘How could my mistress possibly object to anything so good?’

segments.text: Presently the women came back to report that the doctor had gone, and handed up the prescription. The three ladies looked it over. After supplying the household’s regular requirements for each of the four seasons, they could gather what remained and make what they could from it. The accounts would be settled at the end of the year.

‘Something else has just occurred to me,’ Tan-chun said, smiling. ‘If you settle the accounts and hand in the money at the end of the year, naturally it will go to the accounts office. That puts another set of masters over you. You’re in their hands again, with another skin to be stripped off you. By starting this arrangement and appointing you ourselves, we’ve already gone over their heads. They’re angry, even if they can’t say so. What will they do when you come to settle up at the end of the year, if not make you suffer for it? Besides, whatever they manage during the year, for every full share the master has, they take half a share. That’s an old custom of this household, known to everyone. Whatever they take secretly is over and above it.

segments.text: ‘There would still be something left over, but after working hard for a whole year, they ought to have something to spare to help their own families. Increasing income and cutting expenses may be the guiding principle, but we mustn’t be too miserly. Even if you saved another two or three hundred taels, it wouldn’t do if you lost the dignity proper to the household. This way, the accounts office outside would have four or five hundred taels less to pay out each year, without feeling that any severe economies were being made. The women inside would get a little extra too. These old women who have no other means of earning would be better off, the Garden’s trees and flowers would flourish more each year, and you would have the things you need. That should preserve the dignity of the whole arrangement. If saving money were all you wanted, you could scrape together a few cash almost anywhere. segments.text: ‘Otherwise I’ve no business interfering. You all heard my aunt ask me, several times over, to keep an eye on things. Mrs Zhu is busy now, she said, and the other young ladies are still too young. If I refused, I’d only be making my aunt worry. Your mistress has so much illness to contend with, and all the household affairs to attend to as well. I’m an idle person. I ought to help even if we were only neighbours, let alone when my own aunt has asked me. I must put the lesser considerations aside for the greater ones. I can’t afford to worry about people resenting me. Suppose I were to think only of those little personal scruples and win a reputation for being agreeable, and then drunkenness and gambling led to trouble. How could I face my aunt? It would be too late for you to be sorry then. Even the respect you’ve earned with your years would be gone.

segments.text: ‘All these young ladies, and this great Garden, are left in your care because you come of families that have served here for three or four generations and are thought the most reliable in observing our rules. You ought to work together and preserve some proper order. Instead you let others drink and gamble as they please. If my aunt hears of it and gives you a scolding, that’s one thing. But suppose those managing housekeepers hear of it. They needn’t even report to my aunt. They can give you a dressing-down themselves. At your age, to be scolded by women younger than you! They may be housekeepers and entitled to direct you, but wouldn’t it be better to keep your own dignity? Then how could they find a chance to humiliate you?

‘That’s why I’ve thought of this way for you to make something extra: so that you’ll all work together to keep this Garden in the most careful order. When those who hold authority see how strictly and attentively it is managed, without their having to worry about it, surely they’ll feel respect for you. Then my efforts to increase your earnings won’t have been wasted. If we can take the power out of their hands and bring profit to yours, surely we can also govern without meddling and take some of their cares away.

segments.text: They were still speaking when Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife came in.

‘The ladies of the Zhen household in Jiangnan arrived in the capital yesterday,’ she reported. ‘They’ve gone to the palace today to pay their respects. Meanwhile they’ve sent people ahead with presents and enquiries after your health.’
She handed up the list of gifts. Tan-chun took it and read:

‘For imperial use, figured satin and satin with python designs, twelve bolts; for imperial use, satin in assorted colours, twelve bolts; for imperial use, gauze in various colours, twelve bolts; for imperial use, palace silk, twelve bolts; for official use, satin, gauze, silk and damask in various colours, twenty-four bolts.’
Li Wan read it too.
‘Reward the bearers with the first-class gratuity packets,’ she said, and sent word to Grandmother Jia.
Grandmother Jia summoned Li Wan, Tan-chun, Bao-chai and the others to her rooms, where they inspected the gifts. Li Wan received them, but told the women in charge of the inner storerooms:
‘Wait till Her Ladyship has come back and seen them before you put them away.’

‘The Zhens aren’t like other families,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Give the men first-class gratuity packets. I expect they’ll be sending women over to enquire after us at any moment. Have some dress lengths ready.’
Before she had finished, someone announced that four women from the Zhen household had come to pay their respects. Grandmother Jia at once had them shown in.

segments.text: ‘It’s years since you came to the capital,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘I hadn’t expected to see you this year.’
‘Indeed, ma’am,’ they answered, smiling too. ‘This year we were commanded to come by His Majesty.’
‘Has the whole family come?’
‘No, ma’am. Our old lady, the young master, two of the young ladies and the other married ladies have all stayed behind. Only our mistress and the Third Miss have come.’
‘Is she promised to anyone?’
‘Not yet, ma’am.’
‘Both the families your eldest and second young ladies married into are very friendly with ours,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile.
‘Yes, ma’am. Every year, when they write home, they tell us how much they owe to your care.’

‘Care! Our families have been friends for generations, and we’re old relations too. It’s only what’s right. Your second young lady is particularly good. She has no airs about her, and that’s why we see so much of one another.’
‘Your Old Ladyship is too modest,’ the women replied, smiling.
‘And your young master, does he live with your old lady too?’
‘Yes, ma’am. He lives with her too.’
‘How old is he? Has he begun school?’
‘Thirteen this year,’ they said, smiling.

‘There have always been plenty of people with the same name, whether they lived at the same time or generations apart.’
The four women smiled too.

‘After that pet name was chosen, everyone in our household, high and low, had a feeling that someone among our relations or friends had a child with the same name. But it’s ten years or more since we came to the capital, and we couldn’t quite remember.’
‘You honour him,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘It’s my grandson. Someone come here.’
The women and maids answered and stepped forward.
‘Go to the Garden and fetch our Bao-yu. Let these four housekeepers see him and tell us how he compares with theirs.’

segments.text: ‘Ours does nothing but call us stupid. Take his hands! He won’t even let us so much as touch his things. He has only young girls to wait on him.’
Before they had finished, Li Wan and the others burst out laughing. Grandmother Jia laughed too.

‘If we sent people to see your Bao-yu now, and they took his hands, he’d put up with it for a little while too, however reluctantly. Children in families like yours and ours may have all sorts of perverse, outlandish ways, but in front of outsiders they must show the proper manners. If they didn’t, they certainly wouldn’t be allowed their whims. When their elders spoil them, it’s partly because they’re pleasing to look at, but also because they can observe the forms in company every bit as correctly as grown people. They make everyone fond of them, and so they’re indulged a little in private. If a child had no idea how to behave either at home or abroad, and did nothing to make his elders proud, he might be as handsome as you please: he’d deserve to be beaten to death.’
‘Your Old Ladyship is quite right,’ the four women replied, smiling.

segments.text: ‘Naughty and odd as our Bao-yu is, when he meets guests he can be more punctilious and well-mannered than the grown-ups. Everyone who sees him loves him and wonders why anyone should ever beat him. They have no idea how impossible he is at home. He says things his elders would never dream of saying and insists on doing things they’d never think of doing. The master and mistress are exasperated with him and don’t know what to do. Fits of temper are only natural in a child. Spending money recklessly is only natural in a young gentleman. Being afraid of school is natural in a child too. Those things can all be dealt with. But what can one do about this perverse, outlandish disposition he was born with?’
Before they had finished, someone announced that Lady Wang had returned. She came in and paid her respects to Grandmother Jia.

segments.text: Grandmother Jia was so delighted that she told everyone she met about this other Bao-yu, with ways just like their own. The others thought that in so large a world, with so many families of hereditary office-holders, there must be plenty of people with the same name. Grandmothers had always spoilt their grandsons. There was nothing extraordinary in any of it, and they gave it no further thought. Bao-yu alone, being an impractical young simpleton, decided that the four women had merely been saying what would please his grandmother.
Later, when he visited Xiang-yun at Allspice Court, where she lay ill, she said:

‘Now you can make all the trouble you please. Before, it was “One filament makes no thread, one tree makes no forest.” But now you have a partner. When you’ve made enough trouble and been beaten hard enough, you can run away to Nanjing and find the other one.’
‘You believe those lies too?’ Bao-yu said. ‘As though there just happened to be another Bao-yu!’
‘Why was there a Lin Xiang-ru in the Warring States, then, and a Sima Xiang-ru in the Han dynasty?’
‘Very well,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘But the same looks as well? That’s impossible.’
‘Why did the people of Kuang take Confucius for Yang Hu?’
‘Confucius and Yang Hu looked alike, but they had different names. Lin and Sima had the same name, but they didn’t look alike. Must this boy and I have both?’
Xiang-yun could find no answer, and laughed.
‘You only know how to twist things. I shan’t argue with you.

segments.text: ‘Whether there is such a boy or not is no concern of mine.’

She lay down, leaving Bao-yu uncertain again. Say there couldn’t be such a boy, and yet there seemed to be. Say there must be, and yet he had never seen him. Troubled, he went back to his rooms and lay on the couch, turning it over silently in his mind. Before he knew it he had drifted off to sleep, and found himself in a garden.
‘Can there be another garden besides our Prospect Garden?’ he wondered.
While he was puzzling over this, a group of girls came towards him. They were all maids.
‘And can there be girls like these besides Faithful, Aroma and Patience?’ he wondered again.
‘What’s Bao-yu doing here?’ he heard them say with a laugh.
Thinking they meant him, he hurried up with a smile.
‘I happened to stray this way. I don’t know which of our family friends this garden belongs to. Dear sisters, do show me round.’
‘Why, he isn’t our Bao-yu!’ the maids said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘He’s quite nice-looking, though, and he’s got a ready little tongue.’
Bao-yu quickly asked:
‘Sisters, is there another Bao-yu here too?’

‘When we say “Bao-yu”,’ the maids retorted, ‘it’s on the old lady’s and Her Ladyship’s orders, to bring him long life and keep misfortune away. He likes to hear us call him that. What stinking little servant-boy are you, from goodness knows where, to go calling him by his name? Mind that filthy hide of yours! We’ll beat it to a pulp.’
‘Come on,’ another maid said, laughing. ‘If Bao-yu sees us, he’ll say we’ve made ourselves stink by talking to this smelly little boy.’
They went straight off.

Thinking this, he wandered on and soon found himself in a courtyard.
‘Another courtyard like this, besides the House of Green Delights!’
Up the steps he went and into the room. Someone was lying on a couch. Beyond it, several girls were doing needlework, while others laughed and played.

segments.text: The boy on the couch said:

‘I heard Grandmother say there was another Bao-yu in the capital, Chang’an, with a disposition just like mine. I couldn’t believe it. Just now I had a dream. I went into a garden in the capital and met some girls, but they all called me a stinking little servant-boy and wouldn’t have anything to do with me. At last I found his room, but he was asleep. Only his bodily shell was there. Where his true self had gone, I couldn’t tell.’
‘I came here looking for Bao-yu,’ Bao-yu said at once. ‘So you’re Bao-yu?’
The boy on the couch scrambled down and caught hold of him.
‘So you’re Bao-yu! This isn’t a dream, then.’
‘How could it be a dream?’ said Bao-yu. ‘It’s real, quite real.’
Before he had finished, someone came in to say:
‘The master wants Bao-yu.’
Both boys took fright. One Bao-yu hurried away, and the other called after him:
‘Bao-yu, come back! Come back!’

segments.text: Aroma, beside him, heard him calling his own name in his sleep and hurried to shake him awake.
‘Where’s Bao-yu?’ she asked with a smile.
He was awake now, but still dazed. He pointed towards the door.
‘He’s just gone out.’
‘You’re still muddled by your dream,’ Aroma said, laughing. ‘Rub your eyes and look properly. That’s your own reflection in the mirror.’

Bao-yu looked in front of him. There, facing him, was the large fitted mirror, reflecting his image. He laughed too. Someone had already brought a rinsing bowl and strong tea, and he rinsed his mouth.

‘No wonder the old lady is always telling us not to have too many mirrors in children’s rooms,’ said Musk. ‘A child’s soul isn’t fully formed. Too much looking in mirrors frightens them in their sleep and gives them wild dreams. And now we’ve put a bed right by that great mirror. It’s all right when we lower the mirror cover. But before long it’ll be hot, and he may doze off at any time. Who’ll remember to let it down? Just now we forgot. Of course he lay there playing with his reflection first, and when his eyes closed, it turned into a topsy-turvy dream. How else could he see himself and call his own name?

segments.text: Now when Bao-yu heard that Lady Wang had sent for him, he hurried to the front of the house. She wanted to take him to call on Lady Zhen. Delighted, he changed his clothes at once and went with her. The appearance and circumstances of the Zhen household differed little from those of the Rong and Ning mansions; in one or two respects they were rather grander. He made careful inquiries, and there was indeed a Bao-yu. Lady Zhen kept them to a meal, and they did not return until the day was over. Only then was Bao-yu convinced. Back at home that evening, Lady Wang ordered a first-rate banquet and engaged a celebrated troupe to perform a full play, inviting Lady Zhen and her daughter. Two days later the mother and daughter left without a further farewell to return to the family’s official posting. Of this we need say no more.

segments.text: ‘So you’ve taken to invoking Buddha too!’ Nightingale laughed. ‘That is something new.’
‘As they say, “A desperate patient will try any doctor,”’ Bao-yu replied with a laugh.
As he spoke, he noticed that she had on a thinly padded jacket of ink-splashed silk damask, with only a lined blue satin waistcoat over it. He reached out and felt her clothes.
‘You’re wearing so little, and sitting right in a draught. The wind has a bite to it, and there’s sickness about. If you fall ill too, that will make things worse.’

‘From now on we may talk, but keep your hands to yourself,’ said Nightingale. ‘We’re growing older, not younger. It looks improper if people see us. Those wretched creatures say quite enough about you behind your back, but you never take any notice. You go on just as you did when you were little. How can that do? Miss Lin is always telling us not to laugh and joke with you. Haven’t you noticed how she keeps her distance from you lately? She’s afraid she can’t keep far enough away.’
She rose as she spoke and carried her sewing into another room.

segments.text: Bao-yu felt as though a basin of cold water had been poured over his heart. He stared at the bamboos for a while, quite stupefied. Then Mamma Zhu came to dig up shoots and tend the bamboo stems, and he wandered out in a daze. His wits had deserted him; he scarcely knew anything. He sat down at random on a rock and gazed into space, tears falling before he knew it. He remained there long enough for five or six meals, turning a thousand thoughts over in his mind without knowing what he could do.

Snowgoose happened to pass that way on her return from fetching ginseng from Lady Wang’s rooms. Turning her head, she saw someone sitting on a rock beneath the peach blossom, his cheek propped on his hand as he stared before him. It was Bao-yu.
‘It’s so cold,’ she thought in bewilderment. ‘What is he doing here all alone? People with old complaints always have them come back in spring. Perhaps he’s having another fit of silliness.’

segments.text: As she spoke, someone announced that Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife and Shan Da-liang’s wife had come to see the young master.
‘How thoughtful of them,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Let them come and see him.’
At the sound of the name Lin, Bao-yu began thrashing about on the bed.
‘This is terrible! The Lins have come to fetch them. Drive them out at once!’
‘Drive them out!’ Grandmother Jia said hastily. Then she tried to comfort him. ‘They aren’t from the Lin family. The Lin family are all dead. There’s no one to come and fetch her. You needn’t worry.’
‘I don’t care who they are!’ Bao-yu cried. ‘No one is allowed to be called Lin except Cousin Lin!’
‘No one called Lin has come. I’ve driven everyone called Lin away.’

segments.text: As she spoke, she ordered the others, ‘Don’t let Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife into the Garden again. And none of you is to say the word “Lin”. Be good children and do as I say!’

They all hastened to agree, not daring to laugh. Then Bao-yu caught sight of a Western gold mechanical boat on the curio shelves. He pointed to it and cried wildly, ‘There’s the boat that’s come to fetch them! It’s moored over there!’
Grandmother Jia told them to take it down at once. Aroma hurried to do so. Bao-yu held out his hand for it, and she passed it to him. He tucked it under the quilt.
‘Now they can’t go!’ he said with a smile.

segments.text: ‘Just tell me whether it’s dangerous,’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘Who wants to recite medical books with you?’
Doctor Wang bent forward at once and smiled.
‘No danger, ma’am. No danger.’
‘Are you quite sure?’
‘Quite sure. I will answer for it myself.’

‘In that case, please go and sit outside and write a prescription. If he gets well after taking it, I’ll prepare a handsome extra fee and have him bring it to you himself and kowtow. If you let him come to harm, I’ll send men to pull down the hall of the Imperial Medical Academy.’

‘You are too kind, ma’am, too kind,’ said Doctor Wang, bowing and smiling. He had heard the promise of a handsome extra fee, to be delivered by Bao-yu with a kowtow, and was still protesting that he did not deserve such an honour. He had quite missed her subsequent joke about pulling down the Imperial Medical Academy, and was still saying, ‘Too kind.’ Grandmother Jia and the others began to laugh instead.

Soon the medicine was prepared according to his prescription and given to Bao-yu. He did indeed seem calmer than before. But nothing would make him release Nightingale. If she left, he said, it would mean she was going back to Suzhou.

segments.text: By evening Bao-yu was a little easier, and only then did Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang and the others return to their rooms. Several times that night they still sent to ask after him. Nurse Li led Nurse Song and several other elderly attendants in keeping careful watch, while Nightingale, Aroma and Skybright stayed beside him night and day. Sometimes when he fell asleep he would wake in terror, crying that Dai-yu had gone, or that someone had come to fetch her. Each time Nightingale had to soothe him before he would settle. Grandmother Jia also ordered various secret preparations from the imperial pharmacy, including Pills to Expel Evil and Guard the Spirit and Powder to Open the Apertures and Free the Spirit, to be given as directed. The next day he took Doctor Wang’s medicine again and gradually improved.

Bao-yu now understood what had happened. Afraid that Nightingale would go back, he sometimes pretended to be distraught. Nightingale had deeply regretted her actions from that first day, and did not resent the hard work of tending him day and night. Aroma and the others were at ease again.
‘You caused it all,’ they told her with a laugh, ‘and you’ve had to cure it. Did you ever see anyone like our idiot? He hears the wind and thinks it’s raining. What’s to become of him?’
Let us leave them there for the moment.

segments.text: ‘Engaged to whom?’
‘Before the New Year I heard Her Old Ladyship say she wanted to settle a match with Miss Bao-qin,’ Nightingale said with a smile. ‘Why else would she be so fond of her?’

‘Everyone calls me a fool, but you’re a bigger fool than I am,’ Bao-yu said with a laugh. ‘It was only a joke. She’s already promised to Academician Mei’s family. If I really were engaged to her, would you find me like this? When I swore those oaths and tried to smash this wretched thing before, didn’t you try to stop me and say I was mad? I’ve only just got better, and you start provoking me again.’
He ground his teeth as he spoke.

‘I wish I could die this very instant and burst my heart open for you all to see. Then let all of me, skin and bones, turn to ash. No, ash still leaves a trace. Better to turn into smoke. But smoke can gather and still be seen. It would have to be scattered in every direction at once by a great wild wind. Only then would it be right!’
Tears rolled down his face again.

segments.text: The reports of Bao-yu’s condition over the past few days had made Dai-yu still more unwell and set her weeping several times. Now that Nightingale had returned, she asked what had happened. Learning that he was much better, she sent Amber back to attend Grandmother Jia.

That night, when everyone was quiet and Nightingale had undressed and lain down, she said softly to Dai-yu, with a smile, ‘Bao-yu does have a true heart. Only hearing we were going away was enough to put him in that state.’
Dai-yu said nothing. After a long pause, Nightingale went on, as though talking to herself.

‘Better to stay still than to make a move. This is a good enough family. Everything else is easily found, but to have grown up together from childhood, each knowing the other’s temper and ways, that’s the rare thing.’
‘Pah!’ said Dai-yu. ‘Haven’t these last few days worn you out? Why not rest while you can, instead of chewing over such filthy nonsense?’

‘It isn’t idle nonsense,’ Nightingale said with a smile. ‘I’m speaking out of real concern for you. I’ve worried about you for years. With no parents and no brothers, who is there to care whether you’re warm or cold? The important thing is to settle your marriage while Her Old Ladyship is still clear-headed and strong.

segments.text: ‘As the saying goes, “Vigour in old age is like a spring chill or autumn heat.” If anything should happen to Her Old Ladyship, your marriage would still be arranged, but precious time might have been lost, and you might not get what you wanted. There are plenty of noblemen’s sons and grandsons of princes, but which of them doesn’t have three wives and five concubines, looking east today and west tomorrow? Even a heavenly beauty would be forgotten after three or five nights. Some turn against their wives over a concubine or a maid until they’re enemies. It’s a little better if a girl has people with influence in her own family. But for someone in your position, each day Her Old Ladyship is here is a day of protection. Without her, you’d be at their mercy. That’s why it matters to make up your mind. You’re a sensible girl. Haven’t you heard the saying, “Ten thousand taels of gold are easily found; one understanding heart is hard to come by”?’
‘Has this girl gone mad today?’ said Dai-yu.

segments.text: ‘She’s only been away a few days, and suddenly she’s a different person. Tomorrow I shall tell Her Old Ladyship to take you back. I daren’t keep you any longer.’

‘What I’m saying is for your good,’ Nightingale replied with a smile. ‘I’m only asking you to bear it in mind, not to do anything wrong. Why tell Her Old Ladyship and get me into trouble? What good would that do?’

With that she went to sleep. For all Dai-yu’s words, what she had heard had grieved her deeply. Once Nightingale was asleep, she wept the whole night, only dozing off towards daybreak. The next day she forced herself to wash and rinse her mouth and took a little bird’s-nest congee. Grandmother Jia and the others then came in person to see her and gave her a great many instructions.

The following day the Xue household had Xue Ke entertain the business staff to a whole day’s drinking. The bustle lasted three or four days before everything was over.

segments.text: While she was hesitating, she suddenly remembered that Xue Ke was unmarried. The two of them seemed a couple made by Heaven and Earth, and she discussed it with Xi-feng.
‘You know how contrary my mother-in-law can be, Aunt,’ Xi-feng said with a sigh. ‘Let me work out a way to approach her.’
When Grandmother Jia came to see her, Xi-feng said, ‘Aunt Xue has a favour to ask of you, Grannie, but she’s rather shy of mentioning it.’
Grandmother Jia asked at once what it was, and Xi-feng explained the proposed marriage.
‘Why should she be shy about that?’ Grandmother Jia said with a laugh. ‘It’s an excellent idea. I’ll speak to your mother-in-law. She can hardly refuse me.’
On returning to her rooms, she immediately sent for Lady Xing and insisted on acting as matchmaker.

segments.text: Lady Xing thought it over. The Xues came of a good family and were very rich at present; Xue Ke was a handsome young man, and Grandmother Jia was determined to arrange the match. She might as well turn the proposal to her own advantage, and agreed. Grandmother Jia was delighted and sent for Aunt Xue at once. When the two women met, there was naturally a great deal of polite self-deprecation on both sides. Lady Xing immediately sent word to Xing Zhong and his wife. They had come there to depend on her. How could they refuse? They were already declaring that nothing could be better.
‘I do love meddling in other people’s affairs,’ Grandmother Jia said with a laugh. ‘There, I've settled another matter. I wonder how much I'll get in matchmaker's fees.’

‘Of course you must have your fee,’ Aunt Xue answered, laughing. ‘Though if we carried in a hundred thousand taels of silver, I doubt you’d care for it. There’s only one thing: since you are the chief sponsor of the marriage, we ought to have someone else as well.’
‘We may be short of other things,’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing, ‘but our household can still produce a couple of good-for-nothings with useless hands and feet.’
She sent for You-shi and her daughter-in-law. When Grandmother Jia explained the matter, everyone hastened to offer congratulations.

segments.text: ‘You know all our family’s customs,’ Grandmother Jia told You-shi. ‘We never have two sets of in-laws quarrelling over gifts and precedence. You are to act for me in settling things between them. Be neither too stingy nor too extravagant. See that both families are properly provided for, and report back to me.’

You-shi promptly agreed. Aunt Xue was overjoyed. As soon as she returned home, she had a formal invitation written and sent after them to the Ning mansion. You-shi knew Lady Xing’s temper very well and had not wanted to take the business on, but with Grandmother Jia giving her the charge in person she could only accept. She would have to feel her way and act according to Lady Xing’s wishes. Aunt Xue, who would agree to almost anything, would be easier to deal with. Let us leave that for now.

Only then did Lady Xing give up the idea.

segments.text: Xue Ke and Xiu-yan had seen each other once on their earlier journey, and in all probability both were pleased with the match. Xiu-yan was rather more constrained than before, however, and found it awkward to sit and chat with Bao-chai and the other girls. Xiang-yun’s fondness for teasing made her still more uncomfortable. Fortunately she was educated and knew how to conduct herself. She had a young woman’s proper reserve, but was not one of those frivolous creatures forever pretending to be shy and ashamed.

Ever since meeting her, Bao-chai had seen how poor her family was. Other people’s parents were venerable and worthy; hers were a pair steeped in drink, with little regard for their daughter. Lady Xing’s interest in her was a matter of appearances, not real affection. Xiu-yan herself was refined and dignified, while Ying-chun was a corpse that still breathed. She could scarcely look after herself, let alone anyone else. If Xiu-yan lacked any of the ordinary things a girl needed, no one saw to it, and she would not ask. Bao-chai often took pains to help her secretly. She did not dare let Lady Xing know, for fear of provoking suspicion and gossip.
