segments.text: One day Bao-chai was going to visit Dai-yu when she met Xiu-yan on the same errand. She called her over with a smile, and the two went behind a rock face.
‘It’s still so cold,’ Bao-chai asked, smiling. ‘Why have you changed into lined clothes already?’
Xiu-yan lowered her head without answering. Bao-chai knew there must be some reason, and asked again, still smiling.
‘You can’t have had this month’s allowance. Is Feng becoming so careless now?’

‘No, she remembers and gives it on the right day. But Aunt sent word that I couldn’t use two taels of silver a month, and I was to save one and send it out to Father and Mother. Whatever I needed, she said, Cousin Ying-chun had things, and I could manage with some of hers. But you know what Cousin Ying-chun is like, so quiet and unobservant. She may not say anything if I use her things, but which of her nurses and maids is easy to deal with? Which of them hasn’t a sharp tongue?

segments.text: ‘If they were here, Bao-qin could be married, and then we could discuss your wedding. Once you were out of this place, your troubles would be over. But until his sister’s affairs are settled, Xue Ke would never venture to marry first. It is a difficulty. If we wait another two years, I’m afraid you’ll worry yourself ill. I’ll discuss it with Mother. If people bully you, try to bear with them, and whatever you do, don’t make yourself ill with worry. You might as well send the other tael to your parents tomorrow too, and have done with it. Then everyone can be easy in their minds. And you needn’t keep giving those people things to eat for nothing. Let them make their sharp remarks. If it becomes too much to listen to, walk away. If you’re short of anything, don’t stand on the timid pride of a girl from a small family. Come to me.

segments.text: She was about to leave, but Bao-chai caught her by the arm.
‘Off on another mad fit!’ she said, laughing. ‘Sit down at once.’
‘If you were a man, you could go out and fight to right a wrong,’ Dai-yu said with a laugh. ‘But why set yourself up as Jing Ke or Nie Zheng? It’s too ridiculous.’
‘If you won’t let me go and question Cousin Ying-chun, why not bring Xiu-yan to live with us in our court tomorrow? Wouldn’t that be better?’
‘We’ll discuss it tomorrow,’ said Bao-chai, smiling.

segments.text: Jia Zhen and his wife at the Ning mansion could hardly avoid going too. That would leave neither household with anyone in charge. After discussing the problem, they reported that You-shi was in childbirth, thus contriving to have her excused so that she could help manage affairs at both mansions. Aunt Xue was asked to look after the girls and maids in the garden, and had little choice but to move in.

Bao-chai already had Xiang-yun and Caltrop with her. Aunt Li and her daughters had left Li Wan’s rooms for the present, but might still come back for three to five days at a time, and Grandmother Jia had also entrusted Bao-qin to Li Wan’s care. Xiu-yan was staying with Ying-chun. Tan-chun was overwhelmed with household business, and Aunt Zhao and Jia Huan kept coming to pester her, which made her rooms most inconvenient. Xi-chun’s rooms were small. Besides, Grandmother Jia had charged Aunt Xue over and over again to take care of Dai-yu, whom Aunt Xue had always loved and pitied most. The opportunity now offering itself, she moved into Naiad’s House and shared Dai-yu’s room, taking the greatest care over her medicines and food. Dai-yu was endlessly grateful. From then on she called her Mother, just as Bao-chai did, and addressed Bao-chai and Bao-qin directly as her elder and younger sisters. They might all have been born of the same mother, and she felt closer to them than to anyone else.

segments.text: With the masters and mistresses of both mansions so occupied, the stewards too were in a state of bustle. Some accompanied them to court, some attended to the lodgings outside the palace, and others went ahead to inspect accommodation for the journey. Deprived of proper direction, the servants in both households took their ease, or seized the chance to form factions and share in the petty tyranny of those temporarily put in charge. Only Lai Da and a few other stewards remained at the Rong mansion to look after outside affairs. Several of the men Lai Da ordinarily relied on had gone away. Others were appointed in their place, but they were all unfamiliar with the work, and he found nothing went smoothly. They knew no better: one cheated without restraint, another lodged groundless complaints, another recommended people for no good reason. They made trouble everywhere in so many ways that it would be impossible to recount them all.

segments.text: Seeing that the other official households were releasing and sending away all their players, male and female, You-shi and the others decided to raise the question with Lady Wang when she returned. They too wished to send away their twelve girls. Someone suggested, ‘These girls were bought, after all. Even if they no longer learn to sing, we could keep them as servants and simply let their teachers go.’

‘Girls who have learnt to act are not quite the same as girls brought up to serve,’ said Lady Wang. ‘They too are the daughters of respectable families, sold into this work because their parents could not support them. They have spent several years now painting themselves up and playing the fool. Since this chance has come, we should give them a few taels for travelling expenses and let each go her own way. Our ancestors always used to do that. To do otherwise now would damage our hidden store of virtue, quite apart from being miserly.

segments.text: ‘There are still a few older ones here, it is true. Each had some particular reason for not wanting to go home. That is why they stayed on as servants and, when they grew up, were married to our male servants.’

‘Then let us ask all twelve,’ said You-shi. ‘For any who wish to go home, we can send word to their parents to come and fetch them in person, and give them a few taels for the journey. That would be safest. Unless we insist on a parent or close relative coming, some scoundrel might claim a girl under a false name and sell her again. That would defeat the kindness we meant to show. Any who do not wish to go can stay.’
‘That is a sensible arrangement,’ Lady Wang said with a smile.

You-shi and the others sent someone to tell Xi-feng. They also instructed the general steward’s office to give each teacher eight taels of silver and leave them free to depart. Everything at Pear-tree Court was to be checked, entered in an inventory and put safely away, and someone appointed to keep watch at night. Then the twelve girls were summoned and questioned in person. More than half did not want to go home. Some said that though their parents were living, selling them was all their parents cared about, and if they went back they would simply be sold again. Others had lost their parents or had been sold by uncles or brothers. Some had no one to turn to, and some said they could not bear to leave those who had been so kind to them.

segments.text: Only four or five wished to leave. On hearing this, Lady Wang could only let the others stay. The four or five who were going were sent to their godmothers’ homes to wait for their own parents to collect them. Those who did not wish to leave were distributed among the rooms in the garden as servants. Grandmother Jia kept Wen-guan for herself. She assigned Parfumée, who played principal female roles, to Bao-yu; Rui-guan, who played young female roles, to Bao-chai; Ou-guan, who played young male roles, to Dai-yu; Kui-guan, who played major painted-face roles, to Xiang-yun; Dou-guan, who played comic painted-face roles, to Bao-qin; and Ai-guan, who played older male roles, to Tan-chun. You-shi asked for Qie-guan, who played older female roles.

Each now had her place. Like weary birds let out of a cage, they spent their days at play in the garden. Everyone knew they could not sew and were unused to domestic service, so they were seldom scolded.

segments.text: One or two of the more thoughtful girls, however, worried that they would have no useful skill to rely on in future. They too set their former art aside and began learning sewing, spinning, weaving and the other kinds of women’s work.

One day there was a great sacrifice at court. Grandmother Jia and the others left in the fifth watch, went first to their lodgings for some cakes and light refreshments, then entered the palace. When the early breakfast was over, they withdrew to their lodgings, had breakfast there and rested briefly. They then went back to court, remaining until the noon and evening sacrifices were finished. Only then did they return to their lodgings to rest, and after supper go home.

Their lodgings happened to be in the family shrine of a high official, where Buddhist nuns tended the incense and practised their devotions. There were a great many rooms, all very clean, arranged in two courts, east and west. The Rong household rented the eastern court and the Prince of Beijing’s household the western one. The Dowager Princess and the Princess of Beijing rested there each day. With Grandmother Jia and her party in the eastern court, they went in and out together and could look after one another. There is no need to dwell on these outside details.

segments.text: In Prospect Garden, meanwhile, Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang’s daily absences, together with the month away accompanying the coffin before their return, gave all the maids and older women plenty of leisure. They spent much of it wandering in the garden. All the women who had attended the girls at Pear-tree Court had now been withdrawn from there and scattered about the garden to wait on orders, adding several dozen people to its population.

Among Wen-guan and her companions there were proud tempers, girls who relied on their patrons to bully those beneath them, girls who were particular about their clothes and food, and girls with sharp tongues. Most were little inclined to keep quietly within the rules.

segments.text: As it happened, that day was Qingming. segments.text: Bao-yu had not recovered enough to go. After his meal he felt drowsy.
‘It is such a lovely day,’ Aroma said. ‘Go out for a little walk. Don’t put down your bowl of gruel and go straight to sleep, or it will lie heavy inside you.’

Bao-yu could only do as she said. Leaning on a stick, his feet slipped loosely into his shoes, he made his way out of the court. Since the garden had lately been allotted to the older women to manage, each with her own task, everyone was busy. Some were trimming bamboo, some pruning trees, some planting flowers and others sowing beans. On the pond the boatwomen were moving their boats about, scooping up mud to plant lotus roots. Caltrop, Xiang-yun and Bao-qin sat with their maids on the rocks, watching the work for amusement. Bao-yu slowly approached them.
‘Quick, send that boat away!’ Xiang-yun cried with a laugh when she saw him. ‘They have come to take Cousin Lin home!’
Everyone laughed. Bao-yu reddened, but laughed too.
‘No one has a kind thought for someone who has been ill. You have to mimic him and make fun of him as well.’
‘Even the way you are ill is different from everyone else,’ said Xiang-yun, laughing. ‘You invite a laugh, and then you blame us!’
Bao-yu sat down with them and watched the bustle for a while.

segments.text: ‘There is a wind here, and the stone is cold,’ Xiang-yun said. ‘Why not go and sit indoors for a bit?’

Bao-yu had been about to visit Dai-yu anyway. He got up, took his stick, said goodbye and followed the bank by Drenched Blossoms Bridge. The willows trailed golden threads, and the peach trees unfurled rosy clouds. Beyond the rocks stood a great apricot tree. Its flowers had all fallen; thick leaves cast a green shade, and the branches were already set with many little apricots the size of beans.
‘How many days can I have been ill?’ Bao-yu thought. ‘And I have missed the apricot blossom altogether. Already, before I knew it, “Green leaves have made a shade, and branches teem with fruit.”’

He gazed up at the little apricots, unwilling to turn away. Then he remembered that a husband had been chosen for Xing Xiu-yan. Marriage was a great matter for men and women, certainly, and could not be dispensed with; yet it meant one lovely girl fewer. In no more than two years, for her too, ‘Green leaves have made a shade, and branches teem with fruit.’ A few more days and this tree’s fruit would fall, leaving its branches empty. A few more years and Xiu-yan’s raven hair would surely turn to silver, her rosy face wither. The thought grieved him. He stood there weeping and sighing over the apricot tree.

‘Ou-guan! Are you looking to get yourself killed? How dare you bring paper money in here and burn it? I’m going to tell the mistresses. Mind your skin!’

‘Who are you burning it for?’ he asked at once. ‘You mustn’t burn it here. If it is for your parents or brothers, tell me their names. I can have the boys outside make up parcels, write the names on them and burn them for you.’

‘I have told the mistresses already. They are terribly angry.’
Ou-guan was still a child at heart. Afraid of being disgraced and losing face, she refused to go.

‘She wasn’t burning paper money,’ Bao-yu said quickly. ‘Cousin Lin sent her to burn some waste writing paper. You did not look properly, and you have accused her wrongly.’

Even if she were your own daughter, once she had been assigned to her place and given a master or mistress, they would have the right to beat or scold her. So would the senior maids. Who gave her parents leave to step in halfway and interfere? If you all went on controlling them like this, what would be the point of sending them to learn from us?

segments.text: As they talked, they laid out the things for supper. Presently the little maid came in carrying the food box and stood waiting. Skybright and Musk opened it and found only the usual four small dishes.
‘He is better now, and they still won’t give him a couple of light dishes,’ Skybright said, laughing. ‘How long must we go on with this gruel and pickles?’
She arranged the dishes, then looked again in the box. There was a bowl of ham and fresh bamboo-shoot soup. She quickly set it before Bao-yu. He leaned towards the table and took a sip.
‘How hot!’
‘My dear bodhisattva!’ Aroma said with a smile. ‘How many days have you gone without meat, to be as greedy as this?’
As she spoke, she took up the bowl and blew gently on it. Seeing Parfumée beside her, she handed it to her with a smile.
‘You must learn to wait on him too, instead of doing nothing but stare and sleep. Blow gently. Don’t spatter it with spit.’
Parfumée did as she was told and blew on it several times, very properly.

segments.text: Her godmother had meanwhile hurried to bring the rice and stood waiting outside the door. When Parfumée and the other girls had first arrived, their godmothers had been assigned to them outside, and had gone with them straight to Pear-tree Court. These women belonged to the third rank of servants in the Rong household. Their work had been no more than to starch and wash the girls’ clothes; they had never waited in attendance inside and knew nothing of the rules of the inner apartments. Only through the girls had they now gained entry to the garden and followed their goddaughters to their new rooms.

After her dressing-down from Musk, this woman had learnt a little. She was terrified that Parfumée might no longer be allowed to acknowledge her as godmother, costing her a good many benefits, and was intent on winning the maids over. Seeing Parfumée blow on the soup, she hurried in, smiling.
‘She is too inexperienced. She might break the bowl. Let me blow on it.’
She reached for it as she spoke.

segments.text: ‘Get out!’ Skybright shouted. ‘Even if she smashes the bowl, it is not your place to blow on it. When did you find a chance to come in past this partition? Out with you!’
Then she turned on the little maids.
‘Are you all blind? She doesn’t know, but why didn’t you tell her?’

‘We tried to turn her out, and she wouldn’t go,’ they protested. ‘We told her, and she wouldn’t believe us. Now you have got us scolded too. Will you believe us at last? Of the places we are allowed to go, you may enter only half. The other half are out of bounds to you. Yet you go running into a place where even we aren’t allowed, and as if that weren’t enough, you have to put your hands and mouth to work as well!’
As they spoke, they pushed her out. Several older women waiting below the steps to collect the empty boxes and dishes laughed at her.
‘Didn’t you look in a mirror before you went in, sister?’
Burning with shame, resentment and anger, she could only swallow it.

segments.text: Parfumée blew on the soup a few more times.
‘That will do,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Mind you don’t exhaust yourself. Taste a little. Is it ready?’
Parfumée thought he was joking. She only smiled and looked at Aroma and the others.
‘Why shouldn’t you taste it?’ Aroma said.
‘Watch me,’ Skybright said with a laugh, and took a sip.
Parfumée followed her example.
‘It is ready.’

She handed it to Bao-yu. He drank half the bowl, ate a few slices of bamboo shoot, then half a bowl of gruel, and wanted no more. They cleared everything away. A little maid brought a basin, and when he had washed and rinsed his mouth, Aroma and the others went out to eat.

Bao-yu gave Parfumée a look. She was clever by nature and had studied acting for several years. What was there she did not understand? She pretended to have a headache and said she did not want supper.
‘If you are not eating, stay here and keep him company,’ said Aroma. ‘I’ll save this gruel for you. You can have it later if you are hungry.’
They all went out.

segments.text: Alone with Parfumée, Bao-yu told her the whole story in detail, from the moment he had seen the flare of fire: how he had found Ou-guan, how he had lied to protect her, and how she had told him to ask Parfumée. Then he asked who it was she had been making offerings to.
Parfumée was all smiles, but she gave a sigh.
‘It is a story to make you laugh and sigh together.’
Bao-yu eagerly asked her to explain.
‘Who do you think she was making offerings to?’ Parfumée said with a smile. ‘Di-guan, who died.’
‘That is friendship,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Quite right too.’

‘Friendship? Nothing of the sort. It is the maddest notion. She says she played the young male roles and Di-guan the young female roles, and they were always husband and wife. It was only make-believe, of course, but day after day the words they sang and everything they acted were full of real tenderness and loving care. So the two of them went mad. Even when they weren’t acting, at meals or sitting about, whatever they did, they were all love and affection for each other.

segments.text: ‘When Di-guan died, Ou-guan cried till she was half dead herself. She has never forgotten her, and burns paper money at every festival. Afterwards Rui-guan took her place. We saw Ou-guan being just as tender and attentive to her, and asked whether she had found a new love and forgotten the old. She said, “There is a great principle behind this too. Suppose a man loses his wife, and circumstances make it necessary for him to marry again. Then marrying again is what he ought to do. As long as he doesn’t put the dead wife aside and never speak of her, that is deep and faithful love. If he refuses to remarry simply because she is dead, and lives alone for the rest of his life, failing in a great duty, that is not right either. It would only make the dead woman uneasy.” Isn’t she mad and foolish? Isn’t it laughable?’
This foolish speech chimed precisely with Bao-yu’s own foolish nature. He was at once delighted and full of grief, sighing, marvelling and declaring it beyond compare.
‘When Heaven has made people like that,’ he said, ‘what need is there for a foul male creature like me to defile the world?’

segments.text: He caught Parfumée by the hand.
‘In that case I have something to tell her too. It would be awkward to say it to her face. You must tell her for me.’
Parfumée asked what it was.

‘She must never burn paper money again. Paper money is a later heresy, not a teaching handed down by Confucius. Whenever a season or festival comes round, she need only have an incense burner ready and burn incense on the day, in whatever way is convenient. If her whole heart is sincere and reverent, that will reach the spirit. Foolish people do not understand. Whether they worship a god, a Buddha or the dead, they insist on making different grades, each with its own rules. They do not know that everything depends on just one thing: a sincere heart.

segments.text: ‘Even in days of panic and wandering, when you have no incense, any earth or grass will serve as an offering, provided it is clean. Not only the dead, but gods and spirits too will come to receive it. Look at my table: I keep just one incense burner there. I burn incense often, without regard to dates. None of them knows why, but each time I have a reason of my own. If there is plain tea, I offer a cup of tea; if there is fresh water, a cup of water. Or there may be fresh flowers, or fresh fruit, even meat soup or fish dishes. As long as the heart is sincere and the intention pure, even a Buddha may come to receive them. That is why I say it is reverence that matters, not empty forms. Tell her at once that she must not burn paper money again.’
Parfumée agreed. Presently, when supper was over, someone came to report, ‘Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship are home.’

segments.text: At the Rong mansion, Lai Da put extra men on night duty and closed off both sets of halls and courtyards. Everyone coming or going had to use the small side gate on the west. At sunset he had the ceremonial gate shut and allowed no one through. The garden’s front, rear, eastern and western side gates were all locked as well, leaving open only the gate behind Lady Wang’s main rooms which the girls ordinarily used, and the eastern side gate leading to Aunt Xue’s quarters. These two lay within the inner courtyards and did not need to be locked. Inside, Faithful and Silver each shut up the principal rooms and took their maids and older women to sleep in the side rooms. Every day Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife came in with ten or so older women to keep watch at night. A number of young serving-men had also been posted in the passage hall to sit up and strike the watch-clappers. All the arrangements were thoroughly in place.

segments.text: Early one morning Bao-chai woke from her drowsy spring sleep, lifted the bed-curtains and got up. Feeling a slight chill, she opened the door and looked out. The earth in the garden was damp and the moss green: a few drops of light rain had fallen during the fifth watch. She called Xiang-yun and the others to get up. As they washed and dressed, Xiang-yun said that both her cheeks were itching and she was afraid the skin eruption had come back. She asked Bao-chai for some rose medicinal powder.
‘I gave all I had left to my younger cousin the other day,’ Bao-chai told her. ‘Pin-pin has made up quite a lot. I meant to ask her for some, but as I haven’t had any itching this year I forgot.’
She told Oriole to go and fetch some. Oriole had just answered and was starting off when Rui-guan said, ‘I’ll come with you. I can see Ou-guan while I’m there.’
The two of them set out together from Allspice Court.

segments.text: ‘Things to play with, things to use, anything. Let me pick some. I’ll weave a little flower-basket with the leaves still on, and we can put all sorts of flowers in it. That really will be something to play with.’

Putting off the powder errand for the moment, she reached up, drew down the green and parted the gold, and picked a quantity of tender shoots, which she told Rui-guan to hold. She herself went on weaving as she walked, gathering a spray or two of any flowers she saw along the path, until she had made a delicate openwork basket with an arched handle. The twigs were already clothed in their own green leaves, and with the flowers set among them it looked charmingly unusual.
‘Oh, give it to me, sister!’ cried Rui-guan in delight.
‘We’ll give this one to Miss Lin,’ said Oriole. ‘On the way back we can pick some more and make several, for everyone to play with.’

segments.text: While they were talking, Rui-guan and Ou-guan returned.

‘What paper were you burning the other day, after all?’ Swallow asked Ou-guan. ‘My aunt saw you and wanted to report you, but she never managed it. Instead Bao-yu put all sorts of blame on her. She was so angry she told my mother every last detail. What quarrels did you store up in those two or three years outside that you still can’t settle them?’
Ou-guan gave a cold laugh.

‘What quarrels? They’re never satisfied, and then they blame us. In those two years outside, never mind anything else, just think what they made out of our rice and vegetables. Heaven knows how much they took home, more than their whole families could eat. And then there was the money they made every day buying this and that. Whenever we asked them to do the least thing for us out there, they complained to heaven and earth. Have they any conscience? You tell me.’

segments.text: ‘“It’s plainly the same person, so how does she turn into three different things?” It’s nonsense, of course, but there’s something in it. I don’t know about other people. Yesterday the monthly allowance came, so she couldn’t put it off any longer. She bought the things, then told me to wash my hair first.

segments.text: ‘I thought it over. I’ve money of my own, and even if I hadn’t, if I wanted my hair washed, I’d only have to ask Aroma, Skybright or Musk, any one of them, and it would be easy enough. Why should I take advantage of this? It didn’t seem right, so I wouldn’t. Then she made my little sister Xiao-jiu wash hers, and only after that did she call Parfumée. Sure enough, there was a quarrel. Next she wanted to blow on Bao-yu’s soup for him. Wouldn’t it make you die laughing? I told her all the rules as soon as she came in, but she won’t believe me. She has to pretend she knows everything, and all she gets for it is a snub. Luckily there are so many people in the garden that nobody can keep track of who’s related to whom. If anyone did remember, and found it was always our family quarrelling, how would that look?

‘And now you’ve come here to do this! Everything growing along here is in my father’s sister’s charge. Getting this patch meant more to her than coming into an estate to last for ever. She’s up early and to bed late every day, and wearing herself out isn’t enough: she has to make us come and watch it too. She’s terrified someone will spoil something, and then she’s afraid of keeping me from my duties.

segments.text: ‘Now Mother’s come in, the two old sisters-in-law watch over it so carefully they won’t let anyone touch a blade of grass. And here you are picking the flowers and snapping off her young shoots. They’ll be here any moment. Mind they don’t complain.’

‘Other people mustn’t go breaking and picking things at random, but I can,’ said Oriole. ‘Ever since they divided the plots up, every household has had its regular allowance. Never mind things to eat; I’m only talking about flowers and greenery to enjoy. Whoever has charge of them has to send round sprays of all the different kinds each day for the young ladies and their maids to wear, and some for the vases too. We’re the only ones who said, “Don’t send anything. We’ll ask you when we want some.” And we’ve never asked once. If I pick a few today, they can hardly have the face to say anything.’

segments.text: She had scarcely finished when Swallow’s aunt did indeed appear, leaning on a stick. Oriole, Swallow and the others at once offered her a seat. Seeing all the tender willow shoots they had picked, and all the fresh flowers Ou-guan and the others had gathered, the old woman was far from pleased. She watched Oriole weaving, but could not very well say anything to her, so she addressed Swallow instead.

‘I told you to come and keep an eye on things. Now you’ve got so taken up with playing that you won’t go back. If they call for you, you’ll say I sent you on an errand. I’m your charm to make you invisible while you enjoy yourself!’
‘You tell me to do things, and then you’re afraid of the consequences,’ said Swallow. ‘And now you blame me. Am I to split myself into eight pieces?’

segments.text: ‘Don’t believe little Swallow, Auntie,’ Oriole said with a laugh. ‘She picked all this herself and pestered me to weave it for her. I keep telling her to go away, but she won’t.’
‘Do stop teasing,’ Swallow said, laughing. ‘You think it’s all a joke, but Auntie will take you seriously.’

The old woman was stupid and obstinate to begin with, and age had brought her close to dotage. Gain was all she cared for; she had no regard for anyone’s feelings. The sight was tearing her heart out, yet she had been unable to do anything about it. At Oriole’s words she took full advantage of her years, raised her stick and struck Swallow several times.

‘You little hussy! Here I am telling you off, and you still answer back! Your mother hates you till her teeth itch. She’d like to tear your flesh off and eat it. And you’re going to be a stubborn little hardhead with me too!’

segments.text: Stung with shame and distress by the blows, Swallow burst into tears.
‘Oriole was only joking, and you really hit me! Why should Mother hate me? It’s not as if I’ve burnt the wash-water! What have I done wrong?’
Oriole had meant only to tease. Seeing the old woman had lost her temper in earnest, she hurried over to catch her arm.
‘I was joking,’ she said with a smile. ‘If you beat her for that, how am I to hold up my head?’
‘Miss, keep out of our affairs,’ said the old woman. ‘Am I not to discipline a child just because you’re here?’
Such stupid words made Oriole flush with resentment. She let go and gave a cold laugh.
‘You’ve all the time in the world to discipline her, yet you have to begin the moment I make a joke. Go on, then. I’ll watch you do it.’
She sat down and went on weaving her willow basket.

segments.text: Just then Swallow’s mother came looking for her.
‘Why aren’t you fetching water? What are you doing over there?’ she called.
‘Come and look!’ the other old woman called back. ‘Your daughter won’t even listen to me now. She’s standing here telling me off.’
‘Sister, what’s happened now?’ said her mother as she approached. ‘So my girl’s got no mother in her eyes. Has she got no aunt either?’
Seeing Swallow’s mother arrive, Oriole had to explain once more how it had happened. But the aunt would let no one speak. She pointed out the flowers and willow on the rock.
‘Look at what your daughter’s been playing with, a great girl of her age! She brings people to spoil my things, and then how can I say anything to them?’
Swallow’s mother was still angry over Parfumée, and resentful of Swallow for not doing as she wished. She came up and slapped the girl’s face.

‘Little whore! How long have you been too grand for us? You’ve been learning from those brazen little sluts. So we’re not allowed to discipline any of you now? I can’t lay a hand on the one I’m godmother to, but you dropped out of my cunt. Am I to be afraid to discipline you as well?

segments.text: ‘If you hussies can go places I’m not allowed into, you ought to stay there and serve till you drop dead. What are you running out here for, chasing men?’
She snatched up the willow twigs and thrust them in Swallow’s face.
‘What do you call this? Your mother’s cunt, that’s what you’re weaving!’
‘We made that,’ Oriole said at once. ‘Don’t scold one person to get at another.’

The old woman deeply envied Aroma, Skybright and their companions. She had already learnt that the senior maids in the young masters’ and mistresses’ rooms carried themselves with more consequence, and had more power, than women like her. Whenever she met them she felt both fear and deference, which in turn made her angry and resentful, and she took it out on everyone around her. Now there was Ou-guan before her too, her elder sister’s enemy. Anger gathered from every quarter into a single blaze.

segments.text: Crying, Swallow set off for the House of Green Delights. Her mother grew anxious. They would ask why she was crying, and she would tell them she had been beaten, and then there would be more trouble with Skybright and the rest.
‘Come back!’ she hurriedly called. ‘I’ve something to tell you before you go.’

Swallow had no intention of coming back. Frantic, her mother ran after her to pull her back, but Swallow looked round, saw her coming, and fled all the faster. In her haste her mother failed to watch her footing, slipped on the moss and fell, setting Oriole and the other two laughing. Oriole flung all the flowers and willow into the river in a fit of temper and went back to her rooms.
The old aunt was left in such anguish over the loss that she could only call on the Buddha and curse.
‘Spiteful little hussy! Spoiling flowers like that, you’ll have the thunderbolt after you!’
She went on picking flowers herself to send round to the different households, and we shall leave her there.

segments.text: Swallow ran straight into the courtyard and almost collided with Aroma, who was on her way to Dai-yu’s to ask after her. She threw her arms round her.
‘Save me, miss! Mother’s beating me again!’
Seeing her mother coming, Aroma could not help losing her temper.
‘Every other day it’s the same, beating your goddaughter and then your own. Are you showing off how many daughters you’ve got, or do you really not know there’s such a thing as the law?’
In the few days she had been there, the old woman had found Aroma quiet and good-natured.
‘You don’t know anything about it, miss,’ she said. ‘Keep out of our business! You’re the ones who spoil them. What’s the use of interfering now?’

She went on chasing Swallow to hit her. Aroma turned back inside in anger. Musk was under the crab-apple tree airing hand-towels. Hearing the shouting and commotion, she said, ‘Leave her alone, sister. Let’s see what she does.’
At the same time she gave Swallow a look. Swallow understood and ran straight to Bao-yu.
‘Now we’re seeing things we never thought to see!’ everyone said with a laugh.
‘Do cool down a little,’ Musk told the old woman. ‘Don’t all of us count for anything? Can’t we ask you to spare someone and be listened to?’
The old woman saw her daughter run to Bao-yu and saw him take her hand.
‘Don’t be afraid,’ he said. ‘I’m here.’
Still crying, Swallow told him everything that had happened with Oriole and the others.

segments.text: This made Bao-yu still more upset.
‘It would be bad enough if you only made trouble here,’ he said. ‘Must you offend our relations’ people as well?’
Musk turned to the old woman and the others.

‘No wonder our good sister says their affairs are none of our business. We’ve been ignorant enough to interfere where we shouldn’t. Well, now we’ll ask someone who has the authority to deal with it. Then our sister will be convinced, heart and soul, and learn the rules as well.’
She turned to a little maid.
‘Go and fetch Patience for us. If she’s busy, fetch Mamma Lin.’
The girl answered and went out. The other married women came up smiling.
‘Quick, sister, ask the young ladies to call that child back. If Miss Patience comes, you’ll be in trouble.’
‘Whoever this Miss Patience may be, she’ll have to listen to reason,’ said the old woman. ‘Where was it ever heard of that a mother disciplines her daughter and everyone else disciplines the mother?’

‘Who do you think Miss Patience is?’ the women asked with a laugh. ‘She’s Miss Patience from Mrs Lian’s rooms. If she’s feeling kindly you may get a word or two in. If she turns nasty, sister, you’ll have more than you can stomach, and plenty left to carry home!’

segments.text: They were still speaking when the little maid returned.

‘Miss Patience is busy. She asked what I wanted and I told her. She says, “In that case, turn her out. Tell Mamma Lin to give her forty strokes of the board outside the side gate, and have done with it.”’
The old woman was naturally unwilling to leave. Tears streamed down her face as she begged Aroma and the others.

‘It was hard enough for me to get a place in here. And I’m a widow with no one at home. It’s just right for me to give my whole mind to serving you young ladies, with nothing to worry about outside. It’s convenient for you, and it saves some of the expense of keeping me at home.

segments.text: ‘Why bother with her?’ said Skybright. ‘Send her off and have done. Who wants to stand here arguing with her?’
The old woman begged them all again.
‘I know I was wrong. Now you’ve told me, I’ll mend my ways. You’ll be doing a good deed and earning merit.’
Then she appealed to Swallow.
‘It all began with my trying to beat you. In the end I never managed to beat you, and now I’m the one who suffers! Say a word for me too.’
Seeing her so pitiable, Bao-yu could only let her stay, warning her not to make any more trouble. The old woman came up and thanked them one by one, then withdrew.

segments.text: Just then Patience arrived and asked what had happened.
‘It’s all over,’ Aroma and the others told her at once. ‘There’s no need to mention it again.’

‘“Where you can spare someone, spare them,”’ said Patience with a smile. ‘And if we can save ourselves some trouble by letting things pass, so much the better. They’ve only been gone a few days, yet all I hear is that everyone, great and small, is rising in rebellion. Before one affair’s settled another starts. I don’t know which to attend to.’
‘I thought ours was the only rebellion,’ Aroma said with a laugh. ‘So there are others too?’

segments.text: Now Aroma asked Patience what was keeping her in such a bustle.
‘Things no one would ever have thought of,’ Patience said with a smile. ‘They’re funny enough in the telling. I’ll tell you in a few days. Nothing’s clear yet, and I haven’t a moment to spare.’
Before she had finished, one of Li Wan’s maids came in.
‘Is Sister Patience here? My mistress is waiting for you. Why haven’t you come?’
Patience turned and hurried out, calling back with a smile, ‘Coming, coming!’
‘Now her mistress is ill, she’s become a sweet bun herself,’ Aroma and the others laughed. ‘Everyone’s snatching for her, and no one can get hold of her.’
We shall leave Patience to her business.

segments.text: Mother and daughter answered him and set off, chatting as they went.
‘I’m always trying to tell you, Mother, but you won’t believe me,’ said Swallow. ‘Why must you go on till you’ve made yourself look foolish?’
‘Get along with you, little hussy!’ her mother said, laughing. ‘As the saying goes, “No experience, no wisdom.” I know now. And here you are calling me to account as well!’

‘Mother, if you behave yourself and stay in these rooms long enough, there’ll be all sorts of advantages,’ Swallow said with a smile. ‘Let me tell you something. Bao-yu’s always saying that one day he’ll ask Her Ladyship to let everyone in his rooms go free, whether we were born in the household or brought in from outside, every one of us, and leave us and our parents to do as we please. Now tell me, isn’t that one good thing?’
Delighted, her mother asked at once, ‘Is that really true?’

segments.text: ‘Who would make up a lie like that? What for?’ said Swallow.

The old woman went on invoking the Buddha all the way. When they reached Allspice Court, Bao-chai, Dai-yu, Aunt Xue and the others were at their meal. Oriole went to make tea, and Swallow and her mother went straight over to her. Smiling apologetically, they said they had spoken rudely just now, begged her not to take offence, and explained that they had come expressly to ask her pardon. Oriole hastened to offer them seats, smiling, and poured tea for them. Mother and daughter said they had things to do and took their leave.
Suddenly Rui-guan came running after them.
‘Mamma! Sister! Wait a moment!’
She came up and handed them a paper packet. It was rose medicinal powder, she said, for them to take to Parfumée to put on her face.
‘You do make a fuss over trifles!’ Swallow said, laughing. ‘As if there weren’t any for her where she is! You have to go to all this trouble to send her another packet.’
‘What she has is hers. What I give her is mine. Do take it back for me, dear sister.’
Swallow had to accept it. When she and her mother returned, Jia Huan and Jia Cong had just come to ask after Bao-yu and were only now going in.

segments.text: ‘I’ll go in by myself,’ Swallow told her mother. ‘You needn’t come.’

Her mother obeyed. From then on she did whatever Swallow said and dared no longer be obstinate. As Swallow came in, Bao-yu knew she was there to report back and forestalled her with a nod. She understood, said nothing, stood a moment and then went out again, giving Parfumée a look as she did so. Parfumée followed her out, and only then did Swallow quietly tell her about Rui-guan and hand over the powder.

Bao-yu could find nothing to talk about with Jia Cong and Jia Huan, so he asked Parfumée with a smile what she was holding. She at once handed it to him to see, explaining that it was rose medicinal powder for a spring skin eruption.
‘How thoughtful of her!’ Bao-yu said, smiling.
Jia Huan craned his neck for a look. He caught a delicate fragrance, bent down and pulled a piece of paper out of his boot-top, then held it out.
‘Dear Brother, give me half,’ he said with a grin.

segments.text: With Jia Zheng away, and Lady Wang and the others away as well, Jia Huan had been pretending to be ill for several days to get out of school. Now, delighted with his powder, he went to find Cai-yun. She happened to be talking to Aunt Zhao.

‘I’ve got a packet of the good kind too,’ he told Cai-yun with a grin. ‘I’m giving it to you for your face. You always say rose medicinal powder is better for the skin eruption than the silver powder you buy outside. Have a look. Is this it?’
Cai-yun opened the packet and gave a snort of laughter.
‘Who did you get it from?’
Jia Huan told her what had just happened.
‘They’ve made a fool of you, you country bumpkin!’ she said, laughing. ‘This isn’t the medicinal powder. It’s jasmine powder.’
Jia Huan looked. It was indeed a little pinker than the first lot, and when he sniffed it the fragrance was strong.
‘This is good too,’ he said with a smile. ‘Medicine or face powder, it’s all the same. Keep it for your face. As long as it’s better than what you buy outside, that’s good enough.’
Cai-yun could only put it away.
‘As if they’d give you anything good!’ said Aunt Zhao.

Bao-yu’s your elder brother, so you daren’t offend him, of course. But can’t you even question the cats and dogs in his rooms?’

segments.text: ‘Now we’ve got right on our side, it would do us good to give those shameless whores a proper scolding.’
She pointed at Jia Huan.

‘Pah! You spineless little wretch! All you’re fit for is to let those brats ride over you. If I so much as say a word to you, or happen to give you the wrong thing by mistake, you can turn your head away, bulge your veins, glare at me and stamp and slam things about in front of your own mother. But when those little cunts make a fool of you, you put up with it! And you expect the servants in this household to be afraid of you one day? You haven’t a bloody scrap of spirit. I’m ashamed for you.’
Jia Huan was ashamed and angry, but still did not dare to go. He flung out his hands.

‘You’re so good at talking, but you daren’t go yourself. You send me to make the trouble. Suppose they tell the school and I get beaten? Of course, it won’t hurt you! If you’re not afraid of Third Sister, go yourself. I’ll give you credit if you dare.’
That last remark went straight to his mother’s sore spot.

segments.text: Aunt Zhao went straight into the garden, blazing with anger, and ran into Mamma Xia, Ou-guan’s godmother, coming towards her. Seeing the furious look on her face, Mamma Xia asked:
‘Where are you going, ma’am?’

‘Just look at this house!’ said Aunt Zhao. ‘Even the little painted whores from the theatre, who’ve only been here two or three days, have learnt to weigh you up and serve you according to what they think you’re worth. If it were anyone else, I wouldn’t be so angry. But to be made a fool of by those little prostitutes! What does that make us?’
This was just what Mamma Xia wanted to hear. She hurriedly asked what had happened, and Aunt Zhao told her how Parfumée had slighted Jia Huan by passing off face powder as the medicinal sort.

‘My dear ma’am, have you only just found out?’ said Mamma Xia. ‘That’s nothing. Only yesterday they were burning paper money in this very place, all on their own authority, and Bao-yu actually stepped in to protect them. Other people can’t so much as bring anything in without being told it won’t do, it’s unclean, it’s unlucky. And burning paper money isn’t unlucky? Think about it, ma’am. Apart from Her Ladyship, who in this house is above you?

segments.text: ‘You don’t stand up for yourself. If you did, who would dare not be afraid of you? Now, the way I see it, these little painted whores haven’t any proper standing. It won’t matter much if you offend them. You’ve got these two things to go on. Make an example of them, and I’ll be there as your witness. Show them your authority, and afterwards you’ll be able to insist on proper respect in other things too. Even the mistresses and young ladies can hardly blame you for the sake of those little painted whores.’
Hearing this, Aunt Zhao felt more justified than ever.
‘I didn’t know about the paper-burning. Tell me exactly what happened.’
Mamma Xia gave her a detailed account of the earlier affair.
‘You just go and speak your mind,’ she added. ‘If it comes to a row, we’ll be there to help you.’
This pleased Aunt Zhao still more. Her courage strengthened, she went straight to the House of Green Delights.

segments.text: As it happened, Bao-yu had heard that Dai-yu was at Allspice Court and had gone over there. Parfumée was eating with Aroma and the others. At the sight of Aunt Zhao they all got up, smiling, and invited her to join them.
‘Have some food, ma’am. What’s brought you here in such a hurry?’
Aunt Zhao made no answer. She walked up and scattered the powder in Parfumée’s face, pointing at her as she cursed:

‘Little whore! You were bought with my money to learn to sing, nothing but a common painted prostitute! Even the lowest grade of servants in our family is above you. So you know how to change the dish according to the guest, do you? Bao-yu wants to give something, and you get in his way. Was he asking you for anything? You give Huan this to fool him. Do you suppose he doesn’t know the difference? Whatever else they may be, they’re brothers, and both equally your masters. Who are you to look down on him?’
Parfumée could not endure such words. Crying, she answered:
‘I only gave him this because there was none of the medicinal powder left. If I’d said there wasn’t any, I was afraid he wouldn’t believe me. Isn’t this good too?

‘Don’t talk nonsense!’ Aroma said, hastily pulling at her.
In a fury, Aunt Zhao came up and slapped her face twice. Aroma and the others hurried between them, pulling Aunt Zhao back and trying to soothe her.
‘Don’t take a child so seriously, ma’am. Leave us to talk to her.’
After two slaps Parfumée was hardly going to submit. She threw herself about and rolled on the floor, wailing and making a scene.
‘You think you’re fit to hit me? Take a look at yourself before you raise your hand! You’ve beaten me. How can I go on living now?’
She hurled herself against Aunt Zhao’s breast and dared her to hit her. The others tried to calm her and pull her away. Skybright quietly tugged at Aroma.

‘Leave them alone. Let them fight, and see how they get out of it. There’s no rule here now but whoever makes the most trouble. You can hit people, I can hit people. Where will it end if everyone starts doing that?’

segments.text: Ou-guan and Rui-guan were playing together when Kui-guan, the girl who had played major painted-face roles and now served Xiang-yun, and Dou-guan, who served Bao-qin, heard the news. They hurried to find the other two.
‘If someone can bully Parfumée, we’ll look fools too. We must all risk it and make a proper uproar. That’s the only way to get our own back.’

The four were children at heart. Thinking only of their friendship and the wrong done to their companion, they paid no heed to anything else and ran together into the House of Green Delights. Dou-guan charged head first and very nearly knocked Aunt Zhao down. The other three crowded in too, crying at the tops of their voices, tugging with their hands and butting with their heads until Aunt Zhao was surrounded. Skybright and the others laughed and made a pretence of pulling them apart. Aroma was frantic: she would catch hold of one only to have another break away.
‘Are you trying to get yourselves killed?’ she kept saying. ‘If you’ve been wronged, tell someone. How can you behave so outrageously?’

segments.text: You-shi and Li Wan both smiled.
‘Please come to the hall, Aunt. We can talk there.’
Aunt Zhao had no choice but to go out with the three of them, though she was still complaining as she went.

‘Those little maids are only there for our amusement,’ Tan-chun told her. ‘If you like them, you can laugh and talk with them. If you don’t, you can ignore them. Even when they behave badly, it’s no more than a scratch or a bite from a cat or dog. If you can overlook it, do. If you can’t, send for the women in charge and have them speak to the girls and punish them. Why lower yourself, shouting and bellowing till all dignity is gone? Look at Aunt Zhou. Who ever bullies her? She doesn’t go looking for quarrels either. Do go back to your rooms and cool down, Aunt. Don’t listen to those scoundrels egging you on. You only make yourself a laughing-stock, stupidly doing their dirty work for nothing. However furious you are, bear with it these few days. Her Ladyship will deal with it when she comes back.’
This left Aunt Zhao without a word to say. She could only go back to her rooms.

All the girls were fond of her. That day after the meal Tan-chun went to the hall to attend to business, leaving Ebony to mind the rooms. Ebony told Chan-jie to go out and ask a young serving-boy to buy some cakes.
‘I’ve only just swept that great garden,’ Chan-jie said. ‘My back and legs are aching. Can’t you send someone else?’
‘Who else am I to send?’ Ebony said with a smile. ‘Be quick and go. I’ll tell you something for your own good. When you get to the back gate, you can warn your grandmother on the way.’
She told her what Ai-guan had said about Mamma Xia. Chan-jie hurriedly took the money.
‘So that little hussy wants to play tricks on people too! I’ll go and tell her.’
Off she went. At the back gate she found the kitchen people enjoying a quiet interval, all sitting on the steps chatting. Her grandmother was among them.

She went back inside, poked up the fire and set the tea to heat.

segments.text: Holding a hot cake, Parfumée challenged Chan-jie to her face.
‘As if I wanted your cakes! Isn’t this a cake too? I was only joking. I wouldn’t eat yours if you kowtowed to me.’
She broke the cakes in her hand into pieces, tossing them at the sparrows for fun.
‘Don’t begrudge them, Mrs Liu,’ she called, laughing. ‘I’ll buy you two catties to make up for it.’
Chan-jie stared in fury, then gave a cold laugh.

‘Lord Thunder has eyes too. Why doesn’t he strike anyone who does such wicked things? And now she’s trying to provoke me! How could I compare with you? You’ve people bringing you tribute, people volunteering to be your slaves, sucking up to you in hopes of a good word to help them on.’
‘Come, girls, that’s enough,’ the women said. ‘You can’t see each other without squabbling.’
Some of the quicker-witted women, seeing them exchange words and fearing another scene, got to their feet and slipped away. Chan-jie herself did not dare say too much to Parfumée and left, muttering.

segments.text: Liu’s wife had a daughter who was only sixteen that year. A kitchen servant’s daughter though she was, her looks were of a kind with those of Patience, Aroma, Nightingale and Faithful. She was the fifth in her family and so was called Wu-er. Having always been frail and sickly, she had never been given a post. Lately her mother had noticed that there were plenty of maids in Bao-yu’s rooms and the duties were light. She had also heard that he meant to let them all go free one day. She therefore wanted to have her daughter put on the staff there.

At first she could see no way of bringing it about. But she had served at Pear-tree Court, where her attentive care for Parfumée and the other girls had been better even than that of the other godmothers. They in turn were very good to her family. She had now spoken to Parfumée and begged her to put in a word with Bao-yu. Bao-yu had agreed, but lately, with his illness and so many other things going on, he had not yet been able to raise the matter.

segments.text: Wu-er went back, and she and her mother talked gratefully of Parfumée’s kindness.
‘I never expected to get anything like this,’ her mother said. ‘Precious stuff it may be, but too much of it is very heating. If we poured some out and gave it away, that would be a fine favour too.’
‘Who to?’ Wu-er asked.
‘Your uncle’s boy. He’s had a fever since yesterday, and he’s been longing for something like this. I’ll take him half a small cup.’
Wu-er said nothing for a while. She let her mother pour out half a cup, then put the rest, still in the bottle, away in the kitchen cupboard.
‘If it were up to me, I wouldn’t give him any,’ she said with a cold smile. ‘Suppose someone starts asking questions. There’ll be another affair.’

‘If we’re to be frightened of everything like that, where will it end?’ her mother said. ‘We work hard enough. It’s only right we should get a few things out of the household. It’s not as if we stole it.’
She went straight out to her elder brother’s home. Her nephew was lying down. At the sight of what she had brought, her brother, his wife and their son were all delighted.

segments.text: Cool water was fetched from the well at once, and the boy drank a bowl with the essence mixed into it. He felt refreshed, his head and eyes cool and clear. The half-cup that remained was covered with paper and set on the table.

Just then several young servants from the household, friends of her nephew, came to ask after him. Among them was a young fellow called Qian Huai, a nephew of Aunt Zhao’s. His parents kept the accounts at the storehouse, and he himself had been assigned to accompany Jia Huan to school. With some money and influence behind him, and still unmarried, he had long admired Liu Wu-er’s good looks. He had told his parents he wanted her for his wife, and intermediaries and a matchmaker had repeatedly been sent to press his suit. Her parents were willing enough, but Wu-er was determined not to agree. She had never said so outright, yet her behaviour had made it plain, and they had not dared give their consent.

Lately, with her mind on a place in the garden, she had put the match still further out of mind. She meant to wait until she was released in three to five years, then choose a husband outside for herself. The Qian family, seeing her attitude, had let it go. Qian Huai, however, was both angry and ashamed at not being able to get her. He had vowed in his resentment to contrive to make her his wife. Nothing else would satisfy him.

segments.text: He had come with the others that day to visit the sick boy, not expecting to find the boy’s aunt there. Liu’s wife, suddenly faced with a whole party and Qian Huai among them, made the excuse that she could not spare the time, rose and prepared to leave.
‘Why, Auntie, you haven’t even had any tea,’ her brother and his wife said. ‘It was kind of you to remember us.’
‘I’m afraid they’ll be calling for the meal inside,’ she said with a smile. ‘I’ll come and see my nephew when I’ve more time.’
Her sister-in-law took a paper packet out of a drawer and carried it out with her. When they reached the corner of the wall, she handed it to Liu’s wife.

‘Your brother was on duty at the gate yesterday,’ she said, smiling. ‘On this five-day rota it’s been so quiet he hasn’t had a single extra bit of money. Only yesterday an official from Guangdong came to call and brought two little baskets of fuling frost for the masters.

segments.text: ‘Besides those, he gave the men at the gate another basket as a gate gift, and this is what your brother got as his share. That part of the country abounds in thousand-year-old pines and cypresses. So they take the essence of this fuling and mix it with medicine, and somehow make it into this wonderfully fine white frost. They say the best way is to mix it with human milk and take a cupful first thing every morning. Nothing could be more nourishing. Cow’s milk is next best. If there’s nothing else, plain boiled water will do.

‘We thought it would be just the thing for our niece. I sent a little maid round with it earlier in the day, but she said the door was locked and our niece had gone inside the mansion too. I’d meant to come and see her and bring it myself. Then I thought, with the masters away and everywhere under such strict watch, and no duty to take me in, why should I go running about for no good reason? Besides, there’s talk these last two days of the whole place being in an uproar. If I got dragged into it, I’d pay dearly for it. You’ve come just at the right moment, sister. Take it back yourself.’

segments.text: ‘You little monkey!’ Mrs Liu said, laughing. ‘Your own dear auntie’s been looking for a man on the side. That gives you another uncle, doesn’t it? What’s there to wonder about? Don’t make me pull those few cunt-hairs off that chamber-pot lid you call a head! Open the gate and let me in.’
The boy would not open it yet. Still holding her back, he said with a grin:

‘Be a good auntie and steal me some apricots when you get inside. I’ll be here waiting. If you forget, next time you’re out in the middle of the night buying wine or oil, I shan’t open the gate for your ladyship. I shan’t even answer. You can shout till you’re tired.’
Mrs Liu spat.

‘Have you lost your wits? This year isn’t like last year. They’ve shared all those things out among the good ladies. They’ve scratched every scrap of shame off their faces: let anyone so much as pass under a tree, and their eyes are on him like a fighting cock’s. Touch their fruit, indeed! Yesterday I was walking under a plum tree when a bee flew past my face. I waved it away, and your precious aunt happened to see me.

segments.text: ‘She was too far off to see properly and thought I was picking plums. Up went her whore’s screech: “They haven’t been offered to the Buddha yet!” And then, “Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship are away. We haven’t presented the first fruits. Once they’ve had theirs, there’ll be a share for all you sisters.” As if I were sick with craving and waiting for those plums to bring me out in a sweat! Well, I had no kind words for her either. I gave her a proper dressing-down. With two or three of your own relations, your aunts on both sides, in charge of the fruit, why don’t you ask them? Why come to me? It’s the granary rat borrowing grain from the crow: the one sitting over it has none, but the one flying about must have some!’

‘Oh, dear, oh, dear!’ the boy said, laughing. ‘If there aren’t any, say so. What a lot of talk! I suppose you’ll never need me again? Even if our sister’s got herself a good place, she’ll have all the more need to call on us. She’ll have plenty for us to do, answering her calls.’
‘You little monkey-spirit!’ Mrs Liu said with a laugh. ‘More of your sly tricks and nonsense. What good place has your sister got?’

segments.text: ‘Tell her to have them another day.’

‘The other day she wanted tofu, and you gave her some that had gone sour,’ said Lotus. ‘I got a scolding for it. Today she wants eggs, and you haven’t got those either! What a precious delicacy! I don’t believe you haven’t even got eggs. You’d better not let me find any.’
As she spoke, she actually went over and lifted the lid of the food chest. Sure enough, there were ten or so eggs inside.

‘What are these, then? You do like to throw your weight about! The food belongs to our masters, and we’ve our regular allowance. Why should you grudge it us? It’s not as if you laid the eggs yourself and can’t bear to have them eaten.’
Mrs Liu dropped what she was doing and hurried over.

‘Stop that filthy nonsense! It’s your mother who lays eggs! These few are all I’ve kept back for garnishing the dishes. I won’t even use them for that unless the young ladies ask. They’re here in case of need. If you eat them and someone suddenly wants something, there’ll be nothing good to give her, not even an egg.

segments.text: ‘Swallow said, “She doesn’t fancy anything with meat. That’s why she’s asked you to do a separate dish with wheat gluten. And go easy on the oil.” You were so quick to say you must have lost your wits, and off you rushed to wash your hands and cook it. Then you carried it over yourself, frisking along like a dog. But today you pick on me to make an example of, telling me off for everyone to hear!’

‘Blessed Buddha!’ Mrs Liu exclaimed. ‘Everyone here has eyes. Never mind that one time the other day. Ever since this kitchen was set up last year, whenever a young lady or one of the girls in any of the rooms has happened to want an extra dish or two, haven’t they always brought the money first, to buy the extra things? People talk whether they know anything or not. It sounds very nice: I’ve only the young ladies’ kitchen to look after, an easy job with something left over. But the accounts would turn your stomach. There are forty or fifty mouths, young ladies and maids together, and all I can draw each day is two chickens, two ducks, ten-odd catties of meat and a string of cash for vegetables. Work it out for yourselves. What can you do with that? It won’t stretch to the two regular meals, let alone this one ordering one thing and that one another. And when it’s bought, they won’t eat it, and you have to go and buy something else.

segments.text: ‘If that’s how it’s to be, we’d better tell Her Ladyship and have the regular allowance increased. We could do as the main kitchen does for Her Old Ladyship’s meals: write every vegetable under heaven on a wipe-clean menu board, work through them day by day, and settle up at the end of the month. That would be better. Why, the other day the Third Miss and Miss Bao happened to agree that they’d like some wolfberry shoots stir-fried with nothing but oil and salt. They actually sent a maid with five hundred cash for me. I laughed. “Even if the two young ladies had bellies like Maitreya the Buddha, they couldn’t eat five hundred cash’s worth,” I said. “It only costs twenty or thirty cash. I can still afford that.” I hurried over to give the money back, but they wouldn’t take it. They said I was to buy myself some wine. And they said, “Now the kitchen’s inside, we can’t be sure the people in our rooms won’t come bothering you. Salt or sauce, it all costs money. You can hardly refuse them, but if you give it to them, where are you to make up the loss? Keep this money and count it as payment for all the things they’ve been pestering you for.” Those are young ladies who understand and have some feeling for the people below them. We can only pray to the Buddha for them in our hearts.

segments.text: In the midst of this uproar, another messenger came from Chess to hurry Lotus back.
‘Has she died in there? Why doesn’t she come back?’

Lotus went off in a temper and told Chess what had happened, adding a whole chapter of her own. Chess’s anger was duly roused. Once she had finished waiting on Ying-chun at her meal, she came over with the little maids. A number of people were eating when she arrived. Seeing that she meant trouble, they all jumped up, smiling, and offered her a seat.
Chess shouted to the little maids to get to work.
‘Every bit of food in those chests and cupboards, throw it out for the dogs! Then nobody will make anything out of it!’
The little maids needed no second telling. They rushed forward, all hands and feet, rummaging and flinging things about. The others tried to pull them back and calm them while pleading with Chess:

‘Miss, don’t be misled by what a child says. Mrs Liu wouldn’t dare offend you if she had eight heads to lose. Eggs really are hard to buy. We’ve just told her she ought to have known better: whatever you wanted, she should have found some way to get it.

segments.text: ‘She’s seen her mistake now and put them on to steam straight away. If you don’t believe us, miss, look at the stove.’

After all their soothing words, Chess’s anger gradually subsided. The little maids were pulled away before they could finish smashing everything. Chess carried on for a while, scolding and cursing, before the others persuaded her to go. Mrs Liu could only bang down bowls and fling down plates, muttering to herself for a time. She steamed a bowl of eggs and sent someone over with it. Chess tipped the whole bowlful onto the floor. The messenger dared not tell them on returning, for fear of making more trouble.

segments.text: Mrs Liu saw that her daughter had some soup and half a bowl of rice gruel, then told her about the fuling frost. Wu-er wanted to give some to Parfumée, so she wrapped half of it separately in paper. At dusk, when few people were about, she went to find Parfumée, keeping behind flowers and willows as she went. To her delight, no one stopped to question her. She made straight for the gate of the House of Green Delights, but did not like to go in. Instead she stood by a cluster of rose bushes, watching from a distance.

After about the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, Swallow happened to come out. Wu-er hurried forward and called to her. Swallow did not recognise her until she came close enough to see her face, then asked what she wanted.

segments.text: ‘Call Parfumée out,’ Wu-er said with a smile. ‘I want to speak to her.’

‘You’re too impatient, sister,’ Swallow said, laughing quietly. ‘You’ll be coming here in ten days or so anyway. Why keep looking for her? They’ve just sent her out to the front. You’ll have to wait a little. Or tell me what you want to say, and I’ll tell her. You may not be able to wait. I’m afraid they’ll be shutting the garden gate.’
Wu-er handed Swallow the packet, explaining that it was fuling frost, how it was taken and what nourishment it gave.
‘I’ve had some given me, and I’ve brought this for her. Do be so kind as to pass it on.’
Then she said goodbye and went back.

segments.text: She was walking near the knotweed shallows when she suddenly saw Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife coming towards her with several older women. There was no time to hide. She could only go forward and greet her.
‘I heard you were ill,’ said Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife. ‘What are you doing running about here?’

‘I’ve been a little better these last two days,’ Wu-er said with a deferential smile. ‘I came in with Mother for a little diversion. Just now she sent me to the House of Green Delights with some dishes.’

‘That story doesn’t fit. I only shut the gate after I’d seen your mother go out. If she sent you, why didn’t she tell me you were still here? What did she mean by going off and letting me lock up? It’s plain you’re lying.’
Wu-er could find no answer.
‘Mother told me early this morning to take them,’ was all she could say. ‘I forgot, and only just remembered.

segments.text: ‘She must have thought I’d already gone out. That’s why she didn’t tell you, ma’am.’

Her faltering words and uneasy expression made Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife suspicious. Silver had lately reported things missing from the principal rooms over there. The maids were blaming one another, and no culprit had been found. Just then Chan-jie, Lotus and several married servants came along. Seeing what was happening, they said:
‘You ought to question her properly, Mrs Lin. She’s been running in and out of here these last two days in a most suspicious way, all whispering and sneaking about. Who knows what she’s up to?’
‘That’s right,’ Chan-jie put in.

segments.text: ‘Yesterday Sister Silver said the cupboard in Her Ladyship’s side room had been opened and all sorts of little things were missing. Mrs Lian sent Miss Patience to ask Sister Silver for some rose essence, and there was a jar of that missing too. If they hadn’t wanted the essence, they wouldn’t even have known.’
‘I hadn’t heard that,’ Lotus said with a smile. ‘But I did see a bottle of essence today.’
The unsolved thefts were a sore point with Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife. Xi-feng sent Patience to press her about them every day. At this she hastily asked where the bottle was.
‘In their kitchen,’ Lotus replied.
Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife immediately ordered a lantern to be lit and took them all to look.
‘It was Parfumée from Master Bao’s rooms who gave it to me!’ Wu-er cried in distress.
‘Parfumée, Square, Round: I don’t care what she’s called,’ said Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife. ‘We have the stolen goods as evidence. I’ll report it, and you can make your excuses to your masters.’
Still talking, she went into the kitchen, where Lotus led her to the bottle of essence and took it out.

They found a packet of fuling frost as well, seized both, and took Wu-er with them to report to Li Wan and Tan-chun. Jia Lan was ill, however, and Li Wan was attending to no business. She merely told them to go to Tan-chun, who had already retired to her rooms.

segments.text: Their arrival was announced. The maids were all taking the cool air in the courtyard, while Tan-chun was washing inside. Only Scribe went in with the message. After some time she came out.
‘Miss Tan-chun has been told. She says you’re to find Patience and have her report to Mrs Lian.’

Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife had no choice but to take them away again. At Xi-feng’s quarters she first found Patience, who went in to report. Xi-feng had just lain down. On hearing what had happened, she gave her orders:

‘Give the mother forty strokes of the board and turn her out. She’s never to come inside the second gate again. Give Wu-er forty strokes too, then hand her straight over to the country estate, to be sold or married off.’
Patience came out and passed these instructions on to Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife. Terrified, Wu-er knelt before Patience, sobbing, and told her all about Parfumée.

‘That’s easy enough to settle,’ said Patience. ‘We’ll ask Parfumée tomorrow and see whether it’s true. But this fuling frost only came as a gift the other day. No one would dare touch it before Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship came back and saw it. You ought not to have stolen it.’
At this Wu-er hastily told her how her uncle had sent it.

segments.text: ‘So by your account,’ Patience said with a smile, ‘you’re entirely innocent, and they’ve brought you here to take the blame for someone else. It’s late now. My mistress has just taken her medicine and lain down. I can’t pester her with such a little matter at this hour. For the present, hand her over to the night-watch women. They can keep her till morning. I’ll speak to my mistress then, and we’ll decide what to do.’
Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife dared not disobey. She took Wu-er away, handed her over to the married women on night duty and went about her own affairs.

segments.text: Wu-er was kept under guard and dared not move a step beyond where she was allowed. Some of the women lectured her on the disgraceful things she ought not to have done. Others complained:
‘We can hardly get through our proper night watch as it is, and now they’ve given us a thief to look after. If she kills herself or runs away when our backs are turned, it’ll all be our fault.’

Then a number of people who had long been on bad terms with the Liu family, delighted at this turn of events, came to jeer and make fun of her. Wu-er was angry and full of a sense of injustice, but had nowhere to take her grievance. She was already frail and ill. That night, when she wanted tea there was no tea, when she wanted water there was no water, and when she wanted sleep there was neither quilt nor pillow. She sobbed and wept the whole night through.

segments.text: Those who were at odds with mother and daughter could not wait to see them driven out. Afraid that things might change next day, they all rose early and went quietly to win Patience over, bringing little gifts, praising the decisiveness with which she had handled the matter and recounting all sorts of faults in Mrs Liu’s everyday conduct. Patience acknowledged each of them and sent them away. Then she went privately to Aroma and asked whether Parfumée really had given Wu-er the essence.
‘The essence was given to Parfumée,’ Aroma said. ‘I don’t know who she passed it on to.’
She asked Parfumée, who, when she heard what had happened, sprang up in alarm and hastily said that she herself had given it to Wu-er. Parfumée then told Bao-yu, who grew alarmed too.

‘We’ve accounted for the essence, but if they bring up the fuling frost, she’ll naturally tell them the truth about that as well. Once they hear her uncle got it at the gate, he’ll be in trouble too. They meant to be kind, and we’ll have brought trouble on them in return!’
He hurriedly took counsel with Patience.
‘The essence is settled, but there’s still trouble over the frost.

segments.text: ‘Dear sister, tell her to say Parfumée gave her that too. Then it’s all settled.’

‘That may be,’ Patience said with a smile, ‘but she told everyone last night that her uncle gave it to her. How can she now say it came from you? Besides, we still haven’t found who took the essence over there. If we let someone with the stolen goods go free, who are we to look for next? Who’s going to admit it? And people won’t necessarily be satisfied.’
Skybright came over, smiling.
‘No one else took Her Ladyship’s essence. It was plainly Cai-yun, who stole it for Master Huan. You’re all talking at random.’

‘Who doesn’t know that?’ Patience said with a smile. ‘Only now Silver’s so upset she’s crying. If Cai-yun had admitted it when she was asked quietly, Silver would have let it go, and we could all have muddled along without asking any more. Do you think we went looking for this affair? What’s infuriating is that Cai-yun won’t admit it. Worse, she’s putting the blame on Silver and saying she stole it. The two of them started firing at each other inside their own nest till the whole household knew. How could we pretend nothing had happened?

segments.text: ‘We had to investigate. Little do they know that the very person crying theft is the thief. But without the stolen goods to prove it, how are we to accuse her?’
‘All right,’ Bao-yu said. ‘I’ll take the blame for this too. Say I secretly stole Mother’s things to give them a fright for a joke. That will settle both matters.’
‘It would earn you some hidden merit,’ said Aroma, ‘saving someone from the name of thief. Only when Her Ladyship hears, she’ll say you’re childish again, with no sense of right and wrong.’

‘That’s a small matter,’ Patience said, smiling. ‘It would be easy enough to recover the stolen things from Aunt Zhao’s rooms now. I’m only afraid of hurting one good person’s reputation as well. Never mind the others: wouldn’t that one person be upset again? She’s the one I feel for. I won’t smash a jade vase just to hit a rat.’
She held up three fingers. Aroma and the others knew at once that she meant Tan-chun.
‘Of course!’ they all hastened to say. ‘It’s best to let our rooms take the blame.’

segments.text: ‘Still,’ Patience went on, smiling, ‘we must send for those two troublemakers, Cai-yun and Silver, and make certain where we stand. Otherwise they’ll get all the benefit without knowing why. They’ll think I was too useless to find anything out and had to come here to have it settled for me. After that, the thief will steal more than ever, and the one who doesn’t keep watch won’t bother at all.’
‘Quite right,’ Aroma and the others said, laughing. ‘You must leave yourself some ground to stand on too.’
Patience sent for the two girls.
‘Don’t be frightened,’ she told them. ‘The thief’s been found.’
Silver at once asked where the thief was.

‘At Mrs Lian’s quarters now,’ said Patience. ‘Ask her anything, and she admits it. I know perfectly well she didn’t steal the things. The poor girl’s so frightened she’ll confess to anything. Master Bao here can’t bear it and wants to take half the blame for her. I was going to speak out, only the girl who really stole them is an old friend of mine, a sister. The receiver of the stolen things wouldn’t matter, but there’s a good person’s reputation involved too. That’s what makes it difficult. I’ve had to beg Master Bao to admit it, so that everyone can be left in peace.

segments.text: ‘Now I want to ask you two what you mean to do. If from now on everyone will take care and preserve some decency, we’ll ask Master Bao to take the blame. If not, I’ll tell Mrs Lian, rather than let an innocent person suffer.’
Cai-yun blushed. Shame and a sudden revulsion from her own wrongdoing moved her to speak.

‘Don’t worry, sister. We mustn’t wrong a good person or drag someone innocent into it and damage her reputation. As for the theft, Aunt Zhao begged me over and over again. It’s true I took some things for Master Huan. We’ve taken things even when Her Ladyship was at home, all of us, to give to other people. It’s quite usual. I thought they’d make a fuss for a couple of days and then let it drop. But now an innocent person’s suffering for it, I can’t bear it. Take me to our mistress, sister. I’ll admit everything and have done with it.’
Everyone was astonished that she should show such courage. Bao-yu hastily smiled.

‘Sister Cai-yun really is a decent person. But there’s no need for you to admit anything. I’ll just say I stole the things to frighten you for a joke. Now that it’s caused trouble, of course I ought to own up.

segments.text: ‘Only do try to make less trouble in future, sisters, and all will be well.’
‘Why should you admit to something I did?’ said Cai-yun. ‘Live or die, I ought to bear it myself.’

‘That’s not the way to look at it,’ Patience and Aroma said quickly. ‘Once you confess, Aunt Zhao is bound to be dragged in again. Won’t the Third Miss be upset when she hears? It’s much better to let Master Bao admit it and leave everyone in peace. No one beyond the few of us here need know anything about it. How neatly that would settle things! Only everyone must be very, very careful from now on. Whatever you want to take, at least have the patience to wait till Her Ladyship comes home. Then even if the whole house is given away, it’s nothing to do with us.’
Cai-yun lowered her head and thought for a while before agreeing.

‘I had her brought here first thing this morning,’ Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife told Patience. ‘I was afraid there’d be no one to see to the young ladies’ meals in the garden, so I sent Qin Xian’s wife to do it for the time being. ‘Who is Qin Xian’s wife?’ Patience asked. ‘I don’t know her very well.’
‘She keeps the night watch at the south corner of the garden. There’s not much for her to do by day, so you wouldn’t know her. High cheekbones, big eyes, a very clean, capable woman.’
