segments.text: ‘Of course,’ said Silver. ‘How could you forget, sister? She’s Chess’s aunt, the wife of her father’s younger brother. Chess serves the Second Miss. Her parents belong to the Elder Master’s establishment, but this uncle belongs to ours.’
Now Patience remembered.
‘Oh! If you’d said that to begin with, I’d have known who you meant.’
Then she smiled again.

‘You’ve been rather hasty with that appointment. It’s all clear now, from every side. Even the things that went missing from Her Ladyship’s rooms the other day have been accounted for. Bao-yu went over and asked these two wretches for something. They wanted to tease him and said they daren’t give it to him while Her Ladyship was away. So he waited till they weren’t looking, went in himself and took some things out. They knew nothing about it and were thrown into a panic. Only when Bao-yu heard that other people had been dragged into it did he tell me the whole story and bring the things out to show me. There wasn’t a single thing missing. As for the fuling frost, Bao-yu had that from outside and gave it to all sorts of people. It’s not only the people in the garden who’ve had some. Even the older women have asked him for it to take to their relations, and they’ve passed it on to others. Aroma, too, has given some to Parfumée and girls like her.

segments.text: ‘That may be what he says,’ Xi-feng replied, ‘but Bao-yu will take anything on himself, whether it’s right or wrong. Let someone plead with him and say a couple of nice things: put a charcoal basket on his head as if it were a fine hat, and there’s nothing he won’t agree to. If we believe him, what happens when it’s something serious and he does the same? How are we to keep people in order? We must make a thorough inquiry. If I had my way, we’d bring all the maids from Her Ladyship’s rooms here. We can hardly have them beaten on our own authority, but we could make them kneel on broken porcelain in the sun and give them neither food nor tea. A day’s silence, a day on their knees. Even if they were made of iron, they’d confess within a day. Besides, “a fly won’t cling to an egg without a crack.” Mrs Liu may not have stolen anything, but there must have been something to make people accuse her. Even if we don’t punish her as a thief, she should lose her place and never be employed again. The court itself punishes people implicated in someone else’s offence. She couldn’t call it an injustice.’
‘Why give yourself all this worry?’ Patience said. ‘“When you can let go, let go.” It’s nothing so very serious. Why not take the easy chance to do someone a kindness?

segments.text: ‘If you ask me, however much we wear ourselves out over this household, in the end we shall go back to the other branch. Why make enemies of petty people and leave them nursing grudges? Besides, you’ve had one illness and misfortune after another. After all the trouble of conceiving a boy, you lost him at six or seven months. How do we know it wasn’t all the overwork and vexation that harmed you? It’s time you learnt to see half of what goes on and turn a blind eye to the rest. That would be better.’
This speech brought a smile to Xi-feng’s face.
‘Go and settle it as you like, you little hussy. I’ve only just begun to feel more myself. There’s no sense in wearing myself out.’
‘Now that’s sensible!’ Patience said, smiling.

segments.text: Patience came out and gave Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife her instructions.

‘A flourishing household makes large troubles small and small troubles disappear. It’s no way to carry on, making a great to-do with bells and drums over every little thing you can’t put up with. Take mother and daughter back now and let them go on with their duties as before. Send Qin Xian’s wife back to her old place. We needn’t hear any more about this. What does matter is that you keep a careful watch every day.’
With that she got up and left. Mrs Liu and her daughter hastily kowtowed towards her. Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife took them back into the Garden and reported to Li Wan and Tan-chun.
‘We understand,’ they both said. ‘The fewer troubles the better. That’s very good.’

segments.text: Chess and the others had had all their excitement for nothing. Qin Xian’s wife, who had waited so long for an opening to squeeze into, had enjoyed her triumph for no more than half a day. She was still in a bustle in the kitchen, taking over the utensils, rice, charcoal and other stores, when she discovered all sorts of shortages.
‘There are two shi of polished rice missing, and a whole extra month’s ordinary rice has been issued. The charcoal’s short of its quota too.’

segments.text: Meanwhile she had been preparing a present for Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife. Quietly assembling a basket of charcoal, five hundred catties of firewood and a load of polished rice, she had sent sons and nephews from outside to deliver them to the Lin household. She was preparing another gift for the accounts office, and arranging several dishes with which to entertain some of her fellow servants.
‘Now I’m here, I shall depend on all of you. We’re one family from now on. If there’s anything I overlook, do please see to it for me.’
In the midst of these preparations someone came to tell her:
‘You can leave once you’ve seen to breakfast. There was nothing against Mrs Liu after all, and she’s to have charge again.’

The news knocked the spirit out of Qin Xian’s wife. Crestfallen, she struck her colours at once, silenced her drums, rolled up her bundle and left. Much of what she had given away was simply lost; worse, she would have to sell her own belongings to make good the shortages. Even Chess was nearly bowled over with rage. But there was no recovering the position, and they had to let it go.

segments.text: Ever since Silver had made an outcry over the many things Cai-yun had secretly given away, Aunt Zhao had been terrified that an investigation would bring the truth to light. Every day she listened anxiously for news. Then Cai-yun came to tell her:
‘Bao-yu has taken it all on himself. There’ll be no more trouble.’
Only then could Aunt Zhao breathe again. Jia Huan, however, became suspicious as soon as he heard this. He brought out everything Cai-yun had ever given him in secret and flung it at her face.

‘You two-faced creature! I don’t want your things. If you weren’t carrying on with Bao-yu, why would he take the blame for you? If you had the courage to give them to me, you ought not to have let a single other person know. Now you’ve told him, what pleasure is there in my keeping them?’

segments.text: In her distress Cai-yun called down curses on herself to prove her innocence, and at last burst into tears. She tried every explanation, but Jia Huan obstinately refused to believe her.
‘If it weren’t for what there’s been between us, I’d go and tell Cousin Feng you stole them for me and I was afraid to take them. Think that over.’
He flung out his arm and left. Aunt Zhao cursed him in exasperation.
‘You wretched, ill-fated brat! You maggot-hearted little sinner!’
Cai-yun wept until her tears were spent and her heart seemed torn apart. Aunt Zhao did everything she could to comfort her.
‘My good girl, he’s repaid your love badly. I can see that plainly enough. Let me put these away. He’ll come round of his own accord in a day or two.’

She began to gather the things up, but Cai-yun angrily bundled them together herself. When no one was looking she went into the Garden and threw the whole lot into the stream. Some sank; some floated away with the current. That night, bitterly hurt, she cried in secret under her quilt.

segments.text: Now Bao-yu’s birthday had come round. Bao-qin’s, as it happened, fell on the same day. Since Lady Wang was away, there was none of the usual bustle of celebration. Daoist Zhang sent gifts of four kinds and a replacement talisman for the name under which Bao-yu was registered with him. Monks and nuns from several other temples sent choice portions from their offerings, a paper image of the God of Longevity, written prayers, and the annually renewed protective locks for his natal star and the Tai Sui presiding over the year. The women storytellers who regularly visited the house came to offer their birthday wishes. From Wang Zi-teng’s household came the customary set of clothes, a pair of shoes and stockings, a hundred birthday peaches and a hundred bundles of the finest silver-thread noodles, of the grade supplied to the court. Aunt Xue’s gift was on a slightly smaller scale. Of the others in the family, You-shi sent her usual pair of shoes and stockings. Xi-feng gave him a palace-made ‘Fourfold Harmony’ purse, containing a gold figure of the God of Longevity and a toy made in Persia. People were sent to the various temples to distribute alms to the assembled clergy. There were separate gifts for Bao-qin too, too many to enumerate. The girls gave whatever they pleased: a fan, a piece of calligraphy, a painting or a poem, simply to mark the occasion.

segments.text: That morning Bao-yu rose early, washed, dressed his hair and came out in formal cap and sash. In the courtyard before the front hall, Li Gui and the other men, four or five in all, had already set out incense and candles for Heaven and Earth. Bao-yu lit the incense, performed his obeisances, poured the tea libation and burned the paper offerings. He then went over to the Ning mansion and paid his respects in both the clan shrine and the ancestral hall. Coming out onto the terrace, he bowed from afar towards Grandmother Jia, Jia Zheng, Lady Wang and the others. On his way back he called at You-shi’s principal room, saluted her and sat for a while before returning to the Rong mansion. He went first to Aunt Xue, who repeatedly detained him; then he met Xue Ke, and after another exchange of invitations and courtesies he finally entered the Garden.

segments.text: Skybright and Musk accompanied him, with a little maid carrying a felt kneeling-mat. Beginning with Li Wan, he went in turn to the rooms of everyone senior to him. Then he went out through the inner gate again to pay his respects and extend his invitations at the homes of his four nurses, the Li, Zhao, Zhang and Wang women, before returning inside. People tried to make their obeisances to him, but he accepted none. Back in his own rooms, Aroma and the others merely spoke their good wishes. Lady Wang had forbidden the young people to receive formal obeisances, for fear of diminishing their store of good fortune and long life, so no one kowtowed.

segments.text: After he had rested a little, Jia Huan and Jia Lan came with the others. Aroma hastily stopped them from kneeling. They sat a short while and went away. Bao-yu said with a smile that all the walking had tired him, and stretched out on the bed. He had scarcely drunk half a cup of tea when a clatter of voices outside announced a whole laughing troop of maids: Ebony, Xiao-luo, Kingfisher, Picture, Xing Xiu-yan’s maid Zhuan-er, a nurse carrying Qiao-jie, Cai-luan and Xiu-luan, eight or nine of them, coming in with red felt mats in their arms.
‘The birthday visitors are crowding your door off its hinges! Hurry up and give us some noodles!’
They had barely entered when Tan-chun, Xiang-yun, Bao-qin, Xiu-yan and Xi-chun arrived too. Bao-yu hurried out to meet them.
‘You shouldn’t have troubled to come! Quickly, have some good tea ready!’

segments.text: Once inside there was the inevitable exchange of courtesies before everyone sat down. Aroma and the others brought in tea. They had taken only a sip when Patience arrived, dressed as brightly as a flowering branch. Bao-yu hurried out again.
‘I called at Cousin Feng’s door just now and sent in word, but couldn’t see her. Then I sent someone in with an invitation for you too.’

‘I was helping your cousin with her hair,’ Patience said, smiling, ‘and couldn’t come out to answer you. Afterwards, when I heard you’d sent specially to invite me as well, I felt quite unworthy of the honour. So I hurried over to kowtow.’
‘I’m not worthy of that either,’ said Bao-yu.

Aroma had already placed a seat for her in the outer room and invited her to sit. Patience sank into a curtsey, and Bao-yu repeatedly bowed with his hands clasped. She then knelt; he hastily knelt in return, and Aroma hurried to help them up. Patience curtseyed once more, and Bao-yu answered with another bow.
‘Bow again,’ Aroma said, laughing and giving him a push.
‘We’ve finished. Why should I bow again?’
‘Those were her birthday wishes to you.

‘The four of you ought to bow birthday wishes to one another all day long!’

segments.text: The maid went off as instructed. Since Xiang-yun had blurted it out, Xiu-yan could hardly avoid going round the various rooms to extend her own invitations.

‘It is rather amusing,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘Twelve months in a year, and several birthdays every month. With so many of us, these coincidences happen: three people on one day, two on another. Even New Year’s Day isn’t left empty. Our eldest sister has claimed that. No wonder she has such good fortune. Even her birthday comes before everyone else’s. And it was our honoured ancestor’s birthday too.

‘Miss Lin’s is the twelfth of the second month,’ said Aroma. ‘How can you say there’s no one? Though she isn’t one of this family.’
‘What is happening to my memory?’ Tan-chun said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘She and Cousin Lin share the same day,’ Bao-yu said, pointing at Aroma with a smile. ‘That’s why she remembers.’
‘So you two share a birthday too!’ said Tan-chun. ‘And never so much as a birthday kowtow to us from you. We didn’t know Patience’s birthday either. We’ve only just found that out.’

‘People on our sort of register have no right to receive presents or be honoured with birthday greetings,’ Patience said with a smile. ‘What would we have to make a fuss about? We let the day go by quietly. Now she’s gone and made it public. When you young ladies are back in your rooms, I’ll come and pay my respects.’
‘We couldn’t trouble you to do that,’ Tan-chun said. ‘But I shan’t feel easy unless we celebrate your birthday for you today.’
‘Quite right!’ Bao-yu, Xiang-yun and the others said together.
Tan-chun gave a maid her instructions.
‘Go and tell her mistress that we’ve all decided not to let Patience out of here all day. We’re clubbing together to celebrate her birthday.’
The maid went off laughing. After a while she returned.
‘Mrs Lian says to thank the young ladies for doing Patience such an honour.

segments.text: Everyone thought this an excellent plan. Tan-chun sent to ask Li Wan, Bao-chai and Dai-yu, and also sent for Mrs Liu, whom she told to prepare two tables of food and wine immediately in the inner kitchen. Mrs Liu did not understand.
‘But it’s all being prepared in the outer kitchen.’

‘So you don’t know,’ Tan-chun said, smiling. ‘Today is Miss Patience’s birthday. The feast they’re preparing outside is for the family. We’ve privately subscribed a little more for two tables expressly to entertain Miss Patience. Choose some fresh, ingenious dishes and bring them here. Make out your bill and collect the money from me.’
‘So today is Miss Patience’s birthday too!’ Mrs Liu said with a smile. ‘I had no idea.’
She dropped to her knees to kowtow to Patience, who hurriedly pulled her up. Mrs Liu then hastened away to prepare the feast.

segments.text: As soon as they were through the side gate, Bao-chai ordered an older woman to lock it and give her the key, which she kept herself.
‘Why lock this gate?’ Bao-yu protested. ‘Hardly anyone comes this way. Besides, Aunt and all you girls are inside. If you want to fetch anything from home, won’t it be a nuisance?’

‘You can’t be too careful,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘Look at all the things that have been happening on your side these last few days. Not one of our people was involved. segments.text: ‘Better to lock it and restrict Mother and me as well. Nobody comes through. Then even if something does happen, no one can blame the people on our side.’
‘So you know about things disappearing from our side lately?’ Bao-yu asked with a smile.

‘All you know about is the rose essence and the fuling frost. You came to hear of the things because you were concerned about the people. Otherwise you wouldn’t even know about those two. There are several other matters far more serious. If they don’t get unearthed later, it will be everyone’s good fortune. If they do, there’s no knowing how many people will be dragged into them. I’m only telling you because you have nothing to do with running things. Patience is a sensible girl. I told her the other day too. Her mistress hasn’t been out and about, so I thought Patience should understand. If nothing comes out, everyone can be glad to leave it alone. If it does, she’ll already have some idea of how to proceed, and innocent people won’t be wronged. Just listen to me and be careful from now on. You mustn’t repeat this to anyone.’

segments.text: She had scarcely entered when several maids came to look for her and accompanied her to Red Fragrance Court. There the feast was spread in tortoiseshell splendour, the cushions flowered with lotus.
‘Now all our birthday stars are here!’ everyone cried, laughing.
They insisted that the four celebrants should take the four places of honour, but all four refused.

‘I’m getting on in years,’ said Aunt Xue, ‘and I don’t belong in your young company. It makes me feel constrained. I’d be much happier lying down comfortably in the hall. I can’t eat much, and I scarcely drink. They’ll be better off with my place here.’
You-shi and the others would not hear of it.

‘Why not let Mother be comfortable in the hall?’ Bao-chai said. ‘We can send her anything she likes to eat, and she’ll be more at her ease. Besides, there’s nobody in front just now. She can keep an eye on things there.’
‘In that case,’ Tan-chun and the others said, smiling, ‘we shall show our respect by doing as you wish.’

segments.text: ‘Sitting here looking elegant is dull,’ Bao-yu said. ‘We must have a drinking game.’
One person suggested this game, another that.
‘Why not get a brush and inkstone,’ Dai-yu said, ‘write them all down and make them into lots? Whichever we draw is the one we play.’

Everyone thought it an excellent idea. A brush, inkstone and flower-patterned paper were brought. Caltrop, who had lately been learning poetry and now practised her writing every day, could not resist the sight of writing materials. She jumped up.
‘Let me write!’

Between them they thought of ten or so games. As they called them out, Caltrop wrote them down one by one, rolled the slips into lots and dropped them into a vase. Tan-chun told Patience to choose. Patience stirred them round, lifted one out with her chopsticks and opened it. It said ‘The Concealed-Word Game’.

‘You’ve drawn the ancestor of all drinking games,’ Bao-chai said, laughing. ‘The game goes back to antiquity, but the old way of playing it has been lost. This version was made up by later generations, and it’s harder than all the others.

segments.text: ‘Half the people here don’t know how to play it. Why not put it aside and draw another that everyone can enjoy, learned or otherwise?’
‘We’ve drawn it now,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘How can we throw it away? Let’s draw one more. If it’s something everyone can enjoy, they can play that while we play this.’
She had Aroma draw another slip. This time it was ‘Finger-Guessing’.

‘That’s brisk and straightforward,’ Xiang-yun said, laughing. ‘Just my sort of thing! I’m not playing your concealed-word game, hanging my head over some depressing puzzle. I’m going to guess fingers.’
‘She’s the only one who ever disrupts a game,’ said Tan-chun. ‘Cousin Bao, fine her a cup at once.’
Bao-chai would hear no excuses, and made Xiang-yun drink.

segments.text: ‘I’ll drink a cup myself,’ said Tan-chun. ‘I’m mistress of the games. There’s no need for a proclamation. Just do as I tell you.’
She had the gaming dice and dish brought in.
‘Bao-qin throws first, then everyone in turn. Two people with matching throws play the concealed-word game.’
Bao-qin threw a three. Neither Xiu-yan nor Bao-yu nor the others matched it, until Caltrop threw a three as well.
‘We must keep our springtime within these four walls,’ Bao-qin said, smiling. ‘If we start going outside, there’ll be far too much to choose from.’
‘Of course,’ said Tan-chun. ‘Three wrong guesses cost one cup. You give the clue and she guesses.’
Bao-qin thought for a moment, then said, ‘Old.’

Caltrop was new to the game and could think of nothing. All round the room and on the tables she could see nothing that would combine with ‘old’ in a familiar phrase. Xiang-yun had heard the clue too and was looking everywhere. Suddenly she noticed the words ‘Red Fragrance Court’ above the doorway. She knew then that Bao-qin was concealing the inscription’s last word, pu, a garden or gardener, from ‘I am no match for an old gardener.’ Caltrop still could not guess, and the others were drumming to hurry her. Xiang-yun quietly tugged her and whispered that she should say, ‘Medicinal herb.’

segments.text: Xiang-yun had not been able to wait. She and Bao-yu were already playing finger-guessing, shouting ‘Three!’ and ‘Five!’ in a jumble. Across the tables You-shi and Faithful were calling ‘Seven!’ and ‘Eight!’ as they played. Patience and Aroma had paired off too, their bracelets clinking and jingling on their wrists. Presently Xiang-yun beat Bao-yu, Aroma beat Patience, and You-shi beat Faithful. The three winners set their conditions for a drinking prelude and a drinking coda. Xiang-yun declared:

‘The prelude must have one phrase of classical prose, one line of old poetry, the name of a domino combination, the title of a tune, and a phrase from the official almanac, all joined into one connected utterance. The coda must name a fruit or vegetable and relate it to human affairs.’
‘Even her drinking rules are wordier than anyone else’s,’ they all said, laughing. ‘But it is a good idea.’
They urged Bao-yu to begin.
‘Who’s ever heard of such a game?’ he said with a smile. ‘At least give me time to think.’
‘Drink one extra cup and I’ll do it for you,’ Dai-yu said.
Bao-yu really did drink, then listened as Dai-yu began:

‘“Sunset clouds and a lone duck fly together”;
“In the river sky’s fierce wind, wild geese pass crying mournfully.”
Yet it is “A Goose with a Broken Leg”,
Whose cries set “The Heart Turning Nine Times”:
Here are “Wild Geese Arriving as Guests”.’

segments.text: ‘How does that work?’ everyone asked.

‘She says “precious”, bao, and the word to follow it must be “jade”, yu,’ Bao-yu explained. ‘My answer is “hairpin”, chai, because an old poem says, “The jade hairpin is snapped; the red candle is cold.” Doesn’t that give the answer?’
‘You can’t use present-day matters,’ Xiang-yun objected. ‘They should both be fined.’
‘It isn’t only a present-day matter,’ Caltrop put in eagerly. ‘There’s a literary source as well.’
‘There’s no source for “precious jade”,’ said Xiang-yun. ‘You might find it in a New Year’s couplet, but it isn’t in poetry or the classics. That doesn’t count.’

‘The other day I was reading a five-character regulated poem by Cen Jia-zhou,’ Caltrop said, ‘and there was the line, “This land abounds in precious jade.” How have you forgotten it? Afterwards I read a seven-character quatrain by Li Yi-shan with the line, “No day but dust collects upon the jewelled hairpin.” I even laughed about discovering that both their names were in Tang poetry.’

segments.text: ‘That’s stopped you!’ everyone laughed. ‘Drink up!’

Xiang-yun had no answer and had to drink. The dice-throwers went back to matching their throws and the finger-guessers to their game. With Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang away, there was no one to hold them in check. They enjoyed themselves as freely as they pleased, shouting threes and fours, sevens and eights. Throughout the hall red and green fluttered, jade swung and pearls quivered. It was a thoroughly lively scene.

After playing a while they rose from the tables and scattered a little. Suddenly Xiang-yun was nowhere to be seen. At first they assumed she had gone outside to relieve herself and would soon return. But they waited and waited without a sign of her. People were sent to search everywhere, and still she could not be found.

segments.text: Then Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife arrived with several older women. They were afraid there might be some business needing attention. They were also afraid that the young maids, with Lady Wang away, might disregard the authority of Tan-chun and the others, drink to excess and abandon all decorum. They had come to ask whether anything was needed. Tan-chun understood their purpose as soon as she saw them.
‘You can’t trust us, can you?’ she said with a smile. ‘You’ve come to inspect us. We haven’t had much wine. We’re only amusing ourselves, using it as an excuse for games. Don’t worry, mammas.’
‘Go and rest,’ Li Wan and You-shi added, smiling. ‘We wouldn’t dare let them drink too much either.’

‘We know,’ Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife and the others replied with smiles. ‘Even when Her Old Ladyship tells the young ladies to drink, they won’t. With the mistresses away, of course it’s only a game. We thought there might be something to do and came to ask. Besides, the days are long now. When you’ve played a while, you ought to have a little something to eat. You don’t generally eat much between meals. If you have a cup or two of wine and don’t eat more to go with it, we’re afraid it might upset you.’
‘You’re quite right, mammas,’ Tan-chun said. ‘We were just wanting something.’
She turned and ordered refreshments.

segments.text: The maids on either side answered and hurried to have the refreshments brought. Tan-chun smilingly urged the women to leave.

‘We wouldn’t presume to accept,’ Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife and the others replied with smiles.
They stood a little longer, then withdrew. Patience felt her face.
‘My face is quite hot,’ she said, laughing. ‘I’m ashamed to let them see me. I think we ought to clear it all away. It would be no fun having them come round again.’

segments.text: ‘Never mind,’ Tan-chun said with a smile. ‘So long as we don’t settle down to serious drinking.’
Just then a little maid came up, grinning.
‘Misses, come and look at Miss Yun! She’s drunk. She went to cool off and fell asleep on a blue-grey stone bench behind the rockery.’
‘Keep your voice down!’ they said, laughing, and all went to look.

Sure enough, Xiang-yun was lying on a stone seat in a secluded place among the rocks, deep in fragrant dreams. Peony petals had blown over her from every side, scattering red and scent across her hair, her face and the front of her clothes. Her fan lay on the ground, half buried in fallen flowers. A crowd of bees and butterflies bustled round her. She had also wrapped a bundle of peony petals in a fine silk kerchief and made it her pillow. The others watched her with mingled affection and amusement, then hurried forward to shake her gently, call her and help her up. But Xiang-yun was still murmuring the drinking game in her sleep:

‘“The spring is fragrant and the wine is clear”;
“In a jade cup it shines with amber light.”
Drink on till “The Moon Rises over the Plum-tips”,
Be “Helped Home Drunk”:
A day “Favourable for Meeting Friends and Kin”.’

segments.text: They laughed and shook her.
‘Wake up and come to eat! You’ll make yourself ill sleeping on that damp bench.’

Xiang-yun slowly opened her limpid eyes. Seeing the others, she lowered her gaze to herself and only then realised that she was drunk. She had meant merely to cool off somewhere quiet, but the two extra penalty cups had been more than she could bear, and without knowing it she had fallen asleep. Now she felt ashamed. Hastily getting up, she struggled along with the others to Red Fragrance Court. There she washed and drank two cups of strong tea. Tan-chun promptly had the sobering stone brought for her to hold in her mouth, and after a while made her drink some sour soup as well. Only then did she feel a little better.

segments.text: They chose several dishes of fruit and vegetables to send to Xi-feng, who sent some things back in return. Some sat, some stood; some went outside to look at the flowers, others leaned on the balustrade watching the fish. Everywhere there was talk and laughter. Tan-chun began a game of go with Bao-qin, while Bao-chai and Xiu-yan watched. Under a cluster of flowers, Dai-yu and Bao-yu were whispering together about no one knew what.

Presently Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife came in with a group of women, bringing a married servant with them. The woman looked thoroughly miserable. She did not dare enter the hall but stopped below the steps and knelt towards it, knocking her head audibly on the ground. A group of Tan-chun’s stones was under attack. She had calculated and recalculated until the group had its two eyes, then turned to a standard endgame move. Her own two eyes remained on the board, while one hand rummaged among the stones in their box as she considered. Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife had been standing there a long while before Tan-chun turned to ask for tea, noticed her and asked:

segments.text: ‘Wait till tonight and we’ll all have a good drink. Sister Aroma and Sister Skybright can hold their wine too, and they like it, only they’re usually too shy to let on. Today we’ll all break our fast. There’s something else I meant to tell you. I’d forgotten it completely, and only just remembered. From now on I want you to look after Parfumée in everything. If she goes wrong anywhere, remind her. Aroma can’t attend to so many people.’
‘I know,’ said Swallow. ‘You needn’t worry about any of that. Only what about Wu-er?’
‘Go and tell Mrs Liu to let her come straight in tomorrow. I’ll tell the others, and that will settle it.’
‘Now that’s something worth doing,’ Parfumée said, smiling.

Swallow called in two little maids to attend to the hand-washing and pour tea. She cleared away the dishes and gave them to an older woman, washed her own hands and went to find Mrs Liu. Of her errand we need say no more.

segments.text: Bao-yu went out again to find the girls at Red Fragrance Court, with Parfumée behind him carrying his kerchief and fan. They had just left the courtyard when Aroma and Skybright came back hand in hand.
‘What are you doing?’ Bao-yu asked.
‘The meal’s laid out,’ Aroma said. ‘They’re waiting for you to eat.’
Bao-yu laughingly told them about the meal he had just had.

‘You eat like a cat,’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘Whatever smells good takes your fancy. The food in someone else’s pot is always sweeter. Even so, you ought to go and eat a little with them for politeness’ sake.’
Skybright poked Parfumée’s forehead with her finger.
‘You little fox-spirit! When did you slip away to eat? How did you two arrange it without telling us?’
‘They simply happened to run into each other,’ Aroma said, laughing. ‘There was no arrangement at all.’
‘Well, we’re no use any more, then,’ said Skybright. ‘Tomorrow we’ll all go away. Parfumée alone will be quite enough to wait on him.’
‘The rest of us could go,’ Aroma said with a smile, ‘but not you.’
‘I should be the first to go. Lazy, stupid, bad-tempered and no use at all.’
‘And if he burns another hole in that peacock coat, who will mend it when you’ve gone?

segments.text: ‘Don’t try those airs on me. If I ask you to do something, you’re so lazy you won’t lift a needle or stir a thread. And it isn’t my own private work I bother you with. It’s always his, but you still refuse. Then I go away for a few days, and you, ill and half dead, risk your life doing it for him in a single night. What’s the reason for that? Come on, tell me. Don’t just play the innocent and smile at me. That won’t do you any good.’

Talking like this, they reached the hall. Aunt Xue had come over too. Everyone sat down in order for the meal. Bao-yu ate only half a bowl of rice soaked in tea, just to observe the forms. When the meal was over they drank tea, chatted and amused themselves as they pleased.

‘I have Guanyin willow,’ said one.
‘I have arhat pine,’ said another.
‘I have gentleman’s bamboo,’ another said.

‘I have starry green.’
‘I have monthly red.’
‘I have the peony from The Peony Pavilion.’
‘I have pipa, the loquat, from The Lute, the pipa play.’
‘I have sisters’ flowers,’ said Dou-guan.
No one had an answer until Caltrop said:
‘I have married-couple orchids.’
‘I’ve never heard of married-couple orchids,’ Dou-guan said.

segments.text: ‘One flower on a stem makes a lan orchid; several flowers on a stem make a hui,’ Caltrop explained. ‘When a hui has two branches with flowers one above the other, it’s a brothers’ orchid. When the flowers are side by side, it’s a married-couple orchid. These are side by side. Why shouldn’t it be one?’
Dou-guan had no answer. She got up, laughing.

‘By your reasoning, if one branch were big and the other little, it would be a father-and-son orchid. If they flowered with their backs to each other, it would be an enemies’ orchid. Your man’s been away for more than half a year. Are you missing married life? You even drag the orchids into marriage. Shame on you!’
Caltrop blushed and tried to get up to pinch her.
‘You little hussy, may your mouth rot!’ she scolded, laughing. ‘A mouthful of made-up nonsense! Wait till I get up. I’ll beat the life out of you!’
Dou-guan saw her reaching over and would not let her rise. She quickly flung her whole weight on her and pushed her flat, then looked back and appealed laughingly to Rui-guan and the others.
‘Come and help me pinch that lying mouth of hers!’
The two rolled about on the grass.

segments.text: The others clapped and laughed.
‘Oh, look! There’s a puddle there! What a shame, you’ve spoiled her new skirt!’

Dou-guan looked back. There was indeed a pool of rainwater beside them, and half of Caltrop’s skirt was wet and dirty. Embarrassed, she pulled her hands free and ran away. The others could not stop laughing, but for fear that Caltrop would take her anger out on them, they all scattered in a laughing rush.

segments.text: Caltrop got up and looked down. Green water was still dripping from her skirt. She was angrily cursing them when Bao-yu appeared. Having seen them at their plant-name contest, he had gathered some flowers and leaves to join in, only to find that everyone had run away and Caltrop was standing alone, looking down and fussing over her skirt.
‘Why has everyone gone?’ he asked.
‘I had a married-couple orchid. They didn’t know what it was and said I’d made it up. That started the scuffle, and they’ve dirtied my new skirt.’
‘You have a married-couple orchid,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Well, I have a twin-flowered water-caltrop.’
He really was holding a sprig of twin-flowered water-caltrop. As he spoke, he took the married-couple orchid into his hand too.
‘Never mind married couples and twin flowers,’ Caltrop said. ‘Look at this skirt.’
Only then did Bao-yu lower his eyes.
‘Oh dear! How did it get dragged in the mud? What a pity! This pomegranate-red silk damask stains so easily.’
‘It’s some material Miss Qin brought the other day.

segments.text: ‘Miss Bao had a skirt made, and so did I. I put mine on for the first time today.’
Bao-yu stamped his foot and sighed.

‘Your family could spoil a hundred of these a day and think nothing of it. But first of all, Miss Qin brought it, and you and Cousin Bao have only one each. Hers is still good and yours is dirty already. Won’t that seem a poor return for her kindness? Then there’s Aunt, with her sharp tongue. Even as things are, I often hear her saying you don’t know how to manage, that you only waste things and never appreciate your good fortune. If she sees this, there’ll be no end to it.’
He had touched the very heart of Caltrop’s concern. Far from making her more miserable, his words cheered her.
‘That’s exactly it,’ she said, smiling. ‘I have several new skirts, but none the same as this. If I had one like it, I could change at once and all would be well. I could explain afterwards.’
‘Don’t move,’ Bao-yu said. ‘Just stand there, or you’ll drag the mud over your underclothes, your knee-trousers and your shoe uppers as well.

segments.text: ‘I have an idea. Aroma had a skirt made last month that’s exactly like this one. She’s in mourning, so she isn’t wearing it. What if she gave it to you to change into?’
Caltrop shook her head, smiling.
‘No. It wouldn’t be good if they heard about it.’

‘What’s there to be afraid of? When she’s out of mourning, surely you can give her something else she likes? If you insist on refusing, you’re hardly being your usual self. Besides, there’s nothing to conceal. You could tell Cousin Bao. It’s only Aunt’s temper we’re afraid of.’
Caltrop thought it over and saw the sense of it. She nodded and smiled.
‘Then let’s do that. I won’t reject your kindness. I’ll wait here. Only do make sure she brings it herself.’

segments.text: Delighted, Bao-yu promised and hurried back. As he went, he looked down and thought:
‘What a pity for a girl like her. No parents, not even a memory of her own surname, abducted and sold of all people to that tyrant.’

He remembered how unexpected the incident with Patience the other day had been. Today’s was more unexpected still. Turning all these thoughts over, he reached his rooms, took Aroma aside and told her exactly what had happened. No one could help feeling affection for Caltrop. Aroma was open-handed by nature, and she and Caltrop had always been friends. As soon as she heard, she opened her chest, took out the skirt and folded it. She followed Bao-yu to find Caltrop, who was still standing there waiting.
‘You really are too mischievous,’ Aroma told her with a smile. ‘You won’t stop till you’ve made a story worth telling.’
Caltrop blushed and smiled.
‘Thank you, dear sister. Who could have known those little wretches would be so wicked?’
She took the skirt and spread it out. It was indeed identical to her own.

‘Give me the dirty one to take back,’ Aroma said. ‘I’ll clean it and send it to you. If you carry it home and they see it, they’ll still ask questions.’
‘Dear sister, take it and give it to any of the girls you please. Now I have this one, I don’t want it.’
‘You certainly are generous,’ said Aroma.
Caltrop hastily curtseyed her thanks again, and Aroma went off with the dirty skirt.

segments.text: Caltrop saw Bao-yu crouching on the ground. With a twig he had scraped a hole for the married-couple orchid and the twin-flowered water-caltrop. He first gathered fallen blossoms to line it, laid the two sprigs carefully inside and covered them with more blossoms. Only then did he draw the earth over them and smooth it level. Caltrop caught his hand, smiling.
‘And what do you call this? No wonder everyone says you’re always up to these furtive little things that make people squirm. Look at your hands, all black mud and slippery moss! Go and wash them.’

Bao-yu smiled, got up and went to wash. Caltrop walked away too. They had each gone several paces when she turned back and called him. Not knowing what she wanted, Bao-yu came back smiling, his two muddy hands held out clear of him.
‘What is it?’
Caltrop only laughed. Then her little maid Zhen-er came over from the other side.
‘Second Miss is waiting to speak to you.’
Only then did Caltrop say to Bao-yu:
‘You mustn’t tell your cousin about the skirt.’
She turned and went away at once.

segments.text: Now Bao-yu returned to his room to wash his hands and consulted Aroma.
‘We’ll have wine this evening and enjoy ourselves. There must be no standing on ceremony. What shall we eat? We ought to tell them early, so they can get it ready.’

‘Don’t you worry,’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘Skybright, Musk, Ripple and I have put in five qian of silver apiece, making two taels. Parfumée, Emerald, Swallow and Si-er have put in three qian each. We’re not counting those on leave. That makes three taels and two qian altogether. Mrs Liu has had it already, to prepare forty little dishes of things to eat. I spoke to Patience too. A jar of good Shaoxing wine has been carried over and hidden there. The eight of us are giving you a birthday party all our own.’
Bao-yu was delighted.
‘But where do the little ones get money? You shouldn’t have made them pay.’
‘They have no money?’ said Skybright. ‘And we have, I suppose! They each wanted to do it. Even if they stole it, what of it? Just be grateful for their kindness.’
‘Quite right,’ Bao-yu said, laughing.
‘You can’t get through a day without a couple of sharp words from her to put you in your place,’ Aroma said with a smile.
‘You’re getting as bad as the rest,’ Skybright said, laughing. ‘Always stirring things up and fanning the flames.’
At this they all laughed.

segments.text: ‘Let’s shut the courtyard gate,’ said Bao-yu.
‘No wonder they call you Busy About Nothing,’ Aroma said, laughing. ‘Shutting it now would only make people suspicious. We may as well wait a little longer.’
Bao-yu nodded.
‘I’ll take a turn outside. Si-er, fetch some water. Swallow, you come with me. Just you.’
He went out. Finding no one about, he asked her about Wu-er.

‘I’ve just told Mrs Liu. She was delighted. But Wu-er was so upset by the way she was treated that night that when she got home she fell ill again with vexation. How could she come? She’ll have to wait till she’s better.’
Bao-yu sighed deeply, full of regret.
‘Does Aroma know about it?’ he asked.
‘I haven’t told her. I don’t know whether Parfumée has.’

segments.text: ‘I haven’t told her either,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Never mind. I’ll tell her myself.’

He went back in and made a show of washing his hands. It was already lamplighting time. Hearing a party enter at the courtyard gate, they all peeped quietly through the window. Sure enough, Lin Zhi-xiao’s wife was coming with several women in charge of the household, preceded by someone carrying a large lantern.
‘They’re checking the night watch,’ Skybright whispered with a smile. ‘Once they’ve gone, we can shut the gate.’
All those on night duty at the House of Green Delights came out to meet them. Mrs Lin checked that no one was missing.
‘No gambling or drinking, then dropping off and sleeping till broad daylight,’ she told them. ‘If I hear of it, I shan’t let you off.’
‘Who would dare do a thing like that?’ they all said, smiling.
‘Has Master Bao gone to bed?’ she asked.
None of them could say. Aroma hurriedly nudged Bao-yu. He slipped his feet into his shoes and came out to meet her with a smile.
‘I’m not asleep yet.

‘Lately I hear Master Bao has changed his way of speaking,’ Mrs Lin continued with a smile. ‘He’s taken to calling these senior girls by their names.

segments.text: ‘They may be serving in this room, but they still belong to Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship. You ought to show them some respect in the way you speak. Calling a name once in a while is all very well. But if you do it all the time, the younger brothers and nephews may copy you, and then people will laugh at a family that has no regard for its elders.’
‘You’re right, Mamma,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘It really is only once in a while.’

‘You mustn’t do him an injustice,’ Aroma and Skybright said, laughing. ‘He still calls us Sister all the time. He may say a name once or twice when we’re playing, but in front of other people he’s just as he always was.’

‘That’s as it should be,’ said Mrs Lin, smiling. ‘That shows he has learnt his books and his manners. The humbler you are, the more people respect you. Never mind old servants whose families have been here for three or five generations, or girls transferred straight from Her Old Ladyship’s or Her Ladyship’s rooms: even their cats and dogs aren’t to be hurt on a whim. That is how a properly brought-up young gentleman behaves.’
She finished her tea.
‘Do go to bed now. We’ll be off.’
‘Rest a little longer,’ Bao-yu was still saying, but she had already led her party away to inspect elsewhere.

‘Our fine lady has had a cup somewhere. What a lot of jabbering! She’s given us another display of her importance and gone.’

They began setting out the wine and food.
‘We don’t need the table hanging,’ said Aroma. ‘Let’s put the round huali kang table up on the kang and sit there. There’ll be more room, and it’ll be easier.’
They carried it over. Musk and Si-er fetched the dishes on two large tea trays, needing four or five journeys to bring everything. Two old women crouched outside by a brazier, warming the wine.

segments.text: ‘It’s hot,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Why don’t we all take our outer clothes off?’
‘You can take yours off if you like,’ they said, laughing. ‘We still have to take turns giving the formal welcome at your place.’
‘And by the time you’ve all done that it’ll be the fifth watch! You know how I hate those tiresome ceremonies. In front of outsiders they can’t be helped. But to plague me with them now is too bad.’
‘Have it your way,’ they said.

Instead of sitting down, they busied themselves taking off their ornaments and loosening their clothes. Soon their formal dress was laid aside. Their hair was twisted into loose knots, and they all wore long skirts and short jackets. Bao-yu had on only a little scarlet cotton-gauze jacket and lined trousers of green damask patterned with splashes of ink, their legs left loose. He leaned against a new pillow of lined blue-green gauze, stuffed with petals shaken from peonies of different colours, and began a game of finger-guessing with Parfumée. She kept complaining of the heat. All she wore above was a little lined patchwork jacket pieced from three-colour satin, with a willow-green sash about her waist. Below were lined pink trousers scattered with flowers, their legs loose too.

segments.text: A ring of little plaits ran round her forehead and joined at the crown in one thick braid, as broad as a goose’s egg, hanging down behind. In her right ear she had only a tiny jade plug, the size of a grain of rice. From the left hung one large gold-mounted red stone, the size of a ginkgo nut. They made her face look whiter than the full moon and her eyes clearer than autumn water.
‘Those two look like twin brothers,’ everyone said, laughing.
Aroma and the others poured the wine and brought it over one by one.
‘Wait a moment before you go on with your guessing. Even if we don’t give the formal welcome, at least take a sip from each of us.’

Aroma came first, holding out her cup for a sip. The others followed in turn. Only when the round was finished did they all settle in a circle. There was no room for Swallow and Si-er along the edge of the kang, so they brought two chairs and placed them close beside it. The forty dishes were all of the same pale-white Ding ware, no bigger than little tea saucers. In them were delicacies to go with wine, fruits and vegetables from south of the mountains and north of the seas, from China and foreign lands: dried and fresh, from water and earth, all that the world could offer.

‘Why don’t we quietly ask Miss Bao and Miss Lin to come and play?’ Swallow said with a smile. ‘It won’t be too late to go to bed at the second watch.’
‘And make a commotion opening doors and calling people?’ said Aroma. ‘What if you meet the night patrol and they start asking questions?’
‘What’s there to be afraid of?’ said Bao-yu. ‘Our Third Miss drinks wine too. We ought to ask her as well. And Miss Qin.’
‘Leave Miss Qin out of it,’ they all said. ‘She’s staying with the eldest mistress. You’ll stir up too much.’
‘Why be frightened? Go and ask them, quickly.’
Swallow and Si-er needed no second bidding. They hurried to have the gate opened and went their separate ways to invite the guests.

‘Do us this little honour. Only sit with us for a moment, then you can come back.’

segments.text: Another table had to be set beside the first on the kang before there was room for them all.
‘Cousin Lin feels the cold,’ Bao-yu said at once. ‘Come over here by the wooden partition.’

He fetched a back cushion to make her comfortable. Aroma and the others brought chairs and sat in attendance below the kang. Leaning back on her cushion at some distance from the table, Dai-yu smiled at Bao-chai, Li Wan and Tan-chun.
‘Every day you scold other people for getting together at night to drink and gamble. Now we’re doing it ourselves. What will you say to them after this?’
‘Where’s the harm?’ Li Wan said, laughing. ‘It’s only at birthdays and festivals, once in a way. We don’t do it every night. We needn’t worry about that.’

Skybright brought a carved bamboo cylinder filled with ivory flower lots, shook it and set it in the middle. Then she put the dice in a box and shook them. When she lifted the lid, they showed five. Counting round brought them to Bao-chai.
‘So I draw first,’ she said with a smile. ‘I wonder what I shall get.’

‘I wonder what I shall get,’ said Tan-chun, smiling.
She drew a lot, glanced at it herself, then flung it on the floor. Her face reddened as she laughed.
‘This is no good. We shouldn’t play this game. It’s a game for men outside, with all sorts of nonsense written on the lots.’

The others could not understand her. Aroma and her companions hurried to pick it up. It showed a spray of apricot blossom. The heading, in red, read ‘Immortal Flower of the Jasper Pool’, and the verse ran:

segments.text: The note said: ‘She who draws this lot shall surely find a noble husband. Let all congratulate her with a cup and drink a cup together.’

‘So that’s all!’ they said, laughing. ‘These lots were made for girls to amuse themselves with. Apart from two or three with something like this, there’s nothing improper on any of them. What harm can it do? We already have a princess in the family. Are you going to be a princess too? Congratulations! Congratulations!’

They came forward to drink to her. Tan-chun would not drink, but three or four of them, including Xiang-yun, Caltrop and Li Wan, insisted until they had forced the wine down her. She demanded that they discard this game and try another. They would not hear of it. Xiang-yun took her hand and made her throw the dice. Nineteen came up, making it Li Wan’s turn.
Li Wan shook the cylinder and drew a lot. At the sight of it she laughed.
‘Excellent! Look at this. There’s really something in this contraption.’
They looked. An old plum branch was painted on the lot, beneath the heading ‘Cold Beauty at Frosty Dawn’. On the other side was a line of old verse:
Bamboo fence and thatched cottage content my heart.

‘Be off home in that boat, and stop talking!’
Everyone laughed again. They read the note: ‘Since she is “Deep in Fragrant Dreams”, the drawer of this lot should not drink. Only the players on either side must drink one cup each.’
‘Blessed Buddha! What a splendid lot!’ Xiang-yun cried, clapping her hands.

Dai-yu happened to be on one side of her and Bao-yu on the other. Two cups were poured, and they had no choice but to drink. Bao-yu drank half his, then, when no one was looking, passed it to Parfumée. She lifted it and tossed her head back. Dai-yu kept talking to someone and tipped the whole of hers into the rinsing bowl.

Xiang-yun picked up the dice and threw nine. Counting round brought them to Musk, who drew a lot. On one side was a tumi blossom, with the heading ‘Spring’s Glory at Its Height’. On the other was a line of old verse:
When tumi blooms, the season of flowers is done.

segments.text: The note read: ‘Apricot Blossom accompanies her with one cup; anyone present of the same age, one cup; anyone with the same birthday, one cup; anyone with the same surname, one cup.’
‘Now this will be lively!’ they all said, laughing.
They reckoned it up. Caltrop, Skybright and Bao-chai were all Aroma’s age, and Dai-yu shared her birthday. Only someone with the same surname was wanting.
‘My surname’s Hua too,’ Parfumée put in quickly. ‘I’ll drink a cup with her.’
The wine was poured. Dai-yu turned with a smile to Tan-chun.
‘You who are destined for a noble husband, you’re Apricot Blossom. Drink up, so we can drink.’
‘What is she like!’ Tan-chun said, laughing. ‘Sister-in-law, give her a smack while you’re about it.’
‘No noble husband for her, and a beating into the bargain?’ Li Wan said with a smile. ‘I haven’t the heart.’
Everyone laughed.

segments.text: Aroma was just about to throw when someone called at the gate. An old woman hurried out to ask who it was. Aunt Xue had sent someone to fetch Dai-yu.
‘What watch is it?’ they asked.
‘Past the second. The clock has struck eleven.’
Bao-yu would not believe it until he had his watch brought and looked for himself. It was already ten fen into the first quarter of the early zi hour. Dai-yu rose.
‘I can’t keep going any longer. I still have my medicine to take when I get back.’
‘We ought all to be leaving,’ the others said.
Aroma and Bao-yu tried to keep them, but Li Wan and Bao-chai would not agree.
‘It’s too late. This won’t do. We’ve gone far beyond the rules already.’
‘In that case,’ said Aroma, ‘one more cup each before you go.’

Skybright and the others had already filled the cups. Everyone drank, then called for lights. Aroma and her companions saw them as far as the other side of the stream by Drenched Blossoms Pavilion before returning.

segments.text: It was the fourth watch. Between what the old nurses drank openly and what they stole on the sly, the wine jar was empty. The others were astonished to hear it. Only then did they clear away, wash and prepare for bed. Parfumée’s cheeks were rouge-red with drink, her brows and eyes lovelier still. Unable to hold herself up, she lay against Aroma.
‘Dear Sister, my heart’s beating so fast.’
‘Who told you to pour it down as hard as you could?’ Aroma said, laughing.
Swallow and Si-er had been unable to keep upright either and were already asleep. Skybright was still calling out.
‘Don’t call any more,’ said Bao-yu. ‘Let’s lie down as best we can and get a little rest.’

He put his head on the red, fragrant pillow, leaned over and was asleep himself. Seeing how drunk Parfumée was, Aroma feared that moving her about would make her vomit wine. She could only rise gently, ease the girl down beside Bao-yu and leave her to sleep. She herself lay down on the couch opposite.

segments.text: They all sank into deep, sweet sleep, knowing nothing more. At daybreak Aroma opened her eyes to find the light already clear and bright.
‘We’re late!’
She looked across at the bed. Parfumée lay with her head on the edge of the kang, still sound asleep. Aroma hurried up to wake her. Bao-yu had already turned over and woken.
‘We’re late!’ he said with a smile, pushing Parfumée to rouse her.
She sat up, dazed, rubbing her eyes.
‘Have you no shame?’ Aroma said, laughing. ‘Getting drunk and stretching yourself out anywhere, without looking where you were!’
Parfumée looked round and only then realised that she had been on Bao-yu’s bed. Laughing, she scrambled down.
‘How could I have drunk till I knew nothing about it?’
‘I knew nothing about it either,’ Bao-yu said with a laugh. ‘If I had, I’d have smeared your face with ink.’
The maids came in to help him wash and dress.
‘Thank you for entertaining me yesterday,’ he said, smiling. ‘Tonight I’ll give you a feast in return.’
‘Enough, enough,’ Aroma said with a laugh. ‘No more today. If we do it again, people will start talking.’
‘What’s there to be afraid of? It’ll only be twice.

segments.text: ‘You’ve forgotten, Sister,’ Si-er said with a laugh. ‘You sang one too. Was there anyone there who didn’t?’
They all blushed, covered their faces with both hands and laughed helplessly. Just then Patience came in beaming. She had come herself to invite everyone who had been at yesterday’s feast.
‘Today it’s my turn to be hostess. Not one of you is to be missing.’
They hurried to offer her a seat and tea.
‘What a pity she wasn’t here last night,’ Skybright said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘What were you doing last night?’ Patience asked at once.

‘We can’t tell you,’ said Aroma. ‘We had the liveliest time. Even when Her Old Ladyship and Her Ladyship had us all together for a party, it was never as much fun as last night. We finished a whole jar of wine. Everyone drank their shyness away and, before we knew it, we were all singing. It was well into the fourth watch before we dropped off anyhow, sprawled all over the place.’
‘Very nice!’ Patience said, laughing. ‘You wheedle wine out of me, don’t invite me, and then tell me all about it to make me cross.’
‘He’s giving us a feast in return today,’ said Skybright. ‘You’ll be invited, never fear.’
‘Who is “he”? “He” who?’ Patience asked, laughing.
Skybright ran after her to give her a laughing slap.
‘Trust your sharp ears to hear every word!’

‘I’ve things to do now. I can’t stop and talk,’ Patience said with a smile. ‘I’m off to my work. I’ll send someone later to fetch you. If any one of you fails to come, I’ll come and beat down your door.’
Bao-yu and the others tried to keep her, but she had gone.

segments.text: Bao-yu had finished washing and dressing and was drinking tea when he caught sight of a sheet of paper trapped beneath the inkstone.
‘It won’t do, leaving things anyhow under there,’ he said.
‘What is it now?’ Aroma and Skybright asked at once. ‘Who’s done something wrong this time?’
‘What’s that under the inkstone?’ he said, pointing. ‘Someone’s pattern left lying about again, I suppose.’
Skybright quickly lifted the inkstone and pulled it out. It was a written card. She handed it to Bao-yu. On the pink notepaper was written:
‘Adamantina, one outside the threshold, reverently bows from afar in honour of your birthday.’
Bao-yu read it and sprang to his feet.
‘Who took this in? Why wasn’t I told?’
Seeing his agitation, Aroma and Skybright supposed it must be a card from someone of great importance.
‘Who took in a card yesterday?’ they all demanded.
Si-er came running in.
‘Adamantina didn’t come herself yesterday,’ she said, smiling. ‘She only sent an old woman with it.

segments.text: ‘I put it there, and who would have thought a drinking party would drive it clean out of my mind?’
‘And we wondered who it was, to make such a fuss!’ the others said. ‘Hardly worth all this.’
‘Quick, bring paper,’ Bao-yu ordered.

Paper was brought and ink ground. But looking at the words ‘one outside the threshold’, he could not think of a suitable self-description to use in reply. He held his brush and stared, unable to decide even after a long time. ‘If I ask Bao-chai,’ he thought, ‘she’ll only criticise it as eccentric nonsense. Better ask Cousin Lin.’

segments.text: Bao-yu was astonished.

‘She’s so solitary and eccentric, so out of step with everyone. Not one person in ten thousand is good enough for her. If she thinks so highly of you, she must know you’re not one of us common mortals.’

‘She may not really think so highly of me,’ Xiu-yan said, smiling. ‘But we were neighbours for ten years, with only a wall between us. She was practising her devotions at Panxiang Temple. My family were poor, and we rented rooms belonging to the temple. We lived there for ten years. Whenever I had nothing to do, I went over to keep her company.

segments.text: ‘Whatever characters I know, I owe to her teaching. We were friends in poverty, and she was half a teacher to me as well. Then we went away to stay with relations. I heard that she was so out of step with the times that the powerful people there would not tolerate her, and that she had taken refuge here. Now Heaven has brought us together again, and our old affection is unchanged. If anything, she treats me with even greater kindness than before.’
The news struck Bao-yu like a clap of thunder. Delighted, he laughed.

‘No wonder there’s something so free about the way you speak and move, like a wild crane or an idle cloud. So that is where it comes from! I was just puzzling over something to do with her and going to ask someone’s advice. Meeting you is a heaven-sent chance. Do help me.’
He took out the card and showed it to Xiu-yan.

‘She’ll never change,’ Xiu-yan said, laughing. ‘She was born to be extravagant and odd. Whoever heard of signing a visiting card with a private literary name? Just as the saying goes: “Neither nun nor laywoman, neither woman nor man.” What sense does it make?’
‘You don’t understand, Cousin,’ Bao-yu said quickly, smiling. ‘She doesn’t belong to any of those categories. She’s someone beyond the world’s imagining.

segments.text: ‘It is because she credits me with a little understanding that she has sent me this card. But I can’t think how to answer it. I was just going to ask Cousin Lin when I happened to meet you.’
Xiu-yan looked him up and down, studying him for some time before she smiled.

‘No wonder they say hearing of someone is not the same as meeting him. And no wonder Adamantina sent you this card, or gave you all that plum blossom last year. Since even she is like this with you, I must tell you the reason. She is always saying, “Of all the ancients, from the Han and Jin, the Five Dynasties, the Tang and the Song onwards, none wrote good poetry. Only two lines are good:

Your iron threshold may endure a thousand years;
At last one little mound of earth must cover you.”

‘That is why she calls herself “one outside the threshold”. She also keeps praising Zhuang-zi’s prose, so at other times she calls herself “one apart from the world”. If she had signed the card that way, you could have answered as “one in the world”. She means that she is a person standing apart; you humbly describe yourself as one caught in the world’s bustle. That would please her.

segments.text: He found Parfumée had combed her hair, twisted it into a knot and put in flowers and kingfisher ornaments. At once he told her to change her appearance. He had the short hairs round the sides shaved away to show the blue-green scalp, leaving the long hair arranged at the crown.

‘In winter you can wear a big sable headband,’ he said, ‘and little military boots in five colours, with tiger heads and coiling clouds. Or leave your trouser legs loose and just wear plain stockings and thick-soled shoes with an edging.’
Then he added, ‘Parfumée is no good as a name. A boy’s name would be much more distinctive.’
He renamed her ‘Xiong-nu’, Male Slave. She was delighted.
‘In that case, take me with you when you go out. If anyone asks, just say I’m a page like Tealeaf.’
‘They’d still be able to tell,’ Bao-yu said, laughing.

segments.text: ‘You have no imagination,’ Parfumée said with a laugh. ‘There are several families of border tribespeople in our own household. Say I’m a little tribal servant. Besides, everyone says I look well with my hair in paired plaits. Isn’t that a splendid idea?’
Bao-yu was delighted beyond expectation.

‘Excellent!’ he said eagerly, laughing. ‘I’ve often seen officials with attendants of foreign stock, captives presented to them. They like them because they stand up to wind and frost and are nimble in the saddle. If that’s the plan, you ought to have a foreign name too. Let’s call you Yelü Xiong-nu. The sound of Xiong-nu is like Xiongnu, and both are names of the Dog Rong. Besides, those two peoples have been a plague to China ever since Yao and Shun. The Jin, the Tang and other dynasties suffered terribly from them.

segments.text: ‘Luckily for us, we were born in the present age. Our ruler is the true descendant of the great Shun. His holy virtue, merit, benevolence and filial piety, like Shun’s of Yu, shine up to Heaven and shall endure with heaven, earth, sun and moon for countless ages. So all the petty villains who ran riot in earlier dynasties have now been made by Heaven itself to come from far away with folded hands and bowed heads to submit, without our using a single shield or spear. We ought to humiliate them, to add lustre to our sovereign and father.’

‘If that’s so,’ Parfumée said, laughing, ‘you ought to practise archery and riding, learn some martial arts and go out boldly to capture a few rebels. Wouldn’t that be serving him loyally? Why use us? You flap your lips and wag your tongue, making a game of it for your own amusement, then call it praising his achievements and virtues.’

‘That’s where you don’t understand,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Now the four seas acknowledge our rule and all eight quarters are at peace. There’ll be no need for armed preparations for hundreds and thousands of years. Even in our games and jokes we ought to offer praise, so we’re not ungrateful for the peace we enjoy without lifting a finger.’
Parfumée thought this reasonable. The two of them considered their arrangement thoroughly fitting and proper, and Bao-yu began calling her ‘Yelü Xiong-nu’.

segments.text: In fact, both Jia mansions did possess prisoners captured by their ancestors in earlier years and bestowed on them as slaves. They were employed only in tending horses and were of little use for anything more important. Xiang-yun had always been extraordinarily fond of boisterous play. She loved military dress and often put on a bell-hung belt and turned-back sleeves herself. Seeing that Bao-yu had dressed Parfumée as a boy, she dressed Kui-guan as one too. Kui-guan habitually kept her hair shaven short to make it easier to apply stage paint and make-up to her face. She was nimble too, and dressing her up was all the easier. Li Wan and Tan-chun liked what they saw and had Bao-qin’s Dou-guan dressed as a little boy as well: two forked tufts of hair, a short jacket and red shoes. All she lacked was a painted face to be the very image of a lute-boy on the stage.

Xiang-yun changed Kui-guan’s name to Da-ying. Since her surname was Wei, this made her Wei Da-ying, which suited Xiang-yun exactly, with its hidden echo of wei da ying-xiong, ‘Only a great hero can show his true colours’. Why should a boy need rouge and powder? Dou-guan was extremely small and young, as well as wonderfully quick and mischievous; hence her name, Dou-guan, Little Bean.

After the meal, Patience gave her return feast. Saying that Red Fragrance Court was too hot, she had several tables of fresh wine and fine dishes laid in Elm-shade Hall instead.

segments.text: As luck would have it, You-shi had brought Jia Zhen’s two concubines, Pei-feng and Xie-yuan, over for a visit. They were both young, pretty, playful women and seldom came there. Now they were in the garden with Xiang-yun, Caltrop, Parfumée, Rui-guan and the other girls. The sayings ‘Like draws to like’ and ‘Things gather according to their kind’ were proved true enough: there was no end to their chatter and laughter. They paid no heed to where You-shi might be, leaving the maids to attend her while they went about enjoying themselves with the others.

Presently they reached the House of Green Delights and heard Bao-yu call ‘Yelü Xiong-nu’. Pei-feng, Xie-yuan and Caltrop collapsed together in laughter and asked what it meant. Everyone tried calling the name, mispronouncing it or forgetting part, until some even turned Yelü into ‘Wild Ass’. Whoever heard it anywhere in the garden was helpless with laughter.
Bao-yu saw that everyone was making fun of her and feared that she was being humiliated. He hastily spoke again.
‘In Fu-lang-si-ya, west of the seas, I hear they have a precious stone called gold-flecked glass. In their own foreign language they call gold-flecked glass “Wen-du-li-na”.

segments.text: Then word came that two women from the Zhen family had arrived with gifts. Tan-chun, Li Wan and You-shi went out to meet them in the council hall. The others came outside to stroll about. Pei-feng and Xie-yuan went to play on the swing.
‘You two get on,’ said Bao-yu. ‘I’ll push you.’
‘No, no!’ Pei-feng said in alarm. ‘Don’t get us into trouble. We can ask Wild Ass to give us a push.’
‘Dear sisters, do stop joking,’ Bao-yu said quickly, smiling. ‘People will copy you and start calling her names.’
‘We’re weak with laughter. How can we swing?’ said Xie-yuan. ‘You’ll fall off and knock your innards out!’
Pei-feng ran after her to hit her.

‘The Master has ascended to Heaven!’
Everyone started in horror.
‘He was perfectly well. He wasn’t ill. How can he be dead?’

segments.text: ‘The Master practised his devotions every day,’ the servants said. ‘His merit must have reached fulfilment, and he has risen to join the immortals.’

You-shi heard the news. With Jia Zhen, his son and Jia Lian all away, there was not a man close to her whom she could turn to, and for a moment she was at a loss. She could only hurry to take off her ornaments and send orders to Xuan-zhen Abbey that all the Daoists be locked up until her husband came home to question them. Then she hastily took a carriage out of the city, bringing Lai Sheng and a party of household men and their wives. Imperial physicians were summoned too, to discover what illness it had been.

The doctors found him already dead. How could they take his pulse now? They had long known that Jia Jing’s breathing practices were empty nonsense. His worship of the stars and the Dipper, his vigils on gengshen nights and his swallowing of cinnabar had been foolish, futile exertions. In their view, he had so exhausted his mind and strength that he had destroyed his life. Even in death his belly was hard as iron, and the skin of his face and lips was burnt purple-red, shrivelled and cracked.

segments.text: They reported to his daughter-in-law:
‘He died from the burning and swelling caused by swallowing gold and cinnabar in the Daoist manner.’
The Daoists were alarmed.

‘It was the cinnabar elixir the Master had newly prepared by his secret method that did the harm,’ they said. ‘We did warn him that his merit had not yet reached the point where he could take it. We never expected him to swallow it secretly during last night’s gengshen vigil. Then he rose to immortality. Perhaps his devotion has won him the Way, and he has left the sea of suffering, cast off the shell of his flesh and gone free.’

You-shi paid no attention. She merely ordered that they be kept locked up for Jia Zhen to deal with and sent a mounted messenger at full speed to bring him the news. Meanwhile she saw that the place was too cramped for the body to lie there. In any case it could not be taken into the city. She had it dressed at once and carried in a soft litter to the Temple of the Iron Threshold to lie in state. Counting on her fingers, she reckoned that Jia Zhen could not arrive in less than half a month. In the present heat, waiting for him was out of the question. She therefore took charge herself and had an astrologer choose a day for placing the body in its coffin. The coffin had been prepared years before and deposited at this temple, which was a great convenience.

segments.text: Three days later the mourning formally began and mourning clothes were put on. Services for the dead were started while they awaited Jia Zhen. At the Rong mansion Xi-feng could not come out, Li Wan was looking after the girls, and Bao-yu had no understanding of such affairs. Outside business therefore had to be entrusted for the time being to several of the household’s second-rank stewards. Jia Bin, Jia Guang, Jia Heng, Jia Ying, Jia Chang and Jia Ling each had duties assigned to them. Unable to return home herself, You-shi had her stepmother brought to keep house at the Ning mansion.

segments.text: Her stepmother could only bring her two unmarried younger daughters with her. She would not feel easy unless they were all living together.

When Jia Zhen received the news, he immediately applied for leave, as did Jia Rong, who also held an official appointment. The Board of Rites knew how highly the present emperor esteemed filial piety and brotherly duty. Not daring to decide the matter themselves, they submitted a memorial requesting his command. The emperor’s benevolence and filial piety were indeed beyond measure, and he placed particular value on the descendants of meritorious servants. On seeing the memorial, he at once asked what office Jia Jing held. The Board replied:

‘He attained the jinshi degree. The hereditary office of his ancestors has already passed to his son Jia Zhen. Being advanced in years and often ill, Jia Jing had long lived in quiet retirement at Xuan-zhen Abbey outside the capital. He has now died there of illness. His son Zhen and grandson Rong are here in attendance on Your Majesty for the state mourning, and therefore beg leave to return for the coffining.’
On hearing this, the emperor at once issued an edict of exceptional favour:

‘Though Jia Jing held no official appointment and rendered no service to the state, in consideration of the services of his forebears We grant him posthumous office of the fifth rank. Let his son and grandson escort his coffin into the capital by the gate on the northern side, and take it to their private residence for the funeral observances. They are permitted, on completing the full mourning rites, to escort the coffin to their native place. In addition, the Court of Imperial Entertainments shall provide a sacrificial offering according to the highest precedent.

segments.text: ‘All at court, from princes and dukes downwards, are permitted to offer sacrifice and condolences. Respect this.’

When the edict was issued, not only did the Jia family give thanks for the imperial favour, but all the ministers at court acclaimed the emperor’s long life and praised him without end. Jia Zhen and his son rode home at speed through the night. Halfway, they met Jia Bin and Jia Guang galloping towards them at the head of a party of household men. At the sight of Jia Zhen, both rolled from their saddles and offered their respects.
‘What are you doing here?’ Jia Zhen asked at once.
‘Sister-in-law was afraid that once you and my nephew had left, there would be no one on the road to look after Her Old Ladyship,’ Jia Bin replied. ‘She sent the two of us to escort her.’

Jia Zhen was full of praise. He asked how things had been managed at home. Jia Bin and his companion explained how the Daoists had been detained and the body moved to the family temple, and how, fearing there would be no one left in the house, You-shi had asked her mother and the two aunts to stay in the main apartments. Jia Rong had dismounted too. At the news that the two aunts were there, he exchanged a smile with Jia Zhen.

segments.text: ‘Very good, very good,’ Jia Zhen said quickly, and spurred his horse on. They did not stop at inns, but changed horses through the night and galloped on. At last they reached the capital’s gates and went straight to the Temple of the Iron Threshold. It was already the fourth watch. As soon as the night watchmen heard, they shouted to wake everyone.

Jia Zhen dismounted. He and Jia Rong broke into loud weeping and, dropping to their knees outside the main gate, crawled all the way in. Before the coffin they struck their foreheads on the ground and wept as though their tears were blood. They did not stop until daylight, when their voices had grown hoarse. You-shi and the others all came to meet them. Father and son hastened to change into the mourning garments prescribed by ritual and prostrated themselves before the coffin. But business had to be attended to. They could not remain blind to everything, deaf to every sound. They had to restrain their grief a little to direct the household. Jia Zhen recounted the gracious edict in full to their assembled relatives and friends, then sent Jia Rong home ahead of him to prepare for the coffin’s arrival.

segments.text: Jia Rong needed no second bidding. He galloped home and immediately ordered the tables and chairs removed from the front hall, the partition screens taken down and mourning curtains hung. A shelter for the musicians and a ceremonial archway were to be erected at the gate, with the other necessary arrangements. Then he hurried inside to see his grandmother and his two aunts.

Old Mrs You, being elderly and fond of sleep, was usually reclining. His Second and Third Aunts were doing needlework with the maids. When he arrived they offered their condolences. But Jia Rong grinned at his Second Aunt.
‘Second Aunt, so you’ve come again. Father’s been longing for you.’
You Er-jie blushed and scolded him.

‘You little Rong! You can’t bear to go two days without a scolding from me. You’ve less and less idea of proper behaviour. And you a young gentleman from a great family, studying books and manners every day! You’re worse than a lout from some common household.’
She snatched up an iron and aimed a blow at his head. Alarmed, Jia Rong covered his head with his hands and tumbled into her lap, begging for mercy. You San-jie came up to tear at his mouth.
‘Wait till our elder sister comes home. We’ll tell her.’
Laughing, Jia Rong knelt on the kang and begged them to forgive him. The two sisters laughed too.

segments.text: Jia Rong next tried to snatch the sharen seeds his Second Aunt was eating. You Er-jie chewed a mouthful to a pulp and spat it all over his face. He licked it off with his tongue and ate it. The maids could not stand the sight.

‘You’re in fresh mourning,’ they said, laughing, ‘and your grandmother has only just gone to sleep. Those two may be young, but they’re still your aunts. You have no respect for your mother at all. When we tell the Master, you’ll have more trouble than you can carry away.’
Jia Rong left his aunts and began embracing and kissing the maids.
‘My darlings, you’re right. Let’s make those two jealous.’
They hurried to push him away, scolding in disgust.

‘You little devil, may you die young! You have a wife and maids of your own, but you’re always pestering us. Those who know us will say it’s play. Those who don’t, especially some rotten-hearted busybody who likes gossiping and meddling, will make such a noise that everyone in the other mansion will hear. Who isn’t already whispering behind our backs about the filthy goings-on here?’
‘Separate doors, separate households,’ Jia Rong said, laughing. ‘Who’s to mind anyone else’s business? They’ve all got enough of their own.

segments.text: Jia Rong teased his grandmother again.

‘Don’t worry. Father frets about our two aunts every day. He wants to find us two uncles with good family connections, rich, young and handsome, so he can marry our aunts to them. He’s been looking all these years without finding anyone. But just the other day, on the road, he happened to spot one who would do.’
Old Mrs You took him at his word and eagerly asked whose family the man belonged to. Both sisters dropped their needlework and ran after him, laughing and trying to hit him.
‘Mother, don’t believe that thunder-struck wretch!’

segments.text: Now that everything at home was ready, Jia Rong hurried back to the temple to report to Jia Zhen. All that night they assigned the various duties to the servants and prepared the funeral banners, carrying-poles and everything else required. The hour of the Hare on the fourth day of the lunar month was chosen for bringing the coffin into the city, and messages went out to their relations and friends. On the appointed day the funeral procession was a splendid spectacle, with guests in their multitudes. From the Temple of the Iron Threshold to the Ning mansion, the crowds lining the road numbered tens of thousands and more. Some sighed; others envied. There were also half-educated scholars quoting, ‘In funeral rites, better frugal grief than lavish ease.’ All along the route the talk ran on, with everyone having a different opinion.
